fields.name: Susanna Wesley
fields.bio: Susanna Wesley, born in 1669 in London, England, was the mother of John and Charles Wesley, founders of Methodism. A devout Anglican and mother of nineteen children (ten survived to adulthood), she provided rigorous religious education to her children, establishing daily routines of prayer and Scripture study. Despite financial hardships and her husband's absences, she maintained a strong spiritual household.
fields.bio_html:
Susanna Wesley never preached a sermon, never published a book, and never founded a church. She spent her life within the walls of a country rectory in the flat Lincolnshire fenland, bearing children and burying them, teaching them their letters and their prayers, keeping a household together through poverty, fire, and estrangement. Yet from that ordinary kitchen came two of the most consequential lives in Christian history, and a whole movement learned to call her its mother. Hers is a story of grace hidden in the daily round, of a faith that met real sorrow without flinching, and of prayer so woven into the hours that it became the very architecture of a home.

A Dissenter's daughter

She was born Susanna Annesley in London on 20 January 1669, the youngest of some twenty-five children of Dr. Samuel Annesley, a leading Dissenting minister. She grew up in a home of learning and rigorous conviction. Her father's house was a gathering place for ministers, scholars, and Christian thinkers, and the serious theological conversation that filled its rooms became the air the youngest Annesley breathed. Though girls of seventeenth-century England rarely received any formal academic education, Susanna had the run of her father's books, and her education, largely self-directed, was extensive: theology, philosophy, and above all the deep and careful study of Scripture. By the age of thirteen she had, remarkably, thought her way through the controversies of her day and chosen for herself the Church of England over her father's Nonconformity. That early habit of examined, independent belief never left her. In 1688, at nineteen, she married Samuel Wesley, an ambitious and difficult clergyman, and in time settled with him at the rectory of Epworth, where she would spend the rest of her days.

Theirs was not an easy marriage, and Susanna never pretended otherwise. Money was always short; Samuel was imprisoned for debt; his temper and hers could clash. In 1701 the two fell into a bitter dispute when Susanna, out of conscience, refused to say “Amen” to her husband's prayer for King William, whom she did not regard as England's rightful king. Samuel vowed not to live with her until she relented, and for some months he left the household altogether. It was a painful, public rupture, and it reveals a woman who would not surrender her conscience even to the husband she was bound to honour. The estrangement ended, and the son born after their reconciliation was John; but Susanna carried her convictions unbowed to the end of her life.

A house of many children, and many graves

Of the nineteen children she bore, nine died in infancy, including two sets of twins, and one was accidentally smothered by a weary nursemaid. Ten lived to adulthood. It is impossible to read her life without reckoning with that weight of buried children, and Susanna did not hide it behind piety. She grieved, and she went on, and she poured herself into the ones who remained. She resolved to educate every child herself, convinced that education must shape both the mind and the character, and she did so with a discipline that became legendary. School began on a child's fifth birthday; the alphabet was learned in a day; each morning and evening opened and closed with the reading of psalms and Scripture. She held that the first task of a Christian parent was to teach a child obedience, and she wrote of it plainly.

In order to form the minds of children, the first thing to be done is to conquer their will and bring them to an obedient temper. To inform the understanding is a work of time, and must with children proceed by slow degrees; but the subjecting the will is a thing that must be done at once, and the sooner the better.

— Susanna Wesley, letter to John Wesley, 1732

To modern ears this can sound severe, and it was strict; but her aim was never mere control. She wanted each child free from the tyranny of self-will so that reason and religion could take root. And she matched severity with astonishing tenderness of attention. In the great household she set aside a fixed evening every week to be alone with each child in turn, to talk with them about their souls one at a time. Years later, when her grown son John asked her to write down her method, she did, and the letter she sent him in 1732 became one of the most treasured documents of Christian parenting. Behind the method lay a conviction about what a child truly was.

I cannot but look upon every soul you leave under my care as a talent committed to me under trust by the great Lord.

— Susanna Wesley

A brand plucked from the burning

That sense of sacred trust was fired white-hot by the event that came to define her family's story. In February 1709 the Epworth rectory caught fire in the night. The household fled into the darkness, and only when they had gathered outside did they realise that one child, five-year-old John, was still trapped at an upper window. Neighbours formed a human ladder and pulled him out moments before the roof fell in. Susanna received her son back as one raised from the dead, and she never forgot it. John himself would speak of being “a brand plucked from the burning” for the rest of his life. In her private papers his mother wrote a resolution about the boy she had almost lost.

I do intend to be more particularly careful of the soul of this child, that Thou hast so mercifully provided for, than ever I have been, that I may do my endeavour to instil into his mind the principles of Thy true religion and virtue. Lord, give me grace to do it sincerely and prudently, and bless my attempts with good success.

— Susanna Wesley, private meditation

Under the apron

Prayer was not, for Susanna Wesley, an occasional refuge; it was the discipline that ordered everything else. Amid the noise and press of a house full of children, she set apart time every day to be alone with God, and she guarded it fiercely. When she could not leave the room, she would simply draw her long apron up over her head, and every child in the house knew that when Mother was under her apron she was with God and must not be disturbed except in the direst need. Beneath that homespun tent she read her Bible, examined her conscience, and interceded for her household by name.

By her own account Susanna Wesley set apart roughly two hours of every day for private devotion, dividing the time between prayer for her own soul and prayer for each of her children individually. Unable to find a quiet room in so crowded a house, she made one by pulling her apron over her head as a signal that she was at prayer; her children learned to honour it in silence. She counted prayer the chief weapon against temptation, and meditation “incomparably the best means to spiritualise our affections, confirm our judgement, and add strength to our pious resolutions.”

The answer to those prayers came in ways she could see. The child snatched from the flames grew up to be John Wesley, and after him Charles, and between them they carried a gospel of the new birth across Britain and the American colonies, kindling the great evangelical revival and founding the Methodist movement that today numbers in the tens of millions. Susanna's fingerprints are everywhere upon it: in its “method,” born of her ordered rectory; in its love of hymn and psalm; in its insistence that religion is a matter of the heart made new.

The rescue of five-year-old John from the burning rectory in 1709 was, to his mother, a direct providence, and she answered it not with mere relief but with dedication, resolving to be “more particularly careful of the soul of this child” whom God had “so mercifully provided for.” The prayer was answered beyond anything she could have asked: the boy she consecrated at the window became the preacher whose ministry, with his brother Charles, awakened a nation and gave rise to a worldwide movement. The mother who could not preach preached, in the end, through her sons.

A preacher in the kitchen

There is one more scene from Epworth that belongs to this story. During a long absence of her husband, Susanna began holding Sunday evening devotions in the rectory kitchen for her own children, reading a sermon and singing a psalm. Servants asked to come, then neighbours, until the little gathering swelled to two hundred souls, more than filled the parish church. When word reached Samuel and he objected that it was unseemly for a woman, she answered that she could not in conscience abandon so plain a good, and that if he truly wished it stopped he must command her expressly and answer for it before God. He did not. In an age that gave women no pulpit, Susanna Wesley had, without ever intending it, become a preacher of sorts to her village.

Letters to her sons

Susanna's schoolroom never really closed. When her sons left Epworth for university and then for ministries of their own, her teaching simply followed them by post, in long, closely reasoned letters on prayer, obedience, moral discipline, and the nature of true Christian devotion. She published nothing in her lifetime, yet these letters, together with her private meditations, have become treasured by generations of Christians in their own right, and they show a theological mind of real depth at work at the kitchen table. The most famous sentence she ever wrote was her counsel to John on how to recognise sin where Scripture names no rule, a definition he would carry with him all his life.

Whatever weakens your reason, impairs the tenderness of your conscience, obscures your sense of God… that thing is sin to you.

— Susanna Wesley, letter to John Wesley

It is Susanna in miniature: not a list of prohibitions, but a summons to honest self-examination before God. The great themes of her teaching run through all her correspondence, that discipline is essential to spiritual growth, that every believer must answer personally to God for the state of his own soul, and that parents bear a sacred duty for the faith of their children. The movement her sons built, with its class meetings, its self-examination, and its ordered devotion, bears the marks of all three convictions.

Sing a psalm of praise

Her last years were quieter and, at the end, marked by a peace she had long sought. Samuel died in 1735, and the widowed Susanna eventually left Epworth for London, where she spent her final years near her children and watched, with quiet gladness, the first stirrings of the Methodist revival her sons were leading. She died on 23 July 1742, aged seventy-three, with several of her grown children gathered at her bedside. Before her speech failed she gave them a final charge that gathered up her whole life into a single sentence.

Children, as soon as I am released, sing a psalm of praise to God.

— Susanna Wesley, her last words

And when she was gone they did. John Wesley, who preached at her burial in Bunhill Fields to what he called one of the most solemn assemblies he had ever seen, recorded the moment in his Journal: “without any struggle, or sign, or groan, the soul was set at liberty.” She was laid to rest among the Dissenters and the saints of that famous burying ground, a fitting home for a Dissenter's daughter who had crossed into the Church and given it two of its brightest lights.

Susanna Wesley left no grand monument of her own making. She left something rarer: a household so ordered by love and prayer that God built a revival out of it. She reminds every ordinary believer, and especially every weary parent, that the kingdom of God most often comes not through platforms and crowds but through faithfulness in small rooms, through a mother under her apron lifting her children by name before the throne of grace. Her sons changed the world; but she taught them to pray, and she taught them to sing, and that was enough.

faq.q: Who was Susanna Wesley, and why is she called the Mother of Methodism?
faq.a: Susanna Wesley (1669–1742) never preached from a pulpit, founded no church, and published nothing in her lifetime, yet she raised two of the most consequential figures in Christian history, John and Charles Wesley. From her ordered rectory kitchen in Lincolnshire came the habits of prayer, method, and self-examination that would mark the Methodist movement. She is remembered less for anything she built than for the household she shaped, out of which a worldwide revival grew.

faq.q: What kind of home did she grow up in, and how did she come to the Church of England?
faq.a: She was born Susanna Annesley in London in 1669, the youngest child of Dr. Samuel Annesley, a leading Dissenting minister whose house was a gathering place for scholars and ministers. Though girls of her day rarely received formal schooling, she had the run of her father's books and taught herself theology, philosophy, and Scripture. Remarkably, before she was thirteen she had thought her way through the religious controversies of the age and chosen the Church of England over her father's Nonconformity, a habit of examined, independent belief that never left her.

faq.q: What was her marriage to Samuel Wesley like?
faq.a: In 1688 she married Samuel Wesley, an ambitious and difficult clergyman, and settled with him at the rectory of Epworth, where she spent the rest of her life. It was not an easy marriage: money was always short, Samuel was once imprisoned for debt, and in 1701 the two fell into a bitter dispute when Susanna, out of conscience, refused to say 'Amen' to his prayer for King William, whom she did not regard as England's rightful king. Samuel left the household for a time over it, but they reconciled, and their son John was born afterward. She would not surrender her conscience even to the husband she was bound to honour.

faq.q: How many children did she have, and how many did she lose?
faq.a: Susanna bore nineteen children over her years at Epworth, of whom nine died in infancy, including two sets of twins, and one was accidentally smothered by an exhausted nursemaid. Ten lived to adulthood, among them John and Charles Wesley. She did not hide that weight of buried children behind piety; she grieved openly and poured herself into the ones who remained.

faq.q: What happened in the Epworth rectory fire of 1709?
faq.a: One night in February 1709 the rectory caught fire, and the household fled into the darkness before realizing that five-year-old John was still trapped at an upper window. Neighbours formed a human ladder and pulled him out moments before the roof collapsed. Susanna received the boy back as one raised from the dead, and John spoke of himself as 'a brand plucked from the burning' for the rest of his life. In her private papers she resolved to be 'more particularly careful of the soul of this child' whom God had so mercifully spared.

faq.q: How did she educate her children, and how did her method shape Methodism?
faq.a: Susanna resolved to teach every child herself with a discipline that became legendary: school began on a child's fifth birthday, the alphabet was learned in a day, and each day opened and closed with the reading of psalms and Scripture. She held that a Christian parent's first task was to conquer a child's self-will so that reason and religion could take root, writing that 'the subjecting the will is a thing that must be done at once.' When John later asked her to write down her method, the 1732 letter she sent became a treasured document of Christian parenting, and the class meetings, ordered devotion, and 'method' of the movement her sons built bear its clear marks.

faq.q: Did she really give each child her personal attention despite so large a household?
faq.a: She did. In the press of a house full of children, she set apart a fixed evening every week to be alone with each child in turn, to talk with them one at a time about the state of their souls. Behind this lay her conviction that she must 'look upon every soul you leave under my care as a talent committed to me under trust by the great Lord.' She matched her strictness with an astonishing tenderness of individual attention.

faq.q: Is it true she led kitchen services that outdrew the parish curate?
faq.a: Yes. During a long absence of her husband, Susanna began holding Sunday evening devotions in the rectory kitchen for her own children, reading a sermon and singing a psalm; servants asked to join, then neighbours, until the gathering swelled to some two hundred, more than filled the parish church. When Samuel objected that it was unseemly for a woman, she answered that she could not in conscience abandon so plain a good, and that if he truly wished it stopped he must command her expressly and answer for it before God. He did not, and in an age that gave women no pulpit she had, without ever intending it, become a preacher of sorts to her village.

faq.q: What was her life of prayer like?
faq.a: Prayer was not an occasional refuge for Susanna but the discipline that ordered everything else, and by her own account she set apart roughly two hours of every day for private devotion. Unable to find a quiet room in so crowded a house, she would draw her long apron up over her head, and every child knew that when Mother was under her apron she was with God and must not be disturbed except in the direst need. Beneath that homespun tent she read her Bible, examined her conscience, and interceded for her household by name.

faq.q: How did Susanna Wesley die, and what were her last words?
faq.a: Widowed after Samuel's death in 1735, she left Epworth for London and spent her final years near her children, watching the first stirrings of the revival her sons were leading. She died on 23 July 1742, aged seventy-three, with several of her grown children gathered at her bedside. Before her speech failed she gave them a final charge that gathered up her whole life: 'Children, as soon as I am released, sing a psalm of praise to God.' John, who preached at her burial in Bunhill Fields, recorded that 'without any struggle, or sign, or groan, the soul was set at liberty.'

fields.name: Dwight L. Moody
fields.bio: Dwight Lyman Moody, born in 1837 in Northfield, Massachusetts, rose from a fatherless farm boyhood and a Boston shoe store to become the best-known evangelist of the nineteenth century, preaching to as many as a hundred million people across America and Britain. Never ordained and barely schooled, he founded the Northfield schools, the Moody Bible Institute, and a colportage work that put good Christian books within everyone's reach.
fields.tagline: Boston shoe salesman who became the best-known evangelist of the nineteenth century.
fields.bio_html:
Dwight Lyman Moody never finished grade school, never learned to spell with confidence, and was never ordained. Yet in the second half of the nineteenth century this stocky, fast-talking former shoe salesman preached the gospel, by sober estimate, to as many as a hundred million people — without radio, television, or a single microphone — and founded schools, conferences, and a publishing work whose fruit continues to this day. His secret was no mystery to those who knew him. He believed God meant exactly what He said, and he acted on it with all the energy of his big, warm, restless heart.

The Boy from Northfield

Moody was born on 5 February 1837 on a small farm at Northfield, Massachusetts, the sixth of nine children. When he was four his father died suddenly, leaving the family in debt; creditors took even the kindling from the woodshed. His mother, Betsey, refused to break up the family, and the children grew up poor, hard-working, and only lightly schooled. Dwight had perhaps five years of formal education, and his letters bore the scars of it all his life. At seventeen he walked away from the farm to make his fortune, and talked his way into his uncle Samuel’s shoe store in Boston — on the condition, his uncle insisted, that he attend church and Sunday school every week.

A Shoe Store in Boston

The condition proved to be the hinge of his life. His Sunday school teacher at Mount Vernon Congregational Church, a quiet man named Edward Kimball, resolved to speak to each of his boys personally about Christ. On 21 April 1855 Kimball walked into the shoe store, found young Moody in the back wrapping shoes, put a hand on his shoulder, and told him simply of the love of Christ for him. There, among the shelves, Moody gave his heart to the Saviour. Kimball later admitted he had seldom seen anyone whose mind was spiritually darker than his new convert’s — the church examiners, in fact, turned Moody away at his first application for membership because he knew so little doctrine. Heaven measured him differently.

“Crazy Moody”

In 1856 he moved to Chicago, sold shoes with the same drive he did everything, and began renting pews in church — then filling them with young men he had rounded up off the streets. In 1858 he started a Sunday school in a slum district so rough it was called “Little Hell,” holding classes in an old market hall and recruiting scholars with candy, pony rides, and sheer persistence. Within a few years fifteen hundred children were coming, and in 1860 the president-elect himself, Abraham Lincoln, visited the school. That same year Moody made the decision his friends thought mad: he gave up a flourishing business career — and with it his ambition to be worth a hundred thousand dollars — to give God all his time. During the Civil War he ministered tirelessly to soldiers at the front and in the camps; in 1862 he married Emma Revell, whose steady wisdom balanced his impetuosity for the rest of his days; and in 1864 his mission school grew into a church of its own.

Fire and Power

Two events in 1871 broke Moody’s ministry open. On the night of 8 October, preaching to his largest Chicago audience yet, he closed by asking the crowd to go home and consider what they would do with Jesus — and to come back next week with their answer. That night the Great Chicago Fire destroyed the hall, his church, his home, and much of the city; some of his hearers were never seen again. He never forgot it: to the end of his life he refused to let an audience leave without pressing them to decide for Christ that very night.

Behind the second event stood two praying women. Sarah Cooke and her friend Mrs. Hawxhurst had begun sitting on the front bench at Moody’s meetings, telling him plainly that they were praying for him to receive the power of the Spirit. At first it nettled him — he thought he had power enough. Soon he was pleading with God alongside them.

Weeks after the fire, walking down a street in New York where he had gone to raise relief funds, the answer came. God’s presence broke upon him so overwhelmingly that he hurried to a friend’s house and asked to be alone; he rarely spoke of that hour afterwards, except to say that he had to ask God to stay His hand. The sermons, he said, were the same sermons — yet now hundreds were converted where dozens had been before.

Two Nobodies Across the Sea

Moody had already learned, from the young English preacher Harry Moorhouse — who once preached to his Chicago congregation seven nights running on John 3:16 — to preach a God who loves sinners rather than one who merely thunders at them. And he carried in his heart a remark made in his hearing by the evangelist Henry Varley:

The world has yet to see what God will do with, and for, and through, and in, and by the man who is fully and wholly consecrated to Him.

— Henry Varley, words Moody resolved to answer: “By the grace of God, I will be that man.”

In June 1873 Moody sailed for England with a young singer named Ira Sankey, two children in tow and scarcely any invitations worth the name. What followed astonished everyone but God. From York and Newcastle the meetings spread to Edinburgh, where the city’s famously careful divines were won over; then Glasgow, Belfast, and Dublin; then four months in London in 1875, where attendance was counted in the millions. Britain’s newspapers could not explain how an unlettered American, preaching plain anecdotes in a rapid Yankee voice while his companion sang hymns from a little organ, was filling the largest halls in the kingdom. Moody could. “The world has yet to see…” He came home in 1875 the best-known evangelist alive, and gave the next quarter-century to campaign after campaign across America and Britain — Brooklyn, Philadelphia, the New York Hippodrome, and beyond.

Schools and Cheap Books

Moody the evangelist is remembered best, but Moody the builder may have reached further. The man with five years of schooling founded the Northfield Seminary for girls in 1879 and Mount Hermon School for boys in 1881, filling them with students too poor for other doors. His summer conferences at Northfield, begun in 1880, kindled the Student Volunteer Movement, which sent thousands of young missionaries around the world. In 1886 he founded the school that would bear his name, the Moody Bible Institute in Chicago, to train “gap men” who could stand between the pulpit and the crowd. And in 1894 — convinced that good books should not be a luxury — he launched a colportage association printing solid Christian paperbacks cheap enough for a farmhand’s wages, and sent them out by the wagonload.

For all the platforms and institutions, Moody’s own devotion stayed simple. He rose early to keep the first hours of the morning for the Bible and prayer, saying he would rather miss breakfast than miss his time with God, and the books he pressed on others most eagerly were the ones that fed that secret life.

The Coronation

In November 1899, midway through a campaign in Kansas City, his great heart began to fail. He was brought home to Northfield, to the room where he had been born sixty-two years before within sight of the hills he loved. On the morning of 22 December 1899, drifting between sleep and waking, he was heard to say, clearly and without fear:

Earth recedes; heaven opens before me… This is my triumph; this is my coronation day! God is calling me, and I must go.

— D. L. Moody, 22 December 1899

Months earlier he had told an audience what to make of the news when it came:

Some day you will read in the papers that D. L. Moody, of East Northfield, is dead. Don’t you believe a word of it! At that moment I shall be more alive than I am now.

— D. L. Moody

He was buried on Round Top at Northfield, behind the seminary he built. The shoe clerk whom a Sunday school teacher sought out in a back room had been used to move two continents toward heaven — and his plain, warm gospel addresses still do their work wherever they are read.

fields.name: A. B. Simpson
fields.bio: Canadian-born preacher and founder of the Christian and Missionary Alliance, whose "Fourfold Gospel" — Christ as Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer, and Coming King — called readers past every blessing to Christ Himself.
fields.tagline: Canadian preacher who founded the Christian and Missionary Alliance.
fields.bio_html:
Albert Benjamin Simpson had, by his mid-thirties, everything a minister of his era could want: a large salary, a fashionable New York pulpit, and a reputation as one of the ablest preachers on the continent. He laid it all down — the salary, the pulpit, and eventually his denomination’s security — to preach Jesus to the immigrants and working poor no one else wanted in their pews. Out of that surrender came a worldwide missionary movement, the first Bible college in North America, more than a hundred books, and a simple message he never tired of repeating: not the blessing, not the healing, not even the deeper life, but Christ Himself.

A Boy on Prince Edward Island

Simpson was born on 15 December 1843 at Bayview, Prince Edward Island, Canada, into a devout Scottish Presbyterian home where the Sabbath was kept strictly and the catechism learned early. The family soon moved to a farm in western Ontario. As a teenager, studying too hard for the ministry and haunted by a sense that he did not yet know the God he meant to serve, Albert broke down in body and soul. Light came through an old Puritan book, Walter Marshall’s Gospel Mystery of Sanctification, which told him that the first good news of the gospel is that a sinner may come to Christ just as he is. He came — at about fifteen years of age — and never afterwards doubted that Christ had received him.

The Young Presbyterian

He earned his own way to Knox College, Toronto, teaching school and winning scholarships, and while still a student wrote out a solemn covenant of self-dedication — pages long, signed and dated — giving himself to God for whatever service, suffering, or sacrifice might be asked. The document, found among his papers, reads like a prophecy of the life that followed. In 1865, only twenty-one, he was called to Knox Church, Hamilton — one of the largest congregations in Canada — where in eight years some seven hundred and fifty members were added. In 1873 he accepted the pulpit of Chestnut Street Presbyterian Church in Louisville, Kentucky. There, in a city still wounded and divided by the Civil War, he persuaded rival congregations into united evangelistic campaigns and learned to preach for a verdict. And there a deeper crisis found him: outwardly successful and inwardly exhausted by his own striving, he read of the higher Christian life and yielded himself wholly to Christ — discovering, as he later put it, that sanctification is not an attainment to be struggled toward but an indwelling Person to be received.

New York and the Neglected Masses

In 1879 Simpson came to Thirteenth Street Presbyterian Church in New York City. He was soon burdened beyond bearing by the crowds outside his church’s doors — Italian immigrants, dock workers, the unchurched poor — who could never feel at home among rented pews and formal society. When it became plain that his congregation did not share the burden, he resigned, in November 1881, with no salary, no society behind him, and a wife and six children to feed. Margaret Simpson later confessed she thought the decision madness; she came to share the work with her whole heart. Beginning with a handful of followers in a rented hall, he formed an independent Gospel Tabernacle where every seat was free and every class of person welcome.

Healed and Wholly His

Behind that resignation lay another transaction. Simpson had been sickly for years — a heart condition so serious that physicians gave him little hope of continued labour. In the summer of 1881, at Old Orchard Beach in Maine, he heard the scriptures opened on Christ’s ministry to the body, and alone among the pines he made a solemn covenant: he took the Lord Jesus as his healer, promised to use whatever strength was given for God alone, and asked never to be released from the bargain. The chronic trouble lifted; the man whom doctors had written off carried one of the heaviest workloads in American church history for nearly forty more years. From this grew his best-known formulation, the Fourfold Gospel: Jesus Christ our Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer, and Coming King.

Friday afternoons at the Gospel Tabernacle were given to a meeting for healing — but those who came looking for a wonder-worker were gently redirected. Simpson would pray with the sick only after pointing them past the gift to the Giver; the meetings were, before anything else, hours of worship and waiting on God.

The Alliance

Simpson could never see a need without founding something to meet it. In 1883 he opened the Missionary Training Institute — the first Bible college in North America, later settled at Nyack on the Hudson — to prepare ordinary, consecrated men and women for the fields no one else would fill: not scholars only, but clerks and carpenters and widows who had heard the call of God. The same year he sent his first missionary party toward the Congo. In 1887, at Old Orchard, he formed two societies, one for the deeper spiritual life at home and one for the evangelization of the world, which united in 1897 as the Christian and Missionary Alliance. He meant it as a fellowship across the churches, not a new denomination; it became, in time, both a denomination and a missionary force on every continent, from China and India to South America and the Congo basin. The unreached world lay on him like a private grief. His missionary hymn mourns the “hundred thousand souls a day” passing into eternity without the gospel, and answers with Christ’s own commission: all power is given unto Me — go.

Pen and Hymnbook

Out of the same tireless heart flowed the writing: weekly editorials in the magazine he founded (today’s Alliance Life), devotional classics such as Days of Heaven Upon Earth, A Larger Christian Life, and The Fourfold Gospel, Christ-centred expositions spanning the whole Bible, and hymns still sung wherever the deeper life is prized. The best window into the man is the testimony he gave at Bethshan, London, in 1885, published ever since as Himself — the story of how he stopped seeking experiences and found everything in the Person of Jesus. He set it to verse:

Once it was the blessing, now it is the Lord;
Once it was the feeling, now it is His Word;
Once His gift I wanted, now the Giver own;
Once I sought for healing, now Himself alone.

— A. B. Simpson, “Himself”

Those who lived with Simpson said the engine of it all was the early morning — hours kept jealously for the Bible and unhurried communion with God. He wrote that the secret of the deeper life was “a little sanctuary within,” carried through the busiest day, where the soul steals away to Christ between duties.

Rest at Nyack

Simpson preached, travelled, wrote, and administered at full stretch into his seventies, and when his strength finally failed he grieved most that he could no longer carry the missionary burden in prayer as before. He died at Nyack, New York, on 29 October 1919, and was buried on the hillside campus of the institute he founded. The societies he began now number their churches in the thousands and their missionaries around the globe; but his truest monument is smaller and nearer: the reader who, somewhere in his pages, stops chasing the blessing and finds the Blesser — Himself.

fields.name: Amanda Berry Smith
fields.bio: Amanda Berry Smith (1837–1915) was an African-American holiness evangelist who was born into slavery in Maryland and freed when her father bought his family's liberty. A washerwoman by trade, she became one of the most widely traveled preachers of the Wesleyan-Holiness movement, ministering across the United States, Britain, India, and for eight years in West Africa as an independent missionary.
fields.bio_html:
Amanda Berry Smith liked to say that she had been set free twice. The first freedom was bought with a father's sweat; the second was given at the foot of the cross. She was born into slavery on 23 January 1837, in Long Green, a farming settlement in Baltimore County, Maryland, one of thirteen children of Samuel Berry and Miriam Matthews. Her father was an enterprising, tireless man who, after his own long day's labour, worked deep into the nights making brooms and husk mats to earn the price of his family's liberty. One by one he bought them out of bondage. Amanda grew up knowing, in her own flesh, what a costly thing freedom is, and how it can be won by a love that refuses to sleep.

Her schooling amounted to only a few scattered months. What she learned of letters she largely taught herself, spelling out words by lamplight after the housework was done. At thirteen she went into domestic service, and for much of her life she supported herself as a washerwoman, cook, and cleaner in white households across Maryland and Pennsylvania. The world would later call her "the Singing Pilgrim" and print her name in mission reports from three continents; but she never lost the plain speech and worn hands of the laundry tub. It gave her preaching a particular authority. She spoke to the poor as one of them.

Grief, and a heart made clean

Sorrow came early and stayed long. In 1854 she married Calvin Devine; her conversion followed about two years later, during a grave illness in which, near despair, she cried out to God and found herself lifted into peace. Devine went to fight in the Civil War and did not return. In 1863 she married James Smith, a deacon in the African Methodist Episcopal Church, hoping for a settled home and a partner in the work she felt stirring within her. That hope was disappointed; the marriage was hard and often lonely, and he died in 1869. Of the five children born to her across both marriages, four died young. Only her daughter Mazie lived to grow up. By the age of thirty-two, Amanda Berry Smith had buried two husbands and four children. She knew, as few do, the particular silence of a house emptied by death.

It was into this grief that the deepest experience of her life came. In September 1868, at Green Street Methodist Episcopal Church in New York City, she sat under the preaching of John S. Inskip and felt God offering her what the holiness people called "a clean heart" — entire sanctification, the love of God filling every dark corner as sunlight fills a room. She longed to shout for joy, and three times the impulse rose in her; but she was the only Black woman in the crowded church, and fear held her back. A voice whispered that the white worshippers would put her out. At last the fear broke. She rose and shouted "Glory to Jesus!" and from the front Brother Inskip answered, "Amen, Glory to God." Something settled in her that never afterward moved. Out of that night came the sentence she would repeat all her life:

I often say to people that I have a right to shout more than some folks; I have been bought twice, and set free twice, and so I feel I have a good right to shout.

— Amanda Berry Smith

Before she could shout, she had to wrestle. In that Green Street pew she sat gripped by the old fear of what the white congregation might do, the impulse to praise rising and being pressed down, three times over, until at last she surrendered it to God and stood. Her whole ministry was born in that small, hidden act of yielding — the private battle in a crowded room where no one else could see what it cost her to obey.

The washerwoman evangelist

The year after her sanctification, Amanda became convinced that God was calling her to preach. It was an audacious thing. Women preachers were scarcely tolerated in that generation, and a Black woman preaching to mixed and often white congregations was, to many, unthinkable. She had no ordination, no salary, no denomination behind her, and no formal training. What she had was a clear call and an unusual voice. Dressed in a plain Quaker-style gown and poke bonnet — partly from conviction, partly because it was all she could afford — she began to speak and sing at African Methodist Episcopal churches and at the great holiness camp meetings that were sweeping the country.

Her singing disarmed crowds before her preaching convicted them. Camp meetings that might have turned a Black woman away found themselves weeping and shouting under her ministry. She supported herself by taking in washing between engagements, folding the gospel and the laundry into the same long days. She never pretended that the prejudice she met did not wound her; she named it plainly. But she refused to let it define her, and one of the most quietly defiant passages she ever wrote turns the whole question inside out:

Now, to say that being black did not make it inconvenient for us often, would not be true; but belonging to royal stock, as we do, we propose braving this inconvenience for the present, and pass on into the great big future where all these little things will be lost because of their absolute smallness! May the Lord send the future to meet us!

— Amanda Berry Smith

There is no self-pity in that. There is a woman who knows exactly who she is because she knows whose she is. The insults of a segregated church become, in her telling, "little things" measured against the vast inheritance of a child of God.

Across the sea

In 1878 she sailed for England, and what began as a visit stretched into twelve years of travel that carried her farther than almost any American evangelist of her day. She preached across Britain, Ireland, and Scotland, and arranged for Mazie to study in England. From there she went on to India for some eighteen months, at the encouragement of Bishop James M. Thoburn, whose respect for her would later be printed in the introduction to her autobiography. Then came the longest chapter of her overseas work: eight years in West Africa, mainly in Liberia and Sierra Leone, where she preached, championed temperance against the ruinous liquor trade, and took needy African children into her care as her own.

She went as an "independent missionary" — which is a dignified way of saying she went without a society to pay her way or promise her a passage home. She simply prayed, and trusted God to provide the fare and the bread. Again and again in her story, provision arrives at the last hour: a gift pressed into her hand, a sum sent by a stranger, exactly the amount needed and not a day early. Long before, when one of her free-born sisters was seized and sold back into slavery while visiting relatives in Maryland, Amanda had scraped and borrowed the fifty dollars to buy her out. She had learned young that God answers the prayers of those who have run clean out of options.

Facing a task that terrified her, she carried a single verse like a coin in her pocket: "Fear thou not, I will help thee." She had no missionary board, no guaranteed income, no ticket home — only that promise. And the record of her voyages is a record of it being kept: on more than one occasion the exact money for her passage arrived just as it was needed, from hands she had never asked. She went out with empty pockets and a full assurance, and the assurance never failed her.

Obedience, for Amanda Berry Smith, was never abstract. It cost her comfort, safety, and the settled home she had always wanted. But she reckoned the cost of disobedience higher still. Of the pull between staying safe and going where God sent her, she left a line as blunt as her faith:

To stay here and disobey God — I can't afford to take the consequence.

— Amanda Berry Smith

The orphanage, and the long fire of trial

She returned to the United States about 1890, worn down in health, and friends urged her to write her life story. She prayed much over it, unsure whether it was God's will, and at last set to work. An Autobiography: The Story of the Lord's Dealings with Mrs. Amanda Smith, the Colored Evangelist appeared in 1893 — a plain, vivid, five-hundred-page account of privation, hunger, faith, and travel that became a classic of American religious testimony. She wrote it not for fame but for children. The proceeds, together with her savings and a small newspaper she published, went toward a dream she had carried for years.

On 28 June 1899, in Harvey, Illinois, just south of Chicago, she opened the Amanda Smith Orphanage and Industrial Home for Abandoned and Destitute Colored Children — one of the first institutions of its kind for Black children in the state. It was the work of her old age and the object of her deepest anxieties. Money was always short. There were quarrels with staff, complaints from neighbours, failed inspections, and at least one fire. She poured into it the last of her strength and much of her peace. It is honest to say that the orphanage brought her as much heartache as joy; the woman who had trusted God for passage across oceans found the daily grind of feeding and housing destitute children a heavier and less romantic burden. Yet she would not abandon them. She had been a child that the world counted worthless, and she could not bear to let another be.

Sebring, and a long-awaited rest

In 1912, aged seventy-five and unable to carry the work any longer, she handed the home over and retired to Sebring, Florida, where a benefactor had provided a house for her. The institution passed to the state and was later chartered as the Amanda Smith Industrial School for Girls; it burned down in 1918, three years after her death. She did not live to see that loss, and perhaps it was mercy that she did not.

Amanda Berry Smith died in Sebring on 24 February 1915. She had been born a slave in a Maryland cabin and had preached the gospel on four continents; she had lost nearly everyone she loved and had gathered up the abandoned children of strangers; she had been paid in insults and had answered with joy. The holiness movement remembered her as one of its brightest lights, and later generations rediscovered her as a pioneer of Black women's preaching and social reform. But she would have wanted a simpler epitaph — the one her whole life kept spelling out, that a poor washerwoman with a clean heart and an obedient will is richer than she looks, and that the God who set her free the first time by a father's love had set her free forever by His own.

She had spent her life on the road, singing. It seems right to imagine her, at the last, laying down the burden she had carried so far, and finding that the future she prayed for had at last come out to meet her.

fields.name: Samuel Ajayi Crowther
fields.bio: Samuel Ajayi Crowther (c. 1809–1891) was a Yoruba boy from Osogun captured in a slave raid in 1821, rescued by the Royal Navy from a slave ship and landed at Freetown, Sierra Leone, where he was baptized in 1825. Educated by the Church Missionary Society, he became the first African ordained in the Anglican Church (priest, 1843) and, in 1864, its first African bishop.
fields.bio_html:
Samuel Ajayi Crowther is remembered by two names, and both of them are true. The first, Àjàyí, was given to him in a Yoruba town called Osogun around the year 1809 — the name a family gives a child born face-down, a child marked, they believed, for an unusual destiny. The second, Samuel Crowther, was given to him at a font in Sierra Leone in 1825, a borrowed English name laid over an African boy who had already lost almost everything a person can lose and had somehow not lost his faith in life. Between those two names lies one of the most astonishing journeys in the history of the Church: from a slave coffle to a cathedral, from a boy bartered for a horse to the first African bishop in the Anglican communion, from a captive who could not read to the man who first gave the whole Bible to the Yoruba people in their own tongue.

A childhood broken open

He was born into the Oyo country of what is now south-western Nigeria, into a household that farmed and wove and worshipped the old gods. It was a settled, ordinary boyhood — until it wasn't. In 1821 the wars that were feeding the Atlantic slave trade reached Osogun. Fulani and Oyo raiders fell on the town, burned it, and drove its people away in ropes. Àjàyí, about twelve years old, was taken with his mother and his baby brother and marched off among grandmothers and cousins and strangers, all of them now merchandise.

Years later, at the request of the Church Missionary Society, he set down what happened in a long, extraordinarily calm letter — one of the very few first-person accounts of the Middle Passage written by a man who survived it. He does not rage. He measures. He remembers the exact texture of the day his world ended, and he had by then learned to read it two ways at once.

From this period I must date the unhappy, but which I am now taught, in other respects, to call blessed day, which I shall never forget in my life. I call it unhappy day, because it was the day in which I was violently turned out of my father's house, and separated from relations.

— Samuel Ajayi Crowther

What followed was a slow selling-down. He was passed from owner to owner along the trade roads, his price falling as he was carried toward the coast. In one town, he records without self-pity, it was agreed that he should be bartered for a horse; later he was exchanged again for tobacco and rum. He was a boy watching himself become a currency. The despair of it nearly killed him — by his own hand. In the darkness of one of those holding places he tried more than once to strangle himself and could not do it, and afterward he understood that failure as a mercy he had not asked for.

Rescued from the sea

At the coast he was sold to Portuguese traders and packed into a slave ship. He had been aboard only a matter of hours, bound for a lifetime in Brazil or Cuba, when the vessel was intercepted by the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron — the ship HMS Myrmidon — which was hunting slavers under Britain's ban on the trade. The captives were taken off, and instead of a plantation the boy was carried to Freetown in Sierra Leone, a colony founded as a home for the liberated. He stepped ashore in 1822 into a strange kindness: not chains, but a school.

The Church Missionary Society took him in, fed him, and taught him his letters. He learned English quickly and then hungrily, and he began to read the Scriptures — first as a curiosity, then as a claim upon his life. Somewhere in those Freetown years the boy who had survived one slavery came to believe he had been rescued from a deeper one.

About the third year of my liberation from the slavery of man, I was convinced of another worse state of slavery, namely, that of sin and Satan. It pleased the Lord to open my heart.

— Samuel Ajayi Crowther

On 11 December 1825 he was baptized by the CMS missionary John Raban and took the name of an English clergyman he had never met, Samuel Crowther. When the CMS opened Fourah Bay College two years later to train African teachers and pastors, he was its very first student.

He had prayed, in effect, to be made free twice over — freed from men, and then freed from himself. The answer, when it came, he refused to credit to his own searching. "It pleased the Lord to open my heart," he wrote, and the whole grammar of the sentence is grace: the door opened from the inside, but not by him.

A pastor, a husband, a scholar

In 1829 he married Asano, a fellow liberated captive who at her own baptism took the name Susan Thompson; their marriage would last more than half a century. Crowther became a schoolmaster and catechist, and everyone who worked beside him noticed the same thing: a mind of unusual patience and reach, especially for language. He began to take his own mother tongue apart and write it down — sounds, grammar, proverbs — work almost no one had attempted before.

In 1841 the CMS attached him to the ill-fated Niger Expedition, a venture up the great river to plant commerce and Christianity in place of the slave trade. Fever devastated the European members; many died. Crowther survived, and the journal he kept was so observant and so clear that it made his reputation in London. The Society brought him to England, trained him further, and on Trinity Sunday, 11 June 1843, he was ordained a priest — the first African clergyman of the Anglican Church.

The word made Yoruba

Ordained, he turned homeward. In 1846 the Yoruba Mission established itself at Abeokuta, and there the long arc of Crowther's life bent back on itself in a way no novelist would dare invent. Among the townspeople he found his own mother, Afala, from whom he had been torn twenty-five years before. Neither of them, at first, could speak.

We could not say much, but sat still, casting many an affectionate look towards each other, an affection which twenty-five years had not extinguished.

— Samuel Ajayi Crowther

He called the reunion the greatest gift the Lord had ever given him. In time his mother was baptized Hannah, and his sister with her — the captive son become the means of his own mother's salvation.

For twenty-five years a family had been scattered across an ocean of loss, and a boy had grown into a bishop-to-be with an ache no achievement could reach. That God should set his mother down again in front of him, alive, in the town where he had come to preach — Crowther could only sit in the wonder of it. He had learned long before not to name a day unhappy too quickly.

Then came the work that would outlast everything else he did. Crowther gave himself to translating the Scriptures and the Book of Common Prayer into Yoruba, building the grammar and dictionary the task required almost from nothing. Word by word, proverb by proverb, he carried the Bible across into the language his mother had sung to him — the whole of it, the Bibeli Mímọ́, completed under his oversight in his last years. A tongue that had been written in the ledgers of slavers as a price was now made able to carry the words of God. Once, brought before Queen Victoria, he read her the Lord's Prayer in Yoruba, and she is said to have called its sound soft and melodious. The boy sold for a horse now prayed, in his mother's language, before the Queen of the empire whose navy had freed him.

Made a bishop

On St Peter's Day, 29 June 1864, in Canterbury Cathedral, Samuel Ajayi Crowther was consecrated Bishop of the Niger Territories — the first African bishop of the Anglican communion. Oxford gave him a doctorate of divinity. It was a summit of honour, and he wore it as he wore everything, quietly. He gathered African clergy around him, ordained African pastors, and built a mission that was, by design, to be led by Africans for Africa — the very thing the missionary societies had once said they wanted.

The long humbling

It is here that his story darkens, and honesty requires that it be told. As Crowther aged, a new generation of young European missionaries arrived on the Niger, men shaped by the harder racial confidence of the later nineteenth century. They did not believe an African should lead. Through the 1880s they moved against his mission — audits, accusations of mismanagement and corruption levelled at his African staff, dismissals and suspensions, one by one, until the men he had trained were pushed out and replaced with Europeans. The work of a lifetime was taken apart in front of him.

He might have fought it with the weapons of grievance, and no one would have blamed him. He did not. A retiring, soft-spoken man, he made little effort to answer the charges heaped on his people, and in 1890, his own reputation still unbroken, he resigned his authority with a dignity his accusers never matched. There is a particular pain in being undermined by those who owe their very presence to the ground you cleared, and Crowther felt it fully. But he had been made a slave and had not become bitter; he had been made a bishop and had not become proud; and he would not now, at the end, let smaller men make him small. He kept praying, kept serving, kept his eyes on the God who had opened his heart in Freetown sixty years before.

Lord, You who turned an unhappy day into a blessed one, and gave back a mother thought lost forever, and set Your word in our mouths in our own tongue — teach us, when our work is torn from our hands and our names are made low, to hold our peace as Your servant held his, trusting the One who freed us twice to be faithful still.

On the last day of the year 1891 — 31 December — Samuel Ajayi Crowther died of a stroke in Lagos, about eighty-two years old. The men who had displaced his mission gave the bishopric, next, to a European. But the deeper verdict of history has gone the other way. The Yoruba Bible he made is still read; the African church he insisted could stand on its own feet is now vast beyond his imagining; and the boy bartered for a horse is honoured across a continent as a father of its faith. He had been right about the day he was captured all along. It was, in every respect that finally mattered, a blessed one.

faq.q: Who was Samuel Ajayi Crowther?
faq.a: He was a Yoruba man, born around 1809 in the town of Osogun in what is now south-western Nigeria, who rose from slavery to become the first African bishop of the Anglican communion. Captured as a boy and later freed, he gave his life to the church as pastor, scholar, and translator. He is remembered above all as the man who first carried the whole Bible into the Yoruba language and as a pioneering leader of the African church.

faq.q: How did he come to be enslaved as a boy?
faq.a: In 1821 the wars feeding the Atlantic slave trade reached his home town of Osogun, and raiders burned it and drove its people away in ropes. faq.a: At the coast he was sold to Portuguese traders and packed aboard a slave ship, but within hours it was intercepted by the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron, which was hunting slavers under Britain's ban on the trade. The vessel that stopped his ship was HMS Myrmidon, in 1822. Instead of a lifetime on a plantation in Brazil or Cuba, he was carried to Freetown in Sierra Leone, a colony founded as a home for liberated captives.

faq.q: How did he become a Christian and take the name Samuel Crowther?
faq.a: In Freetown the Church Missionary Society took him in, taught him his letters, and set the Scriptures before him, and he came to believe he had been freed from a deeper slavery than the one the Navy had ended. As he later put it, 'About the third year of my liberation from the slavery of man, I was convinced of another worse state of slavery, namely, that of sin and Satan. It pleased the Lord to open my heart.' He was baptized on 11 December 1825, taking the name of an English clergyman he had never met, Samuel Crowther.

faq.q: What was his gift for languages, and what did he do with it?
faq.a: Everyone who worked beside him noticed the same thing: a mind of unusual patience and reach, especially for language. He began taking his own mother tongue apart and writing it down — its sounds, grammar, and proverbs — work almost no one had attempted before, and he produced an early Yoruba grammar and vocabulary. This scholarship laid the foundation for the translation work that would occupy the rest of his life.

faq.q: Did he really find his mother again after being separated by slavery?
faq.a: Yes, and it is one of the most astonishing turns in his story. When the Yoruba Mission settled at Abeokuta, Crowther found among the townspeople his own mother, Afala, from whom he had been torn about twenty-five years before. 'We could not say much, but sat still, casting many an affectionate look towards each other, an affection which twenty-five years had not extinguished,' he wrote. She was later baptized Hannah, the captive son having become the means of his own mother's faith.

faq.q: What is he best known for translating?
faq.a: He gave himself to rendering the Scriptures and the Book of Common Prayer into Yoruba, building the grammar and dictionary the task required almost from nothing and working word by word with African colleagues. The complete Yoruba Bible was finished under his oversight in his later years. A language once written only in the ledgers of slavers as a price was now made able to carry the words of God.

faq.q: How did he become the first African Anglican bishop?
faq.a: His clear, observant journal from the 1841 Niger Expedition made his reputation in England, and he was ordained a priest on Trinity Sunday, 11 June 1843 — the first African clergyman of the Anglican Church. On St Peter's Day, 29 June 1864, in Canterbury Cathedral, he was consecrated Bishop of the Niger Territories, the first African bishop of the Anglican communion. He built a mission meant, by design, to be led by Africans for Africa.

faq.q: Was he treated fairly at the end of his life?
faq.a: No, and honesty requires that it be told plainly. As he aged, a younger generation of European missionaries arrived on the Niger who did not believe an African should lead; through the 1880s they moved against his mission with audits and accusations aimed at his African staff, dismissing and replacing them one by one. A soft-spoken man, he made little effort to answer the charges heaped on his people and resigned his authority in 1890 with a dignity his accusers never matched — undermined by men who owed their very presence to the ground he had cleared.

faq.q: When and how did he die, and what is his legacy?
faq.a: He died of a stroke in Lagos on 31 December 1891, about eighty-two years old, and the bishopric was given next to a European. Yet the deeper verdict of history has gone the other way: the Yoruba Bible he made is still read, and the self-governing African church he insisted could stand on its own feet has grown vast beyond his imagining. The boy once bartered for a horse is honoured across a continent as a father of its faith.

fields.name: Richard Allen
fields.bio: Richard Allen (1760–1831) was born into slavery in Philadelphia, sold as a boy to a Delaware farmer, and converted to Christ as a teenager under Methodist preaching. After his master was himself converted and let him buy his freedom, Allen became a pioneering itinerant preacher; the humiliation of segregated seating at St. George's Methodist Church led him to found an independent Black church, Mother Bethel, in Philadelphia.
fields.bio_html:
Richard Allen was born a slave on the fourteenth of February, 1760, in the city of Philadelphia. His first owner was Benjamin Chew, a prominent Quaker lawyer; and while Allen was still a boy his whole family — mother, father, and children — was sold away to a farmer named Stokeley Sturgis, near Dover in the Delaware country. There, on a modest plantation among the fields and marshes, the future founder of the first independent Black church in America grew up under the plainest and hardest of schools. He learned early what it was to belong to another man, to be counted as property, to watch a family divided at a stranger's convenience. Yet Allen would remember Sturgis, in the end, as a kind master. The bitterness he never forgot was not the man but the thing itself.

I had it often impressed upon my mind that I should one day enjoy my freedom; for slavery is a bitter pill, notwithstanding we had a good master.

— Richard Allen

Awakened in the Fields

When Allen was about seventeen, a Methodist preacher came into the neighbourhood, and the young slave went to hear him. The Methodists in those years were a fervent, unpolished, wandering people who preached to anyone who would listen — the poor, the enslaved, the outcast — and their message went straight to Allen's heart. He came under deep conviction of sin. He describes himself in his memoir as brought low and desperate, certain that unless God had mercy on him he was lost.

I was awakened and brought to see myself, poor, wretched and undone, and without the mercy of God must be lost.

— Richard Allen

For weeks he cried to God day and night, working the fields by day and wrestling in prayer by night, until one evening, alone, the burden broke. The language he chose to describe that moment is the language of a man who had worn literal chains — and now felt spiritual ones fall.

As a young man still in bondage, Allen prayed to God both day and night under conviction of sin, crying out for mercy while he laboured on another man's farm. His conversion did not come in a church or a school, but in the fields, on his knees, where no one could sell his soul.

The deliverance, when it came, was total and joyful. He never forgot it, and he set it down plainly in his own account of his life: all of a sudden my dungeon shook, my chains flew off, and glory to God, I cried. My soul was filled. I cried, enough for me — the Saviour died. From that hour Richard Allen was, by his own reckoning, a free man in the deepest sense long before he was free in the eyes of the law.

Praying His Master Into the Kingdom

The new convert did not keep his joy to himself. He and his brother reasoned that the surest way to honour Christ — and to disarm the slander that religion made slaves lazy — was to work harder and more faithfully than ever, so that no one could say Methodism had ruined a good servant. Allen even worried aloud that his master might think faith had spoiled him, and so he laboured all the more diligently. In time he won Sturgis's permission to hold Methodist meetings in the farmhouse itself.

Preachers came and prayed under that roof, among them the great Methodist itinerant Freeborn Garrettson. One day Garrettson preached from the book of Daniel on the words, weighed in the balances, and found wanting — and applied them without flinching to men who held their fellow creatures in bondage. The word went home. Stokeley Sturgis became convinced that slaveholding was a sin against God, and that he could not meet his Maker with slaves in his fields. He offered Allen and his brother the chance to purchase themselves.

Allen had prayed and laboured for the soul of the very man who owned him. The answer came through a sermon in his master's own house: Sturgis was converted, concluded that slavery was wrong, and opened to Allen the door to freedom. The one who had prayed as a slave would walk out a free man because his prayers had reached his master first.

The terms were set: the brothers were to pay sixty pounds in gold and silver — two thousand dollars in the depreciated continental currency of the Revolution — buying back their own time by their own sweat. Allen agreed, and through years of hired-out labour, sawing wood, hauling bricks, and driving a wagon of salt for the army, he made the payments. By 1783 the debt was cleared and Richard Allen was, at last, legally free. He was twenty-three years old.

The Wandering Preacher

Freedom for Allen meant not ease but errand. He took to the roads as an itinerant preacher, walking and working his way through Delaware, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Maryland, supporting himself with day-labour and preaching wherever a door opened — to white congregations and Black, in barns, in forests, at camp meetings. He attended the historic 1784 Christmas Conference in Baltimore, where American Methodism organized itself as a church, and there he came to know Bishop Francis Asbury, who recognized the young man's gift and once invited him to travel with him through the slave states. Allen declined that particular journey, unwilling to be silenced about slavery, but the two men's paths would remain entwined for life.

In 1786 Allen came to Philadelphia, the city of his birth, and was invited to preach to the Black members of St. George's Methodist Episcopal Church. He preached at five in the morning so as not to disturb the regular services, and under his labours the number of Black worshippers grew quickly. That growth, meant to be a joy, became the occasion of a wound.

"They Were No More Plagued With Us"

As the Black congregation swelled, the white leadership of St. George's grew uneasy. They moved the Black worshippers from their accustomed seats to places along the wall, and then up into the gallery. One Sunday morning Allen, Absalom Jones, and others knelt to pray in the gallery — and a trustee seized Jones by the shoulders, trying to haul him up off his knees in the middle of prayer, hissing that he must not kneel there. Jones begged him to wait until the prayer was finished. He would not. When the prayer ended, the Black members rose together and walked out of the building for good. Allen recorded the moment with a dignity sharper than any protest.

By this time prayer was over, and we all went out of the church in a body, and they were no more plagued with us in the church.

— Richard Allen

They did not walk out of the faith — only out of a house that had shamed them at their prayers. Already, in 1787, Allen and Jones had formed the Free African Society, a mutual-aid and religious fellowship that cared for the widow, buried the dead, and disciplined its members toward sober and godly living. It was one of the first independent Black organizations in the nation, and out of it, and out of the walkout, would come churches.

The Fever of 1793

Before Allen could build his church, the city was visited by terror. In the summer of 1793 yellow fever swept Philadelphia; thousands died, and those who could afford to fled. Physicians, led by Dr. Benjamin Rush, appealed to the Black community to nurse the sick and bury the dead, under the mistaken belief that people of African descent were immune. They were not — many died — but Allen and Jones answered the call anyway, organizing Black Philadelphians to go house to house among the dying, to lift the sick, to carry away the corpses that no one else would touch.

When the city's own citizens fled and its churches emptied, Richard Allen and Absalom Jones rallied the Black poor of Philadelphia to nurse the fevered and bury the dead at the risk of their own lives — and then had to defend their people, in print, against the slander that they had profited from the calamity. It was the answer to their own prayers for a people who could serve Christ freely: a despised community became the city's mercy in its worst hour.

When the epidemic passed, a pamphleteer accused the Black nurses of extortion and theft. Allen and Jones answered with their own published Narrative, defending their people and turning the pen against the whole system that despised them. Allen appended an address to slaveholders that has never lost its force, grounding the cause of the enslaved not in politics but in the character of God Himself.

God himself was the first pleader of the cause of slaves.

— Richard Allen

Mother Bethel and a Church of Their Own

In 1794 Allen bought an old blacksmith's shop, had it hauled to a lot he owned on Sixth Street, and made it into a house of worship. Francis Asbury preached at its dedication, and it was named Bethel — "house of God." The people called it Mother Bethel, and it stands to this day on the oldest parcel of land continuously owned by Black Americans in the United States. That same year Allen was formally recognized in ministry, and in 1799 Bishop Asbury ordained him a deacon — the first Black man so ordained in the Methodist Episcopal Church.

But independence had to be fought for. The white conference tried again and again to bring Bethel back under its control and its property under its power. Allen and his congregation resisted through years of legal struggle, until in 1816 the Pennsylvania Supreme Court affirmed Bethel's right to govern itself. That same year Allen gathered Black Methodist congregations from Philadelphia, Baltimore, and beyond, and together they organized a wholly new denomination: the African Methodist Episcopal Church — the first fully independent Black denomination in America. On the eleventh of April, 1816, Richard Allen was consecrated its first bishop.

As bishop, Allen gave the rest of his life to a people forming themselves in freedom. He built congregations, licensed preachers, opposed the schemes to ship free Black Americans off to Africa through the Colonization Society, championed education, sheltered fugitives from slavery, and in 1830 helped convene the first National Negro Convention in the very rooms of Mother Bethel. His home was a station on the road to freedom; his pulpit was a school of self-respect for a people told daily that they had none.

He had come into the world as another man's property and left it the shepherd of a church that would carry the gospel and the cause of freedom across a continent and beyond. The chains that flew off in a Delaware field had, in the end, loosed a whole people's tongue to pray and to sing in a house that no one could take from them.

He is remembered as bishop, founder, abolitionist, and statesman. But he first knew himself as a slave who had found mercy on his knees — and everything else grew from that.
