fields.name: Festo Kivengere
fields.bio: Festo Kivengere (1919–1988) was a Ugandan Anglican bishop and evangelist of the East African Revival, often called “the Billy Graham of Africa.” Converted from nominal faith during the 1941 revival, he became Bishop of Kigezi in 1972 and a leader of African Evangelistic Enterprise. After Archbishop Janani Luwum's murder in 1977 he fled Amin's Uganda over the mountains into Rwanda, then wrote the celebrated book I Love Idi Amin, a testimony to forgiving the tyrant who had driven him into exile.
fields.bio_html:
Before he was a bishop, before the crowds and the cathedrals and the title the world would fasten on him — the Billy Graham of Africa — Festo Kivengere was a small boy in the high green hills of Kigezi, in the far south-west corner of Uganda, walking behind cattle. He was born in 1919 into a proud, traditional ruling family among the semi-nomadic herders of that country, and his earliest world was one of long grass, mist on the mountains, and the slow patience of the herd. As a boy tending the calves he sometimes turned the pages of little mission picture-books that told the story of a man named Jesus. He could not have guessed that the figure in those pages would one day become the whole meaning of his life — nor how costly that meaning would prove to be.

At about ten he was taken into a mission school newly planted in his village, and because he was quick and bright he was sent away for more education. He learned to read and to reason; he learned the Christian catechism; he was, on paper, a Christian. But it was the faith of a name only. In his teens he drifted from it altogether. At high school he fell in with a crowd untouched by the revival stirring around them, slipped off after dark to the shops, and took up drinking and smoking with a will. By the time he had qualified and returned home as a young schoolteacher, expected by his missionary employers to teach the Bible to children, he taught it with a sneer, unable to resist a sarcastic remark at the sacred text he did not believe.

A flood of light

All this while, the great East African Revival — the movement of the Balokole, the "saved ones" — was moving across the region like wind through the tall grass. It reached Festo not through an argument but through a friend. One day another young man named Festo Rwamunahe came to him, changed past recognition, and said simply, "Three hours ago Jesus became a living reality to me. I know my sins are forgiven." Then he asked Festo's forgiveness for the life they had led together, and promised he would never live that way again. Kivengere had no answer for a joy he could not explain away.

What he did not know was that two small girls had been praying for him by name.

On a Sunday morning early in October 1941, Festo's fourteen-year-old niece told him that she and a twelve-year-old friend named Eva had been praying for his soul — and that God had told them their prayers would be answered that very weekend. The next day it fell to Festo to walk the schoolboys to church. It was an ordinary Anglican prayer-book service, but before ever the sermon began people were rising all over the building to confess their sins and turn to Christ. Festo went down on his knees and surrendered everything. He would say afterward that it was as though a flood of light poured into his soul, and the burdens he had carried simply vanished in the presence of love. Two children had prayed; heaven had kept the appointment.

The conversion was total, and it never wore off. The mocking schoolteacher became one of the youngest and most radiant voices of the revival that was sweeping Uganda, Rwanda, Kenya, and Tanzania. The Balokole lived by open confession, joyful singing — their great song was Tukutendereza Yesu, "We praise You, Jesus" — and a fierce insistence that a Christian must walk continually in the light of the cross, keeping short accounts with God and with every neighbour. Festo drank this in, and it became the marrow of his preaching for the rest of his days.

Called to the whole world

He taught, and he evangelised, and his gift for making the gospel vivid and personal carried him further and further afield. He would eventually serve as an interpreter for Billy Graham when Graham preached in Africa — turning the American's English into words that struck home in Luganda and beyond, and learning the crusade platform from the inside. In 1971 he joined the South African evangelist Michael Cassidy in launching African Evangelistic Enterprise in East Africa, a team of African evangelists carrying the good news into the cities of the continent. He turned down invitations to more comfortable and prominent work — including one from Billy Graham himself — to give his strength to Africa. Ordained a priest, he grew into one of the most beloved evangelists his continent had produced, and in 1972 he was consecrated Bishop of Kigezi, shepherd of the very hills where he had once herded cattle.

He came to the office at the worst possible hour. Idi Amin had seized power, and Uganda was descending into terror.

The years of the beast

Under Amin the disappearances began — the road-blocks, the arrests in the night, the bodies in the forests and the rivers. The church would not stay silent. In February 1977 the Anglican bishops, led by Archbishop Janani Luwum, delivered a protest against the regime's murders. The answer was swift. Luwum was seized, and on 16 February 1977 he was killed. Festo Kivengere was among those closest to him and one of the last to see him alive; he waited outside the building where the archbishop was held until soldiers forced him away at gunpoint. Luwum had already told him, quietly, "They are going to kill me. I am not afraid."

Now the danger closed around Festo. He was a marked man, a bishop who had signed the protest and whose voice carried across the world. On the night after Luwum's murder he and his wife Mera fled. They drove as far as the road would take them, and then, guided by church people who knew the country, they climbed on foot through forest and up the flank of the mountains that divide Uganda from Rwanda, walking through the dark toward the border. He crossed carrying almost nothing but his Bible.

Somewhere on those mountainsides, in the cold and the fear, a bishop and his wife walked and prayed — not knowing whether the next ridge held safety or a soldier, leaving behind a diocese, a home, and a murdered friend. It was the prayer of the hunted: Lord, we have only You left. Bring us over.

"I love Idi Amin"

Safe in exile, Festo could have become a prophet of denunciation. Instead he found a harder road. He discovered bitterness rising in his own heart — the natural, justified hatred of a man who had killed his archbishop and driven his people into terror — and he knew it was poisoning him. In the very year of the terror, as Uganda marked the centenary of the gospel's arrival in the land, he watched imprisoned Christians singing in their cells and men and women streaming to Christ, and he could not carry hatred into that light.

The Holy Spirit showed me that I was getting hard in my spirit, and that my hardness and bitterness toward those who were persecuting us could only bring spiritual loss… So I had to ask for forgiveness from the Lord, and for grace to love President Amin more.

— Festo Kivengere

The turning point came as he contemplated Christ on the cross, praying, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." He saw that the prayer left no one out — not even the tyrant of his own country. He knelt and forgave Amin by name, and peace flooded back into his soul as it had on that October morning long before. Out of that struggle came a small, astonishing book, published in 1977, with a title that scandalised many who saw it: I Love Idi Amin. It was not a book excusing evil. It was a testimony that the love which had saved Festo was strong enough to reach even the man who had tried to destroy him.

On the cross, Jesus said, "Father, forgive them, because they know not what they do." As evil as Idi Amin is, how can I do less toward him?

— Festo Kivengere

Asked how he could possibly love such a man, Festo did not pretend to feel warmly toward him. "I may not like Idi Amin," he said, "but if I am a Christian believer I am obliged to forgive him, love him with Christ's love, and want the highest and best for his life." The prayer he had prayed on his knees in exile — for grace to love his enemy — was answered not in a feeling but in a decision that held, and that set countless other Christians free from the acid of their own hatred.

Homeward, and home

When Amin fell in 1979, Festo went back. He returned to a broken diocese and a wounded nation and set himself to rebuild — restoring churches, caring for orphans and refugees, pouring himself into relief and reconciliation as readily as into preaching. And preach he did, all over the world: in packed African stadiums and in Western cathedrals and university halls, always with the same message he had learned as a young teacher on his knees — that the love of God is real, that it meets us at the cross, and that it is powerful enough to change not only individuals but the bitter history between peoples. He never lost the note of costliness in his gospel.

Peace is not automatic. It's a gift by the grace of God. It comes when hearts are exposed to the love of Christ. But this always costs something. For the love of Christ was demonstrated through suffering, and those who experience that love can never put it into practice without some cost.

— Festo Kivengere

The cost caught up with his body at last. Festo Kivengere died of leukemia on 18 May 1988, still preaching until near the end, still speaking of the Christ who had flooded his soul with light. He was not yet seventy. He left behind a healed man's testimony — that a cattle-herder from Kigezi, once a scoffing schoolteacher, could be so mastered by grace that he would climb a mountain in the dark rather than nurse revenge, and write a tyrant's name in a book about love. His life remains one of the clearest windows the modern church has onto the plain, staggering proposition at the centre of the faith: that on the cross, no one is beyond forgiveness, and that those who have been forgiven much are set free to forgive at any cost.

fields.name: Simeon Nsibambi
fields.bio: Simeon Nsibambi (1897–1978) was an educated, prosperous Muganda health officer in Kampala whose spiritual hunger drove a pivotal September 1929 meeting with the missionary doctor Joe Church at Namirembe. Their weekend of Bible study and prayer over the fullness of the Spirit helped ignite the East African Revival (the Balokole, “saved ones”).
fields.bio_html:
Some of the great awakenings of the church began in cathedrals or crowded revival tents. One of the largest began on a quiet hill in Kampala, over an open Bible, between two men who were tired of being respectable Christians and hungry to be holy ones. Simeon Nsibambi was one of those two men. He was a Muganda of standing — educated, decorated, prosperous, a leader in his people's church — and by every outward measure he had arrived. Yet he carried within him a restlessness that no promotion could quiet, a sense that there was something more of God to be had than he had yet found. When at last he found it, the fire that was lit in him spread across half a continent.

A respected man with a divided heart

Nsibambi was born in 1897 into a prominent Buganda family; his father was a chief among a people who had embraced the Christian faith with remarkable speed a generation before. He was well schooled for his day, studying at Mengo High School and at King's College, Budo, the training ground of Buganda's leaders. During the First World War he served in the African Native Medical Corps and was decorated for distinguished service. Afterward he rose into the government of the Buganda kingdom as a health officer — a sanitation inspector responsible for the wellbeing of Kampala, respected in the streets he walked, secure in salary and in name.

He was also, by the 1920s, a baptised and believing Christian, a member of the Anglican Church of Uganda that the pioneer missionaries and the Baganda martyrs had watered with their blood. But Nsibambi was not content, and his discontent was the holy kind. He looked at himself and at the church around him and saw a faith that was correct but cool, a religion of forms that lacked fire. He had the outward marks of a Christian and the inward hunger of a man who knows he is missing the heart of it. That hunger would not leave him alone.

He had everything a man could want and still knelt as a beggar, asking God for the one thing he could not earn: not more religion, but a living power he had read about in Scripture and had never yet felt in himself. His prayer, in essence, was the oldest prayer of the awakened soul — there must be something more; give it to me.

The weekend on Namirembe Hill

In September 1929 God answered that prayer through a weary Englishman. Dr. Joe Church was a medical missionary of the Ruanda Mission, running the hospital at Gahini, and he too had come to the end of himself — spiritually dry, discouraged, and taking a few days away in Kampala to recover. He was staying on Namirembe Hill, whose name means full of peace, and on the Sunday he climbed to the great cathedral. There the two men met. Nsibambi, sensing in this tired doctor a fellow seeker, pressed him with the question that had been burning in his own chest: what was missing — in the church of Uganda, and in himself?

Church knew the answer, or at least the direction of it, from the "victorious life" teaching he had drunk in at the Keswick conventions of England. He began to speak to Nsibambi of the fullness of the Holy Spirit and of a Christian life lived in victory rather than defeat. The two men could not let the conversation go. Over that weekend — the account remembers it as roughly two days — they sat together with the Bible open, poring over the Scripture and the Scofield notes on the filling of the Spirit, and they prayed. They prayed to lay down every known sin, to be filled, to hold nothing back. It was not a lecture; it was two hungry men coming empty to God together and being filled.

There can be nothing to stop a real outpouring of the Holy Spirit in Rwanda now except our own lack of sanctification.

— Dr. Joe Church, writing of the meeting with Nsibambi

Church went back to Gahini, as those who tell the story put it, in the power of Pentecost. But the deeper change was in Nsibambi, and he did not go quietly back to his old life. He had touched the thing he had ached for all along, and he could not now hold it in.

What began as two discouraged men praying over a shared Bible on a hillside did not stay on that hillside. From that single weekend of surrender the fire ran outward — into Rwanda, into Uganda, and in time across Kenya, Tanzania, Burundi, and beyond — until an awakening now remembered as the East African Revival had touched millions. Few prayer meetings in the history of the church have been so small in the moment and so vast in the answer.

The man who could not stop asking about souls

Nsibambi's transformation was total and, to his respectable neighbours, alarming. He gave up his government post and the security it carried, and gave himself wholly to prayer and to preaching. He took his stand on Namirembe Hill and on the street corners near the cathedral, calling men and women to brokenness, confession, and new life. He led his own younger brother, Blasio Kigozi, to a living faith; Kigozi joined Joe Church at Gahini and became a burning evangelist in his own right before his early death in 1936, and it was Nsibambi who buried him on Cathedral Hill.

Above all, Nsibambi became a man who could not meet a stranger without asking after his soul. He stopped people on the road, in the market, at the gate, and asked them plainly whether they were saved — the kind of buttonhole evangelism that embarrasses the polite and rescues the lost. Not everyone approved. When Joe Church returned to Kampala some months later, an indignant missionary confronted him about what his friend had unleashed:

Oh, he's gone mad and is going round everywhere asking people if they are saved. He's just left my gardener.

— A missionary in Kampala, recounted in the histories of the Revival

It was not madness. It was a man who had finally believed his own gospel. What his critics called excess, the movement he helped birth would call normal Christianity — the natural overflow of a heart that has been genuinely filled. Historians of the awakening have called him, without exaggeration, in many ways the father of the whole Balokole movement — the movement of the balokole, the "saved ones," whose watchword became the sweet Luganda hymn Tukutendereza Yesu, "We praise You, Jesus."

A hidden man of prayer

Around 1941 Nsibambi's health failed. Joe Church described the illness only as a "weakness," and from then on Nsibambi lived increasingly withdrawn, confined much of the time to his home near Namirembe Cathedral. For the leader of a great revival it might have seemed a cruel silencing. It was nothing of the kind. The man who had once stopped strangers in the street now became a fountain of intercession, receiving those who came to him, praying over the movement he had helped to start, holding up in prayer the very leaders whose names would go around the world.

There is something fitting in it. The Revival Nsibambi lit was never chiefly about platforms and crowds; it was about repentance, confession, the "walking in the light" of open honesty before God and one another, and above all prayer. That the man remembered as its father should spend his last decades largely unseen, on his knees, is not a tragedy but a parable. He had already given the movement the only thing that mattered — its hunger for holiness and its habit of prayer — and he went on giving it from the hidden place until the end. He died in 1978, an old man and, in the truest sense, a patriarch.

Lord, give us Nsibambi's holy discontent — the refusal to settle for a correct and comfortable faith when You offer a full one. Make us hungry for more of Your Spirit than we have yet known, bold enough to ask a stranger about his soul, and content, when our strength fails, to serve You unseen upon our knees.

The fire that outlived him

It is hard to overstate what came out of that weekend on Namirembe Hill. The East African Revival that Nsibambi and Church helped ignite swept through the Anglican and Protestant churches of the region for the better part of the twentieth century, breaking down barriers of tribe and race, filling churches with converts, and producing a generation of Christian leaders of extraordinary quality. Among the balokole shaped by the movement were men whose names the whole church would come to honour — Archbishop Erica Sabiti; Bishop Festo Kivengere, the evangelist who preached alongside Billy Graham and answered Idi Amin's terror with a book titled I Love Idi Amin; and Archbishop Janani Luwum, martyred in 1977 for standing against tyranny, dying, as he said, for Uganda and for Christ.

Nsibambi wrote no famous books and left few recorded words of his own. What he left instead was a fire and a family of the faithful. He was a prosperous man who chose to be poor for Christ, a respected officer who was willing to be thought mad, an educated leader who wanted nothing so much as to be holy. He teaches the church a lesson it perpetually forgets: that revival begins not in strategy but in surrender, not in crowds but in a couple of hungry believers who will not get up from their knees until God fills them. From one such surrender, on a hill called full of peace, the peace of God went out to a continent.

fields.name: George Müller
fields.bio: George Müller (1805–1898) was a Prussian-born evangelist who, after a dissolute youth that included theft and a spell in prison, was converted at a prayer meeting in Halle in 1825 and gave his life to living by faith. Settling in Bristol, he founded the Ashley Down orphanages, where he housed and fed more than ten thousand orphans over his lifetime without ever once asking a human being for money — relying on prayer alone and keeping meticulous records of the answers.
fields.bio_html:
George Müller has been remembered, in the hundred and more years since his death, chiefly as the man who fed thousands of orphans without ever once asking a human being for money. But the more remarkable thing is why he did it. He wanted to leave behind him a visible answer to a question that unsettles every anxious heart: does God still hear prayer? He staked his whole life, and the lives of ten thousand children, on the belief that He does — and he kept the ledgers to prove it.

He was born on 27 September 1805 at Kroppenstedt, near Halberstadt, in the Kingdom of Prussia, the son of a tax collector. It would be pleasant to say he was a devout child. He was not. By his own unflinching account he was a liar and a thief almost as soon as he could talk, stealing even from the government money his father was charged to collect. He drank, he gambled, he squandered whatever he could lay hands on, and he was clever enough to hide most of it. At sixteen, run out of money at an inn, he was arrested for fraud and spent several weeks in prison at Wolfenbüttel before his father paid to have him released — and then whipped him, and sent him back to his studies.

The Prayer Meeting at Halle

Destined by his father for the comfortable living of a Lutheran clergyman, Müller entered the University of Halle to read divinity with no more religion in him than ambition and appetite. Then, one Saturday evening in mid-November of 1825, a friend named Beta mentioned that he was going to a small meeting in a private house where people read the Bible, sang, and prayed. Müller, curious and restless, asked to come along. What he found in that plain room undid him. A man knelt down and simply prayed. "I had never seen any one on his knees," Müller later wrote, and he had never himself knelt to pray. He went home that night a changed man, though he could scarcely have explained how. He was twenty years old, and from that evening the whole current of his life reversed.

The change was not instant perfection but a settled new direction. He began to read the Scriptures with hunger, gave up his old companions, and felt a growing pull toward missionary work. In 1828 he was accepted by the London Society for Promoting Christianity Amongst the Jews, and in March 1829 he sailed for England. Within two years he had parted from the society — not in bitterness, but because he could not in conscience keep to rules that seemed to him to bind the freedom of the Spirit. In 1830 he became the minister of a small chapel at Teignmouth in Devon, at a salary of fifty-five pounds a year.

Learning to Live by Faith

At Teignmouth, Müller made a decision that shaped everything after. He gave up his fixed salary altogether. It troubled him that a rented pew system made the gospel a transaction and left the poor ashamed; and more deeply, he wanted to depend on God directly rather than on any arrangement of men. He resolved never again to ask a fellow creature for money, nor even to let his needs be known, but to tell them only to God in prayer and wait. That same year, on 7 October 1830, he married Mary Groves, sister of the missionary Anthony Norris Groves — a woman of quiet strength who would share every privation of the venture without complaint for nearly forty years.

In 1832 the Müllers moved to Bristol, where he would remain the rest of his life, preaching at Bethesda Chapel. Two years later he founded the Scriptural Knowledge Institution for Home and Abroad — to aid schools, circulate Bibles, and support missionaries, all on the same principle of prayer and faith rather than appeals and debt. He would not go into debt for God's work; if the money was not there, he took it that God was not yet calling him to spend. It was a hard school, and he never pretended otherwise.

The only way to learn strong faith is to endure great trials. I have learned my faith by standing firm amid severe testings.

— George Müller

The Orphans of Ashley Down

The orphan work grew out of a burden and an argument. Müller had watched the fatherless children of Bristol beg and starve, and he had grown weary of hearing Christians say, in effect, that they would trust God more if only they had proof He could be trusted. So he decided to become the proof. If a poor man, asking no one but God, could house and feed and clothe and educate orphan children year after year, then the doubting believer might take heart, and the scoffer might be silenced. He was always clear that the children's welfare, dear as it was, was not the first object.

...that it may be seen that God is faithful still, and hears prayer still.

— George Müller

The first orphan house opened in a rented dwelling on Wilson Street in April 1836, taking in a few girls. It filled, and another opened, and another. In time Müller built five great houses on Ashley Down, on the northern edge of Bristol, plain and sturdy and clean, where at their fullest some two thousand children lived at once. Over the course of his life he cared for 10,024 orphans. Not once did he issue an appeal or send round a collecting plate. When money and food ran low — and they often did, sometimes to the last shilling and the last loaf — he prayed, and he waited, and he recorded in his journals, with the precision of an accountant, how the need was met. The published narratives of these dealings ran to volumes and were read across the world.

Müller had learned that he could not pray well from an anxious, empty heart. So before he asked God for anything, he would settle into the Scriptures each morning and not rise until his soul was happy in the Lord. "The first thing to be concerned about," he wrote, "was not how much I might serve the Lord, how I might glorify the Lord; but how I might get my soul into a happy state, and how my inner man might be nourished." Only then did he turn to prayer for the day's thousand needs.

Bread in the Morning

Of the countless recorded answers, one has been told and retold because it gathers up the whole spirit of the place. On a morning when there was no food in the houses and no money to buy any, the children were dressed and seated at the long tables before empty plates. Müller stood and gave thanks to God for the breakfast they were about to receive, as certain of it as if it lay before them.

As the thanksgiving ended there came a knock at the door. It was the baker: he had been unable to sleep in the night, sure that the orphans would need bread, and had risen early to bake for them. Scarcely had the bread been carried in when there was a second knock. The milkman's cart had broken down in the street directly outside the orphanage, and rather than let the milk spoil he begged Müller to take it all. The children who had bowed before empty tables ate a full breakfast of fresh bread and milk.

Such things were not, to Müller, occasional marvels but the ordinary texture of a life lived on prayer. Gifts arrived to the day and often to the exact sum needed; strangers were moved to give without knowing the need existed. He was scrupulously honest that this was no magic and no ease. There were seasons of real want, mornings of genuine dread, prayers that seemed to go unanswered for a long time. He simply refused to stop believing, or to reach for any hand but God's.

Sorrow and Steadfastness

Faith did not exempt him from grief. On 6 February 1870 Mary, his companion in every trial, died of rheumatic fever after nearly forty years of marriage. Fourteen hundred of the orphans followed her coffin. Müller, broken-hearted, insisted on preaching her funeral sermon himself, taking his text from Psalm 119, "Thou art good, and doest good." He would not let his sorrow accuse his God. "God himself has done it," he said of her death; "we are satisfied with him." A son had died in infancy years before; his beloved daughter Lydia, born in 1832, who had grown up among the orphans and married his faithful helper and successor James Wright, would die before him too, in 1890. In 1871 he married again, to Susannah Grace Sanger, who would become his fellow-traveller in the great work of his old age.

The Long Journeys

Most men would have counted the orphan houses labour enough for one life. Müller, past seventy and with the work in Wright's trusted hands, set out to preach. From 1875 to 1892 he travelled on missionary journeys that carried him, by his own reckoning, some two hundred thousand miles across forty-two countries — through Europe, America, India, China, Japan, Australia — preaching to audiences that sometimes numbered thousands, addressing millions in all. He spoke the same message everywhere, in the plain, unhurried way that was his habit: that God is real, that He keeps His word, that prayer is answered, and that a man may safely trust Him with everything.

The Last Morning

He kept working almost to the end. On the morning of 10 March 1898, in his room at the orphanage on Ashley Down, in the ninety-third year of his life, George Müller was found dead beside his bed. He had led evening devotions and retired as usual; in the night, quietly, he had gone to the God he had trusted so long. Bristol mourned him as it had mourned few men. Shops closed, flags flew at half-mast, and tens of thousands lined the streets as his body was carried to the grave, many of them men and women who had once been fed at those long tables as orphaned children.

He died, as he had lived, a poor man; the millions that had passed through his hands had all gone to the work, and he had kept almost nothing for himself. What he left instead was the thing he had set out to leave: a record, honest and enormous and impossible to explain away, of a God who hears. His own words remain the best summary of the ledger he kept for sixty years — a promise held onto until it came true, that it may be seen that God is faithful still, and hears prayer still.

fields.name: Hudson Taylor
fields.bio: James Hudson Taylor (1832–1905) was an English missionary to China and founder of the China Inland Mission. Converted at seventeen while his mother prayed for him miles away, he gave his life to reaching China's unreached inland provinces, pioneering a faith-mission that took no debt and solicited no funds but told every need to God in prayer.
fields.tagline: English missionary who founded the China Inland Mission to reach China’s unreached interior.
fields.bio_html:
Before James Hudson Taylor was born, he had already been given to God. His father, a Methodist chemist in the Yorkshire town of Barnsley, had a burning interest in China and its uncounted millions who had never heard the name of Christ. Kneeling together, James and Amelia Taylor prayed over their expected child a prayer they scarcely dared speak aloud: "Grant that he may work for Thee in China." The boy, born on 21 May 1832, would not learn of that petition until he was a grown man. But heaven had heard it, and the whole of his long life would read like its slow, astonishing answer.

Childhood in a devout home did not make faith automatic. As a teenager Hudson drifted into doubt and a certain worldly coolness, troubled by his own unbelief. Then came a June afternoon in 1849. Seventeen years old and left to himself with a free half-day, he wandered into his father's library, pulled a gospel tract from a basket of pamphlets, and settled down expecting a good story and intending to skip the sermon at the end. The phrase that arrested him was simple: the finished work of Christ. Why finished? Because, as the cry from the cross declared, "It is finished" — a full and perfect atonement, the debt of sin already paid. There was nothing to add, only to receive. Alone in that quiet room, Hudson Taylor knelt and gave himself to the Saviour.

That same afternoon, seventy or eighty miles from home, his mother rose from the dinner table with an intense longing for her son's soul. She went to her room, turned the key in the door, and resolved not to leave until her prayer was answered. Hour after hour she pleaded for him — until at last a settled assurance came that the work was done, and she rose to praise God. When she returned home a fortnight later and Hudson ran to tell her his good news, she smiled: she already knew the very day and hour of his conversion.

The certainty of that shared answer marked Taylor for life. He had learned, before he owned any theology of missions, that prayer moves the hand that moves the world. The old childhood dream of China now returned as a settled call. He began, quite deliberately, to prepare his soul for a country where he would have no salary, no society behind him, and no friend at hand but God.

Learning to Move Men Through God

His training was as much spiritual as medical. Moving to the grim, ditch-side district of Drainside in Hull to work under a doctor and study medicine, he set himself a severe discipline: to live simply, give generously, and depend on God for everything. "When I get to China," he reasoned, "I shall have no claim on any one for anything. My only claim will be on God. How important, therefore, to learn, before leaving England, to move man, through God, by prayer alone." He tested the promise like a man testing ice before he trusts his weight to it.

One incident he never forgot. His employer was chronically forgetful about wages, and one evening Taylor found himself with a single half-crown to his name — no dinner in prospect for the next day. Called out to pray beside a dying woman in a wretched tenement, he was pierced by the poverty of the starving family around her bed. Something told him to give what he had. He struggled; it was his all. At last he pressed the coin into the poor man's hand, telling him that God was indeed a Father who could be trusted. He walked home with an empty pocket and a strangely full heart.

The next morning's post brought a small packet with no name attached. Inside was a pair of gloves, and folded within them, a half-sovereign — four times the coin he had given away. "Ha!" thought the young man, laughing for joy, "this is good interest. That is the bank I can put my money in." He had staked his last shilling on God, and God had settled the account.

In 1853, aged twenty-one, Taylor sailed for China with the Chinese Evangelization Society, tossed for months in a storm-battered sailing ship, arriving in a Shanghai convulsed by rebellion and war. The early years were hard and often lonely. Yet he did something that scandalised many fellow missionaries: he adopted Chinese dress, shaved his forehead and wore the queue, so as to remove every needless barrier between himself and the people he loved. To reach the Chinese, he was willing to become, as far as conscience allowed, Chinese. In 1858 he married Maria Dyer, a missionary's daughter of rare good sense and deep faith, who became the strong companion of his labours.

The China Inland Mission

Ill health forced the Taylors back to England in 1860, but rest gave Hudson no peace. Spread before him was a map of China's vast inland provinces, where whole populations — a million a month, he reckoned, dying without Christ — had no missionary at all. The burden grew unbearable. He longed for God to send workers, yet shrank from the crushing responsibility of asking men to go where he could guarantee them nothing but hardship. The struggle nearly broke his health.

The crisis broke on a Sunday, 25 June 1865. Unable to bear the pretence of worship, he walked out alone along the sands at Brighton. There, as the tide came in, he surrendered the whole weight to God: if God was calling the workers and God would keep them, then the responsibility was God's, not his. On the flyleaf of his Bible he wrote the words that founded a mission: "Prayed for 24 willing, skilful labourers at Brighton, June 25, 1865." Two for each of the eleven unreached inland provinces, and two for Mongolia. The China Inland Mission was born not in a committee room but in a prayer on a beach.

He opened a bank account for the new mission with ten pounds, and fixed its governing principles in prayer: the CIM would go to the unreached interior; it would take workers of any denomination and of ordinary background; it would never go into debt; and it would never appeal for money or solicit funds from any human being. Every need would be told to God alone. It was faith made into a method.

God's work done in God's way will never lack God's supply.

— Hudson Taylor

That principle was tested a thousand times over the following forty years, and it held. Money arrived, often unsolicited and often to the day, from people who could not have known the need. The mission's ledgers became a long, quiet argument for the faithfulness of God. Taylor was no dreamer about it; he counted every penny and kept scrupulous accounts. But he had settled it once for all that the God who calls also provides, and that a work begun and carried on in dependence on prayer would not be allowed to fail for want of funds.

Great Fruit and Great Sorrow

The fruit was immense — and so was the cost. The mission grew, stations opened across province after province, and hundreds of Chinese came to faith. But the same years were soaked in grief. Several of the Taylors' little children were laid in Chinese graves. In 1870, after burying yet another infant son, Maria herself died at the age of thirty-three, her strength spent in the work she had shared so gladly. Taylor, worn and often ill, wrestled with loneliness and with seasons of depression that he did not hide. His secret in those years was not an iron constitution but a discovered rest — the realisation, which transformed him, that the branch has only to abide in the vine, that Christ Himself would supply the strength the servant lacked.

I have not got to make myself a branch. The Lord Jesus tells me I am a branch. I am part of Him and have just to believe it and act upon it.

— Hudson Taylor

Out of that rest came his boldest ventures in prayer. In 1881, with the workers barely numbering a hundred, Taylor and his colleagues knelt and asked God for seventy new missionaries within three years. By the close of 1884, seventy-three had sailed. Emboldened, in 1886 they asked for a hundred new workers in a single year. By November 1887 the mission had accepted a hundred and two. He did not treat prayer as a formula for getting; he treated it as the natural commerce between a child and a Father who delights to give, and he was not afraid to name a number and let God answer it.

I have found that there are three stages in every great work of God: first, it is impossible, then it is difficult, then it is done.

— Hudson Taylor

The Long Shadow and the Homecoming

The deepest sorrow of Taylor's life came near its end. In the summer of 1900 the Boxer Uprising swept north China with fire and slaughter, and the China Inland Mission suffered more than any other society: fifty-eight of its missionaries and twenty-one of their children were killed. Taylor, aged and frail, was in Switzerland when the reports came, and the weight of it nearly crushed him — these were his own people, sent out by his own hand. "I cannot read; I cannot think; I cannot even pray," he confessed in the darkness of it, "but I can trust." When peace returned and the Chinese authorities offered compensation for the mission's losses, Taylor refused every penny, that the meekness of Christ might be shown to a watching nation.

His second wife, Jennie, who had married him in 1871 and stood beside him for over thirty years, died of cancer in 1904. The old missionary, now failing, set his face for one last journey to the land he had given his life to. He reached China in the spring of 1905, was carried through provinces once closed and now dotted with churches, and came at last to Changsha, the capital of Hunan — a city that had long resisted the gospel and now welcomed him. There, on the evening of 3 June 1905, quietly and without a struggle, he slipped away to be with the Christ he had served for more than half a century. He was buried in Chinese soil, among the people for whom his father and mother had prayed before he was born.

He left behind a mission that would grow to more than eight hundred missionaries in his lifetime and, through its successor the Overseas Missionary Fellowship (OMF International), continues to this day. But his truest legacy is not an organisation. It is a demonstration, worked out over seventy-three years and written across a whole continent, that God can be trusted absolutely — that His work, done in His way, will never lack His supply. The praying boy of Barnsley had become the answer to his parents' prayer, and a living proof that heaven still hears.

faq.q: How did Hudson Taylor come to faith, and what part did his mother play?
faq.a: On a free June afternoon in 1849, the seventeen-year-old wandered into his father's library, picked up a gospel tract, and was arrested by the phrase “the finished work of Christ” — kneeling there, he gave himself to the Saviour. Miles away that same afternoon, his mother had locked herself in a room, resolved not to leave until she had prayed her son into the kingdom, and rose at last with the settled assurance that the work was done. When she came home she could tell Hudson the very day and hour of his conversion, and the shared answer marked him for life.

faq.q: What drew Taylor specifically to China?
faq.a: Before he was born, his parents had knelt and prayed over their expected child, “Grant that he may work for Thee in China,” a petition he did not learn of until he was grown. His father, a Methodist chemist in Barnsley, carried a lifelong burden for China's uncounted millions who had never heard of Christ, and after his conversion the old family dream returned to Hudson as a settled call. He sailed for China in 1853, aged twenty-one, with the Chinese Evangelization Society.

faq.q: Did Hudson Taylor really wear Chinese dress, and why was it so controversial?
faq.a: Yes — in his early years in China he adopted Chinese clothing, shaved his forehead and wore the queue, so as to remove every needless barrier between himself and the people he had come to reach. Many fellow missionaries were scandalised, seeing it as beneath a European's dignity, but Taylor was willing to become as far as conscience allowed Chinese in order to win the Chinese. It became a hallmark of the mission he would later found.

faq.q: How was the China Inland Mission founded in 1865?
faq.a: Spread before Taylor was a map of China's inland provinces where whole populations were dying without any missionary at all, yet he shrank from the responsibility of asking men to go where he could promise them only hardship. The crisis broke on Sunday, 25 June 1865, as he walked alone on the sands at Brighton and surrendered the whole weight to God, reasoning that if God called and kept the workers, the responsibility was God's. On his Bible's flyleaf he wrote, “Prayed for 24 willing, skilful labourers at Brighton, June 25, 1865” — two for each unreached province and two for Mongolia — and opened the mission's bank account with ten pounds.

faq.q: Why did the mission never ask anyone for money?
faq.a: Taylor fixed it as a founding principle that the China Inland Mission would never go into debt and would never appeal for funds or solicit money from any human being; every need was to be told to God alone. He had rehearsed this dependence for years in England, once giving away his last half-crown to a starving family and receiving four times as much by the next morning's post. “God's work done in God's way will never lack God's supply,” he said, and over forty years the money arrived, often unsolicited and often to the day.

faq.q: What was the Lammermuir party?
faq.a: On 26 May 1866, Taylor, his wife Maria, their four children, and a band of new recruits set sail from London aboard the tea clipper Lammermuir, the largest group of Protestant missionaries to reach China at one time. The four-month voyage was twice nearly wrecked by typhoons, yet the whole company arrived safely at Shanghai that September. It is often regarded as a turning point in nineteenth-century missionary work, carrying the young mission's first pioneers to the field.

faq.q: Who were Hudson Taylor's wives, and what sorrows did he bear?
faq.a: In 1858 he married Maria Dyer, a missionary's daughter of rare good sense and deep faith who became the strong companion of his labours; several of their little children were laid in Chinese graves, and in 1870 Maria herself died at thirty-three. In 1871 he married Jane Elizabeth “Jennie” Faulding, one of the original Lammermuir party, who stood beside him for more than thirty years until her death from cancer in 1904. Taylor, worn and often ill, did not hide the loneliness and depression these losses brought.

faq.q: What did Taylor mean by the “exchanged life”?
faq.a: In 1869, worn down by struggle and failure, Taylor was transformed by a letter from his colleague John McCarthy pointing him to abiding in Christ, the vine, rather than striving after holiness. He discovered a settled rest in union and communion with Christ, realising that the branch has only to remain in the vine and Christ himself will supply the strength the servant lacks. As he put it, “I have not got to make myself a branch … I am part of Him and have just to believe it and act upon it.”

faq.q: What books did Hudson Taylor write?
faq.a: He wrote A Retrospect, a modest account of his own conversion and early years and God's dealings with him, which has drawn many readers into missionary devotion. He also left Union and Communion, meditations on the Song of Solomon flowing from his deepened inner life, and Separation and Service, reflections drawn from the book of Numbers. All bear the same theme: the sufficiency of Christ for the one who wholly trusts him.

faq.q: How and where did Hudson Taylor die?
faq.a: Frail and aged, he set out for one last journey to the land he had given his life to, reaching China in the spring of 1905 and being carried through provinces once closed and now dotted with churches. On the evening of 3 June 1905 he died quietly, without a struggle, at Changsha, the capital of Hunan — a city that had long resisted the gospel and now welcomed him. He was buried in Chinese soil among the people for whom his parents had prayed before he was born, leaving a mission that would live on through its successor, today's OMF International.

fields.name: Charles G. Finney
fields.bio: Charles Grandison Finney (1792–1875) was a lawyer turned evangelist whose preaching helped drive the Second Great Awakening across upstate New York and beyond. Convinced that revival was not a miracle to be waited for but the right use of God-given means, he pioneered the “new measures” of protracted meetings and direct appeal, saw whole towns transformed, and later became president of Oberlin College.
fields.tagline: Lawyer turned evangelist whose preaching drove the Second Great Awakening.
fields.bio_html:
Charles Grandison Finney came to the gospel late, and by an unlikely road. Born in Warren, Connecticut, in 1792, the youngest of nine, he grew up on the raw frontier of upstate New York, far from settled churches. He never went to college. Tall, striking, and formidably self-assured, he trained instead as a lawyer, reading law in the town of Adams, and he expected to make his life in the courtroom. Religion he regarded coolly — a thing the prayer meetings around him seemed to ask for endlessly and never quite receive.

But the law kept sending him back to the Bible. Blackstone's commentaries cited Scripture; the more Finney read to understand the one, the more the other pressed on him. Through the autumn of 1821 the pressure grew unbearable, until one morning he turned aside into the woods north of the village, resolved not to leave until he had settled the matter with God. There, alone among the trees, his proud lawyer's heart broke, and he gave himself to Christ.

That evening, back in the empty law office, the settlement was sealed in a way he never forgot. As he sat by the fire the presence of God swept over him wave upon wave, until he could scarcely bear it.

The Holy Spirit descended upon me in a manner that seemed to go through me, body and soul… it seemed to come in waves and waves of liquid love.

— Charles Finney, Memoirs

"I said, 'I shall die if these waves continue to pass over me,'" he wrote; "and yet I had no fear of death." The next morning a deacon came to remind him of a court case. "I have a retainer from the Lord Jesus Christ to plead his cause," Finney answered, "and I cannot plead yours." The courtroom had lost him for good.

The lawyer turned evangelist

He studied theology under a local minister, was licensed to preach by the presbytery in 1823–24, and married Lydia Root Andrews the following year. Then he went out into the "burned-over district" — the belt of upstate New York so scorched by successive revivals that observers thought no fire could catch there again. Under Finney it caught as never before. At Evans' Mills, Antwerp, Utica, Troy, and finally in the great Rochester revival of 1830–31, towns were turned upside down. He preached without notes, argued like the advocate he had been, fixed men with his eyes, and pressed for a verdict then and there.

The Rochester revival of the winter of 1830–31 was the crown of it. For six months Finney preached almost daily to the leading citizens of a booming canal town — lawyers, merchants, and their families — and the character of the whole city changed. Grog shops closed, quarrels were made up, and the awakening rippled out along the Erie Canal into town after town. Contemporaries counted conversions in the hundreds locally and believed the ripple touched tens of thousands across the region. It made Finney the most famous revivalist in America and fixed the pattern others would imitate for a century.

His conviction was that revival is not a miracle to be waited on passively but the fruit of ordinary means used rightly — and that ordinary people, convicted of sin, must decide.

A revival is nothing else than a new beginning of obedience to God.

— Charles Finney, Lectures on Revivals of Religion

To bring people to that beginning he pioneered what critics called the "new measures": protracted nightly meetings, plain extemporaneous preaching, the naming of individuals aloud in prayer, women praying in mixed assemblies, and the "anxious seat" — a bench at the front where the awakened sat publicly, unable any longer to hide. These are commonplace now; in the 1820s they scandalized the settled clergy.

The men who prayed him through

Finney never believed the power lay in the measures, or even in his own preaching. Again and again he traced it to hidden intercession. Two men in particular went before him into the fire on their knees.

"Father" Daniel Nash would arrive in a town weeks ahead of Finney, take a room, and give himself almost wholly to agonizing prayer while Finney preached. At Rochester, Abel Clary did the same — so burdened for souls, Finney wrote, "that he was not able to preach much, his whole time and strength being given to prayer." An eyewitness found Clary groaning on the floor, unable to rise.

Finney called Nash one of those men who "had such a powerful Spirit of prevailing prayer," and reckoned that the revivals rose and fell with this unseen labor. It was no accident, he thought, that when Nash died on his knees at the end of 1831, Finney's own itinerant work in the fields soon drew to a close. The visible preacher had always been carried by the invisible pray-ers.

The mill that stopped for God

One scene, told in his own Memoirs, captures the whole pattern — intercessors laboring in secret, and a conviction that fell without a sermon. Walking one morning through Mr. Wolcott's cotton factory near Whitesboro, Finney passed a young woman at a machine who was watching him and whispering, half in mockery, to a companion.

"The thread of one of the machines broke," Finney recalled, "and I observed that the girl's hands trembled so that she could not mend it." He came within a few feet and only looked at her, and she "sunk down, and burst into tears." Conviction ran down the line; operatives wept at their machines. The unconverted owner took one look and gave the order: "Stop the mill, and let the people attend to religion; for it is more important that our souls should be saved than that this factory run." The gates were shut, the hands gathered, and within days nearly the whole mill was converted.

Fire and opposition

Such power made enemies as well as converts. The emotional intensity of the new measures — and Finney's blunt, "denunciatory" preaching — alarmed the leaders of New England religion. The veteran revivalist Asahel Nettleton and the powerful Boston pastor Lyman Beecher set themselves against him, and in 1827 the two sides met face to face at the New Lebanon Convention to thrash it out. Beecher, by later report, warned him off:

I'll meet you at the state line, and call out all the artillerymen, and fight every inch of the way to Boston.

— Lyman Beecher, as remembered

The convention settled nothing, and the criticism only sharpened over the years. Old School theologians charged that Finney's stress on human ability and the sinner's will — worked out later in his Systematic Theology — had traded the sovereign grace of God for mere technique, making revival a thing men could manufacture. He lived under that accusation for the rest of his life. He was, by any reckoning, a controversial man; but tens of thousands dated their new obedience to God from the night they heard him.

Oberlin, and the long labor

From 1832 he pastored in New York City — first at Chatham Street Chapel, then at the Broadway Tabernacle built for him in 1836 — where he barred slaveholders from the Lord's Table, for his gospel had made him a fierce abolitionist. In 1835 he joined the new Oberlin Collegiate Institute in Ohio, an outpost of abolition and of coeducation, teaching theology and eventually serving as the college's president from 1851 to 1866. That same year, 1835, his Lectures on Revivals of Religion appeared and went round the world, shaping how the English-speaking church would think and pray about revival for generations.

The revivals did not end at the church door. Finney taught that a converted heart must show itself in a reformed life and a reformed society, and the awakenings he led poured energy into the great reform movements of the age — the crusade against slavery above all, but also temperance, education, and the opening of Oberlin to women and to Black students. Many of the era's most determined abolitionists dated their zeal to a Finney meeting. To him this was no distraction from the gospel; it was the gospel's fruit, obedience worked out where it cost something.

He preached and taught almost to the end, and died at Oberlin on August 16, 1875, at eighty-two. He left behind a divided verdict and an undivided passion: that no soul need wait, that God's work is done through praying people, and that revival begins the moment a heart turns, from the heart, to obey. "Religion," he insisted, "is something for man to do" — and having done it himself in a wood one autumn morning, he spent fifty years calling others to do the same.

fields.name: David Brainerd
fields.bio: David Brainerd (1718–1747) was a young missionary to the Native American peoples of colonial New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Expelled from Yale for his zeal, he gave his brief life to prayer and itinerant preaching among the Delaware and others, seeing a remarkable awakening shortly before dying of tuberculosis at twenty-nine. His diary, published by Jonathan Edwards, became one of the most influential missionary memoirs ever written.
fields.bio_html:
David Brainerd lived twenty-nine years, spent barely four of them in ministry, saw no great crowds, founded no institution, and died coughing blood in another man's house. By every worldly measure his was a small, failed life. Yet the diary he kept — published after his death by Jonathan Edwards — has sent more men and women to the mission field than the biographies of a hundred famous preachers. He is proof that God measures a life differently than we do.

He was born on a Sabbath day, April 20, 1718, in Haddam, Connecticut, into a devout but sorrow-marked family; both parents were dead before he was fourteen. A serious, melancholy boy, he was much occupied with religion and much troubled by it, keeping fasts and reforming his conduct without finding peace. That came only in his twenty-second year. On July 12, 1739, walking alone at dusk, the weight lifted all at once.

As I was walking in a dark thick grove, unspeakable glory seemed to open to the view and apprehension of my soul… My soul rejoiced with joy unspeakable, to see such a God, such a glorious divine Being.

— David Brainerd, Diary, July 12, 1739

Expelled from Yale

That autumn he entered Yale to train for the ministry, and there his zeal outran his discretion. Caught up in the fervor of the Great Awakening then sweeping New England, the students grew critical of tutors they judged unconverted. Asked in private what he thought of one who had prayed without evident warmth, Brainerd said too much:

He has no more grace than this chair.

— David Brainerd, overheard at Yale, 1742

A freshman overheard and reported it. The rector demanded a public confession; Brainerd, believing the words private and the punishment unjust, refused — and for this, together with his attendance at a forbidden "Separate" meeting, he was expelled in the winter of 1742, in his third year. He never took a degree. The disgrace wounded him deeply and closed the ordinary doors of a New England pulpit to him. It also, providentially, turned him toward the one work for which he is remembered.

To the Indians

Licensed to preach in July 1742, he was taken up by a society for missions to the Native American peoples. In April 1743 he settled at Kaunaumeek, a lonely Housatonic village between Stockbridge and Albany, living in a wigwam and then a rough hut, sleeping on straw, learning the language, eating little, and riding many miles through the wilderness. He was often ill, often cold, and almost always alone. His diary from these years is a long record of physical hardship and spiritual desolation — and of a longing that swallowed every other consideration.

I cared not where or how I lived, or what hardships I went through, so that I could but gain souls to Christ.

— David Brainerd, Diary, July 21, 1744

Ordained by the Presbytery of New York in June 1744, he moved on to the Forks of the Delaware in Pennsylvania, and made hard, fruitless journeys to the Susquehanna. For a long time there was almost nothing to show for it. What sustained him was not results but prayer.

It should be said plainly that Brainerd was not a serene saint. His diary is famous — and to some readers troubling — for its relentless self-searching and gloom. He wrestled all his life with what we would now call depression, recording long seasons of "dejection," calling himself "the vilest creature living," and more than once longing simply to die. Edwards, when he published the diary, worried that its melancholy might mislead the young, and gently cautioned readers to imitate Brainerd's devotion without copying his despondency. Yet that very honesty is part of the book's strange power. Here is holiness not as untroubled triumph but as a sick, sorrowful, self-doubting man clinging to God through the dark — and being carried. It has consoled more discouraged believers than any tale of unbroken victory could.

The wrestling in the woods

Brainerd prayed the way other men work — to exhaustion. He set apart whole days for secret fasting and prayer; he "delighted greatly in sacred retirements," Edwards said, disappearing into the forest to pour out his soul for the people he had come to serve. One evening at the Forks, the night before he faced an idolatrous feast, he prayed until his body gave way.

"I was in such anguish, and pleaded with such earnestness and importunity, that when I rose from my knees I felt extremely weak and overcome," he wrote. "I could scarcely walk straight; my joints were loosed; the sweat ran down my face and body, and nature seemed as if it would dissolve." The next day he "withdrew into the woods" again and gave himself up afresh to God, "for life or death, for all hardships to which he should call me, among the heathen."

The wind at Crossweeksung

In June 1745 he came to Crossweeksung, a scattering of Delaware in New Jersey, and here the long, prayed-over drought broke into rain. He preached, not terror, but the free grace and compassion of Christ — and on August 8, 1745, to about sixty-five hearers, the answer came.

"The power of God seemed to descend upon the assembly 'like a mighty rushing wind,'" Brainerd wrote, "and with an astonishing energy bore down all before it… Almost all persons of all ages were bowed down with concern together, and scarcely one was able to withstand the shock of this surprising operation." Old men who had been "drunken wretches for many years," little children of six and seven, a conjurer, a murderer — all were crying to God for mercy. "I never saw any day like it, in all respects."

The change was not a passing emotion. Drunkenness was abandoned, debts were paid, quarrels were healed; within eleven months thirty-eight had made a public profession of faith, "all of whom appear to have had a work of special grace wrought in their hearts." Brainerd, careful and self-suspicious to a fault, was certain of one thing: he had not manufactured this. It had come as a gift, at the moment his own prospects looked worst, in answer to prayer.

A candle burned out

He had little time to enjoy it. The tuberculosis that had shadowed him for years now closed in; he coughed blood and could no longer ride his circuits. In the spring of 1747 he left the Indians and made his way to the home of Jonathan Edwards in Northampton, Massachusetts. There, nursed through his last nineteen weeks by Edwards's daughter Jerusha, he died at about six in the morning on Friday, October 9, 1747, not yet thirty years old. To the end his one desire was unchanged: "My work is done," he told them; "all my desire is to glorify God."

The little congregation at Crossweeksung was not left orphaned. Brainerd's younger brother John, also a missionary, took up the same work and shepherded the Delaware believers for years afterward, so that the awakening David had prayed into being outlived the man by a generation. What looked, at his deathbed, like a story cut off half-told, God quietly continued.

The diary that would not die

Two years later Edwards published An Account of the Life of the Late Reverend Mr. David Brainerd, built around the diary Brainerd had asked him to weigh. It became one of the most reprinted devotional books in the English language, and its quiet, wasting, faithful obedience lit fires that Brainerd never lived to see. John Wesley abridged and commended it. William Carey carried it to India and pressed it on others as a model. Henry Martyn read it at Cambridge and gave his life to missions in the East. Two centuries on, Jim Elliot filled his own journals in the same spirit before dying young in Ecuador. A short life, poured out among a forgotten people in the woods — and through it, God got to himself a name among the nations, exactly as Brainerd had prayed.

faq.q: Who was David Brainerd?
faq.a: David Brainerd (1718–1747) was a young missionary to the Native American peoples of colonial New Jersey and Pennsylvania. He lived twenty-nine years, spent barely four of them in ministry, saw no great crowds and founded no institution, and died coughing blood in another man's house. By every worldly measure his was a small life — yet the diary he kept, published after his death by Jonathan Edwards, has sent more people to the mission field than the biographies of a hundred famous preachers.

faq.q: How was he converted?
faq.a: Born in Haddam, Connecticut, and orphaned before he was fourteen, he was a serious, melancholy boy much occupied with religion and much troubled by it, keeping fasts and reforming his conduct without finding peace. That came only in his twenty-second year: on 12 July 1739, walking alone at dusk in "a dark thick grove," the weight lifted all at once, and his soul "rejoiced with joy unspeakable, to see such a God, such a glorious divine Being."

faq.q: Why was he expelled from Yale?
faq.a: Caught up in the fervor of the Great Awakening, Yale's students grew critical of tutors they judged unconverted. Asked privately what he thought of one who had prayed without evident warmth, Brainerd said too much — "He has no more grace than this chair" — and was overheard. The rector demanded a public confession; believing the words private and the punishment unjust, he refused, and for that, with his attendance at a forbidden "Separate" meeting, he was expelled in 1742 and never took a degree.

faq.q: What was his work among the Indians like?
faq.a: Licensed in 1742, he settled first at Kaunaumeek, living in a wigwam and then a rough hut, sleeping on straw, learning the language and riding many miles through the wilderness; later he moved to the Forks of the Delaware and made hard, fruitless journeys to the Susquehanna. He was often ill, often cold, and almost always alone. "I cared not where or how I lived, or what hardships I went through," he wrote, "so that I could but gain souls to Christ."

faq.q: Did he struggle with depression?
faq.a: He was no serene saint. His diary is famous — and to some readers troubling — for its relentless self-searching and gloom; he wrestled all his life with what we would now call depression, calling himself "the vilest creature living" and more than once longing to die. Edwards, publishing it, cautioned readers to imitate Brainerd's devotion without copying his despondency. Yet that honesty is part of the book's strange power: holiness here is a sorrowful, self-doubting man clinging to God through the dark and being carried.

faq.q: What was his life of prayer?
faq.a: Brainerd prayed the way other men work — to exhaustion. He set apart whole days for secret fasting and prayer and "delighted greatly in sacred retirements," disappearing into the forest to pour out his soul for the people he served. One evening at the Forks, before facing an idolatrous feast, he prayed until his body gave way: "I could scarcely walk straight; my joints were loosed; the sweat ran down my face and body." The next day he withdrew into the woods again and gave himself afresh to God, for life or death.

faq.q: What happened at Crossweeksung?
faq.a: In June 1745 he came to Crossweeksung, a scattering of Delaware in New Jersey, and preached not terror but the free grace and compassion of Christ. On 8 August 1745, to about sixty-five hearers, "the power of God seemed to descend upon the assembly 'like a mighty rushing wind'... and bore down all before it." Old men who had been drunkards for years, little children, a conjurer and a murderer were all crying to God for mercy. "I never saw any day like it, in all respects."

faq.q: Was the awakening lasting?
faq.a: It was no passing emotion. Drunkenness was abandoned, debts were paid, quarrels were healed, and within eleven months thirty-eight had made a public profession of faith, "all of whom appear to have had a work of special grace wrought in their hearts." Careful and self-suspicious to a fault, Brainerd was certain of one thing: he had not manufactured this. It had come as a gift, at the moment his own prospects looked worst, in answer to prayer.

faq.q: How did he die?
faq.a: The tuberculosis that had shadowed him for years closed in; he coughed blood and could no longer ride his circuits. In the spring of 1747 he left the Indians and made his way to the home of Jonathan Edwards in Northampton, where he was nursed through his last nineteen weeks by Edwards's daughter Jerusha. He died at about six in the morning on 9 October 1747, not yet thirty. "My work is done," he told them; "all my desire is to glorify God."

faq.q: Why has his diary been so influential?
faq.a: Two years after his death Edwards published "An Account of the Life of the late Reverend Mr. David Brainerd," built around the diary Brainerd had asked him to weigh. It became one of the most reprinted devotional books in the English language, and its quiet, wasting, faithful obedience lit fires he never lived to see: John Wesley abridged it, William Carey carried it to India, Henry Martyn read it at Cambridge and gave his life to missions, and two centuries on Jim Elliot filled his own journals in the same spirit.

fields.name: John Bunyan
fields.bio: English writer and Puritan preacher, a Bedford tinker by trade who was imprisoned for more than a decade for preaching without a licence. During that confinement he wrote The Pilgrim's Progress, one of the most published allegories in the English language.
fields.bio_html:
He called himself the chief of sinners, and he meant it. John Bunyan was a mender of pots who spent twelve years in a county gaol rather than promise to stop preaching, and who dreamed there a dream that has been carried into more languages than almost any book but the Bible. He was not a scholar. He had, by his own reckoning, almost nothing when he began — no learning, no standing, no money, and for a long stretch of years, no peace. What he had was a conscience that would not let him alone and a Saviour who would not let him go.

The Tinker’s Son

He was born in 1628 at Harrowden, a hamlet in the parish of Elstow, just south of Bedford, and baptised in the Elstow font on 30 November of that year. His father was a tinker — a mender of pots and kettles — and John took up the trade after him. The family were poor, though not destitute; they owned the cottage they lived in. It was a small world, and Bunyan would spend nearly the whole of his life inside a few miles of it.

He learned to read and write, which was more than many of his neighbours could do, and then, as he tells it, he did his best to forget everything good he had ever been taught. In Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, the autobiography he wrote in prison and published in 1666, he is merciless about his own youth. He was a swearer and a Sabbath-breaker, the ringleader of the village young men in their sports. Modern readers, looking for the great scandal behind such self-accusation, generally fail to find one; his sins were the ordinary sins of an ordinary young man, magnified by a conscience that had been given eyes. That is worth noticing. Bunyan is not confessing to spectacular wickedness. He is confessing to being a sinner — which, it turns out, is harder.

In 1644 his mother and his sister died within weeks of each other, and his father remarried almost at once. That same year, at sixteen, Bunyan was mustered into the Parliamentary army and posted to the garrison at Newport Pagnell under Sir Samuel Luke. He saw little fighting. But he came home with one memory he never lost, and he set it down plainly:

When I was a soldier, I with others, were drawn out to go to such a place to besiege it; but when I was just ready to go, one of the company desired to go in my room: to which, when I had consented, he took my place; and coming to the siege, as he stood sentinel, he was shot in the head with a musket-bullet and died.

— John Bunyan, Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners

Another man stood in his place and took the shot that was meant for him. Bunyan records it among the mercies of his life — and then, with characteristic honesty, admits that at the time it did not move him at all. “Here, as I said, were judgments and mercy,” he writes, “but neither of them did awaken my soul to righteousness.”

Two Books and a Dish and a Spoon

He came home to Elstow, took up the tinker’s trade, and married. The record does not preserve his first wife’s name, which is one of the quiet griefs of Bunyan scholarship, for she may have done more for his soul than anyone before Gifford. They were, he says, as poor as poor might be — “not having so much household stuff as a dish or a spoon betwixt us both” — but she brought a dowry of two books left her by her godly father: The Plain Man’s Pathway to Heaven and The Practice of Piety. They read them together. The books did not convert him, he says, but they began something.

Their daughter Mary was born in 1650, and she was blind. She will matter enormously later.

Then, in the middle of a game of cat on the green — a stick-and-ball game the village young men played — something broke in on him. He had struck the ball one blow and was about to strike it a second time when, he says, “a voice did suddenly dart from heaven into my soul,” asking him whether he would leave his sins and go to heaven, or have his sins and go to hell. “At this I was put to an exceeding maze,” he wrote; “wherefore leaving my cat upon the ground, I looked up to heaven.” He stood there in the field, a young man with a stick in his hand, and felt himself looked at.

Three or Four Poor Women, Sitting at a Door in the Sun

What followed was not a conversion. It was the beginning of a long, wandering, agonising search that would take something like five years. Bunyan became outwardly religious, and rather pleased with himself about it. He was, he says, “a brisk talker” in matters of religion. And then he walked down a street in Bedford one day about 1651 and overheard a conversation that undid him.

They were poor women, sitting at a door in the sun, doing their work and talking. He drew near to listen, expecting to be able to join in. He could not. “I heard but understood not,” he writes, “for they were far above, out of my reach.” Their talk was of a new birth, of the work of God on their hearts, of how God had visited their souls with His love in the Lord Jesus, and of the promises that had held them up under the assaults of Satan. They spoke, too, of their own wretchedness of heart and unbelief, and they despised their own righteousness as filthy and insufficient to do them any good.

Bunyan went away shaken. He had thought himself a religious man. These women were speaking a language he did not know, out of an experience he did not have. He began to seek them out. He told them his condition, and they told their pastor, John Gifford, of him — and Gifford, a man with a hard past of his own, took the tinker in. He invited Bunyan to his house to hear him talk with others about the dealings of God with their souls. Bunyan sat under Gifford’s preaching, and said of him afterwards that his doctrine “was much for my stability.” Gifford taught his people to take no truth on trust from any man, but “to cry mightily to God, that He would convince us of the reality thereof” — because when temptation comes, borrowed convictions do not hold. Bunyan was to test that teaching to destruction. He joined the Bedford congregation in 1653 and was baptised by Gifford in the River Ouse.

The Years in the Dark

Any honest account of Bunyan must slow down here, because he did. The middle of Grace Abounding is one of the most harrowing records of spiritual distress in the English language, and it is the reason the book is still read. For months — years — Bunyan was tormented by the fear that he had committed the unpardonable sin.

The temptation came as a voice, and it came constantly: sell Christ, part with Him, let Him go. He fought it, he says, until he was almost out of breath, twenty times together. And then one morning, worn down, he felt the thought pass through his heart: Let Him go, if He will — and felt his heart consent to it. “Now was the battle won,” he writes bitterly, “and down fell I as a bird that is shot from the top of a tree, into great guilt, and fearful despair.”

What followed was years of horror. He was certain he was Esau, who sold his birthright for one morsel of meat and found no place of repentance afterwards though he sought it with tears. That verse followed him like a hound. It would “fly in my face like lightning.” He heard the sound of Esau’s fall in his ears. He was so raw that every sudden noise sounded to him like Fire! fire! He believed himself damned, and went about his work in Bedford as a man already sentenced.

It is important not to tidy this up. Bunyan was not being coy or rhetorical; he was, by any reasonable description, in profound and prolonged anguish. And he did not pray his way out of it in a week. He wrote it all down, decades later, because he thought some other poor soul in the dark might need to know that a man could be there and still be Christ’s.

The deliverance, when it came, came as suddenly and as unbidden as the despair:

But one day, as I was passing in the field, and that too with some dashes on my conscience, fearing lest yet all was not right, suddenly this sentence fell upon my soul, Thy righteousness is in heaven… I also saw moreover, that it was not my good frame of heart that made my righteousness better, nor yet my bad frame that made my righteousness worse; for my righteousness was Jesus Christ Himself. Now did my chains fall off my legs indeed.

— John Bunyan, Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners

His righteousness was not in his heart, where he had been frantically searching for it and never finding it. It was in heaven, at God’s right hand, and it was a Person. The chains fell off his legs — the man who wrote that sentence had not yet seen the inside of a prison. He would.

The Tinker in the Pulpit

The Bedford church discovered that their tinker could preach. He preached first to small gatherings and then to crowds, with an urgency that came straight out of the pit he had climbed from. “I preached what I felt,” he said — what he smartingly did feel.

Then the King came back. With the Restoration in 1660 the old penal laws returned, and preaching outside the Church of England became a crime. In November 1660 Bunyan rode out to preach at Lower Samsell, a farm near Harlington. He was warned that a warrant was out and that he should not go. He went. He would not, he reasoned, have his people say that their preacher had run at the first sign of trouble. They had just begun the meeting in prayer when the constable came in.

The indictment against him has a lovely, absurd pomposity to it: that John Bunyan, of the town of Bedford, labourer, “hath devilishly and perniciously abstained from coming to church to hear Divine service, and is a common upholder of several unlawful meetings and conventicles.” The sentence was three months. He served twelve years, because at the end of every offer of release stood the same condition — stop preaching — and he would not take it.

When one of the justices told him plainly that he must stretch by the neck for it, Bunyan gave the answer that has outlasted every one of his judges’ names:

I told him, as to this matter, I was at a point with him; for if I was out of prison to-day I would preach the gospel again to-morrow, by the help of God.

— John Bunyan, A Relation of the Imprisonment of Mr. John Bunyan

The Pulling of the Flesh from the Bones
