fields.name: Lemuel Haynes
fields.bio: Abandoned as an infant and indentured until he was twenty-one, Lemuel Haynes (1753–1833) taught himself Scripture, Latin, and Greek by firelight. He served as a Minuteman and marched to Ticonderoga, and in 1785 became the first Black man ordained by a mainstream Protestant denomination in America.
fields.bio_html:
He was born on the eighteenth of July, 1753, in West Hartford, Connecticut, and he was given away before he could remember it. His father was a Black man; his mother was a white woman of a respectable New England family. Neither of them kept him. He did not even carry their name — he bore, most likely, the name of the man in whose house he happened to be born. At five months old he was carried up into the Massachusetts hills, to Granville, and bound out as an indentured servant to a farmer named David Rose until he should turn twenty-one.

It is the sort of beginning that usually ends a story before it starts. His earliest biographer, who had known him from boyhood, wrote of him plainly: he was an orphan “not by the bereaving hand of God, but by the cold neglect of those who ought to have been his most affectionate guardians.” Tradition in Granville held that as a boy he once came upon his mother at a relative’s house in a neighbouring town, and that she slipped away rather than speak to him.

And yet the same providence that let him be abandoned set him down in a house where the Sabbath was kept, where family prayer was offered morning and evening, and where Friday nights were given to teaching the household the Scriptures. Deacon Rose was often sent for to pray beside the sick and the dying. His wife, Lemuel said afterward, “treated me as though I was her own child,” and he remembered a saying among the neighbours: that she loved Lemuel more than her own children. The boy who had been given away had been given, as it turned out, to people who would not let him go.

The chimney corner

The indenture required that he be schooled “in common with other children,” which in a frontier village meant a few winter months a year with a barely-trained master, often missed because there was work to do. So he taught himself. New England chimneys in that generation were enormous — a fireplace eight feet across and a yard deep, with a stone block inside where the children could sit. That block was Lemuel Haynes’s school. He gathered pine knots by day so that he could read by their light at night, because candles were a luxury he rarely had. He read the Bible until he could recite most of the texts bearing on the doctrines of grace and name the book, chapter, and verse of each. And no boy in the neighbourhood did more manual labour than he did.

Meeting an old schoolmate one day, he asked how the young man’s studies were coming, and then offered his own method — a sentence that explains the whole strange arc of his life.

I make it my rule to know something more every night than I knew in the morning.

— Lemuel Haynes

Under the apple tree

Religion frightened him before it comforted him. As a small boy left alone in a thunderstorm he thought the last day had come, and the fear of dying unprepared never entirely left him. Later a display of the northern lights — widely taken then for a sign of the judgment — sent him into weeks of terror. “I cannot express the terrors of mind that I felt,” he wrote long afterward to a friend who had asked him about it. Then, one evening, alone in an orchard: “One evening, being under an apple-tree mourning my wretched situation, I hope I found the Saviour.”

He never lost the modesty of that “I hope,” and he never lost the tree. All his life, whenever he came back to Granville, he went and stood under it, and when he could he picked some of the fruit and carried it home. “It is sweet to my taste,” he said.

“I spent much time in what I called secret prayer,” he wrote of those years. As a boy he would slip away into the woods during the break between the Sabbath services to pray alone; as an old man he was still, in his biographer’s phrase, “much in his closet,” where he “watched, and prayed, and fasted much.” He kept no diary of his soul. The habit was the record.

A minuteman, and a manuscript

His indenture ran out and the Revolution came in. In 1774 he enlisted as a minuteman, drilling one day a week and holding himself ready. After Lexington he marched with the Granville company and joined the army at Roxbury. The next year he volunteered for the expedition north to Fort Ticonderoga; passing through Bennington on a Sabbath, the troops halted, and the young soldier sat and heard a sermon on Romans 5:1 that he remembered for the rest of his life. He came home and nearly died of typhus while getting in a wheat crop, and his neighbours came and finished the field for him.

That same year, 1776, with the ink hardly dry on the Declaration of Independence, he wrote something no one would print for two hundred and seven years. He called it Liberty Further Extended: Or Free Thoughts on the Illegality of Slave-Keeping. He set the Declaration’s own words at the head of it and turned them, without flinching, on the men who had written them. Tyranny, he began, “had its origin from the infernal regions,” and so “it is the duty, and honor of every son of freedom to repel her first motions.” Every privilege men enjoy comes from God, he argued, and any human law contradicting the decrees of heaven “is void.” God, he wrote, quoting Acts 17, “hath pleased to make of one Blood all nations of men.”

Liberty is equally as precious to a Black man, as it is to a white one, and Bondage equally as intolerable to the one as it is to the other.

— Lemuel Haynes

He was twenty-three when he wrote it. The manuscript was never finished and never published in his lifetime; it lay unread in an archive until a historian found it in 1983. Unlike many white antislavery men of the next generation, he never favoured shipping free Black Americans off to Africa. He wanted abolition, and he wanted them to stay.

“It’s Lemuel’s sermon”

The Rose household read a printed sermon aloud on Saturday evenings — Watts, Doddridge, Davies, Whitefield — and Lemuel was the reader. One evening he slid a manuscript of his own into the book and read that instead. The old deacon, whose eyes were dim, was delighted, and asked at the end whose work it was. Was it Davies? Watts? Whitefield? Haynes hesitated, and finally admitted: “It’s Lemuel’s sermon.”

That evening changed everything. Friends urged him toward college, and a door opened at Dartmouth, but “I shrunk at the thought.” Instead he studied Latin with the Reverend Daniel Farrand of Canaan, Connecticut, working in the fields to pay his board, then kept a school at Wintonbury while the Reverend William Bradford taught him Greek so that he could read the New Testament in the original. On the twenty-ninth of November, 1780, a group of ministers examined him “in the languages and sciences” and in “practical and experimental religion,” and licensed him to preach. He was twenty-seven.

They called him back to Granville — the parish where he had been known only as a servant boy — and he preached there five years. In 1783 he married Elizabeth Babbitt, a young schoolteacher whom he had counselled through a long spiritual darkness and who, when she came out of it, proposed to him. He commended the matter to God, asked the advice of several ministers, and accepted. They had ten children.

On the ninth of November, 1785, his old teacher Daniel Farrand preached at his ordination from 1 Chronicles 17:16 — “Who am I, O Lord God, or what is my house, that thou hast brought me hitherto?” No text was ever better chosen. Lemuel Haynes became the first Black man ordained by a mainstream Protestant denomination in America. He went next to Torrington, Connecticut, where one man was so offended that a Black man should be in the pulpit that he sat through the service with his hat deliberately on his head. Years later that man told the story on himself: “The preacher had not proceeded far in his sermon before I thought him the whitest man I ever saw. My hat was instantly taken off and thrown under the seat.” He went home converted.

Thirty years at West Rutland

On the twenty-eighth of March, 1788, he accepted a call to the West Parish of Rutland, Vermont — a raw frontier state with barely four or five Congregational ministers west of the Green Mountains and a confident unbelief circulating among its leading men. He stayed thirty years. He found forty-two members, most of them elderly, and would leave behind a church into which more than three hundred had been gathered.

He preached without regard for what was popular. His only questions about a doctrine, said the man who knew him longest, were: “Is it true? Is it profitable? Is it seasonable?” He wept in the pulpit over people in danger. He said it was “a great deal for ministers to keep ego out of the pulpit,” and when his family praised his preaching after he had gone to his room, he would stop his ears so as not to hear it.

For fifteen years almost nothing happened. Roughly thirty people joined the church in all that time. The prayer meeting was kept up week after week and hardly anyone came. “The spirits of God’s people have been sunk,” he wrote; “our harps were hung upon the willows.” By November of 1802 he had privately decided to resign.

Then, he wrote, “it pleased God to arrest the attention of a very thoughtless youth,” who came to him on a Sabbath evening in distress. They called a meeting that week and the house was packed. “The work spread from week to week, till it was difficult to find any dwelling-house that would hold the people.” In one crowded house the floor gave way and dropped the congregation into the cellar; no one was much hurt, and nobody stopped coming. One hundred and three were added to the church. “Thus it has pleased the Lord to do wonders among us, to the praise of his glorious grace.”

In 1804 the trustees of Middlebury College conferred on him an honorary Master of Arts — the first such degree given to a Black man in America. The next June the Universalist preacher Hosea Ballou came to preach in Haynes’s own pulpit and afterward invited him to add remarks. Haynes rose and delivered, on the spot, a sermon he had built while listening — from Genesis 3:4, “And the serpent said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die.” Universal salvation, he argued, was a very ancient doctrine indeed, and the devil was its first and most successful preacher: “an old preacher,” “a very cunning, artful preacher,” who “mixes truth with error, in order to make it go well.” Printed the following year, it ran through edition after edition on both sides of the Atlantic.

Dismissed

The end at Rutland was not clean. He was an unbending Federalist in a parish and a state torn by party feeling, and he preached politics with a satire that stung. On the twenty-ninth of April, 1818, an ecclesiastical council dissolved the pastoral relation. The record calls it mutual; the council commended him warmly as “a tried and faithful minister of Jesus Christ”; and to his friends he wrote calmly, “No impeachment of my moral or ministerial character was pretended. I fully acquiesce in the event.”

He also said something else. He had lived among the people of Rutland thirty years, he remarked, and they were “so sagacious that at the end of that time they found out” that he was a Black man — the word he actually used was the ugly one — “and so turned him away.” Historians still argue over how much of the dismissal was politics and how much was race. He seems to have known.

He was sixty-four, and it did not stop him. “Since my dismission I have not been idle a single Sabbath,” he wrote that September. “I am astonished, and even ashamed, at the pressing calls I have to preach. I know I am unworthy.” He served the church at Manchester, Vermont, for some three years, and in 1822 settled at South Granville, New York, where he preached for the last eleven years of his life.

Nothing in myself

Early in 1833 he wrote his last sermon, on the words “and serve him day and night in his temple.” That March gangrene appeared in one of his feet, and for three weeks he was in constant pain. When it eased he went straight back to work, and in April preached a funeral sermon on the eternal house not made with hands, looking so pale that people thought he was preaching his own. His final public sermon was from Luke 4:16 — “and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day.” Then he went home to die. The Rutland ministers appointed a committee to see that the old man lacked nothing, and the churches sent help until after his death.

I have been examining myself and looking back upon my past life, but I can find nothing in myself and nothing in all my past services to recommend me at the bar of Jehovah. Christ is my all. His blood is my only hope of acceptance.

— Lemuel Haynes

His last months were not cloudless — he had, his biographer admitted, “seasons of desertion and doubt.” In the same conversation he said, “I have been praying for the faith of assurance, and feel that I have almost attained it. My pains are great; but, blessed be God, they are not eternal. I long to be in heaven.” When a friend who had left his own sick parish to come asked whether he should stay, Haynes answered, “Oh, yes, I want your company to all eternity. Do pray for me.”

He died on the twenty-eighth of September, 1833, aged eighty. A plain marble stone was set over him. Only afterward did his family find, in his own handwriting, the epitaph he had written for himself years before, in the strength of his days.

Here lies the dust of a poor hell-deserving sinner, who ventured into eternity trusting wholly on the merits of Christ for salvation.

— Lemuel Haynes

The inscription went on to invite his children, and anyone who read it, to trust their eternal interest on the same foundation. It is a fitting last word for a man who had been handed nothing, who had learned his Greek by pine-knot light, who had argued for the liberty of his own people while a young nation congratulated itself on freedom, and who wanted it recorded on his gravestone that he had nothing of his own to offer God.

faq.q: Who was Lemuel Haynes?
faq.a: Born on 18 July 1753 in West Hartford, Connecticut, to a Black father and a white mother, Lemuel Haynes was abandoned as an infant and bound out as an indentured servant until he was twenty-one. He taught himself Scripture, Latin and Greek by firelight, served as a Minuteman and marched toward Ticonderoga, and in 1785 became the first Black man ordained by a mainstream Protestant denomination in America.

faq.q: What was his childhood in the Rose household like?
faq.a: Given away before he could remember it, he did not even carry his parents' name. At five months old he was bound out to the farmer David Rose in Granville, Massachusetts. Yet the providence that let him be abandoned set him in a house where the Sabbath was kept, family prayer was offered morning and evening, and Friday nights were given to teaching the Scriptures. Mrs. Rose, he said, "treated me as though I was her own child" — the boy who had been given away had been given to people who would not let him go.

faq.q: How did he educate himself?
faq.a: His indenture promised schooling, but on a frontier that meant a few winter months a year, often missed for work — so he taught himself. New England chimneys then were enormous, with a stone block inside where a child could sit, and that block was his school. He gathered pine knots by day to read by their light at night, and read the Bible until he could recite the texts on the doctrines of grace by book, chapter and verse. His rule, he told a schoolmate, was "to know something more every night than I knew in the morning."

faq.q: How was he converted?
faq.a: Religion frightened him before it comforted him: a thunderstorm as a small boy made him think the last day had come, and a later display of the northern lights, taken for a sign of judgment, sent him into weeks of terror. Then, one evening alone in an orchard, "being under an apple-tree mourning my wretched situation, I hope I found the Saviour." He never lost the modesty of that "I hope," and never lost the tree — all his life he would return to stand under it and carry home some of its fruit.

faq.q: What was his life of prayer?
faq.a: "I spent much time in what I called secret prayer," he wrote of those years. As a boy he slipped away into the woods during the break between the Sabbath services to pray alone; as an old man he was still, in his biographer's phrase, "much in his closet," where he "watched, and prayed, and fasted much." He kept no diary of his soul — the habit itself was the record.

faq.q: What was his military service?
faq.a: His indenture ran out just as the Revolution came in. In 1774 he enlisted as a minuteman, drilling and holding himself ready, and after Lexington he marched with the Granville company to the army at Roxbury. The next year he volunteered for the expedition north to Fort Ticonderoga; passing through Bennington on a Sabbath, the troops halted and he heard a sermon on Romans 5:1 that he remembered for the rest of his life. He came home and nearly died of typhus.

faq.q: What was "Liberty Further Extended"?
faq.a: In 1776, with the ink hardly dry on the Declaration of Independence, the twenty-three-year-old Haynes wrote an antislavery essay that turned the Declaration's own words on the men who had written them: tyranny "had its origin from the infernal regions," and "liberty is equally as precious to a Black man, as it is to a white one, and bondage equally as intolerable." Never published in his lifetime, it lay unread in an archive until 1983. Unlike many white antislavery men, he never favoured shipping free Black Americans off to Africa — he wanted abolition, and he wanted them to stay.

faq.q: What was the "It's Lemuel's sermon" moment?
faq.a: The Rose household read a printed sermon aloud on Saturday evenings, and Lemuel was the reader. One evening he slid a manuscript of his own into the book and read that instead. The old deacon, whose eyes were dim, was delighted and asked whose work it was — Davies? Watts? Whitefield? Haynes finally admitted, "It's Lemuel's sermon." That evening changed everything, turning his friends' minds toward his ministry.

faq.q: How was he ordained, and what were his years at West Rutland?
faq.a: He studied Latin and Greek so he could read the New Testament in the original, was licensed to preach in 1780, and on 9 November 1785 was ordained from the text "Who am I, O Lord God... that thou hast brought me hitherto?" — becoming the first Black man ordained by a mainstream Protestant denomination in America. He then served the West Parish of Rutland, Vermont, for thirty years, finding forty-two members and leaving more than three hundred; in the 1802–03 awakening a crowded house even gave way into the cellar, and nobody stopped coming.

faq.q: How did his ministry end, and what was his epitaph?
faq.a: The end at Rutland came in 1818 amid fierce party politics and race — he said the people were "so sagacious that at the end of" thirty years "they found out" he was a Black man "and so turned him away." He was not idle a single Sabbath afterward, serving churches in Vermont and New York and preaching to the last; he died on 28 September 1833, aged eighty. His family later found the epitaph he had written for himself: "Here lies the dust of a poor hell-deserving sinner, who ventured into eternity trusting wholly on the merits of Christ for salvation."

fields.name: William Law
fields.bio: William Law (1686–1761) was an English priest whose refusal to swear allegiance to George I cost him his Cambridge fellowship and any career in the established church. Barred from preferment, he wrote instead — and A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life (1729) became one of the most influential devotional books in English, shaping John Wesley, George Whitefield, and Samuel Johnson.
fields.bio_html:
In the churchyard of King's Cliffe, a stone village on the edge of the old forest of Rockingham, lies a man who never held a parish of his own, never rose an inch in the church he loved, and never once permitted anyone to paint his portrait. He founded no movement and gathered no following. Yet William Law wrote a book that John Wesley could not shake off, that George Whitefield said worked powerfully upon his soul, that made Samuel Johnson think in earnest about God for the first time in his life, and that Edward Gibbon — the great sceptic, no friend to religious enthusiasm — admitted would kindle any spark of piety in a reader into a flame.

He was born in 1686, the fourth of eight sons in a household of eleven children, to Thomas Law, a grocer of King's Cliffe, and his wife Margaret. A grocer's son with a good head was sent to Cambridge to make something of himself, and on 7 June 1705 William Law was admitted a sizar of Emmanuel College — a poor scholar, earning his keep. He read the classics, mathematics, and philosophy, and by 1711 he had done everything a young man was supposed to do: he took his degree, was elected a fellow of his college, and was ordained. He was twenty-five. The road ahead was straight, respectable, and entirely closed to him within three years.

The oath he would not swear

Queen Anne died in 1714 and the crown passed to George of Hanover. Every man holding office in church or university was required to swear allegiance to the new king and to abjure the exiled Stuart line. Law would not do it. He had already sworn to the House of Stuart, and he held that an oath, once given before God, is not a thing a man revises when the political weather changes. It was a scruple of conscience, and it cost him everything a young clergyman had. Deprived of his fellowship, he became a Non-Juror — one of that small, stubborn company of English clergy who paid for their consciences with their careers and lived on the margins of the establishment for the rest of their lives.

He was never restored. He served briefly as a curate at Fotheringay and in London, but preferment was impossible; when Dean Thomas Sherlock offered him advancement, the oath still stood in the way and Law declined. Instead of a bishopric he got obscurity, private teaching, and time to write. The Church of England's loss of a clergyman was the English-speaking world's gain of a devotional master.

His pen, at first, was a weapon. In 1717 he entered the Bangorian controversy with Three Letters to the Bishop of Bangor, still regarded as the most forcible writing the whole dispute produced. In 1723 he took apart Bernard Mandeville's cynical Fable of the Bees. But in 1726 something deeper surfaced: A Practical Treatise upon Christian Perfection. The controversialist was becoming a physician of souls.

The book that would not let go

By 1727 Law had joined the household of Edward Gibbon at Putney as tutor to the son of the house — the father of the historian who would one day write The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire. He remained ten years and became, in the family's own reckoning, the honoured friend and spiritual director of them all. And there, at the end of 1728, he published the book that carries his name: A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life.

Its argument is disarmingly simple and almost impossible to escape. Everyone grants, Law observed, that prayer must be offered according to the will of God. Very well — then why should the other twenty-three hours be exempt?

Devotion is neither private nor public prayer; but prayers, whether private or public, are particular parts or instances of devotion. Devotion signifies a life given, or devoted, to God.

— William Law

From that seed the whole book grows. He drew portraits — Flavia, who spends on herself and gives the poor her leftovers; Miranda, who divides her fortune with the needy and keeps only her own share of it — so sharply observed that Gibbon thought them not unworthy of La Bruyère. But Law's satire was never cruelty. It was diagnosis. And in the second chapter he laid his finger on the nerve:

And if you will here stop, and ask yourselves, why you are not as pious as the primitive Christians were, your own heart will tell you, that it is neither through ignorance nor inability, but purely because you never thoroughly intended it.

— William Law

That sentence has undone a great many readers. It leaves no room for the comfortable excuse. You are not more holy because you have never seriously meant to be.

Wesley, Whitefield, and the Revival

The effect was extraordinary and almost immediate. Samuel Johnson picked it up at Oxford expecting a dull book he could laugh at, and later told Boswell he had found Law quite an overmatch for him — it was, he said, the first occasion of his thinking in earnest about religion. George Whitefield got hold of a small edition at Oxford and recorded that God worked powerfully upon his soul through it; he began to pray and sing psalms three times a day. Charles Wesley called reading it a turning point. John Wesley first came to see Law at Putney in 1732, and for years he carried the Serious Call and Christian Perfection with him and pressed them on his preachers. Henry Venn, Thomas Scott, James Hervey, John Newton — the men who lit the Evangelical Revival were reading William Law before they were reading each other. Half a century later, in 1784, the young William Wilberforce would be shaken by the same book.

An anonymous benefactor, it is said, pressed a thousand pounds into Law's hands, and Law appears to have turned it straight into a school at King's Cliffe for fourteen poor girls, founded in 1727, who were to be clothed and taught reading, knitting, and every useful kind of needlework. He was giving money away before he had published a word urging others to.

Fixed hours and a rule of life

A third of the Serious Call is about prayer — not prayer as mood, but prayer as appointment. Law urged a rule of life built on fixed hours: early in the morning, then nine o'clock for humility, noon for universal love and intercession, three o'clock for resignation to the will of God, and evening for self-examination and confession. He was blunt about the cost of the first of them: it is as much your duty to rise to pray, he wrote, as to pray once you have risen.

Prayer is the nearest approach to God, and the highest enjoyment of Him, that we are capable of in this life.

— William Law

He kept his own rule to the end. At King's Cliffe he rose every morning at five and gave the hours before breakfast to prayer, meditation, and study; at nine the whole household — family and servants together — gathered for prayers. A servant read a chapter of Scripture aloud and Law explained it. He was at church on Wednesdays, Fridays, and Sundays, and went to bed at nine.

Boehme, and the parting with Wesley

Around 1735 a physician friend, Dr George Cheyne, put into Law's hands a book that led him to the writings of Jacob Boehme, the German shoemaker-mystic. Law was captivated. He taught himself German in order to read Boehme in the original, and his last works — An Appeal to All that Doubt (1742), The Spirit of Prayer (1749–50), The Way to Divine Knowledge (1752), The Spirit of Love (1752–54) — are steeped in him. The moral rigour of the Serious Call gave way to something inward and luminous, all about the birth of Christ within the soul.

Not everyone followed him there, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. This is where Law divided his admirers, and the division has never quite healed. In May 1738, fresh from his Aldersgate experience, John Wesley wrote to his old mentor with a reproach that still stings: how would Law answer it to their common Lord that he had never given Wesley this advice — never directed him first of all to a living faith in the blood of Christ? Law replied, with some dignity, that he had commended Thomas à Kempis and had constantly insisted on the same truth, and asked whether the quarrel was not partly a contest about words. But the friendship was over. In 1756 Wesley published an open letter saying he had scarce met with a greater friend to darkness, except the illuminated Jacob Behmen himself. Law never answered it publicly. He was, we are told, deeply hurt.

Something in that tension is worth sitting with. The man who had taught the Revival to be serious about holiness could not, in the end, walk with the Revival. And yet Wesley went on quoting him with admiration in his sermons for the rest of his life, and went on printing his books. Coleridge and Blake would later prize the Boehme volumes that Law's household paid to publish. Great teachers are rarely tidy.

King's Cliffe: a household of prayer and alms

When old Edward Gibbon died in 1737 the Putney years ended. Law lodged briefly in London and then, towards the close of 1740, went home for good to King's Cliffe. He was not alone for long. Archibald Hutcheson, a member of Parliament, had died that year wishing that his widow Elizabeth should live a retired and religious life under Law's direction; Hester Gibbon, sister of Law's old pupil, made the same choice. By 1744 the three of them were settled in Law's house at King's Cliffe, an ancient manor the village still called King John's Palace.

They set out, quite deliberately, to obey the Serious Call to the letter — to spend in charity everything not strictly necessary. Between them the two women had close to three thousand pounds a year, a very large income for the time. Almost all of it went out again. Law's school for fourteen girls was joined by a school for eighteen boys, raised to twenty in 1746; they built almshouses; Law kept a great theological library. Four cows were kept and their milk given away to poor neighbours. Every day Law tasted the soup made for the poor, and those who knew him said the one thing that could make him short-tempered was soup that had not been well enough made.

His own life was plain to the point of austerity — dinner at noon, tea at which he ate only raisins, a brisk walk in the fields, one pipe and a glass of water before bed. He loved music, insisting that anyone could be taught to sing well enough for devotion, and he was fond of animals and of children.

The charity was not universally admired. The rector complained that the household's giving was indiscriminate, and on 21 February 1753 the more considerable inhabitants of King's Cliffe formally petitioned the justices of the peace that Law and his family were the cause of the miserable poverty of the parish, drawing beggars from miles around. Law signed a reply. They would continue as they had begun; if the parish preferred, they would leave it altogether. They stayed. The beggars, as one historian dryly put it, proved too strong for the considerable inhabitants.

I give to all, because I pray to God to forgive all; and I cannot refuse an alms to those whom I pray God to bless.

— William Law

Almost in the act of singing

He caught a chill at the annual audit of his school, and after a fortnight's illness died on 9 April 1761, aged seventy-five. He had written a letter the day before without so much as mentioning that he was ill. He died, those with him said, almost in the act of singing the Angels' Hymn. He was buried at King's Cliffe, in the village where he was born, a few steps from the schools he had founded. Mrs Hutcheson lived on until 1781 and died at ninety-one; Hester Gibbon until 1790, dying at eighty-six — her nephew the historian noting, not unkindly, that she still lived in a hermitage at Cliffe, having long survived her spiritual guide and faithful companion Mr William Law.

He left no portrait, no monument, no denomination. He left a book. Two and a half centuries later the Church of England and the Episcopal Church still keep his memory on 10 April, and readers who have never heard of the Bangorian controversy or the Non-Jurors still find themselves stopped mid-page by a plain man asking a plain question: not whether they can be holy, but whether they have ever thoroughly intended it.

faq.q: Why did William Law lose his Cambridge fellowship and any hope of a church career?
faq.a: Law had been elected a fellow of Emmanuel College and ordained by 1711, with a straight and respectable road ahead of him. But when Queen Anne died in 1714 and the crown passed to George I, every officeholder was required to swear allegiance to the new Hanoverian king and abjure the exiled Stuart line. Having already sworn to the House of Stuart, Law held that an oath given before God is not revised when the political weather changes, and he refused — a scruple of conscience that cost him his fellowship and any preferment for the rest of his life.

faq.q: What was a "Non-juror," and what did that status mean for Law's life?
faq.a: The Non-jurors were a small, stubborn company of English clergy who would not swear the oath of allegiance to the Hanoverian monarchs and so paid for their consciences with their careers. Law became one of them and was never restored to office. He served briefly as a curate and later declined advancement offered by Dean Thomas Sherlock, because the oath still stood in the way; barred from a parish of his own, he turned instead to private teaching and to writing.

faq.q: Is it true he tutored the family of the historian Edward Gibbon?
faq.a: Yes. Around 1727 Law joined the household of Edward Gibbon at Putney as tutor to the son of the house — the father of the historian who would write The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire. He remained about ten years and became, in the family's own reckoning, the honoured friend and spiritual director of them all. It was during these years, at the end of 1728, that he published the book that carries his name.

faq.q: What is William Law best known for?
faq.a: He is remembered above all for A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life, published at the end of 1728, one of the most influential devotional books ever written in English. Its argument is disarmingly simple: everyone agrees prayer should be offered according to the will of God, so why should the other twenty-three hours of the day be exempt? For Law, devotion meant not a mood or an hour of prayer but a whole life given, or devoted, to God.

faq.q: How did A Serious Call shape John Wesley, Whitefield, and Samuel Johnson?
faq.a: The effect was extraordinary. Samuel Johnson picked it up at Oxford expecting a dull book to laugh at and later told Boswell he found Law "quite an overmatch for me," the first occasion of his thinking in earnest about religion. George Whitefield said God worked powerfully upon his soul through it, Charles Wesley called reading it a turning point, and John Wesley carried it and its companion volume for years and pressed them on his preachers — so that the men who lit the Evangelical Revival were reading William Law before they were reading each other.

faq.q: What are the famous character sketches in the book?
faq.a: Law drew portraits so sharply observed that Gibbon thought them not unworthy of the French satirist La Bruyère — Flavia, who lavishes money on herself and gives the poor only her leftovers, and Miranda, who divides her fortune with the needy and keeps just her own share. Yet the satire was never cruelty but diagnosis. He laid his finger on the nerve with a sentence that has undone many readers: you are not as holy as the early Christians "neither through ignorance nor inability, but purely because you never thoroughly intended it."

faq.q: Why did his later turn to the mystic Jakob Böhme cool some of his admirers?
faq.a: Around 1735 a physician friend put into Law's hands the writings of Jakob Böhme, the German shoemaker-mystic, and Law was captivated — he even taught himself German to read Böhme in the original. His later works grew inward and luminous, all about the birth of Christ within the soul, and not everyone would follow him there. The break with John Wesley was the sharpest: after Wesley reproached him for never pointing him to a living faith in the blood of Christ, the old friendship ended, and in 1756 Wesley published an open letter calling him a friend to darkness — a wound Law is said to have felt deeply, though Wesley went on quoting him with admiration for the rest of his life.

faq.q: How did Law actually live out the holiness he wrote about?
faq.a: Towards the end of 1740 he settled for good at King's Cliffe, the village where he was born, joined by two devout women, Elizabeth Hutcheson and Hester Gibbon, who set out deliberately to obey A Serious Call to the letter and spend in charity everything not strictly necessary. Between them the women had close to three thousand pounds a year, and almost all of it went out again: they ran a school for fourteen poor girls and another for eighteen boys, built almshouses, and gave away milk and soup daily. His own life was plain to the point of austerity — rising at five to pray, keeping fixed hours through the day — and he answered complaints about his indiscriminate giving simply: "I give to all, because I pray to God to forgive all; and I cannot refuse an alms to those whom I pray God to bless."

faq.q: How did William Law die, and what did he leave behind?
faq.a: He caught a chill at the annual audit of his school and, after a fortnight's illness, died on 9 April 1761 at the age of seventy-five, having written a letter the day before without so much as mentioning that he was ill. Those with him said he died almost in the act of singing a hymn. He was buried at King's Cliffe a few steps from the schools he had founded, leaving no movement and no monument, only a book that still stops readers mid-page with its plain question — not whether they can be holy, but whether they have ever thoroughly intended it.

faq.q: Is there any portrait of William Law taken from life?
faq.a: No genuine likeness of him is known to survive, because Law never once permitted anyone to paint his portrait — the later engravings that circulate are not drawn from life. It is of a piece with the man, who founded no denomination, sought no preferment, and gathered no following around himself. He left the world his books and his example rather than his face.

fields.name: Thomas à Kempis
fields.bio: Thomas à Kempis (c. 1380–1471) was a German-born Dutch monk who spent roughly seventy years in a single monastery outside Zwolle, copying manuscripts, keeping his community's chronicle, and teaching its novices. Formed at Deventer among the Brethren of the Common Life, he wrote for those young men four small booklets of counsel that became The Imitation of Christ — after the Bible, the most widely read Christian book ever written.
fields.bio_html:
There is a strange arithmetic at the heart of this man's life. He wrote what is very likely the most widely read Christian book ever composed after the Bible itself — a little volume that has been translated into more languages than almost any other work of devotion, carried in the pockets of soldiers and scholars and dying men for six centuries. And he did it while going almost nowhere, meeting almost no one, and taking such care to leave no trace of himself that for three hundred years learned men argued about whether he had written it at all.

Thomas à Kempis spent roughly seventy years inside a single monastery on a low hill outside a provincial Dutch town. He held no great office. He preached to no crowds. He was never canonised. The record of his days is a record of copying, praying, teaching young men, and writing small books for their use. That is the whole of it — and that is precisely the point. The Imitation of Christ did not come out of a life of incident. It came out of a life of stability, and the two facts belong together.

Better of a surety is a lowly peasant who serveth God, than a proud philosopher who watcheth the stars and neglecteth the knowledge of himself.

— Thomas à Kempis

The hammer's son

He was born Thomas Hemerken — the name means something like "little hammer," and was later Latinised to Malleolus — in the town of Kempen in the Rhineland, in the diocese of Cologne. The year was 1379 or 1380; the sources cannot settle it, and neither should we. He is known to us by the place rather than the family: Thomas of Kempen, Thomas à Kempis.

His parents were John and Gertrude Hemerken, working people. Exactly what his father did is another small uncertainty: some accounts make him a smith, others simply a poor labouring man. His mother, by several accounts, kept a small school in the town. Nothing about the household suggested that one of its sons would be read for six hundred years.

There was an elder brother, John, some fourteen years ahead of him, and John went first — first to school, and later into the religious life. Thomas followed him both times. It is worth pausing on that, because it is a pattern in this life: Thomas rarely struck out. He followed, he stayed, he remained. In a century of restless reformers he was constitutionally a man who did not move.

Deventer, and the Modern Devotion

In 1392, at about twelve or thirteen, Thomas travelled to Deventer in the Netherlands to attend its famous school. He stayed some seven years, and those years made him.

Deventer was the heartland of what came to be called the devotio moderna, the Modern Devotion — a renewal movement begun by Geert Groote, who had died before Thomas was old enough to know him. Groote's followers, the Brethren of the Common Life, were not monks in the old sense. They lived together, worked with their hands, copied manuscripts for their bread, and pursued an interior, practical, unshowy Christianity: less speculation, more obedience. They were suspicious of learning that made a man proud and of devotion that made a man conspicuous.

At Deventer, Thomas came under the care of Florens Radewijns, Groote's successor and the movement's steadying hand. Radewijns took the boy in, paid his way, and shaped him. Decades later Thomas would write the lives of both men — one reason we know as much as we do about the Modern Devotion is that this quiet man in Zwolle wrote its history down. Everything characteristic of The Imitation — the distrust of clever talk, the insistence that Christ is followed rather than discussed, the tenderness toward beginners — is already in the air he breathed there as a schoolboy.

The hill of St Agnes

In 1399 Thomas went to Mount St Agnes, a new house of Canons Regular on a rise outside Zwolle, where his brother John was among the community and would serve as its prior. He arrived at about nineteen or twenty. He would die there, in the same house, at about ninety-one.

He was not, however, rushed into vows. The community was poor and unfinished — there were, in the early days, scarcely any buildings, no garden, no benefactors, no funds — and Thomas seems to have waited years on the threshold. He was clothed as a novice around 1406, when the cloister was at last completed, made his profession in 1407, and was ordained priest in 1413. From arrival to priesthood was fourteen years. Whatever else may be said of his vocation, it was not impulsive.

The poverty of those first years he recorded himself, in his Chronicle of the Canons Regular of Mount St Agnes — a plain, affectionate house-history that is our best window into the world he lived in. He describes evenings when supper ended with almost nothing left to divide the next day, and times when there were no cooking pots, or no suitable food at all. In one passage the cook, Gerard, anxious about the morning, came to Father John and asked sadly, "What shall I set before them to-morrow?" Thomas records the answer: John "consoled his sadness with kindly words, and exhorted him to have faith in the Lord, who doth not fail them that hope in Him."

That same day, Thomas writes in the Chronicle, "when that day had drawn on to evening, Everard of Eza, Curate of Almelo, came unexpectedly in his chariot as if sent by God to comfort the poor." He had brought fine meal and flesh, and gave it to the brothers for their common use. They "gave thanks to God and to Everard that of his bounty he had provided for them and succoured them in their so great need."

The desk, and the whole Bible by hand

What did he actually do, for seventy years?

He copied. This was the Brethren's trade and their discipline, and Thomas was extraordinarily good at it. He copied a missal for the use of his community. He copied out the entire Bible by hand — a labour that survives in several great volumes, and which some accounts say he undertook more than once. Consider what that means as a spiritual exercise rather than a clerical one: years of moving through the whole of Scripture at the speed of a pen, one word at a time, with no possibility of skimming. It is hard to imagine a slower or more thorough way to let a book get inside a man.

Around that work he wrote his own: sermons and short treatises for novices, prayers, hymns, letters, the lives of Groote and Radewijns and of Lidwina of Schiedam, the Chronicle of his house. And, between roughly 1418 and 1427, four small booklets of counsel for young religious that would be gathered together and carried out of that cloister into the whole world.

A Latin motto has long been attached to him — In omnibus requiem quaesivi, et nusquam inveni nisi in angulo cum libro: everywhere I have sought rest, and nowhere found it save in a corner with a book. It is worth being honest about this one, because it is quoted constantly as though it came from The Imitation, and it does not. It survives as a motto associated with his portrait and with early printed editions rather than as a line from his own published text. Whether or not the words are literally his, the description is exact.

Sub-prior, and master of novices

He was twice elected sub-prior of Mount St Agnes — the sources differ on the exact years, some giving 1425 and others 1429 — and once served as procurator, the house's business officer. That last appointment appears not to have gone well; later accounts describe him as simple in worldly matters and inclined to absent-mindedness, a man who withdrew from lively conversation and was relieved to be given back to his books.

But as sub-prior he was master of the novices, and this is the office that produced the book. Everything in The Imitation of Christ was written for particular young men whose faces he knew — anxious, ambitious, distractible beginners, learning to keep silence and to obey. That is why it does not read like theology. It reads like a wise old man talking quietly to someone who is struggling, which is exactly what it was.

I had rather feel contrition than be skilful in the definition thereof.

— Thomas à Kempis

The third and fourth books of The Imitation turn almost entirely into prayer — a dialogue between the soul and Christ, in which the writer stops instructing and starts asking. Anyone who wants to know how Thomas à Kempis prayed need only read them; his own hours, the daily round of the monastic office he kept for seven decades, are woven straight through the text.

"Speak, Lord, for Thy servant heareth. I am Thy servant, grant me understanding, that I may know Thy testimonies. Incline my heart to the words of Thy mouth: let Thy speech distil as the dew." So opens the second chapter of Book III — the prayer of a man who had spent his life copying other men's words and wanted, above all, to hear one Voice speak them.

Exile

The one great disruption came late. In 1429 a bitter dispute over who should hold the see of Utrecht brought an interdict down on the region, and the community was driven from the hill. "Alas! Holy God!" Thomas wrote in the Chronicle, "on the day before the Feast of St. Lambert we ceased from our singing by reason of the Interdict that was published against us!" The silencing of the sung office is the loss he names first.

The exile lasted until 1432. Thomas spent much of it at Bethany, near Arnhem, nursing his brother John, who was old and ill. John died there in November 1432. Thomas had followed him to school, followed him into religion, and now sat with him at the end; then he went home to the hill and stayed there for another thirty-nine years.

The quarrel over the book

The Imitation of Christ went out into the world anonymously, which was entirely in character — the Brethren's whole instinct was to efface the author. In 1441 Thomas completed and signed a codex in his own hand containing all four books together with nine other treatises; that manuscript survives in Brussels and is the single strongest piece of evidence for his authorship.

It did not settle the matter. For centuries rival claims were pressed with real heat: for Jean Gerson, the chancellor of Paris, whose name is close enough to invite confusion, and for a supposed Italian abbot called Giovanni Gersen. National pride, monastic pride, and genuine scholarly puzzlement all played their part. The honest summary is this: the case was seriously disputed for a very long time, and modern scholarship has come down decisively on the side of Thomas à Kempis — on the strength of the autograph manuscript, of contemporary witnesses who named him, and of the Dutch turns of phrase that show through the Latin. There is a fine irony in it: a man who took such pains to disappear behind his subject very nearly succeeded in losing his own book.

The end, and what came after

He died on 25 July 1471, in his ninety-first or ninety-second year, having outlived nearly everyone he had entered with. The Chronicle he had kept for so long was taken up by an anonymous successor, who recorded the death of the brother Thomas Hämerken, born at Kempen in the diocese of Cologne, and noted that he departed after Compline — after the last office of the day, the prayer said as the light goes. Some older reference works give a different date; the house's own chronicle is the better witness.

He was buried at Mount St Agnes. The monastery is long gone; his remains were eventually brought into Zwolle, and in 1897 a monument was raised over them in St Michael's Church bearing the words Honori, non memoriae Thomae Kempensis, cujus nomen perennius quam monumentum — to the honour, not the memory, of Thomas of Kempen, whose name is more lasting than any monument.

A story is often told that when his coffin was opened long after his death, scratches were found inside the lid and splinters under his fingernails, and that the Church therefore refused him canonisation on the grounds that a saint would not have fought so hard to live. It is a memorable tale and it should be labelled plainly: there is little evidence for any part of it. He was in fact never canonised, but the coffin story is legend, not history.

Vanity of vanities, all is vanity, save to love God, and Him only to serve.

— Thomas à Kempis

What remains is the arithmetic we began with. Seventy years in one house; a pen, a choir stall, a cell, a succession of nervous young novices; no travel, no controversy sought, no reputation built. And out of it, a book that has done more to shape ordinary Christian devotion than most councils and most kings — read by Ignatius of Loyola and John Wesley and Thomas More, by Samuel Johnson and by generations of people who never wrote anything down at all.

It is a rebuke to a great deal of what we assume about influence. Thomas à Kempis did not go out and find a hundred million readers. He stayed put, minded his own soul, copied the Scriptures until they were in his bones, and wrote plainly for the twenty young men in front of him. The hiddenness was not the price of the book. It was the soil it grew in.

faq.q: Where and when was Thomas à Kempis born, and what does his name actually mean?
faq.a: He was born Thomas Hemerken in the town of Kempen in the Rhineland, in the diocese of Cologne, around 1379 or 1380; the sources cannot settle the exact year. The surname Hemerken means something like "little hammer" and was later Latinised to Malleolus, probably a nod to his father's trade. He is known to us not by his family but by his birthplace, as Thomas of Kempen, à Kempis. His parents, John and Gertrude, were working people, and he had an elder brother, John, some fourteen years ahead of him whom he tended to follow.

faq.q: What kind of schooling did he have, and what shaped his outlook?
faq.a: At about twelve or thirteen he went to Deventer in the Netherlands, staying roughly seven years at its famous school under the care of Florens Radewijns. Deventer was the heartland of the devotio moderna, the Modern Devotion begun by Geert Groote, whose followers, the Brethren of the Common Life, lived and worked together and copied manuscripts for their bread. Their Christianity was interior, practical, and unshowy: suspicious of learning that made a man proud and of piety that made him conspicuous. Thomas later wrote the lives of Groote and Radewijns, which is one reason we know as much as we do about the movement.

faq.q: What was his life in the monastery like?
faq.a: In 1399 he went to Mount St Agnes, a house of Augustinian Canons Regular on a rise outside Zwolle, where his brother John was among the community and would serve as prior. He was not rushed into vows: the house was poor and unfinished, and he waited years on the threshold, being clothed as a novice around 1406, making his profession in 1407, and being ordained priest in 1413. He remained there for roughly seventy years and died in the same house. The hardship of those early years he set down himself in his Chronicle of the Canons Regular of Mount St Agnes, our best window onto the world he lived in.

faq.q: What did he actually do for seventy years in one place?
faq.a: He copied. Copying manuscripts was the Brethren's trade and their discipline, and Thomas was extraordinarily good at it, producing a missal for his community and copying out the entire Bible by hand; he is generally said to have done so several times over, and one such copy survives in several volumes. Around that labour he wrote his own works: sermons and short treatises for novices, prayers, hymns, letters, saints' lives, and the chronicle of his house. He was twice elected sub-prior and served as master of the novices, and it was for those young men that his most famous book was written.

faq.q: Did he really write The Imitation of Christ, or is that disputed?
faq.a: For centuries it was seriously disputed, with rival claims pressed for Jean Gerson, the chancellor of Paris, and for a supposed Italian abbot called Giovanni Gersen; the work had gone out into the world anonymously, entirely in keeping with the Brethren's instinct to efface the author. Modern scholarship, however, has come down decisively on the side of Thomas à Kempis. The strongest single piece of evidence is a codex he completed and signed in his own hand in 1441, containing all four books, which survives in Brussels. Contemporary witnesses who named him and the Dutch turns of phrase showing through the Latin point the same way.

faq.q: What is The Imitation of Christ about, and why has it been read for so long?
faq.a: It gathers four small booklets of counsel, written between roughly 1418 and 1427 for particular young novices whose faces Thomas knew, on inward devotion, self-denial, and following Christ rather than merely discussing him. That is why it does not read like theology but like a wise old man talking quietly to someone who is struggling. Its temper is caught in a famous line from the first book: "I had rather feel contrition than be skilful in the definition thereof." The later books turn almost entirely into prayer, a dialogue between the soul and Christ.

faq.q: Was Thomas à Kempis famous in his own lifetime?
faq.a: No. He held no great office, preached to no crowds, sought no controversy, and was never canonised; his book carried his name so lightly that for a long time it was hard to prove he had written it at all. This obscurity was of a piece with the Modern Devotion's whole instinct toward self-effacement. A Latin motto is often attached to him, In omnibus requiem quaesivi, et nusquam inveni nisi in angulo cum libro, "everywhere I have sought rest, and nowhere found it save in a corner with a book"; it describes him exactly, though it survives as a motto linked to his portrait rather than as a line from his published text.

faq.q: When and how did he die?
faq.a: He died in 1471, in about his ninety-first or ninety-second year, at Mount St Agnes, having outlived nearly everyone he had entered with. The sources do not fully agree on the exact day: his house's own chronicle and much Catholic tradition give 25 July, while some reference works give a different date. The chronicler who took up the record after him noted that the brother, born at Kempen in the diocese of Cologne, departed after Compline, the last office of the day. He was buried at the monastery; long after, his remains were brought into Zwolle, and in 1897 a monument was raised over them in St Michael's Church.

faq.q: Is the story about scratch marks in his coffin true?
faq.a: It should be labelled plainly as legend. The tale runs that when his coffin was opened long after his death, scratches were found inside the lid and splinters under his fingernails, and that the Church therefore refused him canonisation on the grounds that a true saint would not have fought so hard to live. It is a memorable story with very little evidence behind any part of it. What is true is the plainer fact underneath it: Thomas à Kempis was in fact never canonised, but the coffin story is legend, not history.

fields.name: Clement of Rome
fields.bio: Clement of Rome (c. 35 – c. 99) led the church at Rome in the generation after the apostles and wrote the earliest Christian document to survive outside the New Testament. His one surviving letter was sent to Corinth around AD 96, where a faction had deposed the church's elders, and it argues from Scripture for humility, order and love before closing in prayer for the sick, the imprisoned and the emperor. Three generations later it was still being read aloud in Corinthian worship.
fields.bio_html:
Of all the writers in this library, Clement of Rome is the one we know least and owe most. He stands at the very hinge of the church's story, in the generation that had to learn how to be Christian without the apostles alive to ask. He wrote one letter. It survived. And because it survived we can hear, in ordinary Greek, what a pastor in Rome thought worth saying to a divided congregation while some of the men who had walked with Peter and Paul were still living.

Almost everything else about him is contested, and honesty requires saying so plainly. Irenaeus, writing around AD 180, lists him as the third to hold the office of oversight in Rome after the apostles, following Linus and Anacletus, and says that Clement had seen the blessed apostles and conferred with them. Origen and later writers identified him with the Clement whom Paul names as a fellow worker in Philippians 4:3, whose name is in the book of life. That identification is old and it is attractive, and it cannot be proved. Other traditions made him a freedman of the imperial household, or confused him with the consul Titus Flavius Clemens whom Domitian executed. The letter itself names no author at all. It is sent from the Church of God which sojourns at Rome to the Church of God sojourning at Corinth, in the plural voice of a congregation rather than the singular voice of a bishop. It was the church at Corinth, and then Dionysius of Corinth a lifetime later, who called it Clement's.

What is not contested is the occasion. Some time around AD 95 or 96, word reached Rome that the church in Corinth had done something extraordinary: it had deposed its presbyters. These were men of blameless conduct, Clement says, who had ministered faithfully and given no cause. A younger faction had simply pushed them out. Forty years after Paul had written to the same city about factions and parties, the same city was tearing itself apart again over the same thing.

The letter

Clement does not begin by scolding. He begins by remembering them at their best, and the remembering is so warm that it hurts:

Moreover, ye were all distinguished by humility, and were in no respect puffed up with pride, but yielded obedience rather than extorted it, and were more willing to give than to receive. Thus a profound and abundant peace was given to you all, and ye had an insatiable desire for doing good.

— Clement of Rome, to the Corinthians, chapter 2

Then he names the disease. He calls it jealousy, or envy, and he traces it through the whole of Scripture like a physician tracing an infection: Cain against Abel, Esau against Jacob, Joseph's brothers, Saul against David, and then, terribly and recently, envy in the church itself. In the fifth chapter he turns to his own generation, and gives us the earliest account outside the New Testament of the deaths of Peter and Paul, describing Paul as having reached the limits of the west before his witness before the rulers. He goes on to a great multitude of the elect who, having through envy endured many indignities and tortures, furnished us with a most excellent example. He is writing in a city that has recently watched Christians die, and he is telling a church that its quarrel over which men should serve at the table belongs to the same family of sins as the malice that killed them.

His remedy is not clever. It is order, humility, and love. He points to the ranks of an army, to the harmony of the body, to the seasons that keep their appointed order without complaint, to the sea that does not pass its bounds. He points, at length and with evident delight, to the resurrection, which he argues from day following night, from the sown seed that dissolves before it rises, and from the story of the phoenix, which he plainly believed to be a bird that lived in Arabia. That last argument has embarrassed his readers for nineteen centuries, and it is worth leaving in view: the earliest Christian letter we possess outside the New Testament reasons from natural history that was simply wrong, in the service of a hope that was not. The man is not infallible. He is faithful.

Then, near the end, he writes on love, and the prose lifts:

Who can describe the bond of the love of God? The height to which love exalts is unspeakable. Love unites us to God. Love covers a multitude of sins. There is nothing base, nothing arrogant in love. Love admits of no schisms: love gives rise to no seditions: love does all things in harmony.

— Clement of Rome, to the Corinthians, chapter 49

And he asks the men at the centre of the quarrel to do the hardest thing in the letter: to leave. Whoever among you is noble-minded, he writes, let him say, if it is on my account that sedition and disagreement have arisen, I will go away, only let the flock of Christ live in peace. It is a request nobody could enforce from six hundred miles away. He asks it anyway.

The prayer

The letter closes in prayer, and the prayer is the reason many readers who came for the history stay for the man. He prays for the sick, the fallen, the fainthearted, the hungry, the imprisoned; and then, astonishingly for a Christian writing while Rome was killing Christians, he prays at length for the emperor and the governing authorities, that God would direct their counsel toward what is good.

May God, who seeth all things, and who is the Ruler of all spirits and the Lord of all flesh, grant to every soul that calleth upon His glorious and holy Name, faith, fear, peace, patience, long-suffering, self-control, purity, and sobriety, to the well-pleasing of His Name, through our High Priest and Protector, Jesus Christ.

There is a strange and moving story attached to that prayer. The only manuscript known to Europe for centuries was the great fifth-century Codex Alexandrinus, and a whole leaf of it had been lost. For hundreds of years readers came to the end of chapter 57 and fell into a hole; the long intercession was known only to have existed. Then in 1873 a Greek metropolitan, Philotheos Bryennios, found a complete copy in a library in Constantinople, and the church got its oldest surviving prayer back. Older translations, including the one this library will use, still carry the gap where the leaf was lost.

What came of it

The letter worked. Around AD 170, Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, wrote to Rome that Clement's letter was still being read aloud in the Corinthian assembly on the Lord's Day, three generations after the quarrel it settled had been forgotten.

That is the measure of the man. He had no authority in Corinth that Corinth was obliged to recognise, no office anyone could have defined for him, and no weapon but Scripture, patience, and the memory of what that church had once been. He used them, and a congregation that had thrown out its elders sat down again and listened. Some churches went on reading the letter beside the Gospels for two hundred years; a few ancient manuscripts of the New Testament bind it in.

Of his death, nothing reliable is known. The stories that he was exiled to the Crimea, set to work in the marble quarries, and drowned with an anchor about his neck belong to a much later legend, and the anchor that appears beside him in art comes from that legend rather than from any early record. It is a small irony that a man who wrote so plainly about the danger of exalting oneself should have been given, centuries on, a martyrdom he probably did not have. The letter needs no embellishment. It is the sound of the church, in its second generation, discovering that the gospel would have to be lived out in the unglamorous work of keeping the peace, and choosing to do it.

Why he is worth reading

There is a particular comfort in Clement for anyone who has watched a church quarrel. He does not treat the Corinthian collapse as a scandal that disqualifies the gospel. He treats it as an illness with a known cause and a known cure, and he writes as a man who fully expects the cure to work. He assumes that ordinary Christians can be reasoned with from Scripture, that pride can be repented of, that a congregation which has behaved disgracefully can be spoken to with respect. Nothing in the letter is cynical.

His voice is also, quietly, the voice of a man who prays. The letter is stitched through with Old Testament quotation the way a life is stitched through with habit; he does not reach for the Scriptures to win an argument so much as think in them by reflex. And when he has finished arguing, he does not close with a flourish. He closes on his knees, praying for the sick and the imprisoned and the emperor who may well have been killing his friends. Whatever else is uncertain about Clement of Rome, the letter tells us what he did with his mornings.

Clement of Rome died around the end of the first century; reference works conventionally date him from about AD 35 to about AD 99, though neither end of that span rests on solid evidence and the dates beside his name here should be read as the tradition's best estimate rather than as record. He left one letter, one prayer, and a church at Corinth that stopped fighting.
