fields.name: Joe Church
fields.bio: Dr Joe E. Church (1899–1989) was an English CMS missionary doctor at Gahini Hospital in Rwanda whose two days of Bible study and prayer with the Ugandan layman Simeoni Nsibambi on Namirembe Hill in September 1929 are remembered as the spark of the East African Revival. He served in Africa for over three decades and always insisted the Revival was God’s work, not his own.
fields.bio_html:
Most of the East African Revival belongs to Africans — to the health worker who confessed his pride in front of the hospital, to the layman who preached in the street until people thought he had lost his mind, to the archbishop murdered for refusing to stay silent. Joe Church was none of these. He was an English doctor, a missionary of ordinary rank, sent out to run a hospital in a country that was not his own. What makes his name inseparable from the Revival is not that he led it — he always insisted he did not — but that on a discouraged holiday in 1929 he was asked a question he could not have invented, and had, by grace, the one answer the questioner needed.

A clergyman's son who chose medicine

John Edward Church — Joe to everyone — was born on 10 August 1899 in England, the son of an English country clergyman, Edward Joseph Church. He was sent away to junior school at St Lawrence College, Ramsgate, from the age of eleven, in the settled Edwardian way of the manse.

Then the century broke. He came of age into the First World War and served in the Tank Corps, commissioned a second lieutenant at nineteen — a boy officer in the newest and ugliest machine of that war. When it was over he went up to Emmanuel College, Cambridge, in 1919, on an army grant to study medicine, and there he fell in with the Cambridge Inter-Collegiate Christian Union, the earnest evangelical student body that has shaped generations of English Christians.

His conversion he dated precisely: 29 August 1920. It is worth noticing that a clergyman's son, raised inside the church and already at a Christian union, could still name a day on which the thing became his own. Church knew from his own life that being near the faith is not the same as being filled by it — a distinction that would become the whole burden of his ministry.

He trained at St Bartholomew's Hospital in London and qualified MD in 1926. He was a real doctor, competent and thorough, not a preacher who happened to carry a medical bag. On 28 October 1927 he sailed for Africa with the Church Missionary Society, under its Ruanda Mission, and after some five months of training at Kabale in Uganda he was posted across the border to Gahini, in Rwanda. He arrived to find the district in the grip of a serious famine — his first work in Africa was among the starving.

Namirembe Hill, September 1929

Two years in, Church was worn out and discouraged. The hospital was hard, the fruit was thin, and by his own account he was near the end of his strength. In September 1929 he took a short break in Kampala, staying on Namirembe Hill, where the great cathedral of the Church of Uganda stands. There, near the cathedral, he met a Ugandan layman named Simeoni Nsibambi.

Nsibambi was a man of standing and no small religious energy, and he was profoundly dissatisfied — not with the world, but with himself and with his church. He put to this tired English doctor a question that has echoed through the Revival ever since:

There is something missing in me and the Uganda church. Can you tell what it is?

— Simeoni Nsibambi to Joe Church, Namirembe Hill, 1929

Church did not have a programme to offer him. What he had was the Keswick teaching on holiness he had absorbed as a student — the filling of the Holy Spirit and what its preachers called the Victorious Life — and an open Bible. The two men stayed together for two days and did nothing but study and pray. They worked through the chain-references and notes of Church's Scofield Bible on the filling of the Spirit, tracing the theme from passage to passage, and they prayed. Nsibambi, convicted to the bone, prayed to quit all sin in faith.

Two men on a hill above Kampala — an exhausted foreign doctor and a Ugandan layman who would not be comforted — spent two whole days over one open Bible, following its promises about the Holy Spirit from page to page, until the African prayed to leave every known sin in faith. Neither of them knew they were lighting anything. They thought they were only praying for one man.

Church later wrote of that meeting with unmistakable gladness — of the great joy of telling Nsibambi about the filling of the Spirit and the Victorious Life. He went back to Gahini changed, and wrote home a sentence that turned out to be a prophecy of everything that followed:

There can be nothing to stop a real outpouring of the Holy Spirit in Rwanda now except our own lack of sanctification.

— Joe Church, writing home after the 1929 meeting

Nsibambi did not keep the two days to himself. Ashamed of his old religion and burning with the new, he began to preach in the open air on Namirembe Hill — on brokenness, on repentance, on renewal — until his neighbours thought him unbalanced. Historians of the movement call that meeting between the two men the official spark of the East African Revival. It is a strange thing to trace a fire that swept a continent back to two people praying quietly on their knees, but that is where it goes.

Gahini, and the fire that would not stay put

The centre of Church's own life was the hospital at Gahini, and it was there, and not on the platform of any great meeting, that the Revival is generally said to have originated when it broke out around 1933. In 1930 he had married Decima Tracey — Decie — on 19 May in Uganda; she was herself a trained doctor and worked beside him at Gahini, and they raised five children in that place. The Revival was, from the start, a thing of ordinary work: two doctors, a ward full of the sick, and the slow discovery that the gospel they preached had to be true of them first.

The turn at Gahini came through a hospital worker named Yosiya Kinuka, a dresser, the son of a chief from Ankole, proud and openly resistant to a message of repentance. He bitterly resented being called a Laodicean — lukewarm — and for a time he fought the whole thing. Then conviction found him. He confessed his nominal religion and his spiritual pride in public, was converted, and became one of the first of the evangelistic teams and Church's lifelong co-worker. That pattern — the proud man broken, naming his own specific sin out loud, in company — became the Revival's engine. It ran not on eloquence but on confession, restitution and reconciliation, from the conviction of sin to the reach of grace.

Others came. In 1931 Blasio Kigozi, Nsibambi's younger brother, joined Church at Gahini, and threw himself into the work with an intensity that seemed to know its time was short. He called the church to zukuka — to wake up — and then, on 26 January 1936, he died of tick fever, still a young man. A greater outbreak had already come at Kabale, in Uganda, in 1935, and from there conventions carried the movement outward across East Africa and, in time, to Europe, the Americas and India.

Through all of it the marching song of the Revival was a simple hymn of thanks, sung in Luganda wherever the balokole — the saved ones — gathered:

Tukutendereza Yesu — We praise you, Jesus; Jesus, Lamb of God, your blood cleanses me.

— “Tukutendereza Yesu,” the hymn of the East African Revival

Church would have been the first to say that none of this was his doing. He had brought a Scofield Bible, some Keswick teaching, and a willingness to be undone alongside the Africans he had come to serve. The rest came from somewhere else. If there was an answer to the prayer on Namirembe Hill, it was not a single miracle he could point to. It was the thing itself — the fire at Gahini, the changed life of a proud hospital dresser, the tens of thousands who would name their sins and find them washed.

The two men who prayed on the hill had asked, in effect, for one dry church and one dry man to be filled. What came was a revival that outran them both — Kinuka broken and remade, Nsibambi preaching in the streets, Gahini alight by 1933, and a hymn of thanks sung across East Africa. The honest answer to the 1929 prayer is not a wonder Joe Church worked. It is the Revival.

The long service, and the leaving

Church gave the greater part of his life to that hospital and that country. He served as physician to the king of Rwanda and was decorated by King Baudouin of Belgium — marks of a standing he never sought and rarely mentioned. He wrote, too, though always as a witness rather than an author: a life of Blasio Kigozi, Awake! An African Calling (1937); Forgive Them (1966), the story of the African martyr Yona Kanamuzeyi; and, late in life, his own account of the whole movement, Quest for the Highest (1981), drawn from the journals he had kept for half a century.

The end of his time in Africa was not gentle. In 1961 he left Rwanda amid the ethnic and political violence that was tearing the country apart — the same fractures that would harden into far worse. For a time he helped serve a hospital at Kabarole, in Uganda, before retiring around 1964. He finally left Africa altogether in 1972, during the Amin years, and settled at Little Shelford, near the Cambridge where he had first found his faith as a student. He died there on 29 September 1989, aged ninety.

What he leaves

Joe Church left a hospital, a shelf of modest books, and a movement that never bore his name because he would not let it. What he most clearly leaves is the shape of the 1929 meeting — the proof that the great things of God can begin very small and very low.

He was not a founder in the way ambition understands the word. He was a discouraged doctor on a borrowed holiday who happened to be carrying an open Bible and a teaching about the fullness of the Spirit, and who sat down for two days with an African brother who would not be put off. Out of that came a revival that changed the church across a whole region of the world. His own sentence remains the truest thing he said about it: that nothing could stop an outpouring of the Spirit except a lack of sanctification in those who prayed for it. He spent the rest of his life making sure the lack, at least, would not be his.

fields.name: Yosiya Kinuka
fields.bio: Yosiya Kinuka (c.1905–1981) was a hospital anaesthetist at Gahini in Rwanda who first led the medical staff’s resistance to Dr Joe Church, then — sent to Simeoni Nsibambi in 1931 — returned “an absolutely changed life” and became one of the earliest African leaders of the East African Revival. With Blasio Kigozi he formed the first Bible team around Gahini and stood at the heart of the 1933 convention often named as the Revival’s beginning.
fields.bio_html:
The East African Revival is usually told through its preachers and its martyrs — the men who stood in pulpits or died for what they said. Yosiya Kinuka was neither, at least not at first. He was a hospital assistant: a skilled anaesthetist, the senior African on the medical staff of a mission hospital, and for a while the ringleader of the staff's resistance to the very doctor whose name is now bound up with his. He is one of the earliest African leaders of the Revival, and he stands almost exactly at the point where it caught fire. But he came to that place not as a seeker but as an obstacle, and the story of how the obstacle became a hearth is the most useful thing about him.

A chief's son among the cattle-keepers

He was born around 1905 — the date comes from later summaries rather than any register, so it is best held loosely — into the Bahima, the cattle-keeping people of Ankole in western Uganda. He was a Muhima, the son of an Ankole chief, and by every account proud of that ancestry. It was a proud, self-possessed inheritance, not an obviously promising soil for a religion of brokenness and confession.

In 1928 he married Dorokasi, a woman from the Bufumbira country of Kigezi. Their marriage would outlast every upheaval that followed and their home would later be spoken of as a centre of witness — a model Christian household — but that lay years ahead, on the far side of a change neither of them yet knew was coming.

He was persuaded to join the medical team that Dr Joe Church — J. E. Church of the Ruanda Mission — was assembling for a new hospital at Gahini, across the border in Rwanda. Kinuka proved notably capable; he rose to be chief medical assistant, trusted above all with the delicate work of the anaesthetist, holding a patient's life steady on the table. He was said to have arrived unable to read or write and to have learned quickly, though that detail rests on a single telling and is better offered as something remembered than as fact. What is not in doubt is that he was good at the work, and that when he began he was neither a Christian nor interested in becoming one.

The doctor and the resister

Church wanted more from his staff than medicine. He insisted that the hospital's workers combine their medical duties with evangelism in the villages, and that they be paid on the same scale as the village evangelists rather than as salaried medical men. To a proud and able senior assistant this was both an insult and an imposition, and Kinuka led the staff's resistance to it. The relationship between the two men — employer and chief resister — soured into something close to a standoff.

It is worth staying with this, because it is the opposite of the shape we expect from a revival story. There is no earnest young man asking how to be saved. There is a competent professional digging in against his employer, and a missionary doctor at the end of his ideas about how to reach him. What broke the deadlock was not persuasion. Church, by his own later account, tried persuasion and failed.

Sent to Nsibambi, 1931

In January 1931, as he put it, "as a last resort," Church sent Kinuka up to Kampala to see Simeoni Nsibambi — the Muganda layman whose own hunger for holiness was already a quiet engine of the coming movement. It was not a soft errand, and Nsibambi did not make it one. He offered Kinuka no sympathy and took no side in the quarrel with the doctor. He told him, plainly, that the fault lay not with Church but with Kinuka's own unrepentant heart.

Kinuka's own words about that meeting survive only faintly, in a line remembered rather than recorded: that he had never before seen such a fervent Christian, and that they kept returning to the one subject — of being born again. It is a thin remnant, and it should be held as a memory of what he said rather than a transcript. But it points true. He went up a man defending his grievance and came down a man undone by it.

He returned to Gahini changed. The clearest testimony to it is not his own but the doctor's. Writing home on 5 May 1931, Church summed up in one sentence what had happened to the assistant he had all but given up on:

He has come back an absolutely changed life.

— J. E. Church, of Yosiya Kinuka, 5 May 1931

The tension between the two men turned to reconciliation. Exactly how that healing was enacted between them has grown, in some retellings, into a dramatic scene of mutual kneeling and confession; that scene is not independently verified, and it is enough to say what is certain — that a relationship which had been a standoff became a partnership, and that the mending of it was one of the first sparks of the Revival. What followed makes the outline unmistakable even where the detail is not.

Church, characteristically, put the change to work at once. He took to teaching the Bible by having Kinuka translate and explain what he was trying to say — and in the act of turning the doctor's words into his own language, Kinuka was first challenged and then converted more deeply still. The resister had become the interpreter.

His conversion did not come out of nowhere. Church and Blasio Kigozi had been praying for the African workers for a couple of years, asking for exactly what they could not manufacture. When it came, it came through the hardest man on the staff.

For two years Joe Church and Blasio Kigozi had prayed that the hospital's African workers might be given a living faith. The answer, when it came in 1931, was the last man they would have chosen to bet on — the anaesthetist who had led the resistance against them — sent away in near-defeat and returned, in Church's words, "an absolutely changed life."

The Gahini hearth

From that point Kinuka is at the centre of things. With Blasio Kigozi he formed the first Bible and evangelistic team around Gahini, and the mission station became a hearth from which the fire spread. He is named, from then on, in the same breath as the movement's best-known figures — William Nagenda, Festo Kivengere, Erica Sabiti, Simeoni Nsibambi, Kigozi himself.

At Christmastime in 1933, a convention at Gahini became the moment many later pointed to and said, simply, that the Revival had started. Confession broke out; men and women named their sins aloud and in company; forgiveness was asked and given; broken relationships were restored. The scene was corporate, not any one man's, and Kinuka should not be made its hero — but he was at the heart of the community in which it happened, one of the African leaders who had prepared the ground and who now stood inside the breaking-open.

The practice that surfaced at Gahini in 1933 — specific sin named out loud, in the hearing of others, and then forgiven — was the same medicine that had cured Kinuka himself two years before in a room in Kampala. What Nsibambi had done to one hard man was now happening to a whole convention at once.

Beyond Gahini

The Revival did not stay in the hills of Rwanda. In the mid-1940s Kinuka travelled with William Nagenda and Joe Church to Switzerland and Britain — the first of the movement's overseas tours, an African-led witness carried back into the churches that had sent the missionaries out. That the anaesthetist from Ankole should be standing before European congregations was itself a kind of sermon about who the gospel belongs to.

After the political upheaval that convulsed Rwanda in 1959, Kinuka and Dorokasi moved to Uganda, where he took charge of a camp for Rwandan refugees. He is widely described as having become a church leader in his later years; the specific clerical rank sometimes attached to his name is not confirmed, and it is honest to leave it simply at that — a leader among the saved, spending himself on the displaced. He died around 1981. The circumstances of his last years are sparsely recorded, and it is better to admit the silence than to fill it.

What he leaves

Kinuka left almost no words of his own — one shaky sentence, remembered secondhand, is very nearly the whole of it. What he leaves instead is a demonstration, acted out in his own life before he ever carried it to anyone else.

He is proof that the message of the Revival works on exactly the person least disposed to receive it. He did not come to Gahini hungry; he came proud, capable, and in open opposition to the man God would use to reach him. He was not talked round. He was sent, as a last resort, to be told the plain truth about his own heart — and the truth did what argument could not. The doctor's prayer was answered in the resister; the resister became the interpreter; and the interpreter stood at the hearth when the fire caught. For a movement that would insist, for decades, that the way forward is to name your own sin out loud and let it be forgiven, there could hardly be a truer first witness than the man who had to be broken of his objection before he could be entrusted with the message.

faq.q: Who was Yosiya Kinuka?
faq.a: Yosiya Kinuka (c.1905–1981) was a hospital anaesthetist at Gahini in Rwanda who first led the medical staff's resistance to Dr Joe Church, then — sent to Simeoni Nsibambi in 1931 — returned "an absolutely changed life" and became one of the earliest African leaders of the East African Revival. With Blasio Kigozi he formed the first Bible team around Gahini and stood at the heart of the 1933 convention often named as the Revival's beginning.

faq.q: What was his background?
faq.a: He was born around 1905 into the Bahima, the cattle-keeping people of Ankole in western Uganda — a Muhima, the son of an Ankole chief, and proud of that ancestry, which was not obviously promising soil for a religion of brokenness and confession. In 1928 he married Dorokasi, a woman from the Bufumbira country of Kigezi; their marriage would outlast every upheaval, and their home would later be spoken of as a model Christian household.

faq.q: How did he come to work at Gahini?
faq.a: He was persuaded to join the medical team Dr Joe Church was assembling for a new hospital at Gahini, across the border in Rwanda, and proved notably capable, rising to chief medical assistant, trusted with the delicate work of the anaesthetist — holding a patient's life steady on the table. When he began he was neither a Christian nor interested in becoming one; he was good at the work, and that was all.

faq.q: Why did he resist Joe Church?
faq.a: Church wanted more from his staff than medicine: he insisted the hospital's workers combine their medical duties with evangelism in the villages, and be paid on the same scale as village evangelists rather than as salaried medical men. To a proud and able senior assistant this was both insult and imposition, and Kinuka led the staff's resistance. The relationship soured into something close to a standoff — the opposite of the shape we expect from a revival story.

faq.q: What happened when he was sent to Nsibambi in 1931?
faq.a: In January 1931, as a last resort, Church sent Kinuka to Kampala to see Simeoni Nsibambi, whose own hunger for holiness was already a quiet engine of the coming movement. Nsibambi offered no sympathy and took no side in the quarrel with the doctor; he told Kinuka plainly that the fault lay not with Church but with his own unrepentant heart. He went up a man defending his grievance and came down a man undone by it.

faq.q: How did Joe Church describe the change?
faq.a: The clearest testimony is not Kinuka's own but the doctor's. Writing home on 5 May 1931, Church summed up in one sentence what had happened to the assistant he had all but given up on: "He has come back an absolutely changed life." The tension between the two men turned to reconciliation, and a relationship that had been a standoff became a partnership — one of the first sparks of the Revival.

faq.q: How did the resister become the interpreter?
faq.a: Church put the change to work at once, teaching the Bible by having Kinuka translate and explain what he was trying to say — and in the act of turning the doctor's words into his own language, Kinuka was challenged and converted more deeply still. His conversion had not come out of nowhere: Church and Blasio Kigozi had been praying for the African workers for a couple of years, and the answer came through the hardest man on the staff.

faq.q: What was his part in the 1933 convention at Gahini?
faq.a: With Blasio Kigozi he formed the first Bible and evangelistic team around Gahini, and the mission station became a hearth from which the fire spread. At Christmastime in 1933 a convention at Gahini became the moment many later pointed to and called the beginning of the Revival: confession broke out, men and women named their sins aloud and in company, forgiveness was asked and given, broken relationships restored. The medicine that had cured Kinuka in a room in Kampala was now curing a whole convention at once.

faq.q: Did his witness reach beyond Gahini?
faq.a: Yes. In the mid-1940s Kinuka travelled with William Nagenda and Joe Church to Switzerland and Britain — the first of the movement's overseas tours, an African-led witness carried back into the churches that had sent the missionaries out. That the anaesthetist from Ankole should stand before European congregations was itself a kind of sermon about who the gospel belongs to. After the upheaval of 1959 he and Dorokasi moved to Uganda, where he took charge of a camp for Rwandan refugees.

faq.q: What does his life demonstrate?
faq.a: That the message of the Revival works on exactly the person least disposed to receive it. He did not come to Gahini hungry; he came proud, capable, and in open opposition to the man God would use to reach him. He was not talked round — he was sent, as a last resort, to be told the plain truth about his own heart, and the truth did what argument could not. The doctor's prayer was answered in the resister, and the resister became the interpreter who stood at the hearth when the fire caught. He died around 1981.

fields.name: Blasio Kigozi
fields.bio: Blasio Kigozi (c.1909–1936) was a Ugandan schoolmaster and evangelist, younger brother of the revival co-founder Simeoni Nsibambi, who preached repentance across the villages around Gahini and died of tick fever in January 1936 while carrying his “Zukuka” (“Awake”) call to the Church of Uganda synod. Remembered as the “John the Baptist of the East African Revival,” he was buried at Namirembe beneath a tombstone bearing the single word “Zukuka.”
fields.bio_html:
One word is carved on his grave in the grounds of Namirembe Cathedral, and it is the same word he carried on his last journey to Kampala: Zukuka — Awake. Blasio Kigozi was not yet thirty when he died, a fever burning through him before he could stand and say the thing he had come to say. He wrote no books. Only a handful of his own words survive, and one of them is that single word. Yet those who came after him counted him among the first and most important figures of the East African Revival, and some called him its John the Baptist — the voice that went ahead, cried out that the church was asleep, and was gone almost before the thing he announced arrived.

A younger brother, converted through his elder

He was born a Muganda, in Uganda, around 1909; the exact date, his birthplace, and his parents' names have not come down to us with any certainty. What is well attested is the household he belonged to. His elder brother was Simeoni Nsibambi, the Kampala layman whom the revival's own people regarded as one of its founders — the man who, on a Kampala street, pressed the visiting missionary Joe Church with the question of what was still missing in his Christian life, and would not let it go.

Kigozi was converted in his youth, and he was converted through Nsibambi. This is worth dwelling on, because it is the whole shape of his life in miniature. He did not come to his faith through a foreign preacher or a dramatic meeting. It came to him across a family table, from an older brother who had been gripped himself. The revival was, before it was anything else, this: one person who had been changed refusing to leave the next person unchanged. Kigozi received it that way, and he would spend the rest of his short life passing it on the same way.

The schoolmaster who wanted to be an evangelist

He trained as a schoolmaster. Around 1929 he completed his studies at the teacher-training and theological school at Mukono, and then he was sent south, across the border into eastern Rwanda, to take charge of the network of schools around the mission station at Gahini. He was a teacher by trade and by discipline — not, as one careless telling has it, a barely-literate convert, but a man properly trained to stand in front of a class.

But teaching was not the whole of what burned in him. He carried a fierce desire to follow in the steps of Apolo Kivebulaya, the pioneer Muganda evangelist who had carried the gospel far into the forests to the west. Kigozi wanted that life — the road, the villages, the preaching. And at Gahini he found the setting that would let the teacher become the evangelist.

Around 1931 he joined Dr Joe Church at Gahini Hospital, and the two became close friends. They shared a particular kind of piety — one that would not settle for respectable, half-asleep religion, that insisted on repentance, on moral transformation, on sin named out loud and left behind. Kigozi preached that way for the rest of his life. He was uncompromising to the point of discomfort, denouncing sin wherever he found it, and he gave himself to years of ceaseless itineration, going from village to village on foot, one settlement after another, refusing to let the country sleep.

Two men praying, and the answer that came

Before there was a movement, there were two men praying. Kigozi and Joe Church began to pray together at Gahini for a deeper transformation among the African workers at the station — not for numbers, not for buildings, but for their own colleagues to be genuinely changed. They kept at it for a couple of years, and nothing much seemed to happen.

At Gahini, Kigozi and Joe Church prayed together — steadily, for a long time, and to no visible effect — that the African evangelists and hospital workers around them would be truly, deeply changed, and not merely employed by the mission.

Then in 1931 it happened. Yosiya Kinuka, a fellow worker at the station, underwent a dramatic conversion — a change so real and so public that it could not be explained away. Out of it grew the first small band of African evangelists who would carry the revival, the seed of the teams that soon spread it across the region.

After two years of that quiet, unrewarded praying, their colleague Yosiya Kinuka was suddenly and thoroughly converted in 1931 — the concrete answer that seeded the first African evangelistic team, and with it the movement itself.

It is a small enough episode to miss, but the shape of it matters. The revival did not begin with a strategy or a campaign. It began with two friends asking God, over and over, for one thing they could not manufacture — real change in the people right next to them — and then watching it arrive.

Ordained, and then the road again

In time Kigozi returned north to the theological college at Mukono. He was ordained deacon — the records disagree on the year, and there is no need to pretend to a precision they do not support — and then he went straight back to Gahini, this time to head the school for evangelists. It was exactly the work he was made for: not to sit in a study, but to form the men who would walk the roads he loved.

By 1933 the thing he and Church had prayed for was no longer a hope but a fire. At a convention at Gahini that year, Kigozi stood up to speak alongside his brother Nsibambi, and the accounts remember it as a turning point — the moment when, as the revival's own people put it, the fires began to blaze. The two brothers, the elder who had first been gripped and the younger he had gripped in turn, now stood together in front of a crowd, and the movement took hold.

Awake

By January 1936 Kigozi had one burden left, and it was for the church itself — not the villages this time, but the leadership. He had come to believe that the established Anglican church in Uganda was asleep: respectable, organised, and dead. And he resolved to say so to its face.

He travelled to Kampala to bring a message to the Synod of the church. Its substance can be given in the one word that became inseparable from his name: zukuka — awake. He meant to stand before the assembled leaders of the church and call them to shake off their apathy, to repent, to come alive. The full text of that message has not survived, and it would be a betrayal of the man to invent sentences for him; what is certain is the summons at its heart.

Zukuka! — Awake!

— Kigozi's rallying cry, and the single word later carved on his tombstone

He never delivered it. On his way to the synod he was struck down by tick fever — relapsing fever — and it moved fast. He was taken to the hospital at Mengo, and there, on 26 January 1936, he died. He was around twenty-seven years old. Those who told his story afterward remembered a cry of Awake, awake on his lips at the end; that belongs to tradition rather than to the record, and it is enough to say that the man who died with the word Awake attached to his name never got to shout it at the people he had come to wake.

The word on the grave

His sudden death, before the synod had even opened, did not silence the message. It sharpened it. A man who had crossed the country to tell the church to wake up had died at its door, and the leaders who might have shrugged off a living preacher could not shrug off a fresh grave. His call came to be regarded as prophetic. Within the next year or two, waves of revival swept through the Church of Uganda.

He was buried on Cathedral Hill, in the grounds of Namirembe Cathedral, before a great crowd, and his elder brother Nsibambi — the one who had first led him to Christ — officiated at the funeral. On the tombstone they cut a single word: Zukuka. Awake. It was the whole of his preaching, the whole of his last errand, and now the whole of his epitaph.

Zukuka

— the one word on Blasio Kigozi's grave at Namirembe

Those who weighed the revival afterward were not modest about him. One assessment named him the major founder and developer of the East African Revival in its first decade; others gave him the older, sharper title — the John the Baptist of the movement, the herald who prepares the way and then steps out of it. Both are the same judgement in different words: that a schoolmaster from Uganda who wanted only to walk the roads and preach spent himself so completely, and died so pointedly, that his one word outran his short life.

He is easy to overlook among the revival's louder names. He was not a bishop, not a martyr under a dictator, not the author of anything you can read. He was a younger brother who received his faith at home, a teacher who longed to be an evangelist, a friend who prayed for two unrewarded years before the answer came, and a preacher who died with his message still in his chest. What he leaves is that message, reduced to its irreducible core and set in stone: that the gravest danger to a church is not persecution but sleep, and that the only fitting response is to wake up.

fields.name: William Nagenda
fields.bio: William Nagenda (c.1912–1973) was a Ugandan lay evangelist and the most prominent preacher of the East African Revival. Expelled from theological college in 1941, he chose lifelong lay evangelism over ordination, carrying the revival’s message of brokenness at the Cross across Europe, the Americas, India and East Africa.
fields.bio_html:
The East African Revival threw up its share of bishops and archbishops, men who carried the fire into the highest offices their church could give. William Nagenda went the other way. He was training for ordination, and within a few years of the fire reaching him he was thrown out of the college that would have ordained him — and he decided that this was exactly right, that God was calling him and his friends not to holy orders but to the road. He never took a title, never held a parish, never wore a collar. He remained a layman to the end. And for a generation he was, by the reckoning of nearly everyone who watched the movement, its most prominent and dynamic preacher — the man of whom it was simply said, in convention after convention, that William was the leader.

A chief’s son on Namirembe hill

He was born around 1912 — the year is approximate; no one recorded the day — into a high-status Ganda family. His father, Festo Manyangenda, was a respected Muganda chief on Namirembe hill in Kampala, the very hill where the church’s power sat. It was a large family and a comfortable one, near the centre of things.

He was educated the way a chief’s son was: primary school in Kampala, then King’s College, Budo — the school that trained a generation of Uganda’s leadership — and a diploma at Makerere. He went into government clerical work. On paper he was a young man of Christian upbringing and secure prospects, well-schooled, well-connected, moving up.

And underneath the paper, something was wrong. He came through a genuine moral crisis in these years — a collapse serious enough that he lost his footing, and knew, when he was honest, that the religion he had been raised in was hollow in him. He had learned a great deal about Christ. Christ was not real to him. That is a harder thing to admit than open unbelief, because it comes dressed in respectability, and Nagenda later did not pretend it had been otherwise.

The reality behind the religion

The turn came around 1936, and it came through Simeoni Nsibambi — the Kampala layman whose insistence on the plain claims of the gospel was, more than any single thing, the human spark of the whole revival. Under Nsibambi’s influence the Christ Nagenda had studied so thoroughly stopped being a subject and became a person. The one about whom he had learned so much became, at last, real to him.

The change was total, and it drew him at once into the family and the fellowship of the movement. He married Sala, a daughter of Erasto Bakaluba of the Budo staff; the marriage tied him by blood into the revival’s inner circle, for he became the brother-in-law both of Nsibambi and of the late Blasio Kigozi, the young evangelist whose death in 1936 had shaken the church awake. Nagenda went to Gahini, the mission station just over the border in Rwanda where Joe and Decie Church, Yosiya and Dorokasi Kinuka worked, and where the fire had been burning for several years. He had been a teacher there, and when Kigozi died he was reckoned to have inherited his brother-in-law’s mantle as leader of the revival at Gahini. He and Sala joined the team.

The morning that made the movement

What held that team together was not organisation. It was a habit, and the habit was prayer at dawn. At Gahini the team met early in the mornings for prayer and fellowship, and Nagenda carried that rhythm with him for the rest of his life. It was the engine under everything else he did — the ordinary, unglamorous means by which the fire was kept and passed on.

Before the day began, they met — a small company gathered early in the morning for prayer and for fellowship, confessing to one another whatever the light had shown them since the last time they met. This was the whole method: not a technique, not a programme, but the same few people meeting again at dawn to bring themselves, out loud and in company, back to the Cross. Nagenda kept this pattern to the end of his life.

Out of those meetings came the sound that every reader of the revival’s story eventually hears — the Luganda hymn sung at the opening and close of every gathering, the anthem of the balokole, the saved ones.

Tukutendereza Yesu — we praise you, Jesus; Jesus, Lamb of God, your blood cleanses me; I thank you, Saviour.

— “Tukutendereza Yesu,” the song of the East African Revival

Mukono, 1941

Around 1940 Nagenda entered Mukono — Bishop Tucker Theological College — to train for ordination. If the story had run the ordinary way, he would have come out a priest, as so many of the revival’s leaders did.

It did not run the ordinary way. At Mukono he again gathered a company for the dawn — a group of some forty students who met early in the mornings for prayer and fellowship, as he had at Gahini. Their revival zeal made the staff uneasy. Nagenda insisted, in a colonial church, on the plain racial equality of every soul before the Cross, which was heard as insolence. He and the others criticised what they saw as the missionaries’ liberal theology. And in 1941 the reckoning came: Nagenda and some twenty-eight of his fellow students were expelled.

It would have been natural to read that as a disaster — the door to ministry slammed on the movement’s most gifted young preacher. Nagenda read it as a calling. He became convinced that God was directing his group not toward ordained ministry at all, but toward lay evangelism — that the road, not the pulpit, was their appointment. He did not spend the rest of his life resenting the collar he never wore. He chose against it, deliberately, and stayed a layman for good.

A Christian tea-planter named Lea Wilson gave the expelled students refuge at Namutamba, and the plantation there became Nagenda’s base for the rest of his life — the home ground of a free evangelist. From that ordinary place, with no office and no title, he went out.

A free evangelist to three continents

What followed is one of the more remarkable itineraries in the century’s Christian history, and a layman ran it. In 1946 and 1947 Nagenda was invited to Britain, and to Switzerland, together with the Reverend Yosiya Kinuka and Dr Joe Church — among the very first East Africans to travel to the United Kingdom to bring the gospel rather than receive it. It did not stop there. For some eighteen years, most often in Joe Church’s company, he carried the same message across an astonishing spread of countries — Switzerland, France and Germany; Malawi; Angola and India; the United States and Israel; Brazil. The chief’s son from Namirembe hill preached on three continents.

Those who heard him tried to describe the effect and reached, oddly, for opposite words. There was great energy in him, and yet a quiet sincerity; a penetrating, almost surgical spiritual analysis that could lay a listener bare, delivered in preaching that was gentle. He did not storm. He saw through people, kindly, and told them what he saw. The friend who knew him best summed the whole man up in the title of a small book he wrote about him.

A Great Lover of Jesus.

— J. E. Church, of William Nagenda

The Cross, again and again

Nagenda’s preaching carried a definite theology, and part of its importance is a thing he refused. From about 1944 he decisively rejected the “second blessing” teaching — the idea of a single later crisis that lifts a believer onto a higher, settled plane. He would not have it. What he preached instead was a continual return to the Cross: salvation in the blood of Jesus, a strict moral discipline, and above all brokenness — the daily walking in the light through the constant confession of sin, one believer honest with another.

He set this squarely against okufuba, the striving after holiness by effort and rule-keeping. The Christian life, as he preached it, was not a ladder you climbed and a height you held; it was a place you kept coming back to, low and in company, at the foot of the Cross where the blood still cleansed. It is why the dawn fellowship mattered so much to him. Walking in the light was not a private transaction. It was something you did with other people, out loud, in the morning, before the day could make liars of you.

He asked for no miracle, and the record hands us none — no sudden healing, no wonder tied to his name. The answer to a life spent bringing people back to the Cross was quieter and larger than that: a movement he was reckoned to lead, and confessed, changed lives left behind in country after country across Europe, the Americas, India and his own East Africa. The fruit was the people.

What he leaves

From about 1964 the signs of illness came — by one account Parkinson’s, though the record here is thin — and his last years were spent partly in Oxford. He died in 1973, some sixty years old, a layman still.

He left few of his own words; no famous saying can be safely put in his mouth. What he left is the shape of a life, and it argues two things the church is slow to learn. The first is that the door being shut is not the same as the call being cancelled. Nagenda was thrown out of the college that would have made him a minister, and treated the expulsion as the moment his real appointment became clear. He did not need the office. He needed the road, and he took it.

The second is that a layman with no title, working from a tea plantation, can carry more weight in a church than most of its officers. For a generation William Nagenda was the leading preacher of the largest spiritual awakening East Africa has known, and he did it all without ordination, standing every morning where he told everyone else to stand — broken, in the light, at the foot of the Cross, singing that the blood of Jesus cleanses. He was not a bishop and not a martyr. He was a great lover of Jesus, and he spent himself getting other people to love him too.

It was the engine under everything else: not a technique or a programme, but the same few people meeting again at dawn to bring themselves, out loud and in company, back to the Cross.

faq.q: Why was he expelled from Mukono in 1941?
faq.a: Around 1940 he entered Bishop Tucker Theological College at Mukono to train for ordination, and again gathered a company of some forty students for dawn prayer and fellowship. Their revival zeal made the staff uneasy; he insisted, in a colonial church, on the plain racial equality of every soul before the Cross, which was heard as insolence, and criticised what they saw as the missionaries' liberal theology. In 1941 he and some twenty-eight fellow students were expelled.

faq.q: How did he respond to the expulsion?
faq.a: He read it not as a disaster but as a calling. He became convinced that God was directing his group not toward ordained ministry at all but toward lay evangelism — that the road, not the pulpit, was their appointment — and he chose against the collar deliberately, staying a layman for good. A Christian tea-planter gave the expelled students refuge at Namutamba, and the plantation there became Nagenda's base for the rest of his life, the home ground of a free evangelist.

faq.q: What was his ministry abroad?
faq.a: One of the more remarkable itineraries in the century's Christian history, run by a layman. In 1946 and 1947 he was invited to Britain and Switzerland with Yosiya Kinuka and Joe Church — among the very first East Africans to travel to the UK to bring the gospel rather than receive it. For some eighteen years, most often in Church's company, he carried the same message across Switzerland, France and Germany, Malawi, Angola and India, the United States and Israel, and Brazil.

faq.q: What did people say of his preaching?
faq.a: Those who heard him reached for opposite words: great energy, and yet a quiet sincerity; a penetrating, almost surgical spiritual analysis that could lay a listener bare, delivered in preaching that was gentle. He did not storm — he saw through people, kindly, and told them what he saw. The friend who knew him best, Joe Church, summed the whole man up in the title of a small book about him: "A Great Lover of Jesus."

What he preached instead was a continual return to the Cross: salvation in the blood of Jesus, a strict moral discipline, and above all brokenness — daily walking in the light through the constant confession of sin, one believer honest with another, set against okufuba, the striving after holiness by effort and rule-keeping.

faq.q: What does his life argue?
faq.a: Two things the church is slow to learn. The first is that the door being shut is not the same as the call being cancelled: thrown out of the college that would have made him a minister, he treated the expulsion as the moment his real appointment became clear. The second is that a layman with no title, working from a tea plantation, can carry more weight in a church than most of its officers. He died in 1973, a layman still — a great lover of Jesus who spent himself getting other people to love him too.

fields.name: Yona Kanamuzeyi
fields.bio: Yona Kanamuzeyi (died 1964) was a Rwandan Anglican deacon of the East African Revival who sheltered Tutsi refugees during the violence of the early 1960s. Arrested by soldiers on the night of 23 January 1964 and led away to be shot, he wrote “We are going to heaven” in his diary and sang a hymn as he walked to his death; his name was later inscribed in the roll of modern martyrs at St Paul’s Cathedral, London.
fields.bio_html:
Some of the East African Revival's most remembered figures left books, or led churches, or preached to crowds. Yona Kanamuzeyi left a diary, six children, a wife named Mary, and one sentence written on the last night of his life. He was a deacon in a small place, doing small and dangerous work, when soldiers came for him in the dark. What survives of him is thin, and much of what is repeated about his death cannot be verified. But the core is solid, and it is enough: a man who, being led out to be shot, sang.

A child of two peoples

We do not know when Yona Kanamuzeyi was born. No reliable record fixes the year, or the place, and it would be a disservice to him to invent one. He belonged to the generation of Rwandans who came up in the first decades of the twentieth century, in the years when the Revival that began at Gahini and Kabale was spreading through the hills of Rwanda and Uganda and out across East Africa.

He was the child of a mixed marriage — one parent Hutu, one Tutsi — and was himself generally reckoned a Tutsi. That single fact, an accident of birth he did not choose, would later mark him for death. In the Rwanda of the early 1960s, as the colonial order collapsed and violence broke along the Hutu–Tutsi fault line, a man's parentage could be turned into a sentence. Yona's straddled both sides of the line that was being drawn in blood.

He became an Anglican deacon. Popular retellings sometimes promote him to "Reverend" or "pastor," and there is no great harm in the loose word, but the sources are consistent: he was a deacon, serving at Nyamata, south of Kigali, in the Maranyundo area. A deacon is an ordained servant of the church — the office is defined by service, by the practical care of people in need — and Yona's ministry ran true to the name.

Formed in the Revival

Yona is remembered as a protégé of Blasio Kigozi, one of the pioneers of the East African Revival — which places him squarely in the stream the Revival called the balokole, the "saved ones." To understand him at all, you have to understand that movement, because he had no life apart from it.

The Revival was not a program. It was a recovery of a few plain things the church had let go slack: that sin must be named out loud and specifically, not smoothed over; that a Christian walks in the light with others, hiding nothing; that the cross is the whole of one's standing before God; and that this is cause for enormous, unembarrassed joy. Its people wept and confessed and then sang. Their anthem, "Tukutendereza Yesu" — "We praise you, Jesus" — followed a simple Luganda refrain that could be carried from one country to the next:

Tukutendereza Yesu — We praise you, Jesus; Jesus, Lamb of God, your blood cleanses me.

— "Tukutendereza Yesu," the hymn of the East African Revival

Blasio Kigozi, whose spiritual son Yona was reckoned to be, had prayed for the awakening of a church he found asleep, and died young of relapsing fever in 1936 with the single word Zukuka — "Awake" — associated with his last witness. A movement formed by such men did not treat death as the great catastrophe to be avoided at any cost. It treated a clean conscience and a living hope as worth more than staying alive. Yona was made in that school, and when his own turn came he behaved exactly like a man who had learned its lessons.

The work that made him a target

In the early 1960s the fighting between Hutu and Tutsi sent streams of refugees across the hills, fleeing the violence with whatever they could carry. Yona was asked to help them. He did.

This is the hinge of his whole story, and it is worth sitting with rather than rushing past. He did not die for a doctrine he refused to recant, or for preaching in a forbidden square. He died because he sheltered frightened people. Giving sanctuary to Tutsi refugees marked him, in the eyes of armed men, as a "Tutsi sympathizer" — and a man who could be helped was a man on the wrong side. His crime was mercy shown to the hunted. There is an old pattern here, running back through the whole history of the church: the deacon whose office is the care of the poor and the endangered, and who is destroyed precisely for doing that office faithfully. Yona's refugee work was not a departure from his ministry. It was his ministry, and it cost him his life.

The night of 23 January 1964

The heart of what we know comes down to a single night in January 1964 — the 23rd, though some accounts say the 24th or 25th. Five soldiers came after dark in a jeep and took him away "for questioning." Two other prisoners were held with him.

As he was taken, Yona did two things that tell you who he was. He grabbed the church keys — the deacon still, minding what had been entrusted to him. And he grabbed his diary. In it, that night, he wrote a line that has outlived everything else about him:

"We are going to heaven." — written in his diary on the night of his death. He turned to the two men held with him and asked them about their salvation; and together they sang, "There is a happy land, far, far away."

Consider what that diary entry is. It is not a cry for rescue. It is not a protest of innocence, though he was innocent. It is a statement of destination, written by a man who had every reason to believe he was hours from being killed and who had decided, on the evidence of the gospel he had staked his life on, where he was actually going. He did not write "they are going to kill us." He wrote "we are going to heaven" — and the "we" reached out to include the frightened men beside him, whom he was still, in his last hours, trying to bring along.

We are going to heaven.

— Yona Kanamuzeyi, written in his diary on the night of his death

Then he sang. The hymn on his lips was a children's hymn, "There is a happy land, far, far away," and there is something almost unbearable in the plainness of it — a grown man walking toward his execution with a song a child would know. The soldiers came back amazed that he had sung as he walked toward death. That is the one detail of their reaction that the record vouches for, and it needs no help. Hardened men, sent to do a hard thing, could not get over the fact that the condemned man was singing.

He was taken into the bush. Gunfire was heard. Minutes later the two other prisoners were released. According to the accounts that survive, he was led to a bridge over the Nyabarongo river and shot, and his body was put into the water; the accounts differ about who exactly did the killing, and it would be wrong to pretend to a certainty the sources do not have. Some of the more dramatic scenes attached to his death in later retellings — a final prayer at the river, a soldier converted on the spot — cannot be confirmed, and honesty forbids repeating them as fact. What is attested is quieter and, in its way, harder to shrug off: he sang, and the men who killed him were amazed.

The story did not end in silence

A martyr's "answer to prayer" is rarely a rescue. Yona was not spared. But two things happened that kept his witness from vanishing into the bush with his body.

The two men imprisoned with him were released alive, minutes after the shots — witnesses carried out of the dark. And the diary, with its line "We are going to heaven," made its way back to his wife, Mary. The last word of a man killed in secret did not stay secret.

Those are the honest providences: not a miracle that undid his death, but the small mercies that let his death speak. Mary was left a widow with six children — among them a son later known as John Wesley Kanamuzeyi Gara — and the cost of his faithfulness fell on them, as it always does on the families of the killed. But the diary survived, and so the sentence survived, and so we have it still.

His name was later inscribed in the book of modern martyrs at St Paul's Cathedral in London, entered there by the Dean — a Rwandan deacon set among the church's remembered dead across the whole world. No fixed feast-day marks him, and no confirmed portrait of his face has been found. He is remembered chiefly for the manner of one night: the keys and the diary snatched up together, the question put to his fellow prisoners, the children's hymn sung down a dark road, and one written line that turned an execution into a testimony.

Yona Kanamuzeyi gave his life for people who were not his own people, and met his death singing that he was going home. The Revival taught that the worst the world can do is not the last word. In him, in the plainest possible terms, that claim was put to the test — and a man walked toward the guns, and sang.

fields.name: Janani Luwum
fields.bio: Janani Luwum (c.1922–1977) rose from a herdsboy in northern Uganda to Archbishop of the Church of Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Boga-Zaire. Converted in the East African Revival in 1948, he preached fearlessly and, after leading the bishops’ protest against Idi Amin’s killings, was murdered on 17 February 1977. He is honoured as one of the ten twentieth-century martyrs whose statues stand over the Great West Door of Westminster Abbey.
fields.bio_html:
The East African Revival gave the church a great many quiet people — health officers, teachers, catechists, men and women who confessed their sins in the open and sang the same short song for fifty years. It gave the church a few martyrs too. Janani Luwum was both. He began as a herdsboy in the far north of Uganda and ended as the Archbishop of the whole province, shot dead in a locked room for telling a tyrant the truth. Between the two ends lies a single unbroken line: a schoolteacher who was converted one January morning and never afterward stopped preaching, whatever it cost, and in the end it cost him everything.

A herdsboy from Mucwini

He was born about 1922 at Mucwini, in East Acholi, in the north of Uganda — a long way from the kingdoms and the cathedral cities where the church kept its power. No exact date survives; the year itself is only approximate, as it is for a great many people born in that place and time. His father was a Christian convert, one of the first in the district, which meant Janani was raised inside the faith rather than reaching it as a stranger. As a boy he herded the family’s cattle, goats and sheep, the ordinary apprenticeship of an Acholi childhood.

He was clever, and school carried him up out of the cattle paths. He went to Gulu High School and then to Boroboro Teacher Training College, and became a schoolteacher — a respectable position, a settled future. By his mid-twenties he had a trade, a wife named Mary, and a young daughter. By every ordinary measure he had arrived. What had not yet happened was the thing that would define everything else.

The morning of 6 January 1948

The Revival had been moving through East Africa for more than a decade — out of Rwanda and the mission station at Gahini, up through Uganda, carried by laymen who stood up in ordinary meetings and named their own sins aloud. Its people were called the balokole, the saved ones, and its song was a single Luganda chorus of thanksgiving for the blood of Christ, sung until it wore grooves in the memory of a whole generation.

Tukutendereza Yesu — We praise you, Jesus; Jesus, Lamb of God, your blood cleanses me. I am satisfied in you.

— “Tukutendereza Yesu,” the chorus of the East African Revival

On 6 January 1948 the fire reached Janani Luwum in his own village, while he was still a young schoolteacher. He was converted. It is the defining spiritual event of his life, and everything the rest of the biography records grows from it. There was nothing gradual about what followed. He became an evangelist at once, preaching against drink and tobacco, carrying the plain, uncomfortable, joyful message of the balokole into the villages around him. A man who had been going to be a teacher for the rest of his life had instead been arrested by God, and he never got over it.

The conversion of January 1948 was not a private comfort but a commission. From that morning Luwum preached — first against the small idols of drink and tobacco, then against the great ones — and the clear conscience “before God” that he would one day claim in front of a murderer was already being formed in a village schoolteacher who had simply been told the truth and could not keep it to himself.

Within a year the direction of his life had changed for good. He entered Buwalasi Theological College in January 1949, leaving his wife Mary and their young daughter at home when he first went. He was made a catechist in 1950, returned to train for ordination in 1953, and was ordained deacon on 21 December 1955 — St Thomas’s Day, the feast of the disciple who wanted to see the wounds before he would believe. He was ordained priest the following year.

From the north to the archbishop’s chair

What followed was two decades of steady ascent, though ascent was never the point. In 1966 he became Provincial Secretary of the Church of Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Boga-Zaire — administrative work, the unglamorous machinery of a large church. On 25 January 1969 he was consecrated Bishop of Northern Uganda. It is worth noting who came to that consecration: both Prime Minister Milton Obote and the army chief, Idi Amin, were present. The two men who would between them shape the horror of the next decade both watched the herdsboy from Mucwini become a bishop.

In 1974 the House of Bishops elected him Archbishop of the whole province, succeeding Erica Sabiti, the first African to have held the office. Luwum was the second. He was closely bound to his fellow Revival leader Bishop Festo Kivengere, and the two of them carried into the highest offices of the church the same brokenness and openness they had learned as young men in the meetings. He led as one of the balokole led — plainly, without pomp, and without the instinct to protect himself that high office usually breeds.

That instinct, or its absence, was about to be tested against Idi Amin.

Telling the truth to a tyrant

By the mid-1970s Amin’s Uganda had become a country of disappearances. People were taken in the night and did not return; bodies turned up in rivers and forests. Luwum did not stay silent, and he did not stop meeting the President — a decision that drew criticism from Christians who thought a churchman should keep his distance from a butcher. His answer to them is the fullest surviving statement of how he understood his own position:

I do not know for how long I shall be occupying this chair. I live as though there will be no tomorrow. I face daily being picked up by the soldiers. While the opportunity is there, I preach the gospel with all my might, and my conscience is clear before God that I have not sided with the present government, which is utterly self-seeking. I have been threatened many times. Whenever I have the opportunity I have told the President the things the churches disapprove of. God is my witness.

— Janani Luwum, answering those who questioned his willingness to keep meeting Amin

It reads like the same schoolteacher who could not keep the good news to himself in 1948 — only now the message was rebuke, and the audience was a man who killed the people who displeased him. In early February 1977 security forces raided the archbishop’s residence, claiming to search for weapons. Undeterred, Luwum and the House of Bishops — some eighteen of them — sent an open letter of protest to President Amin in the middle of that month, against the arbitrary killings and disappearances. It was as direct an act of defiance as any churchman in Africa had made.

The answer came quickly. On 16 February 1977 Amin convened a rally in Kampala. “Suspects” were paraded to read out confessions accusing Luwum of being an agent of the exiled Obote, plotting a coup, smuggling arms. Soldiers demanded his execution on the spot. The other bishops were dismissed; the archbishop was held back to see Amin privately. As he was led away, he spoke to Festo Kivengere, who never forgot it.

They are going to kill me. I am not afraid.

— Janani Luwum to Bishop Festo Kivengere, at the rally, 16 February 1977

He was arrested with two of Amin’s own cabinet ministers, Erinayo Oryema and Charles Oboth-Ofumbi. His last words to his fellow bishops, well remembered afterward, were not of fear but of a strange and settled sight:

I can see the hand of the Lord in this.

— Janani Luwum, his final words to his fellow bishops

By 17 February all three men were dead. Radio Uganda announced that they had been killed in a car crash while trying to overpower their driver and escape. It was a lie. When the body was released it was riddled with bullets; Amin’s own Minister of Health, Henry Kyemba, later wrote in A State of Blood that the archbishop “had been shot through the mouth and [had] at least three bullets in the chest.” He was buried near St Paul’s Church at Mucwini, in the ground he had come from.

Those who have kept his memory tell that under interrogation he answered only by praying the Lord’s Prayer, over and over, and that he died praying for the men who killed him. No eyewitness left a verbatim record of such a prayer, and it is repeated as devotion rather than documented as fact — but it is the shape the church instinctively gave to a death it recognised, the shape of the One who prayed for his executioners from the cross.

The witness that outlived the tyrant

There was no rescue. For a martyr the honest answer to prayer is rarely a miracle of deliverance; it is the composure with which the death is met, and the way the witness refuses to die when the man does. Luwum had said he was not afraid, and he was not; he had said he could see the hand of the Lord, and he went to meet it. On 30 March 1977 a memorial service was held for him in Westminster Abbey — a herdsboy from Mucwini honoured under the vaults of England’s coronation church.

Amin fell two years after the man he murdered. Luwum did not. In 1998 his statue was raised over the Great West Door of Westminster Abbey, one of ten twentieth-century martyrs — beside Martin Luther King Jr, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Óscar Romero. The Anglican Communion keeps his day on 17 February; Uganda keeps 16 February as a national holiday in his name. The tyrant sought to make him disappear, as so many had disappeared, and instead made him permanent.

He had once said, simply, that he was prepared to die in the army of Jesus. The Uganda he left behind eventually found room even for reconciliation: in 2019, on the forty-second anniversary, his family and Idi Amin’s kin met in public to make peace — the Revival’s oldest instinct, sin named and forgiveness offered, working its slow way through a nation’s memory.

I am prepared to die in the army of Jesus.

— Janani Luwum

He was a soldier of that army from a January morning in 1948 until a February morning in 1977, and the line between the two never bent. A herdsboy who was told the truth and could not stop telling it; a bishop who kept meeting a murderer so that he could keep rebuking him; a man who saw the hand of the Lord in his own arrest and was not afraid. The chair he sat in he never expected to hold for long. The gospel he preached with all his might is holding still.

fields.name: Lawrence Barham
fields.bio: Lawrence Barham was a British Anglican clergyman and CMS Ruanda Mission missionary who, turned away from China, sailed to central Africa in 1928 and gave his life to Kigezi and Burundi. A front-rank European figure of the East African Revival, he founded the Kabale Bible school that became Bishop Barham University College; his closeness to the Revival cost him a bishopric in 1946, which he finally received in 1964.
fields.bio_html:
Most of the East African Revival's famous names are African, and rightly so — it was an African awakening, carried by African men and women who confessed their sins to one another and sang in the open air. But a handful of Europeans stood inside it rather than above it, and the difference is worth noticing. They did not run the thing from a mission compound; they went into the villages with the teams, took the same road, and let the fire touch them too. Lawrence Barham was one of these. He was an English clergyman who came out to Africa meaning to go somewhere else entirely, spent the rest of his working life in the hills of Kigezi and Burundi, founded the school that still carries his name, and was passed over for a bishop's office for eighteen years precisely because he had thrown in his lot with a revival his superiors did not trust.

A door that closed toward China

He was born in the early twentieth century, an Englishman raised in the Anglican church, and his exact dates are not securely on record. What is clear is where his life turned. In 1926 he offered himself to the Church Missionary Society for China — the great missionary destination of that generation, the field every keen young volunteer dreamed of. China was closing to foreign missionaries just as he applied, and the door he had chosen shut in front of him.

He did not go home. He offered himself instead to the Ruanda Mission, a small and unfashionable CMS venture in the hills between the Belgian and British territories of central Africa, and in 1928 he sailed. That same year he married Julia, née Leakey, who went out with him and shared the work for the whole of it. Their son Kenneth was born in 1936 and would himself become a bishop in Rwanda decades later — the mission became a family calling.

It is worth pausing on the shape of that beginning. Barham did not get the field he wanted. He got the one that was left, and gave it everything. A great deal of the most durable missionary work of the century was done by people whose first plan fell through.

Kabale, and a school that would bear his name

He landed at Kabale, in Kigezi, the far south-west corner of Uganda, and was put straight to work. He was made headmaster of Kigezi High School and given charge of the church's work across the district. But the labour that outlasted everything else was quieter than a headmastership. Barham started a Bible school at Kabale to train African clergy and church-teachers — men who would carry the gospel into their own hills in their own language, which is the only way it ever truly travels.

That small Bible school grew. It became the Bishop Barham Theological College, and it is today the Bishop Barham University College at Kabale, a constituent college of Uganda Christian University. His name is on the gate of an institution that has trained clergy for the best part of a century. He did not set out to build a monument; he set out to train pastors, and the monument followed.

In 1938 Lawrence and Julia moved on to Buye, in Burundi, where he did the same thing again — founding the theological college first known as Canon Warner Theological College, to train clergy and teachers for the mission's churches across Burundi, Rwanda and Kigezi. Wherever the church needed roots, Barham's instinct was the same: raise up local men to lead it, and build them a place to be taught.

Standing inside the fire

By the time the Barhams reached Kabale, the East African Revival was beginning to stir out of the mission station at Gahini in Rwanda, where the doctor Joe Church and his African co-workers were praying and confessing together. From 1931, Barham was among the front rank of those who organised the teaching teams that carried it — named in the same breath as Joe Church, Simeon Nsibambi, Blasio Kigozi, Yosiya Kinuka and Kosiya Shalita, and working hand in hand with his Ugandan colleague Ezekieri Balaba. These men would gather a band of speakers and travel to a convention, and something would break open.

The seminal one in his own district came because he and Ezekieri asked for it. They sent an invitation to Gahini for a team to come to Kabale, and out of that came the Kabale Convention of September 1935 — one of the great outpourings of the revival, remembered ever after. Barham wrote about the year that followed in the mission's quarterly, Ruanda Notes, and his own words survive:

This year has ended up as one of the most blessed in the history of Kigezi. Largely as a result of the convention led by Dr J. Church and a band of men and women from Gahini.

— Lawrence Barham, in Ruanda Notes

What is striking about Barham in these accounts is that he never writes as a manager reporting results. He writes as a man watching something he did not control and would not have dared to invent. When a gardener came under conviction and returned money he had stolen, Barham reached for the only category that fit:

This is not emotionalism… it's stern conviction of the Holy Spirit and it fills us with awe.

— Lawrence Barham, in Ruanda Notes

A gardener, quietly convicted, gave back money he had taken. No preacher stood over him; no meeting worked him up. Barham, who had prayed for this awakening and sent for the team that sparked it, called the restitution what it was — the Holy Spirit's own work — and confessed himself filled with awe. The honest answer to the mission's prayers was not a miracle of healing but a thief giving back what was not his.

The car-load of helpers

A revival is easy to celebrate and hard to shepherd. New converts — the keenites, as they were half-affectionately called — needed teaching, correction, and steadying, or their zeal would run into error and burn out. Barham's letters show him doing exactly this unglamorous follow-up work, Sunday after Sunday, with Ezekieri at his side:

Ezekieri and I with a car-load of helpers have therefore been going out for the last few Sundays to various centres of revival… In between services, we collected a little band of keenites, and after hearing their experiences, were able to point out to them from the Bible, dangers to avoid, as well as encouragements to their faith.

— Lawrence Barham, in Ruanda Notes

Week after week the car went out, full of helpers, to the scattered centres where the fire had fallen. They listened first — heard each young believer's own experience — and only then opened the Bible, to warn of the dangers and to strengthen the faith. This is the labour that never makes the headline of a revival: the patient, weekly work of keeping new life alive.

His steadiness showed most when others wanted to pull back. As the movement spread and grew disorderly, Ezekieri Balaba once told him that things were going rather strangely and they had better keep out of it. Barham would not:

No, we hadn't. We'd better go in it because if these things go wrong the government will clamp down and put these people in prison. We must go around and try to sort it out.

— Lawrence Barham, recalling Ezekieri Balaba

That is a missionary who has decided to be responsible for the people the revival produced, not merely to admire them from a safe distance. He would go in, precisely because it was risky, so that the risk would fall on him rather than on them.

The office that was withheld

His identification with the revival cost him. In 1946 Barham was nominated to be Bishop of Ruanda-Urundi. He was the obvious man — a founder of colleges, a leader of the movement, deep in the life of the church he served. The appointment was blocked by the Bishop of Uganda, because Barham was too closely bound up with the revival, which the Church of Uganda's leadership then regarded with real apprehension. The very thing that made him the right man made him, in their eyes, the wrong one.

He did not leave, and he did not sulk his way through the following years. He kept teaching, kept writing, and for a stretch from the late 1950s served the Ruanda Mission from Britain as its general secretary. The office he had been denied in 1946 came to him only eighteen years later. In 1964, when Jim Brazier retired, Barham was at last consecrated the second Bishop of Rwanda and Burundi — and given the specific, thankless task of preparing the diocese to be divided into two. He served just two years, to 1966, laying down the office almost as soon as he had received it.

Eighteen years is a long time to wait for a chair that half the church did not want you to have, and then to sit in it only long enough to plan its own partition. There is no record of Barham complaining. He had come out in 1928 for a field that was not his first choice, and he gave the rest of his working life to it whether or not it ever rewarded him. The bishopric, when it finally came, changed none of that. The work had already been the ministry.

What he leaves

Lawrence Barham wrote no famous book. What survives of his own voice is a scatter of letters and reports in a mission quarterly, and it is enough to show the man: awed rather than triumphant, patient rather than dramatic, willing to go into the difficult thing so that others would not carry it alone.

He leaves two things that outlasted him. One is a college at Kabale that still bears his name and still trains the pastors he cared most about raising up. The other is a pattern — of a European who did not stand over an African revival but stepped inside it, took the same road, honoured the men beside him, and let it convict and awe him like anyone else. He was passed over for high office for nearly two decades because he had loved that movement too openly, and he counted the movement worth more than the office. When the office finally came, he used it to hand the work on and stepped down.

Not every faithful life is crowned in its own lifetime. Barham's field was chosen for him by a door that closed, his best office was withheld from him by men who feared his friends, and his one verdict on the fruit of it all was that it filled him with awe. That is the honest measure of him — a man who wanted China, was given Kigezi, and gave Kigezi everything he had.
