fields.name: Christmas Evans
fields.bio: Christmas Evans (1766–1838) was the greatest of the Welsh preachers — a poor, self-taught farm laborer, blinded in one eye by an assault in his youth, who became known as the “Bunyan of Wales.” For more than thirty years he oversaw the scattered Baptist churches of Anglesey on a stipend of £17 a year, preaching to thousands in vivid, dramatic open-air sermons. His ministry was revived after a famous covenant with God below Cadair Idris.
fields.tagline: Self-taught farm labourer who became the greatest of the Welsh preachers, the “Bunyan of Wales.”
fields.bio_html:
Christmas Evans was born on Christmas Day, the 25th of December, 1766, in a low thatched cottage at Esgair-wen, near Llandysul in Cardiganshire, Wales. The day gave him his name. It gave him almost nothing else. His parents, Samuel and Joanna Evans, were poor — his father a shoemaker — and when Christmas was nine years old his father died, and the boy was passed to the keeping of an uncle who worked him hard and taught him nothing. He grew up a farm servant, moved from place to place, exposed to rough company and rougher habits, and at seventeen he still could not read a single word, in Welsh or in English. Few lives that God would one day fill to overflowing began so empty.

The filling began in a revival. Somewhere about his seventeenth year the young laborer was drawn into the congregation of David Davies, a Presbyterian minister at Llwynrhydowen, and there, under plain and searching preaching, he was converted. Hungry now to read the Book that had wakened him, he learned his letters as a grown youth, borrowing what light and what pages he could, and made such astonishing progress that within a year or two he was reading Welsh and English and reaching after more. A single eye did all this labor. For while he was still young, a band of youths who bore him a grudge set upon him on the road at night and beat him until he lay senseless; one of them struck him a blow on the left eye that destroyed its sight for the rest of his life. Wales would come to know him as "the one-eyed preacher," and the scarred, half-blind face became one of the most loved in the land.

He never stopped teaching himself, and the wonder of it grew with the years. Books were scarce and dear, and Evans gathered his learning piecemeal, late, and against every disadvantage, yet he pressed at last into the original languages of Scripture. "I was about forty years old," he wrote, "when I learned to read the Hebrew Bible and the Greek Testament, and use Parkhurst's Lexicons in both languages." What he took in he gave out again in the one tongue his hearers loved; the pulpit, never the study, was where all his learning caught fire.

He could not keep the gospel to himself. Coming to Baptist convictions, he was baptized and began to preach, and after early labors in the wild peninsula of Lleyn he crossed, in 1791, to the island of Anglesey. There he settled for more than thirty years as the overseer of its scattered Baptist churches — a bishop in all but stipend, for the pay was a pittance and the roads were long, and he walked or rode them in every weather to preach. It was here that his extraordinary gift came to its height. He preached in the open air to thousands, in the surging, singing cadence the Welsh call the hwyl, and he preached in pictures: whole sermons built as one unfolding scene. His most famous, The Fall and Recovery of Man, tells the entire gospel as a single drama of ruin and rescue, and it earned him a title he has never lost — the Bunyan of Wales.

The secret of it, all who heard him agreed, was an imagination of rare power harnessed wholly to the truth. He did not decorate his sermons with images; he thought in them, until doctrine became landscape and the hearer found himself standing inside the scene. Under such preaching whole congregations were, in the words of his own journals, melted down in tenderness — weeping and crying out together, so that one might suppose the entire assembly, male and female, was dissolved by the gospel, as the word of God became to them "a sharp two-edged sword."

But the gift did not exempt him from the winter of the soul. In the early years of the new century a bitter controversy — the cold, hair-splitting spirit its opponents called Sandemanianism — crept into the Welsh churches and into Evans himself. His congregations were divided and thinned; worse, his own heart went dead. He described the season in a single unforgettable phrase: he was "as dry as Gilboa," barren in the pulpit, in the study, and in secret prayer. For a man whose whole power lay in a burning heart, it was a kind of death.

The thaw came on a lonely mountain road, and it came through prayer. Riding from Dolgelley toward Machynlleth and climbing up toward the great peak of Cadair Idris, Evans judged that he ought to pray, however hard and worldly he felt — and he began, in the name of Jesus, without waiting to feel better first.

Climbing toward Cadair Idris with a cold and reluctant heart, he resolved to pray anyway, "however hard I felt my heart, and however worldly the frame of my spirit was." He spent hours on that ascent in secret wrestling with God — weeping, pleading, and naming his churches one by one — until the numbness broke.

What happened on that ascent he never forgot, and it is his own account, from his journal, that gives the scene its power: the fetters loosening, the hardness softening, the very mountains of frost and snow melting within him.

Having begun in the name of Jesus, I soon felt as it were the fetters loosening, and the old hardness of heart softening, and, as I thought, mountains of frost and snow dissolving and melting within me.

— Christmas Evans

He came down from Cadair Idris a thawed man, and there and then he bound himself to God in a solemn written covenant — thirteen articles, each signed with his initials, giving himself, soul and body, to Christ and pleading for his churches. The first of them set the tone of all the rest.

I give my soul and body unto thee, Jesus, the true God, and everlasting life — deliver me from sin, and from eternal death, and bring me into life everlasting.

— Christmas Evans, from his covenant with God

The prayer on the mountain was answered, in his own words, as "a remarkable refreshing from the presence of the Lord." The deadness lifted and the old fire returned, and the awakening he had begged for came down on the churches of Anglesey: within two years his ten preaching stations on the island had grown to twenty, and some six hundred converts were added to the churches under his care.

The later road was not smooth. His wife Catherine, who had shared the poverty and the endless journeys, died in 1823; he married again in his later years. Troubles and misunderstandings at last drew him away from Anglesey, and the aging preacher — who might have been left to rest — took up new charges instead: at Caerphilly, then at Cardiff, and finally at Caernarvon, still preaching, still traveling, still renewing his covenant with God upon his knees. He had entered the ministry with nothing, and he left it with little; but the churches he had watered were many, and the Welsh nation had taken his sermons into its very memory.

Through it all he remained a poor man, and a humble one. His salary on Anglesey was seventeen pounds a year, and for twenty years he never asked for more, having learned with the apostle that "having food and raiment" a servant of Christ may therewith be content. Yet the little he had he gave away — the sight of want, it was said, always opened his purse — and those who had wronged him found him quick to forgive. Cheerful, self-forgetful, and tender toward every kind of distress, he wore his greatness so lightly that a stranger meeting the shabby, one-eyed traveler on a mountain road would never have guessed he had passed the most powerful preacher in Wales.

In the summer of 1838 he was on a preaching tour in South Wales, an old man of seventy-one, when his last illness overtook him at Swansea. Death held no terror for the one-eyed preacher who had so long proclaimed a risen Christ. At the end he repeated a Welsh verse of trust in his Redeemer, and then, as though the journey were merely changing horses, spoke his last words in English.

Good-bye! Drive on!

— Christmas Evans, his last words, 19 July 1838

With that he turned over as if to sleep, and was gone. He was buried at Swansea. He had come into the world with a pauper's portion and no letters at all, and he went out of it as the greatest preacher Wales had produced — a man whose one eye had seen, and had made a whole people see, the glory of the crucified and risen Lord. Long after his death the Welsh still spoke of his sermons as of scenes they had witnessed rather than words they had heard, and they gathered and translated them so that readers who never knew the hwyl might feel a little of its heat. Those printed sermons remain, and in them the mountain-road fire still burns.

fields.name: Monica of Hippo
fields.bio: Monica of Hippo (c.331–387) was the mother of Augustine, remembered as the great example of a praying mother. For some seventeen years she wept and prayed for her wayward son’s conversion; a bishop assured her that “the son of these tears shall not perish,” and she lived to see him baptized before she died at Ostia.
fields.bio_html:
Almost everything we know about Monica comes from a book her son wrote about God. Augustine’s Confessions, composed a decade after her death, is a long prayer of self-accusation and praise, and inside it stands the fullest portrait of a mother the ancient church has left us. That is worth saying plainly at the start: we see her through the eyes of the boy she wept over, in a book written to glorify not her but the God who answered her. It is a devotional portrait, drawn by a witness who loved her. But it is a portrait from life, and the woman in it is unmistakable — patient past reason, stubborn in prayer, and finally so satisfied that she no longer wished to live.

A wife in Thagaste

She was born around 331 in Thagaste, a small town in Roman North Africa — today Souk Ahras in Algeria — into a devout Christian household of some means. Her name is Berber, and she belonged to a Christian family in a province where the faith was old and deep-rooted. She was raised, Augustine remembered, less by her mother than by an elderly family servant who had carried the household’s children on her back, and who taught the girls to master their thirst and their tongues.

She was married young to Patricius, a pagan town councillor of Thagaste. He was a man of some standing and a difficult husband — hot-tempered and unfaithful. Monica bore all of it with a patience that became famous among the wives of the town. She did not quarrel with him, and when other women showed the marks of their husbands’ anger and asked how she escaped, she told them the fault was often in their own answering tongues. She waited on his temper the way one waits out weather. And over the long years she won him — not by argument but by the steadiness of her life — so that he was baptised a Christian near the end of his life. She and Patricius had at least three children: Augustine, born in 354; a second son, Navigius; and a daughter, of whom Augustine tells us little and whom he does not name.

The years of tears

It was the eldest who broke her heart. Sent away to Carthage to study rhetoric, Augustine fell into the fashionable religion of the Manichees and into a way of living his mother could only grieve over. He took a concubine and fathered a son. He argued for a faith she believed was ruin. For a time she would not have him at her table or under her roof, so sharp was her horror at what he had become — and then, softened by a dream, she took him back and set his place again.

The dream is one Augustine never forgot. Early in her grief, he tells us, she saw herself standing on a wooden measuring-rule, weeping, when a radiant young man came and asked why she wept. She said she was mourning her son’s perdition. He told her to look — and there on the same rule, at her side, stood Augustine. She held to that vision for years as a pledge that where she stood, he would one day stand.

What she did between the dream and its fulfilment was pray. Not once, not in seasons, but as the settled work of her days. Augustine, looking back, could hardly find the bottom of it:

That chaste, pious, and sober widow desisted not, at all the hours of her supplications, to bewail my case unto You.

— Augustine, Confessions III

Nine years she prayed while he was a Manichee; counting from his first straying to the day he was baptised, her intercession ran something like seventeen years. There is no way to make those years sound bearable. They were not a story yet — they were a mother going to God every day about a son who was getting worse, with nothing to show for it but a schoolboy’s dream and her own refusal to stop.

For the better part of two decades Monica wept and prayed for a son who argued against the faith, lived against it, and slipped away from her by night to sail for Rome while she watched at the shore. Her tears looked wasted the whole time. She kept shedding them at every hour of her prayers, because she had heard once, in a dream, that God had already answered — and she believed the answer more than she believed the years.

The son of these tears

At some point in the long grief she went to a certain bishop, himself a former Manichee, and begged him to sit down with Augustine and reason him out of his errors. The bishop refused. Her son, he said, was not yet teachable — he was too pleased with the novelty of the heresy — but he would come round in time; let him alone and pray. Monica would not let it go, and pressed him with tears to intervene. Worn down by her insistence, the bishop gave her the answer she carried for the rest of her life:

Go your way, and God bless you, for it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish.

— a bishop to Monica, Confessions III

Augustine records that she took the words as if they had sounded from heaven. They were only a tired man’s attempt to send a persistent woman home; she received them as a promise from God, and she was right.

Her love was not gentle in the passive sense — it followed. When Augustine determined to leave Africa for Rome and would not take her, he lied to her: he told her he was only seeing a friend to the ship, and while she prayed through the night in a chapel by the shore, he sailed without her. She woke to find him gone. She did not accept the loss. She followed him across the sea, and when his road led on to Milan, she came to Milan too.

There she found a teacher she could give herself to. Ambrose was bishop of Milan, and Monica loved and obeyed him, sitting under his preaching and bending her old African customs to his counsel. Ambrose, for his part, used to tell Augustine how blessed he was in such a mother. Neither of them yet knew how near the end of her waiting was.

The garden and the font

In the summer of 386, in a garden in Milan, the thing she had prayed for happened. Augustine — torn, weeping, unable to give himself wholly to God — heard a child’s voice over a wall chanting take up and read, opened the letters of Paul, and read the sentence that ended his long resistance. He went straight indoors to tell his mother. She had prayed for his soul without ceasing for the better part of his life; now he told her it was done. Augustine writes that she was filled with triumph and blessed God, who is able to do far more than we ask or think.

At Easter of 387, in Milan, Ambrose baptised Augustine. The son Monica had mourned as lost stood in the water a Christian. The dream on the wooden rule had come true to the letter: where she stood, he stood beside her.

Seventeen years of tears were answered in a Milan garden and an Easter font. The son who had argued for heresy and lived against the faith was converted in 386 and baptised in 387 — so completely that his mother, who had begged God for nothing else for half his life, found she had nothing left to ask. The promise she had clung to, that the son of these tears could not perish, had exceeded everything she prayed.

The window at Ostia

They set out for Africa together. Resting at Ostia, the port of Rome, mother and son stood one day leaning at a window that looked over a garden, and fell into a conversation that climbed, as they talked, from the things of earth toward the life of God — reaching, for a moment, past everything they could name. When it was over Monica spoke words Augustine set down almost as she said them: that there was one thing only for which she had wished to linger in this life, that she might see him a Catholic Christian before she died.

My God has exceeded this abundantly, so that I see you withal, despising earthly felicity, made His servant. What do I here?

— Monica at Ostia, Confessions IX

Within about five days she fell into a fever. She had once wished to be buried in Africa beside Patricius, and had spoken of it often; now she let it go entirely. When her sons wondered aloud whether it would not grieve her to die so far from her own city, she gave them the answer of a woman who had finished her business with the world:

Lay this body anywhere; let not the care for it any way disquiet you. This only I ask, that you will remember me at the Lord’s altar, wherever you be.

— Monica, Confessions IX

Nothing, she said, is far from God; she did not fear that at the world’s end He would not know the place from which to raise her. On the ninth day of her sickness she died, in the fifty-sixth year of her age and the thirty-third of her son’s.

What she leaves

She wrote nothing. She founded nothing. She held no office the church could name. What she left is a demonstration that has outlived nearly every institution of her century: that the prayer of a faithful mother is not wasted, however long it goes unanswered, and that God can be trusted with the years in between.

The church came to remember her as the patron of mothers and wives, of hard marriages, and above all of everyone praying for a child who has wandered off and will not come home. A Spanish expedition, centuries later and half a world away, is said to have named a set of springs on the California coast Las Lágrimas de Santa Mónica — the Tears of Saint Monica — and the city of Santa Monica keeps her name to this day. It is a fitting accident. She is remembered by her tears because her tears were the truest thing about her, and because she was right to keep shedding them. The son she wept over became the greatest teacher the Western church has known, and he laid the whole of it at her feet — a mother who would not stop asking, for a God who does more than we ask.

Almost everything we know of her comes from Augustine's Confessions — a portrait drawn from life by the boy she wept over, in a book written to glorify not her but God.

faq.a: Born around 331 in Thagaste in Roman North Africa into a devout Christian household, she was married young to Patricius, a pagan town councillor — a man of some standing and a difficult husband, hot-tempered and unfaithful. Monica bore it with a patience that became famous among the wives of the town; she did not quarrel with him, and told women who showed the marks of their husbands' anger that the fault was often in their own answering tongues. Over the years she won him, and he was baptised near the end of his life.

fields.name: Teresa of Ávila
fields.bio: Teresa of Ávila (1515–1582) was a Spanish Carmelite nun, mystic and reformer who taught that prayer is “an intimate sharing between friends.” She founded the reformed Discalced Carmelites, wrote The Interior Castle, and in 1970 became the first woman named a Doctor of the Church.
fields.bio_html:
Teresa of Ávila is remembered now as a mystic, a saint whose visions were carved into marble by Bernini and whose books are read five centuries after her death. It is worth beginning, then, with the least mystical fact about her: for roughly twenty years she was a nun who could barely pray. She kept the hours, she wore the habit, she was inside the machine of religious life — and by her own account she spent most of those two decades restless, distracted, and half-hearted before God. The woman the Church would one day name its first female Doctor spent her first twenty years in the cloister as an ordinary, struggling, unremarkable religious. That is not a footnote to her holiness. It is the road into it.

A daughter of Ávila

She was born Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada on 28 March 1515, in the walled Castilian city of Ávila. Her family was prosperous but carried a shadow the age did not forgive lightly: her paternal grandfather was a Jew who had converted to Christianity and been reconciled by the Toledo Inquisition in 1485. Teresa was, in the language of the time, of converso descent — a background that meant her family's standing was never quite secure in a Spain obsessed with purity of blood. She grew up bright, sociable, and fond of the world, by turns devout and vain.

Her mother, Beatriz, died when Teresa was about thirteen. The girl, grieving, went to an image of the Virgin and asked her to be a mother in her place — the first act of a life that would keep turning grief and longing into prayer. A few years later her father placed her, for a time, in a convent school; and slowly, against her own resistance and her father's initial opposition, she came to believe she was called to religious life.

In 1535 she entered the Carmelite Monastery of the Incarnation in Ávila, and she professed her vows in 1537. What followed was not a straight ascent. She fell gravely ill, so ill she was once thought dead and a grave was readied for her. She recovered, but her health was broken for life, and her prayer went slack. The Incarnation was a large, comfortable, half-worldly house where nuns received visitors and kept private property, and Teresa — charming, well-liked, easily distracted — drifted with it. She would later be unsparing about those years, blaming no one but herself for a prayer life she called mediocre and mostly abandoned.

The wounded Christ

The turn, when it came, came late and came suddenly. Around 1554, nearly forty years old and nearly twenty years a nun, Teresa passed a statue that had been brought into the convent — an Ecce Homo, an image of Christ scourged and wounded before his death. She stopped. Something in the sight of that suffering broke her open. She threw herself on the ground before it in tears and begged God to strengthen her once and for all. Around the same time she read Augustine's Confessions — one restless soul recognising itself in another — and found there the words for what was happening to her.

This is the hinge of her life. Everything the world now associates with Teresa — the visions, the reform, the books — comes after it, and none of it comes before. The mystic was born not out of natural piety but out of a woman finally surrendering, at forty, after twenty wasted years, in front of a broken image of Christ.

Kneeling before the wounded Christ, nearly forty and worn out with her own half-heartedness, Teresa threw herself down in tears and asked God to strengthen her once and for all, so that she would not offend him again. She dated the real beginning of her prayer from that day.

Prayer as friendship

Out of that surrender came the teaching for which she is loved. Teresa did not think of prayer as performance, or as a technique for the spiritually gifted. She thought of it as a relationship — plain, personal, and available to anyone willing to give it time. Her definition of mental prayer, written in the eighth chapter of her Life, is the most quoted sentence she ever wrote, and it is disarmingly simple:

Mental prayer, in my opinion, is nothing else than an intimate sharing between friends; it means taking time frequently to be alone with him who we know loves us.

— Teresa of Ávila, The Book of Her Life

Everything else in her spiritual writing is an unfolding of that line. In the Life she compared the growth of prayer to watering a garden four ways: hauling water from a well by hand, which is laborious beginner's prayer; turning a water-wheel, which is easier; letting a stream run through, easier still; and at last the rain, which asks nothing of the gardener and is given wholly by God. Years later, in The Interior Castle, she pictured the soul as a castle of clear crystal with seven sets of rooms, and the life of prayer as a journey inward through them toward the innermost chamber where God dwells. She wrote for her own nuns, in a warm, direct, sometimes teasing voice, always insisting that this friendship with God was not reserved for the extraordinary.

The fire and the spear

Teresa's mystical experiences were vivid, and she reported them as plainly as she reported everything else. The most famous, which she describes in the twenty-ninth chapter of her Life and which is usually dated to around 1559, she gives entirely as her own testimony — and it is right to receive it that way, as what she said happened to her. She saw beside her, she wrote, an angel in bodily form, small and beautiful, its face aflame. In its hands was a long golden spear tipped with fire, and it thrust the spear again and again into her heart, piercing to her very entrails. The pain, she said, was so great that she moaned aloud; yet it was so sweet that she could not wish to be rid of it, and it left her all on fire with a great love of God.

It is this scene that Bernini later froze in marble in Rome. Teresa herself would have been wary of the attention; she distrusted spiritual experiences that a soul went looking for, and always turned her nuns back from raptures toward the ordinary, hidden work of love and obedience. The fire in the heart, for her, was never the point. The friendship was.

Barefoot, and on the road

A woman that alive to God could not stay content in a lax and comfortable house. Teresa became convinced that the Carmelite life needed to return to its roots — small communities, strictly enclosed, living in real poverty, at prayer. In 1562 she founded the first reformed convent, St Joseph's in Ávila, consecrated on 24 August. The nuns there owned nothing, took no endowment, wore coarse habits and sandals of rope and straw. From those bare feet came the name that stuck: the Discalced, the "unshod," Carmelites.

The opposition was immediate and fierce. The city authorities of Ávila took her to law, alarmed at an unendowed convent with no visible means of support. Churchmen were uneasy about a woman who taught mental prayer so boldly, in an age when the Inquisition watched such things closely and a nun's inner life could be treated as dangerous. Teresa met all of it with a combination the record keeps insisting on: she was a genuine contemplative and a shrewd, funny, indefatigable organiser. Over the next twenty years, in poor health and over bad Castilian roads, she founded convent after convent across Spain.

In 1567, at Medina del Campo, she met a young friar, small and intense, who wanted to carry the same reform to the men of the order. His name was John of the Cross, and he would become one of the greatest poets and mystics of the Christian tradition in his own right. Together they launched the reform among the friars, whose first house opened at Duruelo in 1568. It was a costly partnership. From around 1575 a bitter jurisdictional war broke out between the Discalced and the older Calced ("shod") Carmelites; John was seized and imprisoned by his opponents; Teresa was, for a time, confined and silenced. Only in 1580 were the Discalced finally recognised as a separate province, and the reform secured.

Through it all she carried a small piece of paper, found after her death in her breviary in her own hand — a few lines that hold the whole temper of a life lived under illness, suspicion, lawsuits and the road:

Let nothing disturb you, let nothing frighten you; all things are passing; God never changes. Patience obtains all things. Whoever has God lacks nothing; God alone suffices.

— Teresa of Ávila, the "Nada te turbe" found in her breviary

For two decades she prayed and worked to give the Carmelites back their poverty and their silence, against lawsuits, imprisonment, and the fear of the Inquisition. She did not live to see the outcome tidy, but in 1580 the reformed houses were recognised as their own province — the work of her latter life made permanent, and still living today.

What she left, and one word she did not say

Teresa died on the night of 4–15 October 1582 at Alba de Tormes, worn out by a last journey. The dates are not a misprint: she died on the very night the Gregorian calendar took effect, when 4 October was followed directly by 15 October, which is why her feast falls on the fifteenth. She left behind a reformed order, a scattering of small poor convents, and four books that have never gone out of print — The Book of Her Life, The Way of Perfection, The Interior Castle, and The Book of the Foundations. She was canonised in 1622. On 27 September 1970, Paul VI named her a Doctor of the Church — the first woman ever so honoured, a week before the same title was given to Catherine of Siena.

One caution belongs in any honest account of her. A much-loved prayer that begins "Christ has no body now but yours, no hands, no feet on earth but yours" is very often printed under her name. It is not hers. It is a later composition, from the nineteenth or twentieth century, and however lovely it is, attaching it to Teresa is a mistake. Her real words stand on their own and need no borrowing.

What she actually leaves is smaller and stronger than any single quotable prayer. She leaves the witness of a woman who was, for twenty years, exactly the sort of tired, distracted, half-serious believer most of us recognise — and who was met, late, in front of a wounded Christ, and became one of the great friends of God. Her whole teaching can be folded back into the one sentence she gave us: that prayer is nothing more, and nothing less, than taking time to be alone with him who we know loves us. She was almost forty before she believed it. She spent the rest of her life proving it was true.

fields.name: Corrie ten Boom
fields.bio: Corrie ten Boom (1892–1983) was a Dutch watchmaker who, with her family, hid Jews from the Nazis in a secret room in their Haarlem home. Arrested and imprisoned in Ravensbrück, where her sister Betsie died, she survived to travel the world for decades preaching God’s forgiveness — even to a former guard of the camp.
fields.tagline: Dutch watchmaker who hid Jews from the Nazis, survived Ravensbrück, and preached forgiveness.
fields.bio_html:
Above a watch shop in the old centre of Haarlem there was a false wall, and behind it a space barely large enough for a few people to stand. It was built into the top-floor bedroom of a woman in her fifties who had never married, who mended clocks for a living, and who had spent her whole life in the same narrow house. When the war reached her door, Corrie ten Boom turned that house into a refuge, lost most of her family for it, survived a place designed to kill her, and came out the other side to spend the rest of her life telling people about forgiveness. She is one of the few in this library who is remembered less for what she wrote than for one thing she did with her hand, years after the war, in a church basement in Munich.

The Beje

Cornelia ten Boom was born on 15 April 1892 in Amsterdam, and grew up in Haarlem, where the family kept a watch shop and a home together in one building. They called it the Beje, after the street it stood on, the Barteljorisstraat. Her father, Casper, was a watchmaker, devout and gentle, of the Dutch Reformed faith; her sister Betsie was her lifelong companion. It was an ordinary, believing, unremarkable household, the kind that produces no headlines for fifty years and then, tested, produces everything.

Corrie learned her father's trade and, in the 1920s (1924, by the museum's record), became the first licensed woman watchmaker in the Netherlands. For most of her life that is the whole story — a single woman, a family shop, church, and the slow work of small mechanisms. She was nearly fifty when the thing happened that the world now knows her for, which is worth remembering for anyone who suspects their real life has not yet started.

The hiding place

Germany occupied the Netherlands in May 1940. As the persecution of Dutch Jews tightened, the ten Booms were drawn into the underground, and their house — old, central, full of odd corners — became a link in a chain that moved Jews and resistance workers to safety. A secret room was built behind a false wall in Corrie's own bedroom on the top floor. The museum that keeps the house today reckons that the family and their network helped save an estimated eight hundred people, most of them sheltered not in the Beje itself but at safe addresses elsewhere. It is an estimate, from those who were there; the point is not the exact number but that each was a person, placed one at a time, at the risk of every life in the house.

On 28 February 1944 the family was betrayed by a Dutch informant. The house was raided and around thirty people were arrested that day, Corrie and Betsie and their elderly father among them. The soldiers never found the secret room. The six people hidden behind the wall, four Jews and two resistance workers, stayed there, silent, for two and a half days, until sympathetic policemen let them out. The hiding place held; the people who built it did not. Nor did all of those it sheltered survive the war: Mary van Itallie, one of the Jewish guests, was arrested again within days at a new address and died at Auschwitz on 1 May 1944, while Meijer Mossel, the cantor the household called Eusie, lived to see the liberation.

Casper ten Boom, who was in his eighties, died about ten days after the arrest. Corrie and Betsie were moved through prison at Scheveningen and the camp at Vught, and then east, into Germany, to the women's concentration camp at Ravensbrück.

Ravensbrück, and Betsie

What happened at Ravensbrück is the heart of Corrie's witness, and almost none of it is about her own courage. It is about her sister. Betsie ten Boom, frail and sick, met that place with a faith that unsettled everyone around her, including Corrie. She insisted that God was not absent from the barracks, that He could be thanked even there, and that they had been brought to this exact hell for a reason — to learn something they would one day have to tell.

Corrie recounts in The Hiding Place (1971) that their overcrowded barracks was infested with fleas, and that Betsie thanked God for them too. Only later did they understand why: the guards would not enter the flea-ridden block, and so the two sisters were left alone to read the Bible aloud to the other women, freely, in a place where such a thing should have been impossible.

Betsie insisted on giving thanks in the barracks for everything, even the fleas — and Corrie, who could not see the sense of it, gave thanks anyway. The guards, as she tells it, avoided the infested block. In the one corner of that camp the guards would not enter, two sisters read Scripture to the condemned.

Corrie also recounts a small bottle of liquid vitamins that she was somehow able to keep, from which she gave a drop each day to Betsie and then to more and more of the sick women around them — and which, she said, went on yielding drops far past the point it should have run dry, until a fresh supply reached them. Betsie compared it to the widow of Zarephath's jar of oil, in the days of Elijah, that did not fail. Corrie tells the story as her own memory, already in her first account of the camps, written in 1945; it belongs to her account of that place, and it is offered here as she offered it.

Betsie died at Ravensbrück on 16 December 1944. Before she died she had told Corrie, again and again, that they must go out afterward and tell people what they had learned there — that there is no darkness so deep that God is not deeper. It is the line most closely associated with the two sisters, and it was Betsie's:

There is no pit so deep that He is not deeper still.

— Betsie ten Boom, as recounted by Corrie in The Hiding Place

Days later, at the very end of December 1944, Corrie was released, for reasons never fully explained. Her first account, written in 1945, suggests the sisters had expected a fixed prison term to run out; years later she was told it had been a clerical error, and in The Hiding Place she recounts that the women of her age were sent to their deaths soon after she left. Whatever the cause, within weeks the camp began gassing the sick and the old. She never claimed to have earned her survival or to fully understand it. She had gone in with a sister and a family; she came out alone, carrying an instruction from a dead woman.

A tramp for the Lord

Corrie kept the instruction. For roughly the next thirty-three years, into her eighties, she travelled — more than sixty countries — as an itinerant speaker with almost no fixed home, calling herself a tramp for the Lord. Her message was not chiefly about the horror she had survived. It was about forgiveness, reconciliation, and the stubborn nearness of God's love in the worst places human beings can make. She had earned the right to say it in the only way such a right is earned.

Then, early in those travels, in 1947, in a church in Munich, the message was put to her directly, as she recounts it.

She had just spoken to a German congregation about God's forgiveness. Afterward a man came forward, beaming, his hand out — and she recognised him. He had been a guard at Ravensbrück, one of the men in the processing room where the sisters, Betsie among them, had been made to file past, naked, under his gaze. He did not recognise her. He told her he had since become a Christian, that he knew God had forgiven him for what he had done there, and he asked whether she, too, would forgive him. And he stood there with his hand held out.

She could not take it. She stood frozen, and the anger rose in her — the memory of Betsie, of that room, of all of it. She knew what her faith required, and she found she did not have it. So she prayed the only prayer she could manage.

Standing before the former guard with his hand out, unable to lift her own, Corrie prayed in silence something close to this: Jesus, I cannot forgive him. Give me Your forgiveness. She had preached forgiveness across Europe, and at the one moment it was demanded of her, she had none of her own to give.

Then, she recounts, she took his hand — woodenly, as an act of the will and not of feeling — and as she did, something moved through her arm and into their joined hands that she knew was not hers. A current of love, she called it, so strong it nearly overwhelmed her. She had willed the deed with a cold heart, and the warmth had been supplied from somewhere else. It is the truth she spent the rest of her life pressing on people, and she stated it plainly:

Forgiveness is an act of the will, and the will can function regardless of the temperature of the heart.

— Corrie ten Boom, Tramp for the Lord

The love she asked for was given the instant she obeyed without it. This is the answer she testified to for the rest of her life: not that God removed her anger and then let her forgive, but that she forgave first, in the will alone, and the feeling followed from Him. The prayer of a woman who had nothing left to give was answered in her own outstretched hand.

What she leaves

In 1967 Yad Vashem recognised Corrie ten Boom as one of the Righteous Among the Nations, for the family's work in hiding Jews. In 1971 she told the whole story in The Hiding Place, written with John and Elizabeth Sherrill and carrying a preface by Billy Graham; a film followed in 1975. The book made a Dutch watchmaker and her dead sister known around the world.

She died in Placentia, California, on 15 April 1983 — her ninety-first birthday, the same date on which she had been born. In her tradition there was an old belief that only specially blessed people die on their birthday, and whether or not that means anything, the neatness of it is hard to ignore: the life closed on the day it opened, a full circle drawn around ninety-one years.

What she leaves is not a system or a book of doctrine. It is a single, tested claim, carried out of a place built to destroy it: that forgiveness is not a feeling you wait for but a thing you do, and that when you do it with a cold heart and empty hands, the love to fill them is given. Betsie promised, dying, that they would have something to tell because they had been there. Corrie spent thirty-three years telling it. The proof was her own hand, in Munich, taking the hand it could not bear to touch.

faq.q: Who was Corrie ten Boom before the war, and what was the Beje?
faq.a: For most of her life she was a watchmaker in Haarlem, an unmarried woman living above the family shop in a narrow house the ten Booms called the Beje, after the street it stood on, the Barteljorisstraat. Her father, Casper, was a watchmaker too, a devout and gentle man of the Dutch Reformed faith, and her sister Betsie was her lifelong companion. It was an ordinary, believing household of the kind that makes no headlines for fifty years, and Corrie was nearly fifty when the events happened that the world now remembers her for.

faq.q: Is it true she was the first licensed woman watchmaker in the Netherlands?
faq.a: So the museum that keeps her house records. She learned her father's trade in the family shop, and in the 1920s (1924, by the museum's record; other sources give 1921 or 1922) she became the first woman licensed as a watchmaker in the Netherlands. For most of her life that was the whole of her story: a single woman, a family shop, church, and the slow work of small mechanisms.

faq.q: How did the ten Boom family come to hide Jews during the occupation?
faq.a: Germany occupied the Netherlands in 1940, and as the persecution of Dutch Jews tightened, the ten Booms were drawn into the underground. Their old, central house, full of odd corners, became a link in a chain that moved Jews and resistance workers to safety. A secret room was built behind a false wall in Corrie's own top-floor bedroom, a space barely large enough for a few people to stand. The museum that keeps the house today reckons the family and their network helped save an estimated eight hundred people, most of them sheltered not in the house itself but at safe addresses elsewhere, placed one at a time, at the risk of every life in the house.

faq.q: What happened when the family was betrayed?
faq.a: On 28 February 1944 a Dutch informant betrayed them. The house was raided and around thirty people were arrested that day, Corrie and Betsie and their elderly father among them. The soldiers never found the secret room: the six people hidden behind the wall, four Jews and two resistance workers, stayed there, silent, for two and a half days, until sympathetic policemen let them out. The hiding place held; the people who had built it did not. Nor did all of those it sheltered survive the war: Mary van Itallie was arrested again within days at a new address and died at Auschwitz on 1 May 1944, while Meijer Mossel, the cantor the household called Eusie, lived to see the liberation.

faq.q: What became of her father and her sister Betsie?
faq.a: Her father, Casper, who was in his eighties, died about ten days after the arrest. Corrie and Betsie were moved through the prison at Scheveningen and the camp at Vught, and then east into Germany, to the women's concentration camp at Ravensbrück. Betsie, frail and sick, died there on 16 December 1944. Before she died she told Corrie again and again that they must go out afterward and tell people what they had learned, and the line most closely associated with the two sisters was hers: "There is no pit so deep that He is not deeper still."

faq.q: What is the story about the fleas and giving thanks?
faq.a: Corrie recounts in The Hiding Place (1971) that their overcrowded barracks was infested with fleas, and that Betsie insisted on thanking God even for them. Corrie could see no sense in it and gave thanks anyway. Only later did they understand: the guards would not enter the flea-ridden block, and so the two sisters were left alone to read the Bible aloud to the other women, freely, in a place where such a thing should have been impossible. In the one corner of that camp the guards avoided, two sisters read Scripture to the condemned.

faq.q: How did Corrie survive when so many did not?
faq.a: At the very end of December 1944, days after Betsie's death, Corrie was released, for reasons never fully explained. Her first account, written in 1945, suggests the sisters had expected a fixed prison term to run out; years later she was told it had been a clerical error, and in The Hiding Place she recounts that the women of her age were sent to their deaths soon after she left. Whatever the cause, within weeks the camp began gassing the sick and the old. She never claimed to have earned her survival or to fully understand it. She had gone in with a sister and a family and came out alone, carrying an instruction from a dead woman to go and tell what they had learned.

faq.q: What is the encounter with the Ravensbrück guard, and why is it remembered?
faq.a: For decades after the war Corrie travelled the world speaking about forgiveness and reconciliation. Then, by her own account, in 1947, in a church in Munich, a man came forward after she had spoken, beaming, his hand out, and she recognised him as a former guard at Ravensbrück. He said he had since become a Christian and asked whether she would forgive him. She stood frozen, unable to lift her hand, and prayed in silence, "Jesus, I cannot forgive him. Give me Your forgiveness." Then she took his hand as an act of the will, and, she recounts, a current of warmth she knew was not her own ran down her arm into their joined hands. She stated the lesson plainly: "Forgiveness is an act of the will, and the will can function regardless of the temperature of the heart."

faq.q: What did she leave behind, and how did her life end?
faq.a: In 1967 Yad Vashem recognised her as one of the Righteous Among the Nations for the family's work in hiding Jews. In 1971 she told the whole story in The Hiding Place, written with John and Elizabeth Sherrill, and a film followed in 1975; together they made a Dutch watchmaker and her dead sister known around the world. She died in Placentia, California, on 15 April 1983 — her ninety-first birthday, the same date on which she had been born. What she leaves is a single, tested claim carried out of a place built to destroy it: that forgiveness is not a feeling you wait for but a thing you do, and that when you do it with a cold heart and empty hands, the love to fill them is given.

fields.name: Lottie Moon
fields.bio: Lottie Moon (1840–1912) was a Southern Baptist missionary who gave nearly forty years to China. Her letters home pressing for prayer, for laborers, and for a Christmas offering for missions built the foundation of Baptist mission giving; she died worn out amid famine and war on Christmas Eve, 1912.
fields.bio_html:
She was small — under five feet — and she spent thirty-nine years in a country that was not hers, in a province most of her supporters at home could not have found on a map. She had one of the first Master of Arts degrees a Southern institution ever gave a woman, and she used it to bake tea cakes for the children of a Chinese village so that their mothers might one day sit and listen to her. Lottie Moon is remembered now mostly for an offering that bears her name and has since gathered more than five billion dollars for missions. But the offering was an afterthought of her real work, which was to give herself away in Shandong until there was nothing left to give.

A Virginia girl who did not believe

Charlotte Digges Moon was born on 12 December 1840 at Viewmont, the family estate in Albemarle County, Virginia. The Moons were affluent and staunchly Baptist, and Lottie was raised inside the faith without belonging to it. She was clever, sharp-tongued, and by her own account religiously indifferent as a young woman — the sort of student who could argue circles around the pious and enjoyed doing it.

Her education was unusual for a woman of her time and place. She read several languages and, in 1861, received from the Albemarle Female Institute one of the first Master of Arts degrees a Southern institution had awarded to a woman. But the decisive change had come three years earlier. In December 1858, under the preaching of John A. Broadus at the First Baptist Church of Charlottesville, the indifferent young woman was converted. The story her friends told afterward was that she had gone to the meetings partly to scoff and stayed to be undone.

For more than a decade after that she taught school. Teaching was one of the few serious occupations open to an educated single woman, and she was good at it. But a conviction was forming in her that the church was leaving half its work undone — that there were women and girls across the world whom no man could ever reach, and that it would take women to reach them.

The call to China

Her younger sister Edmonia went first, sailing for China in 1872 as one of the first single women the Southern Baptists had ever sent. On 7 July 1873, at the age of thirty-two, Lottie was appointed a missionary in her own right, and she followed her sister out to Shandong province. She would remain, with only two furloughs, for the rest of her life.

What she found was not a field prepared for her. It was hard, slow, and often lonely, and she saw quickly that the labour was enormous and the workers pitifully few. Within months of her arrival she was already writing home with the complaint — half lament, half rebuke — that would echo through the rest of her letters.

What we need in China is more workers. The harvest is very great, the laborers, oh! so few. Why does the Southern Baptist church lag behind in this great work?

— Lottie Moon, Tungchow, 1 November 1873

The words were barely her own. They were Christ's, from Matthew's Gospel — the harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few; pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest. Lottie Moon prayed that prayer for nearly forty years, and she prayed it not as a pious sentiment but as a working woman staring at more fields than she could ever reap alone.

Her plea was Jesus' own prayer, taken up and repeated until it became the shape of her life: that the Lord of the harvest would send labourers into a harvest too great for the few already at work. She asked it in her first year in China, and she was still asking it in her last.

Becoming Chinese to win the Chinese

She taught at first in a girls' school in Tengchow, the coastal city where she was based. But the schoolroom chafed at her. The real need, she became convinced, was out in the villages of the interior, among women who had never once heard the name of Christ and never would from a man. So she began to travel — itinerant trips deep into the countryside, and from around 1885 pioneering work at P'ingtu, in the interior, where she often lived and worked alone.

She made a deliberate decision that set her apart from many missionaries of her era: she would not stand over the Chinese as a foreigner but sit among them as a neighbour. She adopted Chinese dress, ate Chinese food, learned the language until it was fluent, and took on the customs of the people she had come to serve. Suspicion of the strange Western woman softened into welcome. Famously, she learned to bake cookies and tea cakes and gave them to the village children, who ran ahead of her from house to house — and behind the children came the mothers, curious about the small woman who fed their little ones and spoke their tongue.

It was patient, unglamorous work, measured in trust slowly earned rather than crowds quickly gathered. And all the while she wrote. Her letters and articles home were the other half of her ministry, and in the long run perhaps the more consequential half. In a steady stream of vivid, unsentimental, sometimes stinging prose, she laid before Southern Baptists the reality of the field and shamed their comfortable neglect of it. She built, almost single-handedly, the foundation of Southern Baptist mission support — and she was blunt about the cost to anyone who might follow her.

Please say to the new missionaries that they are coming to a life of hardship, responsibility and constant self denial. … Let them come "rejoicing to suffer" for the sake of that Lord and Master who freely gave his life for them.

— Lottie Moon, P'ingtu, 9 January 1889

The offering born of a letter

The plea for more workers needed more than prayer; it needed money to send them. In 1887 Lottie Moon wrote home with a concrete proposal: let Southern Baptists set apart the week before Christmas for prayer and for a special offering for missions. She framed it not as a fundraising drive but as a fitting act of worship — a gift given in memory of the great Gift.

Is not the festive season, when families and friends exchange gifts in memory of The Gift laid on the altar of the world for the redemption of the human race, the most appropriate time to consecrate a portion … to send forth the good tidings of great joy into all the earth?

— Lottie Moon, 15 September 1887

The appeal was answered, and answered concretely. The Woman's Missionary Union organized in 1888, and that first Christmas offering raised $3,315 — enough to send three new women missionaries to China, the very labourers she had been begging God to raise up for fifteen years. She had prayed the prayer of Matthew 9; she lived to see it begin to be answered in flesh and blood, in three women stepping off a ship into the field she loved.

The prayer of her first year was answered in her lifetime. Her 1887 letter led the Woman's Missionary Union to organize in 1888 and to gather a Christmas offering of $3,315 — enough to send out three new women missionaries to China, the first fruits of the labourers she had pleaded for. After her death the annual offering was named the Lottie Moon Christmas Offering in her honour, and its cumulative giving has since passed five billion dollars.

She did not live to hear it called by her name; the offering was named for her only after her death, and the Woman's Missionary Union formalized the title in 1918. It is a strange and fitting memorial — not a statue or a book, but a recurring act of giving that has funded generations of the very work she gave her life to.

Poured out

Her last years were lived in the middle of catastrophe. The Qing dynasty fell in 1911 and 1912, and Shandong was swept by regional war, by plague, and by famine. The suffering around her was immense and real, and she carried it in a way that broke her. Never robust and long past her physical prime, she gave and gave into need that had no bottom, and in her final months her health and her mind gave way. From about October 1912 she declined rapidly, ill, worn down, malnourished, and neglecting herself in the midst of a famine that was starving the people she loved.

A popular version of her death holds that she deliberately starved herself, giving away every scrap of food and every coin until she had nothing. It is a moving story, and it is disputed. Historians who have examined her final months carefully — Regina Sullivan among them — conclude that she did not deliberately starve herself, and that she had money in the bank at the end. What is not in doubt is harder and truer than the legend: here was a woman genuinely poured out in a hard place, ill and depressed and undernourished amid real famine, whose body finally failed under the weight of it all. She did not choose death, but she had long since chosen a life that spent itself without reserve, and that life had run its course.

Her colleagues, alarmed, arranged to send her home to recover. She never arrived. On 24 December 1912 — Christmas Eve — Lottie Moon died in the harbour at Kobe, Japan, aboard ship, on her way back to the United States. She was seventy-two, and she had been in China for thirty-nine years. That she should die on the eve of the feast whose offering would carry her name is one of those coincidences that reads like providence.

What she leaves

She left no great book, no theological system, no institution of her own founding. What she left was a body of letters that reshaped how a whole denomination thought about the world, an offering that has sent thousands of workers into the fields she wept over, and an example of a certain kind of holiness — small, stubborn, unspectacular, and total.

Above all she left a prayer she never stopped praying, and the truest picture of her heart is the sentence she wrote after fifteen years in the field, when she had already given more than most and would go on to give everything else.

I would I had a thousand lives that I might give them to … China!

— Lottie Moon, Zhenjiang, 27 August 1888

She had only one life, and she gave it — not thrown away in a single dramatic gesture, but handed over slowly, letter by letter, tea cake by tea cake, village by village, until there was nothing left to hand. The harvest is still great and the labourers still few, and every Christmas the church she scolded and loved takes up an offering in her name and sends a few more.

faq.q: What was Lottie Moon's background and education before she became a missionary?
faq.a: Charlotte "Lottie" Digges Moon was born in 1840 at Viewmont, an affluent Baptist family estate in Albemarle County, Virginia. She received an unusually fine education for a Southern woman of her day, reading several languages and, in 1861, earning from the Albemarle Female Institute one of the first Master of Arts degrees a Southern institution ever awarded a woman. So learned was she that the Baptist preacher John A. Broadus reportedly reckoned her among the best-educated women in the South.

faq.q: Was Lottie Moon always devout, or did she come to faith later?
faq.a: As a young woman she was clever, sharp-tongued, and by her own account religiously indifferent, quite capable of arguing circles around the pious. The change came in December 1858, under the preaching of John A. Broadus at the First Baptist Church of Charlottesville. Friends said she had gone to the meetings partly to scoff and stayed to be undone; she was baptized and gave her life to Christ.

faq.q: How did Lottie Moon end up going to China?
faq.a: Teaching school for over a decade, she grew convinced that there were women and girls across the world whom no man could reach, and that it would take women to reach them. Her younger sister Edmonia sailed for China in 1872, and on 7 July 1873, at thirty-two, Lottie was appointed a missionary in her own right and followed her to Shandong province. She would remain there, with only two furloughs, for the rest of her life.

faq.q: Why did Lottie Moon adopt Chinese dress and customs?
faq.a: She made a deliberate decision that set her apart from many missionaries of her era: rather than stand over the Chinese as a foreigner, she chose to sit among them as a neighbour. She adopted Chinese dress, ate Chinese food, learned the language until she was fluent, and took on local customs, working for years in the interior at P'ingtu, often alone. Famously she baked cookies and tea cakes for the village children, who ran ahead of her from house to house, and behind them came their mothers, curious about the small woman who fed their little ones and spoke their tongue.

faq.q: What did Lottie Moon believe about the role of women in missions?
faq.a: She was convinced that the church was leaving half its work undone, because vast numbers of Chinese women would never hear the gospel from a man. She insisted that women could evangelize women effectively and pressed the point relentlessly in her letters home. Her own patient village work, measured in trust slowly earned rather than crowds quickly gathered, was meant to prove it.

faq.q: How did the Christmas offering that bears her name come about?
faq.a: Her letters home laid the reality of the mission field before Southern Baptists and shamed their neglect of it, begging repeatedly for more workers and more support. In 1887 she proposed setting apart the week before Christmas for prayer and a special offering for missions, framing it not as a fundraising drive but as an act of worship. The Woman's Missionary Union organized in 1888 and gathered a first offering of $3,315, enough to send three new women missionaries to China; after her death the annual offering was named the Lottie Moon Christmas Offering in her honour, a title the Woman's Missionary Union formalized in 1918.

faq.q: Did Lottie Moon ever marry?
faq.a: She never married and spent her long life in China unmarried and often lonely. She had once been drawn to Crawford H. Toy, a scholar she had known in Virginia, and by the early 1880s the two were exchanging letters and contemplating marriage. The engagement came apart over religious differences and over her decision that she could not abandon her depleted mission post; Toy went on to teach at Harvard, and Lottie stayed in China, having concluded that God's claim on her life had to come first.

faq.q: Is it true that Lottie Moon starved herself to death?
faq.a: Her final years were spent amid the collapse of the Qing dynasty and the war, plague, and famine that swept Shandong, and she gave and gave into suffering that had no bottom until her own health and mind gave way. A popular story holds that she deliberately starved herself, giving away every scrap of food and coin, but that account is disputed; historians such as Regina Sullivan have concluded she did not deliberately starve and had money in the bank at the end. What is not in doubt is that she was genuinely poured out, ill and undernourished amid real famine, her body finally failing under the weight of it all.

faq.q: How and when did Lottie Moon die?
faq.a: Alarmed at her decline, her colleagues arranged to send her home to recover, but she never arrived. On 24 December 1912, Christmas Eve, Lottie Moon died aboard ship in the harbour at Kobe, Japan, emaciated and worn out, on her way back to the United States. She was seventy-two and had given thirty-nine years to China.

faq.q: What is Lottie Moon best remembered for?
faq.a: She left no great book, no theological system, and no institution of her own founding; what she left was a body of vivid, stinging letters that reshaped how a whole denomination thought about the world, and an example of a small, stubborn, total devotion. She had once written, after fifteen years in the field, "I would I had a thousand lives that I might give them to China!" She had only one, and she handed it over slowly, letter by letter and tea cake by tea cake, until there was nothing left to give.

fields.name: Mary Slessor
fields.bio: Mary Slessor (1848–1915) was a Dundee mill girl who became a missionary to Calabar in what is now Nigeria. Living among the people and speaking their language, she fought the killing of twins, rescued and raised many children, and became a magistrate in the interior — remembered as “everybody’s mother.”
fields.bio_html:
She was a red-haired jute worker from the Dundee mills, small and plain-spoken, who had stood at a loom since she was a child. She could not have been further from the Victorian idea of a lady missionary. And yet Mary Slessor spent almost forty years in the forests of Calabar, learned to speak Efik like a woman born to it, sat as a magistrate over men who had never taken orders from a woman, and gathered up the twin babies that her neighbours had been taught to throw away. She left behind no great book. What she left was a testimony, repeated to the end of her life, that the whole of it had been carried by prayer.

A hard apprenticeship

She was born on 2 December 1848 in Aberdeen, into poverty. Her father, Robert, was a shoemaker who lost his trade to drink and ended his working life as a mill labourer; the household was held together by her mother and, before long, by the children. In 1859 the family moved to Dundee, to the jute mills that were then swallowing the labour of the poor.

Mary went into the mill young. From the age of eleven she was a “half-timer” — half the day at school, half the day at the loom — and by fourteen she was a skilled worker keeping the long shift, six in the morning until six at night, for the better part of a decade, handing her wages toward the family she was helping to feed. It was not a childhood so much as an apprenticeship in endurance. She learned to work while exhausted, to make do, to stand her ground among rough people, and to read whatever she could snatch. None of it was wasted. The woman who would later walk alone through country where armed men settled arguments with the machete had first been made hard and patient in a Scottish mill.

Her faith grew in those years, in the ordinary furniture of a working-class Presbyterian life — the Sunday school she taught, the mission work in the poor closes of the town. Then, in 1873, David Livingstone died in Africa, and the news of it moved through Scotland like weather. Slessor, already restless, felt the pull of the mission field settle into a call.

The call to Calabar

She was twenty-eight when she applied to the Foreign Mission Board of the United Presbyterian Church in 1876. She trained briefly in Edinburgh, and on 5 August 1876 she sailed for Calabar, on the south-eastern coast of what is now Nigeria — a region with a fearsome reputation among Europeans for its fevers and its violence.

From the first she did the thing that set her apart from most of her fellow missionaries: she went to live among the people rather than beside them. She learned Efik until she was fluent, until she could argue and joke and grieve in it. She ate the local food, went about barefoot, and made her home in the villages rather than the safety of the mission compound. She was not performing humility; she simply could not see the point of a Gospel preached across a fence. The distance most missionaries kept, she closed.

Heaven is now nearer to me than Britain, and no one will worry about me if I go up country.

— Mary Slessor, after the deaths of her mother and sister

Those words came after her mother and her sister died, taking with them the last people in Scotland who watched anxiously for her letters. For most people such a loss would have argued for coming home. For Slessor it cut the last rope. With no one left to worry, she was free to go where no one else would.

Okoyong

In August 1888 she pressed inland to Okoyong, a district where earlier missionaries had been killed and where no European authority reached. She went with a handful of adopted children and very little else. She settled there and stayed for years, and the people came to call her the white queen of Okoyong — a title that says a good deal about how strange her position was and how completely she had made it her own.

What she found in Okoyong she set herself to change. The killing of twins was among the hardest of it. Twins were believed to be cursed, the mark of an evil spirit; the babies were abandoned in the bush or killed, and their mother was driven out. Slessor could not abide it. She went after the abandoned children, carried them home, and raised them as her own — many of them, over the years, among them a daughter she called Janie. She filled her house with the children nobody else would touch, and by keeping them alive and well and loved in plain sight, she made the old belief harder to hold.

It would be a legend to say she abolished the practice single-handed; the killing of twins declined slowly, over decades, through many hands and much labour after hers. What is true, and enough, is that she fought it where she stood, rescued the children she could reach, and made her own household a standing argument against it.

She worked, for the most part, alone — often ill with the malaria that never quite left her, far from any help, with a house full of rescued children depending on her. Her recourse in all of it was prayer, which she rated above the labour it undergirded: “Praying is harder work than doing, at least I find it so, but the dynamic lies that way to advance the Kingdom.”

She set herself, too, against trial by ordeal — the poison bean, fed to the accused so that survival counted as innocence and death as guilt — and against the other cruelties that settled disputes by killing. She threw herself between quarrelling parties and made herself the arbiter, and the accounts most often repeated tell of her facing down armed men and standing between armies to stop a war. Those scenes belong partly to the Victorian storytelling that grew up around her, and the plain record is quieter than the legend; but the fact underneath is not in doubt. A woman with no soldiers and no weapons made herself, by sheer nerve and long-earned trust, the peace of that country.

A magistrate in bare feet

The colonial authorities, watching this, did something unprecedented. In 1892 they made her a vice-consul in Okoyong, giving her charge of the native court — a position of real legal authority that no woman of the time was supposed to hold. She presided over disputes, gave judgment, and was obeyed. Later, in 1905, she took up a similar native-court role at Ikot Obong. In 1913 she was made an honorary associate of the Order of St John in recognition of her work.

It is worth sitting with the picture: a former mill girl, barefoot, plain in speech, ruling on the quarrels of a whole district, her verdicts standing because the people had decided over many years that they trusted her. She had no army behind her and no wealth. What she had was Efik, and courage, and the long credit of a woman who had never once put her own safety ahead of theirs.

One long record of answered prayer

Through all of it she was often gravely ill. Malaria came and went and came again; she was frequently alone, frequently worn past what her body could bear. And through all of it she kept the practice that her biographer would make the centre of her story. She prayed about everything — her health, her decisions, the dangers she walked into, the food that had to appear when there was none — and she believed, plainly and to the end, that it was answered.

My life is one long, daily, hourly record of answered prayer. For physical health, for mental overstrain, for guidance given marvellously, for errors and dangers averted, for enmity to the Gospel subdued, for food provided at the exact hour needed, for everything that goes to make up life and my poor service, I can testify, with a full and often wonder-stricken awe, that I believe God answers prayer.

— Mary Slessor

This was not a doctrine she held at arm’s length. It was the ledger of a life spent alone in dangerous country and somehow carried through it — health sustained when it had no business holding, guidance given at the turnings, dangers averted, “food provided at the exact hour needed.” She did not claim to understand it. She claimed only that, looking back over nearly forty years, she could not tell the story of her service without telling it as answered prayer.

Mother of all the peoples

She died on 13 January 1915 at Use, near Itu, of the fever that had hunted her all her life. She was sixty-six. The colonial government gave her a state funeral, and she was mourned across Calabar and Scotland alike. Among the people she had lived and worked with she was Eka Kpukpru Owo — “mother of all the peoples” — a name earned one rescued child and one settled quarrel at a time. In her own country her memory was kept in the ordinary honours of a nation that had produced her: for years her face looked out from the Clydesdale Bank ten-pound note.

She wrote no famous book and founded no order. What she leaves is harder to frame and more useful. She is proof that God does his largest work through the least likely instruments — that a poor girl from a Dundee mill, given nothing but nerve and a language and a habit of prayer, can change the shape of a country. And she leaves the testimony itself, offered without decoration by a woman who had every reason to know whether it was true: that a whole life, from the loom to the forest, can be one long record of answered prayer.

faq.q: Who was Mary Slessor?
faq.a: Mary Slessor (1848–1915) was a Dundee mill girl who became a missionary to Calabar in what is now Nigeria. Living among the people and speaking their language, she fought the killing of twins, rescued and raised many children, and became a magistrate in the interior — remembered as "everybody's mother." She left no great book, only a testimony, repeated to the end of her life, that the whole of it had been carried by prayer.

faq.q: What was her early life?
faq.a: She was born on 2 December 1848 in Aberdeen into poverty; her father lost his shoemaking trade to drink, and the family moved to Dundee's jute mills in 1859. Mary went into the mill young — a "half-timer" from eleven, half the day at school and half at the loom, and by fourteen a skilled worker keeping the long shift for the better part of a decade. It was less a childhood than an apprenticeship in endurance, and none of it was wasted: the woman who would later walk alone through dangerous country was first made hard and patient in a Scottish mill.

faq.q: What called her to Calabar?
faq.a: Her faith grew in an ordinary working-class Presbyterian life — Sunday school, mission work in the poor closes of Dundee. Then in 1873 David Livingstone died in Africa, and the news moved through Scotland like weather; Slessor, already restless, felt the pull of the mission field settle into a call. She applied to the Foreign Mission Board in 1876, trained briefly, and on 5 August 1876 sailed for Calabar, a region with a fearsome reputation among Europeans for its fevers and its violence.

faq.q: How did she live among the people?
faq.a: From the first she did the thing that set her apart from most missionaries: she went to live among the people rather than beside them. She learned Efik until she was fluent — until she could argue and joke and grieve in it — ate the local food, went about barefoot, and made her home in the villages rather than the safety of the mission compound. She was not performing humility; she simply could not see the point of a Gospel preached across a fence, and closed the distance most missionaries kept.

faq.q: What did she do at Okoyong?
faq.a: In August 1888 she pressed inland to Okoyong, a district where earlier missionaries had been killed and no European authority reached, going with a handful of adopted children and little else. She stayed for years, and the people came to call her the white queen of Okoyong. faq.q: How did she fight the killing of twins?
faq.a: Twins were believed to be cursed, the mark of an evil spirit; the babies were abandoned in the bush or killed, and their mother driven out. Slessor could not abide it — she went after the abandoned children, carried them home, and raised many as her own, filling her house with the children nobody else would touch. By keeping them alive and well and loved in plain sight, she made the old belief harder to hold; the practice declined slowly, over decades and many hands, but she fought it where she stood.

faq.q: How did she become a magistrate?
faq.a: The colonial authorities, watching a woman make herself the arbiter of a whole district, did something unprecedented: in 1892 they made her a vice-consul in Okoyong, giving her charge of the native court — real legal authority no woman of the time was supposed to hold. She presided over disputes, gave judgment, and was obeyed; later, in 1905, she took up a similar role at Ikot Obong. A former mill girl, barefoot and plain in speech, ruled on the quarrels of a district because the people had decided they trusted her.

faq.q: How central was prayer to her work?
faq.a: It was the ground of everything. Often gravely ill with the malaria that never left her, frequently alone and worn past what her body could bear, she prayed about everything — her health, her decisions, the dangers she walked into, the food that had to appear when there was none — and rated prayer above the labour it undergirded: "Praying is harder work than doing, at least I find it so, but the dynamic lies that way to advance the Kingdom."

faq.q: What was her testimony of answered prayer?
faq.a: She summed up nearly forty years in one sentence: "My life is one long, daily, hourly record of answered prayer.
