fields.name: John Stott
fields.bio: John Stott (1921–2011) was rector of All Souls, Langham Place, for his whole ministry and one of the principal architects of modern world evangelicalism — chief framer of the Lausanne Covenant and founder of the Langham Partnership. A clear Bible teacher, lifelong single, and disciplined man of prayer, he gave away his royalties to train pastors across the world.
fields.bio_html:
Most lives that shape a movement do so by restlessness — a man moves from cause to cause, church to church, country to country, and the sum of the motion is the influence. John Stott’s life ran the other way. He was born a short walk from All Souls, Langham Place, in the West End of London; he was converted at school and mentored by letter; he was ordained into that one church and stayed there, in one form or another, until he died. From that single fixed point he did more to shape worldwide evangelical Christianity in the twentieth century than almost anyone alive. He is proof that depth in one place can reach further than breadth across many.

A doctor’s son who heard a sentence

He was born in London on 27 April 1921, the son of Sir Arnold Stott, a Harley Street physician and a convinced agnostic, and of a mother of Lutheran background who took her children to All Souls. It was a household of two settlements — the father’s reason, the mother’s faith — and the boy grew up respecting both.

The decisive thing happened at Rugby School. In 1938 a clergyman named Eric Nash — known to a generation of English schoolboys simply as “Bash” — spoke to the school Christian Union, and on 13 February the seventeen-year-old Stott gave his life to Christ. What made the moment last was what Nash did next. He wrote to the boy every week for about five years, patiently, one letter at a time, teaching him how to follow Christ and how to think. Stott never forgot that a man had taken that much trouble over one young convert. The whole shape of his later ministry — the personal attention, the raising up of the next person, the conviction that the church grows by discipling one soul at a time — was set by those letters.

He went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, took a double first, and was ordained in 1945. His first post was as a curate at All Souls, the church of his childhood. Five years later, in 1950, at the age of twenty-eight, he was made its rector. He would hold that connection for the rest of his life — rector until 1975, then rector emeritus — one man and one church across six decades.

The disciplined morning

To understand everything he built, you have to start where he started every day, because he started it the same way for most of his adult life.

He rose at about five o’clock. Before his feet were properly on the floor, before the post or the diary or the demands of a large parish could reach him, he greeted God — and he greeted him as three Persons, one at a time, so that the first act of the day was not a request but a recognition of who God is. Then came the reading. He followed the plan of Robert Murray M’Cheyne, the young Scottish minister of a century before, working through several chapters of the Bible each day so that the whole of it passed under his eye, year after year, and the Old Testament and the New were always being read together.

Before the day could make its claims on him, John Stott greeted God by name — “Good morning, heavenly Father; good morning, Lord Jesus; good morning, Holy Spirit” — addressing each Person of the Trinity in turn. Rising near five o’clock, he then read his daily portion on the M’Cheyne plan before the parish, the post, or the diary could reach him. The pattern held for the better part of a lifetime: recognition first, requests afterward.

Then the notebook came out. It was a small thing, held shut with a rubber band, its pages covered in tiny handwriting and ruled into four columns — one for evangelism and new converts, one for people facing hard decisions, one for the sick and the bereaved, and one for everything else. Down those columns ran the names of people he prayed for by name, day after day, many of whom never knew they were on the list. The man who would help write the theology of a global movement kept its foundations in a rubber-banded pocket book, praying through a column of names before most of the world was awake.

It is worth saying plainly what this was and was not. It was not a gift of temperament; it was a discipline, kept when he felt like it and when he did not, for decades. The public influence everyone can see grew out of a private practice almost nobody saw.

One church, and a world of pastors

Out of that fixed point the work spread astonishingly. At All Souls he built a preaching ministry admired far beyond his own tradition — careful, biblical, unshowy, always trying to let the text say its own thing rather than making it say his. Between 1952 and 1977 he led some fifty university missions around the world, and from 1959 he was an honorary chaplain to the Queen. He wrote more than fifty books; Basic Christianity, published in 1958, has sold around two million copies in more than sixty languages, and The Cross of Christ (1986) is generally reckoned his masterwork.

Then there was the matter of the money. Around 1969 Stott founded what grew into the Langham Partnership, and to fund it he did something most successful authors never contemplate: he gave away the income from his own books and speaking. The royalties and honoraria that could have made a bestselling clergyman wealthy went instead to train pastors in the majority world — scholarships for gifted teachers from Africa, Asia and Latin America, help for national preachers, the supply of good books where there were none. He had learned from Bash that the way you serve the church is by building up the next person; he simply did it at the scale of continents, and paid for it out of his own pocket. He lived, all his life, simply and single, in a modest flat, and let his wealth become other men’s training.

In 1974 he chaired the committee that drafted the Lausanne Covenant, one of the founding documents of modern world evangelicalism, holding together in a single statement the call to evangelism and the call to social responsibility. In 1982 he founded the London Institute for Contemporary Christianity, to help ordinary believers think Christianly about their work and their world. In 2005 Time named him one of the hundred most influential people alive. Through all of it he remained, to the students and pastors who loved him, simply “Uncle John” — and, in his spare hours, a devoted birdwatcher who could write a whole book, The Birds Our Teachers, on what the created world had to teach about the God who made it.

I could never myself believe in God, if it were not for the cross.

— John Stott, The Cross of Christ

The line is worth weighing. A man who had thought about the faith as rigorously as any of his generation located the whole reason for his believing not in an argument but in a crucifixion — the point at which, he held, the love and the justice of God meet.

“I would pray more”

Late in his life someone asked John Stott what he would do differently if he had his ministry again. The answer he is reported to have given was not about strategy or books or missions. It was two words about the notebook and the early mornings: he would pray more.

Bash had prayed and written for one seventeen-year-old convert, week after week, for five years. That single patient investment produced a man whose books, missions, and given-away royalties trained pastors on every continent — and who, into his old age, still rose before dawn to pray through his own columns of names. The clearest answer to the older man’s labour was the ministry of the younger, multiplied across the world church.

Coming from that man, it is not false modesty and it is not a platitude. It is the most consistent thing he could have said. Everyone else measured his life by its output — the covenant, the institute, the fifty books, the pastors trained. He measured it by the one hidden practice from which all of that had come, and judged that even he, who had kept it for a lifetime, had not given it enough.

Nothing except Christ crucified

He preached and taught into old age, then withdrew quietly to a home for retired clergy. He died on 27 July 2011, at Lingfield in Surrey, at the age of ninety, with friends reading Scripture and playing Handel at his bedside.

His gravestone carries no summary of his achievements. It carries the verse he had preached and lived by — the apostle Paul’s resolve to know “nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified.” It is exactly the epitaph the life asks for. He held one church for one lifetime, gave his wealth away to raise up others, and built a worldwide influence on a rubber-banded notebook and a five o’clock greeting to the Trinity. The doctor’s son who was written to, week after week, by a man who cared about one convert, spent the rest of his years writing back — in letters, in books, in prayers by name, in pastors he would never meet — the same patient answer.

fields.name: Helen Roseveare
fields.bio: Helen Roseveare (1925–2016) was a British missionary doctor who built hospitals and trained African medical workers in the Congo. Beaten and raped during the 1964 Simba rebellion, she spoke of it as being “trusted” by God with suffering, returned to Congo to rebuild, and taught for the rest of her life that the cost is swallowed up in the privilege of knowing Christ.
fields.bio_html:
Most of the people the wider church remembers from the mission field are remembered for what they built or how they died. Helen Roseveare is remembered for something harder to file: for what was done to her, and for what she decided it meant. She was a doctor — a good one, trained at Cambridge — who spent twenty years building hospitals in the north-east of the Congo and teaching Congolese men and women to do the work she had come to do. She is remembered, though, for five months in 1964 when all of that was taken from her by soldiers, and for the sentence she carried out of those months for the rest of her life: that the worst thing that ever happened to her was, somehow, a form of being trusted.

A ration-book childhood and a late conversion

She was born on 21 September 1925 at Haileybury College in Hertfordshire, where her father worked. Martin Roseveare was a mathematician and civil servant who, during the Second World War, designed the British ration book — the ordinary document that fed a nation through its lean years. It is a small thing to note about a daughter who would spend her life measuring out scarce medicine among people who had almost nothing, but it is the kind of small thing that stays with you.

She was clever, driven, and not particularly religious. She went up to Newnham College, Cambridge, to read medicine, and it was there, in 1945, through the Cambridge Inter-Collegiate Christian Union, that she was converted. This matters to the shape of her life. She did not grow up devout and drift into missionary work as the family trade. She came to Christ as a young woman already committed to medicine, and the two callings fused: the science she had chosen and the Lord she had newly found pointed the same direction, toward people who had neither doctor nor gospel.

Ibambi, Nebobongo, and the work of handing it on

She qualified as a doctor and, in 1953, sailed for the Belgian Congo with the Worldwide Evangelization Crusade. She was young, single, and formidable, and she went to a region where a trained physician was a rarity approaching a miracle.

Her first station was Ibambi. From there she moved to Nebobongo — a former leprosy camp, which tells you the condition of the place she was asked to make into a hospital. She built. She built wards and a training school and a maternity unit; she pulled a working medical centre out of a settlement that had been left to the sick. And from the beginning she understood the thing that separates a missionary from a colonist: that her job was not to be indispensable but to make herself unnecessary.

So she trained Africans. She taught Congolese men and women to nurse, to diagnose, to run a ward, to deliver a baby, to carry the work when she was not there — and, as it turned out, when she could not be there. Later she helped establish the medical school and hospital at Nyankunde, a larger training centre meant to send qualified Congolese practitioners across the region. This was the heart of her first decade: not a doctor doing wonders alone, but a teacher multiplying herself into a generation of local hands. When people speak of her hospitals, the more important legacy is the people she taught to run them.

Into the middle of this ordinary, fruitful labour came one of the stories she would tell for the rest of her life — a story small enough to fit in a parcel.

A hot-water bottle

A premature baby had been born at Nebobongo, and its mother had died. There was no incubator, no reliable electricity, and the one hot-water bottle on the station had burst. Roseveare told her nurses and the orphanage children that the baby needed warmth they could not give it. One of the children, at prayers, asked God plainly to send a hot-water bottle — and, since a bottle would be no use arriving next week, to send it that afternoon; and while He was at it, would He send a doll for the baby's sister, so she would know God loved her.

That afternoon a parcel arrived — sent from England five months earlier, before the child had prayed. Among the contents were a hot-water bottle and, near the bottom, a dressed doll. Roseveare told the story for decades not as a marvel about herself but as a rebuke to her own small expectations: the answer had been on its way, packed and posted, before anyone thought to ask.

She would say afterward that she was moved almost to tears — not by the coincidence, but by the realisation that God had answered a prayer before it was prayed, and that her part had merely been to open the box.

1964: five months among the Simba

In 1964 the Congo, only four years independent, tore itself apart. The Simba rebellion swept across the north-east, and the rebel soldiers turned on foreigners and on the mission stations. Roseveare was taken captive. For roughly five months she was held prisoner, and during that captivity she was beaten and raped by rebel soldiers.

It must be said plainly, because she said it plainly. She did not hide it, minimise it, or dress it in euphemism when she came to speak and write about her life; she spoke of the assault openly, in front of audiences, so that other women who had suffered the same thing would not think God had abandoned them for it. To honour her is to state it as she did: she was raped, and she refused to let that fact be unspeakable.

What she also refused was to let it be the last word. In her account of that night and the months around it, she described a sense of God turning her ordeal into a question — not an explanation, which she was never given, but a question she could answer or refuse. She wrote of it, years later, in her book Enough:

Can you thank Me for trusting you with this experience, even if I never tell you why?

— Helen Roseveare, recalling God's word to her in captivity, in Enough (2011)

It is a startling reframing, and it should not be smoothed over. She did not say the suffering was good, or deserved, or a punishment, or a lesson she had needed. She said that being asked to bear it — without an answer, in the dark — was a kind of trust placed in her, a share in what she called the fellowship of Christ's own suffering. The privilege, as she understood it, was not the pain. It was being counted worthy to carry it for Him.

Her surrender, when it came, did not run through an explanation. God never told her why. What she was offered, and what she took, was the chance to say yes to being trusted with something she could not understand — to thank Him not for the experience but for the trust the experience represented.

She went back

The plain fact of the next part is the sermon. In 1966 — two years after the Simba took everything from her — Helen Roseveare returned to the Congo. She went back to the country where she had been imprisoned and assaulted, and she took up the work of rebuilding what the rebellion had wrecked. She stayed until 1973.

People who have not been through it sometimes imagine that faith after trauma is a matter of getting over it. Her return says something harder and truer: she did not go back because the wound had healed and the fear was gone. She went back because she had decided the work, and the people, were worth more than her right to stay safe. The trauma was real; she carried it. She went anyway.

When she finally left the Congo for good in 1973, she settled in the United Kingdom — eventually in Northern Ireland — and became, for the last four decades of her life, one of the most sought-after missionary speakers in the English-speaking world. She wrote the books that carried her testimony far past any lecture hall: Give Me This Mountain (1966), He Gave Us a Valley (1976), Living Sacrifice (1979), Count It All Joy. The titles alone map her theme. It was always the same theme, worked from every side: the cost of following Christ, and what that cost turns out to be worth.

The privilege greater than the price

Her clearest statement of it came at the great student missionary convention at Urbana in 1976. She had every right, of anyone alive, to weigh the cost of obedience and find it too high. Instead she told a stadium of young people that she had learned to stop asking whether it was worth it. The cost was real, she said — but set beside the privilege of being Christ's, it was small, transient, swallowed up.

The cost is swallowed up in the privilege.

— Helen Roseveare, Urbana 1976

She sharpened it elsewhere into the question she said had reordered everything for her. The question, she came to believe, was never really Is it worth it? — a sum you do about God, with yourself as the accountant. The question was whether He was worthy; and to that, she said, the answer is always yes. Once she had settled that, the arithmetic of cost simply stopped mattering. A price you have decided in advance to pay is no longer a price you count.

What she leaves

She died on 7 December 2016 in Northern Ireland, aged ninety-one.

What she leaves is not, in the end, the hospitals, though the hospitals were real and the students she trained carried on long after she was gone. What she leaves is a way of holding suffering that has steadied a great many people who will never build anything. She took the single worst thing that can be done to a person, refused to pretend it had not happened, refused equally to let it define God as absent — and named it, instead, as trust. It is a claim so large it can only be made by someone who has earned the right to make it, and she had.

She was not a martyr; she outlived her ordeal by half a century and told the story with her own mouth. She was not a founder of a movement. She was a doctor who was given more than she asked to carry, went back to the place that had broken her, and spent forty years telling anyone who would listen that the privilege is greater than the price. Coming from her, it is not a slogan. It is a receipt.

fields.name: Jim Elliot
fields.bio: Jim Elliot (1927–1956) was an American missionary speared to death, with four companions, by the Waorani of Ecuador — the people he had come to reach and had resolved not to fight. His journal line, “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain that which he cannot lose,” and the later conversion of the Waorani made his brief life one of the most influential in modern missions.
fields.bio_html:
Jim Elliot was twenty-eight years old when he was killed, on a river sandbar in the Ecuadorian rainforest, by the very people he had crossed the world to reach. He had published nothing. He had pastored no church. He had spent barely four years on the mission field and had not yet learned to speak fluently with the people he died among. By almost every measure the church uses to reckon a life, his was unfinished — and it became one of the most widely told missionary stories of the twentieth century, not for what he built, but for what he was willing to lose, and for a sentence he had written in a private journal seven years before, when he was twenty-two and no one was watching.

A Wheaton devotion

He was born on 8 October 1927 in Portland, Oregon, into a Plymouth Brethren home where the Bible was read plainly and taken seriously. Faith was not, for the Elliots, a Sunday matter; it was the frame of the house. He carried that seriousness into Wheaton College, where he studied from 1945 to 1949, took Greek, and wrestled — he chose the sport, he said, for the discipline it would give a body he meant to spend.

What set the young Elliot apart was less his talent than the ferocity of his devotion. He kept intense journals, and he fed himself on the lives of men and women who had given everything: David Brainerd, worn out among the American tribes before he was thirty; William Carey, the cobbler who would not let the church rest easy about the nations; Amy Carmichael in India. He was not looking for a comfortable Christianity. He was looking for a costly one, and he wrote and prayed his way toward it while still a student.

It was in that spirit, a few months after he graduated from Wheaton, that he made the entry his name is now bound to. On 28 October 1949 he wrote in his journal a line that echoes an older Puritan sentiment but is his own in its phrasing:

He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain that which he cannot lose.

— Jim Elliot, journal, 28 October 1949

It is worth reading slowly, because it is the whole man in one sentence. He was twenty-two. He had lost nothing yet, faced nothing yet, proved nothing yet. He was simply doing the arithmetic of the gospel out loud — that a life, a comfort, a safety, are things a person cannot finally keep anyway, and that to spend them for Christ is not sacrifice but sense. Seven years later the sentence would be quoted over his grave, but he did not write it for a grave. He wrote it for himself, as a young man settling in advance what he would do when the bill came due.

The call to the Waorani

Around 1950 that settled conviction found its object. Elliot was drawn toward the Waorani people of the Ecuadorian rainforest — an isolated group with a long and well-earned reputation for killing outsiders. In that era they were known by a name others had given them, "Auca," a Quichua word meaning "savage." It was a slur, and the people it was aimed at never used it of themselves; they were, and are, the Waorani. That a group was feared and dismissed as beyond reach was, for Elliot, less a warning than an argument. These were exactly the people no one else was going to.

He arrived in Ecuador on 21 February 1952 with his friend Pete Fleming, and began by working among the Quichua at Shandia, learning the country, the language, the patience the work demanded. On 8 October 1953 — his twenty-sixth birthday — he married Elisabeth Howard, herself a missionary and, in time, the chronicler without whom his story would have been lost. Their daughter Valerie was born in February 1955. He was, by then, a husband and a father, with everything a young man might wish to keep.

He had prayed for years that his life would count for God without reserve — in his own words, from his journals, that it might be "an exhibit to the value of knowing God." It is the prayer of a man asking not to be spared the cost, but to be found worth spending.

Operation Auca

The plan to make contact took shape among five young men: Elliot himself; Nate Saint, a pilot with Missionary Aviation Fellowship; Ed McCully; Pete Fleming; and Roger Youderian. Beginning in September and October of 1955, Saint flew over Waorani clearings and lowered gifts on a line from the plane — small tools, trinkets, tokens of goodwill. To their encouragement, the Waorani sent gifts back up. Saint found a narrow sandbar on the Curaray River and named it "Palm Beach," and on 3 January 1956 the five men landed there and made their camp.

On 6 January the first friendly contact came: a small party of Waorani, including a young woman, walked out of the forest to the sandbar. There was curiosity, laughter, even a short flight in the plane for one of the men. For a few days it seemed the impossible might be happening.

Palm Beach

On 8 January 1956, a group of Waorani warriors came to the sandbar and speared all five men to death.

The detail that has held the world's attention for seventy years is this: the men were armed, and they did not defend themselves against the people who killed them. They carried guns, but they had agreed among themselves beforehand that they would not use those guns against the Waorani — that if it came to it, they would not take the life of a man who had not yet heard the gospel in order to save their own. Their reasoning was as plain as Elliot's journal sentence: they were ready for heaven, and the men coming down the beach were not. Accounts of the last minutes differ, and this one will not pretend to a certainty the record does not hold. What is not in doubt is the intent, settled in advance and kept: they had agreed not to use their guns against the men who came to kill them.

He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain that which he cannot lose.

— the line he wrote at twenty-two, and lived out at twenty-eight

The story that outlived the men

The killing might have been a private grief for five young families. Instead it became a public witness. Within weeks Life magazine ran a ten-page photo essay on the men and their deaths, and the story reached far beyond the missionary world. Elisabeth Elliot told the whole account in Through Gates of Splendor in 1957, and her husband's inner life in Shadow of the Almighty in 1958. A generation of young Christians read them and gave themselves to missions. The men had spent what they could not keep, and the gaining had begun.

The gospel reaches the killers

But the deepest part of the story was still to come, and it is the part that turns a tragedy into a testimony.

Rather than leave the Waorani to their reputation and their guilt, two women went to live among them: Elisabeth Elliot, with her small daughter Valerie, and Rachel Saint, the sister of the pilot Nate. They learned the language none of the men had lived to master. They stayed. And over the years that followed, many of the Waorani became Christians — among them some of the very men who had thrown the spears.

The men prayed and sang on the sandbar before their last contact, asking God for the Waorani. They did not live to see the answer. But warriors who had taken part in the killing — among them Mincaye and Kimo — came to faith. Kimo and another, Dyuwi, later baptized Nate Saint's own children in the same Curaray River where the five had died, and Mincaye received Nate's son Steve as a son of his own. The people who made the widows became the family of the fallen. This is the answer to the prayer on the beach.

It is hard to overstate what this reconciliation asks a reader to believe: that the men who murdered a father could raise his son as their own, that the water of a killing could become the water of a baptism, that an enemy could be gathered into the same household as the family he had bereaved. It is exactly the reconciliation the gospel claims to make — normally too slowly, or too privately, for the world to see. Here it was made in a single generation, on a single river, in the sight of everyone who had read the story.

What he leaves

Jim Elliot left no books of his own and few finished works. What he left is a sentence and a demonstration.

The sentence has been carried by millions who never learned to say "Waorani," because it states a truth that does not depend on his death to be true: that everything we clutch — our safety, our years, our comfort — is already slipping through our fingers, and that the only wise thing to do with what cannot be kept is to spend it on what cannot be lost. He wrote it as a student, before it cost him anything, which is the only honest time to write such a thing.

The demonstration is what he and four friends did on a sandbar: they held to a decision made in cold blood — that they would die before they would kill the people they had come to save — and they kept it when the spears came. And the God they trusted answered the prayer they prayed there, not by sparing them, but by giving the killers the very gift the five had carried into the forest to give.

He was twenty-eight. It was enough.

fields.name: Elisabeth Elliot
fields.bio: Elisabeth Elliot (1926–2015) was widowed when her husband Jim and four others were killed by the Waorani of Ecuador — and then went to live among the very people who had killed him, seeing many come to Christ. Through decades of writing and teaching on suffering and obedience, she became one of the most trusted voices of twentieth-century evangelicalism: “do the next thing.”
fields.tagline: Missionary who lived among the Waorani who killed her husband, and wrote on suffering and obedience.
fields.bio_html:
There are missionary stories the church tells because they end well, and there are a few it tells because it cannot quite believe them. Elisabeth Elliot’s belongs to the second kind. Her husband was killed by a people he had gone to reach — speared to death on a river sandbar with four other young men — and two years later she carried her toddler daughter into the forest to live among the very men who had done it. She was not naïve about what they were. She had read the accounts. She went anyway, and she stayed, and she watched a good number of them come to Christ. Then she spent the rest of a long life writing and teaching about the one thing that return had taught her: that obedience is possible in the dark, and that God is to be trusted precisely where He is not to be understood.

A missionary’s daughter, and a hard school

She was born Elisabeth Howard on 21 December 1926 in Brussels, where her parents were serving as missionaries. The family moved to Philadelphia the following year, and she grew up in a home ordered around Scripture and prayer. She went to Wheaton College and studied Classical Greek — not for its own sake, but because she meant to translate the Bible for people who did not yet have it. Afterward she trained further at Prairie Bible Institute. The plan was set early: language, a hard place, a Book put into unwritten speech.

At Wheaton she met Jim Elliot. He was ardent, uncompromising, already given over to the idea of the mission field, and their courtship was famously slow and deliberate — a long discipline of restraint that she would write about decades later, when a younger generation needed someone to tell them that waiting was not a wasted thing. They did not marry until both were in Ecuador. The wedding was on 8 October 1953, in Quito, on Jim’s birthday. Their daughter Valerie was born in February 1955. They settled at Shandia, among the Quichua, and the translation work she had aimed at all her life began in earnest.

The sandbar on the Curaray

Jim and four other missionaries — Nate Saint, Pete Fleming, Ed McCully and Roger Youderian — had set their hearts on reaching the Waorani, a people then known by the insulting name “Auca,” feared across the region for killing outsiders. The men made contact from the air, dropped gifts, and at last landed on a strip of sand along the Curaray River. For a few days it seemed to be working. On 8 January 1956 all five were speared to death.

Elisabeth was twenty-nine, with a ten-month-old daughter, in a foreign forest, suddenly a widow. What she did with the fact — not at once, but soon — became the pattern of everything she taught afterward. She did not treat the killing as the end of the mission. She treated it as, somehow, part of it.

You are loved with an everlasting love — that’s what the Bible says — and underneath are the everlasting arms.

— Elisabeth Elliot, her sign-on for the radio program Gateway to Joy

That sentence, which she would later use to open every one of her broadcasts, was not a slogan she reached for in comfort. It is the thing she had to believe with a spear-widow’s knowledge of what it costs to say it. The everlasting arms are only underneath you when you have fallen far enough to need them.

The return

Here the story turns from grief, which many can imagine, to a decision almost no one can. Rather than go home, Elisabeth stayed in Ecuador and worked toward the one thing the five men had died attempting. In October 1958 she went to live among the Waorani themselves, taking Valerie — by then about three years old — into the group that had made her a widow. She was joined by Rachel Saint, sister of Nate Saint, the pilot killed on the sandbar. The people gave Elisabeth a name in their own tongue: Gikari, the woodpecker. She lived among them until 1961, and in that time — around 1960 — many of the Waorani came to faith in Christ.

She had prayed for years to give the Waorani the words of Scripture. God gave her instead the harder assignment: to give them her own presence, unarmed and forgiving, in the very clearing where they had killed her husband — and to let that be the sermon before there were any words to read.

It would flatten the story to make the two women into a seamless team of saints. They were not. Elisabeth and Rachel Saint differed — in temperament, in theology, in method — and the friction between them was real and is honestly recorded by those who knew them. It is worth saying plainly, because the truth of the return does not depend on the two of them getting along. Two strong, grieving women, each certain of her calling, living in a forest among former killers, did not always agree on how the work should be done. That they persevered anyway, and that the Waorani heard the gospel through them regardless, is more credible for the strain, not less.

Do the next thing.

— the counsel Elisabeth Elliot loved and made famous, from an older poem of uncertain authorship, which she was always careful to credit

A lifetime of telling the truth about suffering

Elisabeth Elliot became, in the decades that followed, one of the most trusted Christian writers of her century — trusted precisely because she never lied about pain. She wrote Through Gates of Splendor (1957), the account of the five men, and Shadow of the Almighty (1958), drawn from Jim’s own journals. She wrote The Savage My Kinsman (1961) about the Waorani. Later came Passion and Purity (1984), which handed her long courtship’s lessons to the young; A Chance to Die (1987), her portrait of Amy Carmichael; The Path of Loneliness in the late 1990s; and Keep a Quiet Heart (1996). From 1988 to 2001 her voice reached households daily through the radio program Gateway to Joy.

Her marriages after Jim were not spared sorrow either. She married the theologian Addison Leitch in 1969 and was widowed again in 1973. In 1977 she married Lars Gren, who cared for her to the end of her life. She knew grief as a repeated visitor, not a single event, and it did not soften her message. It hardened it into something usable.

The center of what she taught was surrender — what she called relinquishment, the handing over of one’s own will to God’s. Her counsel on suffering was direct and unsentimental: accept it, thank God for it, and then offer it back up to Him. Not explain it. Not escape it. Not necessarily even understand it. Accept, thank, offer. She had done exactly that on a riverbank in 1956, and she was not going to prescribe to others a medicine she had refused to swallow.

She is also remembered for three plain words she gave to countless people paralyzed by grief or dread or the sheer size of a hard day: do the next thing. She loved that counsel and made it famous, quoting it constantly — but she was always careful to say she had not coined it. It came from an old poem of uncertain authorship, which she credited rather than claimed. The honesty is characteristic. She popularized it; she did not pretend to have written it. And its wisdom is exactly the wisdom of the return: when the whole road is too dark to see, you are not asked to see the whole road. You are asked to do the next thing.

She had wanted to give the Waorani the gospel. In the end the gospel was given, and given through her — many of the men who had killed her husband came to Christ while she lived among them. It is the plainest answer the record allows: not that her suffering was explained, but that it was not wasted.

The last years, and what she leaves

Elisabeth Elliot stopped public speaking in 2004 as dementia advanced, and she spent roughly her last decade in its long silence. She died at home in Magnolia, Massachusetts, on 15 June 2015, aged eighty-eight, cared for by Lars.

What she leaves is not a system and not a single miracle. It is a demonstration — carried out with her own body, in a real forest, in front of real killers — that the gospel means what it says. She leaves the sentence she began every broadcast with, which is simply true whether or not the day is going well: that you are loved with an everlasting love, and that underneath are the everlasting arms. And she leaves the three words for anyone who cannot see how to go on: not a theory of suffering, but an instruction. Do the next thing. She did, all the way into the forest, and out the other side.

You are loved with an everlasting love — that’s what the Bible says — and underneath are the everlasting arms.

— the words she gave away, day after day, for thirteen years

fields.name: A. W. Tozer
fields.bio: A. W. Tozer (1897–1963) was a self-taught American pastor of the Christian and Missionary Alliance whose books, above all The Pursuit of God and The Knowledge of the Holy, and whose life of prostrate, worshipful prayer made him a prophetic voice calling the church back to the pursuit of God Himself. He pastored for over forty years, most famously at Southside Alliance Church in Chicago, and edited his denomination's magazine until his death.
fields.tagline: Self-taught Alliance pastor and author of The Pursuit of God.
fields.bio_html:
Most pastors are trained for the work before they do it. Aiden Wilson Tozer was not. He never sat in a high school classroom, never took a college course, never spent a day in a seminary. He came off a poor Pennsylvania farm with almost nothing behind him but a habit of reading, and he ended his life regarded across the English-speaking church as a kind of prophet — a pastor who spent more than forty years telling comfortable Christians that they had settled for far less of God than He was offering. The strange thing about Tozer is not that a self-taught farm boy became one of the most quoted devotional writers of his century. It is that a man so hungry for the presence of God could be, at home, so hard to live with.

A farm boy who taught himself

He was born on 21 April 1897, near La Jose — in the Newburg area of Clearfield County, in the rural farm country of western Pennsylvania. There was poverty and there was very little schooling. What there was, instead, was a boy who read everything he could reach. The family later moved to Akron, Ohio, and it was in libraries and second-hand bookshops, not lecture halls, that Tozer got his education. He remained, all his life, entirely self-taught — and the fact is worth resting on, because everything he later became was built on it. The learning that fills his books was gathered by a man who was never given it and went and took it.

The turn came when he was about seventeen. Walking home in Akron, he overheard a street preacher urging his listeners to call on God for mercy. Tozer went home, climbed up to the attic, and there gave his life to Christ. There was no institution in it, no ceremony, no teacher — a sentence heard in the street and a boy alone in an attic. It set the pattern for the whole life: the decisive things would happen between him and God, in private, with the door shut.

In 1918 he married Ada Cecelia Pfautz. They would be married about forty-five years, until his death, and would have seven children. Two years later, in 1920, he was ordained in the Christian and Missionary Alliance — without a single formal credential to his name. He simply began to preach, and the denomination recognised what it was hearing.

The pastor at Southside

The pastorates came in order. Toledo, Ohio, in the early 1920s. Indianapolis for about five years after that. And then, in 1928, the church that would hold him for thirty-one years: Southside Alliance Church in Chicago. It was there that Tozer became Tozer. He preached, he wrote, he read; and from 1950 he also edited the denominational magazine, The Alliance Weekly — renamed The Alliance Witness in 1958 — keeping that editorship until he died. He served a term as a vice-president of the C&MA in the late 1940s as well. In 1959 he left Chicago for Avenue Road Church in Toronto, where he spent his last years.

What people remembered was not the administration. It was the message, which almost never changed. Tozer preached against a Christianity gone shallow and worldly — against entertainment dressed up as worship, against a comfortable, self-satisfied faith that had stopped wanting God Himself. He called believers back to the one thing he thought they had quietly abandoned: the pursuit of God, not for what God gives, but for God. That is why he is so often called a prophet to the church. He tended a flock the way a shepherd does who is more worried about where the sheep are wandering than about being liked by them.

What comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us.

— A.W. Tozer, The Knowledge of the Holy (1961)

That single sentence, the opening line of The Knowledge of the Holy, holds his whole ministry in miniature. He was convinced that the church's troubles were not, at root, moral or organisational but that they came from having too small a thought of God — and that the cure was not a program but a right and reverent vision of who God is.

Face-down on the floor

Behind the preaching was a prayer life that those around him found almost unaccountable. Tozer would arrive at his study early, change out of his suit into old trousers so as not to wrinkle it, and begin to pray on the couch — and then slide down onto the floor, face in the carpet, and stay there. He prayed prostrate, flat on the ground, sometimes for hours. It was worship more than petition. He was not, most of the time, asking God for things. He was gazing at Him.

He described it himself: that there were occasions when for hours he lay prostrate before God without saying a word of prayer or a word of praise — he just gazed on Him and worshipped. This is the man behind the books: not a scholar assembling arguments, but someone lying face-down on a study floor, refusing to leave the presence of God.

This was the engine of everything. The most famous of his books, The Pursuit of God, came out of that same absorbed hunger. According to his biographers, he reportedly drafted much of it in a single night on a train journey to Texas, writing through the dark hours. It was published in 1948, and it is still the book most people mean when they say the name Tozer. Its closing prayers read like the overflow of those hours on the carpet.

O God, I have tasted Thy goodness, and it has both satisfied me and made me thirsty for more.

— A.W. Tozer, The Pursuit of God (1948)

He wrote roughly nine books in his lifetime — among them The Root of the Righteous and The Knowledge of the Holy. Much of the large catalogue that now bears his name is posthumous, compiled from his sermons and editorials by others. He was, in the end, a preacher who happened to write, and his sharpest sentences have the compression of a man who spent his life saying the same thing until it fit on a single line.

The cost at home

It would be dishonest to leave the portrait there. The devotion that made Tozer great in the pulpit was expensive at home, and the ones who paid were his wife and children. He is widely and credibly reported to have been emotionally distant from Ada and the family, absorbed in God and study and writing in a way that left little of himself for them. He handled money so as to keep them poor — giving away or refusing much of the income and royalties that came to him. A biography as sympathetic as Lyle Dorsett's does not hide it. The man who wrote so movingly about longing for God could be, to the people who shared his house, a locked door.

The counterweight is a single sentence, and it belongs here because it is the truth. After Tozer died, Ada in time married again — a man named Leonard Odam. As his biographer Lyle Dorsett recounts, when friends asked whether she was happy, she is reported to have said that she had never been happier in her life: Aiden loved Jesus Christ, but Leonard Odam loves me. It is not a bitter line. It is a quiet, devastating one, and it says something no eulogy would. A man can pursue God with his whole heart and still fail the people nearest him — and both halves of that are real, and neither cancels the other.

One correction is worth making plainly, because it is often got wrong. Tozer is sometimes said to have refused honorary doctorates. He did not. He accepted two — from Wheaton College in 1950 and from Houghton College in 1952 — despite having no earned degree of any kind. What is traditionally said, and fits the man, is that he was uncomfortable with titles and is said to have disliked being called Dr. But he took the degrees. The self-taught farm boy was honoured, in the end, by the schools he never attended.

A man of God

He died on 12 May 1963, of a heart attack, in Toronto, still pastoring Avenue Road Church. He was buried first near Chicago, and his remains were later moved to Ellet Cemetery in Akron, Ohio, back near where he had grown up. The grave is a simple flat marker, and the epitaph on it is as short as one of his own sentences.

A.W. Tozer — A Man of God.

— his gravestone, Ellet Cemetery, Akron, Ohio

It is the right words on the right stone, and it is also, quietly, the harder verdict — for the man under it knew better than anyone what it costs to be that and nothing else. Tozer was a true shepherd, and he tended souls the only way he knew: by chasing after God so hard that his people could not help seeing there was Someone worth chasing. He taught himself everything except the one thing he most had, which was a thirst for the living God that a lifetime never filled. He wrote that self is the veil that hides the face of God from us. He spent his own life trying to get that veil out of the way — succeeding, gloriously, in public, and struggling, honestly, at home. Both are true. That is why the witness holds.

faq.q: Where did A. W. Tozer come from, and what kind of schooling did he have?
faq.a: Aiden Wilson Tozer was born on 21 April 1897 in the poor farm country of Clearfield County, in western Pennsylvania, into a family of little means. There was hardship and there was very little schooling; he never attended high school, never took a college course, and never spent a day in a seminary. What he had instead was a boy's hunger for books, and the education that fills his writing was one he gathered for himself rather than one he was ever given.

faq.q: How did Tozer become a Christian?
faq.a: The turn came when he was about seventeen. Walking home in Akron, Ohio, where the family had moved, he overheard a street preacher urging his hearers to call on God for mercy — to pray, "Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner." Tozer went home, climbed to the attic, and there gave his life to Christ. There was no institution in it and no ceremony, only a sentence heard in the street and a boy alone with God, and it set the pattern for a life in which the decisive things happened in private.

faq.q: If he had no formal training, how did he become a pastor?
faq.a: He was largely self-taught, and it never held him back. He married Ada Cecelia Pfautz, began preaching without a single academic credential to his name, and was ordained in the Christian and Missionary Alliance around 1920. The denomination simply recognized what it was hearing. He went on to serve that fellowship for more than forty years as a pastor, and the learning in his books is the fruit of a man who was never handed an education and went and took one for himself.

faq.q: Where did Tozer spend most of his ministry?
faq.a: After early pastorates he came in 1928 to Southside Alliance Church in Chicago, where he stayed for about thirty-one years — the long middle of his life and the place where he became the Tozer people remember. In 1959 he left Chicago for Avenue Road Church in Toronto, where he spent his final years. From 1950 he also edited his denomination's magazine, The Alliance Weekly, later renamed The Alliance Witness, holding that editorship until his death.

faq.q: What was Tozer's prayer life like?
faq.a: It was the engine of everything else, and those around him found it almost unaccountable. He would come to his study early, change out of his good suit so as not to wrinkle it, and pray — often sliding from the couch down onto the floor to lie prostrate, face to the ground, sometimes for hours. It was worship more than petition; he was not so much asking God for things as gazing at Him. This is the man behind the books: not a scholar assembling arguments, but someone face-down on a study floor, unwilling to leave the presence of God.

faq.q: What are his best-known books?
faq.a: The most famous is The Pursuit of God, published in 1948. By the accounts of those close to him, he drafted much of it in a single night aboard a train bound for Texas, writing through the dark hours with the words coming almost as fast as he could set them down. His other enduring work is The Knowledge of the Holy (1961), a meditation on the attributes of God. Much of the large catalogue that now carries his name is posthumous, gathered from his sermons and editorials, for he was in the end a preacher who happened to write.

faq.q: What was the heart of his message?
faq.a: Tozer preached against a Christianity gone shallow and worldly — against entertainment dressed up as worship, and against a comfortable faith that had quietly stopped wanting God Himself. He called believers back to the pursuit of God, not for what God gives but for God. He was convinced the church's deepest trouble was that it had come to hold too small a thought of God, and the whole of his ministry is caught in the opening line of The Knowledge of the Holy: "What comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us."

faq.q: What was his home life like, and how did he treat money and status?
faq.a: It was plain to the point of austerity. Tozer refused to let money or reputation take hold of him, giving away or declining much of the income and royalties that came to him and keeping his household poor by choice. Honest accounts, including his biographers', also record that the devotion which made him great in the pulpit was costly at home, where he could be distant from Ada and their children. He accepted honorary doctorates from Wheaton and Houghton despite having no earned degree, yet is said to have been uncomfortable with titles and to have disliked being called "Doctor."

faq.q: How is A. W. Tozer remembered?
faq.a: He died of a heart attack on 12 May 1963 in Toronto, still pastoring, and was later buried at Ellet Cemetery in Akron, Ohio, near where he had grown up. The grave is a simple flat marker, and the epitaph on it is as short as one of his own sentences: "A. W. Tozer — A Man of God." It is the right words on the right stone for a man who spent his life chasing after God so hard that his people could not help seeing there was Someone worth chasing.

fields.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
fields.bio: Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906–1945) was a German Lutheran pastor and theologian who opposed Hitler from the first days of the regime, led the Confessing Church's illegal seminary at Finkenwalde, and wrote The Cost of Discipleship with its contrast of cheap and costly grace. Drawn into the resistance conspiracy against Hitler, he was arrested in 1943 and hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp on 9 April 1945, two weeks before its liberation.
fields.bio_html:
Many of the church's pastors were shepherds by long habit — parish priests, seminary heads, missionaries who spent forty quiet years in one place. Dietrich Bonhoeffer had barely begun. He was thirty-nine when they hanged him, and the seminary he is best remembered for leading was illegal and lasted two years before the police shut it. He wrote the book on what it costs to follow Christ, and then the bill came, and he paid it in a concentration camp two weeks before the American army arrived. He is the pastor who counted the cost out loud, in print, years before he knew he was pricing his own death.

A theologian in a house that had no use for one

He was born on 4 February 1906 in Breslau, then in Germany, now the Polish city of Wrocław. The Bonhoeffers were privileged, cultured, and not especially religious. His father, Karl, was one of Germany's leading psychiatrists, and when Karl took the psychiatry chair in Berlin the whole large family — eight children — moved to the capital. Dietrich and his twin sister Sabine were the sixth and seventh of them. It was a house of music and science and careful thinking, the kind of house where a boy might be expected to become a doctor or a lawyer, and where nobody prayed much.

So it surprised them all when, as a teenager, he announced he would become a theologian. His clever, secular-leaning brothers thought he was throwing himself away on a church that was fading. He did not argue the point; he simply went and did it. He studied at Tübingen and Berlin, and by 1927, at twenty-one, he had his doctorate from Berlin with a dissertation on the church as a community of persons — Sanctorum Communio, the communion of saints. He was, by any academic measure, a finished prodigy before he was much of a Christian.

Harlem, and the turn from theologian to disciple

In 1930 he crossed the Atlantic to spend a year at Union Theological Seminary in New York. He was unimpressed by much of what he found in the American academy — too pragmatic, too thin on the substance of the faith. What moved him was somewhere else entirely. Through his friendship with a fellow student, Frank Fisher, he began attending the Abyssinian Baptist Church in Harlem, worshipping regularly with a Black congregation and helping teach its Sunday school. There he heard the gospel preached with a passion and a directness the lecture halls lacked — sin and grace and the love of God and a hope that reached past this world. He also saw, close up, what American racism did to the people singing beside him. Scholars are careful not to make that single year a lightning-bolt conversion, but its mark on him lasted the rest of his life.

Something did shift in him in these years — a change he described later, in a 1936 letter, as moving from a man who owned the Bible as a professional to a man the Bible now owned. He had turned the teaching of Christ, he admitted, into something for his own advantage; and then something happened that changed and transformed his life. The Sermon on the Mount stopped being a text to be mastered and became a set of instructions to be obeyed.

Jamming the spokes of the wheel

He came home to Germany, and Germany was about to hand him the crisis that would define him. Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933. Two days later Bonhoeffer gave a radio address on the idea of the Führer, the Leader — warning that a leader who makes himself into an idol, who acknowledges no authority above himself, becomes a Verführer, a misleader, and leads his people to ruin. The broadcast was cut off before he finished. Exactly why it was cut is not certain, and the honest thing is not to gild it; but the young pastor's instinct, in the regime's first days, was already resistance.

That April the state moved to bar those of Jewish descent from the civil service, and the pro-Nazi faction within the church wanted the same rule applied to its own ministers. Bonhoeffer opposed it at once. In an essay on the church and the Jewish question he argued that the church could not surrender its own standards to a racial ideology, that it had a duty to the state's victims, and that a time might come when the church must not merely bind up the wounded under the wheel but jam the spokes of the wheel itself. His essay carried some of the older assumptions of his tradition about Judaism, and it would be dishonest to make him a fully modern man on that score. But his actions were clean: he stood, early and at cost, for the people the state had marked.

When faithful Protestants broke from the Nazified official church to form the Confessing Church in 1934, Bonhoeffer was with its most uncompromising wing. In 1935 that movement gave him the work he loved best: leading an illegal seminary for its preachers at Finkenwalde, in Pomerania. It was an experiment in shared Christian life — worship, confession, study, and a common table — and it was against the law. The Gestapo closed it in 1937. But out of those two years came the two books he is most read for, The Cost of Discipleship and Life Together.

The first of them made a distinction that has outlived every argument of its decade. Grace, Bonhoeffer said, had been sold cheap — forgiveness without repentance, communion without confession, a grace that costs nothing and so changes nothing.

Cheap grace is the deadly enemy of our Church.

— Dietrich Bonhoeffer, The Cost of Discipleship

Against it he set costly grace: grace that costs a man his life because it cost God the life of his Son, grace that cannot be separated from following. It is the treasure a man sells everything to buy. And in the same book stands the sentence that reads, in hindsight, like a prophecy he wrote over himself.

When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.

— Dietrich Bonhoeffer, The Cost of Discipleship

The pastor and the plot

In June 1939 friends arranged an escape. He sailed to New York, where he could have sat out the coming war in safety and usefulness. Within about two weeks he knew he had made a mistake, and he took a ship home before the war closed the sea. He explained the decision in a letter to the American theologian Reinhold Niebuhr, and the reason he gave is one of the truest things a pastor ever wrote about his people.

I will have no right to participate in the reconstruction of Christian life in Germany after the war if I do not share the trials of this time with my people.

— Dietrich Bonhoeffer, letter to Reinhold Niebuhr, 1939

He was a man with pacifist leanings, a shepherd who believed his place was beside the flock in its worst hour rather than safe across an ocean. The prayer under that decision was not for rescue but for the courage to go back into danger, and it was answered in the going.

Back in Germany, through his brother-in-law Hans von Dohnányi, he was drawn into the Abwehr, German military intelligence, whose leadership had become a nucleus of the resistance against Hitler. On paper he was an agent whose church contacts abroad were useful; in truth the post shielded him from the draft and let him carry the resistance's messages to churchmen overseas, seeking Allied understanding for a Germany after Hitler. He took part in Operation 7, which smuggled a group of Jews to safety in Switzerland.

Here is the hardest turn in his life, and it must be told plainly and without the thrill. This pastor came to support a conspiracy that included plans to kill Hitler. He was not a bomb-maker or an assassin — the popular retellings that cast him as a spy-thriller operative go beyond what the record holds. He was a supporter, a courier, a man who lent the plot his conscience and his cover. He did not pretend the killing was clean. The men of the resistance understood tyrannicide as a grave guilt, and were willing to carry that guilt to stop a greater evil. In the ethics he was writing in these years, unfinished, he wrestled with exactly this: the disciple who, for his neighbour's sake, is willing to step into wrong and answer for it before God rather than keep his own hands clean while others die.

Tegel, Flossenbürg, and a witness that outlived him

In January 1943 he became engaged to Maria von Wedemeyer, from a Pomeranian family he knew; she was far younger than he was, and the engagement was kept quiet at first. On 5 April 1943 he was arrested, along with Dohnányi. The charges were, at first, relatively minor — the Gestapo suspected irregularities in the Abwehr, not yet the plot on Hitler's life. He was held at Tegel military prison in Berlin, and it was there, in his cell, that he wrote the letters and papers his friend Eberhard Bethge would later publish as Letters and Papers from Prison. In them he turned over strange, unfinished ideas about a faith stripped of easy religion in a world come of age, and he wrote poems — among them, in December 1944, one on being sheltered by gracious powers even in the dark, sent as a New Year's greeting to those he loved.

The failed bomb plot of 20 July 1944 changed everything. Seized resistance documents exposed the deeper conspiracy, and Bonhoeffer with it. He was moved to the Gestapo prison, then to Buchenwald, and at last to Flossenbürg. On 8 April 1945 a summary SS court, without real defence or evidence, condemned him. At dawn on 9 April 1945 he was hanged, with fellow conspirators, on what is generally held to have been an order from the very top of the regime after Hitler saw the papers. The camp was liberated by American forces two weeks later.

The account long associated with his death — from a camp doctor who described him kneeling in fervent prayer and going to the gallows composed and unafraid — is one scholars now treat with real caution; the man gave it years later and may have idealized what he saw, or whom. What is better attested comes from a fellow prisoner, Captain Payne Best, who remembered Bonhoeffer's parting words as he was led away, asking that a message be carried to a bishop in England: this is the end — for him, the beginning of life. Even that is a recollection set down five years afterward, not a transcript, and it is honest to hold it as such.

There was no rescue, and it would be a lie to invent one. The answer to the prayers of his last years was not deliverance but the thing he had written of long before — a man who, called by Christ, came and died, and whose witness has sheltered and steadied Christians ever since. The seminary lasted two years; the book he wrote there is still teaching the church what grace costs.

What he leaves

Bonhoeffer left an Ethics he never finished and a stack of prison letters he never meant as a book, and out of those unfinished things came one of the most read Christian voices of the century. He also left a warning against ourselves. So many of his best lines have been sharpened into slogans and, in at least one famous case, put in his mouth though he never wrote them — a reminder that even a martyr can be conscripted for causes he never spoke for, and that honouring him means quoting him truly.

He was a young shepherd, and his crook was broken soon. But he understood something the long-serving shepherds also knew: that a pastor does not lead his people from a safe distance. He shares their trials. He goes back across the ocean when he could have stayed. And when Christ calls, he comes — even when the call, as Bonhoeffer had written with his own hand years before the Gestapo ever knocked, leads him out to die.

fields.name: Martyn Lloyd-Jones
fields.bio: David Martyn Lloyd-Jones (1899–1981), known as “the Doctor,” was a brilliant young London physician — assistant to the King's doctor, Sir Thomas Horder — who left medicine for the ministry, convinced that humanity's deepest disease is spiritual. After eleven years pastoring working people at Sandfields in industrial South Wales, he preached expositionally at Westminster Chapel, London, for thirty years and became a central figure in the twentieth-century recovery of Reformed preaching.
fields.tagline: “The Doctor”: a physician who left medicine to preach at Westminster Chapel for thirty years.
fields.bio_html:
By his early twenties he was working at the top of London medicine — junior assistant to Sir Thomas Horder, physician to the Royal Household, the King's own doctor. A brilliant career lay open in front of him: the qualifications taken in about five years, the research doctorate, the mantle of one of the most eminent physicians of the day apparently his to inherit. And then he walked away from all of it to pastor a mission church among the working people of industrial South Wales. London was astonished. He spent the rest of his life explaining, in effect, why: that a physician can relieve the symptoms of a man but cannot touch the disease at the root of him, and that the root disease is not in the body at all.

A Welsh boy in a London dairy

David Martyn Lloyd-Jones was born on 20 December 1899 in Cardiff, and raised from 1906 in Llangeitho, Cardiganshire — deep Welsh-speaking country, in the heartland where earlier revivals had burned. In 1914 the family moved to London and ran a dairy business in Westminster. He was clever, driven, and quick: from Marylebone Grammar School he went to St Bartholomew's Hospital Medical School, "Bart's," one of Britain's most prestigious teaching hospitals.

The record of those years is a record of relentless ability. He took his medical qualifications with distinction, earned an MD in 1923 for research on infective endocarditis, became a Member of the Royal College of Physicians in 1925, and served as chief clinical assistant to Horder — a man whose diagnostic gift was legendary, and whose gift the young Lloyd-Jones absorbed and never lost. The habit of asking what is really wrong, underneath the presenting complaint, would follow him into the pulpit and stay there for fifty years.

The real disease

Somewhere in the mid-1920s, over roughly two years, the diagnosis turned on the diagnostician. It was not a single dramatic moment — he came under deep conviction gradually — but its conclusion was clear enough to reorder his life. He became convinced that the deepest trouble in the people he treated was not medical but spiritual; that he could send a man home patched up and send him home still lost; that the real disease was sin, and that he himself had been treating everything except the thing that was killing people.

Out of that conviction came a decision that, by every worldly measure, made no sense. The inward matter settled in 1926, and in 1927 he left medicine for the Christian ministry, sponsored by the Presbyterian Church of Wales. On 8 January 1927 he married Bethan Phillips — herself a qualified doctor, and granddaughter of the Welsh revival preacher Evan Phillips. Two physicians, newly married, went straight from their honeymoon not to a Harley Street consulting room but to a mission hall in Port Talbot.

Preaching is theology coming through a man who is on fire.

— D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones, Preaching and Preachers

Sandfields

The church was the Bethlehem Forward Movement Mission Church at Sandfields, Aberavon — the Calvinistic Methodists' home-mission work among the industrial working class. His stipend was about £220 a year. He would stay eleven years, from 1927 to 1938, and it was his first pastorate and his only one in Wales.

What happened there is the reason people still tell the story. Among ordinary working people — dockers, drinkers, men and women whom respectable religion had given up on — lives were visibly and durably changed. Bethan Lloyd-Jones later wrote her own memoir of those years, Memories of Sandfields, and it is full of such transformations: hard men made gentle, ruined homes rebuilt. Those who were there told of the drink-broken finding they could stop, and of at least one who had trafficked in the occult turning from it altogether. Lloyd-Jones did not stage these things or advertise them; he preached, plainly and searchingly, and left the results to God. It confirmed everything he had come to believe: that the gospel reaches the disease that medicine and social improvement never touch.

He gave himself to individuals as well as to crowds — the diagnostic instinct again, the doctor sitting with one troubled soul and asking the patient questions until the real complaint surfaced. He distrusted showmanship, distrusted eloquence that carried no spiritual weight, and longed instead for what he called unction: the anointing of the Holy Spirit on a man's words without which, he believed, preaching was only lecturing.

Westminster Chapel

In 1938 he was called to Westminster Chapel in London, at first alongside the venerable G. Campbell Morgan. On Morgan's retirement in 1943 he became sole minister, and he held that pulpit until 1968, when major surgery for cancer ended his ministry there. For thirty years, week by week, he did one essentially unfashionable thing: he preached consecutively through books of the Bible, verse by verse, sometimes staying with a single epistle for years.

The great series became landmarks — a multi-year Friday-evening exposition of Romans, a long Sunday-morning journey through Ephesians, the Studies in the Sermon on the Mount, and the sermons gathered as Spiritual Depression: Its Causes and Cure. In that last book the doctor's ear is unmistakable, turning a diagnosis into a cure:

Have you realised that most of your unhappiness in life is due to the fact that you are listening to yourself instead of talking to yourself?

— D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones, Spiritual Depression

He set out his whole understanding of the work in lectures given in 1969 and published as Preaching and Preachers. Preaching, he said, was "logic on fire"; a theology that did not catch fire was to him a defective theology. He was, by then, a central figure in a wider recovery — the resurgence of Reformed and Puritan theology in Britain, the founding of the Puritan Conference, the early years of the Banner of Truth Trust, and a long labour among students through the Inter-Varsity Fellowship. He wanted none of it to rest on personality. He kept redirecting attention from the preacher to the Word and the Spirit, and he prayed and preached toward revival — a sovereign outpouring that no technique could manufacture — rather than toward numbers he could produce himself.

He longed, over a lifetime, not for a crowd he could gather by his own gifts but for a genuine visitation of God — and he distrusted every result that owed more to his eloquence than to the Spirit's power. The ambition of his prayers was that God would act, and that the preacher would be only a man on fire with a truth larger than himself.

A costly disagreement

On 18 October 1966, at the National Assembly of Evangelicals in London, Lloyd-Jones made a public appeal for evangelicals to leave doctrinally "mixed" denominations — those that also housed teachers who denied the essentials of the gospel — and to come together in visible evangelical unity. John Stott, chairing the meeting, used the chair to disagree, urging Anglican evangelicals to remain within the Church of England. The exchange opened a lasting breach, and a dividing line ran through British evangelicalism for years afterward.

It is tempting, and wrong, to make one of these men the hero and the other the villain. Both were godly; both believed they were being faithful; both paid for it. Exactly what Lloyd-Jones was calling for — a new denomination, a loose fellowship, or simply withdrawal — is still debated, and his own biographer reads him more narrowly than his critics did at the time. What is not in doubt is that two men who honoured each other found they could not walk together on this, and that the cooling of their fellowship cost them both. It is one of the honest sorrows of the story, and it should be left honest.

Do not hold me back

He preached his final sermon in 1980, at a chapel in Sussex, and then declined through his last months as the cancer advanced. In his last days, too weak to say much, he wrote a note to his wife and family. Iain Murray, his biographer, records its words:

Do not pray for healing. Do not hold me back from the glory.

— his dying note, in Iain Murray, The Fight of Faith

It was the settled verdict of a man who had spent his youth learning to postpone death and his manhood learning what death could not touch. The physician who had once fought disease at Bart's now asked to be released to the only cure that had ever finally interested him.

He asked his family not to pray for his recovery — and their answer to that prayer was to let him go. He died peacefully in his sleep on 1 March 1981, St David's Day, at Ealing, and was buried at Newcastle Emlyn in the west Wales country he had come from. The note was not resignation but confidence: the glory he had preached, he now went to see.

What he leaves

Lloyd-Jones left a large body of expository sermons still read and heard, a recovered seriousness about biblical preaching, and the memory of a man who gave up one of the most enviable careers in Britain because he had decided what was really wrong with people. "The Doctor," everyone called him, long after he had stopped practising — and the name kept telling the truth about him. He had simply changed patients, and changed the disease he was treating, and never stopped taking the case history until the real complaint came out.

He was not a martyr and not a mystic. He was a Welsh physician who read the human heart the way he had been trained to read a body, found the sickness under the symptoms, and spent fifty years offering the one remedy he had come to trust. To an ordinary reader who has never heard of him, that is the thing worth knowing: he believed the deepest trouble in every one of us is curable, and he gave up everything he had to say so.

faq.q: Who was Martyn Lloyd-Jones?
faq.a: David Martyn Lloyd-Jones (1899–1981), known as "the Doctor," was a brilliant young London physician — assistant to the King's doctor, Sir Thomas Horder — who left medicine for the ministry, convinced that humanity's deepest disease is spiritual. After eleven years pastoring working people at Sandfields in industrial South Wales, he preached expositionally at Westminster Chapel, London, for thirty years and became a central figure in the twentieth-century recovery of Reformed preaching.

faq.q: What was his medical career?
faq.a: Born in Cardiff in 1899 and raised in Welsh-speaking Cardiganshire, he moved with his family to London and trained at St Bartholomew's Hospital, one of Britain's most prestigious. The record of those years is one of relentless ability: qualifications with distinction, an MD in 1923 for research on infective endocarditis, membership of the Royal College of Physicians in 1925, and a post as chief clinical assistant to Sir Thomas Horder, physician to the Royal Household. The habit of asking what is really wrong beneath the presenting complaint would follow him into the pulpit.

faq.q: Why did he leave medicine?
faq.a: In the mid-1920s, over roughly two years, the diagnosis turned on the diagnostician. He became convinced that the deepest trouble in the people he treated was not medical but spiritual — that he could send a man home patched up and still lost, that the real disease was sin, and that he had been treating everything except the thing killing people. In 1927 he left medicine for the ministry, married Bethan Phillips (herself a qualified doctor), and the two went straight from their honeymoon to a mission hall in South Wales.

faq.q: What happened at Sandfields?
faq.a: From 1927 to 1938 he pastored the Bethlehem Forward Movement Mission Church at Sandfields, Aberavon, among the industrial working class, on a stipend of about 220 pounds a year. Among ordinary people whom respectable religion had given up on — dockers, drinkers, ruined homes — lives were visibly and durably changed. He did not stage or advertise these things; he preached plainly and searchingly and left the results to God, and it confirmed what he had come to believe: that the gospel reaches the disease medicine and social improvement never touch.

faq.q: What did he do at Westminster Chapel?
faq.a: In 1938 he was called to Westminster Chapel in London, at first alongside G. Campbell Morgan, becoming sole minister in 1943 and holding the pulpit until 1968. For thirty years, week by week, he did one unfashionable thing: he preached consecutively through books of the Bible, verse by verse, sometimes staying with a single epistle for years. The great series became landmarks — a multi-year exposition of Romans, a long journey through Ephesians, the Studies in the Sermon on the Mount, and the sermons gathered as "Spiritual Depression."

faq.q: What did he teach about preaching?
faq.a: He set out his whole understanding in lectures published as "Preaching and Preachers," defining preaching as "logic on fire" and "theology coming through a man who is on fire" — a theology that did not catch fire was, to him, a defective theology. He longed for what he called unction, the anointing of the Holy Spirit on a man's words without which preaching was only lecturing, and he distrusted showmanship and eloquence that carried no spiritual weight.

faq.q: What did he teach about the mind and spiritual depression?
faq.a: The doctor's ear is unmistakable in his best-known counsel: "Have you realised that most of your unhappiness in life is due to the fact that you are listening to yourself instead of talking to yourself?" His "Spiritual Depression: Its Causes and Cure" turned a diagnosis into a remedy — teaching the downcast believer to preach truth to his own heart rather than passively absorb its moods, exactly the instinct he had brought from the sickbed to the pulpit.

faq.q: What was his disagreement with John Stott?
faq.a: On 18 October 1966, at the National Assembly of Evangelicals, Lloyd-Jones appealed for evangelicals to leave doctrinally "mixed" denominations and come together in visible evangelical unity; John Stott, chairing, used the chair to disagree, urging Anglican evangelicals to remain in the Church of England. The exchange opened a lasting breach across British evangelicalism. Both men were godly and believed they were being faithful, both paid for it, and the cooling of their fellowship is one of the honest sorrows of the story.

faq.q: How did he die?
faq.a: He preached his final sermon in 1980 and declined through his last months as cancer advanced. Too weak to say much, he wrote a note to his family: "Do not pray for healing. Do not hold me back from the glory." It was the settled verdict of a man who had spent his youth learning to postpone death and his manhood learning what death could not touch. He died peacefully in his sleep on 1 March 1981, St David's Day, and was buried in the west Wales country he had come from.
