fields.name: Alexander Maclaren
fields.bio: Alexander Maclaren (1826–1910) was a Scottish Baptist preacher who served Union Chapel, Manchester, for forty-five years — “the prince of expository preachers,” whose lifelong daily reading of the Greek and Hebrew Scriptures fed the sermons gathered in his Expositions of Holy Scripture.
fields.tagline: Scottish Baptist of Union Chapel, Manchester: “the prince of expository preachers.”
fields.bio_html:
Alexander Maclaren was born in Glasgow on 11 February 1826, the son of David Maclaren, a merchant who was also a Baptist lay preacher — so the boy grew up hearing the Scriptures opened at home before he ever opened them in a pulpit. He was quick, bookish, and devout. He studied first at Glasgow University, and when the family moved to London he was set to train for the ministry at Stepney College, the Baptist ministerial school, entering in 1842. There he came under a teacher who shaped him for life: the Hebraist Benjamin Davies, who grounded his young student so thoroughly in Greek and Hebrew that Maclaren never afterwards let a day pass without them. It was the making of the expositor: a man who would spend half a century drawing sermons out of the very words of Scripture had first been taught to love those words in the tongues they were written in. He took the London University degree in 1845, winning a prize in the Scripture examination, and at twenty he was ready — younger than most men are when they first begin to listen to preachers, he had already been called to be one.

A three-month supply that lasted twelve years

His first charge was Portland Chapel in Southampton, which he began to serve on 28 June 1846. He was invited as a temporary supply, for perhaps three months, to a small congregation — a room for three hundred hearers, a membership of twenty, and a modest guaranteed stipend. The three months became twelve years. It was a hard, unglamorous apprenticeship, and it taught him the craft that would make him famous: how to take a single text and open it until a plain congregation saw the whole gospel standing in it.

In 1858 he was called to Union Chapel, Manchester, and there he stayed — not for a season, but for the rest of his working life. From 1858 to 1903, forty-five years, he preached to substantially the same people, in the same city, from the same book. It is one of the most remarkable long pastorates of the century, and out of it came the reputation that clung to him ever after: the prince of expository preachers. Crowds came from across the city and beyond to hear him, and young ministers came to learn; yet the man himself never courted the fame, and would have counted a single soul helped toward Christ a better return than a full gallery. Twice the Baptist Union made him its president, and when the Baptist World Alliance first gathered in London in 1905 it made the old man of Manchester its first president. But the honours never drew him from his desk, and he wore them lightly, an expositor to the last rather than a dignitary.

The study, not the lounge

Maclaren's power in the pulpit was the fruit of a discipline in the study that never relaxed. Every morning he read a chapter of the Old Testament in Hebrew and a chapter of the New in Greek — not as a scholar sharpening tools, but as a worshipper, the Word read on his knees before it was ever preached from the platform. He entered his study at nine o'clock, and — so the story went among those who knew him — he would take off his slippers and pull on a pair of heavy outdoor work boots, to remind himself that what he was about to do was hard labour. His study, he insisted, was a study, not a lounge and certainly not an office; there was no telephone, and interruptions were not welcome. He warned young ministers against letting themselves be pitch-forked into committees and tea-meetings when they ought to be at their desks with the text.

His prayer life and his study were not two things but one. The daily half-hour in the Hebrew Scriptures and the Greek New Testament was itself his devotion — the Word taken in on his knees each morning, so that when he stood to preach it, he was only handing on what he had already received in communion with God.

He refused to prepare his sermons weeks in advance. “I must give it red-hot,” he said, and he meant it — the message had to come warm from that morning's fire, not reheated from a cold week's notes. He preached, famously, without a manuscript. The habit was born of a small accident early in his ministry: notes he had tucked into his Bible blew away during a service, and he resolved on the spot never again to face his people with a scrap of paper between them. For half a century afterward he wrote out only his first few sentences and preached the rest from a single sheet of the barest headings — and the stenographers who took him down found little to correct.

What he preached

His sermons had a shape as recognisable as his voice. They ran to some forty minutes and four thousand words, close-knit to the text and almost always divided into three clear heads — so reliably that a friendly critic said he served the bread of life with a three-pronged fork. But the structure was never a cage; it was a way of carrying a congregation, point by point, into the heart of a passage until they saw it whole. He preached to persuade, not to display, and he guarded that aim jealously. To get himself out of the way, so that nothing stood between his hearers and the Christ of the text, he held to be among a preacher's first duties — and forty-five years in one pulpit, refusing the platforms and committees that would have made him a public man, was the long practice of that conviction.

What he gave his people, red-hot and note-free, was Christ — Christ set out of the text with a clarity that made men see what they had read a hundred times and never noticed. He had a gift for the memorable sentence that lodged in the memory and would not leave, and again and again his theme was the one thing he was surest of: that the human heart is made for God and is restless until it rests in him.

This world's gifts cloy and never satisfy; God satisfies and never cloys.

— Alexander Maclaren

He did not preach an anxious religion. The rest he commended was not the reward of a strenuous striving but the natural repose of a soul that has found its true home, and he pressed his hearers toward it as toward a settled and all-sufficient good.

We are at rest when we have God, and to long for Him is to insure the possession of an absolute and all-sufficing good.

— Alexander Maclaren

The forty-five years of sermons were gathered, in the end, into the great work by which most readers now know him: the Expositions of Holy Scripture, a running exposition of the whole Bible drawn straight from the pulpit of Union Chapel. It has never gone out of use. Generations of preachers who never heard his voice have learned from those volumes how to find the sermon that is already hidden in the text — how to open a verse until it yields its Christ, and then to keep out of the way while it does its work. They are not lectures but sermons still, warm off the page, and readers who come to them for a commentary find themselves preached to instead. Maclaren himself reckoned that a preacher's own comfort and effectiveness rose and fell exactly with the depth of his daily communion with God; his own long fruitfulness was simply the visible proof of a hidden life. The forty-five years at Union Chapel, the daily hour on his knees with the Greek and Hebrew, the plain sermons in their three plain heads — all of it flowed from the same conviction, that a man cannot give out what he has not first taken in.

The end of a long faithfulness

Maclaren gave up the active pastorate of Union Chapel in 1903, on the day forty-five years to the date from the day he had begun it, and was made pastor emeritus. In 1909 he retired to Edinburgh, and there, on 5 May 1910, he died, in his eighty-fifth year. His was not a life of signs and wonders — there is no famous deliverance to relate, no dramatic answer to a desperate prayer — but of something rarer and, in its way, harder: a faithfulness so steady and unbroken that it can be easy to overlook. He read the same two Testaments every morning, entered the same study, and preached to the same people, for the better part of half a century, and the freshness never failed because the fountain never failed. His life is the quiet argument of his own preaching — that the soul which has God wants for nothing, and that a man who keeps close to the fountain will never run dry.

fields.name: Isaac Watts
fields.bio: The father of English hymnody: a frail Dissenting minister who taught the church to sing the gospel in its own words, giving it “When I Survey the Wondrous Cross,” “Our God, Our Help in Ages Past” and “Joy to the World.” Laid aside by illness for years and sheltered for thirty-six by the Abney family, he also wrote Divine Songs (1715), the songs generations of children learned by heart.
fields.bio_html:
Millions of people who could not tell you who Isaac Watts was can sing his words by heart. They sing them at Christmas without knowing he never meant them for Christmas, at funerals without knowing he wrote them as a paraphrase of a psalm, and at the Lord’s Table without knowing that a small, sickly Dissenting minister first wrote them out for a communion service in London in 1707. He is called the father of English hymnody, and the title is fair. Before him, most English congregations of his tradition sang only the psalms of David, set in stiff metre. After him, the church had learned to sing the gospel in its own words.

Born beside a prison

He was born in Southampton on 17 July 1674, the eldest of a large family. His father, also Isaac, was a clothier among the town’s Dissenters, and a man who paid for his convictions: he was imprisoned for nonconformity in 1674, 1678 and 1683. Family tradition says that while he lay in the gaol, his wife sat on a stone by the prison door nursing their infant son. The story may have grown in the telling, but the world it describes is real. The boy was born into a church that was being fined, harried and locked up for meeting at all.

He was astonishingly quick. From 1680 to 1690 he was schooled at the free grammar school in Southampton under John Pinhorne, a Church of England clergyman, and by the usual account he had Latin, Greek and Hebrew while still a boy. His gift for rhyme showed itself early, and so did his seriousness. A local doctor, John Speed, offered to send him to university; but acceptance would have meant conforming to the Church of England, and the young Watts declined. He would remain a Dissenter all his life, with every door that conformity might have opened left closed behind him.

“Taught to trust in Christ”

His own record of his conversion is almost startling in its brevity. In the private memoranda he kept of the chief events of his life, he wrote that he “fell under considerable convictions of sin” in 1688, and that the following year he “was taught to trust in Christ, I hope.” That is all. There is no dramatic scene, no named preacher, no date and hour — only a boy of fourteen made serious about his sin, and a boy of fifteen finding his refuge in a Saviour, recorded with a caution that reads like humility rather than doubt. It is the quiet shape of a great many real conversions, and it is worth noticing that the man who would give the church so many words for its joy described his own beginning in so few.

From 1690 to 1694 he studied at the Dissenting academy at Stoke Newington, then a village north of London, under Thomas Rowe. There he read widely and worked hard — too hard, by most accounts, for a constitution that was never strong.

Something better to sing

After the academy he came home to Southampton, and there, around the age of twenty, the work of his life began. The story is told that he complained to his father about the dreary singing at the Above Bar chapel, where the congregation laboured through metrical psalms that were often clumsy and sometimes barely Christian in their outlook, and that his father answered, in effect, that he should write something better. He did. The hymn usually named as his first, “Behold the glories of the Lamb,” is built on the fifth chapter of Revelation, and it was received well enough that hundreds more followed.

What troubled him was not only the verse but the worship. Years later, in the preface to his hymnbook, he wrote that “the dull Indifference, the negligent and the thoughtless Air that sits upon the Faces of a whole Assembly, while the Psalm is on their Lips, might tempt even a charitable Observer to suspect the Fervency of inward Religion.” He believed the fault lay partly in the words themselves. Many of the old metrical psalms, sung exactly as David wrote them, were, as he put it, “foreign to the State of the New Testament.” The church was being asked to praise a Christ it was not allowed to name. His answer was twofold: fresh hymns of praise written from the whole of Scripture, and a new rendering of the Psalms themselves as a Christian who has seen the cross might sing them.

A pastor in London

In 1696 he went to live at Stoke Newington as tutor to the son of Sir John Hartopp, a leading Dissenting layman, and it was in that household that he gave himself to study and to preaching. He preached his first sermon on his twenty-fourth birthday, 17 July 1698. The next year he became assistant to Dr Isaac Chauncy at the Independent congregation in Mark Lane in the City of London, one of the most distinguished Dissenting pulpits in the capital. On 8 March 1702 — the day King William III died — he accepted the call to succeed Chauncy as pastor, and he was ordained on 18 March.

His health was poor from the start. By 1703 the church had to give him an assistant, Samuel Price, who was later made co-pastor. The congregation moved to Pinner’s Hall in 1704 and in 1708 built a new meeting-house in Bury Street. Watts remained its pastor for the rest of his life, though for long stretches he could do little more than pray for it.

Hymns and Spiritual Songs

In 1707 he published Hymns and Spiritual Songs, and English worship was never quite the same. The first edition carried some two hundred hymns in three books, and it was enlarged in 1709. Among them was one he had written for a communion service, under the plain heading “Crucifixion to the World by the Cross of Christ.” It begins, “When I survey the wondrous cross,” and it ends with a stanza that has been answered by generations of worshippers at the Lord’s Table:

Were the whole realm of nature mine, / That were a present far too small; / Love so amazing, so divine, / Demands my soul, my life, my all.

— Isaac Watts, “When I Survey the Wondrous Cross” (1707)

Matthew Arnold, more than a century later, was reported to call it the greatest hymn in the English language. What made it new was that it was not a paraphrase at all. It was a Christian standing before the cross in his own words — what Watts called a hymn of “human composure” — and many in his day thought such a thing presumptuous. He defended it patiently, and time was on his side.

Twelve years later came the other half of his reform: The Psalms of David Imitated in the Language of the New Testament (1719). Here he kept the psalms but let them speak of Christ. His rendering of the ninetieth psalm opened with words that have steadied English-speaking Christians ever since:

Our God, our help in ages past, / Our hope for years to come, / Our shelter from the stormy blast, / And our eternal home.

— Isaac Watts, from Psalm 90, The Psalms of David Imitated (1719)

John Wesley altered the first word to “O God” in 1738, and both forms are still sung. In the same book the ninety-eighth psalm became “Joy to the World,” printed under the title “The Messiah’s Coming and Kingdom” — a hymn about Christ’s reign rather than his birth, which the church later took up for Christmas. The seventy-second psalm became “Jesus shall reign where’er the sun.” Between his hymns and his psalms, Watts is usually credited with some seven hundred and fifty pieces.

The long illness, and a week that lasted a lifetime

In September 1712 he was struck down by a violent fever. It shook his constitution and left his nerves weakened for the rest of his life, and for more than four years — until October 1716 — he could not carry on his public ministry at all. Price shouldered the congregation.

It was in this season that Sir Thomas Abney, a Dissenter and former Lord Mayor of London, and his wife Mary invited him to their house at Theobalds in Hertfordshire to recover. He came, as he later said, intending to stay a single week. He stayed for thirty-six years, living with the family at Theobalds and, after Sir Thomas died in 1722, with Lady Abney at Stoke Newington, where she moved in 1735. His early biographers record him remarking, many years into the arrangement, that he had come to the house of his good friend Sir Thomas Abney “intending to spend but one single week” under his roof, and had extended the visit to thirty years. Lady Abney is said to have answered at once: “Sir, what you term a long thirty years’ visit, I consider as the shortest visit my family ever received.”

He never married. It was in her house, and under her care, that most of his later books were written. In the dedication to his songs for children in 1715 he said plainly that it was to her “unwearied Tenderness, and many kind Offices by Night and Day, in the more violent Seasons of my Indisposition, that (under God) I own my Life, and Power to write or think.”

Songs for children, and a guide to prayer

That same year, 1715, he published Divine Songs Attempted in Easy Language for the Use of Children. He explained to parents why he had put the faith into rhyme: “What is learnt in verse is longer retained in memory and sooner recollected.” A song running in a child’s mind, he thought, might keep off a temptation when no verse of Scripture was at hand. The little book taught generations to praise God for creation, to fear lying and idleness, and to think soberly about death. It opens with a child daring to join the praise of heaven:

Then let me join this holy train, / And my first offerings bring; / Th’ eternal God will not disdain / To hear an infant sing.

— Isaac Watts, “A General Song of Praise to God,” Divine Songs (1715)

The same year also saw A Guide to Prayer, written by a man who had spent three years too ill to preach. It is a practical book, full of directions, but its heart is a conviction about what prayer is.

To Watts, prayer was “the conversation which God allows us to maintain with himself above, while we are here below” — a converse in which the soul of a saint often gets near to God and, for a short time before heaven, dwells with its Father. He wrote his guide to help ordinary Christians learn that holy skill.

A wide mind, and an honest struggle

The invalid of Theobalds was also one of the busiest minds in England. His Logick (1725) became a standard introduction to reasoning, used for generations at Oxford, Cambridge and Yale. He wrote on education, on astronomy and geography, on the mind and its improvement, and a great deal of theology. In 1728 the universities of Edinburgh and Aberdeen made him a Doctor of Divinity. Samuel Johnson, no friend to Dissent, admired the range of it: every sensible man, he wrote, would “look with veneration on the writer who is at one time combating Locke, and at another making a catechism for children in their fourth year.”

Not all his thinking brought him peace. From The Christian Doctrine of the Trinity in 1722 onward, he struggled for years to find a way of explaining the Trinity that satisfied both his reason and his Bible, and some of his speculations troubled his friends and have been argued over ever since. What is striking is where the struggle finally went: not into a pamphlet but into a prayer.

Among his last writings, published after his death, is The Author’s Solemn Address to the Great and Ever-Blessed God. It opens, “Righteous art thou, O Lord, when I plead with thee concerning thy judgments,” and asks leave to plead “with all that humble reverence, and that holy awe of thy majesty, which becomes a creature in the presence of God.” He brought his hardest questions to God himself, on his knees.

It is an honest picture of a real believer: a man who had given the church some of its surest words, still wrestling in old age, and choosing to wrestle in the presence of God rather than away from him.

Lying down with comfort

His last years at Stoke Newington were quiet and increasingly frail. His friends recorded that when he went to bed he would often say:

I bless God. I can lie down with comfort; not being solicitous whether I awake in this world or another.

— Isaac Watts, in his last years

David Jennings, who preached his funeral sermon, preserved some of his dying sayings, among them that he believed the promises of God “enough to venture an eternity on them.” His amanuensis wrote, the day before the end, that he had passed the night quietly and was peaceful and serene. He died on 25 November 1748, aged seventy-four. He was buried in Bunhill Fields on 5 December, attended at his own request by two ministers from each of the three Dissenting denominations — Independent, Presbyterian and Baptist — together. Jennings took for his text, “He being dead yet speaketh.”

What he leaves

A monument to him stands in Westminster Abbey, carved by Thomas Banks; statues were raised in Abney Park, on the old grounds where he lived, and in his native Southampton. But the truer memorial is sung. Jennings said at his funeral that no man then living had works in such constant use or translated into so many languages, and that has only become more true.

His life is an encouragement in a particular direction. He was small, unwell and often unable to work; he was barred from the universities by his conscience, and dependent for most of his life on the kindness of friends. Out of that weakness came words that taught the church to look at the cross, to trust God across the generations, and to let its children sing. He did not preach to great crowds. He gave the crowds something to sing, and they have not stopped.

faq.q: Who was Isaac Watts?
faq.a: Isaac Watts (1674–1748) was an English Dissenting minister, poet and writer, remembered as the father of English hymnody. Born in Southampton, he pastored the Independent congregation that met at Mark Lane and later Bury Street in London, and he is usually credited with some 750 hymns and psalm versions. Before him, most congregations of his tradition sang only metrical psalms; after him, the church had learned to sing the gospel in its own words.

The hymn usually named as his first is “Behold the glories of the Lamb,” built on Revelation 5.

faq.a: He left only a very brief record of it. In the private memoranda he kept of the chief events of his life, he wrote that he “fell under considerable convictions of sin” in 1688, when he was fourteen, and that the next year he “was taught to trust in Christ, I hope.” There is no dramatic scene in the account, only a boy made serious about his sin and finding his refuge in Christ, recorded with a caution that reads like humility.

faq.a: He meant a hymn written in a believer’s own words from the whole of Scripture, rather than a close metrical paraphrase of a psalm. “When I Survey the Wondrous Cross” is the classic example: a Christian standing before the cross and answering, “Love so amazing, so divine, / Demands my soul, my life, my all.” Many in his day thought such hymns presumptuous, and Watts defended them patiently. He also rendered the Psalms themselves so that they spoke of Christ.

faq.q: Was “Joy to the World” written as a Christmas carol?
faq.a: No. Watts published it in 1719 in The Psalms of David Imitated as his Christian rendering of Psalm 98, under the title “The Messiah’s Coming and Kingdom.” It celebrates Christ’s reign rather than his birth, and it was the church that later took it up for Christmas. In the same way, “Our God, Our Help in Ages Past” is his version of Psalm 90; John Wesley changed its first word to “O God” in 1738, and both forms are still sung.

faq.a: In September 1712 a violent fever broke his health, and he could not carry on his public ministry until October 1716. In 1715 he wrote that to her tenderness “(under God) I own my Life, and Power to write or think.” He never married.

faq.a: Yes. In 1715 he published Divine Songs Attempted in Easy Language for the Use of Children, explaining to parents that “what is learnt in verse is longer retained in memory and sooner recollected.” The book taught generations of children to praise God for creation, to fear lying and idleness, and to think soberly about death; “How doth the little busy bee” and “’Tis the voice of the sluggard” come from it. It opens with a child joining the praise of heaven: “Th’ eternal God will not disdain / To hear an infant sing.”

faq.q: What did Isaac Watts teach about prayer?
faq.a: In A Guide to Prayer (1715), written after years too ill to preach, Watts called prayer “the conversation which God allows us to maintain with himself above, while we are here below,” in which the soul draws near to God. He practised it in his hardest questions too: late in life he wrestled for years over how to explain the Trinity, and his last word on it was not a pamphlet but a prayer, his Solemn Address to the Great and Ever-Blessed God.

faq.a: He died peacefully at Stoke Newington on 25 November 1748, aged seventy-four. In his last years he would often say at bedtime, “I bless God. I can lie down with comfort; not being solicitous whether I awake in this world or another,” and he was remembered as saying he believed God’s promises “enough to venture an eternity on them.” He was buried in Bunhill Fields, attended at his request by ministers of all three Dissenting denominations, and a monument to him stands in Westminster Abbey.

fields.name: Jesse Lyman Hurlbut
fields.bio: Jesse Lyman Hurlbut (1843–1930) was an American Methodist minister who spent over fifty years training Bible teachers through the Sunday school and the Chautauqua movement. His Story of the Bible (1904) and Life of Christ (1915) retold Scripture plainly and faithfully, adding nothing, so that young readers would be led straight to the Bible itself.
fields.bio_html:
Some servants of the church are remembered for a single hour — a sermon, a revival, a martyrdom. Jesse Lyman Hurlbut is remembered for something slower and humbler: more than half a century spent teaching people how to teach the Bible, and then, in his sixties and seventies, sitting down to tell its story himself in words a child could follow. He was a Methodist pastor, an editor, an organiser of classes and circles and leagues. But the thread that runs through every part of his long life is the conviction that the Scriptures belong to ordinary people, and that the best gift a teacher can give is to lead a learner straight to the Book itself.

A New York boyhood and a Methodist calling

Hurlbut was born in New York City in 1843. The record of his early years is thin. We know nothing certain of how his own faith began — no account of a conversion survives in the sources available to us — and it would be wrong to invent one. What is plain is where it led. He went to Wesleyan University in Middletown, Connecticut, the Methodist college of New England, and graduated in 1864, while the Civil War was still being fought.

That same year he taught languages at Pennington Seminary in New Jersey, a Methodist school, and soon afterwards he entered the Newark Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church. His first station was Roseville, New Jersey, in 1865–66. There followed the ordinary itinerant life of a Methodist preacher: a few years in one pulpit, then the bishop’s appointment to the next. His pastorates read like a map of northern New Jersey — Newark, Montclair, Paterson, Plainfield, Hoboken, Morristown, Orange and Bloomfield. He married Mary Matilda Chase, and together they raised a family in the parsonages of those towns.

It is worth pausing on those years, because nothing about them is famous. A young minister preaching on Sundays, visiting the sick, burying the dead, and — as every Methodist pastor of his day was expected to do — watching over the Sunday school. It was there, in the least glamorous corner of the church’s life, that Hurlbut found the work that would become his own.

Beside the lake at Chautauqua

In August 1874 two Methodist men — John Heyl Vincent, a minister who had given himself to improving the Sunday school, and Lewis Miller, an Ohio manufacturer — gathered Sunday-school teachers at Fair Point on Chautauqua Lake in western New York. They called it the National Sunday School Assembly. The idea was simple and, for its time, bold: teachers of the Bible should themselves be taught, with a real course of study, real examinations, and a diploma earned rather than given.

Hurlbut came to the lake in 1875, the assembly’s second summer, and he never really left. He became one of Vincent’s closest helpers, supervising the Normal Courses — the teacher-training classes that were the heart of the early assemblies. They were not easy. By Hurlbut’s own account only about a tenth of those who attended the classes passed the examination and took the diploma. He wanted the Bible taught well, and he did not think that could be done cheaply.

Over the following decades he became one of Chautauqua’s best-loved teachers. He taught an adult Bible class each Sunday afternoon, spoke from the great platform, and lectured in Palestine Park, the scale model of the Holy Land laid out along the lake shore, where students could walk the length of the land in a few minutes and see its hills, lake and river laid out before them. The same impulse lies behind his Manual of Biblical Geography of 1882, later known as his Bible atlas: a teacher who wants his class to understand the story must first help them see the land where it happened.

When Vincent launched the Chautauqua Literary and Scientific Circle in 1878 — a four-year course of home reading that eventually reached vast numbers of ordinary men and women across America, many of whom had never had the chance of college — Hurlbut worked alongside him in its direction. He was one of the presidents of the Circle’s first graduating class, the Class of 1882, the “Pioneers.”

He loved the place and its stories. In his history of the movement he told how the famous Chautauqua Salute began in 1877: a deaf lecturer had finished speaking, and Vincent, realising the man could not hear the applause, asked the audience to wave their white handkerchiefs instead. The gesture caught on and became one of Chautauqua’s cherished customs — a small picture of what Hurlbut prized in the whole enterprise, a community that took thought for the one who could not otherwise share in it.

An editor for the Sunday schools

From 1879 Hurlbut’s work moved from the parish to the wider church. He was drawn into the Sunday-school and tract work of the Methodist Episcopal Church, and when Vincent was elected a bishop in 1888, Hurlbut took up the editing of the denomination’s Sunday-school literature and the work of its Sunday-School Union and Tract Society. For years he prepared commentaries and notes on the International Sunday-School Lessons — the Bible passages studied week by week in thousands of classrooms.

In May 1889 a group of Methodist leaders met at Cleveland to form the Epworth League, a society for the young people of the church, and Hurlbut served as its general secretary from 1889 to 1892, through its first years. Young people, Sunday-school teachers, adult learners at the lake: in every case his instinct was the same — organise, train, supply good books, and then trust the Word of God to do its work.

His manuals for the Sunday school are plain and practical. In Organizing and Building Up the Sunday School (1910) he insisted that a school’s success “depends not on a constitution, whether written or unwritten, but upon a man” — the superintendent — because an able leader will call forth or train up able workers. It is the conviction of a man who had spent his life raising up teachers.

The story-teller of the Bible

Out of all this came the books for which he is chiefly remembered. In 1904, at sixty-one, he published Hurlbut’s Story of the Bible, which retold the whole of Scripture, from Genesis to Revelation, in one hundred and sixty-eight stories, each complete in itself and together forming a connected narrative. He explained in his preface why he had done it:

Those who in childhood learn the Story of the Bible are fortunate, for they will never forget it.

— Jesse Lyman Hurlbut, preface to Hurlbut’s Story of the Bible (1904)

His aim, he wrote, was not merely to gather the most striking episodes but to tell all the principal stories in their order, so that a reader would find not only “stories from the Bible” but the “story of the Bible.” He deliberately kept close to the language of Scripture itself, so that the book would lead the young reader to the Bible and not away from it. Wise parents, he observed, already told these stories to their little children, and both parents and children found them the most fascinating of books. The volume went through edition after edition, and its distributors have counted more than four million copies in circulation since it first appeared.

In 1915 he did the same for the Gospels in Hurlbut’s Life of Christ for Young and Old. He held himself to a strict rule. So that the book would not lead its readers “away from the Bible, but directly toward it,” he introduced no imaginary scenes and no invented conversations.

The design has been to write the biography of Jesus, not a romance founded upon his life.

— Jesse Lyman Hurlbut, preface to Hurlbut’s Life of Christ (1915)

The opening chapter of that book shows the teacher at his best. Why should everybody know the life of Christ? Hurlbut gives his reasons one by one, the way he might have given them to a class: because Jesus is the most famous man who ever lived; because his story is full of wonders, and true; because he came to show us what God is like; because his life is the pattern for ours; because wherever he is known the world is made better; and, best of all, because through him our sins may be forgiven. He tells of an artist asked to paint a man who had died years before, who painted the father by studying the face of the son — and so, he says, if we know Christ, we know God. And to the child who hears a wonderful tale and looks up to ask, “Is it all true?”, he gives a direct answer:

Wonderful indeed are the stories told of Jesus; and the greatest wonder is that they are all true.

— Jesse Lyman Hurlbut, Hurlbut’s Life of Christ (1915)

Prayer runs quietly through those pages. He tells children that God is their Father, the Father of every one in all the world, to whom any child may go as he would go to his own father for whatever he needs.

“If Jesus had done no more for us than to teach us the Lord’s Prayer, beginning with the words ‘Our Father who art in heaven,’ he would have done enough to make us love him.” So Hurlbut wrote to his young readers — and he sent the book out with a prayer of his own: “May it help many, young and old, to know Jesus better, to love him more, and to follow him more closely!”

He wrote for the church’s memory too. The Story of the Christian Church (1918) traced the church from Pentecost to his own day in a clear, compact narrative, with outlines in the margins for teachers and students. Like his Bible stories it has outlived him; in Spanish, as Historia de la Iglesia Cristiana, it is still in print and still studied.

The last years

Hurlbut never stopped being a pastor at heart. From 1909 until his retirement in 1914 he served as superintendent of the Newark District of his conference, overseeing the churches of the region where he had begun his ministry half a century before. In retirement he kept writing. In 1921 he published The Story of Chautauqua, a history of the movement told by one who had been there almost from the first summer, and dedicated to its two founders, Lewis Miller and John Heyl Vincent.

In 1924, when Chautauqua kept its fiftieth anniversary, Hurlbut — by then past eighty and one of the very few still living who had known its beginnings — gave an address on “Memories of Early Days.” He was speaking of summers he had seen with his own eyes, when the idea of teaching the teachers of the Bible was still new.

He died in New Jersey in 1930, at the age of eighty-seven. The following year a church was opened on the Chautauqua grounds and named in his memory: the Hurlbut Memorial Church, where a Methodist congregation still worships beside the lake where he taught for more than fifty summers.

A legacy of plain words

Hurlbut was not an original theologian, nor a great preacher whose sermons are still read, nor a missionary who crossed oceans. His gift was of another kind, and the church needs it just as much. He believed that the Bible could be understood by anyone who was patiently and faithfully taught, and he spent his life making that true — training teachers by the thousand, editing the lessons they taught, and at last telling the old story himself, so simply that a child could follow it and so faithfully that the child would want to go on to the Bible.

Generations of children first met Abraham and Joseph, Ruth and David, and above all Jesus, in his pages. Whenever one of them went on from his pages to the Scriptures themselves, it was exactly what he had hoped for. There are worse epitaphs for a Christian teacher than that his books led people past themselves to the Book he loved.

fields.name: F. F. Bosworth
fields.bio: F. F. Bosworth (1877–1958) was an American evangelist and early Pentecostal pioneer whose healing campaigns of the 1920s filled auditoriums across the United States and Canada. His book Christ the Healer (1924) became one of the most widely read works on divine healing, and in old age he travelled with William Branham to Africa and beyond.
fields.bio_html:
Fred Francis Bosworth spent most of his life telling sick people that God was willing to heal them, and he could tell them so because he had once been given up to die himself. He became one of the best-known healing evangelists of the twentieth century, but the moments that show him most clearly are not the packed auditoriums. They are a night walk along a Texas railway line with a broken wrist, and a family putting their heads one by one into an empty bread tin and saying “Glory.”

A prairie boy with a cornet

He was born on 17 January 1877 on a farm near Utica, Nebraska, and raised in a Methodist home. His father, Burton, was a Civil War veteran. At a soldiers’ reunion he heard a cornet played, and he wanted one so badly that he eventually traded animals for it and taught himself to play. Music stayed with him for life.

He left home at sixteen, and around that time, at a revival meeting in Omaha, he gave his life to Christ. As a young man he was diagnosed with tuberculosis and told his case was hopeless. “I coughed much of the time for ten years,” he later said, “and finally got up from what I supposed would be my death bed and went from Illinois to Georgia for the purpose of saying good-bye to my parents and brothers and sisters before going to heaven.”

His family had moved to Fitzgerald, Georgia. There, at a Methodist meeting led by a woman evangelist (his son later named her as Mattie Perry), the dying young man was prayed for. His first biographer records that she laid her hands on him and prayed that he might be healed, and “from that self-same hour Fred began to mend.”

He stayed in Fitzgerald, working as a barber, a bookkeeper and for two years the city clerk, a post he lost after backing a prohibition candidate. He led the town band, and around 1900 he married Estella Hyde. They were to have two daughters and a son.

Zion, and a new fire

In the early 1900s the Bosworths moved to Zion City, Illinois, the community that John Alexander Dowie had built around his teaching on divine healing. Bosworth kept books there until Dowie heard him play and put him in charge of the Zion band. When Dowie’s empire collapsed under debt and scandal, Bosworth lost confidence in the man, but not in the God he had preached.

In September 1906 Charles Parham came to Zion preaching the baptism in the Holy Spirit, and the Bosworth home became one of the places where seekers gathered. On the night of 18 October 1906 Fred Bosworth received the experience himself, and with it a call he dreaded. “I feared that if I gave up all to God that He would ask me to preach the Gospel,” he admitted. “I would say, ‘Lord if you should call me to preach how could I support my family; what would we live on?’” He went anyway. He evangelised with Cyrus Fockler, met William Seymour of Azusa Street in 1907, and held meetings in Indiana and across the South. About 1909 he took his family to Dallas to plant a church.

They knew one family in Dallas, and it moved away the day they arrived. For three months they prayed for revival, and they prayed for bread. Bosworth later remembered a fifty-pound lard tin where the bread was kept, and a little family custom “whenever the tin got empty — each of us in turn would put our heads into the tin and say ‘Glory.’” Once a stranger came to the door with food. The church grew into a centre of revival. In 1912 Maria Woodworth-Etter held months of meetings there.

The road to Calvert

In August 1911 Bosworth was asked to come to Hearne, Texas, where Black Pentecostals were holding a camp meeting under a tent. White onlookers who would not enter the tent had asked for a white preacher to teach them. Bosworth stood on a platform between the two crowds and preached to both. Afterward armed white men stopped him, accusing him of putting the races on a level. He told them he would not resist: “I am ready to die and will offer no resistance to anything God permit you to do.” They let him go, if he took the next train. At the station a mob of about twenty-five men beat him to the ground again and again with clubs made from boat oars. His left wrist was broken, his back was beaten raw all the way down to his knees, and they would not let him board the train.

He picked up his suitcase with his good arm and walked nine miles through the night to Calvert. Under the clubs he had prayed only that his spine would not be broken. On the walk, he wrote to his mother, “the walk to Calvert in the dark with moon light was the most heavenly experience of my life and the Lord gave me wonderful intercession for those men that He should forgive them and prepare them for his coming.” It was a month before he could lie on his back.

In that letter, written to keep his mother from worrying, he told her that if the mob had come because of some unwise thing he had done he would be very sorry, “but since it came for plain obedience in preaching His gospel to every creature, it has given me great joy.” Then he added a line that sums up the man:

I would much prefer to be faithful and have some little tribulation now than to fail to overcome and have to pass through the great tribulation soon to come.

— F. F. Bosworth, letter to his mother, August 1911

A costly conviction, and a heavier loss

When the Assemblies of God was formed in 1914, Bosworth was among its early leaders. He brought his Dallas church into the fellowship and served a term on its executive presbytery. The new denomination soon made speaking in tongues the required “initial evidence” of the baptism in the Spirit. Bosworth had spoken in tongues himself, but he did not believe Scripture taught that every Spirit-baptised believer must. He argued his case before the General Council, published a pamphlet titled Do All Speak with Tongues?, and in April 1918 resigned rather than hold credentials on terms he could not accept. His church split, and one fellow minister misrepresented him to the council and to his own congregation. He joined the Christian and Missionary Alliance and started again.

Then came his worst sorrows. His little son Vernon died at four. In November 1919 Estella died, worn out by years of hard work and weakened by influenza and tuberculosis, and she left him with two young daughters. It should not be passed over that a man about to become famous for preaching healing had just buried his wife and his son. He did not stop believing, and he did not stop preaching.

“If people didn’t get saved”

In August 1920 he held meetings in Lima, Ohio. They began so slowly that the team drove a Ford around town ringing an engine bell to draw a crowd. The pastor then asked him to preach on divine healing. He believed in healing and had prayed for the sick, but he had never made it the plain message of a campaign. The question he took to God was an honest one.

“I said to the Lord, ‘But suppose I preach Healing and the people come and then don’t get healed?’ And the Lord said, ‘If people didn’t get saved you wouldn’t stop preaching the Gospel.’” He studied and prayed until, he said, he “saw that it was God’s will to heal as well as to save.” He preached it and invited the sick to come. A visiting minister reported “a mighty revival wave” in Lima, with crowds so large that Memorial Hall had to be rented. The place that had looked hopeless became, in his words, the place where God worked most mightily.

From Lima the invitations poured in. Through the 1920s he and his brother B. B. Bosworth held long campaigns in city after city across the United States and Canada. In October 1922 he married Florence Valentine, a Nyack-trained Alliance evangelist who preached at his side for the rest of his life. The best-remembered campaign was seven weeks in Ottawa in 1924. By his own count six thousand came forward for healing and about twelve thousand for salvation, and he was sure which drew which: “I doubt if there would have been more than one thousand for salvation had it not been for the miracles of healing which displayed the compassion of the Lord.”

That same year he published his sermons as Christ the Healer, written, its preface admits, “under great pressure and weariness” between revivals. Its argument is that healing, like forgiveness, was purchased at the cross, and that faith cannot rest on a hope that God might heal. It has to rest on a knowledge that He wills to.

Faith begins where the will of God is known.

— F. F. Bosworth, Christ the Healer (1924)

Appropriating faith is not believing that God can but that He will.

— F. F. Bosworth, Christ the Healer (1924)

Enlarged in later editions, it has never gone out of print. Its teaching has also been seriously contested. Many Christians do not accept that healing is guaranteed in the atonement, and its emphasis on confession fed later “faith” teaching that others have criticised sharply. Bosworth never claimed everyone went home healed, and he himself lived with diabetes that was never cured.

A wandering, and a return

He published a magazine, Exploits of Faith, and from Chicago became a pioneer of gospel radio with the National Radio Revival. In the 1930s he also embraced British Israelism, the teaching that the Anglo-Saxon peoples descend from the lost tribes of Israel, and it cost him his standing in the Alliance. It was an error, and in 1944 he said so. He publicly apologised for having been wrong and was welcomed back.

“He did not believe in … retirement”

By 1948 he was past seventy, semi-retired and wondering, his son said, whether his course was run. Then he went to hear William Branham at a healing campaign in Miami. The two men took to each other at once, and Bosworth joined Branham’s team as a teacher and elder adviser. Branham would become a deeply controversial figure, and by one account Bosworth told him to his face in 1951 that he was wrong. But it was South Africa, that year, that changed Bosworth. Past seventy-four, he preached three and four times a day and taught crowds of tens of thousands in Durban. He spent his last years returning to Africa again and again, and preaching in Cuba, Japan and Europe.

He came home to Miami in failing health, with heart trouble and a stroke on top of the diabetes, and told his family his work was done. His son remembered the family gathered by the bed, talking, laughing and singing, when the old man looked past them all and began “to greet and hug people — he was enraptured,” for several hours. Then he lay back smiling and went to sleep. He died on 23 January 1958, six days after his eighty-first birthday.

He made real mistakes, and admitted at least one of them in public. But the young man who rose from his deathbed, the pastor who prayed all night for the men who beat him, and the old man who would not retire while anyone remained unreached are the same man. He preached above all the compassion of Christ, and he had tested it himself on a dark road outside Calvert.

fields.name: Smith Wigglesworth
fields.bio: Smith Wigglesworth (1859–1947) was a Yorkshire plumber who could not read as a boy, worked in a woollen mill from the age of seven, and became one of the best-known evangelists of early Pentecostalism. With his wife Polly he led the Bowland Street Mission in Bradford for many years; after receiving the baptism in the Holy Spirit at Sunderland in 1907 he preached faith and divine healing across Europe, America, Australasia, India and Africa, and his sermons were gathered in Ever Increasing Faith and Faith That Prevails.
fields.bio_html:
Smith Wigglesworth never pretended to be anything but what he was: a working man from the West Riding of Yorkshire, with a plumber’s hands and almost no schooling, who had been laid hold of by God. When he first visited America in 1914, the Pentecostal paper that received him put it simply: “He lays no claim to learning.” Yet the Bradford plumber who could not read as a boy became one of the most travelled preachers of his generation, and his whole message could be gathered, as he gathered it himself, into two words: only believe.

Six until six

He was born in June 1859 in Menston, a village near Bradford, to John and Martha Wigglesworth, a family so poor that there were days with no food in the house. Smith went to work at six, pulling and cleaning turnips in the fields until his small hands were sore. At seven he and his older brother went into a woollen mill. The children rose at five and worked twelve hours. “It’s a long time from six until six in the mill,” he told his father once, and his father, with tears in his eyes, answered, “Well, six o’clock will always come.” By nine he was working full time. “Schooling was not compulsory in those days,” he said long afterward, “and so I was robbed of an education.”

What the mill could not take from him was a hunger he could not remember being without. Neither of his parents knew God, but the boy would kneel in the fields and ask Him for help.

I can never recollect a time when I did not long for God.

— Smith Wigglesworth, telling his story to Stanley Frodsham

His grandmother, an old-time Wesleyan Methodist, took him to her meetings, and when he was eight a revival came to her chapel. Early one Sunday morning, as the simple congregation sang and clapped around the big stove about “the Lamb, the bleeding Lamb,” the boy looked to Christ and knew that he was born again. He saw then, he said, that God “has made the condition as simple as He possibly could — ‘Only believe.’” The first soul he won was his own mother.

But he had no words. When he stood up in testimony meetings he could only weep. In Bradford, where the family moved when he was thirteen, he carried a Testament everywhere, though he could make out little of it. Chosen with six other boys to give a fifteen-minute missionary talk at the Wesleyan chapel, he prepared the only way he knew: “For three weeks I lived in prayer.”

The plumber and the preacher

At sixteen he threw himself in with the Salvation Army, newly arrived in Bradford, whose all-nights of prayer and fierce zeal for souls matched his own. At the mill a godly Plymouth Brethren steam-fitter taught him plumbing, believer’s baptism and the hope of the Lord’s return. In his early twenties, in Liverpool, he spent nearly all his wages feeding the barefoot children of the docks and fasted every Sunday. Asked to speak, he could never get through without tears: “like Jeremiah,” he said, “I was a man with a fountain of tears.”

Back in Bradford at about twenty-three, he set up in business for himself as a plumber and there met, in his own words, “the best girl in the world.” Mary Jane Featherstone — Polly — was a Salvation Army preacher of real gifts, and on 4 December 1882 they were married at St Peter’s Church, Bradford. It was Polly who taught her husband to read, and the Bible remained, as he often said, almost the only book he ever read. They had five children: Alice, Seth, Harold, Ernest and George.

Together they opened a small mission in Bowland Street, in the Manningham district of Bradford, which was their spiritual home for some thirty years. For twenty years they sat on the platform there together — Polly the practised preacher, Smith the plumber who still could hardly speak in public without tears. He was honest in later years about what she had to bear. “I can remember the time when I used to go white with rage, and shake all over with temper,” he confessed. He waited on God for ten days, and Polly testified to the difference: “I never saw such a change.”

A faint glimpse of the Healer

His healing ministry began almost by accident. Stanley Frodsham records how Wigglesworth used to pay the fares of poor and sick neighbours and take them each week to a divine-healing meeting in Leeds. When the Leeds leaders went away to the Keswick Convention, they left the protesting plumber in charge. Fifteen came forward for prayer, among them a man on crutches who, as Frodsham tells it, was soon jumping about without them. “I am sure it was not my faith,” he said, “but it was God in His compassion coming to help me in that hour of need.”

He and Polly made a strict vow that no medicine or doctor would come into their house, and soon it was tested. For six months he had suffered from appendicitis. One Sunday the pain brought him down at an open-air meeting and two men helped him home.

He had, he said, only “a faint glimpse of Jesus as the Healer.” That night he and Polly prayed until morning. “All night I was praying, pleading for deliverance,” he remembered, “but none came.” By daylight he was worse. Polly sent for the doctor, who found him too weak even for an operation and left the house without hope.

After the doctor had gone, an elderly woman known for her prayers came to the door with a young man. While she prayed, the young man laid hands on the sick plumber and rebuked the evil in Jesus’ name, and Wigglesworth says he was instantly free of pain. He got up and went off with his tools to a plumbing job. The doctor returned to find the bed empty and warned, “They will bring him back a corpse, as sure as you live.” Years later, telling the story from the platform, Wigglesworth added: “Well, I’m the corpse.”

Sunderland

In late October 1907 Wigglesworth went to All Saints’, Monkwearmouth, in Sunderland, where Alexander Boddy was vicar and people were said to be speaking in tongues as at Pentecost. Convinced he already had all there was to have, he questioned and argued until, he admitted, “the people wished I had never come.” But he was hungry.

One night, having left his key in his other clothes, he went home with a missionary he had been quarrelling with. “But do you think we went to bed that night? Oh, no, we spent the night in prayer.” For four days, he said, “I wanted nothing but God.”

On his last day, with a train to catch at four, he went to the vicarage to say goodbye and asked Mary Boddy, the vicar’s wife, to lay hands on him. “It isn’t tongues you need,” she told him, “but the Baptism.” She prayed, and was called out of the room, and he was left alone with God. He saw, he said, the empty cross and Jesus glorified, and was so overwhelmed by a sense of cleansing that he cried “Clean! Clean! Clean!” — and found himself worshipping in tongues.

Polly was not immediately impressed. “I am as much baptized in the Holy Ghost as you are,” she said, and sat at the back to watch him preach alone. Before long she was saying to herself, “That is not my Smith that is preaching. Lord, you have done something for him.” By the end of the evening, he said, fourteen people were on the floor under the power of God, “my own wife included.”

The plumbing business could not survive the calls that followed. He knew how unlikely a preacher he was:

There never was a weaker man on the platform. Language? None. Inability — full of it.

— Smith Wigglesworth, Ever Increasing Faith

“Her work is done”

In 1913 the partnership ended. Polly had once said to him, “You watch me when I’m preaching. I get so near to heaven when I’m preaching that some day I’ll be off.” He was leaving for Glasgow, having said goodbye to her before her evening meeting, when a doctor and a policeman met him at the door with the news that she had collapsed and died at the door of the mission. He told the story many times afterward, and told it plainly: he went up to her body and commanded death to give her up, and “she came back to me for a moment. Then God said to me, ‘She is Mine; her work is done.’” At the coffin he asked his children, “Is she there?” “No, father,” they said.

I knew she had got what she wanted.

— Smith Wigglesworth, on Polly’s death

He was fifty-three, and the widest part of his life still lay ahead.

To the ends of the earth

In 1914 he crossed to America for the first time. After the war the invitations multiplied. In 1920 he held crowded meetings in Switzerland, where doctors in one town tried to have him arrested. In 1921 he was in Norway, Sweden and Denmark, where police on horseback held back the crowds; when the Swedish authorities forbade him to lay hands on the sick, he simply asked the people to lay hands on themselves while he prayed. Writing home from Scandinavia, he did not describe himself as a conqueror.

I am at the feet of Jesus, and weep through my address, and God breaks up the people, and there are rows of people each night seeking salvation.

— Smith Wigglesworth, letter from Scandinavia, 1921

In 1922 he sailed to Australia and New Zealand; in 1926 he preached in India and Ceylon; he ministered widely in the United States in the later 1920s, and went on to South Africa, the Pacific and much of Europe. His daughter Alice, who had married the Congo missionary James Salter, often travelled and ministered with him; one woman he prayed for remembered him asking Alice to lay her hands on her alongside his own. His sermons, taken down as he spoke, were gathered into two books, Ever Increasing Faith (1924) and Faith That Prevails (1938).

He was not an easy man, and it would be dishonest to make him one. He was blunt, impatient with what he called unbelief, and at times rough with the very people he prayed for; one who knew him recalled him striking the afflicted part of the body and insisting it was the devil he was hitting. The no-medicine vow of his early years was a hard standard. And the legends grew faster than the records: the number of people he is said to have raised from the dead runs from three to more than a hundred, depending on who is telling it, and such stories cannot now be checked. What can be read, in his own words, is a man who gave God the credit every time, who wept as he preached, and who pressed on ordinary people the simple conviction that God means what He says.

Going home

He went on preaching into his late eighties. On 12 March 1947, at Glad Tidings Hall in Wakefield, he attended the funeral of his friend Wilf Richardson, and there, at the age of eighty-seven, he died. He was buried at Nab Wood Cemetery, near Shipley. The next year Frodsham published Smith Wigglesworth: Apostle of Faith, and the name stuck.

It is a fair title, so long as the faith is understood as he understood it — never as his own. The mill boy who could not find words, the plumber whose wife taught him his letters, believed to the end that everything he had came from a God who wanted him more than he wanted God, and who had made the condition as simple as He possibly could.

fields.name: John G. Lake
fields.bio: John G. Lake (1870–1935) was a Canadian-born Pentecostal preacher and faith healer who, after his wife’s healing in the circle of John Alexander Dowie, helped found the Apostolic Faith Mission of South Africa (1908–1913). Returning to America, he opened his “Divine Healing Rooms” in Spokane and later worked in Portland, leaving a lasting and much-debated legacy in the healing movement.
fields.bio_html:
John Graham Lake was born on 18 March 1870 at St. Mary’s, Ontario, one of sixteen children in a household that knew more of the sickroom than most. His parents, he remembered, were strong and healthy people, yet one after another their children sickened, and before Lake was a grown man the family had buried eight of them. Looking back over his boyhood, he recalled it as a long procession of doctors and nurses, hearses and gravestones, a brokenhearted mother and a grieving father trying to hold together those who were left. When he was a teenager the family moved across the border to Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan. The question that would govern his whole life — does God still heal? — was pressed on him early.

A house of sickness, and a turning

He grew up in the Methodist church and later said he had been ordained a Methodist minister at twenty-one, though no record of seminary study has been found. What the records do show is a young man working with his hands: the 1900 census lists him as a carpenter, and the historian Barry Morton has traced him as a small builder and roofer who bought, repaired and sold houses. In February 1893 he married Jennie Stevens of Newberry, Michigan. They would have six children and adopt a seventh.

Very soon after the wedding, as Lake told it, the shadow that had followed his father’s family fell on his own. Jennie developed heart disease and tuberculosis. She would lose consciousness without warning; he would find her collapsed on the floor, and the doctors turned at last to nitroglycerine tablets to keep her heart beating. At the same time his brother, an invalid for twenty-two years, and two of his sisters were dying.

Into that darkness came the preaching of John Alexander Dowie, the healing evangelist whose “Healing Homes” in Chicago drew the desperate from across the continent. Lake’s family carried the brother there, and, by Lake’s account, he rose from what had seemed his deathbed and walked. A sister with cancers followed, carried in on a stretcher. Another sister, Lake wrote, was brought back from the edge of death while he knelt with his parents at her bed and rebuked the power of death in the name of Jesus.

Jennie was the last. Her husband later described the morning when a fellow minister, with tears in his eyes, advised him to be reconciled to letting her die, and how, going home in a storm of grief, he threw his Bible on the table and it fell open at Acts 10:38 — Jesus “healing all that were oppressed of the devil.” From that verse he drew the conviction that sickness was the devil’s work and not God’s will, a conviction that shaped, for good and for ill, everything that came after.

In April 1898, in the orbit of Dowie’s ministry, Lake and Jennie fixed an hour — half past nine in the morning — and he telephoned and telegraphed friends to pray with them. Lake wrote that he knelt at her deathbed and called on the living God, and that she threw back the bedclothes and stood on the floor, crying, “Praise God, I am healed!” Newspapers carried the story, and people began coming to the Lakes’ door asking for prayer. “We were forced into it,” he wrote.

That same year Lake opened a small branch of Dowie’s Christian Catholic Church in Sault Ste. Marie, meeting in the attic of his parents’ home. In 1901 he moved his family to Zion, Illinois, the theocratic town Dowie had built north of Chicago, and worked in its construction department.

Business, and the claim to have left it

Lake would later tell a dramatic story about these years: that he moved to Chicago, made a fortune in real estate, bought a seat on the Board of Trade, and was paid fifty thousand dollars a year to organize a trust of insurance companies — and that he laid it all down for the gospel. In his own telling, his heart became so divided that business interviews kept turning into prayer meetings, until he told his company president he could not go on. He took three months to preach, and at the end of them, he said, he made his decision.

I am through forever with everything in life but the proclamation and demonstration of the Gospel of Jesus Christ.

— John G. Lake

Honesty requires a caution here. Morton’s research in local newspapers and church directories found Lake still living in Zion throughout these years, working after 1905 as a salesman of real estate and of fire and life insurance in nearby Waukegan — in Morton’s words, “an ordinary, small-town insurance salesman.” Even Lake’s sympathetic biographer, Kemp Burpeau, found no evidence beyond Lake’s own word for his dealings with great financiers. Lake was a gifted storyteller, and the story of the surrendered fortune grew in the telling. What remains beyond dispute is that he did give himself wholly to preaching, and never went back.

Pentecost in Zion

After Dowie’s fall, Zion was a shaken and divided town, and in 1907 Charles Parham’s Pentecostal tent meetings found many hearers there. Lake was among them. He began to seek what Pentecostals called the baptism in the Holy Spirit, and he sought it for a long time.

“I prayed for the Baptism of the Holy Spirit for nine months,” Lake said, “and if a man ever prayed honestly, and sincerely in the faith, I did.” The answer came in 1907, as he knelt to pray with a friend in Zion City. He described it ever after as the most vivid spiritual experience of his life — an overwhelming sense of Christ’s love for a lost and suffering world, and an anguished promise to follow Him all the way, even unto death.

The Pentecostal circle in Zion did not stay peaceful. In 1907, after Parham’s departure, violent attempts at exorcism among the Pentecostal remnant ended in deaths, and Zion’s new overseer, Wilbur Voliva, publicly held Parham, Lake’s friend Tom Hezmalhalch and Lake himself partly responsible. Lake and Hezmalhalch moved to Indianapolis. Morton reads this as flight from an angry town; the South African Pentecostal scholar Marius Nel argues that the evidence does not bear that reading out. Either way, the Indianapolis winter was a turning point. There, Lake said, the call to Africa he had felt since boyhood became clear, and in February 1908, after he and Tom had knelt together by Tom’s bed to pray for the two thousand dollars the journey would cost, four drafts of five hundred dollars each arrived by post.

South Africa

The party sailed that spring — by Lake’s count his family of eight and four others, by Morton’s reckoning seventeen people in all — and landed at Cape Town with almost nothing in hand. In Johannesburg an American missionary, Mrs. C. L. Goodenough, met them and gave them a home. Within months Lake and Hezmalhalch had gathered many of the scattered followers of Dowie’s South African work and founded the Apostolic Faith Mission of South Africa. Lake preached at the Apostolic Tabernacle in Johannesburg and travelled widely across the country.

The first year cost him dearly. On 22 December 1908, only some six months after their arrival, Jennie died in Johannesburg; by the usual telling Lake was away preaching when she was taken. He called her death “Satan’s masterstroke.” He stayed on for four more years, raising seven children with the help of his sister Irene.

Those years were marked by great fruit and by serious controversy, and both belong in the record. Some of the men Lake worked beside became pillars of African Christianity. Elias Letwaba, a Black preacher of deep prayer, went on to found and run the Patmos Bible School for more than twenty years; Edward Lion became a founder of the Zionist churches of southern Africa and a mentor of Engenas Lekganyane, who founded the Zion Christian Church, today among the largest churches in the region. Lake’s influence on the whole Pentecostal and Zionist movement there is not in doubt.

Neither are the questions. In 1909 and 1910 Lake faced accusations of misusing mission funds, of ruling the young church like “a second Dowie,” and of exaggerating the revival to supporters abroad. The AFM’s leaders cleared him, and a Los Angeles mission that had sent money declared itself satisfied that it had been well spent. Yet as early as January 1909 the AFM’s own executive council admitted there was “only too much truth” in complaints of exaggerated healing reports, and Morton has shown that at least one expedition Lake later described as a triumph was reported at the time as a fiasco. Lake reported healings and converts in enormous numbers; those figures come from Lake and his admirers and cannot now be checked. Morton goes further and charges deliberate fraud; Nel answers that Morton’s case rests too often on assumption and on a worldview that rules out the miraculous from the start. A reader can hold both things together: a man who was, as even Nel concedes, “prone to exaggerate,” and a ministry through which a great many people came to faith.

The Healing Rooms

Lake returned to America early in 1913, and that September he married Florence Switzer; they had five children. After a year of travelling ministry he settled in Spokane, Washington, by the summer of 1914, and there he opened the work for which he is best remembered in America: “Lake’s Divine Healing Rooms,” run from 1915 until 1920 in the Rookery Building downtown. Lake trained workers he called “healing technicians,” and the sick came for prayer day after day, some from great distances. The large totals of healings later attached to those five years are, again, the ministry’s own reckoning. He wrote that some came from five thousand miles away.

In 1920 he moved to Portland, Oregon, for a similar work of about five years, then carried it down the California coast and as far as Houston, Texas, before returning to Spokane in 1931 to open one last church and healing room.

The consecration

Among Lake’s papers is a written consecration, a set of principles by which he meant to live. It speaks of holding every possession in trust for God, of paying workers justly, of guarding the sanctity of marriage, of refusing to spread evil reports. One promise concerns prayer — that he would never “cease to cry to God and implore Him to deliver mankind from the effects of sin so long as sin lasts.” Another reads almost as a confession of what he knew he needed.

I shall live my life in meekness, never defending my own personal rights, but shall leave all judgment to God who judges righteously.

— John G. Lake, from his consecration

He did not always live up to those words, as the record shows; but they show what he reached for.

In 1935 he suffered a serious stroke, and on 16 September 1935 he died in Spokane, aged sixty-five. He left behind a complicated inheritance. His sermons are still read and his name still carried by healing ministries on several continents; his South African church and the African preachers he stood beside have long outgrown anything he built alone. His stories, too, have outlived him, and some of them cannot bear the weight that has been put on them. Yet beneath the legend is a man whose childhood was spent at gravesides and who never stopped believing that the Christ of the Gospels still meets the sick and the dying. He prayed for them by the thousands, from a Michigan bedside to a Johannesburg tabernacle to a Spokane office building, and he spent his life telling anyone who would listen that the days of Jesus’ compassion were not over.
