fields.name: John R. Mott
fields.bio: John R. Mott (1865–1955) was an American Methodist layman who gave his life to “the evangelization of the world in this generation.” Converted to lifelong service as a Cornell student, he led the Student Volunteer Movement, founded the World’s Student Christian Federation, chaired the 1910 Edinburgh Missionary Conference, and shared the 1946 Nobel Peace Prize. A tireless traveller and a man of the “morning watch,” he helped lay the foundations of the International Missionary Council and the World Council of Churches.
fields.bio_html:
John Raleigh Mott was born on the 25th of May, 1865, at Livingston Manor in Sullivan County, New York, the third of four children and the only son. When he was four months old his parents, John and Elmira Mott, carried him west to Iowa, and the boy grew up in Postville, a prairie village of fewer than five hundred people near the Mississippi. His father prospered in the lumber trade and became the town’s first mayor; his mother read constantly and never missed a Methodist prayer meeting. He later said those boundless plains had kindled his imagination for worldwide plans.

In the winter of 1878–79 a Quaker evangelist named J. W. Dean, secretary of the Iowa Young Men’s Christian Association, spent several weeks in Postville. Scores of townspeople were converted, the elder Mott among them, and his thirteen-year-old son felt the first serious stirrings of faith. The local Methodist pastor, Horace Warner, took the boy in hand, directed his reading, and persuaded his father to send him to college. At sixteen he went to Upper Iowa University at Fayette, where he won prizes in debate. But he meant to be a lawyer and a politician, and partly to escape the pressure toward religious work, he moved in 1885 to Cornell University.

Three sentences at Cornell

He was lonely at first, and restless. Within two months he was writing home that he had long felt he was “meant for something more than a business life,” though in what sphere he could not yet say. That winter J. E. K. Studd, the Cambridge cricketer and brother of C. T. Studd, came to Cornell. On Friday evening, the 15th of January, 1886, Mott hesitated a long while before going to hear him, arrived late, and slipped into a seat at the back of the botanical lecture room just as Studd gave out his text. Decades later Mott told a student convention what happened.

These words went straight to the springs of my motive life. I have forgotten all else that the speaker said, but on these few words hinged my life-investment decision. I went back to my room not to study but to fight.

— John R. Mott

The words were three short sentences: “Seekest thou great things for thyself? Seek them not. Seek ye first the Kingdom of God.” The next afternoon he found the courage to call on Studd, who sent him back to the New Testament itself and urged him to rest the guidance of his life on a personal relationship with Christ. But the ground had been prepared for weeks, and the struggle had been waged on his knees.

Two days after Studd’s address, Mott wrote to his parents that the decision had not come suddenly. Through the previous term, he said, “I then went to God in prayer and night after night I implored Him to reveal to me in an unmistakable manner what He would have me do in this world.” Answer seemed slow in coming; then one afternoon he and a friend put their textbooks aside, examined their motives honestly, and went down on their knees together, and he knew that he “must work in His vineyard.”

The letter began: “I have glad news for you for your prayers have been answered.” Later he told his father to dispose of the business he had held for his only son. The fuller surrender, Mott always said, came gradually. He spent much of that year serving prisoners in the county jail, and set himself to a hard, honest study of the resurrection, and he never forgot the day when, with his notes spread across the desk and the faded rag carpet, he could say with Thomas, in full intellectual honesty, “My Lord and my God.”

The Mount Hermon hundred

That summer Cornell sent him as its delegate to the first international Christian student conference, called by Dwight L. Moody at Mount Hermon, Massachusetts, in July 1886. Two hundred and fifty-one young men from eighty-nine colleges gathered for four weeks, and for nearly two of them nobody spoke of foreign missions. But a Princeton student, Robert Wilder, had come after weeks of prayer, backed by the prayers of his sister Grace, convinced that God would call many of those men to the mission field.

Wilder gathered the students who were even thinking about missionary service. Twenty-one came, though only three or four had decided, and this small group began to pray that God would set apart many men for the work. In Mott’s own account, “In a few days they were to see their faith rewarded far more than they had dared to claim.” After a night of appeals by young men of ten nations, the twenty-one had become exactly one hundred by the close of the conference, and John Mott was one of them.

From that pledge grew the Student Volunteer Movement for Foreign Missions, formally organized in 1888, with Mott as chairman of its executive committee for the next thirty-two years. The movement took as its watchword “The Evangelization of the World in This Generation.” In 1900 Mott explained the phrase in a book of that title. He insisted that it did not promise the conversion of the world: “It means to give all men an adequate opportunity to know Jesus Christ as their Saviour and to become His real disciples.” And he never let the plan stand apart from prayer. “The missionary church is a praying church,” he wrote. “The history of missions is a history of prayer.”

He graduated from Cornell in 1888 with Phi Beta Kappa honours. That September, after long searching of heart, he agreed to serve for one year as a travelling college secretary of the YMCA. He stayed with the work for the rest of his life. In November 1891 he married Leila Ada White of Wooster, Ohio. She shared his work for more than sixty years, and they had two sons and two daughters.

The morning watch

In 1895, at Vadstena Castle in Sweden, Mott and the Swede Karl Fries founded the World’s Student Christian Federation. As its general secretary Mott set out at once on a world tour through some two dozen countries, helping to form national student movements in India, Ceylon, China, Japan, Australia, and New Zealand. He pressed on students everywhere the “morning watch,” by which he meant spending at least the first half-hour of every day alone with God in Bible study and prayer. He called the first hour “preeminently the still hour,” and urged his readers to form “an undiscourageable resolution” to keep it.

The true object should be (and it is necessary to remind ourselves of this constantly) to meet God, to hear His voice, to receive guidance and strength from Him, which will enable me to please Him today in thought, in word, in activity.

— John R. Mott, The Morning Watch

Some of his most vivid lessons in the practice came from the students he met abroad. In Japan he was woken more than an hour before daybreak and led across the city and the valley to the crest of a hill, where the members of a college Christian association met for prayer as they always did. “Let then these nations teach us,” he wrote, the deeper meaning of the early Christians’ practice.

Travel became the pattern of his life. He crossed the Atlantic more than a hundred times and the Pacific fourteen times, and by one reckoning he covered some two million miles, at an average of thirty-four days a year at sea. He studied each country’s history and religion before he arrived, and the Nobel Committee later remarked that he never carried the gospel abroad “in an American style.”

Edinburgh, and a world at war

In June 1910 he presided over the World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh, where some twelve hundred delegates of the Protestant missionary societies met for ten days of careful study. On the closing evening, the 23rd of June, Mott rose to send them home.

The end of the Conference is the beginning of the conquest. The end of the planning is the beginning of the doing.

— John R. Mott, closing address, Edinburgh, 1910

The rest of that address was more searching than triumphant. The conference, he said, had humbled them as they discovered “that the greatest hindrance to the expansion of Christianity lies in ourselves.” He asked leaders to go quietly home and revise their plans “not in the light of our resources, but of His resources and wishes.” He admitted how flat and timid their intercession had been. He chaired the committee that carried Edinburgh’s work forward, and in 1921 that committee became the International Missionary Council, which he led until 1942.

Four years after Edinburgh the world went to war, and much of what Mott had built across borders was torn apart. Christian students who had prayed together now faced each other across the trenches. Mott had already declined President Wilson’s offer of the ambassadorship to China. He now served on a commission to Mexico in 1916 and on the special diplomatic mission to Russia in 1917. As general secretary of the YMCA’s National War Work Council he raised vast sums for work among soldiers and for the relief of prisoners of war on both sides, and he received the Distinguished Service Medal. When the Nobel Committee later spoke of his long life, it said plainly that it had brought him “profound disappointments,” and that these had never broken his spirit.

There were other disappointments too. The watchword that had fired a generation drew criticism from the German mission historian Gustav Warneck and others who thought it overconfident, and the generation it named passed without its fulfilment. After the peak of the student conventions around 1920, the Student Volunteer Movement began to lose its focus on Bible study, evangelism, and the missionary call. Mott remained steady through it all. He presided at world missionary conferences at Jerusalem in 1928 and Tambaram in 1938, and in the Second World War again gave himself to aid for prisoners of war.

The servant of all

In 1946, at eighty-one, he shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Emily Greene Balch, “for his contribution to the creation of a peace-promoting religious brotherhood across national boundaries.” In his Oslo lecture on the 13th of December he spoke of the leadership the post-war world required. Leaders must rely, he said, on “the superhuman resources,” and above all on “the superhuman power of prayer.” He ended with the words of Christ: “He who would be greatest among you shall be the servant of all.” Two years later, at Amsterdam, the new World Council of Churches elected him its honorary president, and the old man stood in his academic robes before the assembly of churches whose unity he had spent his life preparing.

Leila died in 1952, after more than sixty years of marriage. The next year, in his late eighties, he married Agnes Peter. John R. Mott died at his home in Orlando, Florida, on the 31st of January, 1955, at the age of eighty-nine, and was buried in the Washington National Cathedral. At the memorial service in New York his friend Ralph Sockman summed up the secret of his influence: he was so great a master of men, Sockman said, because he was so truly a servant of God. Yet the heart of his life lies further back than any movement he founded: in a young man praying night after night in an Ithaca rooming house, in a hundred students on a New England hillside, and in the first half-hour of each day given to God. A prayer of his, printed in the YMCA’s memorial folder, asks the Father that each one present might be placed “afresh at Thy disposal in Thine unerring and loving hands.” That is where John Mott had tried to live since the winter night at Cornell.

fields.name: Billy Sunday
fields.bio: Billy Sunday (1862–1935) was an American baseball player turned evangelist, a Chicago White Stockings outfielder converted outside the Pacific Garden Mission who became the most famous revivalist of the early twentieth century. Preaching in wooden tabernacles to vast crowds, he called hundreds of thousands to “hit the sawdust trail” for Christ and was a leading voice in the campaign for Prohibition.
fields.bio_html:
Billy Sunday never saw his father. William Sunday, a bricklayer, enlisted in the Twenty-third Iowa Infantry in the summer of 1862, and four months later, on the 19th of November, his wife gave birth to a third son in a two-room log cabin near Ames, Iowa, and named the boy after the soldier who was away. Private Sunday died of disease in a camp at Patterson, Missouri, on the 22nd of December, a little more than a month after the child was born. The boy who would one day draw larger crowds than any American evangelist before him began his life as one of the war’s many small casualties: fatherless, poor, and very soon on his own.

A soldier’s orphan

His mother, Mary Jane, kept her three boys together as long as she could, with help from her father. But the wolf, as Sunday put it, scratched at the cabin door, and at last she told her sons she was sending two of them to the Soldiers’ Orphans’ Home. Woken at a hotel in Ames for a train in the small hours, he saw that his mother’s eyes were red. “All the time Ed and I slept,” he said, “mother had been praying.” She put an arm around each boy on the platform and sobbed as though her heart would break.

He spent about two years in the orphanages at Glenwood and Davenport. By fourteen he was shifting for himself — doing farm chores in Nevada, Iowa, attending the high school there without graduating, working as a school janitor. He liked to say he had crawled out of “the university of poverty and hard knocks.”

The fastest man in the National League

In Marshalltown, Iowa, where he ran with the fire brigade team and played ball for the town, he was noticed by Cap Anson, the captain of the Chicago White Stockings, the champions of the National League. In 1883, not yet twenty-one, Sunday went straight from the Iowa sandlots to Chicago. He never became much of a hitter, but he was reckoned the fastest runner in the league, and the bleachers loved his diving catches and head-first slides. He played five seasons in Chicago and then moved to Pittsburgh and Philadelphia.

A curbstone recruit

One Sunday afternoon in Chicago — in 1886 or 1887; the sources differ — he and several teammates came out of a saloon and sat down on a curb. Across the street a band from the Pacific Garden Mission was playing horns and trombones and singing the gospel hymns he had heard his mother sing in the log cabin. The memories came flooding back, and he sobbed. A young man from the band invited them down to the mission. Sunday stood up and spoke to his friends.

I’m through. I am going to Jesus Christ. We’ve come to the parting of the ways.

— Billy Sunday, recalling the street corner in Chicago

Some of them laughed and some mocked. He went to the mission again and again, and there, after conversation and prayer with Mrs. Clark, the wife of the mission’s founder, he made his decision. “I groped my way out of darkness into the arms of Jesus Christ,” he said long afterwards, “and I fell on my knees and cried ‘God be merciful to me a sinner!’” He dreaded the ridicule waiting at the ballpark, but the first man to meet him inside the gate the next morning was the team’s great star, Mike “King” Kelly: “Bill, I’m proud of you! Religion is not my long suit, but I’ll help you all I can.” Anson and the rest followed with the same encouragement.

The change in him was plain to teammates and fans alike. He gave up swearing, gambling and the saloon, refused to play ball on the Lord’s Day, and joined the Jefferson Park Presbyterian Church, where he threw himself into the mid-week prayer meeting and the Christian Endeavor society. There he met Helen Amelia Thompson — Nell — the capable daughter of a prosperous Scottish Presbyterian in the dairy business. Her father did not want a professional ballplayer for a son-in-law; her mother took Billy’s side, and in the end her father relented. They were married in the Thompson home on the 5th of September, 1888, and spent their honeymoon travelling with the team. For the next forty-seven years he would make almost no decision without her.

The parting of the ways

Sunday’s Christianity kept pulling him away from the diamond. He was in demand at YMCA meetings, though he was then a poor, stumbling speaker. In the spring of 1891, bound by a three-year contract with Philadelphia, he put the question to God in the plainest terms he knew: if God wanted him out of baseball and in Christian work, let the club release him before the 25th of March. On the 17th a letter came from the club’s president granting the release. Then the Cincinnati club arrived with a contract for $3,500 and a first month’s pay in advance. His father-in-law told him he was a fool not to take it.

Sunday went home and went to bed, but he could not sleep. By his own account he “prayed that night until five o’clock,” until he “seemed to get the thing straight” — and then he said, “No, sir, I will not do it.” He had asked God for a sign, the release had come, and he would not go back on his word.

He went to work for the Chicago YMCA as an assistant secretary for about eighty-three dollars a month — money that was sometimes months late. For three years he visited the sick, prayed with the troubled, and carried invitations into saloons, learning at close range what drink could do to a family. In 1893 he became the assistant to J. Wilbur Chapman, one of the best-known evangelists of the day — his advance man, organizing prayer meetings and choirs, driving tent pegs, and listening night after night to a master preacher at work. Chapman taught him to build a sermon, and pressed on him the importance of prayer.

Then, over the holidays of 1895–96, a telegram came: Chapman was returning to the pastorate, and the work was over. Sunday had a wife, two children, no job, and no money. He could not go back to baseball.

“I laid it before the Lord,” he told the journalist William T. Ellis, “and in a short while there came a telegram from a little town named Garner, out in Iowa, asking me to come out and conduct some meetings.” He knew no one there. He had eight sermons, enough for ten days. He went in January 1896 — and from that day, he said, he never once had to seek an invitation to preach.

I have just gone on, as the Lord opened the way, trying to do his work. I had no plan for this sort of thing. It is all the Lord’s doings.

— Billy Sunday, to William T. Ellis

The sawdust trail

For twelve years he worked what he called the “kerosene circuit,” some seventy small towns, most of them in Iowa and Illinois, without electric light. When a snowstorm in Salida, Colorado, flattened his tent in 1906, he began to insist that towns build him plain wooden tabernacles, their floors strewn with sawdust to deaden the noise. In the Puget Sound country, among loggers who knew what it was to follow a sawdust trail home out of the forest, walking forward at the invitation became “hitting the sawdust trail.” From 1908 Nell travelled with him and ran the whole enterprise, leaving the younger children with a nanny; a staff grew around them, among them the song leader Homer Rodeheaver.

On the platform Sunday was unlike anything American religion had seen. He ran, stood on the pulpit, smashed chairs, and slid across the stage like a runner stealing home, in a torrent of slang. Many ministers were scandalized, and not without reason — he could be coarse and cruel. But beneath the performance lay something the crowds did not always see.

Before a hammer was lifted on a tabernacle, the churches of a city were divided into districts and blocks for cottage prayer meetings, held wherever possible in the homes of the unconverted. Conversions were often reported before the evangelist arrived.

Before the Pittsburgh campaign of 1913–14, in the weeks of December alone, 4,137 prayer meetings were held in private homes across the city, with a combined attendance of 68,360 people. With such a sea of prayer beneath him, Ellis concluded, any preacher could have had a revival.

Sunday’s own habit was the same. Ellis heard him pray in his room before going out to preach, in exactly the plain, conversational way he prayed on the platform.

I never preach a sermon until I’ve soaked it in prayer. Never.

— Billy Sunday, from his sermon “Teach Us to Pray”

Between 1915 and 1917 he preached in Philadelphia, Boston, Detroit, Buffalo and other great cities, and in the spring of 1917, as the United States entered the First World War, he held his largest campaign, in New York, from April to June. More than 98,000 people came forward, and he gave the entire offering there to war charities, as he gave his Chicago offering to the Pacific Garden Mission where he had been converted. Over his career something like a million people walked the sawdust trail. His most famous sermon was against strong drink, and he did as much as any man to arouse the nation for Prohibition; on the night it took effect in January 1920 he staged a mock funeral for “John Barleycorn” in Norfolk, Virginia.

Trials

The honest record has shadows. The campaigns made the Sundays wealthy, and critics questioned the offerings. His patriotism could curdle into harshness; in the 1920s he accepted gifts from members of the Ku Klux Klan and, hired by coal operators, spoke contemptuously of striking miners. After the war the crowds thinned, but he kept preaching wherever he was invited.

The deepest sorrow was at home. The children had been raised largely by others while their parents travelled, and the three sons struggled with drink and failed marriages; the Sundays paid money to keep scandals quiet. In 1930 Nora Lynn, the nanny who had become family, died. In 1932 their daughter Helen died after a long, wasting illness. In 1933 their eldest son, George, whom they had rescued from financial ruin, took his own life. Sunday had once prayed aloud before a tabernacle crowd, with a candour that made the critics wince, words that read very tenderly now.

Well, Jesus, I’m not up in heaven yet. I don’t want to go, not yet… I don’t want to leave Nell and the children. I like the little bungalow we have out at the lake.

— Billy Sunday, a tabernacle prayer

Early in 1935 he suffered a heart attack, and his doctor told him to stay out of the pulpit. He did not. About a week before he died he preached on the jailer’s question, “What must I do to be saved?” — the question that had found him on a Chicago curb half a century before. He died on the 6th of November, 1935, at the Chicago home of Nell’s brother, William Thompson, just short of his seventy-third birthday, and was buried in Forest Home Cemetery at Forest Park, Illinois.

He was a man of large faults and larger zeal. He was a soldier’s orphan who never forgot his mother praying through the night, and a ballplayer who asked God for a sign and kept his side of the bargain. The chair-smashing has dated. What remains is the simple gospel he heard from a mission band on a street corner and preached for forty years: that any sinner, however far gone, may still get up, turn his back on the old crowd, and go to Jesus Christ.

fields.name: Charles S. Price
fields.photo_attribution: Flower Pentecostal Heritage Center, via AG News
fields.bio: Charles S. Price (1887–1947) was an English-born Pentecostal evangelist who, as a liberal Congregational pastor in Lodi, California, went to Aimee Semple McPherson’s 1921 San Jose meetings to expose them and was converted instead. His healing campaigns across North America drew huge crowds, notably in Victoria and Vancouver in 1923, and his book The Real Faith (1940) taught that true faith is not worked up but imparted by God.
fields.bio_html:
Charles S. Price spent the first dozen years of his ministry explaining God away. He was a gifted, popular, well-read preacher who could account for every religious feeling by the laws of psychology, and who never once, by his own confession, asked a sinner to come to Christ. Then he went to a tent meeting in San Jose to gather material for a sermon that would expose it, and the meeting exposed him instead. He spent the rest of his life as a healing evangelist, preaching to arenas of ten thousand — and, at the height of it, wrote a book confessing that his heart had been heavy for those who went home unhealed.

A Sheffield boy who drifted

Charles Sydney Price was born on 7 May 1887 in Sheffield, England. He never knew his mother. She died while he was still very small, and he was told that before she died she took him in her arms and dedicated him to the service of the Lord. His father married again, and Charles grew up loving his stepmother dearly. It was her insistence, and his parents’ sacrifice, that gave him a good schooling; he attended Wesley College, a Methodist school.

Somewhere in those years, he wrote, he began to drift. He came to think his parents’ faith old-fashioned and rather narrow. He worked for a time with a Sheffield law firm and was fascinated by the courtrooms, but he grew restless, and as a young man of about twenty he crossed to Canada, where the legal career he hoped for did not come and he ended up doing rough work instead. From Canada he felt drawn to Spokane, in Washington State.

A lamp post in Spokane

One night in early autumn he was leaning against a lamp post in Spokane, listening to a little band of mission workers sing in the street. When the meeting ended, an old woman stopped him and asked whether he knew that God wanted him. He was uncomfortable, excused himself rather rudely, and hurried off. Halfway across the Monroe Street Bridge he stopped. A feeling of dread and awe had come over him, a sense that God had spoken through her. He turned round and walked back to the mission. When the leader gave the altar call that night, he later wrote, he sprang to his feet, squared his shoulders and marched to the front, and gave himself to God.

He threw himself into the work of that Free Methodist mission, and before long he was ordained into the Methodist ministry. He married and began to raise a family. Then came the turning point he would regret all his life. News had reached Spokane of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit in Los Angeles, and Price, convicted, promised to meet with some workers to pray to be filled. On his way to that prayer meeting an older minister caught him by the arm and begged him not to wreck his future. Price spent the afternoon in the man’s study instead and went home with half a suitcase of books. He did not go to the prayer meeting.

The books did their work. He came to believe, he said, that he could explain every religious emotion from the standpoint of psychology. Pastorate followed pastorate, and his reputation climbed. He left the Methodists for the broader Congregational Church, spent a season in Alaska, and then took pulpits in Santa Rosa and Oakland, California. In the First World War he spoke from Oakland’s theatre stages as one of the “Four Minute Men,” work that earned him a letter from President Woodrow Wilson. At last he came to the First Congregational Church of Lodi, a fine church with generous people.

I never gave an altar call—never led a soul to Jesus—never preached the glory of the born-again experience. I was spiritually blind, leading my people into the ditch.

— Charles S. Price, The Story of My Life

The tent at San Jose

In 1921 Aimee Semple McPherson held a great tent campaign in San Jose, and members of the Lodi church began coming home from it saying they had been saved. Price laughed, and then grew bitter. He put an advertisement in the newspaper announcing that his next Sunday sermon would be titled “Divine Healing Bubble Explodes,” and drove to San Jose with pen and paper to take notes.

The first shock was the sponsor’s name on the banner: William Keeney Towner, pastor of the First Baptist Church in Oakland, a friend from Price’s Oakland years. The tent held about six thousand and was packed. Towner found him in the crowd, gripped his hand and told him that this was real and that it was what he needed. The only empty seat was in the section reserved for the crippled. The altar call undid him; he did not sleep that night. The next night the preaching, as he put it, punctured his theology until it looked like a sieve.

Back in his hotel room after that second night, Price threw himself on his knees and cried out to God. By his own account the heavens were black above him and no answer came, yet in sincerity of heart he promised God that he would change. The following evening he sat on the platform among the ministers praying for strength to do what he had resolved.

When the call for sinners came, he stood. A prominent minister beside him put a hand on his shoulder and whispered that she was calling for sinners, for people who needed to be saved. Price whispered back that he knew, and went down the steps. As he knelt, he wrote, the glory of God broke over his soul and an ocean of divine love rolled across his heart; he threw up both hands and shouted Hallelujah. Night after night afterwards he tarried in prayer at the Baptist church, and one night, praying for hours in a corner behind a piano until Towner came and urged him into the middle of the room, he was baptized in the Holy Spirit.

He went home to Lodi fully expecting to lose his pulpit. Instead the church was packed the next Sunday, and he told them plainly what they would hear from now on.

As long as I am pastor, you will hear one burning message from this pulpit—Jesus Christ and Him crucified.

— Charles S. Price, The Story of My Life

More than eighty people knelt at his first altar call. Prayer meetings multiplied, attendance reached a thousand, and a Lodi Gospel Team of close to a thousand members drove out in convoys to hold street meetings in nearby towns. When church authorities began to interfere, the revived congregation formed an independent church, Bethel Temple. On 17 August 1922, with a sad parting, Price left Lodi for the evangelistic field.

Arenas of ten thousand

His first campaign was in Ashland, Oregon, where the churches closed their own services to join him. When the first person he prayed for fell under the power of God, he admitted, he was afraid. Then came Albany, Roseburg and Eugene, and in April 1923 an invitation from Methodist ministers in Victoria, British Columbia. The meetings outgrew the Metropolitan Methodist Church and moved to an arena. Among those prayed for was Ruby Dimmick, a young woman crippled for years and the daughter of a Methodist minister; her healing was reported across Canada and the United States. In May he went on to Vancouver, where the Denman Arena held ten thousand, and its owner, Frank Patrick, reckoned that more than a quarter of a million people came in three weeks.

Honesty requires the rest of the story. The healings were contested from the start. Later in 1923 a committee of Vancouver ministers, doctors and others followed up some 350 people who had been prayed for, and reported that most showed no lasting change and that thirty-nine had died within months. Some who had endorsed him drew back, saying they had supported his preaching rather than his healing. Price’s supporters answered with testimonies of people still well years later, and he went on returning to Canada; converts from those campaigns helped fill Pentecostal churches in British Columbia and the prairies for a generation.

From 1926 he sent out a monthly magazine, Golden Grain, carrying his sermons and the testimonies of the healed. He held campaigns across Canada and the American Midwest, and in the late 1930s preached in Europe and the Middle East. The travelling was relentless, and it cost him. His marriage did not survive those years; he and his wife separated and later divorced. It is a sorrow his public story tends to pass over.

The faith that is given

The weariness of that life shows through in his own pages. One night in a tabernacle, with some five hundred sick people waiting to be anointed and no strength left to preach, he looked through a crack in the wall at the sufferers and felt like running away.

“Oh, Jesus,” he cried, dropping to his knees on the office floor and weeping, “I can’t. I have not the strength.” He wrote that a still, small voice answered in his heart, asking why he did not take the Lord’s strength instead. He walked out without his notes, and at midnight he was still laying hands on the sick. Going home, he was not too tired to kneel again and thank God for what He had done.

Out of such nights came his best-known book, The Real Faith, published in 1940. It opens with a confession. For years, he wrote, he had known that something was wrong. He had gone home from meetings with shouts of victory ringing in his ears, only to weep before the Lord for those who dragged their sick bodies home as needy as they came. He would not shrug off the gap between what was preached and what happened. His answer was that faith cannot be worked up by effort of will; it is not the same as believing a promise, but a gift that God Himself imparts to the heart.

We have made faith a condition of mind, when it is a divinely imparted grace of the heart.

— Charles S. Price, The Real Faith

The book is full of prayer rather than technique. He tells of a woman confined to an institution, whom he prayed for one morning with no visible answer, while her husband held him by the coat and begged him not to give up.

Price called his own church and others to a whole day of prayer for her. About four o’clock that afternoon, praying near the altar, he felt the Spirit of the Lord come upon him and rose to announce that the answer was on the way. He telephoned the husband. The next day, after a brief time of prayer and anointing, he wrote, she was delivered and went home to her husband and children.

Just as honestly, he recorded nights when nothing happened and he felt, in his word, empty. When two men once pressed him to settle a controversy, he admitted he did not know the answer.

Brethren, the important thing is not what you believe, but in whom you believe.

— Charles S. Price, The Real Faith

In 1945 he felt the Lord calling him to stay at home, and he gave his last years in Pasadena to writing, local preaching, rest and prayer. He died there on 8 March 1947, aged fifty-nine, and was buried at Forest Lawn in Glendale. Golden Grain went on being mailed out for years after his death, and The Real Faith is still reprinted today.

He was not a theologian, and he carried griefs and failures along with the triumphs. But the man who once explained every emotion by psychology ended his life insisting that faith was not something he could produce, and that every good thing he had seen had come from Jesus alone. That confession is still what his books make.

fields.name: John Foxe
fields.bio: John Foxe (c. 1516–1587) was an English Protestant historian and preacher who gave up his Oxford fellowship for conscience, fled Queen Mary's persecution, and in exile and after gathered the records of those who died for the Reformed faith into Actes and Monuments (1563), known ever since as Foxe's Book of Martyrs. In old age he pleaded with Queen Elizabeth to spare even the heretics he opposed from the fire.
fields.bio_html:
Most of the people in John Foxe's great book died young, and violently, and in public. Foxe himself lived to about seventy and died quietly in his own house in London. He was not a martyr and never claimed to be one. He was the man who sat at a desk for thirty years so that the martyrs would not be forgotten — gathering their letters, their trial records, the words of the people who had stood near the fire — and who, having written down more burnings than any Englishman before him, spent part of his old age begging his own queen not to burn anyone else.

A boy from Boston

He was born at Boston, in Lincolnshire, about 1516; the exact year is not certain. His father died while John was very young, and his mother married again, to Richard Melton, a prosperous yeoman of the nearby village of Coningsby. It seems to have been a kind home. Years later Foxe dedicated one of his early writings, An Instruccyon of Christen Fayth, to his stepfather, with every mark of affection.

He went up to Oxford, and in July 1538 he became a probationer fellow of Magdalen College, a full fellow a year later. He lectured in logic in 1539–40 and proceeded Master of Arts in July 1543. Somewhere in those Oxford years — the record does not tell us exactly when or how — he came over to the Reformed faith, and came over thoroughly.

Leaving Magdalen

It cost him his place. The college statutes required a fellow to attend chapel regularly and to take priest's orders within a set time, and priest's orders in the 1540s meant celibacy. Foxe would not conform to either rule, and he objected plainly to celibacy being forced on the fellows. In 1545 he resigned his fellowship.

It was a hard step for a poor scholar. A fellowship was a living, a roof and a future, and he walked away from it with nothing in hand. He found work as a tutor in the household of Sir William Lucy at Charlecote, in Warwickshire, teaching the young Thomas Lucy. There, on 3 February 1547, he married Agnes Randall, the daughter of a Coventry merchant. She would share every hardship that followed, and outlive him.

Then came London, and real want. The memoir of his life that his son Simeon wrote many years later tells how Foxe was sitting one day in St Paul's, worn out with long fasting, when a stranger he had never seen sat down beside him, pressed a sum of money into his hand, and bade him be of good cheer. Within a few days he was taken into the household of the Duchess of Richmond as tutor to the orphaned children of her brother, the poet Earl of Surrey, who had lately been executed. Foxe, the memoir says, never found out who the stranger was. Modern scholars treat the story with some caution — Simeon was born long afterwards and wrote from scattered recollections — and it was very likely through evangelical friends that the post came to him. But the post itself is certain, and so is the want that went before it. Foxe taught the Howard children from about 1547 to 1553; the eldest, Thomas, would one day be Duke of Norfolk. On 24 June 1550 Nicholas Ridley, Bishop of London, ordained him deacon.

Flight

In 1553 Mary came to the throne, and the Reformed faith that had been the law of the land under her brother Edward became a crime. The fires began. Foxe was a marked man, and in 1554 he fled.

It was a close thing. He and Agnes, who was expecting a child, took ship for the Continent. Officers of Bishop Stephen Gardiner came with a warrant for his arrest and broke down the door of the house where he had been hiding — but the ship had gone. Then a storm drove it back to port. To throw his pursuers off, Foxe hired a horse and made as though he were riding off into the country; that night he slipped back aboard, pleaded with the master to carry them to safety, and was away. Two days later they landed at Nieuport, in Flanders.

The exile was poor and unsettled. At Strasbourg he met Edmund Grindal and saw through the press, in 1554, a Latin history of the persecutions of the faithful from the days of Wycliffe onward — the seed of all his later work. At Frankfurt he found the English exiles quarrelling bitterly over how they ought to worship; he urged Peter Martyr to come and reconcile them, and in January 1555 sat with John Knox, William Whittingham, Anthony Gilby and Thomas Cole on a committee that drafted an order of service. It was rejected. Peacemaking was not always rewarded.

He moved on to Basel, and there poverty drove him to the printing house of Johannes Oporinus, where he worked as a reader of proofs. It was humble work, but it put him at the heart of the Protestant book trade. Oporinus printed his Latin drama Christus Triumphans in 1556. And all the while news came over from England, much of it by way of Grindal: names, dates, examinations, letters smuggled from prison, the last words of men and women burned at Smithfield and Oxford and Canterbury. Foxe gathered it all. In 1559 Oporinus published his great Latin folio of some 740 pages, running from Wycliffe to Cranmer, and Foxe dedicated it to his old pupil, now Duke of Norfolk.

The book

Mary died in November 1558, and Foxe came home under Elizabeth. For a time he lived in the Duke of Norfolk's house at Aldgate, and in 1560 Grindal, now Bishop of London, ordained him priest. He threw himself into turning the Latin work into something far larger, in English, for the ordinary reader — and he found in the London printer John Day a partner equal to the task.

In 1563 Day published the Actes and Monuments: a vast folio of 1,827 pages. Foxe told his readers plainly why he had written it:

I have addressed this present history, to the end, first, that the wonderful works of God in His Church might appear to His glory.

— John Foxe, Actes and Monuments

That is the key to the whole enormous book. It is not first a catalogue of cruelty, though it records cruelty without flinching. It is a history of the faithfulness of God — Christ's promise that the gates of hell should not prevail against His Church, tested and kept through fifteen centuries. The apostles and the Roman persecutions are there, and the Waldenses, and Huss, and Tyndale. But the heart of it is England under Mary: John Rogers, the first to burn; John Hooper; Rowland Taylor; Latimer and Ridley at Oxford — Ridley, who had made Foxe a deacon; Cranmer thrusting into the flame the hand that had signed his recantation; and scores of weavers, housewives, apprentices and labourers whom no one else would have remembered. Foxe gave the humble the same care he gave the bishops.

The book was loved and attacked in equal measure, and Foxe answered his critics by working harder. The second edition of 1570, in two volumes, ran to 2,354 pages, with the woodcuts increased from about sixty to some one hundred and fifty. In 1571 the Convocation of Canterbury ordered that a copy of "that full history entitled Monuments of Martyrs" be set up in every cathedral church, beside the Bible, and that church dignitaries keep copies in their houses for servants and visitors to read. Further editions followed in 1576 and 1583, the last in Foxe's lifetime. Chained in the churches and read aloud in households for generations, it became, after the Bible, perhaps the most widely read book in Protestant England. The popular abridgments that carry his name to this day, among them William Byron Forbush's edition of 1926, cut his work down and added chapters he never wrote; but its spirit is his.

The preacher and the peacemaker

Honours were offered him, and he took few of them. At the suggestion of Bishop Jewel of Salisbury he was given a prebend in Salisbury Cathedral, with the lease of the vicarage of Shipton, in May 1563. But he had a conscientious objection to wearing the surplice, and he would not pretend otherwise. The respect in which he was held was such that he kept his prebend until he died, nonconformity and all. His way of life stayed simple.

On Good Friday 1570, at Grindal's bidding, he preached at Paul's Cross, the great open-air pulpit of London. The pope had just excommunicated the queen, and the city was tense. Foxe preached Christ crucified. The sermon was printed at once, with a prayer, and reissued several times in his lifetime. In it he told his hearers what it truly means to know the cross:

To know the crucified sacrifice of Christ's body to be a perfect deliverance of all his people, to be a full satisfaction once, and for ever, for all our sins … this is to know Christ Jesus crucified.

— John Foxe, A Sermon of Christ Crucified, preached at Paul's Cross, 1570

Two years later his loyalties were tested in the most personal way. His old pupil and patron, the Duke of Norfolk, was condemned for conspiring with Mary Queen of Scots and the Catholic nobility against Elizabeth. Through the spring of 1572 Foxe and Alexander Nowell, Dean of St Paul's, ministered to the condemned man, and on 2 June they went with him to the scaffold. Foxe did not abandon the boy he had taught, even when the boy, grown, had chosen a cause Foxe hated.

Nor was his pastoral work only for the great. He was known as a man people sent for in trouble of soul.

In 1574 Foxe was called to Robert Briggs, a lawyer of the Temple in London, who was in great affliction and was thought to be possessed by the devil. Foxe prayed with him and led those standing by in prayer, and left behind a written prayer for them to use if the attacks returned. Accounts of that ministry were copied and passed from hand to hand, and shaped how English Protestants prayed over the afflicted for years to come.

"Spare their lives"

The most striking moment of Foxe's later years came in 1575. That spring a congregation of Dutch Anabaptists was arrested at a meeting near Aldgate, and two of them, Jan Pieters and Hendrik Terwoort, were condemned to be burned. Foxe had no sympathy with their teaching. But no one had been burned for religion in England for seventeen years, since the Marian fires he had spent his life recording, and he could not bear to see them lit again by Protestant hands. He wrote in Latin to the queen, to Lord Burghley and to the Lord Chief Justice, pleading that the punishment was out of all proportion to the offence, and that men erring from blindness rather than malice might yet be won. Banish them, he urged; imprison them; but do not burn them.

I have no favour for heretics, but I am a man and would spare the life of a man.

— John Foxe, from his Latin letter to Queen Elizabeth, 1575 (in translation)

He did not win. A month's respite was granted, and on 22 July 1575 both men were burned at Smithfield. But the letter was remembered. Later church historians such as Thomas Fuller praised it, and it stands as one of the most humane things written by any churchman of his age. Foxe was not a modern believer in toleration; he wanted heresy driven out of England. But he had looked too long at the fire to think that the fire could serve the gospel.

The end of a long labour

His last years were spent in London, in the parish of St Giles, Cripplegate, still revising, still preaching, still writing. His sons grew up: Samuel, the elder, and Simeon, who became a physician and wrote the memoir of his father's life.

According to that family memoir, Foxe knew his end was near. He loved his sons dearly, but he did not wish them to watch him die, and a short time before his death he sent Samuel off on a journey of several days about some business, and asked that Simeon and Robert not be sent for. He wanted, it seems, to meet his Lord quietly and alone. He died on 18 April 1587, at about seventy years of age, and was buried in St Giles, Cripplegate, where Samuel set up a monument to him.

He had lived through four reigns and every turn of the English Reformation, and he never wore a martyr's crown. What he did was simpler and harder: he remembered. He made a nation remember the weaver and the bishop, the blind woman and the archbishop, who would not deny Christ, and he told their stories not so that readers would hate but so that they would see, as he put it, the wonderful works of God in His Church. The Church he wrote about has not failed yet, and the book he gave his life to is still read.

faq.a: On Good Friday 1570, at Grindal's bidding and just after the pope had excommunicated the queen, Foxe preached at Paul's Cross in London on Christ crucified. In it he said that to know the crucified sacrifice of Christ's body to be a perfect deliverance of all his people and a full satisfaction once and for ever for all our sins is to know Christ Jesus crucified.

faq.q: Did John Foxe oppose burning heretics?
faq.a: Yes. In 1575 two Dutch Anabaptists, Jan Pieters and Hendrik Terwoort, were condemned to the fire. Foxe rejected their teaching, but no one had been burned for religion in England for seventeen years, and he wrote in Latin to the queen, Lord Burghley and the Chief Justice, urging banishment or prison instead. He wrote that he had no favour for heretics, but was a man and would spare the life of a man. The two were burned at Smithfield on 22 July 1575.

faq.q: When and how did John Foxe die?
faq.a: Foxe died in London on 18 April 1587, at about seventy years of age. According to a family memoir, he knew his end was near and did not wish his sons to watch him die, so he sent his son Samuel away on a journey of several days and asked that Simeon and Robert not be sent for. He was buried in St Giles, Cripplegate, where Samuel set up a monument to him.

fields.name: Arthur T. Pierson
fields.bio: Arthur Tappan Pierson (1837–1911) was an American Presbyterian pastor and missions statesman whose 1886 address at Mount Hermon helped launch the Student Volunteer Movement, and who filled Spurgeon's pulpit in London from 1891 to 1893. A close friend of George Müller, he wrote George Müller of Bristol (1899), the authorized memoir of Müller's life of prayer and faith.
fields.bio_html:
Arthur Tappan Pierson spent most of his life telling other people's stories. He wrote the memoir of George Müller, filled Charles Spurgeon's pulpit, gave a generation of students its watchword, and edited for more than twenty years a magazine whose whole business was reporting what God was doing in other lands. It is easy, reading about him, to see only the crowds he stood in front of. But the turning points of his own life were small and private: a Sunday evening in Detroit, a railway carriage between Utah and Chicago, a few hours in his study with an old man who would not let him get away with an argument that had no Bible in it.

A New York boyhood

He was born on 6 March 1837 in Chatham Street, New York — the street now called Park Row — and was named in honour of Arthur Tappan, the New York merchant and abolitionist. His father was Stephen Haines Pierson. It was a name that carried a conscience with it, and in time the boy would grow into it.

At thirteen he was sent away from home to the Collegiate Institute at Tarrytown-on-the-Hudson. That year, 1850, a series of revival meetings was held in the Methodist church in the town, and there the Presbyterian schoolboy publicly professed faith in Jesus Christ. It is worth noticing where it happened. The man who would spend his life among Presbyterians, and end it outside their ranks, came to Christ at a Methodist meeting. He never afterwards had much patience with the walls between believers.

He went on to Hamilton College in Clinton, New York, graduating in 1857, and then to Union Theological Seminary in New York to prepare for the ministry.

A young pastor and a growing household

In 1860 he married Sarah Frances Benedict, and the same year took his first pastorate, at Binghamton, New York. Three years later he moved to Waterford, in the same state, and stayed six years. These were the quiet, formative years in which a young minister learns to preach week by week to the same faces.

The Piersons had seven children. It is recorded of them that every one came to faith before the age of fifteen, and that all grew up to serve Christ as missionaries, pastors or lay leaders. His eldest son, Delavan, would one day write his life. Whatever else is said of Pierson's public ministry, it began at a family table.

Detroit, and a church that burned

In 1869 he was called to the Fort Street Presbyterian Church in Detroit, one of the most prestigious congregations in the city, with one of the finest church buildings in the land. He was an eloquent preacher and a growing Bible scholar, and he was, by every outward measure, a success.

Something was already stirring. In 1874 he hosted the evangelist Major D. W. Whittle and the singer P. P. Bliss for meetings in Detroit, and their simple, direct gospel left him seeking more of God's abiding presence and power in his own life and ministry. He was not looking for a larger church. He was beginning to suspect that the one he had was not reaching the people who most needed it.

On a Sunday in March 1876 Pierson preached with a power he felt was not his own, and that evening he was pressed in spirit with a strong sense that the time was very near when God would open a new way for him to the unsaved — above all to the masses who never came near a church.

Within days, in March 1876, the Fort Street church caught fire. The interior was gutted, the roof destroyed, and the spire came crashing down into the street. The congregation moved its services into the Detroit opera house while the building was restored.

It was in the borrowed theatre that the thing he had sensed came to pass. People who would never have walked into the fashionable church on Fort Street walked into the opera house. And Pierson, standing on a stage instead of in a pulpit, found himself looking honestly at the ministry he had been building. He came to see that he had grown proud, that he had been courting the approval of the wealthy, and that his handsome church had been, without meaning to, a closed door to the poor.

The revival he had felt coming broke out in the opera house. By his own account more souls were converted in that one year than in the whole of his previous ministry — and almost all of them were the "outsiders" the church had never before reached.

He did not leave the lesson in the theatre. In the years that followed he led his congregation to turn outward toward Detroit's poor. He set himself against the system of pew rents, by which the best seats belonged to those who could pay, and he came to take his own salary on a basis of faith rather than fixed contract. None of this was comfortable in a wealthy church. It was the beginning of a life of obeying convictions at a cost.

A train from Ogden

For more than twenty years Pierson had followed at a distance the career of George Müller of Bristol, the man who fed thousands of orphans without asking anyone but God for money. In May 1878 he was in San Francisco when Müller was to speak on a Sunday afternoon at Oakland, just across the bay. Pierson had a conscientious objection to needless Sunday travel, and so he stayed where he was and let what seemed his only chance go by.

God, it turned out, was not bound by his timetable. When Pierson's train reached Ogden, in Utah, Mr. and Mrs. Müller boarded it, and they travelled to Chicago together. Pierson introduced himself and talked with the old man about the things of God every day of the journey. At his invitation Müller came to Detroit on his next tour, and in January 1880 preached at Fort Street on two Sundays and two weeknights between them.

He also met Pierson privately in his study, for an hour at a time over several days. Pierson brought his questions, and his objections. He had argued persistently against the premillennial view of the Lord's return, and he laid out every argument he had. Müller heard him through and gave a single answer: that the arguments had one fatal defect — not one of them was based on the word of God — and that he would never reach the truth until he laid his prejudices aside and asked, like a little child, what Scripture actually said.

Pierson also told him of the convictions that had been growing since the fire: that the worship of the churches had lost its first simplicity, that pew rents were pernicious, that fixed salaries were unscriptural, and that the duty of Christians to the masses outside the churches was grossly neglected. As Müller rose to leave, he said:

My beloved brother, the Lord has given you much light upon these matters, and will hold you correspondingly responsible for its use. If you obey Him and walk in the light, you will have more; if not, the light will be withdrawn.

— George Müller to Pierson in Detroit, 1880, as Pierson recorded it

Nearly twenty years later Pierson wrote that those words had never left him:

It is a singular lesson on the importance of an anointed tongue, that forty simple words, spoken over twenty years ago, have had a daily influence on the life of him to whom they were spoken.

— Arthur T. Pierson, George Müller of Bristol (1899)

Philadelphia, and a voice for the world

In 1882 he moved to Second Presbyterian Church in Indianapolis, and the next year to Bethany Presbyterian Church in Philadelphia, where he served from 1883 to 1889. Bethany was a church that worked among the city's urban poor, and there Pierson ran a missionary training school. The man who had once preached to Detroit's wealthy was now training workers for the streets and for the ends of the earth.

Missions had become his great theme. At one of D. L. Moody's Bible conferences in 1885 he called on the Protestant churches to launch a worldwide missionary campaign, and in 1886 he published The Crisis of Missions, which became the leading missionary book of its day.

In July 1886 Moody gathered college students for a summer conference at Mount Hermon, near Northfield, Massachusetts. Pierson spoke to them on God's providence in modern missions and urged them to evangelize the world in their own generation. By the end of the conference one hundred students had volunteered for service overseas. Out of that response grew the Student Volunteer Movement for Foreign Missions, which in 1888 took as its watchword a phrase traced to Pierson's address: "the evangelization of the world in this generation." By the year of his death the movement had sent some five thousand volunteers abroad from America alone.

From 1888 until he died he edited The Missionary Review of the World, which he and a colleague expanded into a monthly and made the most important nondenominational missions journal of its time. Month after month, for twenty-three years, he gathered the news of the gospel's advance and set it before the churches.

In Spurgeon's pulpit

In the autumn of 1891 Charles Spurgeon, gravely ill, left London for the warmer air of Mentone in the south of France, and Pierson was asked to fill the pulpit of the Metropolitan Tabernacle in his absence. It was a striking choice: a Presbyterian who had never been baptised as a believer, preaching to the great Baptist congregation. When Spurgeon died on 31 January 1892, the Tabernacle asked Pierson to stay, and he carried the pulpit until 1893, when Spurgeon's son Thomas took it up.

The question of baptism would not leave him. Some time later he became persuaded from Scripture that baptism belonged to believers, and on 1 February 1896, at the age of fifty-eight, he was baptised by James Spurgeon, Charles's brother. It cost him his standing: he left the Presbytery of Philadelphia over it. It was the same principle Müller had pressed on him sixteen years earlier, and he paid its price in the same coin.

That same year, 1896, he was holding meetings in Bristol and heard Müller, then in his ninety-first year, preach at Bethesda Chapel on the seventy-seventh Psalm — on prayer, his favourite subject. Pierson asked "his beloved father Müller" to speak at the close of his own series, and the old man gave a forty-five-minute address on prayer and missions with a vigour that seemed to deny his age.

Pierson became a familiar voice at the Keswick Convention in England, whose teaching on the Spirit-filled life he loved, and in 1903 he published The Keswick Movement in Precept and Practise.

The witness to a prayer-hearing God

Müller died in March 1898, and the next year Pierson published George Müller of Bristol, soon received as the authorized memoir. He did not write it to add to the facts, which Müller had already recorded in exhaustive detail. He wrote it, he said, "simply and solely" to "extend, emphasize, and perpetuate George Müller's witness to a prayer-hearing God." Its pages carry things Müller told him personally, among them this:

Not once, or five times, or five hundred times, but thousands of times in these threescore years, have we had in hand not enough for one more meal, either in food or in funds; but not once has God failed us; not once have we or the orphans gone hungry or lacked any good thing.

— George Müller to Arthur T. Pierson

Reading the book now, it is hard not to hear Pierson's own story underneath his friend's. The chapter that tells of their meeting ends not with praise of Müller but with a warning to the reader, drawn from Pierson's own experience of light received and light obeyed:

We risk the forfeiture of privileges which are not employed for God, and of obscuring convictions which are not carried into action. God's word to us is "use or lose."

— Arthur T. Pierson, George Müller of Bristol (1899)

The last journey

He never stopped working. Across his life he preached more than thirteen thousand sermons and wrote more than fifty books, and he served as a consulting editor of the Scofield Reference Bible, published in 1909 by his friend C. I. Scofield.

In 1910, past seventy, he set out to visit the missions of East Asia — the fields he had spent a quarter of a century writing about. In Korea he taught the Bible in a number of churches. But he fell ill on the journey and had to turn for home. He died in Brooklyn on 3 June 1911, at the age of seventy-four, and was buried in Green-Wood Cemetery.

Even then the missionary cause had the last word. He left funds in his will for a Bible institute in Korea, and the Pierson Memorial Bible Institute was founded in Seoul in his name; it continues today as Pyeongtaek University. The year after his death his son Delavan published his life under the title A Spiritual Warrior, Mighty in the Scriptures.

Pierson's life is sometimes told as a list of platforms — Detroit, Philadelphia, Northfield, London, Keswick. It reads better as a list of obediences. A proud young pastor let a fire humble him. A Presbyterian let an old Brethren preacher correct his theology. A man with a great reputation let himself be baptised again at fifty-eight and lose his place for it. Each time, as Müller had promised, the light he obeyed was followed by more. And the book he left behind still does the thing he most wanted it to do: it sends its readers not to George Müller, and not to Arthur Pierson, but to the God who hears prayer.
