fields.name: Blaise Pascal
fields.bio: Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) was a French mathematician, physicist and Christian thinker whose experiments on the vacuum and work on probability made him famous across Europe. On the night of 23 November 1654 he met the living God in an experience he recorded in his Memorial and carried sewn into his coat for the rest of his life. His Provincial Letters and the unfinished defence of the faith published after his death as the Pensées remain among the most searching Christian writings ever composed.
fields.bio_html:
Few people in history have been as brilliant as Blaise Pascal. At sixteen he wrote a treatise on geometry that the older mathematicians of Paris could hardly believe was his own. At nineteen he built one of the first mechanical calculating machines. Before he was thirty his experiments on the vacuum had overturned an idea as old as Aristotle, and his letters with Pierre de Fermat had laid the foundations of probability theory. Yet the most important night of his life had nothing to do with numbers. He spent it alone in his room with a Bible open before him, and when it was over he wrote one word in capital letters: FIRE.

A Gifted Child in a Grieving House

Blaise Pascal was born on 19 June 1623 in Clermont, in the mountainous Auvergne region of central France. His father, Étienne Pascal, was a respected magistrate and a gifted amateur mathematician. His mother, Antoinette Begon, died when Blaise was three, and Étienne never remarried. He gave himself to raising his three children: Gilberte, the eldest, Blaise, and little Jacqueline. In 1631 he moved the family to Paris and taught them himself.

Étienne had a clear plan. Blaise would learn Latin and Greek first and mathematics only later, so the father kept his geometry books out of the boy’s reach. The plan did not survive the child. According to his sister Gilberte, the young Blaise, not yet knowing the proper names of things, worked out for himself many of the first propositions of Euclid, drawing figures in charcoal on the floor. After that, Étienne opened the books and brought his son to the gatherings of scholars around Father Marin Mersenne, where the finest scientific minds in France met to talk.

From childhood Pascal was also frail. Gilberte later recalled him saying that from the age of eighteen he never passed a day without pain. Headaches, digestive torment and at times near-paralysis followed him for the rest of his short life. His whole genius had to work through a body that was always failing him.

In 1639 Étienne was appointed a royal tax commissioner in Rouen, in Normandy. The work meant endless arithmetic. To lighten his father’s load, Blaise designed a machine of gears and wheels that could add and subtract. He built some fifty prototypes over the following years, and the “Pascaline” is still remembered as a milestone in the history of computing.

The First Awakening

In January 1646 Étienne slipped on the ice in Rouen and badly injured his hip. Two gentlemen skilled in bone-setting, the brothers Deschamps, came to live with the family for some months while he recovered. They were devout followers of the Abbé de Saint-Cyran and of the movement centred on the convent of Port-Royal. That movement, later called Jansenism, stressed humanity’s total dependence on the grace of God and called believers to a serious, wholehearted Christian life.

The brothers brought books with them, and the Pascal household began to read. Blaise read, and was deeply moved. For the first time he saw Christianity not as a respectable inheritance but as a demand on the whole of life. The entire family was changed. Jacqueline, the most ardent of them, began to long for the religious life.

But this first conversion did not yet go to the root. Pascal remained a scientist of burning ambition. In 1647 and 1648 he set out to prove that a true vacuum could exist in nature. At his direction his brother-in-law, Florin Périer, carried a column of mercury up the Puy de Dôme, the old volcano above Clermont, and showed that the mercury fell as he climbed. The air had weight, and the idea that “nature abhors a vacuum” had to be dropped. The experiment made Pascal famous across Europe.

The Worldly Years

Étienne Pascal died in September 1651. Jacqueline, now free, soon entered Port-Royal as a nun. Blaise opposed her decision at first, partly out of loneliness and partly over the matter of her inheritance, and the break hurt them both. With his father gone, his sister in the convent and his doctors urging rest and amusement, Pascal entered the salons of Paris. He made friends with the young Duc de Roannez and with polished men of the world, and he studied gambling and games of chance. From that study came his famous correspondence with Fermat in 1654, which founded the mathematics of probability.

Later he would look back on these years with sorrow. Yet even in the midst of them he felt, as he later told Jacqueline, a growing disgust with the world and a strange sense of abandonment by God. Brilliance, company and fame had not filled him. By the autumn of 1654 he was visiting his sister at Port-Royal and pouring out his emptiness to her.

The Night of Fire

On Monday, 23 November 1654, Pascal was alone in his room in Paris. What happened there he never spoke of. After his death a servant felt something stiff in the lining of his coat and found a folded piece of parchment, and inside it an older sheet of paper, both carrying the same words in Pascal’s hand. He had sewn the record into each new coat he wore for eight years. It begins with the date and the hour, “from about half past ten in the evening until about half past midnight,” and then:

FIRE. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and the learned. Certainty, certainty, feeling, joy, peace. God of Jesus Christ.

— Blaise Pascal, the Memorial

The Memorial is less an essay than a prayer set down in fragments: “Joy, joy, joy, tears of joy.” It confesses, “I have separated myself from Him,” and cries, “Let me never be separated from Him.” It ends with a vow of “total submission to Jesus Christ and to my director,” and with the words of Psalm 119: “I will not forget thy word.”

The God Pascal met that night was not the “first cause” of the philosophers, whom a clever man might reason his way towards. He was the living God of the Bible, the God who had called Abraham and who is known only through Jesus Christ. From that night the centre of Pascal’s life moved. He did not give up thinking, but he no longer lived for his own glory.

In January 1655 he went on retreat at Port-Royal-des-Champs, the convent in the valley south-west of Paris. There he talked at length with its spiritual director, Isaac Le Maistre de Saci, about the pagan philosopher Epictetus and the sceptic Montaigne. He came away convinced that each saw half the truth about man, his greatness or his wretchedness, and that only the gospel held the two together.

The Provincial Letters

Within a year Pascal’s pen was needed. In early 1656 Port-Royal’s leading theologian, Antoine Arnauld, was on trial before the Sorbonne, and the friends of Port-Royal wanted the public to understand what was at stake. Under the pen name “Louis de Montalte,” Pascal wrote a letter supposedly addressed to a friend in the provinces. It was so clear, so witty and so readable that it sold out at once, and seventeen more letters followed between January 1656 and March 1657.

In the Provincial Letters Pascal turned his fire on the moral theology taught by some Jesuit writers of his day. It was a system of subtle distinctions, he argued, that let people keep their sins while still feeling at peace with God. He quoted their books against them, with devastating irony. The letters were condemned and burned by order of the authorities, but they could not be unread. They are still counted among the founding works of modern French prose. Behind the wit lay a pastor’s concern: that the love of God should not be traded away for an easy conscience.

The Holy Thorn

In the middle of that struggle, something happened in Pascal’s own family. His ten-year-old niece and god-daughter, Marguerite Périer, Gilberte’s child, was a pupil at Port-Royal in Paris. For more than three years she had suffered from a lachrymal fistula, a festering ulcer at the corner of her eye that swelled her face and gave off a foul discharge. Her doctors held out little hope except a painful cautery.

On 24 March 1656 the nuns of Port-Royal, praying over a relic they revered as a thorn from Christ’s crown, touched it to Marguerite’s eye. Within days the ulcer had healed. Physicians examined her and the Church authorities of Paris formally recognised the cure in October that year. The community received it as God’s answer to their prayers, and Pascal as a sign that God had not forsaken them.

Pascal was deeply stirred. He took for his seal an eye surrounded by a crown of thorns, with the words of Paul, Scio cui credidi, “I know whom I have believed.” The event also turned his mind to a larger work. If God still gave signs, why did so many still not believe? How could the honest sceptic, the pleasure-seeker, the indifferent man of the world be brought to take Christ seriously?

The Great Apology

Pascal set out to write a defence of the Christian faith unlike any before it. He did not mean to begin with proofs from nature, which he thought convinced no one. He would begin with man himself: his greatness and his misery, his restlessness, his endless diversions from the one question that matters. He wanted to show that Christianity alone explains that riddle, and then to show that it is true.

Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed.

— Blaise Pascal, Pensées

He worked on it for years, jotting thoughts on scraps of paper, sorting them into bundles and threading them together on string. Illness kept breaking into the work. By 1659 he could often do little at all, and the great book was never finished. What remained after his death, nearly a thousand fragments, was published by his friends at Port-Royal in 1670 as the Pensées, or “Thoughts.” Among them is the famous wager, in which Pascal presses the doubter to see that he cannot avoid staking his life on one side or the other. And among them is a line that has outlived its author by centuries:

The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.

— Blaise Pascal, Pensées

By “the heart” Pascal did not mean mere feeling. He meant the part of us that grasps first truths directly and loves or refuses God. Faith, he believed, is “God felt by the heart, not by the reason.” Yet the Pensées are not only argument. Some of their most moving pages are meditation, above all “The Mystery of Jesus,” written as Pascal knelt in spirit beside Christ in Gethsemane. There he hears the Lord say to him, “Console thyself, thou wouldst not seek Me, if thou hadst not found Me,” and he writes:

Jesus will be in agony even to the end of the world. We must not sleep during that time.

— Blaise Pascal, Pensées

Sickness Rightly Used

Pascal’s last years were marked by sorrow and pain. In October 1661 his beloved sister Jacqueline died, on her thirty-sixth birthday. Her death came soon after the nuns of Port-Royal had been pressed to sign a formulary against the teachings they held dear. Pascal’s own health collapsed further. He gave up every comfort he could spare, sold much of his furniture and gave the money to the poor. He took a characteristic interest in a new scheme: the first public carriages in Paris, the “five-sol coaches,” which began to run in March 1662. It was the city’s first omnibus service, and Pascal had pledged his share of its income to the poor.

In his illness Pascal wrote a Prayer to Ask God for the Right Use of Sickness. In it he gave thanks that God had taken from him the health he had misused on the world, and asked that he might suffer as a Christian, joined to the sufferings of Christ, seeking in his pain not relief but God himself.

His charity followed him to the end. He had taken a poor family into his home, and when one of the children fell ill, he did not turn them out. Instead he left his own house and moved to Gilberte’s. There, in the summer of 1662, he grew steadily worse. He begged to be carried to the Hospital for Incurables so that he might die among the poor, and when his doctors would not allow it, he asked that a poor sick man be brought into the house and cared for as he was. He longed to receive Communion, and in his last hours, when a lucid moment came, he received it with joy.

“May God never abandon me” were among his last words. Blaise Pascal died at one o’clock in the morning on 19 August 1662. He was thirty-nine years old. He was buried in the church of Saint-Étienne-du-Mont in Paris, a short walk from where he died.

Legacy

Pascal left behind a scientist’s legacy that would have satisfied most people: Pascal’s triangle, Pascal’s law of pressure, the foundations of probability, the calculating machine. A modern unit of pressure and a computer language bear his name. But it is the notebook of unfinished thoughts that has done the most good. For more than three centuries the Pensées have spoken to people who would never open a book of theology: students, sceptics, the bored and the restless, anyone who has sensed that their diversions are hiding something from them. Pascal meets them there, with an honesty about the human condition that is hard to escape.

He also shows that a great mind and a humble heart are not enemies. The same man who weighed the air above a mountain knelt in the dark of Gethsemane and heard Christ say, “I thought of thee in Mine agony.” He had tested the claims of reason further than almost anyone of his age, and he found its limit. His whole life came to rest in the few words he carried in his coat: “God of Jesus Christ… Joy, joy, joy, tears of joy.”

faq.q: Who was Blaise Pascal?
faq.a: Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) was a French mathematician, physicist and Christian thinker whose experiments on the vacuum and work on probability made him famous across Europe. On the night of 23 November 1654 he met the living God in an experience he recorded in his Memorial and carried sewn into his coat for the rest of his life. His Provincial Letters and the unfinished Pensées remain among the most searching Christian writings ever composed.

faq.q: When and where was Blaise Pascal born?
faq.a: He was born on 19 June 1623 in Clermont, in the mountainous Auvergne region of central France. His father, Étienne Pascal, was a respected magistrate and gifted amateur mathematician; his mother, Antoinette Begon, died when Blaise was three. Étienne never remarried and raised his three children, Gilberte, Blaise and Jacqueline, himself, moving the family to Paris in 1631 and teaching them at home.

faq.q: What is Blaise Pascal known for in mathematics and science?
faq.a: As a child he worked out many of Euclid's first propositions for himself, drawing figures in charcoal on the floor. At nineteen he began building a calculating machine, the Pascaline, to ease his father's tax work. In 1647 and 1648 his brother-in-law carried mercury up the Puy de Dôme at his direction, proving that air has weight and overturning the idea that nature abhors a vacuum. His 1654 letters with Fermat founded probability theory.

faq.q: How did Blaise Pascal first come to a serious faith?
faq.a: In January 1646 his father injured his hip on the ice in Rouen, and two bone-setting brothers named Deschamps lived with the family while he recovered. They were devout followers of the movement centred on the convent of Port-Royal, later called Jansenism, which stressed total dependence on God's grace. Through their books Pascal first saw Christianity as a demand on the whole of life. But this first conversion did not yet go to the root, and his scientific ambition remained.

faq.q: What was Blaise Pascal's Memorial?
faq.a: On Monday, 23 November 1654, from about half past ten in the evening until half past midnight, Pascal had an experience of God alone in his Paris room. He wrote it down and sewed the record into each new coat for eight years; a servant found it after his death. It begins, "FIRE. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and the learned," and cries, "Joy, joy, joy, tears of joy." It ends with a vow of total submission to Jesus Christ.

faq.q: What were Pascal's Provincial Letters about?
faq.a: In early 1656, when Port-Royal's leading theologian Antoine Arnauld was on trial before the Sorbonne, Pascal wrote under the pen name Louis de Montalte a letter supposedly addressed to a friend in the provinces. Seventeen more followed until March 1657. With devastating irony he attacked moral theology taught by some Jesuit writers, which he argued let people keep their sins while feeling at peace with God. The letters were condemned and burned, but remain founding works of French prose.

faq.q: What was the miracle of the Holy Thorn?
faq.a: Pascal's ten-year-old niece and god-daughter, Marguerite Périer, a pupil at Port-Royal, had suffered for over three years from a festering ulcer at the corner of her eye. On 24 March 1656 the nuns touched to her eye a relic they revered as a thorn from Christ's crown, and within days it had healed; Church authorities recognised the cure that October. Pascal took as his seal an eye in a crown of thorns with the words "I know whom I have believed."

faq.q: What are Pascal's Pensées?
faq.a: Pascal set out to write a defence of Christianity that began not with proofs from nature but with man himself, his greatness and misery. Illness kept it unfinished, and nearly a thousand fragments were published by his friends at Port-Royal in 1670 as the Pensées, or Thoughts. They include the famous wager, the line "Man is but a reed... but he is a thinking reed," and the meditation The Mystery of Jesus: "Jesus will be in agony even to the end of the world."

faq.q: What did Pascal mean by the heart has its reasons?
faq.a: In the Pensées Pascal wrote, "The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know." By the heart he did not mean mere feeling but the part of us that grasps first truths directly and loves or refuses God. Faith, he believed, is "God felt by the heart, not by the reason." The God he met on his night of fire was not the first cause of the philosophers but the living God of the Bible, known only through Jesus Christ.

faq.q: How did Blaise Pascal die?
faq.a: Frail from childhood, he said he had not passed a day without pain since eighteen. After his sister Jacqueline died in October 1661, his health collapsed further; he gave much to the poor and wrote a Prayer to Ask God for the Right Use of Sickness. Having left his home to a poor family with a sick child, he died at Gilberte's house at one in the morning on 19 August 1662, aged thirty-nine, saying, "May God never abandon me." He was buried in Saint-Étienne-du-Mont, Paris.

fields.name: C. S. Lewis
fields.bio: C. S. Lewis (1898–1963) was an Oxford and Cambridge scholar of medieval and Renaissance literature who came back from atheism to Christian faith in 1931 and became the twentieth century's best-loved defender of it — in the wartime broadcasts that became Mere Christianity, in The Screwtape Letters, and in the seven Chronicles of Narnia. His own books are still in copyright; Ochorus offers its own companions to his life and teaching, and the older classics he loved.
fields.bio_html:
C. S. Lewis spent the first half of his life arguing against God, and the second half explaining Him to more people than almost any writer of his century. He was not a pastor or an evangelist, and he never thought of himself as a theologian. He was an Oxford don who lectured on medieval allegory and Renaissance poetry, smoked a pipe, walked enormous distances, and answered every letter he received. Yet a wartime radio talk, a short book of letters from a senior devil, and seven stories for children carried the Christian faith into homes, barracks and nurseries across the world — and they are still doing it. Few lives show more plainly how God can take a reluctant, clever, wounded man and make him a servant of joy.

A Belfast boyhood, and a prayer that seemed to fail

Clive Staples Lewis was born on 29 November 1898 in Belfast, the younger son of Albert Lewis, a solicitor, and Flora Hamilton Lewis, a clergyman's daughter who had taken a degree in mathematics at a time when few women did. He had one brother, Warren, three years older, who would be his closest companion for the rest of his life. As a small boy he announced that his name was now "Jacksie," after a beloved dog; the family shortened it to Jack, and Jack he remained to everyone who knew him.

The house was full of books, and the two brothers filled the wet Ulster afternoons by inventing whole imaginary countries of their own. But the happy childhood ended abruptly. In 1908, when Jack was nine, his mother was found to have cancer. He prayed, with all a child's earnestness, that she would be made well. She died that August. Within weeks his grieving father sent both boys away to a grim boarding school in England, and something in Jack closed.

As a nine-year-old he prayed with all his heart for his mother's healing, and when she died he still half-expected a miracle. Years later he judged that he had come to God that day not as a Saviour or a Judge but as a kind of magician who was expected to perform and then go away — and when nothing happened, the disappointment quietly laid a foundation for his unbelief.

By his mid-teens he had abandoned the faith of his childhood altogether. He was sent at last to a private tutor in Surrey, William Kirkpatrick — "the Great Knock" — a fierce, logical old atheist who taught him to argue, to read Greek and Latin as living languages, and to accept nothing he could not defend. Lewis thrived on it. In the same years, though, something else was stirring. On a railway bookstall in 1916 he bought a copy of George MacDonald's Phantastes, and found in it a holiness he had no name for. He would later say that the book had baptised his imagination long before anything touched the rest of him.

The trenches, and a promise kept

Lewis won a scholarship to University College, Oxford, but the war came first. Commissioned into the Somerset Light Infantry, he reached the front line in France on his nineteenth birthday. On 15 April 1918, near Arras, a British shell fell short and burst beside him. He was wounded in the leg, hand and chest; the sergeant standing next to him, Harry Ayres, was killed. Lewis was invalided home and carried fragments of that shell in his body for the rest of his life.

Before going to France he had made a pact with a friend from training, Paddy Moore: if either of them did not come back, the survivor would look after the other's family. Paddy was killed. Lewis kept his word. For more than thirty years he shared a home with Paddy's mother, Janie Moore, and her daughter Maureen, supporting them through lean years as a young lecturer and nursing Mrs Moore patiently through her long final illness until her death in 1951. It was not always an easy household, and he rarely spoke of it, but it was a promise kept at real cost.

The most reluctant convert

Back at Oxford he took three first-class degrees — in classics, philosophy and English — and in 1925 was elected a Fellow of Magdalen College, where he would teach for nearly thirty years. He was, by every outward sign, a settled and slightly combative unbeliever. But his own reading kept betraying him. The writers he loved most — MacDonald, Chesterton, the old poets — seemed to know something he did not. His sharpest friends turned out to be Christians. And all his life he had been ambushed by sudden, piercing moments of longing for something no earthly thing could satisfy, a longing he called Joy.

Slowly, against his will, he was cornered. One evening in the summer term of 1929, alone in his rooms at Magdalen, he stopped resisting.

I gave in, and admitted that God was God, and knelt and prayed: perhaps, that night, the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England.

— C. S. Lewis, Surprised by Joy

That was belief in God, not yet in Christ. The second step came two years later. On the night of 19 September 1931 he walked for hours along Addison's Walk by the Cherwell with two friends, J. R. R. Tolkien and Hugo Dyson. Lewis had always been moved by the old myths of a dying and rising god; Tolkien and Dyson pressed on him that the story of Christ is that same myth — but this time it really happened, in history, at a particular place and under a particular governor. Nine days later, riding in the sidecar of his brother's motorcycle on the way to Whipsnade Zoo, he found that he believed Jesus Christ was the Son of God. He could not remember deciding; when they set out he did not believe, and when they arrived he did.

A layman's ministry

The convert set to work with the tools he had. Lewis joined his parish church, Holy Trinity at Headington Quarry, near the house called the Kilns which he shared with Warren and the Moores, and he took Communion faithfully. His first Christian book, an allegory of his own journey, appeared in 1933. With Tolkien and a circle of friends — the "Inklings" — he met weekly to read aloud what they were writing; The Lord of the Rings and much of Lewis's own fiction were first heard in those rooms.

The war made him famous. In 1940 The Problem of Pain faced honestly the question every grieving person asks. The next year a series of imaginary letters from an experienced devil, Screwtape, to his junior nephew began appearing in a church weekly; as a book in 1942 it became a bestseller, and it is still read by people who would never open a book of theology. In 1941 the BBC asked him to speak on the radio, and for three years his plain, reasonable, faintly gruff voice explained the Christian faith to a nation at war. He travelled to RAF stations to talk to airmen who might be dead within the week. Those broadcasts, gathered and revised, became Mere Christianity — an account of the faith held in common by Christians of every tradition, which has led countless readers out of unbelief.

I believe in Christianity as I believe that the sun has risen: not only because I see it, but because by it I see everything else.

— C. S. Lewis, "Is Theology Poetry?" (1944)

Fame cost him. Some colleagues at Oxford thought it unbecoming that a scholar should write popular religion, and he was passed over for chairs he had earned. He accepted it without bitterness. He gave away most of the royalties from his religious books, quietly, through a charitable trust, and he answered by hand the flood of letters from strangers — the anxious, the bereaved, children, the doubting — often several hours a day, for the rest of his life.

From October 1940 Lewis went almost every week to an elderly Anglican priest of the Cowley Fathers in Oxford, Father Walter Adams, for confession and spiritual direction, and continued until Father Adams died in 1952. Under his guidance Lewis kept a disciplined life of prayer — morning and evening, praying through the Psalms, and holding before God by name the long list of people who had asked for his prayers.

Narnia, and a new chair

In 1950, in his fifties, he published a story for children about four evacuees who step through a wardrobe into a frozen land and meet a great lion. Six more Chronicles of Narnia followed over six years. Lewis insisted that they were not allegories, but he did not hide who Aslan is: the stories are his attempt to let children meet the goodness, the terror and the joy of Christ before they have learned to be bored by religious words. They have been read by tens of millions of children ever since.

In 1954 Cambridge created a new chair of Medieval and Renaissance Literature for him at Magdalene College. He took it gladly, spending the week in Cambridge and the weekends at the Kilns. He continued writing serious scholarship alongside the books for which he is loved, and published his own spiritual autobiography, Surprised by Joy, in 1955. He thought he would remain a bachelor. He was wrong.

Joy

Among his many correspondents was Joy Davidman, an American poet of Jewish birth and a former Communist, who had come to Christ partly through his books. They met in 1952, and over the next few years a friendship of minds became something more. In April 1956 Lewis married her quietly in an Oxford register office — at the time he called it a formality, to allow her and her two sons to remain in England. That autumn she was found to have cancer throughout her bones, and he discovered that he loved her.

She was not expected to live long. On 21 March 1957, at her hospital bedside, they were married with the blessing of the Church by Peter Bide, a priest and former pupil of Lewis's. At Lewis's request Bide also laid hands on her and prayed for her healing.

Against every expectation, Joy did not die. Over the following months her disease receded, the diseased bones began to rebuild, and she was able to walk again; Lewis brought her home to the Kilns. At the same time he himself developed a painful loss of calcium in his own bones, and he wondered in his letters whether God had allowed him to bear something in her place. They were given three happy years — he said he had never expected such happiness — including a long-dreamed-of visit to Greece in the spring of 1960.

The cancer returned in 1959, and Joy died on 13 July 1960. Lewis's grief was savage. He wrote it down in a notebook, raw and unguarded, and published it under a pseudonym as A Grief Observed. It is one of the most honest books ever written by a Christian: it does not hide the doubt, the anger, the sense of a door slammed in his face. But it also records, slowly and without false comfort, the return of trust — not answers, but the presence of the One he had been shouting at. Many who have lost someone have found that book the only one they could bear to read.

Home

Lewis cared for Joy's sons, David and Douglas, and wrote on, but his own health was failing. In the summer of 1963 his heart and kidneys gave out; at one point he fell into a coma and received the last rites, then woke again, and spoke afterwards, half in jest, of being almost sorry to have been sent back. He resigned his Cambridge chair and spent the autumn quietly at the Kilns with Warren, reading and answering letters. On 22 November 1963, a week before his sixty-fifth birthday, he died at home in the late afternoon. The news was all but lost: the same day President Kennedy was shot in Dallas. He was buried in the churchyard of Holy Trinity, Headington Quarry, where he had worshipped for thirty years.

Aim at Heaven and you will get earth "thrown in": aim at earth and you will get neither.

— C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity

Half a century later he was given a memorial stone in Poets' Corner in Westminster Abbey. His books have never gone out of print, and Christians of almost every tradition count him as a friend; evangelical readers often differ with him on particular points, and he would have been the first to say that he was a layman, not an authority. What he gave the church was not a system but a voice: clear, humble, reasonable and glad, convinced that the longing at the heart of every human life was meant to lead home to God. His own books are still in copyright, so you will not find them here yet — but the older writers who led him there are on these shelves: George MacDonald, whose Unspoken Sermons he treasured; G. K. Chesterton, whose The Everlasting Man helped bring him back to faith; Athanasius, whose On the Incarnation he loved; Augustine; Thomas à Kempis; John Bunyan; and William Law.

Lewis (1898–1963) was an Oxford and Cambridge scholar of medieval and Renaissance literature who spent the first half of his life arguing against God and the second half explaining Him to more people than almost any writer of his century. fields.name: G. K. Chesterton
fields.bio: G. K. Chesterton (1874–1936) was an English journalist, poet and novelist who passed through near-despair as an art student and came out of it into a lifelong gratitude that led him to Christ. In Orthodoxy (1908) and The Everlasting Man (1925) he defended the Christian creed with wit, paradox and joy, and the second of them helped bring C. S. Lewis to faith.
fields.bio_html:
G. K. Chesterton was a huge man, more than six feet tall and broad in proportion, with a cloak, a wide-brimmed hat, a sword-stick and a pair of pince-nez that never sat straight. Behind the comic figure was one of the clearest Christian minds of the twentieth century. He wrote some eighty books, hundreds of poems, about two hundred short stories and thousands of essays, and in an age that was confident it had outgrown the faith, he argued for it so cheerfully that even his opponents loved him. More than anything else he was a man astonished by the world, and grateful for it.

A Kensington boyhood

Gilbert Keith Chesterton was born on 29 May 1874 in Kensington, London, the elder son of Edward Chesterton, whose family ran an estate agency, and Marie Louise Grosjean, whose family was of Swiss-French descent. His brother Cecil, five years younger, became his lifelong companion and sparring partner; the two boys argued, it was said, from the day Cecil could talk. Their father was a gentle, inventive man who built a toy theatre for the children, and Gilbert never forgot the little cardboard world with its painted scenes and tiny proscenium. The home was liberal, kindly and only loosely religious, and the boy grew up with a love of fairy tales, ballads and pictures more than of doctrine.

He went to St Paul's School, where he seemed to his teachers dreamy and slow, but where he and a circle of friends founded a debating club and a little magazine. In 1893 he enrolled at the Slade School of Art, part of University College London, to train as an illustrator. Those years became the darkest of his life.

Near despair, and a thread of thanks

The art world of the 1890s was full of a weary, clever pessimism, and the young Chesterton breathed it in. Alone with his imagination and his doubts, he fell into a period he afterwards described as a kind of madness. He filled notebooks with morbid drawings, until friends who found them wondered whether he was losing his mind, and he and Cecil experimented with the planchette and the Ouija board. He later said that whatever power moved the board, the one thing he could say with certainty about it was that it told lies; and he gave it up with what he called a bad smell in the mind. He came to feel that he had been playing with something dangerous.

What brought him back was not at first an argument but gratitude. Even at the lowest point, he said, he had held on to religion by a thin thread of thanks: the simple, overwhelming sense that it was good to exist at all, that a dandelion or a lamp-post was a gift that need not have been given. Out of that thread he began, slowly, to rebuild. Orthodoxy, written years later, tells the story of how the instincts of the nursery — wonder, gratitude and the sense that joy depends on keeping some small condition — turned out to fit the Christian creed like a key in a lock.

The test of all happiness is gratitude; and I felt grateful, though I hardly knew to whom.

— G. K. Chesterton, Orthodoxy

In the notebooks of those recovering years, kept long before he was well known, he wrote that other people said grace before meals, but he would say grace before the play and the opera, before the concert and the pantomime, before he opened a book, before sketching, swimming, fencing, walking and dancing — and grace before he dipped the pen in the ink. It was the habit of the rest of his life: everything received as a gift, and a gift meant thanks.

Frances

In 1896 Chesterton met Frances Blogg, the eldest daughter of a family in the artistic suburb of Bedford Park. Everyone around her talked endlessly about religions; what astonished him was that she actually practised one. She had been brought up in an Anglo-Catholic school, she went to church, she prayed, and she seemed entirely untouched by the fashionable moods of the people around her. He fell in love with her almost at once. They were married on 28 June 1901 at St Mary Abbots, Kensington, and through her faith and the clergy and Anglican friends she brought into his life, he found his way into the Church of England.

It was a deeply happy marriage, and also one marked by a quiet sorrow. They longed for children, and for many years hoped; at last Frances underwent an operation in the hope of being able to have them, but none came. Chesterton sat for two hours on the stairs of her nursing home, blocking the way, because he would not take her the sonnet he had written for her recovery until he had got its last line right. In later years their secretary, Dorothy Collins, became almost a daughter to them, and the children of their friends and neighbours filled the house at every Christmas party.

A journalist in the great debates

Chesterton had left the Slade without a degree and gone to work for a publisher, but he soon found his calling in journalism. He wrote reviews and essays for The Speaker and the Daily News, and from 1905 a weekly column for the Illustrated London News that he kept up for the rest of his life. He loved an argument, and he chose the biggest opponents he could find. In 1903 and 1904 he answered the atheist editor Robert Blatchford in the pages of The Clarion. For thirty years he debated George Bernard Shaw, in print and on public platforms, and the two remained affectionate friends throughout. He crossed swords with H. G. Wells over socialism, progress and the meaning of history. He held that ordinary people's instincts — for home, for property, for freedom, for faith — were wiser than the theories of the intellectuals who despised them.

In 1905 he published Heretics, a book of essays on the leading thinkers of the day, from Kipling to Shaw. Its critics, among them the writer G. S. Street, complained that he had attacked everybody else's philosophy without stating his own. Chesterton accepted the challenge. The answer, published in 1908, was Orthodoxy: not a textbook of theology but, as he said in its preface, an account of how he personally had come to believe. He tells it as the story of a man who set out to discover a new truth and found, to his embarrassment, that it had been discovered already.

I am the man who with the utmost daring discovered what had been discovered before.

— G. K. Chesterton, Orthodoxy

Orthodoxy was written when Chesterton was an Anglican, and it defends the faith of the Apostles' Creed rather than the claims of any one church. That is part of why Christians of every tradition have loved it ever since.

Father Brown and Beaconsfield

On a lecture tour in Yorkshire in 1904 he met a young Catholic priest, Father John O'Connor, who became one of his closest friends. Chesterton was astonished to find that this shy, kindly man knew more about the dark places of the human heart than any worldly-wise undergraduate. From that surprise came Father Brown, the small, round, unremarkable priest who solves crimes because he understands sin from the inside. The first collection, The Innocence of Father Brown, appeared in 1911, and the stories have been read and filmed ever since.

In 1909 Gilbert and Frances left London for Beaconsfield, a quiet market town in Buckinghamshire. They lived first in a small house called Overroads and later in Top Meadow, across the road, where the large studio became the scene of plays, parties and endless visitors.

Illness, and a brother lost

Late in 1914, worn out by work and the first months of the war, Chesterton collapsed. His heart was failing, and on Christmas Eve he fell into a coma from which, for weeks, he hardly woke. Frances nursed him through the winter, writing anxious letters to Father O'Connor and asking him to pray. Slowly, in the early months of 1915, he came back.

Frances wrote to Father O'Connor through those weeks begging him to pray for Gilbert, and herself prayed that God would restore him. In January 1915 she was able to write that by the mercy of God she dared to hope he would be given back to them. He recovered, and lived more than twenty years longer. Both of them afterwards spoke of his recovery as a miracle.

Sorrow came again at the war's end. Cecil Chesterton, who had enlisted as a private, fell ill in the last weeks of the fighting and died in a military hospital in France on 6 December 1918. Gilbert grieved for him deeply, and for years kept going the small political paper, The New Witness, whose editorship he had taken over when Cecil enlisted — out of loyalty to his brother, and at great cost to his own time and purse.

Into the Catholic Church

For many years Chesterton had been moving closer to the Roman Catholic Church. On 30 July 1922 he was received into it by Father O'Connor, in a makeshift chapel in a corrugated-iron hall belonging to the Railway Hotel in Beaconsfield, since the town had no Catholic church. Frances wept through the ceremony; she found the step hard, and followed him four years later, in 1926. Chesterton was entirely candid about where he had gone and why, and many Catholics count him among their great converts. Protestant readers, for their part, have never stopped finding in his books a warm and fearless defence of the faith they share — the Creed, the incarnation, the cross and the resurrection.

His greatest Christian books came in the years that followed. St Francis of Assisi appeared in 1923. In 1925 came The Everlasting Man, his answer to Wells's popular Outline of History: a retelling of the whole human story, from the paintings in the prehistoric cave to the child born in the cave at Bethlehem, to show that man is no mere animal and Christ no mere teacher. Among its readers was a young Oxford don named C. S. Lewis, then still an unbeliever. Lewis later wrote that in The Everlasting Man he first saw the whole Christian outline of history set out in a form that seemed to make sense, and he counted it one of the books that brought him to faith. St Thomas Aquinas followed in 1933, a short book that scholars of Aquinas have admired ever since.

Joy, which was the small publicity of the pagan, is the gigantic secret of the Christian.

— G. K. Chesterton, Orthodoxy

The last chapter

In the spring of 1936, after finishing his Autobiography, Chesterton's strength began to fail; the doctors found that his heart could no longer carry his enormous frame. Waking from a long reverie near the end, he said that the issue was now quite clear: it was between light and darkness, and everyone must choose his side. He died at Top Meadow on 14 June 1936, with Frances beside him, and was buried in the Catholic cemetery at Beaconsfield. Frances died two years later and was buried with him.

Chesterton never thought of himself as a saint, and he would have laughed at the idea of being a theologian. He was a journalist who wrote too much and too fast, and some of what he wrote has not aged well. But he gave the church something rare: a joyful, fighting faith that refused to be embarrassed, that found the creed not a cage but a playground with walls, and that saw the world, from the dandelion to the stars, as a gift that calls for thanks. Orthodoxy and The Everlasting Man are still finding readers who, like Lewis, discover in them that the old faith is far larger, stranger and gladder than they had been told.

faq.q: Who was G. K. Chesterton?
faq.a: Gilbert Keith Chesterton (1874–1936) was an English journalist, poet, novelist and Christian writer. He wrote some eighty books, hundreds of poems, about two hundred short stories and thousands of essays, and in an age confident that it had outgrown the faith he defended it so cheerfully that even his opponents loved him. He is best remembered for Orthodoxy, The Everlasting Man and the Father Brown detective stories.

faq.q: Where and when was Chesterton born?
faq.a: He was born on 29 May 1874 in Kensington, London, the elder son of Edward Chesterton, whose family ran an estate agency, and Marie Louise Grosjean. His brother Cecil, five years younger, was his lifelong companion. He went to St Paul's School and in 1893 enrolled at the Slade School of Art to train as an illustrator.

faq.q: What happened to Chesterton during his years at the Slade School of Art?
faq.a: The Slade years were the darkest of his life. Breathing in the weary pessimism of the 1890s art world, he fell into what he later called a kind of madness, filled notebooks with morbid drawings, and with his brother experimented with the planchette and the Ouija board. He gave it up, concluding that whatever moved the board told lies. What brought him back was gratitude: he said he had held on to religion by a thin thread of thanks for the sheer goodness of existing.

faq.q: How did Chesterton's wife Frances influence his faith?
faq.a: He met Frances Blogg in 1896 and was astonished that, among people who talked endlessly about religions, she actually practised one; she had been brought up in an Anglo-Catholic school, prayed and went to church. They married on 28 June 1901 at St Mary Abbots, Kensington, and through her faith and the Anglican friends she brought into his life he found his way into the Church of England.

faq.q: Did G. K. Chesterton have children?
faq.a: No. Gilbert and Frances longed for children and hoped for many years; Frances even underwent an operation in the hope of being able to have them, but none came. Their secretary, Dorothy Collins, later became almost a daughter to them, and the children of friends and neighbours filled their house at Christmas parties.

faq.q: Why did Chesterton write Orthodoxy?
faq.a: In 1905 he published Heretics, essays on the leading thinkers of the day. Critics, among them the writer G. S. Street, complained that he had attacked everybody else's philosophy without stating his own. Orthodoxy (1908) was his answer: not a textbook of theology but an account of how he personally came to believe, told as the story of a man who set out to discover a new truth and found it had been discovered already. He wrote it as an Anglican, and Christians of every tradition read it.

faq.q: Who did Chesterton debate?
faq.a: He loved an argument and chose the biggest opponents he could find. In 1903 and 1904 he answered the atheist editor Robert Blatchford in The Clarion. For thirty years he debated George Bernard Shaw, in print and on public platforms, and the two remained affectionate friends. He also crossed swords with H. G. Wells over socialism, progress and the meaning of history.

faq.q: Who inspired Father Brown?
faq.a: On a lecture tour in Yorkshire in 1904 Chesterton met a Catholic priest, Father John O'Connor, who became one of his closest friends. He was astonished that this shy, kindly man knew more about the dark places of the human heart than any worldly-wise undergraduate. From that surprise came Father Brown, the unremarkable priest who solves crimes because he understands sin from the inside; the first collection, The Innocence of Father Brown, appeared in 1911.

faq.q: When did Chesterton become a Catholic?
faq.a: After many years of moving towards it — through a near-fatal illness in 1914–15, from which both he and Frances spoke of his recovery as a miracle, and the death of his brother Cecil in France in December 1918 — Chesterton was received into the Roman Catholic Church on 30 July 1922 by Father O'Connor, in a makeshift chapel belonging to the Railway Hotel in Beaconsfield. Frances followed him four years later, in 1926.

faq.q: How did The Everlasting Man influence C. S. Lewis?
faq.a: The Everlasting Man (1925) retells the whole human story, from the paintings in the prehistoric cave to the child born at Bethlehem, to show that man is no mere animal and Christ no mere teacher. C. S. Lewis, then a young Oxford don and still an unbeliever, read it and later wrote that in it he first saw the whole Christian outline of history set out in a form that seemed to make sense; he counted it among the books that brought him to faith. Chesterton died at Beaconsfield on 14 June 1936.

fields.name: George MacDonald
fields.bio: George MacDonald (1824–1905) was a Scottish Congregational minister who lost his only pulpit young and spent the rest of his life preaching through novels, fairy tales, poems and his three series of Unspoken Sermons. The author of Phantastes, At the Back of the North Wind and The Princess and the Goblin, he taught that God is a Father whose love will not rest until his children are made good — and C. S. Lewis called him his master.
fields.bio_html:
George MacDonald lost the only pulpit he ever held before he was thirty, and spent the next half-century preaching anyway — in novels, in fairy tales, in poems, and in three volumes of sermons he called “unspoken,” because no congregation ever heard them. He lived most of those years poor and often ill, buried several of his children, and was distrusted by many in the churches he had grown up in. Yet the one conviction that runs through everything he wrote never wavered: that God is a Father, wholly good, whose love will not rest until his children are made like his Son.

A boy from Huntly

He was born on 10 December 1824 in Huntly, a small town in Aberdeenshire in the north-east of Scotland, into a family of farmers and weavers. His mother died when he was eight, and he was raised by his father, also named George, a man whose patience and goodness the son never forgot. Many readers have seen that father behind the wise, gentle fathers who fill MacDonald’s books, and behind the way he would later speak of God.

The religion of his boyhood was the stern Calvinism of the Scottish Congregational chapel, and the young MacDonald struggled with it. He could not make himself believe that God had chosen some for glory and passed the rest by, and he could not stop wanting God all the same. He studied at King’s College, Aberdeen, then went south to London to train for the ministry at Highbury College, a Congregational seminary.

Arundel, and the loss of a pulpit

In 1850 he was called as minister of Trinity Congregational Church in Arundel, Sussex, and in 1851 he married Louisa Powell. Their marriage would last more than fifty years, and they would have eleven children — six sons and five daughters.

Arundel did not go well. Within two years some of the leading men of the congregation had charged their young minister with heresy: he had suggested that the heathen who never heard the gospel might yet have an opportunity beyond death, and he was said to be tainted with German theology. Rather than dismiss him, they cut his salary of £150 a year, hoping he would leave. MacDonald answered that this was bad news, but he supposed he must try to live on less — and for a time he did, helped by gifts from his poorest parishioners, who did not share their deacons’ views. In May 1853 he resigned. He never held a pastorate again.

The years after Arundel were years of real want, with a growing family and a husband often too ill to work. MacDonald trusted his Father in heaven for their daily bread, and the family saw their needs met again and again, often at the last moment — the poor of Arundel bringing fruit, potatoes and cabbages to the manse; Lady Byron, the poet’s widow, who sought him out after reading his poem Within and Without and insisted she would be “the obliged person” if he let her help; and, years later, friends who clubbed together so that the family could build a home in Italy.

Poverty, sickness and the pen

The family moved to Manchester, where MacDonald preached to small groups and taught, until his lungs failed him. He suffered all his life from the tuberculosis that would take several of his children, and there were seasons when he could do nothing but lie still. Lady Byron, who became his patron in 1856, made possible a winter in the dry air of Algiers, which restored him for a time.

Shut out of the pulpit, he turned to writing. Within and Without, a long dramatic poem, appeared in 1855. In 1858 came Phantastes, “a faerie romance for men and women,” in which a young man named Anodos wanders through a dreamlike Fairy Land, meets his own shadow, and learns at last that it is better to love than to be loved. It sold poorly. To support his family MacDonald began writing novels of Scottish life — David Elginbrod (1863), Alec Forbes of Howglen, Robert Falconer and many more — full of crofters, schoolmasters and ministers, and of characters who find their way out of a hard religion into the love of God. They made his name, and for the rest of his life he wrote steadily, more than fifty books in all.

He also wrote for children, and it is for these books that many people know him best: At the Back of the North Wind (1871), about a poor London cab-driver’s boy and the mysterious lady who carries him through the night, and The Princess and the Goblin (1872), with its great-great-grandmother spinning in the attic and her thread that leads a child safely home through the dark. Fairy tales such as “The Light Princess” and “The Golden Key” followed. MacDonald did not think he was writing only for children. “I do not write for children,” he said in his essay “The Fantastic Imagination,” “but for the childlike, whether of five, or fifty, or seventy-five.” The same thought runs all through “The Child in the Midst,” the sermon that opens his Unspoken Sermons.

Among the friends of the family was a young Oxford mathematician, Charles Dodgson. He brought the MacDonalds the manuscript of a story he had written for a little girl named Alice, and Louisa read it aloud to the children to see whether it was worth publishing. Their small son Greville declared he wished there were sixty thousand copies of it. Dodgson took the hint, and Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland appeared in 1865 under the name of Lewis Carroll.

The unspoken sermons

All the while MacDonald went on preaching wherever he was asked, and writing sermons no congregation heard. The first series of Unspoken Sermons appeared in 1867, the second in 1885, the third in 1889. They are not easy reading — he called them “ears of corn, gathered and rubbed in my hands upon broken Sabbaths” — but they are where he speaks most directly. Again and again he returns to the same few things: that God is our Father and we are truly his children; that obedience, not opinion, is the way to know him; and that God’s love is not soft but fierce, a fire that will burn away everything in us that is not good.

Nothing is inexorable but love.

— George MacDonald, “The Consuming Fire”

He had a horror of any teaching that seemed to make God less good than the best of men, and he said so without hedging. He taught that every punishment God sends is meant to heal; and that a soul shut out in the outer darkness is still pursued there by a love that will not let it go “till he has paid the uttermost farthing.” He hoped — and in the end taught — that God’s love would finally win every one of his children home.

It should be said plainly that on this point, and on others, many Christian readers part company with him. MacDonald was a Christian universalist, though not a careless one. In his sermon “Justice” he rejected the doctrine of the atonement as it was commonly preached in his day — that God punished the innocent Christ in place of the guilty — calling the idea of laying the pain upon the righteous “in the name of justice” simply monstrous. Evangelicals who hold to penal substitution and to the finality of judgement will find much here to argue with, and they are not wrong to argue. But even those who disagree with him most have often found that he sends them back to the Gospels with fresh eyes, and few writers make the goodness of God feel so near.

The hardest, gladdest thing in the world is, to cry Father! from a full heart.

— George MacDonald, “Abba, Father!”

America, and the house called Courage

In 1872 the Boston Lyceum Bureau invited MacDonald to lecture in the United States, and from the autumn of that year into 1873 he travelled from city to city, speaking on Burns, Shakespeare and other poets to large audiences. He made many friends there. In 1877 Queen Victoria granted him a Civil List pension of £100 a year, which eased the long strain on the family purse.

Sorrow came too. Their daughter Mary Josephine died of tuberculosis in 1878, and their son Maurice the following year. Grace died in 1884, and Lilia, the eldest — who had nursed so many of the sick in the family — in 1891. In 1880, in the years of those first losses, MacDonald privately printed A Book of Strife in the Form of the Diary of an Old Soul: a seven-line prayer for every day of the year, with a blank page beside each one for the reader to add prayers of his own.

The Diary of an Old Soul is one long prayer — a poem for each day of the year, written in a season of grief and sickness, in which MacDonald brings his doubts, his weariness and his longings straight to God. It was printed with a blank page facing every page of verse, so that whoever read it might pray alongside him.

For the sake of the family’s lungs they had begun to winter on the Italian Riviera, and around Christmas 1880 they moved into a large house at Bordighera that friends had helped them to build. They called it Casa Coraggio, the House of Courage. It became a gathering place for the English community there, with readings and music; the second series of the Unspoken Sermons is dated from it.

The long silence

MacDonald’s last major book, Lilith (1895), is a strange, dark dream of death and resurrection, in which even the most rebellious soul is at last brought to lie down and sleep in hope. After it he wrote little. By 1898 a stroke had taken his speech, and he spent his last years almost entirely silent, cared for by his family. Louisa died in January 1902. MacDonald lived on three more years, and died on 18 September 1905 at Ashtead, in Surrey. His body was cremated, and his ashes were buried in the English cemetery at Bordighera, beside Louisa and their daughters Lilia and Grace.

Obedience is the opener of eyes.

— George MacDonald, “The Way”

The master of C. S. Lewis

MacDonald’s reputation faded after his death, and it might have faded further but for one reader. In 1916 a seventeen-year-old named Clive Staples Lewis, waiting for a train at Leatherhead station, bought a cheap copy of Phantastes from the bookstall. He was then an atheist, and remained one for years. But he later wrote that the book had worked on his imagination long before the rest of him followed, and that it carried a quality he could only afterwards name as holiness.

C. S. Lewis came to regard MacDonald as his master. In 1946 he published an anthology of 365 short readings from MacDonald, drawn mostly from these Unspoken Sermons, because he wanted to spread MacDonald’s religious teaching rather than revive his literary fame. In The Great Divorce he made MacDonald himself the narrator’s guide through the outskirts of heaven. Through Lewis, and through the writers who learned from them both, MacDonald’s Fairy Land has reached millions who have never heard his name.

What they were reaching for was what MacDonald had spent his life holding out: a God who is light with no darkness at all, who hides nothing that can be revealed, and who is not content to forgive his children until he has made them good. The first series of his sermons ends with a prayer that might stand for the whole of his life’s work — that Christ, “the child, the obedient God,” would come, “that we may be one with thee, and with every man and woman whom thou hast made, in the Father.”
