fields.name: John Milton
fields.bio: John Milton (1608–1674) was an English poet and pamphleteer, Secretary for Foreign Tongues to the Commonwealth’s Council of State, who went blind at forty-three and then dictated Paradise Lost, the great English epic of the fall of man, written to “justify the ways of God to men.”
fields.bio_html:
John Milton wrote the greatest poem in the English language about the fall of man, and he wrote it blind, out of favour, and lucky to be alive. He had spent twenty years of his prime arguing in prose for causes that lost, and had buried two wives and two of his children. Then, in a small house in London, with friends and hired readers taking down his lines, he set out to tell the whole story of sin and grace — from the war in Heaven to the promise of a Redeemer — and to “justify the ways of God to men.” Christians of every tradition have been reading it with profit ever since.

A scholar from Bread Street

He was born on 9 December 1608 in a house on Bread Street, in Cheapside, in the City of London. His father, also John Milton, was a scrivener and in his leisure a composer of real accomplishment. Under tutors and at St Paul’s School the boy learned Latin, Greek and Hebrew, French and Italian, and he later remembered that from the age of twelve he seldom went to bed before midnight, a habit he believed began the ruin of his eyes.

At sixteen he went up to Christ’s College, Cambridge, where his fair looks and fastidious manners earned him the nickname “the Lady of Christ’s.” He had been expected to enter the ministry of the Church of England, but he came to feel that he could not in conscience take the oaths a clergyman must swear under the bishops of his day. He gave himself instead to six more years of private study in his father’s houses outside London, in the hope, as he later wrote, of leaving something so written to aftertimes as they should not willingly let it die.

The early poems

The poet showed himself early. On Christmas morning 1629, at twenty-one, he wrote “On the Morning of Christ’s Nativity,” an ode in which the pagan oracles fall silent and the old gods flee before the Child in the manger; it is still read at Christmas. In 1637 a Cambridge acquaintance, Edward King, was drowned in the Irish Sea, and Milton’s elegy for him, “Lycidas,” turned a conventional lament into a meditation on early death and on corrupt shepherds of the Church, and ends in heaven, where the saints “wipe the tears for ever from his eyes.”

Italy, and the call home

In 1638 he set out on a long tour of the Continent. In Florence he visited Galileo, old, blind and a prisoner of the Inquisition in his own house at Arcetri — the one contemporary named in Paradise Lost. He meant to go on to Sicily and Greece, but news of the troubles between King and Parliament turned him back.

Twenty years of prose

Back in London he took in pupils, and from 1641 he poured out pamphlets against the rule of bishops. In 1642 he married Mary Powell, the young daughter of a Royalist family in Oxfordshire. Within weeks she went home to her parents and did not come back for three years. In that bitter interval Milton wrote The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce and three further tracts, arguing that a marriage without “fit conversation” — without true companionship of mind — was no marriage, and that Scripture allowed it to be dissolved. It scandalised his Puritan allies, and most Christians since have judged it too easy on the gospel’s hard words about divorce, though it was the work of an unhappy man reading his own trouble by the light of Scripture. In 1645 Mary returned — kneeling to beg his pardon, his nephew Edward Phillips remembered — and he took her back. They had four children together.

When Parliament moved to license every book before it could be printed, he answered with Areopagitica (1644), the most famous defence of a free press in English. “Give me the liberty to know, to utter, and to argue freely according to conscience, above all liberties,” he wrote. His liberty had its limits — he would not extend toleration to Roman Catholics — but the book has outlived the age that ignored it.

After the execution of Charles I in 1649, Milton defended the deed in print, and in March of that year the new Council of State made him its Secretary for Foreign Tongues, writing the Republic’s Latin letters to the courts of Europe. He served Cromwell’s government almost to the Restoration, and his Latin Defence of the English People (1651) made him famous across the Continent.

Blindness

His sight had been failing for years, and he was warned that the work on his Defence would cost him what remained of it. He finished it anyway, and by early 1652 he was totally blind, at forty-three. The same year brought heavier losses. Mary died in May 1652, a few days after the birth of their third daughter, Deborah, and within weeks their only son, John, died in infancy. Milton was left in darkness with three small girls. In 1656 he married Katherine Woodcock, and by every account the marriage was happy; but she died in February 1658, a few months after giving birth to a daughter who died soon after her.

Out of the first darkness came the sonnet later editors titled “On His Blindness.” It wrestles with the parable of the talents: how can a servant whose one gift is buried render a true account to his Master? Patience gives the answer.

When I consider how my light is spent,
Ere half my days in this dark world and wide,
And that one talent which is death to hide
Lodged with me useless, though my soul more bent
To serve therewith my Maker, and present
My true account, lest he returning chide;
“Doth God exact day-labour, light denied?”
I fondly ask. But Patience, to prevent
That murmur, soon replies, “God doth not need
Either man’s work or his own gifts; who best
Bear his mild yoke, they serve him best. His state
Is kingly. Thousands at his bidding speed,
And post o’er land and ocean without rest:
They also serve who only stand and wait.”

— John Milton, Sonnet XIX

The Restoration

When the monarchy returned in 1660 Milton had every reason to fear for his life. He had defended the killing of a king. He went into hiding; his books defending the regicide were burned by the common hangman; and in the autumn he was arrested and held in custody. He was released on 15 December 1660, after paying fees that his friend the poet Andrew Marvell, then a member of Parliament, protested in the House were excessive. In 1663 he married Elizabeth Minshull, a young woman who cared for him faithfully to the end.

His early biographer John Aubrey recorded the shape of Milton’s blind days. He rose early, at four in the morning, even after he lost his sight, and had a man read to him; the first thing read was the Hebrew Bible, and then he sat in contemplation. Only after Scripture and silence did he turn to dictating.

Paradise Lost

He composed the great poem in the late 1650s and early 1660s, dictating in blank verse — without rhyme, which he called the invention of a barbarous age. When plague came to London in 1665, a young Quaker who read to him, Thomas Ellwood, found him a cottage at Chalfont St Giles in Buckinghamshire, and there Ellwood was lent the finished manuscript. In April 1667 he sold the rights to a printer for £5, with £5 more to come, and Paradise Lost appeared that autumn in ten books. In 1674, the year of his death, he issued the second edition, dividing two of the books to make twelve and setting a prose “Argument” before each — the form in which the poem is read here.

Its opening prayer to the Holy Spirit gives the whole purpose of the work.

What in me is dark / Illumine, what is low raise and support; / That to the highth of this great argument / I may assert the Eternal Providence, / And justify the ways of God to men.

— John Milton, Paradise Lost, Book I

The poem opens in Hell, where Satan and his angels lie stunned on a burning lake, and Satan is magnificent — so magnificent that William Blake would say Milton was “of the Devil’s party without knowing it.” But Milton is showing how splendid evil can look, and how it shrinks: by the end Satan is a serpent hissing in the dust. In Heaven the Son offers himself to die for man while all the angels stand mute; in Eden Adam and Eve live in a love that is innocent and full of joy; then the temptation, the fall, the bitter quarrel, and at last their tears of repentance before God. In the final books the archangel Michael shows Adam the history to come, down to the Seed of the woman who will crush the serpent’s head, and Adam bursts out in wonder at a grace that can bring good from his own ruin.

O Goodness infinite, Goodness immense! / That all this good of evil shall produce, / And evil turn to good.

— John Milton, Paradise Lost, Book XII

The blind poet’s prayer for inner sight stands at the head of the third book, where he turns from Hell to Heaven and calls upon the holy Light he can no longer see: “So much the rather thou, celestial Light, / Shine inward, and the mind through all her powers / Irradiate: there plant eyes, all mist from thence / Purge and disperse, that I may see and tell / Of things invisible to mortal sight.”

When Ellwood returned the manuscript at Chalfont, he asked Milton what he had to say of Paradise found. Later Milton showed him Paradise Regained, a shorter epic of Christ’s victory over Satan’s temptations in the wilderness, and told him he owed the poem to that question. It was published in 1671 together with Samson Agonistes, a tragedy of the blind champion of Israel, “eyeless in Gaza.”

An honest account

Milton was a man of strong and sometimes stubborn convictions, and not all of them were the Church’s. After his death a long Latin treatise, De Doctrina Christiana, lay forgotten among state papers until it was found in 1823 and published in 1825. In it he argued from Scripture that the Son, though divine, was neither coeternal nor equal with the Father — a view near to the ancient Arian heresy — and that the whole person, soul with body, sleeps in death until the resurrection. It also defended his views on divorce and denied that Scripture forbade polygamy. Christians who honour him have to say plainly that on the Trinity the treatise departs from the creeds. Readers still argue over how much of it reaches the poem, but many have found in Paradise Lost nothing a believer cannot read with gladness.

Death and legacy

Milton died of gout, quietly, on 8 November 1674, and was buried beside his father in the chancel of St Giles Cripplegate in the City of London. Readers of every Christian tradition have found in it the biblical story made vivid: the pride of the fallen angel, the goodness of creation, and the grace that answers sin with a Saviour. In 1942 C. S. Lewis published A Preface to Paradise Lost, defending the poem against critics who found it cold or who made Satan its hero. Lewis argued that Milton’s theology is, in the main, the common faith of Christendom, and that Satan, for all his splendour, is a study in self-deceiving pride, never meant to be admired.

The poem ends not in despair but in hope. Adam and Eve, forgiven and promised a Redeemer, shed some natural tears and wipe them soon. “The world was all before them, where to choose / Their place of rest, and Providence their guide.” Hand in hand they go out of Eden. It is a fitting picture of the man who wrote it: blind, bereaved and defeated in everything the world counts success, yet still trusting that the ways of God are good.

faq.q: Who was John Milton?
faq.a: John Milton (1608–1674) was an English poet and writer, born in Bread Street, Cheapside, in the City of London. After the early poems he wrote at Cambridge and twenty years of prose pamphlets, he served the Commonwealth as Secretary for Foreign Tongues, went totally blind by early 1652, and afterwards dictated Paradise Lost, his epic of the fall of man, written to “justify the ways of God to men.”

faq.q: Where did John Milton study?
faq.a: Milton learned Latin, Greek and Hebrew, French and Italian under tutors and at St Paul’s School in London, and at sixteen went up to Christ’s College, Cambridge, where his looks and manners earned him the nickname “the Lady of Christ’s.” He had been expected to enter the ministry, but felt he could not in conscience take the oaths a clergyman had to swear under the bishops of his day, and gave himself instead to six more years of private study.

faq.q: What were Milton’s early poems?
faq.a: On Christmas morning 1629, at twenty-one, Milton wrote “On the Morning of Christ’s Nativity,” an ode in which the pagan oracles fall silent and the old gods flee before the Child in the manger; it is still read at Christmas. In 1637 he wrote “Lycidas,” an elegy for the drowned Edward King that becomes a meditation on early death and on corrupt shepherds of the Church, and ends in heaven.

faq.q: Did John Milton meet Galileo?
faq.a: Yes. On his tour of the Continent in 1638 Milton visited Galileo in Florence, when the astronomer was old, blind and a prisoner of the Inquisition in his own house at Arcetri. Galileo is the one contemporary named in Paradise Lost. Milton meant to travel on to Sicily and Greece, but news of the troubles between King and Parliament turned him back to England.

faq.q: What did Milton argue in Areopagitica and the divorce tracts?
faq.a: After his young wife Mary Powell went home to her family, Milton wrote The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce and three further tracts, arguing that a marriage without true companionship of mind was no marriage and could be dissolved; it scandalised his Puritan allies. In Areopagitica (1644) he opposed the licensing of books before printing: “Give me the liberty to know, to utter, and to argue freely according to conscience, above all liberties.” He would not extend that toleration to Roman Catholics.

faq.q: When did John Milton go blind?
faq.a: Milton’s sight had been failing for years, and he was warned that writing his Latin Defence of the English People (1651) would cost him what remained of it. He finished it anyway and was totally blind by early 1652, at forty-three. Out of that darkness came the sonnet later editors titled “On His Blindness,” which ends: “They also serve who only stand and wait.”

faq.q: What losses did Milton suffer in his family?
faq.a: His first wife, Mary, died in May 1652, a few days after the birth of their third daughter, Deborah, and within weeks their only son, John, died in infancy. In 1656 he married Katherine Woodcock, a happy marriage, but she died in February 1658, a few months after giving birth to a daughter who also died. In 1663 he married Elizabeth Minshull, who cared for him faithfully to the end.

faq.q: What happened to Milton at the Restoration?
faq.a: Having defended the execution of Charles I and served Cromwell’s government, Milton went into hiding when the monarchy returned in 1660. His books defending the regicide were burned by the common hangman, and in the autumn he was arrested and held in custody. He was released on 15 December 1660, after paying fees that his friend Andrew Marvell protested in Parliament were excessive.

faq.q: How did Milton write Paradise Lost?
faq.a: Blind, he dictated the poem in blank verse to friends and hired readers. John Aubrey recorded that he rose at four in the morning, had the Hebrew Bible read to him first, and then sat in contemplation before dictating. The poem appeared in ten books in 1667; in 1674, the year of his death, Milton issued the second edition in twelve books with a prose Argument before each. Paradise Regained and Samson Agonistes followed in 1671.

faq.q: Was John Milton orthodox in his beliefs?
faq.a: Not entirely. His Latin treatise De Doctrina Christiana, found in 1823 and published in 1825, argued that the Son, though divine, was neither coeternal nor equal with the Father, a view near to the ancient Arian heresy, and that soul and body sleep in death until the resurrection. Readers still argue how much of it reaches the poem, and C. S. Lewis’s A Preface to Paradise Lost (1942) defended the poem’s theology as, in the main, the common faith of Christendom.

fields.name: Julian of Norwich
fields.bio: Julian of Norwich (1343 – after 1416) was an English anchoress whose Revelations of Divine Love, written after sixteen “shewings” she received in May 1373 when she was thought to be dying, is the first book in English known to have been written by a woman. Enclosed in a cell at St Julian’s church in Norwich, she spent twenty years pondering what she had seen, and came to one answer: love was his meaning, and all shall be well.
fields.bio_html:
We do not know her name. She is called Julian because she lived for many years in a cell built against the wall of St Julian’s church in Conisford, a parish of the busy river city of Norwich, and in her own book she calls herself only “a simple creature unlettered.” Yet that book, written in English by a woman who had been shut away from the world, is the first book in the English language known to have been written by a woman — and six centuries later it is still read and prayed over because it insists, against everything its age had seen, that the deepest truth about God is love.

A city of plague

Julian tells us that she was thirty and a half years old in May 1373, so she was born late in 1342 or early in 1343. Norwich was then one of the great towns of England, a city of wool and trade, of cathedral, priories and crowded parish churches. When she was about six the Black Death reached it. The pestilence of 1349 carried off a great part of the city, and it came back again and again through her childhood and youth. A woman of her generation grew up among funerals.

In 1381 the Peasants’ Revolt swept through Norfolk; in her later years the burning of heretics began in England. Julian’s serenity was won in a hard century.

Of her family we know nothing. Some have guessed that she was a widow who had lost a husband and children to the plague, and so learned the mother’s love she later wrote about; others that she was a nun of the Benedictine priory of Carrow, which held the church of St Julian. Neither guess can be proved. She tells us almost nothing of herself, because she wanted her readers to look past her: “Because of the Shewing I am not good but if I love God the better.”

Three gifts

What she does tell us is how she prayed. As a young woman she asked God for three gifts. She wanted to have been with Mary Magdalene and the others at the cross, to see with her own eyes what the Lord suffered; she asked for an illness when she was thirty, so severe that she and everyone around her would believe she was dying; and she asked for three wounds.

Of the third gift she writes: “by the grace of God and teaching of Holy Church I conceived a mighty desire to receive three wounds in my life: that is to say, the wound of very contrition, the wound of kind compassion, and the wound of steadfast longing toward God.” The first two petitions she offered with a condition — “if it be not Thy will, good Lord, be not displeased: for I will nought but as Thou wilt” — and in time forgot them. The third she asked without any condition, and it dwelt with her continually.

May 1373

When she was thirty and a half, she fell ill. For three days and nights she lay sick; on the fourth night she received the last rites, and no one expected her to live till morning. She lingered two more days. By then her body was dead from the waist down, and those who were with her thought she was passing. Her parish priest was sent for. He set a crucifix before her face and said, “I have brought thee the Image of thy Maker and Saviour: look thereupon and comfort thee therewith.” Everything in the room grew dark except the cross, on which she saw “a common light.” Then, suddenly, all her pain was taken away.

The petitions she had long since forgotten were answered together. The sickness came at thirty, as she had asked, so near to death that all who saw her believed she was dying; and as she gazed on the crucifix she saw what she had longed to see — the red blood trickling down from under the crown of thorns, “hot and freshly and right plenteously,” and with it a joy that filled her heart. She took it, she says, as strength for the hour of her temptation, “for all creatures living, against all the fiends of hell.”

Over the next hours she received what she called “shewings.” The first began about four in the morning, and they followed one after another until past nine. She saw the face of the crucified Christ change colour as he died. And in one of the best loved passages in all Christian writing, she saw the whole of creation held in the hand of God.

It lasteth, and ever shall [last] for that God loveth it. And so All-thing hath the Being by the love of God.

— Julian of Norwich, on the little thing, “the quantity of an hazel-nut,” in the palm of her hand

God made it, God loves it, God keeps it — and no soul is at rest till it rests in him. Later that day, when the pain came back, she told a visiting religious that she had been raving — and then was ashamed, because he took her shewings more seriously than she had. That night she dreamed that the Fiend had her by the throat, and woke to a smell of smoke that no one else could smell; she fled to what she had been shown and to the faith of the Church, and peace came. Then came the sixteenth shewing, in which she saw Christ dwelling in the soul as in a city, and heard the words that close the revelations.

He said not: Thou shalt not be tempested, thou shalt not be travailed, thou shalt not be afflicted; but He said: Thou shalt not be overcome.

— Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love

Twenty years of pondering

Julian wrote down what she had seen; that first account, the Short Text, survives in a single fifteenth-century copy. But she did not stop there. For two decades she turned the visions over, prayed through them, and asked what they meant. She tells us that she desired “oftentimes” to know what the Lord meant, and that the answer came more than fifteen years after the shewings, in her understanding:

Learn it well: Love was His meaning. Who shewed it thee? Love. What shewed He thee? Love. Wherefore shewed it He? For Love.

— Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love

One vision had baffled her most: a lord who sends his servant on an errand, and the servant who runs off in his eagerness, falls into a ditch, and lies there hurt and unable to rise, unable even to turn his face to his master. The lord does not blame him at all, and means to reward him beyond anything he lost. Twenty years after the shewings, “save three months,” she was taught to see in the servant both Adam and Christ — fallen humanity, and the Son who came down into its fall to lift it. Out of these years of reflection came the much fuller book now called the Long Text, eighty-six chapters in which the visions open out into a theology of God’s love.

The anchoress of St Julian’s

At some point Julian became an anchoress. An anchoress was enclosed for life in a cell joined to a church, with one window onto the altar and another for those who came for counsel. Her days were given to prayer, to the services of the church and to the people who sought her out. The four wills that mention her show that she was known and valued: in 1394 a Norwich rector left twelve shillings to “Julian anakorite”; in 1404 a priest left money to Julian, anchoress at St Julian’s, Conisford, and to Sarah who lived with her; in 1415 a Norwich man remembered the anchoress there with her maid and her former maid Alice; and in 1416 Isabel, Countess of Suffolk, left twenty shillings to “Julian reclus a Norwich.”

The most vivid glimpse of her comes from another woman. In about 1413 Margery Kempe of Lynn, whose tears and visions had made her many enemies, came to Norwich to ask the anchoress whether her experiences were from God. Julian encouraged her to be obedient to God’s will, and told her that the Holy Spirit never moves anyone to anything against charity, for then he would be contrary to himself. Margery remembered “holy dalliance” between them over many days, and wrote it down in her own book.

All shall be well

What Julian saw, and what she spent her life understanding, is that God is love — not as a sentiment, but as the ground of everything. She saw no wrath in God; the wrath, she said, is on our side, and God’s mercy works to bring us peace. She saw the cross as the highest proof of that love: Christ told her that if he could suffer more for her, he would. She wrote boldly of Jesus as our Mother, who bears us to joy and endless life as an earthly mother bears her children to pain and death, and feeds us with himself in the Sacrament. The image was not new — Anselm and Bernard had used it, and Christ himself spoke of gathering Jerusalem as a hen gathers her chickens — but no one has drawn it more tenderly.

And she faced the hardest question of her century head on. If God is love, why was sin not prevented? Why so much sorrow? The answer she was given has become her most famous sentence:

It behoved that there should be sin; but all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.

— Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love

She did not take this as a cheap comfort. She saw that there is a great deed the Trinity will do at the last day, hidden now in God, by which he will make well all that is not well. Some modern readers have pressed these words into universalism, the belief that in the end every soul will be saved. Julian herself would not go there. She set beside the promise the teaching of the Church that many shall be condemned, and confessed honestly that she could not see how both could stand. The answer she received was this: “That which is impossible to thee is not impossible to me: I shall save my word in all things and I shall make all things well.” So she held to the faith of the Church in every point, trusted God with what she could not see, and left the tension in his hands.

After her

We do not know when Julian died. She was alive in 1416, and probably did not live many years beyond it. Her Long Text survived because English Benedictine nuns, living in exile at Cambrai and Paris in the seventeenth century, copied the old contemplative writers for their own prayer; one of their chaplains, Serenus Cressy, printed it in 1670. In 1901 Grace Warrack brought out the version from the manuscript in the British Museum that is printed here; with it Julian found a new audience. In 1942 T. S. Eliot gave her words to the closing lines of Little Gidding, and in the same year a German bomb destroyed St Julian’s church. It was rebuilt and reopened in 1953, with a chapel on the site of her cell. She is remembered on 8 May in the calendars of the Church of England and other churches.

She wrote for all her “even-Christians,” her fellow believers, and wanted them to look past her to the Lord who had shown her his love. In her last chapter she says that the book is begun but “not yet performed” — a fitting word from a woman whose whole message was that the love of God is greater than anything we have yet understood of it.

faq.q: Who was Julian of Norwich?
faq.a: Julian of Norwich was an English anchoress who lived in a cell built against the wall of St Julian’s church in Conisford, Norwich. Born late in 1342 or early in 1343, she received sixteen visions of the love of God in May 1373, when she was thirty and a half and thought to be dying. Her account of them, Revelations of Divine Love, is the first book in the English language known to have been written by a woman. She was still alive in 1416, and the date of her death is not known.

faq.q: Was Julian of Norwich her real name?
faq.a: No one knows her real name. She is called Julian after the church of St Julian in Conisford, where she lived as an anchoress, and in her book she calls herself only “a simple creature unlettered.” Of her family nothing is known. Some have guessed that she was a widow who had lost a husband and children to the plague, others that she was a nun of the Benedictine priory of Carrow, which held the church; neither guess can be proved.

faq.q: What three gifts did Julian of Norwich ask of God?
faq.a: As a young woman Julian asked God for three gifts. She wanted a sight of the Passion, as if she had stood with Mary Magdalene at the cross; she asked for an illness at thirty so severe that everyone would believe she was dying; and she asked for three wounds: the wound of very contrition, the wound of kind compassion and the wound of steadfast longing toward God. The first two she asked only if they were God’s will, and in time forgot them. The third she asked without any condition.

faq.q: What happened to Julian of Norwich in May 1373?
faq.a: When she was thirty and a half she fell so ill that she received the last rites and no one expected her to live. Her parish priest set a crucifix before her face and told her to look on the image of her Maker and Saviour. Suddenly her pain was taken away, and as she gazed on the cross she saw the blood trickle down from under the crown of thorns. Fifteen shewings followed from about four in the morning until past nine, and a sixteenth came the following night. Her forgotten petitions had been answered together.

faq.q: What is Julian of Norwich’s vision of the hazelnut?
faq.a: In one of her first shewings Julian saw a little thing, the size of a hazelnut, lying in the palm of her hand, as round as a ball. When she asked what it might be, she was answered that it is all that is made. She wondered how it could last, it was so small, and was told: “It lasteth, and ever shall [last] for that God loveth it.” In it she saw three things: that God made it, that God loves it and that God keeps it.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Short Text and the Long Text?
faq.a: Julian first wrote down her visions in a brief account now called the Short Text, which survives in a single fifteenth-century copy. She then spent some twenty years praying over what she had seen. More than fifteen years after the shewings she was taught that love was the Lord’s meaning, and twenty years after them, save three months, she came to understand the vision of the lord and the servant. Out of that reflection came the much fuller Long Text, eighty-six chapters in which the visions open out into a theology of God’s love.

faq.q: What was an anchoress, and how do we know Julian was one?
faq.a: An anchoress was a woman enclosed for life in a cell joined to a church, with one window onto the altar and another for those who came for counsel. Four wills record Julian there: a Norwich rector left money to “Julian anakorite” in 1394; a priest remembered Julian, anchoress at St Julian’s, Conisford, and Sarah who lived with her, in 1404; a Norwich man remembered the anchoress and her maids in 1415; and Isabel, Countess of Suffolk, left twenty shillings to Julian, recluse at Norwich, in 1416.

faq.q: Why did Margery Kempe visit Julian of Norwich?
faq.a: In about 1413 Margery Kempe of Lynn, whose tears and visions had made her many enemies, came to Norwich to ask the anchoress whether her experiences were from God. Julian encouraged her to be obedient to God’s will, and told her that the Holy Spirit never moves anyone to anything against charity, for then he would be contrary to himself. Margery recalled their holy conversation over many days and wrote it down in her own book.

faq.q: What did Julian of Norwich mean by “all shall be well”?
faq.a: Julian had wondered why God did not prevent sin, since without it all would have been well. She was answered: “It behoved that there should be sin; but all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.” She understood that the Trinity will do a great deed at the last day, hidden now in God, by which he will make well all that is not well. Some modern readers have taken this as universalism, but Julian held to the Church’s teaching that many shall be condemned, confessed that she could not see how both could stand, and left the tension in God’s hands.

faq.q: Why does Julian of Norwich call Jesus our Mother?
faq.a: Julian saw that God is love, the ground of everything, and wrote of Jesus as our Mother, who bears us to joy and endless life as an earthly mother bears her children to pain and death, and who feeds us with himself in the Sacrament. The image was not new, for Anselm and Bernard had used it and Christ spoke of gathering Jerusalem as a hen gathers her chickens, but no one has drawn it more tenderly. She also saw no wrath in God, only on our side.

fields.name: Brother Lawrence
fields.bio: Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection (Nicolas Herman, c. 1614–1691) was a lay brother of the Discalced Carmelites in Paris — a former soldier and footman who cooked for his community for fifteen years and later mended its sandals. His conversations and letters, gathered after his death as The Practice of the Presence of God, teach a life lived hour by hour in God's company, and have been loved by Catholics and Protestants alike.
fields.bio_html:
He was never a priest, never a preacher, never a scholar. He was a lame lay brother who cooked for a Paris monastery and, in his old age, mended its sandals. Yet the few pages gathered after his death — four conversations and a handful of letters — have been read for three centuries by Catholics and Protestants alike, by anyone who has wondered whether God can be known in a kitchen as well as in a chapel. Brother Lawrence’s answer was that he can, and that the whole of the spiritual life comes down to living, hour by hour, in his company.

A peasant’s son from Lorraine

He was born Nicolas Herman in Hériménil, a village near Lunéville in the Duchy of Lorraine, around 1614. The year is uncertain; in a late letter he calls himself “almost eighty,” which would put it a few years earlier. His parents were poor country people, and devout. In his youth the Thirty Years’ War brought soldiers, plague and famine to Lorraine’s villages.

The turning point of his life came in a winter when he was about eighteen. He told the story himself, decades later. Seeing a tree stripped of its leaves, and considering that in a little while the leaves would be renewed, and after them the flowers and the fruit, he received, as he put it, “a high view of the Providence and Power of God,” which never afterwards left him. That bare tree set him loose from the world and kindled in him a love for God so great that, forty years on, he could not tell whether it had grown since.

Soldier and footman

The tree did not send him straight into a cloister; he went for a soldier. According to the accounts of his early life, he was taken prisoner by German troops who suspected him of being a spy and threatened to hang him; he answered them so calmly that they let him go. In 1635, at Rambervillers, not far from home, he was badly wounded in the leg. The injury lamed him for the rest of his life.

After a time of recovery at his parents’ home he went into service as a footman to M. Fieubert, the treasurer. He remembered himself in that post with rueful humour as “a great awkward fellow who broke everything.” He went into religion thinking, he said, that in a monastery he would be made to smart for his awkwardness and his faults, and so would sacrifice to God his life and its pleasures. But God, he added, “had disappointed him”: he met with nothing there but satisfaction.

The Carmelites of the rue de Vaugirard

In 1640, at about the age of twenty-six, he entered the house of the Discalced Carmelites on the rue de Vaugirard in Paris as a lay brother. He received the brown habit in August of that year and took the name by which the world knows him, Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection, making his profession two years later. He would spend the rest of his life in that community, unlearned and largely unnoticed.

His first years there were not peaceful. He was, he said, long troubled by the conviction that he would be damned, and nothing anyone said could persuade him otherwise. For four years the fear lay on him. What carried him through was a resolution:

In the years he believed himself lost, he reasoned with himself before God: “I engaged in a religious life only for the love of God, and I have endeavored to act only for Him; whatever becomes of me, whether I be lost or saved, I will always continue to act purely for the love of God. I shall have this good at least, that till death I shall have done all that is in me to love Him.”

In a letter he wrote that for his first ten years he suffered much: his past sins were always before him, and all creatures, reason and God himself seemed against him, with faith alone for him. Then, when he had resigned himself to ending his days in that trouble, he found himself “changed all at once,” and his soul, until then in turmoil, felt “a profound inward peace, as if she were in her centre and place of rest.” He came to see that the trouble had arisen from want of faith, and from then on, he said, he passed his life in perfect liberty and continual joy.

The kitchen

For some fifteen years Brother Lawrence was the community’s cook. He had, by his own account, a great natural aversion to the work. He did not escape it; he changed the way he did it, doing everything there for the love of God and praying on every occasion for grace to do it well, until he found it easy.

When he began his work in the kitchen he would say to God, with a son’s trust: “O my God, since Thou art with me, and I must now, in obedience to Thy commands, apply my mind to these outward things, I beseech Thee to grant me the grace to continue in Thy Presence; and to this end do Thou prosper me with Thy assistance, receive all my works, and possess all my affections.” When he had finished, he gave thanks if it had gone well, asked pardon if not, and began again without discouragement.

Those who watched him saw that in the greatest hurry of the kitchen he was never hasty and never loitering. In his own words, the ones he is best remembered by:

In the noise and clatter of my kitchen, while several persons are at the same time calling for different things, I possess God in as great tranquility as if I were upon my knees at the blessed sacrament.

— Brother Lawrence, Fourth Conversation

The monastery sometimes sent him on errands he was badly fitted for. Once he was dispatched to Burgundy to buy the community’s wine, a task he dreaded: he had, he said, no head for business, and he was so lame that he could get about the boat only by rolling himself over the casks. He gave himself no uneasiness, but told God that it was His business he was about, and afterwards found that it had all been very well done.

He made it his rule, whenever some hard duty or some virtue was asked of him, to turn to God and say, “Lord, I cannot do this unless Thou enablest me.” And then, he told his friend, he received strength more than sufficient.

In later life he was moved from the kitchen to the sandal-maker’s bench, where he repaired the footwear of a large community. He was well pleased with it, he said, and as ready to leave it as the old one, since in every condition he found his pleasure in doing little things for the love of God — even taking up a straw from the ground for His sake.

The practice

What Brother Lawrence called the practice of the presence of God was not a technique, and he distrusted techniques. He had read many books describing different methods of going to God, he said, and found that they puzzled him more than they helped. So he resolved to “give the all for the all”:

I renounced, for the love of Him, everything that was not He; and I began to live as if there was none but He and I in the world.

— Brother Lawrence, First Letter

From then on he kept his mind in God’s presence, and when it wandered he brought it back without fretting. In time it became habitual. It was a great delusion, he said, to think that the times of prayer ought to differ from other times; his prayer was nothing else but a sense of the presence of God.

He was frank that it was hard at first. It did not matter greatly what one did, for God “regards not the greatness of the work, but the love with which it is performed.” Our sanctification, he said, does not depend on changing our works, but in doing for God’s sake what we commonly do for our own. He believed anyone could live this way, and said so plainly:

Were I a preacher, I should, above all other things, preach the practice of the presence of God; and, were I a director, I should advise all the world to do it, so necessary do I think it, and so easy too.

— Brother Lawrence, Fifth Letter

The friend who wrote it down

Brother Lawrence would have left no trace at all but for Joseph de Beaufort, a priest who later served as vicar general to Cardinal Louis-Antoine de Noailles, Archbishop of Paris. De Beaufort first visited him on 3 August 1666 and came back three more times, in September and November of that year and in November 1667, writing down afterwards what the old brother had told him. He asked only sincerity: if de Beaufort truly meant to serve God, he might come as often as he pleased; if not, he ought not to come at all.

Others sought him out by letter. The letters that survive are short and practical, written to a priest, to friends in religion and in the world, and, in the last of them, to a correspondent who was gravely ill. To the sick he did not promise relief; he prayed that God would give them strength to bear their pains as long as He pleased, and told them that God is often nearer to us in sickness than in health. “We have but little time to live,” he wrote to one friend; “you are near sixty-four, and I am almost eighty. Let us live and die with God.”

Death and the little book

His last letter ends with the hope that God would grant him “the favor to see Him within a few days.” The editor’s note beneath it records that he took to his bed two days later and died within the week. He died in the Carmelite house in Paris on 12 February 1691, after half a century in the community. De Beaufort’s account of his death says that when a brother at his bedside asked him what he was doing, he answered that he was doing what he would do for all eternity — blessing God, praising Him, adoring Him and loving Him with all his heart.

De Beaufort gathered what he could. In 1692 he published Brother Lawrence’s spiritual maxims and his letters, with a short eulogy of his life, and in 1694 a second small volume containing an account of his ways and the four conversations. They had the misfortune to appear just as the quarrel over Quietism — the controversy around Madame Guyon and Archbishop Fénelon, who admired Brother Lawrence — was making all talk of simple, wordless prayer suspect in France, and for a long time the lay brother was more honoured outside his own church than within it. It was a Protestant, Pierre Poiret, who reprinted him among the classics of the inner life, and through such editions he passed into English.

So a Roman Catholic lay brother, who never left his order and never wished to, became one of the best-loved devotional writers of the Protestant world. John Wesley included him among the works he published for the early Methodists in his Christian Library. E. M. Bounds set his words at the head of a chapter of Purpose in Prayer; and A. W. Tozer commended him often as one who had learned to make the kitchen as holy as the chapel. Carmelites, for their part, have always counted him one of their own.

He would have been surprised by all of it. He asked his first correspondent to show his letter to nobody. What he left behind is less a method than an invitation, made to everyone: to think often of God, by day, by night, in business and even in diversions — “He is always near you and with you: leave Him not alone.”
