faq.q: Who was Brother Lawrence?
faq.a: Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection, born Nicolas Herman, was a lay brother of the Discalced Carmelites in Paris in the seventeenth century. He was never a priest, a preacher or a scholar: he cooked for his community for some fifteen years and in later life mended its sandals. The four conversations and the letters gathered after his death as The Practice of the Presence of God have been loved by Roman Catholics and Protestants alike for three centuries.

faq.q: Where and when was Brother Lawrence born?
faq.a: He was born Nicolas Herman in Hériménil, a village near Lunéville in the Duchy of Lorraine, around 1614. The year is uncertain; in a late letter he calls himself almost eighty, which would put his birth a few years earlier. His parents were poor and devout country people, and in his youth the Thirty Years' War brought soldiers, plague and famine to the villages of Lorraine.

faq.q: What happened when Brother Lawrence saw a bare tree in winter?
faq.a: In a winter when he was about eighteen he saw a tree stripped of its leaves and considered that in a little while the leaves would be renewed, and after them the flowers and the fruit. He said that it gave him a high view of the Providence and Power of God which never afterwards left him. The sight set him loose from the world and kindled such a love for God that, forty years on, he could not tell whether it had grown since.

faq.q: Was Brother Lawrence a soldier?
faq.a: Yes. Before he entered religion he went for a soldier in the Thirty Years' War. According to the accounts of his early life he was taken prisoner by German troops who suspected him of being a spy and threatened to hang him, and he answered so calmly that they let him go. In 1635, at Rambervillers, not far from his home, he was badly wounded in the leg, and the injury lamed him for the rest of his life.

faq.q: Why did Brother Lawrence become a Carmelite?
faq.a: After recovering from his wound he served as a footman to M. Fieubert, the treasurer, and remembered himself in that post as a great awkward fellow who broke everything. He went into religion thinking that in a monastery he would be made to smart for his awkwardness and faults, and so would sacrifice his life and its pleasures to God. But God, he said, had disappointed him: he met with nothing there but satisfaction.

faq.q: When did he join the Carmelites, and why is he called Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection?
faq.a: In 1640, at about the age of twenty-six, he entered the house of the Discalced Carmelites on the rue de Vaugirard in Paris as a lay brother. He received the brown habit in August of that year and took the name Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection, making his profession two years later. He spent the rest of his life in that community, unlearned and largely unnoticed.

faq.q: Did Brother Lawrence struggle in his faith?
faq.a: Yes. In his first years in the monastery he was long troubled by the conviction that he would be damned, and for four years the fear lay on him. He held on by resolving to act purely for the love of God whether he was lost or saved. In a letter he wrote that for his first ten years he suffered much, until he found himself changed all at once and felt a profound inward peace. From then on, he said, he passed his life in perfect liberty and continual joy.

faq.q: What did Brother Lawrence mean by the practice of the presence of God?
faq.a: It was not a technique; he found that books of methods puzzled him more than they helped. He resolved to give the all for the all, renouncing for the love of God everything that was not He, and to live as if there were none but God and himself in the world. He kept his mind in God's presence, brought it back without fretting when it wandered, and held that the times of prayer ought not to differ from other times. His prayer, he said, was nothing else but a sense of the presence of God.

faq.q: How did Brother Lawrence pray in the kitchen?
faq.a: He had a great natural aversion to kitchen work, but he did everything there for the love of God and prayed on every occasion for grace to do it well, until he found it easy. When he began his work he asked God for the grace to continue in His presence and to receive all his works. He said that in the noise and clatter of his kitchen, with several people calling for different things, he possessed God in as great tranquility as if he were on his knees at the blessed sacrament.

faq.q: Who wrote down Brother Lawrence's words, and how did his book spread?
faq.a: Joseph de Beaufort, a priest who later served as vicar general to Cardinal de Noailles, Archbishop of Paris, visited him four times in 1666 and 1667 and wrote down his conversations. After Brother Lawrence died on 12 February 1691, de Beaufort published his maxims and letters in 1692 and the conversations in 1694. The Quietist controversy made such writing suspect in France, but the Protestant Pierre Poiret reprinted him, John Wesley included him in his Christian Library, and later E. M. Bounds and A. W. Tozer commended him.

fields.name: Samson Occom
fields.bio: Mohegan minister and writer (1723–1792), converted in the Great Awakening, ordained in 1759, who preached across Britain for Native education, wrote a landmark execution sermon and hymnbook, and helped found the Christian Indian town of Brothertown.
fields.bio_html:
Samson Occom was born in 1723 in a wigwam at Mohegan, near New London in Connecticut, on a day he never knew. His father, Joshua, was a hunter who ranged abroad in the season of the chase and came home when the snows began; his mother, Sarah, was a woman of uncommon strength and affection who in time joined the church of the nearby English parish. “I was Born a Heathen and Brought up in Heathenism,” Occom wrote of those years, describing parents who lived “a wandering life.”

He was about sixteen when, as he put it, “we heard a Strange Rumor among the English, that there were Extraordinary Ministers Preaching from place to Place and a Strange Concern among the White People.” The Great Awakening had come to eastern Connecticut, and by summer its preachers had come to Mohegan. For about six months he went to every meeting he could reach, “under Trouble of Mind,” and in the same season he bought a primer and began to learn his letters. Eleazar Wheelock later credited his conversion to the preaching of the revivalist James Davenport.

Come just as you are, with all your sins and abominations, with all your blood-guiltiness, with all your condemnation, and lay hold of the hope set before you this day.

— Samson Occom

A discovery of the way of salvation

At seventeen the long struggle ended. “I had, as I trust, a Discovery of the way of Salvation through Jesus Christ,” he wrote, “and was enabled to put my trust in him alone for Life & Salvation. From this Time the Distress and Burden of my mind was removed, and I found Serenity and Pleasure of Soul, in Serving God.” What followed was compassion: he felt “an uncommon Pity and Compassion to my Poor Brethren According to the Flesh.”

When he was in his nineteenth year his mother went to Lebanon, Connecticut, and Occom asked her to find out whether the Reverend Eleazar Wheelock, who kept a small school for English boys, would take him for a week or two. Wheelock wanted to see him at once. “So I went up, thinking I Should be back again in a few Days,” Occom remembered; “he received me With kindness and Compassion and instead of Staying a Forthnight or 3 Weeks, I Spent 4 Years with him.” He arrived on 6 December 1743 and threw himself into Latin, Greek and later Hebrew, but he strained his eyes so badly over his books that by the winter of 1748–49 he had to give up formal study altogether.

Schoolmaster at Montauk

In 1749 Occom went with some of his people on a fishing trip to Montauk, at the eastern tip of Long Island. He went from wigwam to wigwam holding meetings instead, and the Montaukett people asked him to stay and open a school. He stayed about twelve years. “I kept School,” he wrote, “and Carried on the Religious Meetings as often as ever, and attended the Sick and their Funerals, and did what Writings they wanted, and often Sat as a Judge to reconcile and Decide their Matters.” Every school day began the same way: “as Soon as the Children got together, and took their proper Seats, I Prayed with them.” On the Sabbath he sang Watts’s psalms and hymns with the people and opened the Scriptures “in Familiar Discourse.” A revival followed, and many at Montauk, he wrote, were “hopefully converted to the Saving knowledge of God in Jesus.”

He lived as his people lived. His home was a wigwam, moved with the seasons. His salary was tiny and sometimes unpaid, so he hunted and fished, farmed a plot of corn, carved spoons, ladles, pails and gunstocks, and bound books for the English families of East Hampton, often working at night by torchlight. In the autumn of 1751 he married Mary Fowler, a Montaukett woman whose brothers David and Jacob became his pupils and lifelong co-workers. They raised at least ten children. On 30 August 1759, at East Hampton, the Presbytery of Suffolk ordained him a Presbyterian minister.

The Indian preacher in Britain

After missions to the Oneida people of New York in the early 1760s, Occom settled again at Mohegan. Wheelock’s school at Lebanon now trained Native American missionaries, and George Whitefield believed a converted Indian who could preach would win it British support. In December 1765 Occom left his family in God’s care and set out for Boston with the Reverend Nathaniel Whitaker. Opponents in Boston scoffed that he had been a Christian all his life and could not even speak his own language. He wrote to Wheelock:

Waiting in Boston for a ship, uncertain whether he would see his wife and children again, Occom committed the journey to God: “I have a struggle in my mind at times, knowing not where I am going. I dont know but I am looking for a spot of ground where my bones must be buried and never see my poor Family again, but I verily believe I am called of God by a strange Providence and that is enough.”

He landed in England in February 1766 and preached for the first time on 16 February, in Whitefield’s Tabernacle in London, to a packed house. For more than two years he travelled through England and into Scotland, preaching by most counts between three and four hundred times. He met the Earl of Dartmouth and John Newton and won a firm friend in the merchant John Thornton; King George III gave £200. By the time Occom sailed home in the spring of 1768, the tour had raised more than £12,000, a sum without precedent for a missionary cause in the colonies. He was offered Anglican orders and refused them: “I had no such view when I came from home.”

“Because I am a poor Indian”

He came home to trouble. Support promised to his family had come slowly. Mary had been forced to write to Wheelock, “I am out of Corn and have no Money to buy any with and am affraid we shall suffer for want.” In September 1768 he wrote a short account of his life. It is one of the earliest autobiographies written in English by a Native American, and it was not printed until 1982. It ends with a grievance he could no longer keep quiet about. For twelve years of service as both schoolmaster and minister, he had been paid what another mission received in a single year. “I was my own Interpreter,” he wrote. “I was their Ear, Eye & Hand, as Well as Mouth.”

I believe it is because I am a poor Indian. I Can’t help that God has made me So; I did not make myself so.

— Samson Occom

A deeper hurt followed. In 1769 Wheelock received a charter for Dartmouth College and moved his school to the woods of New Hampshire, and the money Occom had preached for went more and more to educating white missionaries rather than Native students. Wheelock sincerely believed this would serve the Indians best; Occom felt it as a betrayal of everything he had told the givers in Britain. He warned Wheelock, with a pun, that the school meant to be an Alma Mater to his people would prove an Alba Mater, a white mother. A friendship of a quarter-century never fully recovered.

A fall, confessed

In those dark days Occom fell. Ill, without employment and discouraged, he was overcome by drink on one occasion early in 1769. He did not hide it, but accused himself before his own presbytery: “I have been shamefully overtaken with strong drink, by which I have greatly wounded the cause of God, blemished the pure religion of Jesus Christ, blackened my own character and hurt my own soul.” After hearing him in person, the Suffolk Presbytery concluded in November 1769 that he had drunk only a small quantity of spirits after going all day without food, while in what it called “a very gloomy and desponding Frame of Mind,” and it cleared him. Wheelock reported a second lapse the following summer. His English friend John Thornton answered, “I fear he had hard usage and that drove him into the horrid sin of drinking. Pray my dear Sir, use him tenderly, for I am much mistaken if his heart is not right with God.” When rumours prompted his presbytery to investigate in 1791, nothing was found against him. The record shows a man who named his sin before God and his brethren, and got up again.

A sermon at the gallows

That experience lies behind his best-known work. In 1772 Moses Paul, a Native American man condemned for killing a man after he was turned out of a tavern for drunkenness, asked that Occom preach the sermon before his execution. On 2 September, a stormy day, Occom preached in the crowded meeting-house at New Haven from Romans 6:23: “For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” To the condemned man he spoke as kin, “You are the bone of my bone, and flesh of my flesh.” If Moses would believe, he said, “instead of a melancholy day, it would be a wedding day to your soul.” To the Native people present he spoke frankly about drink. Then he walked with Moses Paul to the gallows and prayed with him there. The sermon was printed that October and went through at least nineteen editions in America and Britain, and was later translated into Welsh.

Two years later, in 1774, he published A Choice Collection of Hymns and Spiritual Songs, gathered “for the Edification of sincere Christians, of all Denominations” and including hymns that seem to be his own. The hymn most often sung under his name, “Awaked by Sinai’s awful sound,” is not in that book. It appeared only after his death, revised from an earlier text, “Wak’d by the gospel’s pow’rful sound,” that hymn scholars believe was his. Its refrain could stand over his whole life: “The sinner must be born again.”

Brothertown

Occom’s last great work was to gather the scattered Christian Indians of southern New England into a single town of their own. He led the plan with his son-in-law Joseph Johnson and his brothers-in-law David and Jacob Fowler. The Oneida nation granted them land in New York in 1774, but the Revolution scattered the first settlers. On 7 November 1785, in a clearing near David Fowler’s house, they organized themselves at last. “We Named our Town by the Name of Brotherton,” Occom wrote in his diary, and its people “Concluded to live in Peace, and in Friendship and to go on in all their Public Concerns in Harmony.” They asked him to be their teacher, and he agreed to make the town “my Home and center.”

The next day, 8 November 1785, the neighbouring Stockbridge people kept a day of fasting and prayer for their own new settlement and asked Occom to lead it. He wrote that the fast was held “to confess their sins before God, and to repent and beg the pardon of all their sins and desire the Blessing of God upon them.” He preached twice, and “it was a solemn Fast Day, many were deeply afected, all attended like criminals before the Barr.”

Two years later, the leaders of Brothertown and New Stockbridge wrote that his preaching “came with great weight upon our Minds,” and they testified: “we must confess to the Glory of God, that God has made him an Eminant Instrument amongst us, of a Great and Remarkable Reformation.” They called him to be their settled minister, and he accepted.

He moved his own family west in 1789 and also preached in the barns and cabins of the new frontier settlements. Shortly before his death he wrote that the church at Brothertown had placed itself under the Presbyterian order, and that it was “the first Indian Presbyterian Church that ever was formed by Indians themselves, for we had no white man to assist us.” His last years were troubled by a bitter quarrel over the leasing of Brothertown land to white settlers, and in the winter of 1791–92 he moved a few miles west to New Stockbridge.

On 14 July 1792, on his way to a cedar swamp to look for timber, he stopped, asked for water, and told the man with him, “I have done.” He folded his hands on his chest and died within minutes, in the sixty-ninth year of his age. More than three hundred Native people from many nations gathered the next day to hear Samuel Kirkland preach his funeral sermon from Matthew 24:44: “Therefore be ye also ready.” His grave was never marked. Honoured in London, slighted at home, fallen and restored, he remained to the end what he had become at seventeen: a man who had put his trust in Christ “alone for Life & Salvation,” and who spent the rest of his life telling his own people, just as they were, to come.

faq.q: Who was Samson Occom?
faq.a: Samson Occom (1723–1792) was a Mohegan minister, teacher and writer who came to faith in the Great Awakening and became an ordained Presbyterian minister in 1759. He preached across Britain to raise funds for Native education, wrote one of the earliest autobiographies in English by a Native American, published a famous execution sermon and a hymnbook, and led the Christian Indians of southern New England to found Brothertown in New York.

faq.q: What was his early life like?
faq.a: He was born in 1723 in a wigwam at Mohegan, near New London, Connecticut, to Joshua, a hunter, and Sarah, who later joined a Christian church. He described himself as born and raised in his people's traditional ways, in a family that lived a wandering life. Nothing in his childhood pointed toward the pulpit.

faq.q: How was he converted?
faq.a: When he was about sixteen, preachers of the Great Awakening came to Mohegan, and he spent some six months under deep conviction, going to every meeting he could reach and teaching himself to read from a primer. At seventeen, he wrote, he had a discovery of the way of salvation through Jesus Christ and put his trust in him alone. The burden lifted, and he felt a new compassion for his own people.

faq.q: How did he come to study with Eleazar Wheelock?
faq.a: In his nineteenth year he asked his mother to find out whether the Reverend Eleazar Wheelock of Lebanon, Connecticut, would teach him for a week or two. Wheelock took him in on 6 December 1743, and he stayed four years, studying Latin, Greek and Hebrew. Badly strained eyesight finally ended his formal education in the winter of 1748–49.

faq.q: What did he do at Montauk?
faq.a: From 1749 he spent about twelve years among the Montaukett people of Long Island as schoolmaster, preacher, scribe and judge, opening each school day with prayer and seeing a revival among them. He lived in a wigwam, hunted, fished, carved woodenware and bound books to support himself on a very small salary. He married Mary Fowler, a Montaukett woman, in 1751, and the Presbytery of Suffolk ordained him on 30 August 1759.

faq.q: What happened on his preaching tour of Britain?
faq.a: From early 1766 to 1768 Occom and Nathaniel Whitaker toured England and Scotland raising money for Wheelock's school for Native students. Occom preached between three and four hundred times, met the Earl of Dartmouth and John Newton, and the tour raised more than 12,000 pounds, including 200 from King George III. Before sailing he wrote that he believed he was called of God by a strange providence, and that this was enough.

faq.q: Why did he feel betrayed afterward?
faq.a: He came home to find his family left short of food, and in 1768 he wrote a short narrative of his life protesting that he had been paid far less than white missionaries, adding that he believed it was because he was a poor Indian. Then in 1769 Wheelock received a charter for Dartmouth College in New Hampshire and increasingly used the British funds to educate white missionaries. Occom saw this as a betrayal of the donors' purpose, and the friendship never fully recovered.

faq.q: What was his confession of drunkenness?
faq.a: Early in 1769, ill and discouraged, Occom was overcome by drink on one occasion, and he accused himself before his own presbytery, saying he had wounded the cause of God and hurt his own soul. The Suffolk Presbytery examined him and concluded he had taken a small quantity of spirits after a day without food, and cleared him. Wheelock reported a second lapse in 1770, but a 1791 inquiry by his later presbytery found nothing against him.

faq.q: What were his execution sermon and hymnbook?
faq.a: On 2 September 1772 he preached at New Haven before the execution of Moses Paul, a Native man condemned for murder, from Romans 6:23, urging him to come to Christ just as he was. The sermon went through at least nineteen editions and was later translated into Welsh. In 1774 he published A Choice Collection of Hymns and Spiritual Songs; the famous hymn Awaked by Sinai's awful sound, often credited to him, appeared only after his death as a revision of an earlier text believed to be his.

faq.q: What was Brothertown, and how did he die?
faq.a: Brothertown was a Christian settlement on Oneida land in New York, gathered from several New England Native communities and formally organized on 7 November 1785, with Occom as its minister; he moved his family there in 1789 and called its church the first Indian Presbyterian church formed by Indians themselves. He died suddenly at New Stockbridge on 14 July 1792, telling a companion, I have done, before folding his hands and dying. More than three hundred Native people attended his funeral.

fields.name: Absalom Jones
fields.bio: Born enslaved in Delaware, Absalom Jones (1746–1818) bought his wife’s freedom and his own, nursed Philadelphia through the 1793 yellow fever, and became founding pastor of St. Thomas’s — the first Black priest in the Episcopal Church.
fields.bio_html:
Absalom Jones was born on November 6, 1746, in Sussex County, Delaware, a slave in the household of the Wynkoop family. He was still small when his master took him from the fields to wait on him in the house, and there a quiet hunger took hold of him. He saved the pennies that visitors gave him, bought himself a primer, and, as he later wrote, “begged to be taught by any body that I found able and willing to give me the least instruction.” A spelling book followed, and then, among his growing stock of books, a Testament. While other boys spent their leisure hours at play, he read. “By this course,” he remembered, “I became singular, and escaped many evils, and also saved my money.”

Half a century later, preaching on the day the slave trade ended, the boy with the Testament would tell his people what a lifetime had taught him:

The great and blessed event, which we have this day met to celebrate, is a striking proof, that the God of heaven and earth is the same, yesterday, and to-day, and for ever.

— Absalom Jones

In 1762, when he was sixteen, his world was broken apart. His mother, five brothers and a sister were sold, and he was brought to Philadelphia with his master, Benjamin Wynkoop, to wait in the store, pack goods and carry them out. Yet even here he found a way forward: a clerk set him copies to imitate, and he was soon able, as he put it, “to write to my mother and brothers, with my own hand.” In 1766 he asked leave to attend a night school for one quarter and spent it learning arithmetic — addition, subtraction, weights and measures — the plain tools of a man who meant to earn his way.

Freedom bought by the hour

In 1770 Absalom married Mary Thomas, who was also enslaved. Almost at once he set about buying her freedom, before his own. Her mistress, Sarah King, named a price of forty pounds. With his father-in-law, John Thomas, he drew up an appeal and called on leading Quakers of the city; some lent and some gave, and they raised thirty pounds. Sarah King forgave the rest. Then, for seven years, while still serving his own master by day, Jones worked until twelve or one o’clock at night to help Mary earn a living and to pay back every borrowed shilling.

Only when that debt was cleared did he ask for his own freedom. In 1778 his master refused. Jones bought a small house and lot instead, knowing that as long as he was a slave even that could be taken as his master’s property, and he kept asking. On the first of October, 1784, at the age of thirty-seven, he received his manumission. He stayed on in Wynkoop’s service at good wages, built two more small houses on his lot, and wrote of the whole long struggle without bitterness, as “the little estate that a kind Providence has put in my hands.”

On their knees at St. George’s

By the 1780s Jones was worshipping at St. George’s Methodist Episcopal Church on Fourth Street, where many of the Black people of Philadelphia gathered, and where he and his friend Richard Allen served as lay preachers among them. Allen was a younger man, born a slave in Philadelphia, converted under Methodist preaching, and like Jones a buyer of his own freedom. The two were drawn together by a shared burden. In April 1787 they founded the Free African Society, a mutual-aid fellowship that pledged a shilling a month to support members in sickness and to care for widows and fatherless children; its founding minute says the two men had “often communed together” in sorrow over the condition of their people.

As the Black congregation at St. George’s grew, it was told to sit apart, in the newly built gallery. Allen left the only eyewitness account of what happened next. The elder had just said, “Let us pray,” and the people had gone down on their knees, when Allen heard scuffling and looked up to see one of the trustees pulling Absalom Jones off his knees: “you must get up — you must not kneel here.”

Pulled from his knees in the middle of prayer, Absalom Jones would not argue and would not leave before the prayer was done. “Wait until prayer is over,” he answered, “and I will get up and trouble you no more.” When the prayer ended, the Black worshippers rose and walked out of St. George’s together, and never returned.

The date of that walkout is disputed. Older accounts, following Allen’s memoir, place it in 1787; many historians now argue for late 1791 or 1792, when the gallery was actually being built and the officials Allen describes were in office. Whatever the year, the meaning is the same. A man had been told he was not fit to kneel beside his brothers before God, and he answered by building a house of prayer where no one could tell him so again.

The African Church

Out of the Free African Society grew a plan for a church, raised with the help of Quaker friends and of Dr. Benjamin Rush. When the question came of which communion to join, the two friends parted ways in peace. Allen could not leave Methodism and went on to found Bethel Church, the mother church of the African Methodist Episcopal denomination. The majority chose the Episcopal Church and asked Jones to be their pastor. The African Church was opened and dedicated for worship on July 17, 1794, and that autumn it was received into the Episcopal Church of Pennsylvania as the African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas — the first Black Episcopal congregation in the United States.

Jones did not take up the call lightly. His letter of acceptance to the trustees, dated October 21, 1794, is the clearest window we have into his heart. The call, he wrote, was “of such a serious nature as to cause me to tremble at the thought of such an undertaking.”

Trembling at the call to shepherd St. Thomas’s, Jones looked to God and remembered Jacob crossing the brook with nothing but his staff: “on my looking up to Him who is the Sovereign Ruler of all things … I was led to put my trust in God, and become your servant in Christ; and in all things begun, continued, and ended in his name, I hope He will be glorified, and our souls eternally profited.”

The church’s convention dispensed with the usual requirement of Greek and Latin, and in August 1795 Bishop William White ordained him a deacon. He was later ordained priest — on September 21, 1802, by the Episcopal Church’s own reckoning, though the church’s nineteenth-century historian records him as reported a priest in 1804 — and so became the first Black priest in the Episcopal Church. He had been forty-eight at his first ordination — a man who had learned his letters from pennies and a primer.

The fever year

Before St. Thomas’s had even opened, Jones and Allen faced the gravest test of their lives. In the late summer of 1793 yellow fever swept Philadelphia, killing thousands and emptying the city of everyone who could flee. A notice in the papers asked the people of colour to come forward and nurse the sick, on the mistaken belief that they could not catch the disease. Jones, Allen and a few others met to decide what to do.

We found a freedom to go forth, confiding in him who can preserve in the midst of a burning fiery furnace, sensible that it was our duty to do all the good we could to our suffering fellow mortals.

— Absalom Jones and Richard Allen, 1794

The first house they entered held a dying man, his wife already dead beside him, and two helpless children. They nursed the sick, procured nurses, bled patients under Dr. Rush’s direction and carried away the dead when almost no one else would touch them. The belief proved false: Black Philadelphians caught the fever and died like everyone else. When the plague was over, the publisher Mathew Carey printed an account that singled out Black nurses for profiteering. Jones and Allen answered in January 1794 with A Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People, During the Late Awful Calamity in Philadelphia, laying out their accounts to the penny: they had buried several hundred poor people and strangers without asking anything, and were out of pocket by £177. To that defence they added a plea to the slaveholders of America, grounded in Scripture: “We wish you to consider, that God himself was the first pleader of the cause of slaves.”

Recalling those first days among the dying, when they had gone out trusting God to keep them in the furnace, Jones and Allen wrote simply: “The Lord was pleased to strengthen us, and remove all fear from us, and disposed our hearts to be as useful as possible.”

A pastor and a petitioner

For more than twenty years Jones served St. Thomas’s, and the people loved him less for his preaching than for his presence. A later rector of St. Thomas’s, William Douglass, wrote that his sermons were earnest and impressive, but “it was never thought that his forte was in the pulpit”; what endeared him to all was his evenness of temper and “his repeated visitations among the people, especially the sick of his flock.” He kept a day school, and the church’s registers record 268 adult baptisms and 927 infant baptisms between 1796 and 1818. A portrait painted by Raphaelle Peale in 1810 shows him in clerical black, a book in his hands — calm, broad-shouldered, attentive.

That gentleness did not make him quiet about injustice. In 1797 and again in 1799 he joined other free Black men of Philadelphia in petitioning Congress — first on behalf of freed people who had fled re-enslavement in North Carolina, and then against the slave trade and the cruelties of the fugitive slave law. The House received the second petition with open hostility and declined to give it any encouragement. Jones kept praying and kept pressing.

The God who comes down

On January 1, 1808, the law ending the importation of slaves into the United States took effect, and Jones preached a thanksgiving sermon at St. Thomas’s on Exodus 3:7–8: “I have surely seen the affliction of my people.” It is searing in its description of the slave ships, the auction block and the overseer’s whip, and yet overflowing with praise. God, he told his people, had not been indifferent: “every tear they shed, was preserved, and every groan they uttered, was recorded.”

He has seen the affliction of our countrymen, with an eye of pity.

— Absalom Jones

Jones told his congregation in 1808 that heaven had heard them: God “has heard the prayers that have ascended from the hearts of his people; and he has, as in the case of his ancient and chosen people the Jews, come down to deliver our suffering country-men from the hands of their oppressors.” He closed with prayer: “Oh thou God of all the nations upon the earth! We thank thee, that thou art no respecter of persons, and that thou hast made of one blood all nations of men.”

He did not let the celebration end in the church. He urged his hearers to carry their thanks home to their families and their closets, to pray for those still in bondage, to live humbly and soberly, and above all to teach their children “the principles of the gospel of Jesus Christ, whereby they may become wise unto salvation.” He prayed that enslaved people would be given the means to read the Scriptures, so that “even while they are the slaves of men,” they might become “the freemen of the Lord.” He even wondered aloud whether God might bring some good out of the whole dark history — perhaps raising up a Joseph among their children to carry the gospel back to Africa — a hope many Black Christians of his generation shared, offered not to excuse the trade but to refuse to believe that God had abandoned them in it.

Absalom Jones died on February 13, 1818, at the age of seventy-one, and was buried beneath the shadow of the church he had founded. His epitaph remembered a man who, “born a slave,” was “principally instrumental in founding the African Church of St. Thomas,” where he served faithfully for twenty-two years. The Episcopal Church now keeps February 13 in his memory. He had begun life saving pennies for a primer, and ended it having taught a whole people to pray, to read, and to kneel before God without asking anyone’s leave.

faq.q: Who was Absalom Jones?
faq.a: Absalom Jones (1746–1818) was born enslaved in Delaware, bought his wife’s freedom and then his own, and became the founding pastor of the African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas in Philadelphia. Ordained by Bishop William White, he was the first Black priest in the Episcopal Church, and he spent his life shepherding his people and pleading their cause before God and the nation.

faq.q: How did he learn to read?
faq.a: Taken from the fields as a small boy to wait on his master in the house, he saved the pennies visitors gave him and bought a primer, begging anyone willing to teach him. A spelling book followed, and then, among other books, a Testament. He later wrote that his love of books kept him apart from the amusements of other boys and helped him escape many evils.

faq.q: What happened when he came to Philadelphia?
faq.a: In 1762 his mother, five brothers and a sister were sold, and he was brought to Philadelphia with his master to work in a store. A clerk set him copies to imitate so that he could write to his mother and brothers in his own hand, and in 1766 he was allowed one quarter at a night school, where he learned arithmetic.

faq.q: How did he win freedom for his wife and himself?
faq.a: In 1770 he married Mary Thomas, who was enslaved, and soon bought her freedom for thirty pounds raised from Quaker friends, her mistress forgiving the remaining ten. For seven years he worked until midnight or later to repay the debt. His own request for freedom was refused in 1778, but he kept asking, and on October 1, 1784, his master, Benjamin Wynkoop, granted his manumission.

faq.q: What happened at St. George’s Methodist Church?
faq.a: Jones and Richard Allen were lay preachers among the Black members of St. George’s in Philadelphia. When Black worshippers were told to sit in the new gallery, a trustee pulled Jones off his knees during prayer; Jones asked him to wait until prayer was over, and then the Black members walked out together. Older accounts date this to 1787, but many historians now place it in late 1791 or 1792.

faq.q: What was the Free African Society?
faq.a: Founded by Jones and Allen in April 1787, the Free African Society was a mutual-aid fellowship whose members paid a shilling a month to support one another in sickness and to care for widows and fatherless children. It grew into the congregation that became the African Church of Philadelphia.

faq.q: What did he do in the 1793 yellow fever epidemic?
faq.a: When yellow fever emptied Philadelphia, Jones, Allen and others answered a public call to nurse the sick, trusting the God who preserves in the burning fiery furnace. They nursed, bled patients under Dr. Benjamin Rush, and buried the dead, often unpaid. When Mathew Carey accused Black nurses of profiteering, they answered in 1794 with A Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People, showing they had lost money in the work.

faq.q: How did he become the first Black Episcopal priest?
faq.a: The African Church was dedicated on July 17, 1794, and received into the Episcopal Church that autumn as St. Thomas’s, with Jones as its pastor; he accepted the call trembling, putting his trust in God. The requirement of Greek and Latin was waived, Bishop White ordained him deacon in August 1795, and he was ordained priest in 1802 (one older source says 1804).

faq.q: What is his Thanksgiving Sermon of 1808?
faq.a: On January 1, 1808, the day the American ban on importing slaves took effect, Jones preached on Exodus 3:7–8, declaring that God had seen the affliction of his people and come down to deliver them. He urged his congregation to give daily thanks, pray for those still enslaved, live humbly, teach their children the gospel, and keep the first of January each year as a day of thanksgiving.

faq.q: How is Absalom Jones remembered?
faq.a: He served St. Thomas’s for twenty-two years, loved for his gentle manner and his visits to the sick, and joined other free Black men in petitioning Congress in 1797 and 1799. He died on February 13, 1818, aged seventy-one, and was buried at the church he founded; the Episcopal Church keeps February 13 in his memory.

fields.name: Maria W. Stewart
fields.bio: Orphaned, widowed and robbed of her inheritance, Maria W. Stewart (1803–1879) met Christ in Boston, wrote prayer-filled meditations, became one of the first American women to lecture publicly, and spent fifty years teaching Black children.
fields.bio_html:
Maria W. Stewart was born Maria Miller in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1803, and by the time she was five years old she had lost both her parents. The orphan girl was bound out to a clergyman’s family, where — as she put it many years later — she “had the seeds of piety and virtue early sown” in her mind, though she was denied the schooling her soul thirsted for. She left that household at fifteen and went on attending Sabbath schools until she was twenty, gathering what learning she could. The book she knew best, she said, was the Bible: through childhood and youth it was the book she “mostly studied,” and its language would run through everything she ever wrote.

In 1826, in Boston, she married James W. Stewart, an older man who had served in the United States Navy during the War of 1812 and who made a good living as a shipping agent, fitting out vessels. For three short years she lived in comfort among the free Black community on the north slope of Beacon Hill, where the Stewarts knew the abolitionist David Walker, whose fiery Appeal she would later honor. Then, in December 1829, James fell ill and died.

A widow at the bedside

The loss broke her open. She sat by his sickbed through the long last days, and years afterward she still wrote of it in the present tense of grief — the dying groans, the restless head turning from side to side, the dim eye turned on her for relief. What wounded her most was that he seemed to die without hope in Christ: “he had no God to look to!”

As her husband lay dying, Maria Stewart cried to God for his life and for a surrendered heart if the answer was no: “Spare his life, O God, if consistent with thy will, was my cry; if not, make me to say: ‘Thy will be done.’”

Worse followed. The will James had made two days before his death was carried out of the house by one of its executors before she ever heard it read, and the white executors stripped her, through the courts, of everything he had left her. She was young, childless, without a single living relative, and suddenly poor. A friend who examined the case nearly fifty years later wrote that the executors had “literally robbed and cheated her out of every cent,” and that she was a woman who “would have suffered wrong rather than defend her rights.”

It was in that ruin that she met Christ. In 1830, she wrote, she was, “as I humbly hope and trust, brought to the knowledge of the truth, as it is in Jesus,” and in 1831 she made a public profession of her faith. In her own retelling, conversion came as surrender: “borne down with a heavy load of sin and shame,” she was “at last brought to accept of salvation as a free gift, in and through the merits of a crucified Redeemer.” It was not easy. It was hard, she admitted, to say “Thy will be done” when she saw her earthly prospects blasted; but she “was at last made willing to be anything or nothing for my Redeemer’s sake.”

A voice for her people

From the moment of that change she felt, she said, a strong desire to give the rest of her days to God and to her people. Soon after her profession, at a gathering, she was moved to speak before many — and walked home ashamed, not knowing where to hide herself. Then came the inward word that set the course of her life.

Lord, if thou wilt be with me, then will I speak for thee so long as I live.

— Maria W. Stewart

In 1831 she walked into the office of William Lloyd Garrison, who had just begun publishing The Liberator, and put a manuscript into his hands. Garrison was so struck by it that he set it in type himself and printed it as a tract: Religion and the Pure Principles of Morality, the Sure Foundation on Which We Must Build. It is an astonishing document — part sermon, part prayer, part summons. She reminded her Black readers that God had “formed and fashioned you in His own glorious image,” that “it is not the color of the skin that makes the man, but it is the principle formed within the soul.” She pleaded with mothers to plant in their children “a thirst for knowledge, the love of virtue,” urged the women of her community to pool their earnings for a high school, and turned on America itself: “O, America, America, foul and indelible is thy stain!” And through it all she pressed the gospel, plainly and personally.

Religion is pure; it is ever new; it is beautiful; it is all that is worth living for.

— Maria W. Stewart

The next year Garrison printed her Meditations from the Pen of Mrs. Maria W. Stewart, presented to the First African Baptist Church and Society of Boston. It is a little book of devotion, written about a year after Christ “first spoke peace to my troubled soul” and soon after her baptism: fourteen meditations, most closing with a written prayer. They are the prayers of a grieving widow learning to trust — confessing sin, interceding for her church and pastor, pleading for her unconverted friends and for “the benighted sons and daughters of Africa,” and begging God to “rivet this heart alone upon thyself.” Alexander Crummell, who knew her soon afterward, later recalled that she had so little schooling that a young girl had written out the words for her.

In the thirteenth of her Meditations the orphaned widow turned her losses into thanksgiving: “For wise and holy purposes best known to thyself, thou hast seen fit to deprive me of all earthly relatives; but when my father and mother forsook me, then thou didst take me up.” She asked the same mercy for “all widows and fatherless children, and for the stranger in distress,” that they might know God as “a prayer-hearing and prayer-answering God.”

Four lectures in Boston

Then she did something almost no woman in America had done: she spoke in public, on matters of faith and justice, before audiences of men and women. Over 1832 and 1833 she gave four lectures in Boston — to the Afric-American Female Intelligence Society; at Franklin Hall on 21 September 1832; at the African Masonic Hall on 27 February 1833; and a farewell address that September. She is often called the first American-born woman known to lecture publicly on political themes, and the first Black woman to do so. She stood up as a Christian first. At Franklin Hall she told how the question had come to her in prayer: “Who shall go forward and take off the reproach that is cast upon the people of color? Shall it be a woman?” And her heart answered, “If it is Thy will, be it even so, Lord Jesus!”

She asked hard things of everyone. She urged free Black Bostonians to education, thrift, and self-respect, and rebuked the white North for shutting Black girls out of every trade but service. She rebuked the church too, longing to see believers “not holding religion in one hand and the world in the other.” Not everyone welcomed it. Some told her to stop talking so much about religion; others resented a woman lecturing at all. In her farewell address she defended her calling from Scripture.

What if I am a woman; is not the God of ancient times the God of these modern days?

— Maria W. Stewart

Did not God raise up Deborah to judge Israel, she asked, and Esther to save her people? Was it not Mary Magdalene who first declared the resurrection, and the woman of Samaria who called her town to come and see the Christ? Christ, she said, would not condemn “this worthless worm”: “The bruised reed he will not break.” But she left Boston wounded. It was, she said, “contempt for my moral and religious opinions in private that drove me thus before a public,” and she had found it “no use for me, as an individual, to try to make myself useful among my color in this city.” Even so she would not leave in bitterness. “The bitterness of my soul has departed from those who endeavored to discourage and hinder me,” she said, “and I can now forgive my enemies, bless those who have hated me, and cheerfully pray for those who have despitefully used and persecuted me.” In 1835 Garrison gathered her writings into one volume, Productions of Mrs. Maria W. Stewart.

The long years of teaching

Her public speaking ended at thirty, and almost fifty years of quiet labor followed. In New York she joined a Female Literary Society, studied eagerly with the help of other young women, and became a schoolteacher in New York and in Williamsburg, Long Island. In 1852, having lost her position there and hearing that the Black people of the South were more God-fearing, she moved to Baltimore. There, at the foot of the cross, she resolved to make the best of hard circumstances, printed her own circulars, and opened a school — charging so little that she was always poor. Soon after President Lincoln took office she went on to Washington, a stranger, praying all the way.

Arriving in Washington alone, she had asked God for one small mercy: “I had prayed to the Lord that there might be standing by the cars some lad to conduct me where I wanted to go, for I was a perfect stranger. And upon my arrival, there stood a young man looking as if he wished he had something to do.” He led her past the White House to the family she was seeking. Years earlier, told that no one might take her in, she had said, “God will take care of me, if He sends an angel to do it!” — and she found that he did.

The Washington years were the hardest. She had become an Episcopalian, and when the free school she taught in during the war would keep her only if she gave up her church, she refused: “before I will give up my religious sentiments for dollars and cents I will beg my bread from door to door.” She very nearly did. She kept a day school, a night school, a Sunday school, and a prayer meeting in a room with a stove too small to warm it; one bitter night she waited and no one came to pray. When gossip turned her rector against her and he withdrew his support, she wrote that “no tongue can portray my agony of mind.” She prayed God to show him “that I was a clean woman before the Lord,” went to church on Ash Wednesday as if nothing had happened, and committed her cause, she said, “to Him who judgeth righteously.” In time the rector sent for her, and she brought thirteen of her night scholars to help found St. Mary’s, a church for Black Episcopalians in Washington. Later, near the Freedmen’s Hospital, she opened a Sunday school and raised money to buy it a building, gathering poor children of the neighborhood so that they might be taught, a friend wrote, “to fear God and keep His Commandments.” A Washington pastor whose own children she taught remembered her walking the streets in the dead of winter looking for children who should have been in school, whether or not their parents could pay.

Remembered at the last

By the late 1870s she was matron of the Freedmen’s Hospital in Washington. In 1878 Congress opened pensions to widows of the War of 1812, and a friend went to Boston, found four old witnesses who had known her and James, and proved her claim; in March 1879 she was granted a pension of eight dollars a month. Her friend saw it as an answer to long years of prayer: “surely God was good to her and did answer her prayers.” That spring she visited Garrison in Boston, forty-six years after they had last met, and he wrote to her of “your intelligence and excellence of character.” With the pension money she republished her Meditations in 1879, adding letters from old friends and her own account of her wartime sufferings, written so that “souls may be brought to the knowledge of the truth as it is in Jesus.”

She died at the Freedmen’s Hospital in December 1879, the year the book appeared, at about seventy-six. She had stood almost alone for most of her life — “I have neither kindred nor friends,” she had written in 1831 — yet she never stopped praying for her people, teaching their children, and pointing them to Christ. Her own confidence, written at the start, held to the end: “though all the powers of earth and hell were to combine against me … still would I trust in the Lord, and joy in the God of salvation.”

faq.q: Who was Maria W. Stewart?
faq.a: Maria W. Stewart (1803–1879) was a Black Christian writer, lecturer and teacher from Boston who is often called the first American-born woman known to lecture publicly on political themes. Converted as a young widow, she wrote prayers and essays that William Lloyd Garrison printed, spoke four times in Boston in 1832–33, and then spent nearly fifty years teaching Black children in New York, Baltimore and Washington.

faq.q: What was her early life like?
faq.a: Born Maria Miller in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1803, she was orphaned at five and bound out to a clergyman's family until she was fifteen. She was denied formal schooling but went on attending Sabbath schools until she was twenty, and she said the Bible was the book she most studied in childhood and youth.

faq.q: What happened in her marriage?
faq.a: In 1826 in Boston she married James W. Stewart, a Navy veteran of the War of 1812 who made a good living fitting out ships. He died in December 1829 after only three years of marriage, and the white executors of his will took everything he had left her, leaving her young, childless, without living relatives, and poor.

faq.q: How did she become a Christian?
faq.a: Out of that grief and loss she wrote that in 1830 she was "brought to the knowledge of the truth, as it is in Jesus," and in 1831 she made a public profession of faith and was baptized. She described accepting salvation as a free gift through the merits of a crucified Redeemer, and being made willing to be anything or nothing for Christ's sake.

faq.q: What did she write?
faq.a: In 1831 Garrison printed her tract Religion and the Pure Principles of Morality, which called Black Americans to faith, education and self-respect and rebuked America for slavery and prejudice. In 1832 he printed her Meditations, fourteen devotional pieces, most ending in a written prayer, and in 1835 he gathered her writings and lectures as Productions of Mrs. Maria W. Stewart.

faq.q: What were her Boston lectures?
faq.a: Between 1832 and 1833 she gave four public lectures in Boston, including one at Franklin Hall on 21 September 1832 and one at the African Masonic Hall in February 1833, speaking to audiences of men and women. She said the call came in prayer, when she heard the question "Shall it be a woman?" and answered, "If it is Thy will, be it even so, Lord Jesus!"

faq.q: How did she defend a woman speaking?
faq.a: In her farewell address of September 1833 she asked, "What if I am a woman; is not the God of ancient times the God of these modern days?" She pointed to Deborah, Esther, Mary Magdalene and the woman of Samaria, and trusted that Christ, who does not break the bruised reed, would not condemn her. She left Boston hurt by contempt for her views but said she forgave her enemies and prayed for them.

faq.q: What did she do after leaving Boston?
faq.a: She moved to New York, studied with a Female Literary Society, and taught school in New York and Williamsburg, Long Island. In 1852 she went to Baltimore and opened her own school, and soon after Lincoln took office she moved to Washington, where she kept day, night and Sunday schools and prayer meetings, often in deep poverty.

faq.q: How did she hold to her faith in Washington?
faq.a: When the free school she taught in would keep her only if she left the Episcopal Church, she refused, saying she would rather beg her bread from door to door. Slandered and left without support for a time, she prayed, kept going to church, and committed her cause to God; she later helped gather the first members of St. Mary's Church and ran a Sunday school near the Freedmen's Hospital.

faq.q: How did her life end?
faq.a: By the late 1870s she was matron of the Freedmen's Hospital in Washington, and in 1879 she won a widow's pension for her husband's War of 1812 service, which friends saw as an answer to her prayers. She used it to republish her Meditations with an account of her later sufferings, and she died at the Freedmen's Hospital in December 1879, still praying that souls would come to know Jesus.

fields.name: Zilpha Elaw
fields.bio: Black Methodist preacher (c. 1790–1873) who, after meeting Christ as a servant girl, preached holiness across the northern states, in the slave South at risk of kidnap, and for years in England. Her 1846 Memoirs tell the story.
fields.bio_html:
Zilpha Elaw was born around 1790 in Pennsylvania, near Philadelphia, to Black parents she remembered simply as “religious parents.” In her father’s house the day began and ended with prayer: family devotion morning and evening, the praises of God sung aloud. It was the only such home she would know as a child. When she was about twelve her mother died after giving birth to her twenty-second child. Her father placed Zilpha with a Quaker family, Pierson and Rebecca Mitchel, to serve them until she was eighteen. Eighteen months later he too was dead, and the girl had no one on earth to look to but the household she had been sent to serve.

The Mitchels were kind, but their religion was kept “in the secret silence of the mind,” and no one spoke of God in her hearing. The change from her father’s praying house was hard. Left without guidance, she says, she ran into folly with the other young people of the house, though often she slipped away to weep before God where no one could see. Once, swearing to make her companions laugh, she looked up and seemed to see God frowning down on her, and her tongue stopped mid-word. That night she dreamed of the Day of Judgment, and woke so shaken that her mistress asked what had changed in her.

A vision in the cowshed

About this time the Methodists began holding meetings in that part of the country, and Zilpha was allowed to attend them every other Sunday afternoon. Under their preaching the darkness slowly lifted, but for months she had no assurance that her sins were forgiven, and she prayed for it every day. The answer came one evening in the most ordinary of places. She was milking the cow and singing a hymn — “Oh, when shall I see Jesus, and dwell with him above?” — when she turned her head and saw a tall figure in a long white robe coming towards her, who stood beside her with open arms and smiled. She felt that his very looks spoke, and said, “Thy prayer is accepted, I own thy name.”

She tells the story without embarrassment, and adds that even the cow saw it, bowing her knees and cowering to the ground. Readers may weigh such things as they will; Elaw herself declared that she wrote “as before God and Christ.” What is beyond doubt is what followed. “From that day to the present,” she wrote more than thirty years later, “I have never entertained a doubt of the manifestation of his love to my soul.” In 1808 she joined the Methodist Episcopal society. When the preacher asked whether anyone present wished to join, she rose and answered, “Yes, bless the Lord, here is one.” Looking her over, he remarked, “Well, this seems a bold champion indeed.”

The rest of the household did not share her joy. She was mocked by the young people, scolded by her mistress, and lived among them, she said, “as a speckled bird.” But the loneliness drove her to God. Her two-mile night walks to class meeting, past graveyards and through dark woods, became “seasons of sweet communion with my God.”

An unequal yoke

In 1810 she married Joseph Elaw, a fuller by trade, “a very respectable young man,” as she put it, “but he was not a Christian.” Within a year of the wedding Joseph had set out to make her give up her religion. He took her to a ball in Philadelphia, hoping the music would win her over; she stood in the ballroom and could only weep before God, and he never tried it again. The couple moved to Burlington, New Jersey, where, to her delight, the Methodist class met a few doors from her house. A daughter, Rebecca, was their only child.

At a camp meeting in the woods, Elaw came into the experience Methodists called entire sanctification. She sank to the ground under the preaching and lay there a long while, and heard a voice say, “Now thou art sanctified.” When she came to herself she felt “as pure as if I had never sinned in all my life.” This was Wesleyan holiness teaching, the conviction that God can cleanse the heart and fill it with love. For the rest of her life she counted it the heart of the gospel she preached. Soon after, she was praying aloud in the meetings, and for five years she carried what she called a “household ministry” through Burlington, visiting families rich and poor to speak with them about their souls.

The call she resisted

The call to preach came first through her sister Hannah. Dying in Philadelphia, Hannah told Zilpha she had seen Jesus, and that an angel had bidden her tell Zilpha “that she must preach the gospel.” Zilpha kept it to herself for years. Her husband’s opposition weighed on her, and so did her sense of being unfit.

“How often have I said, ‘Lord! send by whom thou wilt, only send not by me; for thou knowest that I am ignorant: how can I be a mouth for God! — a poor, coloured female: and thou knowest we have many things to endure which others do not.’ But the answer was, ‘What is that to thee? follow thou me.’”

A long illness brought her to the edge of death. Her doctor tried a last, brutal treatment, burning her side with caustic, and it nearly killed her. During her recovery she saw, one midnight, a figure by her bed bringing her word from God, and from that hour she began to mend. Fifteen months later a camp meeting was announced. She had no money and no suitable clothes. Then her old master Mitchel, hearing she had been ill, sent his son and daughter to find her in Burlington with a gift of money. It was the first such favour she had ever received from him, and to her it showed “the ever-mindful care of God.” At that meeting, on a Sunday at midday before thousands of people, she began, almost without meaning to, to exhort the crowd. When she sat down she heard the same voice again: “Now thou knowest the will of God concerning thee; thou must preach the gospel; and thou must travel far and wide.”

This is my commission for the work of the ministry, which I received, not from mortal man, but from the voice of an invisible and heavenly personage sent from God.

— Zilpha Elaw

The local ministers approved. Her own class did not. All but three of the Black class members who had loved her abandoned her: “Like Joseph, I was hated for my dreams.” Joseph Elaw heard the news from a neighbour who taunted him with it, and he begged her to stop. “Now child,” he told her, “we are undone.” Then his health failed. He died of consumption on 27 January 1823, still, as far as she could tell, a stranger to Christ, though he grew gentler near the end and admitted that her conduct had always been blameless. She turned down friends’ offers to pay for his funeral, wanting to do this last thing for him herself.

Teacher, debtor, preacher

Widowed and in debt, she put her daughter into service, went into service herself until her health broke, and then opened a school in Burlington for Black children, whom the white schools would not admit. Local Quakers gave her books and brought visitors to see “a female of colour teaching the coloured children.”

Oh! that men would outgrow their nursery prejudices and learn that “God hath made of one blood all the nations of men that dwell upon all the face of the earth.”

— Zilpha Elaw

But the commission would not leave her alone. She told herself it would be a sin to set out while she owed any man money, and she stayed two years in that state with no savings to show for it. She asked God for a sign within three months. None came, and she fell ill again, and then into a darkness so deep she could not pray. Her young daughter put it plainly: “I believe thou art going to be like some of the queer old women.” Elaw took the words as a rebuke from God.

That day she pledged herself to God: if He would give her the help of His Holy Spirit again, she would go out in His ministry just as she was, not waiting for any further provision or preparation, but trusting only in His word. The next Sunday her tongue was loosed, and she told her congregation she must leave them.

Still anxious about how she could ever leave, she was teaching her pupils one morning when one of the little boys began to read Psalm 125: “They that trust in the Lord shall be as Mount Zion, which cannot be removed.” Her tears dried; everything fell into place by the appointed hour. In Philadelphia every congregation she preached to took up a collection for her, and within three weeks she had all she needed. She came home after seven months and paid every debt.

On the soil of slavery

In 1828, leaving Rebecca with relatives, she went south into the slave states, into Maryland, Virginia and the District of Columbia. She knew exactly what she risked: a free Black woman with no protector could be seized and sold, and the law would allow it. In one small town the news that a Black woman was preaching to the enslaved drew a crowd, and as she watched them point at her through the door, terror took hold of her. She went off to a corner of the room and asked herself where the fear came from. Then her faith returned.

Get thee behind me Satan, for my Jesus hath made me free.

— Zilpha Elaw

She came out of her corner and went on with the meeting. White Methodists then opened the courthouse for her. She preached in Baltimore, Washington, Alexandria and Annapolis, to slaveholders in the body of a chapel and enslaved people in its gallery, all of them weeping together. Even so, she noted, “the production of the documents of my freedom was not once demanded during my sojourn on the soil of slavery.”

Over the next decade she travelled through New York, Connecticut, Massachusetts and Maine, preaching from chapel pulpits and from open wagons. In Hartford a leading Presbyterian minister vowed to have her stopped and ended up telling his own people that the work was of God. At an Oyster Bay camp meeting her own daughter cried out for mercy while she preached, and was converted before it ended. For some years she made her home on the island of Nantucket.

A stranger in a strange land

In 1828 she had heard a voice tell her she would see London. On 10 June 1840 she parted from Rebecca and two small grandsons. “Mother, we part now,” her daughter said, “but I think we shall yet meet again.” Elaw sailed from New York on 1 July and landed at the London Docks on 25 July. England was not easy. A Wesleyan committee in London examined her, she said, as “the proud do the needy.” In Liverpool a superintendent told her, “Do you not know that we do not allow women to preach?” She held, as she wrote, that the God who raised up Deborah had sent her, and that Paul’s rule for ordinary church order was never meant to limit the Holy Spirit’s extraordinary call. Primitive Methodists, Wesleyans and independent chapels opened their doors to her across Kent, Yorkshire, Lancashire and the north-east. She preached about two hundred times in nine months around Manchester, as well as to fishermen on Holy Island, and was nursed through a five-month illness by English friends.

In 1846, after five years in England, she published her Memoirs in London and dedicated them to “the Saints and faithful Brethren in Christ” who had heard her, meaning to cross “the pathless bosom of the foaming Atlantic” and go home. Her memoir ends there, and for more than a century it was not known what became of her. Historians searching English records have since found that a widow named Zilpha Elaw married Ralph Shum at Bow, in east London, in 1850, and was widowed again in 1854, and that a Zilpha Shum, aged 80, was buried in Tower Hamlets Cemetery in August 1873. If these records are hers, as scholars believe, she never sailed home, and she died in London. We do not know whether she preached in those last years, or whether she saw Rebecca again.

What she left is the testimony she wrote so that others might take heart: the story of a motherless servant girl who met Christ while milking a cow, and a widow who left her school with an empty purse. In slave country she told her fear, “my Jesus hath made me free.”
