faq.q: Who was Zilpha Elaw?
faq.a: Zilpha Elaw (c. 1790–1873) was a Black Methodist preacher born near Philadelphia. Against fierce opposition she preached across the northern states and in the slave states of Maryland, Virginia and the District of Columbia, then spent years preaching in England. Her 1846 Memoirs are one of the earliest spiritual autobiographies by an African American woman.

faq.q: What was her childhood like?
faq.a: She grew up in a praying household, where family devotion was held morning and evening. When she was about twelve her mother died after giving birth to her twenty-second child, and her father placed her with a Quaker family, Pierson and Rebecca Mitchel, to serve until she was eighteen. Eighteen months later her father died too, leaving her with no one to look to but the household she served.

faq.q: How was Zilpha Elaw converted?
faq.a: Under Methodist preaching she prayed for months to know her sins were forgiven. One evening, while milking a cow and singing a hymn, she saw a figure in a white robe who stood by her with open arms, and she felt his looks say, "Thy prayer is accepted, I own thy name." She wrote that she never doubted Christ's love for her from that day on, and in 1808 she joined the Methodist Episcopal society.

faq.q: What was her marriage like?
faq.a: In 1810 she married Joseph Elaw, a fuller, whom she described as respectable but not a Christian. Within a year he was trying to make her give up her religion, once taking her to a ball in hopes of winning her over, where she could only weep before God. He later begged her to stop preaching, and he died of consumption on 27 January 1823.

faq.q: What happened to her at the camp meeting?
faq.a: At a Methodist camp meeting she came into the experience of entire sanctification. She lay on the ground a long time under the preaching, heard a voice say, "Now thou art sanctified," and felt as pure as if she had never sinned. This Wesleyan holiness teaching became the heart of her message, and for five years she carried a household ministry, visiting families in Burlington, New Jersey.

faq.q: How was she called to preach?
faq.a: Her dying sister Hannah told her that an angel had said Zilpha must preach the gospel, but for years she held back, pleading that she was a poor, coloured female. After a long and nearly fatal illness, she began to exhort the crowd at a camp meeting before thousands, and heard a voice say, "thou must preach the gospel; and thou must travel far and wide." She called this her commission, received not from mortal man but from God.

faq.q: What did she do after her husband died?
faq.a: Widowed and in debt, she went into service until her health failed, then opened a school in Burlington for Black children whom the white schools would not admit. For two years she would not set out to preach while she owed money. Then she pledged to go just as she was. In Philadelphia every congregation took up a collection for her, and she came home after seven months able to pay every debt.

faq.q: Did she preach in the slave states?
faq.a: Yes. From 1828 she preached in Maryland, Virginia and the District of Columbia, including Baltimore, Washington, Alexandria and Annapolis, at real risk of being seized and sold. When fear overtook her in one town she answered it, "Get thee behind me Satan, for my Jesus hath made me free," and went on. She noted that she was never once asked to produce the papers proving her freedom.

faq.q: Why did she go to England?
faq.a: She believed God had told her in 1828 that she would see London and declare his name there. In 1840 she left her daughter Rebecca and sailed from New York, landing at the London Docks on 25 July. Over the next five years she preached across Kent, Yorkshire, Lancashire and the north-east, including about two hundred sermons in nine months around Manchester, though some Wesleyan ministers refused to allow a woman to preach.

faq.q: When did Zilpha Elaw die?
faq.a: Her Memoirs, published in London in 1846, end with her hoping to return to America, and for a long time her fate was unknown. Historians have since found records of a Zilpha Elaw marrying Ralph Shum in east London in 1850, and of a Zilpha Shum, aged 80, buried in Tower Hamlets Cemetery in August 1873. If these are hers, as scholars believe, she died in London without returning home.

fields.name: Fanny Jackson Coppin
fields.bio: Born enslaved in 1837, Fanny Jackson Coppin led Philadelphia’s Institute for Colored Youth for over thirty years, organized A.M.E. women for missions, and served as a missionary in South Africa — a teacher whose vocation grew from faith.
fields.bio_html:
Fanny Jackson Coppin was born in 1837 in Washington, D.C., born a slave. Her earliest memory was of a one-room cabin where she had been sent to keep her grandmother company, and of a ladder up to the loft where they slept. “Mammy,” as the children called her, made a long prayer every night before bed. The little girl remembered only one word of it — “offspring” — because she wondered what it meant. Her grandmother was asking God to bless her children and her children’s children. The girl in the loft would spend her life helping to answer it for thousands of other people’s children.

“Mammy used to make a long prayer every night before going to bed,” Fanny remembered seventy years later; “she would ask God to bless her offspring.” Of all that was said in that cabin, it was the one word that stayed with her — the first thing she knew of prayer was a slave grandmother committing her family to God in the dark.

Her grandfather had saved money and bought himself, then four of his children. He would not buy Fanny’s mother. So it was an aunt, Sarah Orr Clark, working for six dollars a month, who saved one hundred and twenty-five dollars and bought the child’s freedom, when Fanny was about twelve. Long afterward Fanny inscribed her book to that aunt, “my beloved aunt Sarah Orr Clark, who, working at six dollars a month, saved one hundred and twenty-five dollars, and bought my freedom.”

Deep in her soul

Freed, she was sent north to relatives in New Bedford and then Newport, Rhode Island, where at fourteen she found a place as a servant in the household of George Henry Calvert, a writer, and his wife Elizabeth. Mrs. Calvert grew fond of her, taught her to sew and darn, and took her along to bathe in the sea, after which the shaking agues of her sickly childhood went away. Fanny was given one hour every other afternoon for private lessons, and without telling anyone she took music lessons on a piano at her aunt’s house until she could play the little organ in the Union Church. When Mrs. Calvert found out, she did not scold her: “Well, Fanny, when people will go ahead, they cannot be kept back.”

She was happy there, and when the time came to leave, Mrs. Calvert asked whether money would keep her. It would not.

It was in me to get an education and to teach my people. This idea was deep in my soul.

— Fanny Jackson Coppin

She passed the examination for the Rhode Island State Normal School at Bristol, where her eyes were “first opened on the subject of teaching.” Then, with her aunt still helping and a scholarship of nine dollars a year from Bishop Daniel A. Payne of the African Methodist Episcopal Church — a debt she said she would never forget — she went in 1860 to Oberlin College in Ohio.

Oberlin: “Are you a Christian?”

Oberlin was one of the few colleges in the country that admitted Black students and women, and it was steeped in the revival preaching of its president, Charles G. Finney. Fanny remembered that when Finney met a new student, his first words were, “Are you a Christian? and if not, why not?” — and that he would follow the question up with a persistence that could not be resisted until it was settled. She lived for years in the homes of two Oberlin professors, and credited those “two Christian homes,” where she was treated as one of the family, with forming the character that would carry her through what came after.

She took the “gentleman’s course” — Latin, Greek, and as much mathematics as one could shoulder — which the faculty did not forbid to women but did not advise. She felt the weight of every recitation: “I never rose to recite in my classes at Oberlin but I felt that I had the honor of the whole African race upon my shoulders.” In 1863 the faculty gave her a preparatory class to teach, warning her that if the white pupils rebelled they would not force the matter. No one rebelled. The class grew so large it had to be divided. And in her last year, as freed people began to arrive in Ohio from the South, she opened an evening class to teach them to read and write. It moved her deeply to see old men “painfully following the simple words of spelling; so intensely eager to learn.” She graduated in August 1865.

The Institute for Colored Youth

A Quaker school in Philadelphia, the Institute for Colored Youth, had written to Oberlin asking for a Black woman who could teach Greek, Latin, and higher mathematics. The answer came back: “We have the woman, but you must wait a year for her.” She arrived in 1865 to head the girls’ department, and in 1869, when the principal, Ebenezer Bassett, was appointed United States Minister to Haiti, she was made principal of the whole school — among the first Black women anywhere in the country to lead such an institution. She would hold the post for more than thirty years.

Philadelphia met her with the old humiliations: on her arrival a streetcar conductor made her stand in a rainstorm until a car marked for colored people came by. On a later visit to Oberlin, Finney asked her how she was growing in grace. She told him she was growing “as fast as the American people would let me.” It was a joke with a wound in it.

In Philadelphia she worshipped first as an Episcopalian, at the Church of the Crucifixion, a mission of St. Thomas, where she sang alto in the choir. Her teaching was frankly Christian. She wanted children to learn the Ten Commandments in verse, and said that Scripture a child could understand — “Jesus loves me this I know, for the Bible tells me so” — would be the teacher’s “first ally.” She taught that love was the root of discipline: “Love wins when everything else will fail.” And she knew that a teacher could not guard a child’s heart by technique alone.

“There is always an active enemy who is doing his sowing at the same time,” she warned teachers, remembering the parable of the tares, “and for this reason we must humble ourselves and pray that the Lord of the Harvest may protect our child’s mind from the sower of evil.”

She also saw that most of her people could not live on Greek. In Philadelphia, she told the city’s school directors, the only places a Black boy could learn a trade were the House of Refuge and the penitentiary. For years she spoke in churches and halls across the city and beyond, taking up a collection everywhere — but asking no one for more than a dollar, because she wanted the poor to have a share before the rich were asked. The fund grew in quarters and dollars, the Quaker managers joined the cause, and an Industrial Department was built at the Institute teaching a dozen trades. In 1879, raising money for the struggling Christian Recorder, she wrote that self-help was “the best help that any man can have, next to God’s,” and that her people’s “faith is firmly fixed in that ‘Eternal Providence’” that would in its own time justify the ways of God to man.

Marriage, and a wider field

At that very fair for the Recorder she met the Rev. Levi Jenkins Coppin, a young A.M.E. pastor, who walked her home and kept walking her home. “Her intellect was great,” he wrote later, “but her heart was greater.” They were married on December 21, 1881, by Bishop Payne, the same man who had once given her nine dollars toward Oberlin. She joined her husband’s African Methodist Episcopal Church, and asked him what work it would expect of her. He told her that the church gave a certain portion of its missionary work to its women.

She took that seriously. She became president of the A.M.E. Woman’s Home and Foreign Missionary Society, and her husband recorded that in 1892 she brought the General Conference a new constitution organizing the church’s women into conference branches and local auxiliaries, which gave their missionary giving new life. In 1888 the Society sent her to London as its delegate to the Centenary of Missions. She dreaded the voyage, knowing no one aboard.

“And so I had it out with the Lord,” she wrote. “Thou seest, O Lord, that I have no one to help me, and if I get nausea I may faint and be very troublesome to those about me. Thou seest, O Lord, that I must not get sick.” Then, simply: “And I wasn’t sick.”

In London she sat entranced among the gray-headed missionaries who had carried the gospel to the far places of the earth. When a minister warned the women there not to assume ecclesiastical functions, she rose to answer that “the Lord God alone gives the limit to the functions of woman’s religious work” — though she added that she had always considered the pulpit a sacred place and had never sought to speak from it. Black women only lately out of slavery, she told the assembly, had already sent missionaries to Haiti, Trinidad, and Sierra Leone, though they had only a crust to share.

The spirit of missionaries, the spirit of mission work, is the spirit of sharing all we have.

— Fanny Jackson Coppin

Africa

In 1900 her husband was elected a bishop and assigned to South Africa. After thirty-seven years in the schoolroom, she laid down her work at the Institute and followed him, counting it a privilege to end her active life in “the home of the ancestors” of the young people she had taught. They anchored in Table Bay on Sunday morning, November 30, 1902. In Cape Town, where her husband had bought a building for a school and mission house, Bethel Institute, she gathered the Christian women of the congregation and began temperance and missionary societies among them, and then in mission stations across the Cape. At the first conference at Port Elizabeth she watched women who had never before spoken in public for Christian work stand and speak — some in Dutch, some in broken English, “and some in their own God-given native language.”

She travelled with the bishop as far as Bulawayo, more than thirteen hundred miles north. There, worn out, she fainted while speaking through an interpreter — the first time, she said, she had ever “fallen at my post” — and was carried out tenderly by African women while her husband went on with the meeting. Government informers sat in on such meetings, fearing the missionaries would stir up the people; she answered that they were missionaries, not politicians, and that if people grew discontented, the fault lay in injustice and “a general lack of the Christian spirit of brotherhood.” Yet she counselled patience, not violence.

The Kingdom of God does not proceed in its conquests by the employment of carnal weapons, and right can afford to be patient because it is bound to win in the end.

— Fanny Jackson Coppin

“We were graciously kept from disease,” she wrote of the African years, “even the bubonic plague that came to our very door.” She went with her husband through most of his field, speaking to the women “upon the subjects of righteousness, temperance and the judgment to come,” content if some seed took root that would never be wholly uprooted.

The long evening

They returned to America in the spring of 1904, and her strength began to give way. For about eight years she was largely confined to the house in Philadelphia — no single illness, her husband wrote, but a gradual breaking down of a constitution that had answered every call of duty. Her mind stayed clear to the end. She read the papers and, above all, the Bible. In those quiet years she wrote Reminiscences of School Life, and Hints on Teaching.

Fanny Jackson Coppin died on January 21, 1913. Her funeral was held at Bethel Church, and her friends founded a scholarship in her name for struggling students, which they thought she would have liked best of all. In South Africa, A.M.E. women later raised money to name a building at Wilberforce Institute the Fanny Jackson Coppin Hall, and in 1926 a teacher-training school in Baltimore took her name. — today’s Coppin State University. One eulogy said that for forty years she had been “the inspiration of thousands,” and that her name “was a synonym for character.” But the root of it all is in her own pages: a slave grandmother praying in the dark for her offspring, an aunt’s six dollars a month, a college president asking whether she was a Christian, and a woman who believed that whatever God had given her — mind, learning, or a crust — he had given in order that it be shared.

faq.q: Who was Fanny Jackson Coppin?
faq.a: Born enslaved in Washington, D.C., in 1837, Fanny Jackson Coppin became one of the most respected Christian educators of nineteenth-century America. She led Philadelphia's Institute for Colored Youth for more than thirty years, organized the missionary work of the A.M.E. Church's women, and ended her active life as a missionary in South Africa.

faq.q: How did she gain her freedom?
faq.a: Her grandfather bought himself and four of his children but would not buy Fanny's mother. Her aunt, Sarah Orr Clark, working for six dollars a month, saved one hundred and twenty-five dollars and bought Fanny's freedom when she was about twelve. Fanny later inscribed her book to that aunt.

faq.a: Working as a servant in Newport, Rhode Island, in the household of the writer George Henry Calvert, she studied whenever she could. She said it was in her to get an education and to teach her people, an idea deep in her soul, and no offer of comfort could turn her from it. She went on to the Rhode Island State Normal School and then, in 1860, to Oberlin College.

faq.q: What did Oberlin mean for her faith?
faq.a: Oberlin's president, Charles G. Finney, greeted new students with the question, "Are you a Christian? and if not, why not?" Fanny lived for years in two Christian professors' homes and credited them with forming her character. While still a student she taught a preparatory class and, in her last year, an evening class for freed people learning to read.

faq.q: What did she do at the Institute for Colored Youth?
faq.a: She arrived at the Quaker-founded Institute in Philadelphia in 1865 to head its girls' department and became principal of the whole school in 1869. She taught Greek, Latin and mathematics, trained teachers, and campaigned for years, a dollar at a time, to add an Industrial Department where young people could learn trades.

She organized temperance and missionary societies among African and Coloured Christian women and travelled as far as Bulawayo, speaking on righteousness, temperance and the judgment to come.

She died on 21 January 1913. A scholarship, a hall at Wilberforce Institute in South Africa, and Coppin State University in Baltimore all bear her name.

fields.name: Kateri Tekakwitha
fields.bio: Mohawk-Algonquin convert (1656–1680) who, scarred by smallpox and mocked by her village, was baptized at twenty, fled two hundred miles to the Christian mission at Kahnawake, and gave her whole life to Christ. The first Indigenous North American woman canonized.
fields.bio_html:
Kateri Tekakwitha was born in 1656 in the Mohawk village of Ossernenon, on the south bank of the Mohawk River near present-day Auriesville, New York — the same village where, ten years before, the Jesuit Isaac Jogues had been put to death. Her father was a Mohawk; her mother was an Algonquin woman who had been taken captive in war and brought into the Mohawk country, and who was a baptized Christian. The girl grew up in the longhouses of the village with a Christian mother she would barely remember and a people who, for the most part, wanted nothing to do with the faith of the French blackrobes.

When she was about four, smallpox swept through the village. It took her father, her mother, and her small brother within a few days of one another, and left the child alone. She survived, but the disease marked her for life: her face was scarred, and her eyes were so weakened that for years she could not bear strong light. She learned to keep indoors, and when she had to go out she drew her blanket over her head to shade her eyes.

She was taken in by her father’s brother, a chief of the village, and by her aunts. After a French expedition burned the Mohawk towns in 1666, the family rebuilt on the north bank of the river, at a village later known as Caughnawaga, near present-day Fonda. There Tekakwitha grew into a quiet, capable young woman — shy, skilled in the crafts of the longhouse — and, to her relatives’ frustration, determined not to marry. When her aunts arranged a match and the young man came to sit beside her in the lodge, she rose and walked out of the cabin — a refusal that cost her years of hard words and harder work.

The blackrobe at the door

Jesuits had lived among the Mohawks since 1667, but her uncle disliked the French and their religion, and she did not dare to go looking for a priest. The meeting, when it came, came almost by accident. In 1675 she had injured her foot and was sitting idle in the lodge while the other women worked in the cornfields. Father Jacques de Lamberville, new to the mission, was walking through the half-empty village visiting the sick and the old, and meant to pass her uncle’s cabin by. Something moved him to step inside.

For years Tekakwitha had carried a hidden longing to know the God her mother had prayed to, yet she dared not seek out the priest. Then, laid up with a wounded foot, she looked up to find him in the doorway. “Never was an encounter more fortunate,” Father Chauchetière wrote — for the girl, “who wished to speak to the Father, and who dared not go to seek him,” and for the priest, “who found a treasure where he expected to find no one.”

She opened her heart to him at once and told him she wanted to become a Christian whatever it cost. Lamberville, a careful man, instructed her through the winter and asked quietly around the village about her life — and was surprised to find that no one, not even those who treated her badly, could say anything against her. On Easter Sunday, 1676, at the age of twenty, she was baptized in the little bark chapel and given the name Catherine — in the Mohawk tongue, Kateri.

“The Christian”

Baptism did not bring her peace in her uncle’s lodge; it brought the opposite. Because she would not work in the fields on Sundays and feast days, her relatives refused her food on those days. Children were sent to throw stones at her on her way to the chapel, and drunken men followed her and threatened her life, until she took long roundabout paths to reach her prayers. Her uncle turned against her, and one aunt spread a slander about her that the priest saw through at once. The village children stopped calling her by name at all. Chauchetière records that they called her only “the Christian,” in a tone that meant dog, until people forgot her old name entirely — and that, far from grieving over it, “she was happy to have lost her name.”

She said plainly, when she had to, that she would die rather than give up her faith. Yet later, looking back from the safety of the Christian village, the thing she most reproached herself for was not that she had suffered but that she had sometimes given way — that she had let herself be driven into the fields on the Lord’s Day, and had, as she put it, feared death more than sin. It is an honest glimpse of a young convert who knew both courage and fear.

Lamberville saw that she could not long survive as she was, and urged her to go north to the mission of Saint-François-Xavier at the Sault Saint-Louis, on the St. Lawrence opposite Montreal — Kahnawake, where Christian Iroquois had gathered to live and pray together. In the autumn of 1677, with the help of three Christian men from that village, she slipped away. Her uncle set out after them with a loaded gun; her companions hid her in the undergrowth, and he passed by. The journey north was some two hundred miles, by trail, river, and lake.

Of that long flight through the forests to the Christian village, Father Chauchetière wrote simply: “Her journey was a continual prayer, and the joy that she felt in approaching Montreal could not be expressed.”

The treasure of the Sault

She arrived at Kahnawake carrying a letter from Lamberville to the Fathers there. As the mission remembered it, its message was short: “I send you a treasure; guard it well.” She was taken into the longhouse of Anastasia Tegonhatsiongo, an older Christian woman who had known her mother, and who became her teacher and guide. She gave herself to prayer with an intensity that startled even the missionaries, in the chapel before dawn and again through the day, learning the catechism and the life of Christ with a hunger that seemed never satisfied. Her one question, the Jesuits remembered, was this:

Who will teach me what is most pleasing to God, that I may do it?

— Kateri Tekakwitha

At Christmas 1677, after only a few months at the mission, she was admitted to her first Communion — an unusual mark of trust, since new converts at the Sault were normally made to wait much longer. The next spring she was received into the Confraternity of the Holy Family, a society of the most devout women of the village. And there she found a friend. Marie-Thérèse Tegaiaguenta, an Oneida widow who had come through her own hard years, became her constant companion. The two worked and prayed side by side, and with another woman even dreamed of founding a little community of Native women on an island near the mission — until the priests judged them too young in the faith and set the plan aside.

Her relatives at the Sault, meaning only her good, pressed her again to marry: a husband, they said, would keep her from want. When she brought the matter to her confessor, Father Pierre Cholenec, he put to her, to test her, every reason she ought to marry. Her answer was immediate.

I am not any longer my own. I have given myself entirely to Jesus Christ, and it is not possible for me to change masters.

— Kateri Tekakwitha

He told her to take three days to pray about it. She came back within a quarter of an hour. “It is settled,” she said; “my part has long since been taken. No, my father, I can have no other spouse but Jesus Christ.” On 25 March 1679, the Feast of the Annunciation, with Cholenec’s consent, she made a private vow of perpetual virginity — so far as anyone knew, the first such vow made by a Native woman of North America.

Love that would not count the cost

The last part of Kateri’s life must be told honestly. In the Christian village there was a fervent, sometimes extreme movement of penance among the women, and Kateri threw herself into it. She fasted, spoiled the taste of what little she ate, exposed herself to the winter cold, and with Marie-Thérèse went out in secret to a lonely cabin by the cemetery to scourge one another. Once she held a burning brand between her toes; once she slept three nights on a bed of thorns.

Kneeling in that cold cabin, Kateri prayed aloud, as Marie-Thérèse later reported: “My Jesus, I must risk everything with you. I love you, but I have offended you.” Often, her friend said, tears and sobs choked her before she could finish, and she would speak of the three nails that held the Saviour to the cross as the figure of her own sins.

These practices were not what her teachers asked of her, and they are not a pattern for anyone to follow. It was Thérèse who first, finding her pale and exhausted, warned her that she would offend God by such things without her confessor’s leave; and when Kateri went to Cholenec, he rebuked her and told her to throw the thorns into the fire, which she did at once. The priests who wrote her life admired her fervour and were also alarmed by it, and they record again and again how they tried to rein it in. What moved her was a fierce longing to give something back to the Christ who had been crucified for her. But her body, already weak from childhood illness, could not bear it, and her life was almost certainly shortened by it.

“I will love you in heaven”

Through the winter of 1679–80 she grew steadily weaker, with a low fever that would not leave her. In Holy Week, when she could no longer be carried to the chapel, Father Cholenec did what had never been done at the mission and brought Communion to her in the longhouse, the village kneeling outside.

On the morning of Wednesday in Holy Week, 17 April 1680, Thérèse knelt beside her. Chauchetière, who was there, recorded Kateri’s farewell to her friend: to take courage, to hold fast, to listen to the Fathers, and never to forget what they had done together.

I am going to die. … I will love you in heaven — I will pray for you — I will help you.

— Kateri Tekakwitha

The accounts of her very last words differ a little. Cholenec wrote that she spoke the holy names of Jesus and Mary before her voice failed; later tellings, repeated by Pope John Paul II at her beatification, give them as “Jesus, I love you.” She died about three o’clock that afternoon, peacefully, “as if she had gone to sleep.” She was twenty-four years old.

Then came the thing that the Jesuits never forgot. About a quarter of an hour after her death, Cholenec wrote, her face — “thus emaciated and marked” by smallpox, sickness, and penance — “changed all at once” and became “so beautiful and so fair” that he cried out in astonishment and called the other priest, and the whole village came to see. Chauchetière described the same change. Both men were eyewitnesses and took it as a sign of God’s favour; it is their testimony, to be weighed as such.

The Lily of the Mohawks

Kateri Tekakwitha left no writings of her own. Everything we know of her words comes through the two Jesuits who knew her best, Claude Chauchetière and Pierre Cholenec, who wrote her life in the years after her death, and through the memories of Marie-Thérèse and Anastasia that they gathered. Chauchetière also painted her portrait from memory — usually dated to the 1690s, it is the oldest image of her that survives. Their accounts carry the devotional habits of their age and must be read with care; but the young woman they knew stands out clearly.

Devotion to her spread quickly among Native and French Christians alike, and many healings and favours were credited to her prayers. The Catholic Church declared her venerable in 1943, and Pope John Paul II beatified her in 1980. In 2012, after the Church attributed to her intercession the recovery of Jake Finkbonner, a boy of Lummi descent in Washington State, from a flesh-eating infection, Pope Benedict XVI canonized her — the first Indigenous woman of North America to be named a saint by the Catholic Church.

For at the heart of her story is not a miracle but a choice, made again and again by a scarred and half-blind orphan who had every reason to keep her head down. She chose Christ in a village that mocked her for it, chose Him again on a two-hundred-mile road through the forest, and chose Him once more when every voice around her urged an easier life. “I am not any longer my own,” she said. Few have said it more simply, or meant it more completely.

faq.q: Who was Kateri Tekakwitha?
faq.a: Kateri Tekakwitha was a Mohawk-Algonquin woman, born in 1656 in what is now upstate New York, who became a Christian at twenty in the face of fierce opposition from her own village. She fled to the Christian mission at Kahnawake near Montreal, gave her life wholly to Christ, and died there in 1680 at twenty-four. In 2012 she became the first Indigenous woman of North America canonized by the Catholic Church.

faq.q: What was her childhood like?
faq.a: She was born at Ossernenon, near present-day Auriesville, New York, to a Mohawk father and a Christian Algonquin mother. When she was about four, smallpox killed her parents and her little brother, and left her face scarred and her eyes so weak that she shaded them with her blanket for years. She was raised by her uncle, a village chief who disliked the French and their religion, and by her aunts.

faq.q: Why did she refuse to marry?
faq.a: As she grew into a shy, capable young woman, her aunts tried to arrange a marriage for her. When the young man came to sit beside her in the lodge, she rose and walked out of the cabin. The refusal cost her years of hard words and harder work, and later, after her conversion, she explained that she had given herself entirely to Jesus Christ.

faq.q: How did she meet Father de Lamberville?
faq.a: In 1675, laid up with an injured foot while the other women worked in the fields, she looked up to find the Jesuit Jacques de Lamberville in the doorway; he had meant to pass the cabin by. She had longed to speak to a priest but had not dared to seek one out. Father Chauchetière later wrote that the priest "found a treasure where he expected to find no one."

faq.q: When was she baptized?
faq.a: Lamberville instructed her through the winter and quietly asked around the village about her life, finding that no one could say anything against her. On Easter Sunday, 1676, at the age of twenty, she was baptized in the bark chapel and named Catherine, in Mohawk Kateri.

faq.q: What did she suffer for her faith?
faq.a: Because she would not work in the fields on Sundays, her relatives refused her food on those days. Children threw stones at her on the way to the chapel, drunken men threatened her life, and the village called her only "the Christian," in a tone that meant dog. Father Chauchetière recorded that she was happy to have lost her name.

faq.q: How did she escape to Kahnawake?
faq.a: Lamberville urged her to go to the Christian mission of Saint-François-Xavier at the Sault Saint-Louis, opposite Montreal. In the autumn of 1677, with the help of three Christian men from that village, she slipped away on a journey of some two hundred miles; when her uncle came after them with a gun, they hid her in the undergrowth. Chauchetière wrote that her journey was a continual prayer.

faq.q: What was her life like at the mission?
faq.a: She lived in the longhouse of Anastasia Tegonhatsiongo, an older Christian woman who had known her mother, made her first Communion at Christmas 1677, and became close friends with Marie-Thérèse Tegaiaguenta. Her constant question was "Who will teach me what is most pleasing to God, that I may do it?" On 25 March 1679 she made a private vow of virginity, telling her confessor, "I am not any longer my own."

faq.q: What about her severe penances?
faq.a: Kateri took part in an intense movement of penance among the women of the village: fasting, exposure to cold, scourging, even a bed of thorns. These were not what her teachers asked of her, and they are not a pattern to follow; when her confessor, Father Cholenec, learned of the thorns he rebuked her and had her throw them into the fire. Her weakened body could not bear such things, and her life was almost certainly shortened by them.

faq.q: How did she die, and how is she remembered?
faq.a: She died at Kahnawake on 17 April 1680, Wednesday of Holy Week, telling her friend Thérèse, "I will love you in heaven." The two Jesuits present reported that her smallpox-scarred face became beautiful shortly after her death. She left no writings; her words come to us through Fathers Chauchetière and Cholenec. She was beatified in 1980 and canonized in 2012.

fields.name: Kanzo Uchimura
fields.bio: Samurai's son, Christian writer, and founder of Japan's Non-Church movement, Kanzō Uchimura was brought to the cross at Amherst College and spent his life calling Japan to Christ — loving, as he said, "two J's": Jesus and Japan.
fields.bio_html:
Kanzo Uchimura was born in Edo — the city soon to be renamed Tokyo — in March 1861, into a family of the samurai class. “My family belonged to the warrior class,” he wrote, “so I was born to fight.” His grandfather longed for a battle he never saw; his father was a Confucian scholar who could recite the sayings of the sage almost entirely from memory. From him the boy took the old virtues of loyalty to one’s lord, reverence for parents and teachers, and an honour that would rather starve than bend. He took, too, a crowded and anxious religion. He prayed each morning to the gods of the four points of the compass, kept vows of abstinence for one god after another until eggs and beans were forbidden him, and would walk a longer road to school to pass fewer shrines. “With so many gods to satisfy and appease,” he remembered, “I was naturally a fretful timid child.”

In 1877 he entered the new government Agricultural College at Sapporo, on the northern island of Hokkaido. The American scientist William S. Clark had spent the college’s first year there and had already left, but behind him he left a document he had written out in English — the “Covenant of Believers in Jesus” — signed by every student of the first class. The older boys set about converting the newcomers. Uchimura resisted them as a patriot resists a foreign invader; one afternoon he went to a nearby shrine and prayed, with all the sincerity he had, that the guardian god would extinguish the new enthusiasm and punish its converts. It was no use. Before the year was out the sixteen-year-old had signed the covenant, pressed into it, he admitted, “against my will.”

And yet the forced step opened a door. The covenant taught him there was one God and not eight million, and the discovery set him free. “One God, and not many, was indeed a glad tiding to my little soul,” he wrote. He walked past the temples with his head up and kept talking and laughing all the way to school. On 2 June 1878 he and six classmates were baptized by a visiting Methodist missionary, kneeling and answering “Amen” when asked to own “the name of Him who was crucified for our sins.” He took the Christian name Jonathan, for the love of Jonathan for David, and with his friends began a little church in their dormitory rooms.

Into Christendom

The joy of those student years did not last untroubled. After graduating in 1881 he entered government service, working on the fisheries of his country, and in 1884 he married Take Asada. The marriage ended in sorrow within months, and the young Christian who had thought himself strong found himself crushed by guilt, grief, and a heart he could not master. That November, with little money and less peace, he sailed for the United States, hoping that the Christian lands which had sent him the gospel might give him the peace he could not find.

His first refuge was not a church or a college but an asylum. At Elwyn, Pennsylvania, the superintendent of a training school for children with intellectual disabilities, Dr. Isaac Kerlin, took him on as an attendant, and for some eight months the samurai’s son washed and fed and watched over the least of the children. He went there, he confessed, much as Luther went into his convent — to earn peace by good works. But on his very first night of duty a voice in his heart answered him: “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.” He was learning, slowly, that he could not make himself clean.

Look to the Crucified

In 1885 he made his way to Amherst College in Massachusetts, to meet its president, Julius Seelye, whose writings he had read in Japan. He arrived with seven silver dollars and expected a stern, unapproachable scholar. Instead the door opened on a large man with tear-filled eyes and a warm grip. “From that time on,” Uchimura wrote, “my Christianity has taken an entirely new direction.” Seelye gave him a room in the dormitory and had the janitor find him a bed and a chair. Uchimura settled into the top floor, resolved never to leave it “till the Almighty should show Himself unto me.”

Seelye’s word to him, as Uchimura later remembered it, was simple: stop looking within yourself, and look to Jesus, who paid for your sins on the cross. The lesson took. In the spring of 1886 he wrote in his diary the words that marked the turning of his life:

Never was the atoning power of Christ more clearly revealed to me than it is to-day. In the crucifixion of the Son of God lies the solution of all the difficulties that buffeted my mind thus far.

— Kanzo Uchimura

Months later he put the same discovery another way: “death to sin” comes “not by looking into my sinful heart, but by looking up to Jesus crucified.” He meditated on Christ as he hauled scuttles of coal up the dormitory stairs, and once set them down on the landing to burst into thanksgiving. One September evening, so grateful that he longed to remember the Lord’s death, he pressed juice from wild grapes into a little dish, cut a piece of biscuit, gave thanks, and received them. Through a New England winter without a stove and with his bills unpaid, he called himself “a real optimist.” He would say that he was truly converted at Amherst, some ten years after his baptism.

In the spring of 1887 he wrote out his morning prayer: “I come unto Thee, not because I am clean and pure and loving. I came unto Thee that I may be filled by Thee… I am unclean; I pray Thee to cleanse me. I have no faith; give Thou me faith.”

He graduated from Amherst in 1887 and entered Hartford Theological Seminary that autumn, but he had come on condition that he would never be ordained, and the dry debates of the classroom wearied him. Ill and impatient, he left in early 1888. Fifty days at sea brought him home in May with seventy-five cents in his pocket and, he said, nothing to show his parents but the gospel, “unto the Jews a stumbling-block, and unto the Greeks foolishness.”

The bow he would not make

In 1889 he married again, and in January 1891 he was teaching at the First Higher Middle School in Tokyo when the school held a ceremony for the new Imperial Rescript on Education, which bore the Emperor’s signature. Teachers and students filed forward to bow deeply before it as before a sacred object. When his turn came, Uchimura hesitated, and made at most a slight bow. To his conscience a reverent bow came too near to worship; he would honour the Emperor, but worship God alone. The press called it a national insult. Students, newspapers, and patriots denounced him as a traitor, and he was forced to resign.

The storm broke his health. He fell gravely ill, and his young wife Kazu, who had nursed him and stood between him and the angry crowds, caught the sickness herself and died that spring, only twenty-one months after their wedding. He was left without work, without a wife, and with his name a byword across Japan. In these years of poverty he began to write — and in 1895 published, in English, How I Became a Christian: Out of My Diary, the book from which most of what we know of his conversion comes. With his third wife, Shizu, whom he married at the end of 1892, he went through want so severe that she pawned her wedding kimonos to keep them out of debt.

Two J’s

He never stopped loving the country that rejected him. As a columnist for the Tokyo daily Yorozu Chōhō from 1897 he attacked corruption without fear. When war with Russia loomed in 1903, he declared himself a Christian pacifist and opposed it, almost alone, while even many church leaders cheered it on. He resigned rather than soften his view, and once more lost his living; again he was called a traitor, and there were days when the family went hungry rather than fall into debt. All his life he held two loves together:

I love two J’s and no third; one is Jesus, and the other is Japan.

— Kanzo Uchimura

He likened his faith to an ellipse with two centres. But the order was never in doubt. In the front of his English Bible he had written the four lines he wanted on his grave — himself for Japan, Japan for the world, the world for Christ, “and All for God.”

In 1900 he began a monthly, Seisho no Kenkyū (Biblical Study), which he published until his death, and he gathered readers into Sunday Bible lectures in Tokyo, many of whose hearers were students. From this grew what came to be called Mukyōkai, the “Non-Church” movement. It had no ordained clergy, no denominational structure, and no sacraments administered by a church; its believers met in homes and lecture halls to study the Bible under lay teachers. Uchimura described the ideal as “a fellowship, not an institution,” calling no man bishop or pastor save Jesus Christ. Some missionaries and churches branded him a church-destroyer, and the absence of baptism and the Lord’s Supper as church ordinances is a real departure a careful reader should know. Yet the faith he taught was historic and evangelical: the Bible as the Word of God, salvation through the atoning death of Christ on the cross, His bodily resurrection, and His return. Uchimura did not oppose churches as such — he spoke in them when asked — and he insisted only that no institution could stand between a soul and its Saviour.

A daughter and a hope

His daughter Ruth — Rutsuko — had been his comfort through the years of abuse. In January 1912, at eighteen, she died. At her burial in Tokyo, as the mourners sang “Rock of Ages” and the coffin was lowered, her father took up a handful of earth, lifted it high, and cried “Ruth, banzai!” — a shout of victory. Some thought grief had unhinged him. He meant that she had gone, not to the grave, but to glory. Years later he told a friend that without her death he would never have become the evangelist he was, and that those who had never lost a child might not understand the hope of Christ’s coming, “however many theological books they would read.”

That hope became the burden of his later preaching. For three decades an American businessman, David C. Bell, whom he had met by chance on a Washington tram car in 1885, had been praying for him on exactly this point.

In 1918 Uchimura wrote that Bell “has prayed every day for more than thirty years that I might believe in the Second Coming of Christ. And now that his prayers were answered, and God opened my eyes… all things became new to me.” What no argument could do, he said, “God’s Spirit in answer to the prayers of one of His saints accomplished in full.”

That year he joined the holiness evangelist Jūji Nakada and others in a series of meetings across Japan proclaiming the Lord’s return, which drew large crowds. He would not set dates or speculate about the details, and he drew back after a time from views of his colleagues he could not share. But the hope itself never left him.

All for God

Kanzo Uchimura died of heart disease in Tokyo on 28 March 1930, at sixty-nine. He was buried in Tama Cemetery, and on the stone were carved, as he had asked, the words from the front of his Bible:

I for Japan; Japan for the World; The World for Christ; And All for God.

— Kanzo Uchimura

His disciples became professors, university presidents, and Bible teachers across Japan, and every spring since his death they have gathered near the anniversary to remember him and open the Scriptures. Branded a traitor by his country and a heretic by some of his fellow Christians, he was neither. He was a samurai’s son who had been conquered at last — not by the bigger boys at Sapporo, but by the crucified Son of God — and who spent his life asking his own people to look where Julius Seelye had told him to look.

fields.name: Josephine Bakhita
fields.bio: Sudanese-born former slave (c. 1869–1947) who found Christ in Venice, won her freedom in an Italian court, and served fifty years as a Canossian sister in Schio, forgiving those who had enslaved her.
fields.bio_html:
She never knew her own birthday, and she could not remember the name her mother gave her. Josephine Bakhita was born around 1869 in Olgossa, a village in Darfur in the west of present-day Sudan, one of the Daju people. Her father, a respected and reasonably prosperous man, was brother to the village chief; she grew up among three brothers and three sisters, and when she came to dictate her memories forty years later she began with that lost home: “I lived a very happy and carefree life, without knowing what suffering was.”

Taken

Slave raiders had already carried off her eldest sister. Then, around 1877, when she was perhaps eight or nine, they came for her. She was marched barefoot hundreds of miles toward El Obeid and sold and bought twice before she even reached the town. The Canossian account says that terror drove her own name out of her memory, and that the name she bore for the rest of her life was the one her captors gave her: Bakhita, Arabic for “fortunate.” Only much later would it come to seem, without anyone intending it, a true word.

Over the following years she was sold again and again — five times in the slave markets of Sudan, Pope Benedict XVI would later write. She once tried to escape, and was recaptured. In El Obeid an owner’s son beat and kicked her so savagely that she lay for more than a month unable to rise from her straw mat. Her worst years were in the household of a Turkish general, serving his wife and his mother-in-law. “During all the years I stayed in that house,” she remembered, “I do not recall a day that passed without some wound or other. When a wound from the whip began to heal, other blows would pour down on me.”

There, too, came the ordeal she named as the most terrifying of all. With their mistress standing over them, whip in hand, Bakhita and the other slave girls were marked: a woman drew patterns on their skin in white flour, cut along the lines with a razor, and filled the wounds with salt so that the scars would never fade. “I felt I was going to die any moment,” she said, “especially when they rubbed me in with the salt.” She carried those marks, and the marks of the lash, to her grave; Benedict XVI counted 144 scars. Yet even in that darkness, by her own testimony, something in her was reaching toward God before she knew his name. “Seeing the sun, the moon and the stars,” she remembered, “I said to myself: Who could be the Master of these beautiful things? And I felt a great desire to see him, to know Him and to pay Him homage.”

A different kind of master

In the early 1880s the Mahdist uprising swept toward El Obeid, and the general sold off his slaves before leaving. In Khartoum Bakhita was bought by the Italian consul, Callisto Legnani — and for the first time since her capture, she noticed, no one used the lash when giving her orders. In his house she knew peace and even moments of joy, though they were shadowed by longing for the family she would never see again. When the siege of Khartoum forced Legnani to flee, Bakhita begged to go with him. They escaped across the desert by camel to the Red Sea port of Suakin and sailed for Italy, arriving at Genoa in 1885.

She was not yet free. At Genoa, Legnani gave her to the wife of his friend and fellow-refugee Augusto Michieli, and she went with the Michieli family to their villa at Zianigo, near Mirano, in the Veneto. When their daughter Alice — called Mimmina — was born in 1886, Bakhita became her nanny and devoted friend. Then Augusto Michieli bought a hotel at Suakin and resolved to move his family to Africa for good. While the Italian property was being sold, his wife needed somewhere to leave the child and her nurse, and on the advice of the family’s agent, Illuminato Checchini, she placed both with the Canossian Sisters at the Institute of the Catechumens in Venice in late November 1888.

It was there, from the sisters, that Bakhita heard of Jesus Christ. She later said they had introduced her to “that God who from childhood I had felt in my heart without knowing who He was,” and she spoke of their teaching as given “with heroic patience.” Pope Benedict, retelling her story at the opening of his encyclical on hope, put his finger on what that teaching meant to someone who had known only owners. Learning the Venetian dialect, Bakhita called God by the word for a master of a household — paron. All her life she had known masters who despised her, beat her, or at best found her useful. Now she heard of a Paron above all masters, who was good, who knew her, who had made her and loved her — and who had himself been flogged, and was waiting for her at the Father’s right hand.

“Here, I became a daughter of God”

When Signora Michieli came back for her daughter and her slave, Bakhita did something no one had ever allowed her to do: she said no. With a firmness that startled everyone, she refused to leave the sisters and the God she had found among them. For three days Michieli tried to force the matter. The superior of the catechumenate appealed to the Patriarch of Venice, and the question went to the authorities. On 29 November 1889 the ruling came: slavery had been outlawed in Sudan before Bakhita was born, and Italian law had never recognized it at all. In the eyes of the law she had never been anyone’s property. For the first time in her life her future was her own, and she chose to stay.

The longing she had felt as a slave child under the Darfur stars — “a great desire to see him, to know Him” — found its answer in Venice. On 9 January 1890 she was baptized, confirmed and received her first Communion, taking the name Josephine. She hardly knew how to contain her joy, and for years afterward she was seen kissing the baptismal font and saying, “Here, I became a daughter of God!”

Freedom did not send her away from the sisters but deeper among them. She remained at the catechumenate, felt the call to give her whole life to Christ, and in December 1893 entered the novitiate of the Canossian Daughters of Charity. On 8 December 1896, in Verona, she made her vows. Her heart, even then, was in Africa.

On the day she consecrated her life to God she prayed: “O Lord, I wish I could fly southward to my people, to preach to all, loudly, your goodness. Oh! How many souls I could win for you! First among all, my mother, and my father, my brothers and my sister, as yet a slave... Grant, O Lord, that they, too, may know and love you!”

Madre Moretta

She never did fly south. In 1902 she was sent to the Canossian house at Schio, a small industrial town in the foothills of the Alps near Vicenza, and there, apart from a few years away, she spent the rest of her life. Her work was the plainest work a convent has: cooking, sewing and embroidery, the sacristy, and above all the door. As portress she greeted everyone who knocked, and she would lay her hands gently on the heads of the children coming in each day to the Canossian school. During the First World War part of the convent became a military hospital, and she helped care for wounded soldiers. The people of Schio came to love her. They called her Sor Moretta and Madre Moretta — “our little brown sister,” “our black mother” — and the names were affection, not mockery.

What they remembered was her gentleness, her musical Venetian with the rhythm of another country in it, and a smile that did not seem to wear out. Her counsel was always short and always pointed toward God: “Be good, love the Lord, pray for those who do not know Him. What a great grace it is to know God!”

In 1910, in obedience to her superiors, she dictated the story of her life, and it is from that notebook that nearly everything we know of her childhood comes. In 1931 Ida Zanolini published it as Storia meravigliosa — “a wonderful story” — and the book made her famous across Italy. From 1935 to 1939 her order sent her travelling from house to house, based at the missionary novitiate at Vimercate near Milan, to tell her story and help prepare young sisters for Africa. She went because, as Benedict XVI wrote, the hope that had redeemed her was not something she could keep to herself.

Forgiveness

The question people most wanted to ask her was the hardest one. A student once asked what she would do if she ever met the men who had kidnapped her. She answered at once.

If I were to meet the slave-merchants who kidnapped me and even those who tortured me, I would kneel and kiss their hands. If what happened to me had never taken place, how could I become a Christian and a religious?

— Josephine Bakhita

It would be easy to misread those words as if she thought the slavers had done well. She did not. She simply refused to let them have the last word over her life, and she refused to hate them. “I pity them!” she said on another occasion. “No doubt they were unaware of the anguish they caused me.” When a priest pressed her — even those who tortured you? — she replied, “Why not? poor things! They did not know the Lord.” The mercy that had found her was the measure of the mercy she extended. Her grief, when she spoke of her slavery, was not for what she had suffered but for the years she had lived without knowing Christ: “If I were to kneel my whole life, it would not be enough to express my gratitude to the good Lord.”

As the Master desires

Through the Second World War, when Schio, a centre of industry, came under bombing, the townspeople looked on the old African sister as a kind of shelter among them. When her superior, worn down by the hardships of those years, confided her troubles, Bakhita answered in her usual way: “Dear Mother, why do you wonder that the Lord is giving you some trouble? If He were not to come to us for sharing some of his sufferings, to whom will He go?” She would pray, she said, “but only that the Will of God be done.”

Her last years were long and painful. Illness confined her to a wheelchair, but the smile stayed. When visitors asked how she was, she gave the answer that became her motto: “As the Master desires.” Asked whether she was afraid to die, she said, “When a person loves another very much, she greatly wished to meet that person. Why then should I be afraid of death? Death brings us to God.”

He is the Master, I am only his humble creature.

— Josephine Bakhita

At the very end, her mind went back to the slave roads of her childhood. More than once she begged the nurse beside her, “Please, loosen the chains... they are heavy!” Then the old terror passed, and she died peacefully at the convent in Schio on 8 February 1947, about seventy-eight years old, with her sisters around her. Crowds came for three days to see their Madre Moretta for the last time.

Fortunate

The Catholic Church opened her cause twelve years after her death, beatified her in 1992 and canonized her on 1 October 2000; as the process requires, the Church credited healings to her intercession, but her life needs no wonders added to it to speak. When John Paul II visited Khartoum in 1993 he honoured her on her own soil — “Rejoice, all of Africa! Bakhita has come back to you” — and she is now regarded as patron of Sudan and of those who work against human trafficking. In 2007 Benedict XVI chose her, of all the saints, to open his encyclical Spe Salvi, as the clearest modern picture of what Christian hope is: not the small hope of finding a kinder owner, but the great hope of knowing oneself “definitively loved” by God.

That is the strange truth hidden in the name her kidnappers gave her. The girl who forgot her own name was found, named and claimed by a Master who wounds no one and was wounded for all. She spent fifty years opening a convent door to strangers, and through that small door a great many people have since glimpsed the God she called Paron — and found that he is good.

faq.q: Who was Josephine Bakhita?
faq.a: Josephine Bakhita (c. 1869–1947) was a Sudanese woman kidnapped into slavery as a child who, after being brought to Italy, came to faith in Christ, won her freedom in an Italian court, and spent fifty years as a Canossian sister in the town of Schio. Her forgiveness of those who enslaved her and her quiet joy made her one of the best-loved Christian witnesses of modern Africa, and she was canonized by the Catholic Church in 2000.

faq.q: Where did she come from?
faq.a: She was born around 1869 in Olgossa, a village in Darfur in the west of present-day Sudan, one of the Daju people; she never knew her exact birth date. Her father was brother to the village chief, and she grew up among three brothers and three sisters, remembering later that she lived a very happy and carefree life without knowing what suffering was.

faq.q: How did she become a slave, and where does the name Bakhita come from?
faq.a: Around 1877, when she was perhaps eight or nine, slave raiders who had already taken her eldest sister kidnapped her and marched her toward El Obeid. The Canossian account says the terror made her forget her own name, and she kept the one her captors gave her: Bakhita, Arabic for "fortunate." She was sold five times in the slave markets of Sudan.

faq.q: What did she suffer in slavery?
faq.a: She was beaten so badly by one owner's son that she lay for more than a month unable to rise, and in the house of a Turkish general she was whipped almost daily. She and other slave girls had patterns cut into their skin with a razor and filled with salt so the scars would last; she said she felt she was going to die, especially when the salt was rubbed in. Pope Benedict XVI counted 144 scars on her body.

faq.q: How did she come to Italy?
faq.a: In Khartoum she was bought by the Italian consul Callisto Legnani, in whose house no one used the lash. When the Mahdist siege forced him to flee, she begged to go with him, and they reached Genoa in 1885. There he gave her to the wife of his friend Augusto Michieli, and she became nanny to the Michielis' daughter Mimmina at their villa near Mirano.

faq.q: How did she come to faith in Christ?
faq.a: In late 1888 Signora Michieli left Mimmina and Bakhita with the Canossian Sisters at the Institute of the Catechumens in Venice while she joined her husband in Sudan. There the sisters introduced her, as she put it, to the God she had felt in her heart from childhood without knowing who He was. Learning Venetian, she called God "Paron" — the Master — a good Master who knew and loved her, unlike every master she had known.

faq.q: How did she win her freedom?
faq.a: When Signora Michieli returned to take her back to Africa, Bakhita refused to leave the sisters, and for three days the matter was contested until it reached the authorities. On 29 November 1889 the ruling came that slavery had been outlawed in Sudan before her birth and had never been recognized in Italy, so she had never legally been a slave. On 9 January 1890 she was baptized as Josephine, and afterwards she would kiss the font, saying, "Here, I became a daughter of God!"

faq.q: What was her life as a sister?
faq.a: She made her vows as a Canossian Daughter of Charity on 8 December 1896, praying that God would let her fly south to tell her people of His goodness. From 1902 she lived at the convent in Schio, near Vicenza, working as cook, seamstress, sacristan and doorkeeper, and the townspeople called her Madre Moretta, their black mother. Her memoir, dictated in 1910 and published by Ida Zanolini in 1931, made her known across Italy, and from 1935 to 1939 she travelled telling her story to help prepare sisters for Africa.

faq.q: What did she say about the people who enslaved her?
faq.a: Asked what she would do if she met her kidnappers, she said she would kneel and kiss their hands, because if those things had not happened she would not have become a Christian and a religious. She did not excuse the evil, but she refused to hate: "I pity them," she said, and of her torturers, "Poor things! They did not know the Lord."

faq.q: How did she die, and how is she remembered?
faq.a: In her last years illness confined her to a wheelchair, and when asked how she was she would answer, "As the Master desires." She died at Schio on 8 February 1947, at the end reliving her slavery and begging that the chains be loosened. The Catholic Church canonized her in 2000, and in 2007 Pope Benedict XVI opened his encyclical on hope, Spe Salvi, with her story as a picture of a soul that knows itself definitively loved by God.

fields.name: Soonderbai Powar
fields.bio: Soonderbai Powar (1856–1921) was an Indian Christian evangelist and teacher, Pandita Ramabai’s trusted helper at the Sharada Sadan, a voice in London against the opium trade, and founder of the Zenana Training Home for Bible-women in Poona.
fields.bio_html:
Soonderbai Hannah Powar was born on July 29, 1856, into a family that had already crossed a great divide. Her parents, Ramachandra and Ganderbai Powar, had been high-caste Hindus who became Christians early in their lives, and so their daughter grew up in a home where Christ was named and the Bible was read. An American journal that introduced her in 1892 put the consequence plainly: because of her parents’ faith, Soonderbai “was spared the usual fate of Brahmin girls, early marriage and zenana seclusion.” She received a Christian education, learned to speak English fluently, and grew up free to go where most women of her birth could never go. She spent that freedom, for the rest of her life, on the women who had none.

Her childhood is thinly recorded; she left no memoir, and most of what is known of her comes from the friends who worked beside her. But the shape of her calling is clear. By her early twenties she was at work among the women of Bombay, and by 1892 she had given fifteen years to missionary work in that city. She was received, it was said, into an unusual number of zenanas, the secluded women’s quarters of high-caste homes, where an Indian Christian woman could sit, read, and talk as no foreign missionary easily could. In 1889 the Bombay Guardian reported her in charge of schools of the Methodist mission there, carrying on work begun by the Rev. W. W. Bruere: a school for high-caste girls that she taught herself, and a mixed school of low-caste children. That Christmas she wrote to the paper asking for gifts so that the children of three schools might have presents.

It is through prayer that hearts are reached.

— Soonderbai Powar

A friendship that shaped two lives

In March 1889 Pandita Ramabai opened the Sharada Sadan, her home and school for high-caste Hindu widows, in a house behind the sea-front at Chowpatty in Bombay. Ramabai had become a Christian, but she had promised Hindu families that the school would be neutral in religion, and the widows were free to keep their caste. Soonderbai came to visit. While Ramabai was out of the room, she took the chance to read the Bible to the girls. Ramabai’s little daughter, Manorama, then about eight or nine, won her heart by insisting that she was a Christian and that the Bible was her Shastra.

The friendship between the two women grew until, at Ramabai’s request, Soonderbai gave up her Bombay work and came to live at the Sharada Sadan, by then moved to Poona. The girls called Ramabai “Bai,” and Soonderbai “Akka,” elder sister. Helen Dyer, who visited often over the next seven years, remembered that the pupils followed Ramabai about like bees out of school hours, while Soonderbai’s little room was usually crowded with girls coming and going, sure of a hearing and help with any difficulty. When the bell rang for bed, wherever Bai and Akka were found, the whole household flocked in for a good-night kiss, from the forty-year-old Brahmin cook to the youngest child-widow. Dyer called her, simply, Ramabai’s “right hand.”

A voice for the silent

Soonderbai’s compassion did not stay inside the walls of a school. She saw what opium was doing in Indian homes: husbands enslaved to a drug the British government licensed and drew revenue from, wives and children left hungry. And she knew that the women who suffered most, shut away in the zenanas, had no way to be heard. So she went to be heard for them. She made more than one journey to Britain to speak against the opium trade, the first in 1888–89, with the support of the Bombay Guardian and the women’s anti-opium movement.

Before one of these journeys, she gathered messages from the women themselves. In Poona, Ramabai brought together a large company of Hindu and Christian women. In Lucknow, in October 1891, Muslim women who had lived their whole lives in seclusion came together at a public meeting and, one after another, stood up to charge Soonderbai with their messages to England. On January 12, 1892, she carried those messages to a crowded anti-opium meeting in Exeter Hall, London. Dressed in her own country’s clothes, speaking in forceful English, she put a question to a Christian nation:

There are millions of broken-hearted women spending their days in misery, because their husbands have been poisoned by the agents of the government.

— Soonderbai Powar

She reminded her hearers that they were sending missionaries to preach Christ in India while the same government licensed men to sell the poison, and she closed without softening anything: if Britain could not rule India justly and righteously, the best plan was to give it up. That year she published a pamphlet, An Indian Woman’s Impeachment of the Opium Crime of the British Government, and she was back in England in 1892–93, seated at Frances Willard’s right hand at a great London welcome for the American temperance leader. She was invited on to America for a women’s congress, but she declined. She was sorry she could not go, she wrote to Willard, “but think it better to return to my native country and help our dear Ramabai.”

Blamed on earth

She came home to Poona in the spring of 1893 to find that something had happened while she was away. Ramabai and the girls who were her own family had been meeting for Bible study and prayer from five to six each morning, and the door had been left open to any who wished to come. By the time Soonderbai returned, about half the widows were attending.

In the May holidays Ramabai ordered carriages for a festival picnic and told the girls that she and Akka needed a day alone with God; any who wished could stay and join them. Out of sixty or more, somewhere between twenty-five and thirty stayed. The whole day was given to the Scriptures, prayer, and exhortation. “We had meetings all day at home,” Soonderbai wrote afterwards, “and nineteen girls prayed, seventeen testifying that they believed in Jesus and knew their sins were forgiven.”

The news got out, and a storm broke over the Sharada Sadan. Hindu supporters said Ramabai was making the girls Christians, and many put the blame on the Christian woman who lived with her. Soonderbai bore it with a smile. Dyer recorded her remark:

It is altogether too bad that I should have all the blame on earth, and Ramabai all the reward in heaven.

— Soonderbai Powar

Dyer added that she was plainly glad of what had happened, and not much troubled by the blame.

Famine, plague, and the work of faith

The two friends prayed together about everything. When Ramabai began to wonder how the school might one day support itself, she thought of buying land in the country and planting fruit trees. Taking hold of Christ’s promise that if two agree on earth touching anything they ask, it shall be done, she and Soonderbai prayed together that God would send the money if the plan was his.

Ramabai and Soonderbai began to pray for a farm in 1892. Gifts trickled in, and two years later the money was in hand. A hundred acres of rough land were bought at Khedgaon, about forty miles from Poona. When famine struck and the Poona house could not hold the girls Ramabai rescued, that rocky ground became the site of Mukti, the great home of salvation that grew to shelter about two thousand women and girls.

The famine of 1896–97 tested them to the limit. Ramabai went into the famine districts and sent rescued girls to Poona in parties of ten and twenty, starving, filthy, and many of them sick. The work of receiving and caring for them fell to Soonderbai and the Christian girls of the Sharada Sadan. When plague reached Poona, the magistrate ordered that the number living at the Sharada Sadan must not grow, and Ramabai hired tents and sent the household into open country twenty miles away. Soonderbai went in charge of the girls. In 1898, when Ramabai went to America for most of the year, Soonderbai was left in full charge of the Sharada Sadan, with plague still in the city. Dyer says she told of how the household would gather to pray whenever a girl fell sick with fever, and how, even when five or six were unwell at night, their temperatures were normal when the inspectors came round the next day. It was a hard time, and she carried it. Around the same time a letter of hers, sent to England, reported the baptism of more than two hundred girls, many of them famine orphans. “Is this not good news,” she wrote, “for you and for all God’s children?”

The record of these years also carries things a careful reader should weigh for themselves. Dyer reports that Ramabai, after years of consulting doctors in vain, began to pray for her own healing, that Soonderbai joined her in prayer for half an hour every day, and that within two months Ramabai spoke of being completely healed. Dyer gives it as Ramabai’s testimony, and so it is given here.

A home of her own

Around the turn of the century, when the Sharada Sadan was moved out to Khedgaon, Soonderbai left Ramabai’s work. Dyer says only that she was “led by circumstances” to withdraw, that some friends were grieved, and that it later proved to be of the Lord, because it set her free for a work of her own. In Poona she founded the Zenana Training Home. There she trained the daughters of Indian Christians to be Bible-women, carrying the gospel to women in their homes for other missions, and she took in famine orphans as well. Like Ramabai, she ran it on faith lines, looking to God rather than to any society for daily needs.

In 1905, when revival spread from Mukti across western India, it reached her school too. Two girls began a prayer meeting; within days the whole household of about a hundred and twenty was praying. Soonderbai described the scenes honestly: girls who trembled, laughed, or shook; shy girls who found their tongues; nights of prayer that went on until two or three in the morning; and four girls who said they had seen visions of Jesus. Such things were controversial even among friends of the revival, and she did not hide them. “I do not interfere,” she wrote, “for fear I might hinder God’s work.” She judged the revival by its fruit: the girls loved one another and longed to win others, and the Bible-women began to preach in the open road, “an unusual thing for Indian women to do.” The lesson she drew was a humble one, and she wrote it down:

I have never felt in my life such a power in prayer as I have experienced in these days.

— Soonderbai Powar

She had spent years trying to convince people by speaking well, she said; now her Bible-women prayed more with the women they visited and spoke much less, because they had learned that it is through prayer that hearts are reached. Around 1907 she published Hinduism and Womanhood, a collection of personal histories of Indian women, written for British Christian women, with an account of her call and work by Helen Dyer.

Faithful to the end

Soonderbai Powar died on December 15, 1921, aged sixty-five. That year was a year of grief for the household she had helped to build: Manorama, the little girl who had once told her that the Bible was her Shastra, had died that summer, and Ramabai herself would follow a few months later. Dyer wrote of Soonderbai as Ramabai’s “greatly valued friend and former associate” and noted that many of the Bible-women trained in her Poona home and sent out to other missions had been famine orphans. In 1924 a short biography was published in London under a title that sums her up well: Soonderbai Powar, for 45 Years an Earnest Worker for God in India.

She is less remembered than the friend whose right hand she was, and she would likely not have minded. She was an Indian woman who spoke for silenced women in Exeter Hall, a sister who answered children’s questions in a crowded little room, and a teacher who learned, late and gladly, that the work was God’s and not her own. She took the blame on earth with good humour and left the reward to heaven.

faq.q: Who was Soonderbai Powar?
faq.a: Soonderbai Hannah Powar (1856–1921) was an Indian Christian evangelist and teacher who worked among the secluded women of Bombay and Poona. For years she was Pandita Ramabai's closest helper at the Sharada Sadan, she spoke in London against the British opium trade, and she later founded the Zenana Training Home in Poona to train Indian Bible-women.

faq.a: She saw opium, licensed by the British government for revenue, ruining Indian homes and leaving wives and children hungry. Helen Dyer remembered her as Ramabai's greatly valued friend and noted that many of the Bible-women she trained had been famine orphans. A biography published in 1924 called her an earnest worker for God in India for forty-five years.

fields.name: William J. Seymour
fields.bio: Son of formerly enslaved parents, the one-eyed holiness preacher William J. Seymour (1870–1922) led the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles, where Black and white believers prayed side by side and the Pentecostal movement spread worldwide.
fields.bio_html:
William Joseph Seymour was born on May 2, 1870, in Centerville, Louisiana, in the sugar country of St. Mary Parish. His parents, Simon and Phillis Seymour, had both been born into slavery and freed by the war. He grew up poor, in the hard years when Reconstruction was being torn down and the South was building the walls of segregation around its Black citizens. He was raised a Baptist and had little formal schooling. Those who knew him later spoke of a boy given to dreams and visions, and of a hunger for God that seems to have been with him from the start.

As a young man he went north looking for work. In Indianapolis he waited tables and worked as a railroad porter, and there and in Cincinnati he found the holiness movement. He joined a group called the Evening Light Saints, who preached that God was gathering one holy people out of the divided churches, Black and white alike. He took from them a conviction he never gave up: that the blood of Christ makes believers one. In Cincinnati he caught smallpox. He survived, but it cost him the sight of his left eye. He accepted a call to preach and began to travel.

A student in the hallway

In 1903 he moved to Houston, Texas, partly to look for relatives, and there he became friends with Lucy Farrow, a Black holiness pastor. Through her he heard about Charles Parham, a white Kansas preacher who taught that the baptism in the Holy Spirit was a distinct gift after salvation and sanctification, marked by speaking in other tongues as on the day of Pentecost. When Parham opened a short-term Bible school in Houston in the winter of 1905–06, Farrow urged Seymour to attend.

Texas law and custom kept Black and white students apart, and Parham was a man of his time and place. Seymour was allowed to listen, but not to sit with the others. He took his lessons from the hallway, outside the classroom door. He did not let the humiliation drive him away. He studied the Scriptures Parham opened, became convinced that the teaching was true, and began to seek the experience for himself.

John G.
