Lake, who knew him, remembered Seymour telling him in a Chicago hotel about those years: “Before I met Parham, such a hunger to have more of God was in my heart that I prayed for five hours a day for two and a half years.” In Los Angeles, Seymour said, the hunger only grew, and when the Spirit told him to pray more, he raised his hours of prayer to seven. Lake was writing from memory long afterward, and his figures may not be exact. The picture of a man who gave whole days to prayer fits everything else that is known about him.

Locked out

Early in 1906 a woman from a small holiness mission in Los Angeles met Seymour while visiting Houston, and the congregation invited him to come as its pastor. He arrived on February 22, 1906, and preached in the mission on Santa Fe Street. He preached from Acts 2:4, that the baptism in the Holy Ghost would be accompanied by tongues. Many in the congregation believed they had already received the Spirit when they were sanctified, and they would not accept it. Months later he told the story in his own paper: “one night they locked the door against me.” The leaders of the local holiness association were called in to correct him. Seymour stood his ground, though he did not yet have the experience he was preaching.

He was now a stranger in a strange city with no pulpit and no income. A church member, Edward Lee, took him in, and the little group began to meet for prayer in homes, soon at the house of Richard and Ruth Asberry at 214 North Bonnie Brae Street. Most of those who came were Black working people, many of them domestic servants and washerwomen. Seymour told them plainly that he had not received what he preached. He was seeking it too, and wanted them all to pray with him until every one of them had received it. Every afternoon at three o’clock they met to ask God for the power from on high. Lucy Farrow came from Houston to join them.

They kept on through opposition and very little visible fruit, fasting and praying. On the evening of April 9, 1906, as the mission’s paper later put it, “the fire of God fell in a cottage on Bonnie Brae.” Edward Lee and then others in the crowded house began to speak in tongues and praise God. One of them was Jennie Evans Moore, who later became Seymour’s wife. Three days later Seymour himself received the experience he had sought so long. Crowds packed the street, and he preached to them from the front porch.

312 Azusa Street

The house could not hold the people, and within days the meetings moved to 312 Azusa Street, an old Methodist church building near downtown. Part of it had been turned into a tenement, and the meetings were held in the large room left on the ground floor, which the paper called “unplastered, barn-like.” On April 18, 1906, the same day an earthquake devastated San Francisco, the Los Angeles Times ran a mocking story under the headline “Weird Babel of Tongues.” The ridicule only drew more people. For the next three years meetings ran almost every day, often from morning until long after midnight. Visitors came from across the country and then from around the world, and many of them carried the message home with them, to Chicago and Memphis, and as missionaries to India, China and Africa.

What visitors noticed first was who was in the room. In a city and a country ruled by the color line, Black and white, Mexican and Chinese, rich and poor knelt together at the same altar, and women as well as men testified, prayed for the sick and went out as preachers. The journalist Frank Bartleman, a white holiness evangelist who was there almost from the beginning, wrote years later that at Azusa Street “the ‘color line’ was washed away in the blood.” The mission’s own paper said it simply: “No instrument that God can use is rejected on account of color or dress or lack of education.” It saw in this a sign of the times: “One token of the Lord’s coming is that He is melting all races and nations together.”

Seymour himself stayed in the background. He did not want the movement to depend on him. When people asked who had founded the work, the paper answered that the Lord was its founder, and that “Bro. Seymour is simply a humble pastor of the flock.” William H. Durham of Chicago, who received the baptism at Azusa in 1907, wrote of him in the paper: “He is the meekest man I ever met. He walks and talks with God.”

Bartleman remembered how Seymour led the meetings: “Brother Seymour generally sat behind two empty shoe boxes, one on top of the other. He usually kept his head inside the top one during the meeting, in prayer.” The best-known figure of the revival spent most of its services with his head bowed, waiting on God.

The Apostolic Faith

In September 1906 the mission began to publish a free paper, The Apostolic Faith. There was no money for it. The first issue told how the workers had knelt in the little office upstairs to ask for it.

“We start with not a cent in sight,” the first issue said, “but in the little upper room office above the mission on Azusa Street, we dropped on our knees and asked Him to send the means to publish the paper. In a short time, the money began to be sent in.” The first printing was five thousand copies. By the third issue it was twenty thousand, and within a year tens of thousands of copies were going out by mail across the world, with no subscription charged and no debt incurred.

Seymour wrote much of the paper’s teaching himself, in plain, warm sermons signed “W. J. Seymour.” He wrote about the atonement, sanctification, healing and the Spirit’s power, and he kept turning back to the cross. He warned against counterfeits, against treating the Spirit’s gifts as a show, and against faith that could not reach past the boundaries of human creeds.

Above all, let us honor the blood of Jesus Christ every moment of our lives, and we will be sweet in our souls.

— William J. Seymour

He also wrote practical counsel for the poor and the zealous. He warned new believers not to abandon their families in the name of faith and not to borrow what they could not repay. For those called out to preach with nothing, he gave the advice he had lived by:

Get down and pray. Make your wants known unto God and He will send it in.

— William J. Seymour

Wounds from friends

The trials, when they came, came mostly from friends. In October 1906 Seymour invited Charles Parham, his old teacher, to preach at Azusa Street, and the paper had at first called him the movement’s leader. Parham was disgusted by what he found. He objected to the noise and, above all, to the mixing of Black and white worshippers, and he denounced the meetings from Seymour’s own pulpit. The mission’s leaders asked him to leave, and he never stopped condemning the revival. Two months later the paper admitted that it had been hasty, and that “the Lord should be our leader.”

On May 13, 1908, Seymour married Jennie Evans Moore, one of the first to receive the Spirit on Bonnie Brae Street, who became his partner in the ministry. Some in the mission objected to the marriage. Florence Crawford, a gifted white evangelist who had begun a work in Portland, Oregon, believed the Lord’s return was too near for marrying, and she was not alone. That year Clara Lum, the white secretary who edited The Apostolic Faith, joined Crawford in Portland. She took the paper with her, and with it the national and international mailing list. Seymour lost his voice to the movement he had helped to start, and the loss was never undone.

More trouble followed. In 1911, while Seymour was away preaching, William Durham returned to preach at Azusa with a new teaching on sanctification, and many of the congregation followed him. Seymour came home and locked the doors against him, and much of the crowd left with Durham. Then, after 1913, came the “Oneness” controversy, which swept through the young Pentecostal churches with teaching that rejected the Trinity and baptized in the name of Jesus only. Seymour would not follow it. He held to baptism “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.”

The love that is Pentecost

By 1915 the mission was a small, mostly Black congregation. That year Seymour published The Doctrines and Discipline of the Azusa Street Apostolic Faith Mission, a manual for its life and order. It shows a man who had thought hard about what had happened in those years. The tongues he had once preached as the necessary sign of the Spirit were no longer at the center of his teaching. Instead he wrote that the baptism in the Holy Ghost “means to be flooded with the love of God and power for service, and a love for the truth as it is in God’s word.” The book also records his hurt. Its constitution required that the bishop, vice bishop and trustees of the mission be “people of color.” After years of watching white colleagues leave and take the work with them, he gave the leadership of Azusa Street to the people who had stayed. He still preached that the blood of Jesus makes one family.

He had never lost that conviction. In its last Los Angeles issue, in May 1908, his paper printed a sentence that sums up the revival at its best: “The Pentecostal power, when you sum it all up, is just more of God’s love. If it does not bring more love, it is simply a counterfeit.”

William Seymour died in Los Angeles on September 28, 1922, after heart attacks. He was fifty-two, and he died in Jennie’s arms. He was buried in Evergreen Cemetery in East Los Angeles. Jennie Seymour pastored the mission until her own death in 1936, and soon afterward the old building was torn down. Outside Pentecostal circles, few people at the time noticed his death. Today hundreds of millions of Pentecostal and charismatic Christians around the world trace their story back to the revival he led. He had little schooling, one good eye and few friends among the powerful, and he started a movement that went around the world by spending long hours on his knees.

faq.q: Who was William J. Seymour?
faq.a: William Joseph Seymour (1870–1922) was a Black holiness preacher, the son of formerly enslaved parents, who led the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles from 1906. The revival, where Black and white believers worshipped together, became one of the main sources of the worldwide Pentecostal movement. He pastored the Apostolic Faith Mission on Azusa Street until his death.

faq.q: What was his early life like?
faq.a: He was born on May 2, 1870, in Centerville, Louisiana, to Simon and Phillis Seymour, who had both been enslaved. He grew up poor in the years when segregation was being built across the South and had little formal schooling. As a young man he worked as a waiter and railroad porter in Indianapolis and Cincinnati, where he joined the Evening Light Saints, a holiness group that taught that Christ makes believers one. In Cincinnati smallpox cost him the sight of his left eye.

faq.q: How did he come to Charles Parham's Bible school?
faq.a: In 1903 he moved to Houston, where the Black holiness pastor Lucy Farrow introduced him to Charles Parham's teaching on the baptism in the Holy Spirit with speaking in tongues. When Parham opened a short Bible school in Houston in the winter of 1905–06, segregation kept Seymour from sitting with the white students, so he listened from the hallway. He became convinced the teaching was true and began to seek the experience himself.

faq.q: How did he come to Los Angeles?
faq.a: A small holiness mission on Santa Fe Street invited him to be its pastor, and he arrived on February 22, 1906. When he preached that the baptism in the Spirit would be accompanied by tongues, the congregation rejected the teaching, and he later wrote that one night they locked the door against him. Edward Lee took him in, and he began to lead prayer meetings in homes, soon at 214 North Bonnie Brae Street.

faq.q: What happened at Bonnie Brae Street?
faq.a: The small group, mostly Black working people, met every afternoon at three o'clock to pray for the power from on high, and they fasted as well. Seymour told them openly that he had not yet received what he preached. On April 9, 1906, as the mission's paper later put it, the fire of God fell in the cottage on Bonnie Brae, and three days later Seymour received the experience he had long sought.

faq.q: What was the Azusa Street Mission like?
faq.a: Within days the meetings moved to 312 Azusa Street, an old Methodist church building, and for about three years they ran almost daily. Black and white, Mexican and Chinese, men and women worshipped and prayed together, and Frank Bartleman wrote that there the color line was washed away in the blood. Seymour stayed in the background; Bartleman remembered him sitting behind two stacked shoe boxes with his head inside the top one, in prayer.

faq.q: What was The Apostolic Faith?
faq.a: It was the mission's free paper, first published in September 1906. The workers began with no money and knelt in the upstairs office to ask God for the means, and the money came in. The first printing was five thousand copies, and within a year tens of thousands were going out around the world. Seymour wrote many of its sermons, urging readers above all to honor the blood of Jesus Christ every moment of their lives.

faq.q: What trials did he face?
faq.a: His old teacher Charles Parham visited in October 1906 and denounced the revival, especially the mixing of races. After Seymour married Jennie Evans Moore on May 13, 1908, Clara Lum, who edited the paper, joined Florence Crawford in Portland and took the paper and its mailing list with her, cutting Seymour off from most of his readers. In 1911 William Durham drew away much of the congregation, and Seymour locked the doors against him.

faq.q: What did he teach in his later years?
faq.a: In 1915 he published The Doctrines and Discipline of the Azusa Street Apostolic Faith Mission. In it he described the baptism in the Holy Ghost as being flooded with the love of God and power for service, and he did not make tongues the center of it. He held to baptism in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost against the Oneness teaching. Wounded by the departures of white colleagues, he required the mission's bishop, vice bishop and trustees to be people of color.

faq.q: How did he die, and what is his legacy?
faq.a: He died in Los Angeles on September 28, 1922, after heart attacks, at the age of fifty-two, and was buried in Evergreen Cemetery. Jennie Seymour led the mission until her death in 1936. Today hundreds of millions of Pentecostal and charismatic Christians trace their story to the revival he led, and he is remembered as a man of long prayer and a preacher of the love that makes believers one.

fields.name: Sadhu Sundar Singh
fields.bio: Sikh-born Indian evangelist who met Christ in a vision in 1904 and became a barefoot Christian sadhu, preaching across India, into Tibet, and around the world before disappearing on a final Himalayan journey in 1929.
fields.bio_html:
Sundar Singh was born on September 3, 1889, at Rampur, in the Sikh state of Patiala in the Punjab, the youngest son of a wealthy and well-connected family. He grew up in comfort, and all his life he would contrast that soft, uneasy luxury with the hard and happy road of a wandering preacher. His parents were Sikhs, but their home was open to the teachers of Hinduism as well, and the boy was steeped in both. By seven, his biographers were told, he knew most of the Bhagavad Gita by heart. He would say later that he had not been a Sikh but a seeker.

The great influence of his childhood was his mother. She took him to holy men and temples, held before him the ideal of the sadhu — the renouncer who leaves the world to seek God — and told him that one day he must seek the Peace that alone satisfies. Years afterwards, when a minister suggested he might take a course at a theological college, he answered that he had already been to the best one in the world: his mother’s lap. She died when he was fourteen, and her death left him desolate. He went on seeking — through scripture, through ritual, through a sadhu’s instruction in yoga — and found nothing that would quiet his heart.

A Bible in the fire

At the Presbyterian mission school in his village he first met the New Testament, and he hated it. It seemed to him an insult to the faith of his fathers and to the pride of his Sikh blood. He threw stones at Christian preachers and urged others to do the same. Then, in his own words, came the act he would confess for the rest of his life: “In the presence of my father I cut up the Bible and other Christian books and put kerosene oil upon them and burnt them.” He was faithful to every ceremony of his religion, and still he had no peace — so little that he resolved to die.

Three days after burning the Bible, in December 1904, the fifteen-year-old rose at three in the morning, bathed in cold water, and prayed: “O God, if there is a God, wilt thou show me the right way or I will kill myself.” If no answer came, he meant to lay his head on the railway line when the five o’clock train passed. He prayed, and prayed, and prayed half an hour longer.

At half past four, as he told it, the room filled with a great light, and in the light he saw the form of Jesus Christ — “It had such an appearance of glory and love” — and heard a voice in Hindustani: “How long will you persecute me? I have come to save you; you were praying to know the right way. Why do you not take it?” It was the very One he had been insulting. “The thought then came to me, ‘Jesus Christ is not dead but living and it must be He Himself.’ So I fell at His feet and got this wonderful Peace which I could not get anywhere else.”

The vision passed, but he said the peace never did. He went straight to his father and told him he was a Christian. His father told him to go back to bed — only the day before yesterday he had burned the Bible. “Well,” the boy answered, “I have discovered now that Jesus Christ is alive and have determined to be His follower. To-day I am His disciple and I am going to serve Him.”

Driven out, and the first night in heaven

His family tried everything to turn him back: promises of wealth and position, reminders of the shame he would bring on the family name, an appeal from a friendly Raja to his pride of race, and months of humiliation. When none of it moved him he was disowned and sent away — and, as his early biographers recorded it, with food in which poison had been mixed, since it was better he should die than disgrace them. His first night as an outcast was spent in the cold under a tree.

I remember that night as my first night in heaven.

— Sadhu Sundar Singh

“In the midst of luxuries and comfort I could not find peace in my heart,” he said of it. “The presence of the Saviour changed the suffering into peace.” On his sixteenth birthday, September 3, 1905, he was baptized in the Church of England at Simla.

A Christian sadhu

As a young Christian he made the choice that shaped everything after. He put on the saffron robe of a Hindu holy man and took to the roads as a sadhu — but a sadhu of Jesus Christ. He owned a robe, a blanket, and a New Testament. He took no money, ate what was offered, and slept in caves, under trees, or in the houses of anyone who would have him. The robe opened doors closed to a foreign missionary; it also meant that reverence could turn quickly into fury when a village learned whom this holy man preached. He walked through the Punjab, Kashmir, Baluchistan, and Afghanistan, and made a base at Kotgarh, a Himalayan village some fifty miles from Simla.

There he worked for a time alongside Samuel Stokes, a young American who had given away his fortune to live as a friar in India; together they nursed lepers at Sabathu and served in a plague camp near Lahore. Stokes, tending him through a bout of fever, heard him murmur under his breath, “How sweet it is to suffer for His sake.” He studied at St. John’s Divinity College in Lahore and was licensed to preach, but handed the licence back to Bishop Lefroy rather than be ordained, so that he could preach freely among Christians of every name. Sundar never founded an order, never baptized his own converts — he sent them to the local churches — and refused to be anyone’s guru. “How can I make you my disciple,” he once told a would-be follower, “when I myself am only a disciple?”

The record of those years is full of rough handling. One witness, a member of the Arya Samaj, wrote to a Christian weekly describing how he watched a young sadhu sit down on a log in a hill village, wipe his face, and begin to sing of Christ, until a man struck him to the ground. Sundar bound up his bleeding hand with his turban and went on singing, praying for those who had hit him. The man who struck him later asked to be baptized, and was.

Tibet, and stories that were questioned

From 1908 the closed land of Tibet became his chosen field. Few had carried the gospel there, and the cold and danger drew him rather than deterred him. For years he spent the warmer months trying to cross the frontier and the winters preaching in India.

In his twenty-third year, against the advice of friends, he attempted a fast of forty days in the jungle between Hardwar and Dehra Dun, counting the days with a heap of stones until he grew too weak to throw them aside. Woodcutters found him and carried him out in his blanket. He said afterwards that the fast had settled a doubt: as his body failed, his peace grew stronger, and he concluded it was a peace given from heaven and not welling up from himself. He admitted, too, that he was prone to irritation when tired and pressed with questions — “when you write your book you ought to write about my weaknesses also.”

From these years come the stories that made him famous — and that were most disputed. He told of being arrested at a town called Rasar, thrown into a dry well among the bones of earlier victims, and drawn out on the third night by a rope from an unseen deliverer, the lid locked again behind him; the head lama, he said, found the key still on his own girdle. He spoke of a vast secret brotherhood of Christian sannyasis, and of an ancient hermit, the “Maharishi of Kailash,” living in a cave high in the Himalayas. These are what Sundar recounted; no one else witnessed them. In the 1920s the Jesuit scholar H. Hosten and the Swiss pastor Oskar Pfister published sustained attacks arguing that such stories could not be verified or were untrue, and some charged him with imposture. Others, including the German scholar Friedrich Heiler, made inquiries in India and defended his sincerity. The question has never been settled, and readers can hold these accounts with reserve. What is clear is how Sundar himself weighted them: “People have made too much of this incident in my life,” he said of the hermit. “My work is, not to preach the Rishi, but to preach Christ.” Heiler recorded that he bore the attacks calmly and spoke of his opponents only with love.

To the ends of the earth

In 1918 a visit to Madras turned an obscure itinerant into a figure known across the world. Thousands came to hear him in South India and Ceylon, then in Burma, Malaya, China, and Japan. In 1920 he sailed for England and went on to the United States and Australia; in 1922 he travelled through Switzerland, Germany, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, and Holland. He spoke in Luther’s church at Wittenberg and in Uppsala Cathedral, with Archbishop Söderblom as his interpreter. His father, once his fiercest opponent, had by now become a Christian himself and helped pay his passage. When the father asked his son to baptize him, Sundar sent him to the ordinary ministers of the church: his work, he said, was not to baptize but to preach the gospel.

Christ alone is salvation. He who lives in Him becomes dead to sin and enters into eternal life.

— Sadhu Sundar Singh, at Basle, 1922

In Ceylon a mother begged him to lay hands on her dying son. “There is no power in these hands,” he told her, “only in the pierced hands of Christ.” At last he went to the hospital, prayed, and laid his hand on the boy’s head; three days later he saw the boy sitting with his mother at one of his meetings. But when people insisted on treating him as a wonder-worker, he gave up praying for the sick in that way, lest they look to him and not to Christ.

Fame frightened him more than persecution had. Crowds called him a saint; a former Russian empress asked his blessing, and he refused, saying his hands had torn up the Holy Scriptures. He liked to say that when Jesus rode into Jerusalem it was the donkey that walked on the garments, and it would have been foolish for the donkey to think the honour was for him. The West also disappointed him: he found many in Christian lands living as though Christ were absent, and said so — without laying the blame on Christ.

At the Master’s feet

In the 1920s, between his journeys, he wrote a series of small books in Urdu, quickly translated into English: At the Master’s Feet, Reality and Religion, The Search After Reality, Meditations on Various Aspects of the Spiritual Life, and finally With and Without Christ, signed at Sabathu in August 1928. Full of parables from the hills and rivers he knew, they return again and again to prayer, the cross, and the living presence of Christ. In At the Master’s Feet, written as a conversation between a disciple and his Lord, he insists that prayer “is not a form of begging” but “an effort to lay hold of God Himself.” (A further book, Visions of the Spiritual World, describes ecstatic visions of the life beyond, including conversations with the departed; even admirers have read it with caution, and it is not where his testimony is strongest.)

Christianity is Christ Himself.

— Sadhu Sundar Singh, The Search After Reality

He had long said he expected to die in Tibet, and that he would welcome it. “Do not then think ‘He is dead,’” he told a Swiss audience, “but say: ‘He has entered Heaven and Eternal Life; he is with Christ in the perfect life.’” In April 1929, against the advice of his friends, he set out once more for Tibet. He was last seen at Kalka, below Simla. He never returned, no trace of him was ever found, and after a time the government presumed him dead.

Perhaps that is fitting for a man who would not let anyone build on him. He wanted no order, no disciples of his own, no reputation for wonders. He wanted only to point past himself to the One who had met a desperate boy at dawn and given him a peace that never left — the peace he had found, as he put it, under a tree on the first night in heaven.

faq.q: Who was Sadhu Sundar Singh?
faq.a: Sundar Singh was a Sikh-born Indian who met Christ in a vision as a teenager in 1904 and spent the rest of his life as a barefoot Christian sadhu, a holy man in a saffron robe who owned nothing and preached Jesus across India, into Tibet, and around the world. He wrote several small devotional books and disappeared on a final journey toward Tibet in 1929.

faq.q: What was his childhood like?
faq.a: He was born on September 3, 1889, at Rampur in the Sikh state of Patiala, the youngest son of a wealthy family. His devout mother took him to holy men and temples and held before him the ideal of the sadhu who renounces the world to seek God. She died when he was fourteen, and he searched the scriptures of several religions without finding peace.

faq.q: Why did he burn a Bible?
faq.a: At the mission school in his village he met the New Testament and hated it as an insult to the faith of his fathers. He threw stones at Christian preachers, and in his father's presence he cut up a Bible and other Christian books, poured kerosene on them, and burned them. He confessed that act for the rest of his life.

faq.q: How was he converted?
faq.a: Three days later, in December 1904, he rose before dawn and prayed that if there was a God, He would show him the right way, or he would kill himself on the railway line. As he told it, the room filled with light and he saw Jesus Christ, who asked, "How long will you persecute me?" He fell at Christ's feet and received a peace he said never left him.

faq.q: What happened when he told his family?
faq.a: His family tried promises, shame, and months of humiliation to turn him back, and finally disowned him; his early biographers record that he was sent away with poisoned food. He spent his first night as an outcast under a tree in the cold, and remembered it as his first night in heaven. He was baptized at Simla on his sixteenth birthday, September 3, 1905.

faq.q: Why did he become a Christian sadhu?
faq.a: He put on the saffron robe of a Hindu holy man so that he could present Christ in a form India recognised, owning only a robe, a blanket, and a New Testament. He took no money, slept in caves or under trees, nursed lepers and plague victims, and refused ordination so he could preach among Christians of every church. He never baptized his own converts or let anyone make him their guru.

faq.q: What about his journeys into Tibet?
faq.a: From 1908 he spent much of each year trying to preach in Tibet. He told of being thrown into a dry well at Rasar and rescued on the third night, and of meeting an ancient hermit called the Maharishi of Kailash. No one else witnessed these events, and in the 1920s writers such as Father Hosten and Oskar Pfister disputed them, while others like Friedrich Heiler defended his sincerity. Sundar himself said his work was not to preach the hermit but to preach Christ.

faq.q: How did he become known around the world?
faq.a: A visit to Madras in 1918 made him famous, and he went on to preach in Ceylon, Burma, Malaya, China, and Japan. In 1920 he travelled to England, the United States, and Australia, and in 1922 across Europe, speaking in Luther's church at Wittenberg and at Uppsala. His father, once his fiercest opponent, had become a Christian and helped pay his passage.

faq.q: How did he handle fame?
faq.a: He feared fame more than persecution. When asked to bless people or heal them, he said there was no power in his hands, only in the pierced hands of Christ, and he stopped praying over the sick when people began treating him as a wonder-worker. He compared himself to the donkey that carried Jesus into Jerusalem: the honour on the road was never meant for the donkey.

faq.q: What did he write, and how did his life end?
faq.a: In the 1920s he wrote small books in Urdu, including At the Master's Feet, Reality and Religion, The Search After Reality, and With and Without Christ, all centred on prayer, the cross, and the living Christ. In April 1929, against his friends' advice, he set out again for Tibet and was last seen at Kalka, below Simla. He was never found, and the government eventually presumed him dead.

fields.name: Phillis Wheatley
fields.bio: African-born poet of Boston (c. 1753–1784), kidnapped as a child and enslaved, who became the first African American to publish a book of poems (1773) and wrote of the "Impartial Saviour" and the God-given love of freedom.
fields.bio_html:
No one knows the name her mother gave her. She was born somewhere on the coast of West Africa around 1753, taken from her home as a small child, and carried across the Atlantic on a slave ship called the Phillis. In the summer of 1761 she was put up for sale in Boston, a thin, sick girl wrapped, as the family’s memoir later remembered it, in nothing but a scrap of dirty carpet. Susannah Wheatley, the wife of a prosperous Boston tailor and merchant, chose her over sturdier girls because of her “humble and modest demeanor,” and took her home in the family chaise. They guessed her age at about seven because she was shedding her front teeth. They named her after the ship.

Of Africa she kept only one memory, which she passed on to the family: that every morning her mother poured out water before the rising sun. It is worth holding that loss in mind, because the young woman who grew from that child would write with real gratitude of the faith she found in America — and would also write, in the same breath, of what it had cost her parents to lose her.

A child who learned to read the Scriptures

The Wheatleys soon saw that the girl was extraordinary. She was found trying to form letters on the wall with chalk or charcoal, and the Wheatleys’ eighteen-year-old daughter Mary began to teach her. John Wheatley later wrote that within sixteen months of her arrival, without any schooling, she had learned English — a language “to which she was an utter Stranger before” — well enough to read “the most difficult parts of the Sacred Writings, to the great Astonishment of all who heard her.” She went on to Latin, to Pope’s Homer and to Milton, to geography and ancient history; but the book that shaped her most was the Bible. By 1765, when she was perhaps twelve, she had written a letter to Samson Occom, the Mohegan preacher then raising money in England — the beginning of a friendship between two people of colour who both preached Christ to a world that doubted them.

She remained enslaved. The Wheatleys kept her close, spared her most heavy work, and gave her a light and writing things by her bed so she could set down lines that came to her in the night. Yet her place was always uncertain: invited into the houses of Boston’s great families, she would ask to eat at a side table rather than presume a seat among the guests.

In August 1771 she was received into the church that met at Boston’s Old South Meeting House, entered in its register simply as “Phillis, Servant to Mr. Wheatley.” Her letters from these years, written to her friend Obour Tanner, an enslaved African woman in Newport, show a heart that had taken the gospel deeply to itself. When Obour wrote of her own conversion, Phillis rejoiced with her over “the saving change,” and agreed that “there was nothing in us to recommend us to God.”

Inexpressibly happy should we be could we have a due sense of the beauties and excellence of the crucified Saviour.

— Phillis Wheatley, to Obour Tanner, 1772

She was glad, she told Obour, “to hear of so many of my nation, seeking with eagerness the way to true felicity,” and she prayed that they would all “meet at length in that happy mansion.”

The elegy for Whitefield

The poem that made her name was a funeral elegy. On 30 September 1770 George Whitefield, the great preacher of the awakening, died at Newburyport, north of Boston. Within weeks a broadside appeared, printed under the name of “Phillis, a servant girl, of 17 years of age,” who had “been but 9 years in this country from Africa.” It was reprinted across the colonies and in London. In it she remembered Whitefield’s “incessant cries” of prayer, and she put into his mouth an invitation that no one else in print was making:

“Take him, ye Africans, he longs for you, / Impartial Saviour is his title due.”

The Christ she knew was impartial — offered on the same terms to Africans as to anyone. That conviction runs through her best-known poem, “On being brought from Africa to America,” eight lines that have been read both as gratitude and as rebuke. It begins, “’Twas mercy brought me from my Pagan land,” and it ends by turning on the very Christians who looked down on her: “Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain, / May be refin’d, and join th’ angelic train.” Modern readers sometimes wince at the opening line. But it is the testimony of a believer who counted her knowledge of the Saviour a mercy — and it was written by a woman who, as her later letters show, never mistook that mercy for a defence of slavery.

Poems on Various Subjects

Boston printers would not risk a book of verse by an enslaved African girl. Many simply did not believe she had written it. So in the autumn of 1772 the Wheatleys gathered an attestation signed by eighteen of the most prominent men in Massachusetts — the governor Thomas Hutchinson, the lieutenant-governor, John Hancock, John Wheatley himself, and ministers including Charles Chauncy, Mather Byles and Samuel Cooper — assuring the world that the poems had been “written by Phillis,” a young woman “under the Disadvantage of serving as a Slave.” Even with that, the book found its publisher in London, with the support of Selina, Countess of Huntingdon, Whitefield’s patron, to whom it was dedicated.

In May 1773, in poor health, Phillis sailed for England with the Wheatleys’ son Nathaniel. For a few crowded weeks she was received in London society: the abolitionist Granville Sharp took her to see the Tower, and she met, among others, the Earl of Dartmouth and Benjamin Franklin. To Dartmouth she had already addressed a poem that explained where her love of liberty came from. She had been, she wrote, “snatch’d from Afric’s fancy’d happy seat,” and she asked what “pangs excruciating” must have torn at her parents, and how “steel’d” the soul that “from a father seiz’d his babe belov’d.” Then word came that Susannah Wheatley was gravely ill, and Phillis sailed home before her book came off the press in September 1773, with an engraved portrait of her at her writing desk as its frontispiece. Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral was the first book of poems published by an African American.

The year before the voyage, sick through the winter and spring and sent to the country for better air, she asked Obour Tanner to pray for her: “Let me be interested in your prayers that God would please to bless to me the means us’d for my recovery, if agreeable to his holy will. While my outward man languishes under weakness and pain, may the inward be refresh’d and strengthen’d more abundantly by him who declar’d from heaven that his strength was made perfect in weakness!”

Back in Boston in the autumn of 1773, she wrote to Obour that the voyage had “conduced to the recovery (in a great measure) of my health,” and that the kindness she had met in England filled her “with astonishment” — which, she hoped, would have “the happy effect of lessening me in my own esteem.” “The God of the seas and dry land, has graciously brought me home in safety,” she wrote. “Join with me in thanks to him for so great a mercy.”

In the same letter she pressed on her friend the thing that mattered most:

Dear Obour, let us not sell our birthright for a thousand worlds, which indeed would be as dust upon the balance.

— Phillis Wheatley, 1773

Free, and speaking of freedom

That October she told a friend that “since my return to America my Master, has at the desire of my friends in England given me my freedom.” Freedom did not make her comfortable — she lived largely on the sale of her books, and asked Obour to find subscribers “as it is for my benefit” — but it let her speak more plainly than before.

In February 1774 she answered a letter from Samson Occom, who had written in defence of the natural rights of Black Americans. Her reply, printed in the Connecticut Gazette that March, is her clearest word on slavery, and it is a Christian argument from first to last. She believed, she wrote, that “the divine Light is chasing away the thick Darkness which broods over the Land of Africa,” and that civil and religious liberty were so bound together “that there is little or no Enjoyment of one Without the other.” The Israelites in Egypt had longed for freedom; so did her people.

In every human Breast, God has implanted a Principle, which we call Love of Freedom; it is impatient of Oppression, and pants for Deliverance.

— Phillis Wheatley, to Samson Occom, 1774

“By the Leave of our modern Egyptians,” she went on, “I will assert, that the same Principle lives in us.” She prayed, “God grant Deliverance in his own Way and Time,” and added that she wished this “not for their Hurt,” but to show the slaveholders “the strange Absurdity of their Conduct” — men who cried for liberty while exercising “oppressive Power over others.” It did not, she remarked drily, “require the Penetration of a Philosopher to determine” how badly the two agreed.

When war came, she wrote a poem to the new commander of the Continental Army and sent it with a letter in October 1775. George Washington answered from Cambridge in February 1776, praising “your great poetical Talents” and writing, “If you should ever come to Cambridge, or near Head Quarters, I shall be happy to see a person so favourd by the Muses.”

A seemingly frowning Providence

Then the losses began. Susannah Wheatley died in March 1774. “I was a poor little outcast & a stranger when she took me in,” Phillis wrote to Obour; “I was treated by her more like her child than her servant.” She had watched her mistress die in what she called “earnest longings, & impatient thirstings for the upper courts of the Lord.”

In her grief she asked her friend to carry the household to God: “Do, my dear friend, remember me & this family in your closet, that this afflicting dispensation may be sanctify’d to us.” A few weeks later she wrote that she hoped “to be resigned to the afflicting hand of a seemingly frowning Providence,” and praised God that “while he strikes one comfort dead he raises up another. But O that I could dwell on & delight in him alone above every other object!”

John Wheatley died in March 1778; Mary, her first teacher, died that September; Nathaniel, in England, died in 1783. In April 1778 Phillis married John Peters, a free Black man of Boston. The family memoir of 1834, drawn from relatives of the Wheatleys, paints him harshly as proud and improvident, and says he failed in business and once went to jail for debt; later historians think that portrait may be unfair, and the truth of the marriage is hard to recover. What is certain is that the war years were desperately poor ones, and that Phillis bore three children, of whom two died young.

She kept writing. In 1779, as Phillis Peters, she advertised proposals for a second volume of poems and letters, to be dedicated to Benjamin Franklin. Too few subscribers came forward in a ruined wartime economy, and the book never appeared; most of its manuscripts are lost. In 1784 she published a poem, Liberty and Peace, celebrating the end of the war. To Obour, in a short note of 1778, she had written that the upheavals of those years should “convince us of the uncertain duration of all things temporal,” and stir “an ardent desire of, & preparation for” a state “more suitable to the immortal mind.”

Remembered at the last

Phillis Peters died in Boston on Sunday, 5 December 1784, about thirty-one years old, and her last infant died with her. The Independent Chronicle noted that she was “known to the literary world by her celebrated miscellaneous poems.” She was buried, with her child, in an unmarked grave.

She had not been forgotten for long. Abolitionists reprinted her poems as proof of what they had always claimed, and every generation since has returned to her. But for a Christian reader she is more than a literary first. She is a young African woman who, stolen from her mother and sold as property, found Christ in the land of her captivity, called him the “Impartial Saviour,” and told the slaveholders of a revolutionary age, in the language of Exodus, that God had planted the love of freedom in every human heart. Her own counsel to Obour is a fair summary of how she tried to live: that “by the assistance of divine grace,” they would “live the life,” and so “die the death of the Righteous.”

faq.q: Who was Phillis Wheatley?
faq.a: Phillis Wheatley (c. 1753–1784) was an African-born Christian poet in Boston and the first African American to publish a book of poems, Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (London, 1773). Kidnapped as a child and enslaved by the Wheatley family, she became a church member, was freed in 1773, and wrote of Christ as the "Impartial Saviour" and of the love of freedom God implants in every heart.

faq.q: What was her early life like?
faq.a: She was born in West Africa around 1753 and carried to Boston on a slave ship called the Phillis, where she was sold in 1761 to Susannah Wheatley at about the age of seven. The only memory of Africa she kept was of her mother pouring out water before the rising sun each morning. The family named her after the ship.

faq.q: How did she learn to read and write?
faq.a: The Wheatleys' daughter Mary taught her, and John Wheatley wrote that within sixteen months she could read the most difficult parts of the Bible. She went on to Latin, classical literature and history, and by about 1765 she had written a letter to the Mohegan preacher Samson Occom.

faq.q: What was her faith like?
faq.a: In August 1771 she was received into the church at Boston's Old South Meeting House. Her letters to her friend Obour Tanner, an enslaved woman in Newport, speak of the saving change of conversion, of having nothing in herself to recommend her to God, and of longing for a due sense of the beauty of the crucified Saviour.

faq.q: Why was her elegy on George Whitefield important?
faq.a: When the evangelist George Whitefield died in September 1770, she published an elegy as a 17-year-old servant girl, and it was reprinted across the colonies and in London. In it she pictured Whitefield inviting Africans to Christ as their "Impartial Saviour," and the poem made her name known.

faq.q: How was her book published?
faq.a: Boston printers doubted that an enslaved girl could have written the poems, so in 1772 eighteen leading Bostonians, including the governor and John Hancock, signed an attestation that she was the author. The book was published in London in 1773 with the support of the Countess of Huntingdon, to whom it was dedicated, and carried an engraved portrait of her as its frontispiece.

faq.q: What happened on her trip to England?
faq.a: She sailed to London in May 1773 for her health and was received by figures such as Granville Sharp, the Earl of Dartmouth and Benjamin Franklin. She returned to Boston before the book appeared because her mistress was gravely ill, and she thanked God for bringing her home safely and largely restoring her health.

faq.q: What did she write about slavery and freedom?
faq.a: Soon after her return she was freed. In a 1774 letter to Samson Occom, printed in the Connecticut Gazette, she wrote that God had implanted in every human breast a love of freedom that is impatient of oppression, compared enslaved Africans to Israel in Egypt, and prayed that God would grant deliverance in his own way and time.

faq.q: What trials did she face in her later years?
faq.a: Susannah Wheatley died in 1774, and John and Mary Wheatley in 1778. That year she married John Peters, a free Black man, and the war years brought deep poverty; two of her three children died young, and her 1779 proposal for a second volume failed to find subscribers. In her letters she spoke of resigning herself to a seemingly frowning Providence and longing to delight in God alone.

faq.q: How did her life end?
faq.a: She died in Boston on 5 December 1784, about thirty-one years old, and her last infant died with her; they were buried in an unmarked grave. Abolitionists later reprinted her poems, and she is remembered as a believer who found Christ in the land of her captivity and spoke boldly for the freedom of her people.

fields.name: Old Elizabeth
fields.bio: Born enslaved in Maryland about 1766, Old Elizabeth was freed around age thirty and preached for decades without a licence, facing church elders and slave-state magistrates alike. She died in Philadelphia in 1866.
fields.bio_html:
Almost everything we know about the woman remembered as Old Elizabeth comes from sixteen small pages. In her ninety-seventh year, living in Philadelphia, she told her story to friends who wrote it down “mainly from her own lips,” keeping her plain language as closely as they could, and in 1863 it was printed as Memoir of Old Elizabeth, a Coloured Woman. No other name for her survives, no portrait was ever made, and no letter or sermon in her own hand is known. What remains is a voice — direct, unafraid, and soaked in Scripture — telling how a girl born into slavery became a preacher of the gospel for some forty-five years.

She was born in Maryland, by her own account in 1766. Her parents were enslaved, and both belonged to the Methodist Society. Every Sabbath morning her father read the Bible aloud to his children, and even at five, she said, she felt “the overshadowing of the Lord’s Spirit” without understanding what it meant.

Nobody but God

When she was eleven, her master sent her to another farm several miles from her family. So lonely she thought she would die, she went without leave, walked twenty miles to find her mother, and stayed several days. Then she was sent back. At parting her mother told her that she had “nobody in the wide world to look to but God.” The child walked back repeating the words. The overseer tied her with a rope and whipped her, and she carried the marks for weeks.

Left alone with her mother’s words, the eleven-year-old turned to God: “I betook myself to prayer, and in every lonely place I found an altar.” She prayed in the corners of the fields and under the fences, mourning, she said, “like a dove.”

For about six months she wept and could hardly eat, though she was still made to do all her work. One evening, so weak she expected to die, she cried out that she was a sinner, unfit for God’s presence, yet longing for His pardon. What followed she described as a vision seen “with my spiritual eye,” and it is told here as her own testimony. Brought to the edge of a fiery gulf, she prayed the Lord’s Prayer, the only prayer she knew, and then a shorter one: “Lord have mercy on me — Christ save me.” She was shown that her hope hung by no more than a hair, yet told to pray on, for it would be sufficient. Every cry lifted her higher, until she saw the Saviour with His hand stretched out to receive her and heard Him say, “peace, peace, come unto me.”

She felt her sins forgiven and fell at His feet crying, “Thou hast redeemed me.” Asked whether she was willing to be saved in the Lord’s own way, she answered, “Yes Lord, in thy own way.” Then she was shown the world lying in wickedness and told she must go and call people to repentance. The message lay on her like a heavy yoke, until a voice promised that though some would laugh and scoff, “while thou doest my will, I will be with thee to the ends of the earth.” She was not yet thirteen. The next day she felt “like a new creature in Christ.”

Freedom and a long silence

There was no preaching where she lived, so she worshipped alone behind the haystacks. Later she was sold to a stranger, and then for a term of years to a Presbyterian who did not think it right to hold anyone enslaved for life. She served out the term, and he gave her her freedom in about her thirtieth year — the mid-1790s.

Free, and able to attend religious meetings, she sometimes felt moved to speak but shrank back, “so great was the cross to my nature.” At forty-two the old message pressed on her again. She could read only a little, and every religious leader she consulted told her there was nothing in Scripture for such a calling. It was hard enough for men to travel, they said — “and what would women do?” She turned back to the Lord, “feeling that I was nothing, and knew nothing,” and asked Him to make His will plain. A light seemed to fall on her that banished her fears, and she resolved to go on “to prison and to death” if that should be her portion.

“A good racket”

Her first meeting was in a poor widow’s house on one of the worst streets in Baltimore, among a few Black sisters. A watchman walked in and said he had been sent to break it up, because the neighbours could not sleep for the racket. The other women fled. Elizabeth answered him: “a good racket is better than a bad racket.” Why, she asked, were people left alone when they danced and fiddled till midnight, but stopped when they praised God?

The man who came to silence her went away blessing her. As Elizabeth spoke, she said, the watchman “turned pale and trembled,” begged her pardon, promised never again to disturb a religious meeting, and wished them success.

Opposition from inside the church was harder to bear. The elders forbade the meetings and said “that woman” must be quieted. Ministers looked on her, she said, “as a speckled bird”; some called her an enthusiast, others said the Methodist Discipline allowed no such work. Hunted from place to place, in one dark season she was even tempted to throw herself into the dock, until the Lord lifted the gloom “in his own time.” An aged sister opened her house for a meeting at the risk of being put out of the church, and there “a victory was gained over the power of darkness.” The meetings went on for years, she said, to the conversion of many.

If the Lord had ordained me, I needed nothing better.

— Old Elizabeth

That was her answer in Virginia, a slave state, where people would not believe a Black woman could preach and tried to imprison her because she spoke against slavery. Asked whether she had been ordained, she said she preached “not by the commission of men’s hands.” In Maryland a crowd came to take her before the squire after a sermon on “Woe to the rebellious city,” and she said the Lord delivered her. She held meetings in remote places with no meeting-house and travelled to settlements of Black people in Canada.

Among Friends

On her journeys she stayed with many Quakers and received from them “much kindness and sympathy, and no opposition.” Once, finding a Friends’ meeting-house open, she sat in silence with a Friend and his little daughter — a meeting of three — and felt the presence of God as much as anywhere in her life. From there she went to Michigan, where she worked four years and founded a school for Black orphans. It was Philadelphia Friends who later printed her story, but the memoir never says she left the Methodists or joined them. In her eighty-seventh year, ill and released from further travel, she came to Philadelphia, where she lived the rest of her life.

When I went forth, it was without purse or scrip.

— Old Elizabeth

Shackles broken

A later edition, published by the Tract Association of Friends in 1889, adds an account of her death. Its writers did not make her a plaster saint: they admit that early in her illness her “inflexibility” and irritable temper sometimes showed, and that her plain speaking against hollow religion gave offence — mostly, she said, among “high professors” of her own people. Her last months were spent in great pain from gangrene in one leg. She called out to those around her, “Oh come, come to Jesus, I have always found Him the never failing Friend.”

In the worst of her pain she prayed: “Oh, thou God of love, have mercy upon thy poor old hand-maiden; hide not thy face from thy servant, and if it be thy holy will, suffer this cup to pass from me; Jesus before me asked this.”

Two hours before the end, her mind quite clear, she said that she longed to see her Saviour’s face, and then: “My shackles are broken.” She asked to be left quiet for two hours, and at the end of that time her breathing gently stopped. It was 11 June 1866, half a year after the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery in the United States; her friends reckoned her nearly a hundred and one.

The record is thin, and it is right to leave it thin. She preached long before Jarena Lee and Zilpha Elaw published their own accounts of the same battle for a woman’s right to preach. She left no books and no portrait — only the testimony of a girl who learned at eleven that she had nobody but God, and found Him faithful for ninety years.

faq.q: Who was Old Elizabeth?
faq.a: Old Elizabeth (c. 1766–1866) was a Black Methodist woman, born enslaved in Maryland, who preached the gospel for some forty-five years in Maryland, Virginia, other states and Canada without any church licence. Her story survives only in a short memoir taken down from her own lips in her ninety-seventh year and printed in Philadelphia in 1863. No other name for her and no portrait are known.

faq.q: What was her early life like?
faq.a: She was born in Maryland, by her own account in 1766, to enslaved parents who both belonged to the Methodist Society. Her father read the Bible aloud to his children every Sabbath morning, and she said that even at five she felt the overshadowing of the Lord's Spirit at those times.

faq.q: What happened when she was eleven?
faq.a: Her master sent her to a farm several miles from her family. She ran off, walked twenty miles to find her mother, and on parting was told she had nobody in the wide world to look to but God. Back at the farm the overseer tied her and whipped her, and from then on she prayed in every lonely place she could find.

faq.q: How did she come to faith?
faq.a: After months of grief, believing she was about to die, she cried out to God as a sinner. She described a vision in which she prayed, "Lord have mercy on me, Christ save me," saw the Saviour reach out to receive her, and felt her sins forgiven. She was not yet thirteen, and she said she believed she was then called to preach repentance.

faq.q: How did she gain her freedom?
faq.a: After being sold more than once, she was sold for a term of years to a Presbyterian who did not think it right to hold people enslaved for life. When she had served the term he set her free, in about her thirtieth year, which would be the mid-1790s.

faq.q: Why did she wait so long to preach?
faq.a: She felt the call strongly but shrank from it, and she could read only a little. When she was about forty-two she asked one religious leader after another for help, and all told her Scripture gave no sanction to such a calling for a woman. She turned back to prayer, and said a light fell on her that banished her fears.

faq.q: What happened at her first meeting?
faq.a: She led a prayer meeting with a few Black women in a poor widow's house in Baltimore, and a watchman came to break it up. She told him a good racket is better than a bad racket, and asked why people were left alone to dance till midnight but stopped for praising God. She said he trembled, begged her pardon and wished them success.

faq.q: What opposition did she face?
faq.a: Methodist elders forbade her meetings because she was a woman, and ministers called her an enthusiast. In Virginia people tried to imprison her for speaking against slavery, and when asked whether she was ordained she answered that if the Lord had ordained her she needed nothing better.

faq.q: What was her connection with the Quakers?
faq.a: On her travels she stayed with many Quaker families and said she received kindness and no opposition from them. Philadelphia Friends later printed her memoir and an account of her death, but the memoir never says she left the Methodists or became a Quaker. She also spent four years in Michigan, where she founded a school for Black orphans.

faq.q: How did her life end?
faq.a: In her eighty-seventh year she settled in Philadelphia. In her last months she suffered terribly from gangrene in one leg, yet urged those around her to come to Jesus, calling Him the never failing Friend. She died on 11 June 1866, shortly after saying, "My shackles are broken."

fields.name: Catherine Ferguson
fields.bio: Born enslaved in New York, Katy Ferguson (c. 1774–1854) gained her freedom, earned her living making cakes, raised forty-eight neglected children, and gathered street children for Sunday catechism teaching in her home.
fields.bio_html:
Catherine Ferguson — “Katy” to everyone who knew her — was born a slave, and she was born on the move. Her mother gave birth to her while being carried from Virginia to New York City, where the two of them belonged to a man known in the records only as “R. B.,” who lived on Water Street and was an elder in one of the city’s Presbyterian churches. Her name then was Katy Williams. The year is uncertain: the man who later wrote down her story gave her age at death once as about seventy-five and once as about eighty, so she was born around 1774 or 1779. Almost everything we know of her comes from that one man, the antislavery merchant Lewis Tappan, who sat with her on 25 March 1850 and took down the facts of her life “from Mrs. Ferguson’s own lips.” The record is thin. But what it holds is luminous.

Given to God

When Katy was still a little girl — about eight, according to Benson Lossing, who retold her story a year after her death — her master sold her mother away. They never saw each other again. Decades later, an old woman, Katy still remembered the last thing her mother did.

Before we were torn asunder, she knelt down, laid her hand on my head, and gave me to God.

— Catherine Ferguson

The grief marked her for life, and it turned into something holy. The memory of her own anguish at that parting, she told Tappan, was what made her feel such compassion for children. Her mistress told her that if she turned out as good as her mother, she would do well. At ten she went to her master with a bargain of her own: if he would give her her liberty, she would serve the Lord for ever. He refused.

She was never taught to read. “My mistress,” she said, “would not let me learn.” Yet she was quick — her mistress once admitted, “You know more now than my daughters,” and one of the sons in the house complained that if he read the Bible wrong or stumbled over his catechism, Katy caught it at once. She was allowed to attend public worship, and what she heard there she kept. Lossing says her retentive memory stored up a great treasury of Scripture, which she gave away for the rest of her life to anyone who would listen.

A trembling girl at the pastor’s door

At about fourteen she came under conviction of sin. She resolved to go and see the minister whose church she attended, Dr. Mason of the Scotch Presbyterian congregation — the elder John Mason, Lossing says. She was frightened: afraid the family would find out, afraid she would not be let in, afraid that a great man would have no time for a little slave girl.

“While I stood at the door ringing the bell,” she remembered, “I can not describe my feelings; and when the door opened, and Dr. Mason himself stood before me, I trembled from head to foot.” If he had spoken harshly or turned her away, she said, she might almost have died of grief, and perhaps lost her soul. He did neither. Before she could say a word, he asked her, “Have you come here to talk to me about your soul?” The question lifted the weight from her. She went in and opened her heart to him, and she left his house, in Lossing’s words, with a heart full of joy. A history of the congregation records that she was received into its membership as a girl of fifteen.

Freedom, marriage and loss

When she was sixteen or seventeen, a lady of the city bought Katy’s freedom for two hundred dollars, giving her six years to pay it back. Later the lady agreed to take eleven months of Katy’s work for half the sum, and the merchant Divie Bethune raised the other hundred dollars. Historians identify the lady as Isabella Graham, Bethune’s mother-in-law, a Scottish widow and schoolmistress who belonged to the same church and who spent her life founding societies for widows, orphans and the poor. The liberty Katy had asked for at ten had come at last, through the generosity of fellow believers.

At eighteen she married a man named Ferguson. She bore two children, and she lost them both. Nothing more is recorded of her husband; he too seems to have died early. In 1850 she summed it up for Tappan without self-pity: “They are dead, and I have no relations now, and most of my old friends are gone.” For almost fifty years she earned her living as a cake-maker, and she became one of the best known in New York: her wedding and party cakes were, Tappan said, unrivalled, and many who ate them also remembered her sensible conversation and her godly talk.

Forty-eight children

Bereaved of her own, Katy gathered other people’s. Over the course of her life she took in forty-eight children — twenty of them white — some from the almshouse and some from parents who could not or would not keep them. She raised them in her home, or kept them until she could find good places for them, spent her money on them, and followed them afterward with her prayers. When Tappan asked whether she had laid up any property for her old age, she answered at once.

How could I, when I gave away all I earned?

— Catherine Ferguson

While she lived at 51 Warren Street, she noticed the neighborhood children running wild in the street on the Lord’s day. She began collecting them into her house every Sunday, black and white together, and since she could not read to them herself she found suitable people to come in and hear them say their catechism. Isabella Graham would sometimes invite Katy and her scholars to her own house to recite and be taught. Then the minister of the congregation — by now Dr. John Mitchell Mason, the son, who was building a new church on Murray Street — heard of the school and walked in on it one Sunday. “What are you about here, Katy,” he said, “keeping school on the Sabbath?” She feared it was a rebuke. It was not. “We must not leave you to do all this,” he told her, and he had the church’s lecture room opened and the children moved into it, with helpers found for her. That, Tappan wrote, was the origin of the Sunday school of the Murray Street church, and it was believed that Katy’s was the first Sunday school in the city. Isaac Ferris, later chancellor of New York University, told Lossing that he had given his first expositions of Scripture as a theological student in Katy’s Sunday school.

Later writers fixed the founding in 1793, and she is often called the founder of New York’s first Sunday school. No document from her lifetime confirms either the date or the claim; Tappan himself only says it was “believed,” and ties the move to the years when the Murray Street church was built, around 1810. What is certain is that a freed slave who could not read gathered the neglected children of her street and made sure they heard the Word of God.

A house of prayer

For more than forty years, up to the end of her life, Katy kept a prayer meeting in her home every Friday evening, and for her last five years another every Sunday afternoon. She gathered in the poor and neglected children of the neighborhood and adults who went to no church anywhere, and always found some good man to lead. Wherever she lived in the city, tract distributors and city missionaries noticed, “the whole aspect of the neighborhood was changed.”

Tappan, who had known many reformers, put the secret of her usefulness down to a “fervent, uniform, and consistent piety” — no one, he said, could be with her even briefly without feeling it. She grieved over the vice and poverty of the city and was blunt about what was ruining it: “The ruination of both white and colored people, in this city, is gambling.” She had told one gambler she would rather live on bread and water than do it.

Her heart reached past New York. In the last years of her life a young missionary bound for West Africa with the American Missionary Association came to her little meetings once or twice before he sailed, and Katy took him and all his companions into her care in the only way she could.

A few months before her death Tappan met her in the street, and she pressed him at once for news of the Mendi Mission in Sierra Leone. For three years, she told him, not one day had passed without her praying for those missionaries.

I have never missed a day but I have prayed for those dear missionaries.

— Catherine Ferguson

“All is well”

In the summer of 1854 cholera was in New York. On Tuesday morning, 11 July, after feeling unwell for several days, Katy went out to see a physician, came home and lay down, and grew rapidly worse. Within a few hours it was plain that it was cholera and that she was dying, at her home at 74 Thompson Street. The summons was sudden, Tappan wrote, but she was ready, her mind calm and clear. “Oh!” she said to a friend standing by, “what a good thing it is to have a hope in Jesus!” Her last words were, “All is well.”

Ten days later Tappan went to her rooms to look through a barrel of pamphlets she had left behind. While he was there a little girl from the neighborhood came in and asked for a book “to remember Aunt Katy by,” and he gave her one. Tappan’s obituary, printed in the New York Daily Tribune and the American Missionary, carried her story far beyond Warren Street; Lossing set her portrait — engraved from a daguerreotype Tappan had arranged in 1850 — among his eminent Americans, and the American Tract Society published her life as Katy Ferguson; or, What a Poor Colored Woman May Do. In 1920 a home for young Black women in Harlem was named for her. She left no writings, no property, and no children of her own. She left instead a neighborhood changed, forty-eight children brought up in her house, and the witness of a woman whose mother had given her to God — and who, once free, gave herself away.

faq.q: Who was Catherine Ferguson?
faq.a: Catherine "Katy" Ferguson (c. 1774–1854) was a formerly enslaved Black Christian woman in New York City who earned her living as a cake-maker and gave her life to neglected children. She took forty-eight children into her home, gathered street children for Sunday catechism teaching that grew into the Murray Street church's Sunday school, and held a weekly prayer meeting in her house for more than forty years.

faq.q: What was her early life like?
faq.a: She was born a slave while her mother was being taken from Virginia to New York City, and was owned by a Presbyterian elder on Water Street. When she was about eight her mother was sold away and they never met again. Her mistress would not let her learn to read, but she memorized a great deal of Scripture.

faq.q: What did her mother do before they were parted?
faq.a: Katy remembered that before they were separated her mother knelt down, laid her hand on her head, and gave her to God. She said the memory of her own anguish at that parting was what gave her such compassion for children.

faq.q: How did she come to faith?
faq.a: At about fourteen, under conviction of sin, she went trembling to the house of her pastor, Dr. Mason of the Scotch Presbyterian Church, afraid he would turn her away. Before she could speak he asked whether she had come to talk to him about her soul, and she opened her heart to him and left full of joy. She joined the congregation at about fifteen.

faq.q: How did she gain her freedom?
faq.a: At sixteen or seventeen a lady of the city, identified by historians as Isabella Graham, bought her freedom for two hundred dollars. Katy repaid half of it with eleven months of work, and the merchant Divie Bethune raised the other hundred dollars.

faq.q: What happened to her own family?
faq.a: She married at eighteen and had two children, but both died, and nothing more is recorded of her husband. Late in life she said she had no relations left and most of her old friends were gone.

faq.q: How many children did she care for?
faq.a: Over her life she took in forty-eight children, twenty of them white, from the almshouse or from parents who could not keep them, and raised them or kept them until she found good homes. Asked if she had saved any property, she replied that she could not, because she gave away all she earned.

faq.q: Did she found New York's first Sunday school?
faq.a: While living on Warren Street she gathered neighborhood children into her home each Sunday and brought in helpers to hear their catechism. Dr. John Mitchell Mason found her at it and moved the school into the lecture room of his Murray Street church, and Lewis Tappan wrote that hers was believed to be the first Sunday school in the city. The often-quoted founding date of 1793 and the claim to be first have never been confirmed by documents from her lifetime.

faq.q: What was her prayer life like?
faq.a: For more than forty years she held a prayer meeting in her home every Friday evening, and in her last years another on Sunday afternoons, for poor children and adults who attended no church. City missionaries said the whole neighborhood changed wherever she lived. In her last years she prayed every day for the missionaries of the Mendi Mission in West Africa.

faq.q: How did she die and how is she remembered?
faq.a: She died of cholera at her home on Thompson Street on 11 July 1854, after only a few hours' illness, saying how good it was to have a hope in Jesus; her last words were "All is well." Lewis Tappan's obituary spread her story, Benson Lossing included her among eminent Americans, and in 1920 a home for young Black women in New York was named for her.

fields.name: Mary Prince
fields.bio: Bermudian-born woman enslaved in Bermuda, Turks Island and Antigua, converted through Moravian missionaries, whose 1831 History of Mary Prince — the first published life of a Black woman in slavery in Britain — testified for abolition.
fields.bio_html:
Mary Prince was born into slavery at Brackish Pond, in Bermuda, on a farm belonging to a Mr. Charles Myners, around the year 1788. Her mother was a household slave; her father, whose name was Prince, was a sawyer owned by a shipbuilder at Crow Lane. When she was an infant old Mr. Myners died, the household was divided, and she and her mother were bought by Captain Darrel and given to his granddaughter, little Miss Betsey Williams, a child of her own age. Mrs. Williams was a kind woman, and Mary’s first years were, she said, “the happiest period of my life,” because she was too young to understand what it meant to be a slave.

She learned soon enough. At about twelve she was hired out to a neighbouring household. Then Mrs. Williams died, and Captain Williams, needing money for his own remarriage, sent Mary and two of her sisters to be sold. On the morning of the sale her mother dressed the girls in new osnaburg cloth and said, “See, I am shrouding my poor children; what a task for a mother!” At the market they were stood in a row against a wall, handled by strangers, and sold one by one to different owners. “Our poor mammy went home with nothing.”

I have been a slave—I have felt what a slave feels, and I know what a slave knows; and I would have all the good people in England to know it too, that they may break our chains, and set us free.

— Mary Prince

The years of the whip

The story she later told in London does not soften what followed, and it should not be softened here. Her new master, a ship’s captain at Spanish Point, and his wife flogged their slaves for the smallest fault. Mary watched a fellow slave named Hetty, who had been the only friendly face in the house, beaten while pregnant until her child was born dead and her own health broke; after Hetty died, all her work fell on the girl. For a cracked jar that came apart in her hands Mary was given a hundred lashes. Once she ran away to her mother, who hid her in the rocks, until her father brought her back and begged the captain, “for the love of God,” to be kinder to her. He was not.

Years later she would look back on that time and see a hand she could not then name. “There was no end to my toils—no end to my blows,” she said. She lay down at night and rose in the morning in fear, and often wished she could join Hetty in the grave.

But the hand of that God whom then I knew not, was stretched over me; and I was mercifully preserved for better things.

— Mary Prince

After about five years she was sold again and shipped to Turks Island, where her new master owned salt ponds. There she stood up to her knees in brine from four in the morning, the sun raising salt blisters on her skin and the salt eating boils into her legs and feet, sometimes to the bone. She saw old and lame slaves tortured and killed. “Oh the horrors of slavery!” she said. “But the truth ought to be told of it.” She worked the ponds for about ten years. Once, on a Sunday, a sloop came in loaded with new slaves, and on its deck she found her own mother, so shaken by the voyage that she did not know her daughter.

Her master later took her back to Bermuda, where she had to bear his drunken rages and his indecency. In the end she asked to be sold to John Wood, a Bermudian merchant who lived in Antigua. Looking back, she said, “It was ordained to be, I suppose; God led me there.” Wood bought her for three hundred dollars, some fifteen years before she told her story.

A sinner at a prayer meeting

Antigua brought new suffering. In the Wood household Mary fell ill with rheumatism and a burning infection in her leg, and lay for months in an outhouse full of vermin. “If the Lord had not put it into the hearts of the neighbours to be kind to me,” she said, “I must, I really think, have lain and died.” Mary worked on her own account whenever she could, taking in washing and selling coffee and yams to ships’ captains, and saved toward buying her freedom. Twice friends offered to buy her; twice Wood refused.

She had been baptized in the English church in 1817, after learning to repeat the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, but the faith had not yet reached her heart. That happened one Christmas when the Woods took her to the country at Date Hill. A slave woman invited her to a Methodist prayer meeting on a nearby plantation, and she went. They were, she said, “the first prayers I ever understood.” A woman prayed, they sang a hymn, and then each spoke in turn of their own griefs as sinners.

That night Mary Prince saw her own heart: “I felt sorry for my sins also. I cried the whole night, but I was too much ashamed to speak. I prayed God to forgive me.”

The meeting, she said, “led my spirit to the Moravian church.” Back in town she asked to have her name written in the missionaries’ book, and she followed the church at every chance — without telling her mistress, who she knew would forbid it. Three Moravian women, Mrs. Richter, Mrs. Olufsen and Mrs. Sauter, taught her to read in a class of old and young, most of them free. After spelling they read the Bible together, and the missionary gave out a hymn. “I dearly loved to go to the church, it was so solemn,” she said. “I never knew rightly that I had much sin till I went there.” Frightened by what she found in herself, she used to pray God to pardon her sins for Christ’s sake, and she went home to her work turning over what she had heard. In time she was admitted as a candidate for the Holy Communion.

In the Moravian congregation she met Daniel James, a carpenter and cooper, a widower who had bought his own freedom. When he asked her to marry him she would not say yes until he had gone to church with her and joined the Moravians. They were married about Christmas 1826 in the Moravian chapel at Spring Gardens. The Woods were furious, and Mary was flogged with a horsewhip for taking a husband. When she again begged to buy her freedom, Mrs. Wood asked who had put freedom into her head. “To be free is very sweet,” Mary answered.

Free in London, and not free

In 1828 the Woods sailed to England and took Mary to look after their child. She hoped the voyage might cure her rheumatism, and her husband had heard a rumour that she would be freed. Instead she was set to the heavy washing, though her joints were so swollen she had to kneel at the tub. Slavery had no legal standing in England; four times he and his wife told her to do the work or get out. The fourth time, after thirteen years in their service, she went.

She carried her trunk to the only people she knew in England, the Moravian missionaries at Hatton Garden, and they took her things in and told her to come to church.
