A poor shoe-black and his wife nursed her through months of illness. In November 1828 she went to the Anti-Slavery Society, whose lawyers told her the hard truth: the laws of England could not make her free in Antigua. If she went home to Daniel, she would go home a slave. She told them she would rather go into her grave than go back a slave, “though I wish to go back to my husband very much—very much—very much!”

The Society tried to buy her freedom and was refused. A petition setting out her case was presented to Parliament in 1829. Wood went back to Antigua and would not move. Quaker ladies brought her warm clothing and money — “thus I had great cause to bless God in my affliction,” she said — and she worked as a charwoman and in service. In December 1829 Thomas Pringle, the Society’s secretary, took her into his own household as a servant.

There she read the Bible daily, went to church three times on Sundays, and sat under the preaching of the parish clergyman, the Rev. Mr. Mortimer. “He never keeps back the truth,” she said, and she trusted she had profited by it. Mortimer told her that he could not open the eyes of her heart for her: she must pray to God to change her heart, “and make me to know the truth, and the truth will make me free.”

I still live in the hope that God will find a way to give me my liberty, and give me back to my husband.

— Mary Prince

She did not pretend that waiting was easy. She tried to keep down her fretting and to leave everything to God, she said, “for he knows what is good for me better than I know myself. Yet, I must confess, I find it a hard and heavy task to do so.”

The book that told the truth

The idea of a book was her own. She wished it, Pringle wrote, “that good people in England might hear from a slave what a slave had felt and suffered.” She dictated it to Susanna Strickland, a young writer staying in the house, and Pringle edited it. The History of Mary Prince, a West Indian Slave, Related by Herself appeared in London early in 1831 — the first account of a Black woman’s life in slavery to be published in Britain — and ran through three editions that year. It closed with her own plain challenge to those who said slaves were content: “All slaves want to be free—to be free is very sweet.”

Mary Prince ended her story by asking English Christians to keep praying: “I hope they will never leave off to pray God, and call loud to the great King of England, till all the poor blacks be given free, and slavery done up for evermore.”

The book was attacked at once. A pro-slavery writer, James MacQueen, denounced it in Blackwood’s Magazine, and Wood called her a woman of bad character. A former neighbour in Antigua, Joseph Phillips, answered that she had been her owners’ most trusted household slave. Mrs. Pringle and three other women examined her body and reported that her back was “chequered” with the scars of old floggings. Pringle himself wrote of her honesty and trustworthiness, and he was candid about her faults too: a hasty temper, some pride, and a faith that was still young. Her religious knowledge, he said, was “but very limited,” but her profession of faith had “nothing of insincerity.”

In February 1833 the quarrel reached the courts. Pringle sued the publisher of Blackwood’s, Thomas Cadell, for libel and won, though the damages were only three pounds. Then Wood sued Pringle for libelling him in the book, and won twenty-five pounds, because Pringle could bring no witnesses from the West Indies. Mary Prince testified in both trials. Under hostile cross-examination she was questioned about relationships with men before her marriage, which the published History had left out, and she said that she had told Miss Strickland more than was printed. Phillips had already written that an earlier connection with a white sea captain was, he believed, broken off when she became “seriously impressed with religion.” Hers was the story of a real woman, owned body and soul by others, who came to Christ out of that life — not of a saint without a past.

What became of her

After the trials of 1833 Mary Prince disappears from the record. We do not know whether she ever went back to Antigua or saw Daniel James again, or when or where she died. No portrait of her is known to exist.

But the year she vanishes is the year Parliament passed the Slavery Abolition Act, which took effect across most of the British Empire on 1 August 1834. No one can measure how much one small book did toward that, but it put the voice of an enslaved woman before the British public, in her own words, during the very years the campaign was won. In 2012 Bermuda named her a National Hero.

Sold as a child, worked in the salt until her legs broke open, beaten for taking a husband, she came at last to a prayer meeting where she wept all night over her own sins, and to a Moravian class where she learned to read the Bible. And she used the freedom she had — a stranger, sick, and far from home — to tell the truth so that others might be set free.

faq.q: Who was Mary Prince?
faq.a: Mary Prince (c. 1788–after 1833) was a Bermudian woman born into slavery whose life story, The History of Mary Prince, a West Indian Slave, Related by Herself, was published in London in 1831. Converted through a prayer meeting in Antigua and a member of the Moravian church, she told her story so that English Christians would know what slavery was and work to end it.

faq.q: What was her childhood like?
faq.a: She was born at Brackish Pond, Bermuda, to an enslaved household servant and a sawyer named Prince. Her earliest years with a kind mistress were, she said, the happiest of her life. When she was about twelve her mistress died and she and two of her sisters were sold at auction to different owners.

faq.q: What did she suffer as a young slave?
faq.a: Her owner at Spanish Point and his wife flogged her severely for small faults, once giving her a hundred lashes over a cracked jar. She was then sold to Turks Island, where for about ten years she raked salt standing in brine from before dawn until her legs were covered in boils. Later she said the hand of a God she did not yet know had preserved her through it all.

faq.q: How did she come to Antigua?
faq.a: After years back in Bermuda under a violent master, she asked to be sold to John Wood, a merchant who lived in St. John's, Antigua, and she felt afterwards that God had led her there. In the Wood household she suffered long illness from rheumatism, harsh treatment, and repeated refusals when she tried to buy her own freedom with money she had saved.

faq.q: How did Mary Prince become a Christian?
faq.a: She had been baptized in the English church in 1817, but her heart was reached one Christmas at a Methodist prayer meeting, where she heard the first prayers she ever understood. That night she cried for her sins and prayed God to forgive her. The meeting led her to the Moravian church, where missionaries' wives taught her to read the Bible and she prayed to be pardoned for Christ's sake.

faq.q: Whom did she marry?
faq.a: About Christmas 1826 she married Daniel James, a free Black carpenter and cooper, in the Moravian chapel at Spring Gardens, Antigua. She would not accept him until he went to church with her and joined the Moravians. Her owners were furious and had her flogged for taking a husband.

faq.q: What happened when she came to England?
faq.a: In 1828 the Woods brought her to London, worked her hard despite her illness, and four times told her to obey or leave. She left and took her trunk to the Moravian missionaries at Hatton Garden, and the Anti-Slavery Society took up her case. Because Wood refused to free her, she could not return to her husband in Antigua without becoming a slave again.

faq.q: How did her book come to be written?
faq.a: In December 1829 Thomas Pringle, secretary of the Anti-Slavery Society, took her into his household as a servant, where she read the Bible daily and went to church. Writing her story was her own idea; she dictated it to Susanna Strickland and Pringle edited it. Published in 1831, it ran through three editions that year and ended with her plea that English Christians keep praying until slavery was ended.

faq.q: What were the 1833 libel trials?
faq.a: In February 1833 Pringle won a small libel award against the publisher of Blackwood's Magazine, which had attacked the book, and John Wood won a libel suit against Pringle. Mary Prince testified in both. Under cross-examination she was questioned about relationships before her marriage that the book had left out, and she said she had told more than was printed.

faq.q: What happened to Mary Prince in the end?
faq.a: After 1833 she disappears from the record, and no one knows when or where she died, whether she saw her husband again, or what she looked like, since no portrait is known. Her book appeared in the years when Britain's abolition campaign succeeded, and the Slavery Abolition Act was passed in 1833. Bermuda named her a National Hero in 2012.

fields.name: Nancy Prince
fields.bio: Free-born Black Baptist from Massachusetts (b. 1799) who lived nine years at the Russian imperial court, survived the 1824 St. Petersburg flood, taught freed children in Jamaica, and told it all in her Narrative (1850).
fields.bio_html:
Nancy Gardner was born in Newburyport, Massachusetts, on 15 September 1799, into a family whose story already carried the wound of slavery. Her mother’s father, Tobias Wornton, had been stolen from Africa as a boy and held as a slave by Captain Winthrop Sargent of Gloucester — “but, although a slave,” she wrote, “he fought for liberty.” He served in the Revolutionary army and was at the battle of Bunker Hill. Her grandmother was a Native American woman. Her father, Thomas Gardner, a man of African descent born on Nantucket, died when she was three months old.

Her mother married again, and Nancy’s stepfather was another kidnapped African, who had escaped the slave ship by swimming ashore at night while it lay at anchor off the New England coast. He was not kind to Nancy or her older sister Silvia, and during the War of 1812 he was pressed into British service and died far from home. Her mother, left with eight children and, as Nancy put it, “with no hope in God, and without the knowledge of her Saviour,” never recovered from the blow.

A girl carrying a family

Nancy left her mother’s house at eight to work in other people’s families. She remembered her grandfather with special tenderness: a member of a Congregational church who took the children with him to meeting every Sunday morning, and from whom, she said, “I early knew the difference between right and wrong.”

At fourteen she went to Salem for better wages and found a household that rang the bell for her at two on a Monday morning to begin the wash, and scolded her for being slow. “I often looked at my employers,” she wrote, “and thought to myself, is this your religion?” Within three months her health was broken.

In February 1816 word came that Silvia, who had gone to Boston as a nursery maid, had been lured into a brothel. Nancy set out the next morning on foot in bitter cold and reached Boston with her feet, hands and ears frostbitten. A Mr. Brown went with her, carrying a large cane. She found her sister by the fire among the others. The woman who kept the house tried to drag Silvia down into the cellar, crying that the girl owed her money; Mr. Brown held her off, and Silvia said, “I will go.” Nancy never doubted whose help it had been: “Without his aid, how could I ever have rescued my lost sister?” The next day, when the stage driver from their own town would only let the two young women ride on the open roof in the freezing cold, a Black man they had never met helped them hire a sleigh — and Nancy gave “ten thousand thanks to our colored friend, and to our Heavenly Father.”

Peace with God

The years that followed were a long burden. Her mother suffered spells of mental illness and could not hold the family together; her brother George went to sea and did not come back; one younger brother after another landed on Nancy’s hands to be boarded or fitted out from her own wages. She had made many resolutions, but she had not yet given her heart to God. Then, when “all hope but in God was lost,” she turned to Him.

In the worst of her cares, with her mother wandering and the younger children scattered, Nancy Gardner sought the Lord: “I resolved, in my mind, to seek an interest in my Saviour, and put my trust in Him; and never shall I forget the place or time when God spake to my troubled conscience.”

Justified by faith I found peace with God, the forgiveness of sin through Jesus Christ my Lord.

— Nancy Prince

On 9 May 1817 the Rev. Thomas Paul, pastor of Boston’s African Baptist Church in the African Meeting House on Beacon Hill, baptized her with seven others. She was seventeen, and had lived, she said, sixteen years “without hope, and without a guide.” Her faith was the plain evangelical faith of new birth and trust in Christ; years later, in Jamaica, she would press on church leaders “the necessity of being born of the spirit of God before we become members of the church of Christ.”

Nine years in St. Petersburg

On 1 September 1823 Nero Prince, a Black New Englander who had gone to Russia in 1810 and become one of the twenty Black footmen of the imperial household, arrived in Boston. They were married on 15 February 1824, and in April they sailed for Russia, reaching St. Petersburg in June. Soon after, she was presented at court to the Emperor Alexander and the Empress Elizabeth, who received her graciously and gave her a watch. There, she noticed, “there was no prejudice against color.”

At the first parties she attended she declined the dancing and dice, telling her hosts that her religion did not allow them, and they respected her for it. “By the help of God,” she wrote, “I was ever enabled to preserve my stand.” She learned Russian in six months, took children into her home as boarders, and started a business making baby linen and children’s clothes, with a journeywoman and apprentices. The Empress herself bought garments from her for her own children.

That first autumn the Neva flooded the city — the great St. Petersburg flood of 1824, in which many were drowned. Nancy was alone at home, still unable to speak the language; she beckoned people in from the street until the water stood two inches below her window. That night she set out with a lantern to find the boarders’ families and fell into a pit where the earth had caved in.

Sinking in the dark, she grasped once and the earth gave way; she grasped again and caught hold of the leg of a drowned horse, and by it drew herself up out of the mire. “Had not the horse been there,” she wrote, “I should never again have seen the light of day.” And she gave the glory where it belonged: “Thus through the providence of God, I escaped from the flood and the pit.”

She lived through the death of Alexander, the Decembrist rising of 1825, when cannon were fired into the crowd and she saw the snow and ice stained with blood, and the cholera of 1831. Through it all she found her spiritual home in the small Protestant congregation of the Rev. Richard Knill (she spelled it “Kenell”). When the flood damaged the society’s Bibles, its members worked so that the poor could still have them, and Nancy, encouraged by the matron of the Empress’s children, carried Bibles into the palace itself and sold many there. She also helped found an asylum for children in the city.

Home to Boston

The Russian winters weakened her lungs, and physicians warned her not to stay another cold season. Nero, unable to leave the emperor’s service at will, meant to follow in two years; she sailed in August 1833 and reached Boston that October. He never came — he died in Russia. Her mother and Silvia had both died in 1827, Thomas Paul was dead, and the old church was in confusion.

She did not sit still. Seeing Black orphans shut out of every asylum in the city because of their color, she called a meeting and proposed a home for them like the one she had helped begin in St. Petersburg. It opened with eight children, but for want of funds it soon failed. She joined the antislavery meetings that William Lloyd Garrison and his friends had begun, and refused to lose heart over her country’s prejudice; were it not for the promises of God, she wrote, “one’s heart would fail.”

Jamaica

When slavery ended in the British West Indies, her heart turned to Jamaica. The Rev. David Ingraham, an American missionary who had spent seven years there, urged her to come; she told him she would go if she could be useful, though she knew how limited her education was. On 16 November 1840 she sailed. The voyage brought a week-long storm and a suspected pirate ship. She kept a little diary: “Monday, and we mortals are still alive. Tuesday, thus far the Lord has led us on.”

Dropping anchor at St. Ann’s Bay on 6 December 1840, “we blessed the Lord for his goodness in sparing us to see the place of our destination.” She set down there her whole purpose: to help “raise up and encourage the emancipated inhabitants, and teach the young children to read and work, to fear God, and put their trust in the Saviour.”

Jamaica tested her hard. She taught school at St. Ann’s for some months, but clashed with a class-leader and the missionary over a church system in which, as she saw it, people were admitted on paying for tickets without any sign of a changed heart; she spoke of the new birth and was let go. In Kingston she visited the markets, the jail and the poor, gave away tracts and Bibles, and defended the freed people against the charge of idleness: “here surely we see industry.” Where she saw their failings, she laid them at slavery’s door: “Forgive them, this is the bitter fruit of slavery.” Friends in Kingston formed a society to provide a house for a school for destitute girls, and she sailed home in July 1841 to raise money for it. That year she also published a short account of the islands, The West Indies.

Back in America, despite a fall that dislocated her shoulder, she collected in Boston, New York and Philadelphia for her “Free Labor School,” made up the shortfall from her own purse, and in April 1842 sailed again. She landed in Kingston into an island in turmoil. The society that had promised her support drew up a constitution under which its members would “take charge of all she has brought”; she alone refused to stand for the vote, and the meeting broke up. Once a gun was fired through a window she had just left. With no school possible, she took refuge at the Mico Institution and left in August 1842.

Perils by sea

The voyage home was the hardest passage of her life. The captain secretly steered for Key West, where a new law ordered any free Black person who stepped ashore to be jailed, and he tried every inducement to get her off the ship; she would not go. A gale near Texas left her sitting on a trunk for thirty-six hours with water pouring over her, and the wreck was towed into New Orleans. There, kept aboard while the white passengers went ashore, she watched chained men and women driven through the streets, and she rebuked those who came to stare at her. When they told her she ought to be concerned about herself, she answered them.

I am sure the Lord will take care of me; you cannot harm me.

— Nancy Prince

A second ship was dismasted in another storm, and she reached New York on 19 October 1842 nearly starving. For three days she went from door to door for the money to release her baggage, until Nathaniel Southard and Lewis Tappan raised it. She reached Boston on 1 August 1843, “poor in health, and poor in purse, having sacrificed both, hoping to benefit my fellow creatures.” She trusted that it was acceptable to God, “who in his providence preserved me in perils by land, and perils by sea.”

A hiding place

Her later years in Boston were years of illness, losses and poverty. She was robbed, broken up in business three times, and laid low by sickness in 1848 and 1849. A neighbor recalled long afterward that in 1847 she led the women of her Beacon Hill street in driving off a slave-catcher who had come for a fugitive woman. To support herself without leaning on any charity she published her Narrative of the Life and Travels of Mrs. Nancy Prince in 1850, with new editions in 1853 and 1856; by the third she had “lost the power of my arms.” The book ends not in complaint but in Scripture and praise — “more than conquerors,” Christ “made perfect through suffering,” and a hymn naming Jesus as her hiding place.

I am a wonder unto many, but the Lord is my strong refuge, and in him will I trust.

— Nancy Prince

After 1856 the record grows faint. When and where Nancy Prince died is not certainly known: most reference works say only that she died after 1856, while some recent accounts give a death in Boston in November 1859, resting on a single newspaper notice. No portrait of her is known. What survives is her own voice — a free-born daughter of New England who knew the Russian court and the New Orleans wharf, who carried Bibles into a palace and rebuked cruelty from a wreck, and who, through every loss, kept saying that the Lord would take care of her.

faq.q: Who was Nancy Prince?
faq.a: Nancy Prince (born Nancy Gardner, 1799) was a free Black Christian woman from Massachusetts who lived nine years at the Russian imperial court in St. Petersburg, worked as a missionary teacher in newly emancipated Jamaica, and wrote A Narrative of the Life and Travels of Mrs. Nancy Prince (1850). She was a Baptist, converted and baptized in Boston in 1817.

faq.q: What was her family background?
faq.a: She was born in Newburyport, Massachusetts, on 15 September 1799. Her grandfather Tobias Wornton had been stolen from Africa and enslaved, yet fought in the Revolutionary army at Bunker Hill; her grandmother was Native American. Her father, Thomas Gardner, died when she was three months old, and her stepfather, another kidnapped African who had escaped a slave ship by swimming ashore, died in British service during the War of 1812.

faq.q: What was her childhood like?
faq.a: She left home at eight to work in other families, and from her teens she carried much of the burden of supporting her mother and younger brothers and sisters. At fourteen she worked in a Salem household so hard that her health broke, and she wondered at employers who prayed morning and evening but treated her unkindly. She credited her grandfather, a Congregational church member, with teaching her right from wrong.

faq.q: How did she rescue her sister?
faq.a: In February 1816 she learned that her older sister Silvia had been lured into a brothel in Boston. Nancy walked there through bitter cold, arriving frostbitten, and with the help of a Mr. Brown and his cane she brought Silvia out of the house. She said she could never have rescued her sister without God's aid.

faq.q: How did she become a Christian?
faq.a: Weighed down by family cares, she resolved to seek her Saviour and put her trust in him, and she wrote that, justified by faith, she found peace with God and the forgiveness of sin through Jesus Christ. On 9 May 1817 the Rev. Thomas Paul baptized her with seven others into the African Baptist Church in Boston.

faq.q: Why did she go to Russia?
faq.a: On 15 February 1824 she married Nero Prince, a Black New Englander who served as one of the footmen of the Russian imperial household. They sailed that April and she lived in St. Petersburg until 1833, was received at court by Emperor Alexander and Empress Elizabeth, and ran a business making baby linen and children's clothes, which the Empress herself bought.

faq.q: What did she experience in St. Petersburg?
faq.a: She survived the great flood of 1824, when she fell into a pit in the dark and pulled herself out by the leg of a drowned horse, crediting the providence of God. She witnessed the Decembrist rising of 1825 and the cholera of 1831, worshipped in the Protestant congregation of the Rev. Richard Knill, carried Bibles into the palace for sale, and helped found an asylum for children.

faq.q: What did she do after returning to Boston?
faq.a: Poor health sent her home in 1833, and her husband died in Russia before he could follow. In Boston she started a home for Black orphans who were shut out of other asylums, though it soon failed for lack of funds, and she took part in antislavery meetings.

faq.q: What was her mission to Jamaica?
faq.a: After emancipation in the British West Indies she sailed for Jamaica in November 1840, hoping to teach freed children to read and work, to fear God, and trust the Saviour. She taught at St. Ann's Bay, pressed the need for new birth before church membership, raised funds in America for a school for destitute girls, and returned in 1842, but unrest, theft and a society that tried to take her goods made the school impossible.

faq.q: How did her life end?
faq.a: Her voyage home in 1842 took her through storms, a stop at Key West where free Black people were jailed if they went ashore, and New Orleans, where she told her questioners the Lord would take care of her. Back in Boston she lived in illness and poverty and published her Narrative in 1850, 1853 and 1856 to support herself. When she died is not certainly known; some accounts give November 1859, and no portrait of her is known.

fields.name: Harriet Tubman
fields.bio: Born into slavery in Maryland, Harriet Tubman (c. 1822–1913) escaped in 1849 and returned some thirteen times to lead about seventy people to freedom, trusting God to guide every step; later a Union nurse and scout, she spent her last years caring for the aged in Auburn, New York.
fields.bio_html:
Harriet Tubman was born Araminta Ross, called “Minty,” in Dorchester County on the Eastern Shore of Maryland, around 1822. Her parents, Ben Ross and Harriet “Rit” Green, were enslaved, and so were their children; no one wrote down the day she was born. Her first biographer, Sarah Bradford, who knew her well, wrote that she was brought up by parents “possessed of strong faith in God,” and that she seemed never to have known a time when she did not trust Him. Before she could read a word — and she never learned to — she knew that God heard the prayers of slaves.

Childhood was hard and short. She was hired out from a very young age to other households, and she carried the scars of it all her life. Bradford tells of a mistress who made the little girl sit up all night rocking a sick baby, with a whip under the pillow for the moment her head nodded. Later she was sent into the fields, where she grew so strong that grown men wondered at her. Then, as a young girl, she was struck on the head by a heavy iron weight thrown in a fit of rage — by the account most historians follow, an overseer’s throw at another slave who had run from a village store. It broke her skull. For the rest of her life she suffered sudden spells in which she fell into a deep sleep that no one could rouse her from, and with them came dreams and visions that she understood as coming from God.

Praying for her master

The injury left her so weak that her owner, Edward Brodess, tried to sell her and could find no buyer. All that winter, as men came to look her over and name their price, she lay sick and prayed for the man who owned her. It was, she told Bradford, a kind of praying without ceasing: at the horse-trough, washing her face, she asked the Lord to wash her clean; taking up the broom, she asked Him to sweep every sin out of her heart.

Sick and unsellable, Minty prayed through the long nights for her owner: “Oh, Lord, convert ole master; Oh, dear Lord, change dat man’s heart, and make him a Christian.” When she heard that she and her brothers were to be sold south in the chain-gang, she changed her prayer and asked the Lord to take him out of the way if his heart would never change.

It is to her credit that she told this story against herself. In March 1849 Brodess died, and she never forgot it. “Oh, den it ’peared like I would give de world full of silver and gold, if I had it, to bring dat pore soul back,” she said. “I would give myself.” She had wanted him converted, not dead, and the memory grieved her for the rest of her life.

Around 1844 she had married John Tubman, a free Black man, and taken the first name of her mother, Harriet. But her husband scoffed at her fears, and with Brodess dead the danger of being sold away was real. Two of her sisters had already been carried off south. In her dreams she kept seeing a line, with green fields and open arms on the other side of it, and she could never quite reach it.

Across the line

In the autumn of 1849 she fled. A first attempt with two of her brothers ended when they lost their nerve and turned back, taking her with them. Soon afterward she went alone, guided by the North Star and passed along by people she learned to trust, and walked the long way into Pennsylvania. She remembered the moment of crossing for the rest of her life: “When I found I had crossed dat line, I looked at my hands to see if I was de same pusson. There was such a glory ober ebery ting.”

The joy did not last. She was free, but everyone she loved was still in Maryland, and there was no one to welcome her. “I was free, and they should be free,” she told Bradford. “I would make a home in the North and bring them there, God helping me.” Then she prayed: “I said to de Lord, ‘I’m gwine to hole stiddy on to you, an’ I know you’ll see me through.’”

Moses

She found work in Philadelphia and at Cape May, cooking and scrubbing, and spent her wages on going back. In December 1850 she helped her niece Kessiah and Kessiah’s two children escape from Baltimore — the first of her rescues. Over roughly the next ten years she made about thirteen trips into Maryland and brought out some seventy people, most of them family and friends, and gave directions to dozens of others who found their own way. Older books said she rescued three hundred people on nineteen trips; careful historians have since shown the real number was smaller, and no less astonishing. Thomas Garrett, the Quaker merchant of Wilmington who helped her on many journeys, guessed from what he knew of her work that she had brought away “from 60 to 80 persons,” and that no one under her care had ever been caught.

She travelled by night and usually began on a Saturday, so that a Sunday would pass before advertisements could be printed. She hid her parties in woods, swamps and potato holes, and signalled to them with hymns: one tune meant the way was clear, another meant danger. When frightened people wanted to turn back, and so endanger everyone, she carried a revolver and made it plain that they would go on. In 1851 she went back for her husband and found that he had taken another wife; she let him go, and took others north instead. After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made the free states unsafe, she led her people all the way to St. Catharines, in Ontario, and made her own home there for a time. At Christmas 1854 she brought out three of her brothers just before they were to be sold, and in 1857 she carried away her aged parents in a makeshift cart drawn by an old horse.

Asked how she dared go back with a price on her head, she always gave the same answer: “Don’t, I tell you, Missus, ’twan’t me, ’twas de Lord!”

I trust to you. I don’t know where to go or what to do, but I expect you to lead me.

— Harriet Tubman

That was her prayer, she said, “an’ he always did.” Garrett, who did not believe easily, wrote in 1868 that he had “never met with any person, of any color, who had more confidence in the voice of God, as spoken direct to her soul.” She told him that she talked with God and He talked with her every day of her life, and that she went only where God sent her. Garrett recalled a cold March night when she was leading two men some thirty miles below Wilmington. She said God told her to stop, then to leave the road and turn left; she came to a stream with no boat or bridge, and was told to go through. She waded in up to her armpits, and the men followed. The next day, they learned, a reward had been posted for those very men at the railway station on the road she had left.

Taking a frightened young woman named Tilly north by steamboat, Tubman found that the clerk suspected them and ordered them to stand aside. Having no other help, she knelt in the bow of the boat, her head in her hands, and prayed over and over, “Oh, Lord! You’ve been wid me in six troubles, don’t desert me in the seventh!” The clerk came, touched her shoulder, and said only, “You can come now and get your tickets.” She never knew what changed his mind. She said it was the Lord.

Garrett told another story he could not explain. Tubman walked into his store one day and said, “God tells me you have money for me.” He had in fact just received money sent for her by friends in Scotland — and she asked for almost exactly the sum he held. The Quaker would not say whether it was clairvoyance or “the divine impression on her mind from the source of all power,” but he was sure she had a guide within herself.

Scout, spy and nurse

In 1858 she met John Brown, who called her “General Tubman” and trusted her with his plans; she grieved deeply when he was hanged at Charles Town in 1859. When the Civil War came, friends in Massachusetts sent her south to the Union lines on the coast of South Carolina in 1862. There she nursed sick and wounded soldiers and freed people, washing wounds through long days in the heat, then baking pies and gingerbread at night and selling them to support herself, for she drew almost no pay. She knew roots that eased dysentery and went without fear among those sick with smallpox and fever. The Lord, she said, would take care of her until her time came.

She also scouted and spied. On 2 June 1863 she guided Colonel James Montgomery’s Black troops up the Combahee River in a raid that destroyed plantations and supplies and carried some seven hundred enslaved people to freedom. She remembered them streaming down to the gunboats, mothers with children on their backs and pots of rice still smoking on their heads. When the crowds clung to the rowboats and would not let go, Montgomery called out, “Moses, you’ll have to give ’em a song,” and she sang them aboard.

On the way home at the war’s end, with her pass as a government nurse, she was thrown out of a railway car by a conductor and three other men and badly injured. William Seward, who had sold her a small property in Auburn, New York, wrote of her that “a nobler, higher spirit, or truer, seldom dwells in the human form.” Frederick Douglass, writing to her in 1868, put it more simply: “The midnight sky and the silent stars have been the witnesses of your devotion to freedom and of your heroism.”

Auburn

Auburn was home for the rest of her life. She cared for her aged parents there until they died, took in the poor, the sick and the old, and was rarely without hungry people at her table. In 1869 she married Nelson Davis, a Union veteran, and later adopted a little girl named Gertie. Sarah Bradford wrote Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman that same year, and the proceeds helped save the mortgaged house; a second book, Harriet, the Moses of Her People, followed in 1886. For decades she pressed the government for the wages and pension she had earned, and only in 1899 did Congress grant her a pension, partly for her service as a nurse.

She belonged to the African Methodist Episcopal Zion church in Auburn and spoke for her people and for the rights of women. At a suffrage convention in 1896 she summed up her years on the Underground Railroad in a sentence that has been repeated ever since.

I never ran my train off the track and I never lost a passenger.

— Harriet Tubman

Her last great work was a home for the aged and poor. She bought land beside her own in 1896 and later deeded it to the AME Zion church so that the church would run it. She had told Bradford that this was “her last work,” and that she only prayed the Lord to let her live until it was well started. The Harriet Tubman Home for the Aged opened in 1908.

A place prepared

In her final years she became a resident of the home she had founded. She died there of pneumonia on 10 March 1913, at about ninety years old, with friends and ministers of her church around her. Those at her bedside reported that among her last words were the words of Jesus: “I go to prepare a place for you.” She was buried in Fort Hill Cemetery in Auburn with military honors.

She had told her worried friends long before, when they begged her not to go south again, that she was not afraid to die. The apostle John had seen twelve gates in the heavenly city, she reminded them, and three of them were on the south side; if they killed her down there, she reckoned she would get into one of those. She had asked the Lord to lead her, and He had. Bradford wrote in her first book of her hope that one day a gentle voice would say to Harriet, as to the guest in Christ’s parable, “Friend, come up higher.”

faq.q: Who was Harriet Tubman?
faq.a: Harriet Tubman (c. 1822–1913) was an American Christian woman who escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and then went back again and again to lead others to freedom on the Underground Railroad. She later served the Union Army as a nurse, scout and spy, and spent her last decades in Auburn, New York, caring for the poor and the aged. Those who knew her said her courage rested on a constant, childlike trust in God.

faq.q: What was her early life like?
faq.a: She was born Araminta Ross, called Minty, around 1822 in Dorchester County on Maryland's Eastern Shore, to enslaved parents Ben Ross and Harriet Green. She was hired out as a small child and later worked in the fields. As a young girl she was struck on the head by a heavy weight thrown in anger, an injury that left her with sudden sleeping spells, dreams and visions for the rest of her life.

faq.q: How did she pray for her master?
faq.a: While she lay sick and her owner, Edward Brodess, tried to sell her, she prayed through the nights that the Lord would convert him and change his heart. When she heard she was to be sold south, she changed her prayer and asked God to take him out of the way if his heart would not change. When he died in March 1849, she grieved and said she would have given anything to bring him back.

faq.q: How did she escape from slavery?
faq.a: In the autumn of 1849, fearing she would be sold away, she fled north. A first attempt with two brothers ended when they turned back, so she went alone, following the North Star and helped along by people she learned to trust. She said that on crossing into freedom she looked at her hands to see if she was the same person.

faq.q: How many people did she lead to freedom?
faq.a: Historians today estimate that over about ten years she made around thirteen trips into Maryland and brought out some seventy people, mostly family and friends, while giving directions to dozens more. Older books gave a figure of three hundred, which careful research has not supported. Her friend Thomas Garrett estimated sixty to eighty, and said no one under her care was ever caught.

faq.q: What part did faith play in her rescues?
faq.a: She said that she talked with God and He talked with her every day, and that she went only where God sent her. When people asked how she dared to go back, she answered that it was not her but the Lord, and that she had always told Him she trusted Him to lead her. She prayed through dangers, as when a suspicious boat clerk suddenly let her and a young fugitive buy their tickets.

faq.q: What did she do in the Civil War?
faq.a: From 1862 she worked with Union forces on the South Carolina coast as a nurse to soldiers and freed people, and as a scout and spy. On 2 June 1863 she guided Colonel James Montgomery's troops up the Combahee River in a raid that freed some seven hundred enslaved people. She received almost no pay for her service.

faq.q: What was her life in Auburn like?
faq.a: She settled on a small property in Auburn, New York, bought from William Seward, where she cared for her aged parents and took in the poor and sick. In 1869 she married Nelson Davis and later adopted a daughter, Gertie. Sarah Bradford's books about her, published in 1869 and 1886, helped support her, and in 1899 Congress finally granted her a pension.

faq.q: What was the Harriet Tubman Home for the Aged?
faq.a: It was her last great work: a home for elderly and poor Black people on land she bought beside her own in 1896. She deeded the property to the AME Zion church, to which she belonged, so the church would run it, and it opened in 1908. She had prayed that the Lord would let her live until it was well started.

faq.q: How did her life end?
faq.a: She became a resident of her own home for the aged and died there of pneumonia on 10 March 1913, at about ninety. Those at her bedside reported that among her last words were Jesus' words, "I go to prepare a place for you." She was buried in Fort Hill Cemetery in Auburn with military honors.

fields.name: Tiyo Soga
fields.bio: Xhosa minister, missionary, hymn writer and translator (1829–1871), the first Black South African ordained to the ministry, who founded the Mgwali and Tutura missions and gave his people Pilgrim’s Progress in Xhosa.
fields.bio_html:
Tiyo Soga was born in 1829 at Gwali, in the green Tyhume valley of the Eastern Cape, in the homestead of a powerful man. His father, Soga, was one of the chief councillors of the Ngqika chief — a tall, fierce-eyed traditionalist with eight wives and thirty-nine children, who dreaded the new religion of the missionaries as the herald of a revolution. Yet the same man was the first of his people, it was said, to drive a plough and to lead the water of a running stream onto his fields. Tiyo’s mother, Nosuthu, was Soga’s great wife, and Tiyo was the seventh of her nine children.

Nosuthu became a Christian. She separated from her husband’s marriage bed while remaining at his homestead, and she let the boy go to live with the missionary at the nearby Chumie station, the Rev. William Chalmers, who had grown fond of the slender, truthful child in a sheepskin kaross. When Tiyo was a very small boy, an old Christian later recalled, his mother had said she did not know what to do with him — when they knelt to pray, he would take the prayer out of her mouth and offer it himself.

“The salvation of mankind”

In 1844 Chalmers had to choose which of his pupils to send to compete for a free place at the Lovedale seminary. He asked the boys which was the greatest work of God. Each answered, “The work of creation.” Tiyo answered, “The salvation of mankind, because it shows God’s love” — and his teacher, as Tiyo told it, clapped his hands and shouted, “Well done, well done, Tiyo!” At Lovedale itself the frightened boy failed the examination, but Chalmers would not give him up, and William Govan took him into the seminary anyway. He climbed from the bottom of his class to the top.

Then, in 1846, came the War of the Axe. Lovedale was broken up, the Chumie station was burned to the ground, and Tiyo and his mother were refugees at Fort Armstrong. Night after night she gathered sneezewood splinters so her son could read by the firelight. When the homeless missionaries resolved that Govan should take the boy to Scotland, the Rev. James Laing went to ask her consent. Her answer has come down to us whole: “My son is the property of God; wherever he goes, God goes with him.” If he was willing to go, she said, she would not object, for he was as much in God’s keeping across the sea as he was near to her. Her husband and kinsmen were at that moment in arms against the colony.

A son of Africa in Glasgow

Tiyo sailed with Govan in July 1846. In Glasgow he was taken up by the John Street United Presbyterian Church and its minister, Dr. William Anderson, who — Tiyo wrote long afterwards — took possession of his soul and feelings in a Sunday school one evening, not by anything he said, but by his “exceeding fellow-feeling towards a strange boy.” There, far from home, the seed sown at the Chumie came up. On 7 May 1848 Tiyo Soga made his public confession of faith in Christ and was baptized by Dr. Anderson in John Street Church.

He went home that year as a young catechist, interpreting for the missionary George Brown — with whom he also read Jonathan Edwards’s Religious Affections — and then teaching and preaching at the new station of Uniondale among people who had never heard the gospel. His message to old warriors and young braves alike was the one word “Repent,” and it was mostly ignored. Because he had refused the initiation rite of manhood, parents pulled their children from his school, and some threatened his life. It was in these lean years that he began to write hymns in Xhosa; the 1850 hymnbook already contained some from his pen.

On Christmas Day 1850 war broke out again. The Uniondale station was looted and burned, and Tiyo escaped through the Amatole bush by night, outrunning men who chased him in the dark. When the chief Maqoma sent him captured letters to translate, he returned every one: he would have no part in a contest that carried death to his fellow-creatures.

Before he sailed for Scotland a second time, in 1851, he was offered the post of government interpreter at a good salary. He turned it down.

I had rather beg my bread from door to door in your streets to gather up what will pay my fees at College, and thereafter attend the Theological Hall in order to learn better how to preach Christ as my known Saviour to my heathen countrymen who know Him not.

— Tiyo Soga

The first of his race

He studied at the University of Glasgow and the United Presbyterian Theological Hall in Edinburgh. He was never a prize-winner — he had begun English at fifteen, and his schooling had been broken by two wars — but his professors vied to praise his diligence, and his fellow students loved him. One of them, Robert Johnston, said that meeting Tiyo turned his whole life toward the mission field. He taught Sunday school in a poor district and did city mission work, where at least once he was cursed down a staircase for his colour.

On 23 December 1856, in a crowded John Street Church, the Presbytery of Glasgow ordained him to the ministry — the first Black South African to be ordained. On 27 February 1857 Tiyo married Janet Burnside, a Scotswoman, and in April they sailed together for the Cape. From London he wrote that she had made all the sacrifice, not he, and that he trusted the sense of it would make him “a tenderly affectionate husband.”

Coming home to a famine

He landed at Algoa Bay in July 1857 into two kinds of storm. A Black minister with a white wife drew stares in every street. And his own people were dying. In 1856–57, following the prophecies of Nongqawuse, the Xhosa had killed their cattle and burned their grain, believing the ancestors would rise and the land be renewed. Tiyo called it, with grief, a nation that had believed a lie. Near Peelton he helped dig the grave of a mother and two little children who had lain down under one blanket and starved in their sleep. He wrote to Glasgow begging the John Street people for money to feed the starving. Yet he refused despair: “It is by terrible things that God sometimes accomplishes His purposes,” he wrote; affliction might yet soften hearts toward the truth.

In September 1857 he and Robert Johnston reached the Mgwali stream, in a valley emptied by famine, with the scattered Christians of the old Chumie mission following them. The two young graduates cut poles and sods with their own hands and finished the little church themselves. At its opening in 1858 Tiyo served the Lord’s Supper to about forty communicants — among them his eldest brother, who had first taught him the alphabet — and they sang the old hymn of Ntsikana, the early Xhosa Christian prophet, until the little church was full of sobs. The Mgwali grew; Alexander Duff, the great Scottish missionary to India, wrote after visiting in 1864 that he had found no mission station in all South Africa more orderly than his.

The dark years

The work was not easy, and Tiyo felt every blow. Members fell into sin, and a group of Christian boys took up the initiation rite and openly defied him, with two elders taking their side. “I have had disappointment after disappointment,” he wrote in 1862. That year his throat and chest broke down, and he lay for weeks at King William’s Town unable even to speak aloud. His second son was growing up lame. And through the colony there ran the steady humiliation of colour — a grieving father who at first refused to let a Black minister bury his child, policemen who demanded his pass, an innkeeper who ordered him out. He bore most of it in silence.

Prostrate with illness in December 1862, he wrote that he was not anxious about himself and wished to leave himself entirely in the Lord’s hands: “my prayer, yea, my earnest prayer — oh may He in mercy hear it! — is, that this affliction may be sanctified for the good of my soul.”

His private journal from these years, written partly in Greek letters so no one else would read it, is one of the most searching records any missionary has left. He accused himself of irresolution, coldness, temper and unbelief, and cried out like a child to his Father: “O God, by Thy spirit move me, and Thou shalt have the entire glory.” Slowly he came to see that his trouble was looking at his sins so long that he could not see Christ. “The promises are all on my side,” he wrote in May 1863. “Why should I doubt?” Those who knew him said that this hidden struggle was the secret of the humility that shone in his face.

Pilgrim’s Progress in Xhosa

Bunyan had been Tiyo’s companion since his student days, and he had already roughed out a translation in Scotland. On the night of 21 November 1866 he wrote in his journal that he had finished, “through the goodness of Almighty God,” the first part of John Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress — “my fingers aching with writing.” Printed at Lovedale as U-Hambo lom-Hambi, it was read aloud at mission stations everywhere. One reader, hearing the fight with Apollyon, refused to believe that the writer had not seen it with his own eyes. His hymns — not translations, but his own meditations on Scripture — entered the worship of his people. The hymn “Lizalis’ idinga lakho,” traditionally ascribed to him, is still sung in South African churches today. From 1869 he also sat on the board of seven missionaries from seven churches revising the Xhosa Bible, insisting that the text be pure and idiomatic. “It is no task,” he wrote, “but a delightful privilege and duty.”

To the Tutura

In 1867 the Xhosa paramount chief Sarhili asked for a missionary who spoke his language, and named Tiyo as the man he wanted. In June 1868 Tiyo left the Mgwali with his family to found a new station at the Tutura, beyond the Kei, among people who often stared blankly at the hymns he sang. In 1870, knowing his strength was failing, he sent his three eldest sons — William Anderson, John Henderson and Kirkland Allan — to be educated in Scotland. For them he wrote a small book, “The Inheritance of My Children,” of sixty-two short counsels. Never be ashamed, he told them, that your father was a Xhosa; take your place in the world as Black men; love all men; set your face against scandal; insult no one, but fear no one when you are in the right.

God has made from creation no race of men mentally and morally superior to other races.

— Tiyo Soga

Trust in no right hand of your own, but in the living God, to do anything great or honourable.

— Tiyo Soga

Sunset

In mid-1871 he sent the Bible board his translation of Acts as far as chapter twenty-three, with a line in Xhosa at the end: strength had failed him at that point. Though desperately weak, he left his bed on two days that July to vaccinate the people who came to him for help, and relapsed.

“Although I despaired of life,” he wrote in his last letter, “the Lord Jesus Christ sustained me by His grace and enabled me to commit all to Him without fear.” To a visiting minister he said that his mind was kept in peace, that he had no fears, and that all would be well.

On the night of 11 August he gathered his strength and prayed aloud in Xhosa: trusting himself wholly to Christ, and pleading for his scattered countrymen, for every preacher of the gospel, for the little church at the Tutura, for the children in the schools, for those who had grieved him, and for his sons across the sea — that they might come home and teach his people. When a friend asked whether he found the Saviour precious, he whispered “Yes.” He died the next afternoon, 12 August 1871, aged forty-two, in the arms of his old Lovedale schoolfellow Richard Ross. His aged mother, who had nursed him day and night, stood calmest of all at the grave in the orchard he had planted.

His long illness is identified by later historians as tuberculosis. His prayer for his sons was answered: William Anderson Soga came home as a doctor and medical missionary in the Transkei, and John Henderson Soga served as a missionary and completed the second part of the Xhosa Pilgrim’s Progress that his father had begun. On the wall of the church at the Mgwali a tablet called Tiyo Soga “the first ordained preacher” of his people, “a Friend of God,” “a Lover of His Son,” and “a Devoted Missionary who spent himself in his Master’s service.” It is a fair summary of a man who carried the gospel, the burdens of his nation and the wounds of his colour, and asked only that all of it be sanctified to the good of his soul.

faq.q: Who was Tiyo Soga?
faq.a: Tiyo Soga (1829–1871) was a Xhosa minister, missionary, translator and hymn writer from the Eastern Cape. Ordained in Glasgow in 1856, he was the first Black South African to be ordained to the Christian ministry. He founded mission stations at Mgwali and Tutura and translated the first part of John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress into Xhosa.

faq.q: What was his early life like?
faq.a: He was born in 1829 at Gwali in the Tyhume valley, the son of Soga, a chief councillor of the Ngqika, and of Nosuthu, Soga's great wife. His mother became a Christian, and as a boy he went to live with the missionary William Chalmers at the nearby Chumie station. In 1844 he entered the Lovedale seminary, where he rose from the bottom of his class to the top.

faq.q: How did he come to go to Scotland?
faq.a: When the War of the Axe broke up Lovedale in 1846, the missionaries resolved that William Govan should take him to Scotland to be educated. His mother consented, saying that her son was the property of God and that wherever he went, God went with him. He studied in Glasgow from 1846 to 1848.

faq.q: When did he become a Christian?
faq.a: The faith sown in him at the Chumie came to open profession in Scotland. On 7 May 1848 he publicly confessed his faith in Christ and was baptized by Dr. William Anderson in John Street United Presbyterian Church, Glasgow.

faq.q: What did he do between his two visits to Scotland?
faq.a: From 1849 he worked as a catechist, interpreter and schoolteacher, first at the Chumie and then at Uniondale in the Amatole, preaching repentance to people who largely ignored him. When war broke out on Christmas Day 1850 the station was burned and he escaped through the bush by night. He refused to translate captured letters for the chief Maqoma and turned down a paid post as government interpreter.

faq.q: How was he trained and ordained?
faq.a: Returning to Scotland in 1851, he studied at the University of Glasgow and the United Presbyterian Theological Hall, supported by John Street Church. He was licensed to preach in December 1856 and ordained by the Presbytery of Glasgow on 23 December 1856. In February 1857 he married Janet Burnside, and they sailed for South Africa that April.

faq.q: What did he find when he returned home in 1857?
faq.a: He arrived during the famine that followed the Xhosa cattle-killing of 1856–57, when thousands died after following prophecies that the dead would rise. He helped bury starving families, appealed to Glasgow for money for food, and in September 1857 founded the Mgwali mission with Robert Johnston among the returning survivors.

faq.q: What trials did he face as a missionary?
faq.a: He suffered discouragement from moral failures and defiance at his station, a serious breakdown of his throat and chest in 1862, a lame son, and repeated insults because of his colour. His private journal records long struggles with doubt and coldness of heart, and his prayer that his affliction would be sanctified for the good of his soul.

faq.q: What were his literary achievements?
faq.a: He finished translating the first part of Pilgrim's Progress into Xhosa in November 1866, and it was printed at Lovedale as U-Hambo lom-Hambi. He wrote original Xhosa hymns, including Lizalis' idinga lakho, traditionally ascribed to him and still sung today. From 1869 he served on the board revising the Xhosa Bible and helped complete the four Gospels.

faq.q: How did his life end?
faq.a: In 1868 he moved to found a station at Tutura among the people of the chief Sarhili, and in 1870 he sent his three eldest sons to Scotland with a book of counsel called The Inheritance of My Children. Weakened by long illness, which later historians identify as tuberculosis, he died at Tutura on 12 August 1871, aged 42. His last letter said that the Lord Jesus Christ had enabled him to commit all to Him without fear.

fields.name: Pastor Hsi (Xi Shengmo)
fields.bio: Confucian scholar and opium addict converted through David Hill in 1879, Pastor Hsi (Xi Shengmo, c. 1836–1896) took the name “Overcomer of Demons” and founded self-supporting opium refuges across Shanxi, China.
fields.bio_html:
Xi Zizhi — the man the English-speaking church came to know as Pastor Hsi — was born about 1836 in the Western Chang village (Xiliangzhuang), at the foot of the mountains about ten miles from the city of P’ing-yang (modern Linfen) in the province of Shanxi, northern China. He was the youngest of four sons in a family of scholars and hereditary physicians, and his father’s favourite. Even as a small boy he was haunted by questions no one around him could answer. His biographer, who heard his story from his own lips, records that at eight years old he asked himself, “What is the use of living in this world? Men find no good. And in the end?” No missionary had ever lived in Shanxi; the only thing that had reached it from the Christian West, as his biographer bitterly put it, was opium.

He was clever and ambitious. Married at sixteen, he won his first literary degree the same year, and grew into a man of property and influence: a village leader, a writer of lawsuits who moved easily among the mandarins’ offices, feared for his scholarship, his nerve, and a temper that was the terror of anyone who crossed it. He despised foreigners. But the restlessness of his childhood never left him. His first wife died, and in his grief he turned to Taoism, hoping it held the secret of a life that could outlast the grave. Around the age of thirty he married again — a bright young woman from a neighbouring village, who would become the great partner of his life. But his health was breaking, and the Taoist promise of immortality proved empty. Sick and failing, he gave in to friends who urged a few pipes of opium for the pain.

“The opium that eats the man”

The descent was swift. For a year and a half he hardly left his couch. Studies, profession, and farm all slipped away, and he loathed himself and the habit he could not break. Then came the terrible North China famine of 1876–79, in which millions died. Famine relief brought the first Protestant missionaries into Shanxi, among them a gentle English Methodist, David Hill, who reached Shanxi in 1878 and made his home in P’ing-yang. Hsi thought it shameful that anyone should even accept their help.

In the autumn of 1879, as thousands of scholars gathered at the provincial capital for the great examinations, Hill and his colleague Timothy Richard handed out packets of Christian books along with an offer of prizes for essays on Christian themes, one of them on how the opium curse might be broken. Hsi had not gone to the examination; but a brother brought the papers home. Seeing a chance to make money out of the foreigner without ever meeting him, Hsi read the accompanying books and wrote several essays under different names. He won three of the four prizes.

Hill would hand the silver only to the writer himself, so Hsi had to go to the mission house in person. He went expecting sorcery. Instead he looked up into David Hill’s face. “One look, one word, it was enough,” he said years later. “That face told me I was in the presence of a true, good man.” A few days later Hill asked him to become his Chinese teacher, and Hsi went to live in the missionary’s house.

Kneeling at Gethsemane

On the table in his little room lay a New Testament, which he needed for his lessons and found himself reading for hours. The life of Jesus grew real to him; and with it the weight of his own guilt and his slavery to opium grew unbearable. At last he knelt on the floor with the book before him and read on through the story of the cross. When he reached the agony in Gethsemane, as he himself recorded, the Holy Spirit moved his soul, and “with tears that flowed and would not cease” he yielded himself to Christ as his Saviour and his God. His later colleague D. E. Hoste said that from that hour Hsi lived as one who had seen the living Christ.

Hill, cautious, suggested he wait a few weeks before joining the believers openly, lest he go back as quickly as he had come. Hsi’s reply was characteristic.

From this day until death and beyond, I will never, never draw back.

— Pastor Hsi

He knew at once that the opium must go — entirely and for ever. What followed was a week of agony. For seven days and nights, by his biographer’s account, he scarcely ate or slept; Hill’s medicines, native and foreign, did nothing. Hsi came to believe that he was fighting not only a craving but a spiritual enemy.

In the height of his withdrawal Hsi brought the struggle, as he put it, before the Lord’s face daily, crying out: “Devil, what can you do against me? My life is in the hand of God. And truly I am willing to break off opium and die, but not willing to continue in sin and live!” At last, reading of the Comforter in his Bible, he cast himself on God and prayed for the gift of the Holy Spirit.

The answer, he said, came suddenly and completely, and the craving never returned.

He did what man and medicine could not do. From that moment my body was perfectly at rest.

— Pastor Hsi

Soon after, sensing that the Christian life would be a war, he took a new name. Instead of an elegant literary title he chose Shengmo — “Overcomer of Demons.” When David Hill left Shanxi in the spring, Hsi walked beside his cart out of the city and stood weeping on the old stone bridge until it was out of sight. They never met again.

A new man in the Western Chang village

The village was scandalised: the scholar Hsi had “eaten the foreign religion.” He burned his idols, was cut off by the gentry, and later even had his degree taken from him by the education chancellor (it was eventually restored). But people could not ignore the change. He brought home the aged stepmother he had once driven out, and humbly sought peace with the brothers he had quarrelled with for years.

Then Mrs. Hsi fell into a terrible affliction that the whole village took for demon possession — a judgment, they said, on the “Conqueror of Demons.” Prayer seemed to do nothing, and she grew weaker. Hsi called his household to a three-day fast; then, by the account he gave his biographer, he laid his hands on her and in the name of Jesus commanded the evil spirits to leave. She was delivered at once, never suffered so again, and from that day declared herself a Christian and his partner in the work. Accounts of healing and deliverance in answer to prayer run all through his story. His biographer and Hoste record them as the Chinese Christians described them, without claiming to explain them; they are best read the same way, as the testimony of believers who simply took the Gospels at their word.

Hsi wrote that because of the onslaughts of Satan, he and his wife for three years seldom undressed to sleep, so as to be ready to watch and pray. “Sometimes in a solitary place, I spent whole nights in prayer,” he recalled, and his mother would see a light burning in their room toward midnight and know they were still waiting before their heavenly Father.

He grew slowly, and he made mistakes. In his early zeal he dragged a persecution case before the mandarin with all his old lawyer’s force, and grew opium for one more summer before his conscience caught up with him. Setting out alone one evening on a seventeen-mile walk to pray with a dying woman, he found himself surrounded in the dark by wolves.

Hsi fell to his knees on the mountain road and cried aloud to God. “Everything,” he recorded, “grew strangely still. I know not when the wolves disappeared, or where they went. But they returned no more. Truly the Lord was my shield and my protector.”

The opium refuges

Hsi’s great work grew out of the need around him. In Shanxi, people joked that eleven men out of ten smoked opium, and he knew from experience how hopeless the habit was. With his friend Fan, a convert from a local religious sect, he began receiving addicts into homes where they were nursed through withdrawal, surrounded with prayer and hymns, and pointed to Christ. In 1883, when the missionaries’ supply of medicine ran out and patients were left in the middle of their cure, Hsi fasted and prayed and then compounded anti-opium pills from native drugs. They worked, and the refuges no longer depended on supplies from the coast. The refuges were self-supporting and run by Chinese Christians. Patients joined in worship morning and evening, because Hsi had no faith in medicine alone: as he had learned on his own knees, only Christ could break the chain. His refuges spread across Shanxi and into Henan and Shaanxi, often where no missionary had yet gone.

His home filled with former addicts, inquirers, and men in training, and he fed whoever came. In one lean year, facing a large debt, he won the first prize in a second Christian essay competition with a set of poems — the beginning of a gift for hymn-writing that gave the Shanxi churches some sixty songs in their own idiom.

Pastor of the flock

The Christians had long called him “our Pastor,” a title he tried hard to stop. In the summer of 1886 Hudson Taylor, founder of the China Inland Mission, came to southern Shanxi, and at the Hung-tung conference the missionaries and Chinese leaders asked Hsi to become superintending pastor of the churches across the three districts. He refused again and again: “Full of weakness and failings myself, how should I assume oversight of all the churches?” Only when the mission’s deputy director, J. W. Stevenson, told him that God had already called him to the work did he give way. In August 1886, pale from prayer and fasting, he knelt before Hudson Taylor in the first ordination service ever held in Shanxi.

The next year brought the darkest trial of his life. Some fellow workers, Fan among them, resented his new standing, and Hsi himself — his biographer does not hide it — gave them an opening by a lack of tact and humility, preaching once in a way that sounded like boasting over his own reward. In 1887 Fan led a mob that seized the Hung-tung refuge and, sword in hand, tried more than once to attack him. The rebels opened rival refuges beside his in more than twenty places. Hsi fasted for days at a time; “the tears that I shed,” he wrote, “were beyond knowledge.” He would not go to law. Within a few years the rival refuges had collapsed, and long afterwards Fan came to pay his respects to his old friend at the New Year.

Those years broke something in him and made something new. He drew close to Hoste, and the proud Confucianist became, by the testimony of those who lived with him, a servant. In 1891 he and Hoste led the Hung-tung church to renounce appeals to foreign treaty rights and trust the Lord alone in persecution. When a neighbour moved his boundary stones and took a patch of his best land, he let it go. “It is my Master’s land,” he said. “I hold it only for His service.” His quick temper still sometimes got the better of him, and when it did he would turn at once to prayer, saying, “Truly, I am nothing. I am unfit to shepherd the flock of God.”

The path that Jesus follows, leads to the Cross.

— Pastor Hsi

Higher service

In August 1895, at about sixty, Hsi gathered two hundred refuge workers at his home and preached a last, searching sermon on the rich man and Lazarus. A few days later he collapsed at Hung-tung. Doctors spoke of exhaustion after years of overwork, and of his heart. He was carried home and lay for six months, too weak at last to kneel or speak. “The Lord is taking away my strength,” he said. “It must be because my work is done.” He died on 19 February 1896, and was buried on a hillside overlooking the plain. By Hoste’s count about seven hundred people had been baptized in the churches under his care. Mrs. Hsi, weeping beside him, said, “I think of Jesus — and He is enough.” She carried on the women’s refuges after him and survived the Boxer persecution of 1900.

Three months after Hsi’s death, David Hill also died, in Central China. His story reached the wider church through two books by Hudson Taylor’s daughter-in-law, Geraldine Taylor. Its lesson is the one Hsi himself drew from his week of agony: that the chains of sin give way only to the living Christ, by the power of His Spirit.

faq.q: Who was Pastor Hsi (Xi Shengmo)?
faq.a: Pastor Hsi, or Xi Shengmo (c. 1836–1896), was a Confucian scholar from Shanxi in northern China who was set free from opium addiction when he became a Christian in 1879. He founded a network of self-supporting opium refuges that brought addicts to Christ, and in 1886 he was ordained pastor of the churches of southern Shanxi alongside the China Inland Mission.

faq.q: What was his early life like?
faq.a: He was born about 1836 in the Western Chang village near P'ing-yang (modern Linfen), the youngest son in a family of scholars and physicians. From the age of eight he was troubled by the fear of death. He won his first literary degree at sixteen and became an influential village leader and lawyer, feared for his temper and hostile to foreigners.

faq.q: How did he become addicted to opium?
faq.a: After his first wife died he turned to Taoism looking for immortality, but his health broke down. Around the age of thirty, sick and failing, he gave in to friends who urged him to smoke opium for the pain. He soon became a complete slave to it, lying on his couch for a year and a half while his studies and property slipped away.

faq.q: How did David Hill's essay prize lead to his conversion?
faq.a: In 1879 the missionary David Hill, who had come to Shanxi during the great famine, offered prizes for essays on Christian themes. Hsi read the Christian books to write his entries and won three of the four prizes. When he collected the money in person he was won over by Hill's kindness, became his Chinese teacher, and began reading the New Testament in Hill's house.

faq.q: How did he come to faith in Christ?
faq.a: Alone in his room, overwhelmed by his guilt and his slavery to opium, he knelt and read the story of the cross. When he reached Jesus' agony in Gethsemane he yielded himself to Christ with tears, as his Saviour and his God. When Hill urged him to wait before joining the believers, he answered, "From this day until death and beyond, I will never, never draw back."

faq.q: How was he freed from opium?
faq.a: He gave up opium at once and endured about a week of agony that no medicine relieved. Believing he was fighting a spiritual enemy, he prayed for the gift of the Holy Spirit, and he testified that the craving left him completely and never returned. He then took the name Shengmo, "Overcomer of Demons."

faq.q: What happened to his wife?
faq.a: Soon after his conversion his wife fell into an affliction the whole village believed was demon possession. After a three-day household fast, Hsi laid hands on her and commanded the evil spirits to leave in Jesus' name, and he and his biographer record that she was immediately delivered. She became a Christian and his lifelong partner in the work.

faq.q: What were the opium refuges?
faq.a: Starting with his friend Fan around 1882, Hsi took addicts into homes where they were nursed through withdrawal and surrounded with worship and prayer. In 1883 he compounded his own anti-opium pills after fasting and prayer. The refuges were self-supporting, staffed by Chinese Christians, and spread across Shanxi and into Henan and Shaanxi.

faq.q: When was he ordained, and what trials followed?
faq.a: In August 1886, at a conference attended by Hudson Taylor, he was ordained superintending pastor after repeatedly refusing the post as unworthy. In 1887 jealous fellow workers led by Fan seized one of his refuges, attacked him with a sword, and set up rival refuges. He refused to go to law, fasted and prayed, and grew humbler and gentler through the trial.

faq.q: How did his life end?
faq.a: In August 1895, after a conference at his home, he collapsed from years of overwork and lay weak for six months, saying the Lord was taking his strength because his work was done. He died on 19 February 1896, leaving churches in which about seven hundred people had been baptized. His wife carried on the women's refuges after him.

fields.name: Virginia W. Broughton
fields.bio: Fisk graduate of 1875 and Memphis teacher who became a Baptist missionary, leading the Bible Band movement among Black women in Tennessee and helping found the National Baptist Woman’s Convention.
fields.bio_html:
Virginia Walker was born in Nashville, Tennessee, in 1856, into a family that had paid dearly for its freedom. Her father, Nelson Walker, a native of Virginia, had been allowed by his master to hire out his own time, and with what he earned he bought his own freedom and then his wife’s. Virginia was named for the state he never stopped praising. Writing of herself fifty years later, she counted it “the godly heritage of being well born of honorable parents who had secured their freedom at great cost.” Before the Civil War she attended a private school, and she was still a child “when the new day of freedom dawned upon the race.”

When Fisk opened its doors to the freedpeople in 1867, she was among its very first pupils. Ten years of steady study later, in May 1875, she graduated from Fisk’s college department in its first graduating class. She believed she was “the first college graduate of womankind south of Mason and Dixon line,” and later historians have repeated her claim. Immediately after graduation a telegram called her to Memphis and a place in its public schools. For twelve years she taught in the Memphis public schools, rising to principal of the North Memphis school and then assistant principal of the Kortrecht grammar school, the most advanced public school for Black children in the city. She married Julius A. O. Broughton, and the couple raised a family of daughters and a son.

A meeting for women only

In January 1886 a white Baptist missionary named Joanna P. Moore came to Memphis, holding Bible readings in the churches by night. One day Moore called on her and invited Mrs. Broughton to a missionary meeting “for women only.” Such a thing, she remembered, “was an entirely new thing under the sun,” and she went chiefly out of curiosity. Out of that meeting came what they called a Bible Band, a circle of women pledged above all to “the daily study of the Bible.” The bands spread through the city; soon, she wrote, “every Monday afternoon women could be seen in all sections of the city with Bibles in their hands.” By March, Moore recorded, a city union of fifteen churches had enrolled 136 women, and “V. W. Broughton” was chosen its president.

She had no thought yet of missionary work. Then her mother died, “the deepest sorrow Virginia had ever known,” and the world seemed lonely and drear. Her own health failed. In the spring of 1887 she fell so seriously ill that her life was despaired of; she chose her burial clothes and gave everything up — “husband, children and all other earthly ties.”

Lying on what she believed was her deathbed in 1887, Virginia Broughton waited quietly “on the Lord for the expected summons.” Instead, she testified, she was “overshadowed with the veritable presence of God,” and made to understand “in language spoken to the soul, that God was not ready for her then, but He had a work for her to do.” Her strength began to return from that hour.

She came back to the Bible class so full of joy that at her first meeting she spoke twice. When a district association asked for a Bible woman to visit its country churches, her church sent her. Her first journey went up the Mississippi. She was afraid of water, and she set out only after being assured of something she never forgot.

God is on the water as well as on the land.

— Virginia W. Broughton

That first trip took her across the river in a leaking skiff, by night in an ox wagon, and on horseback through flooded bottomland to a settlement where, she said, “a women missionary of no race had ever gone.” She came home rejoicing, all her expenses met. For several years afterward she taught school five days a week and gave the other two to the country churches as far as fifty miles away, often walking from the railroad station into her classroom on Monday morning without having slept or eaten.

Opposition in the churches

In the spring of 1888 the board of the Bible and Normal Institute in Memphis, a new Baptist school left in debt by the murder of its benefactor, sent two Bible women out through West Tennessee to organize the women and children: Broughton and her friend Emma King. Everywhere they went, she wrote, “the people were aroused, some for them and many against them.” In September 1888 the first women’s district meeting gathered at Stanton, the first of ten annual meetings. The women urged on one another simple living, temperance, the education of “heart, head and hand,” and “above all things, loyalty to Christ.”

At the district meeting in Trenton so many women came that the food ran out after the first day. Mrs. Broughton told the sisters plainly how things stood and asked them to pray that God would feed the delegates. “Praise God!” she wrote. “The windows of Heaven were opened.” The white grocers, bakers and butchers of Trenton told the committee to take whatever supplies they needed, “without money or price,” for as long as the meeting lasted.

The deeper the work took root, the fiercer the resistance became. Most of the men, she said, “really believed the work unlawful and forbidden by the Scriptures” because of Paul’s words about women keeping silence in the churches. As the Bible women spoke out against drink, snuff-dipping and church fairs, ministers rose against them. Church houses were locked, and some women were beaten for trying to hold meetings.
