Another man said he would rather “flail the life out of a woman than to hear her speak in the church.” Some of these opponents were won over — one minister, who had come to gather evidence against her, stood up at the end to confess that he had been “washed, rinsed, starched, hung up, dried, sprinkled and ironed, and am now ready for service.” But for a season, she admitted, the work “seemed to stand still,” the women’s association broke up, and many bands disbanded while the women waited in prayer. In one dark stretch she longed to go home and rest, until Christ’s words came to her: “I must work the work of Him that sent me while it is day.” She saw, she wrote, that she was “only required to do the work assigned her and leave the results with God.”

“You two must settle it”

The hardest opposition came from home. Her husband was not yet a Christian, and he was strongly against her frequent journeys. Relatives sided with him, saying it was “unlike God to call a woman of family so frequently from her home duties.” One day he asked her, “When is this business going to stop?” Her answer became the hinge of her life.

I don’t know; but I belong to God first, and you next; so you two must settle it.

— Virginia W. Broughton

She left the matter in God’s hands, and, as she told it, God settled it. After a long struggle her husband yielded to Christ, made an open profession of faith, and was baptized on the same day as their two eldest daughters, Emma and Elizabeth. For the rest of her missionary life he looked after much of its business.

But the family talk had shaken her. At a meeting in Stanton she told one of the women that she did not know whether she would come again, “for it seems that I ought to be at home with my children.” Soon afterward her third daughter, little Selena, fell ill. Her mother stayed home, called a doctor, and sat by her bed, and still the child grew worse. Mrs. Broughton came to see, she wrote, that she could stay home with every help medicine could give and God might still take her children if He willed. The little girl died peacefully after praying, “Lord Jesus, help me,” and patting her mother’s cheek with the words “Poor little mama.” She was buried on a Friday; on Saturday morning her mother went out on her mission. God used her so powerfully that day that her bitterest critics said, “Let that woman alone, God is truly with her.” She never again let fear for her home keep her from her calling.

We praise God for afflictions; for in mercy they are all sent to bring us near to God.

— Virginia W. Broughton

A missionary of faith

Giving up her teaching post was its own struggle — “a substantial, sure support” traded for “work of faith, with no visible means of support.” For many years her custom was to read the Bible through, and it was on an afternoon when she had just finished one such reading that the call to leave the classroom came home to her, and she surrendered. Not long afterward the Woman’s Baptist Home Mission Society of Chicago commissioned her as its missionary for western Tennessee. For the Society she also toured the North, speaking at the Northern Baptist anniversary meetings at Saratoga, New York, where she was the only Black woman among the speakers.

She believed God still heals, and her book tells of prayers at sickbeds, among them those for her brother John, a physician, who recovered from a grave illness after the doctors and his family had given him up. She was careful to add that this “does not discard the use of means,” and that she believed “in the science and practice of medicine as one of the divinely appointed means to man’s physical healing.” In the later 1890s she also took up the Holiness teaching of sanctification — a deeper surrender to Christ and fullness of the Holy Spirit — at a time when the controversy was splitting Baptist churches in the South. She pressed for “holiness of heart and uprightness of daily deportment” but urged her Bible women to stay in their own churches, and the persecution that followed grew so heavy that for a time it seemed aimed at her very life.

During that conflict the Bible women of Woodlawn called a special meeting at their church to pray for their leader. She recorded that God “then and there assured them that they would see their sister again standing as usual in their church to tell the blessed story of Jesus and his love” — and she lived, she wrote, to see God’s power and wisdom in her deliverance.

Wider fields

In December 1899 the Broughtons moved back to Nashville, the city of her birth. For three years she worked at Sunshine Home, the headquarters of Joanna Moore’s Fireside School, as one of Moore’s secretaries and assistant editor of Moore’s Bible-study paper Hope, and for six months as its supervisor. Moore described her as one of the helpers who had “proven wise, kind and efficient,” and Broughton called those years her “post course in Bible study.”

For years she had pleaded at the National Baptist Convention for a women’s organization of their own. In 1900, at Richmond, Virginia, it was formed: the Woman’s Convention, Auxiliary to the National Baptist Convention, with Virginia Broughton as recording secretary and Nannie Helen Burroughs as corresponding secretary. When some sought to disband it the next year, the women held firm. At Birmingham she was made educational secretary, charged with preparing a course of Bible lessons for the convention’s paper. In 1904 she published Woman’s Work, as Gleaned from the Women of the Bible, setting out from Scripture the place God had given women in the home and the church. Her own sermon outline on the subject drew on Deborah, Esther, Ruth and Lydia and rested on Galatians 3:28: “All believers one in Christ.”

From 1905 she lectured for the John C. Martin Educational Fund, organizing women’s Bible unions across the South, and in 1906–07 she taught Bible at the Agricultural and Mechanical College at Normal, Alabama. In 1907 she published her life story, Twenty Year’s Experience of a Missionary, writing of herself as “Virginia” and hoping it would “encourage others to dedicate their lives to the Master’s service.”

Faithful to the end

She did not stop. She kept travelling and teaching for the women’s missionary work in Tennessee for almost three decades more. Her husband died in 1930. In 1929 the Tennessee women’s convention honored her with words that capture her life: because of “her intellectual advantages and religious fervor, she has not exalted herself but humbled herself and become one with those who did not have her advantages, and helped them to see the light.” She died on September 21, 1934, at seventy-eight.

She had begun as a schoolteacher curious about a meeting “for women only,” and she lived to see Black Baptist women organized across the South, studying their Bibles at their own firesides. She knew opposition from pulpits and from her own family, and the grief of a little grave. Through it all she held to the hymn she said God gave her when she rose from her sickbed in 1887, “How firm a foundation, ye saints of the Lord,” and to the conviction that settled every quarrel: she belonged to God first.

faq.q: Who was Virginia W. Broughton?
faq.a: Virginia W. Broughton (1856–1934) was a Black Baptist teacher and missionary from Tennessee who led the Bible Band movement among Black women from the late 1880s. A member of Fisk University's first graduating class in 1875, she spent nearly fifty years organizing women for Bible study and mission work, and in 1907 told her story in Twenty Year's Experience of a Missionary.

faq.q: What was her early life like?
faq.a: She was born Virginia Walker in Nashville in 1856. Her father, a Virginian, hired out his own time and used his earnings to buy his freedom and then his wife's, and he named his daughter for his native state. She attended a private school before the Civil War and was among the first pupils when Fisk opened to the freedpeople in 1867.

faq.q: What did she do after Fisk?
faq.a: She graduated from Fisk's college department in May 1875 and believed she was the first woman college graduate south of the Mason–Dixon line. She went straight to Memphis, where she taught in the public schools for twelve years, becoming a principal and then assistant principal of the Kortrecht grammar school. She married Julius A. O. Broughton and raised a family.

faq.q: How did the Bible Band work begin?
faq.a: In January 1886 the Baptist missionary Joanna P. Moore invited her to a missionary meeting for women only, and out of it came a Bible Band devoted to daily Bible study. The bands spread across Memphis, and by March a city union of fifteen churches and 136 women had chosen Broughton as its president.

faq.q: What happened in her illness of 1887?
faq.a: After her mother's death her own health broke, and in the spring of 1887 she was so ill that she chose her burial clothes and gave up every earthly tie. She testified that God's presence came over her and made her understand that He was not ready for her yet and had a work for her to do. Her strength returned, and she began going out to the country churches as a Bible woman.

faq.q: What opposition did she face?
faq.a: Many Baptist ministers and laymen believed Scripture forbade women to speak in church, and they fought the women's work hard: churches were locked, some women were beaten, and for a time the women's association broke up. Some opponents were won over after hearing her, and she resolved simply to do the work assigned her and leave the results with God.

faq.q: How did she answer her husband's objections?
faq.a: Her husband was not yet a Christian and opposed her frequent journeys. When he asked when this business would stop, she answered that she belonged to God first and to him next, so the two of them must settle it. In time he professed faith in Christ, was baptized with their two eldest daughters, and helped with the business of her mission.

faq.q: What did she believe about healing and holiness?
faq.a: She believed God still heals in answer to prayer and recorded recoveries she had prayed for, including her brother John's. She also insisted that medicine is one of God's appointed means of healing. In the later 1890s she embraced the Holiness teaching of sanctification, which brought fierce persecution, but she urged her Bible women to stay in their own churches.

faq.q: What were her later years of work?
faq.a: From 1899 she worked in Nashville with Joanna Moore's Fireside School and helped edit its paper Hope. In 1900 she helped found the Woman's Convention, Auxiliary to the National Baptist Convention, serving as its recording secretary and later as educational secretary. She published Woman's Work, as Gleaned from the Women of the Bible in 1904 and lectured and taught Bible across the South.

faq.q: How is she remembered?
faq.a: She kept up her mission work in Tennessee until her death on September 21, 1934, at seventy-eight. In 1929 the Tennessee women's convention praised her for humbling herself to become one with those who lacked her advantages and helping them to see the light. Her autobiography remains a rare first-hand record of Black Baptist women's mission work in the South.

fields.name: Krupabai Satthianadhan
fields.bio: Indian Christian writer (1862–1894), daughter of Brahmin converts, among the first women at Madras Medical College and one of the first Indian women novelists in English, author of Saguna and Kamala.
fields.bio_html:
Krupabai Satthianadhan lived only thirty-two years, and for much of that short life she was ill. Yet she left behind two novels in English that made her, in the words of the friend who wrote her memoir, “the first of Indian women novelists” — and, running beneath both books, the quiet testimony of a young woman who had met Christ in her loneliness and never let Him go. In her last months, dictating chapters to her husband with a raging fever, she gave the reason she kept on writing.

Let me show that even a simple Indian girl can do something useful.

— Krupabai Satthianadhan

A Brahmin household turned to Christ

She was born at Ahmednagar, in the Bombay Presidency, on 14 February 1862, the thirteenth child of Haripunt and Radhabai Khisty. Her parents were remembered as the first Brahmin converts to Christianity in the Bombay Presidency. Their great struggle was over before any of their children were born, but Krupabai grew up on its story, and years later she told it — lightly fictionalised, with her father renamed Harichandra — in her first novel. It is difficult, her memoirist wrote, to over-rate what a Brahmin gave up in renouncing the faith of his fathers: friends, position, wealth, nearly everything men hold dear.

In her daughter’s telling, Haripunt’s turning came one evening as the Gospel he had been reading rose before him in a new light: Christ stooping beside a blind beggar, healing the sick, raising the fallen, and at last dying on Calvary. “Such love! I will follow Thee, my Saviour,” she has him cry. “All I have I leave to follow Thee.” Radhabai, a child-wife, at first felt herself trapped in a missionary’s house and polluted by it; she threw her jewels at her husband’s feet and begged him to take her home. Only slowly, through his patience and the kindness around her, did she yield — and in the end, her daughter wrote, she “found a rich harvest of joy and happiness” in the religion her husband had embraced.

Haripunt spent the rest of his life as a Christian missionary, and the home the Khistys made was, in Krupabai’s words, one where “the Christian life … was of a simple apostolic type.” The children wore coarse clothes their mother sewed, the girls owned no jewels, and the boys took to manual labour as readily as to books. Radhabai never learned to read, but she set no barrier in the way of her children’s schooling. Krupabai’s father died while she was still small, and an elder sister and her brother Bhasker took up the work of teaching the younger ones.

Bhasker and the mountain-top

Bhasker, much older than she, became the great influence of her childhood. She was a fiercely bright little girl who insisted on sitting in while her brothers studied — and who corrected their sums — and it was Bhasker who stood her friend. When the family moved to the hills of the Upper Deccan for his failing health, the two walked the mountain paths together at dawn. On one such morning, watching the sun break through the mist, he told her that a land before the light of Christianity comes is like that dark hillside, and that the Gospel brings everything into its true beauty, as the sun does.

On their last morning in the hills, she remembered, they climbed above the clouds before the stars had faded, and Bhasker turned to her: “It was in this place with such a scene before me some years ago that I determined that my life should be pure and holy. Oh how our lives are wasted. Promise to me that yours will be devoted to God’s glory.” Then, she wrote, “We were alone, alone with God on the mountain top and we fell on our knees and prayed.”

Bhasker did not live long. Her account of his death in Saguna is among the most moving pages she wrote: the brother telling their mother, “We are all pilgrims. I am going before, and you will follow me,” charging his younger brothers to “Be real torch-bearers,” and the little sister clinging to his neck crying that he must not die. For months afterwards the children would gather round their mother at dusk, and she would hold them and say, “Yes! God, God alone is left now.” But Krupabai confessed that she “failed to understand God’s ways,” and that her grief was “intense, almost rebellious.” Her health suffered for months.

Lonely at school, found by Christ

Partly in hope of rousing her, she was sent to study with missionary ladies and then to the Zenana Mission school in Bombay. She was so far ahead of girls her age that she could not be placed in any class and was allowed her own course of study. She was also, her memoirist admitted, intensely self-conscious and over-sensitive, and the school was not easy for her. In Saguna she tells of being labelled the “ungodly one” by the pious girls of a prayer union, and of fleeing to the garden afterwards to weep. There, misunderstood on every side, she found herself longing for a love “that can cover even one’s deficiencies,” and a silent prayer rose “to Bhasker’s God and mine.”

She needed, she wrote, one “who had lived the life of man in this world, and who understood human motives and human longings … the loving God made man in Christ.” And then: “Him I needed, and He came and I found joy.” Her prayer in that hour was a cry of surrender: “I cannot let Thee go. I could not do without Thee. Thou knowest the future and Thou wilt guide me. Stand by me, Christ, and all will be right.”

In the novel the bitterness drained out of her that day; she wanted to embrace the very girls who had hurt her, and the words kept singing in her ears, “Jesus is near and all is well.” Saguna is a novel, and its scenes are shaped and idealised; but her friend and memoirist, who knew her from her student days, called it “essentially an autobiography,” and these pages ring with the sound of a real conversion.

The first Indian woman at Madras Medical College

At the Bombay school she came under the influence of an American woman doctor, and set her heart on medicine. Her friends hoped to send her to England to study, but her health was judged too frail. Madras Medical College had just opened its doors to women, and so, still in her teens, she travelled alone from Bombay to Madras. She was received there into the home of the Rev. W. T. Satthianadhan, a respected Tamil clergyman, and his wife and daughters, and spent a happy year with them while attending lectures. When she first entered the lecture hall, the whole body of students rose and cheered her: she was, her memoirist wrote, the first Indian lady to join their ranks. By the end of the year she had won several prizes and stood first in every subject but chemistry. A former head of the college later remembered her as “one of the sweetest characters I ever knew.”

But after the strain of examinations her health broke down completely, and she was never strong enough to return to her medical studies. It was one of the griefs of her life that the dream of qualifying, perhaps in England, was never fulfilled.

A marriage of shared purpose

In 1881 she married Samuel Satthianadhan, the son of the household that had welcomed her, just returned from nearly four years at Cambridge. It may have cost her something: she had once written, “How hard it seemed to my mind that marriage should be the goal of a woman’s ambition.” But she found in him a companion whose aims matched her own, and whose feet, as she put it, were “planted on the Rock of Ages.”

Christ was ours. God was ours. Heaven was ours, and our lives were to be one full and joyous song.

— Krupabai Satthianadhan

For nearly two years they lived at Ootacamund in the Nilgiri hills, where Samuel was headmaster of the Breeks Memorial School. The mountains revived her, and she set out at once to be useful. She spent hours each week visiting women in their zenanas, helped improve the teaching at the Hobart School for Indian girls, and started a small school for Muslim girls, whom no one had yet provided for; it later grew into a sizeable school under the Church Missionary Society. Here too she began to write — descriptive pieces for the South India Observer, published as the work of “an Indian lady.”

Writing through weakness

In 1884 Samuel was posted to Rajahmundry. There she broke a blood-vessel without warning and spent about a year as a complete invalid. At Kumbakonam her strength slowly returned, and she loved to gather people of every condition round her sofa to hear their joys and sorrows. In 1886 they moved to Madras, where Samuel later became professor of logic and philosophy at the Presidency College. There, urged by her husband and a friend, she began to write about what she knew best — her own childhood. The result was Saguna: A Story of Native Christian Life, serialised in the Madras Christian College Magazine in 1887–88 and later published as a book in 1895. It was reviewed warmly in English journals, and Queen Victoria herself accepted a copy.

Not every reader was pleased. Her satirical chapter on a Christian village of poor converts was taken as an attack by some of the very people she meant to serve, and her memoirist felt it fair to her memory to explain that she had wished only to describe its quaintness and the troubles of converts left without careful oversight. The book’s heart, though, was her own home — a picture, the memoirist thought, that should be read by all who doubted what Christianity had done for India.

Soon after the last chapter appeared, her only child was born — a baby lent to its parents, her memoirist wrote, “for a few short months.” The little one’s death nearly cost Krupabai her own life, and her husband wrote that “she was never herself after this great loss.” Yet she did not complain, but moved about quietly, trying to make herself useful. A journey to her old home in Bombay only exhausted her, and in a Madras hospital she was told that her illness — tuberculosis, as later accounts name it — must sooner or later prove fatal. She received the news, her friend wrote, “with her usual quiet strength and sweetness.” The deaths of her husband’s mother and father, whom she had loved since they first took her in, followed close behind.

Kamala, and the last months

She wrote all the more. A history of her father-in-law’s conversion came first, then sketches of her mother-in-law’s life and schools, and then a second novel, Kamala: A Story of Hindu Life. Some of its chapters she worked out in her hospital bed; much of it was written at Coonoor in the Nilgiris in 1893. When she could no longer hold a pen she dictated, and some of the last chapters were taken down by her husband while her temperature stood at 104 degrees.

Kamala is the story of a Hindu child-wife, and it shows how deeply Krupabai loved the women of her country who did not share her faith. She wrote with tenderness of the burdens they bore — “Blame not the poor Indian woman for her love of jewellery,” she pleaded, since jewels were often all that would be left to her if she were widowed. She drew Kamala’s quiet goodness with a loving hand, and pleaded with English readers to understand such women.

She lived to see Kamala appear in the same journal that had carried Saguna. In April 1894 she was taken again to Coonoor, tenderly nursed by her husband and his sister. Her friend wrote that her cheerfulness never forsook her, and that “her strong faith burnt more brightly as death approached.” Tennyson’s “Crossing the Bar” — “Sunset and evening star, and one clear call for me” — was often on her lips. She returned to Madras, but the sudden death of the sister-in-law who had nursed her was more than her weakened body could bear, and she died peacefully in August 1894. She was buried beside her child in the cemetery at Purasawalkam in Madras. Kamala was published as a book that same year, and Saguna the next.

Within months of her death her name was given to memorials in Madras — remembered at the medical college that had cheered her and at the University — honouring a young woman who had opened doors for those who came after her. She left no children, and she never sought fame. But the vow she made with Bhasker on the mountain-top was kept. Her books carry, as her memoirist wrote, “the pure and earnest spirit which breathes in every line,” and in them a lonely schoolgirl’s prayer still sounds: “Stand by me, Christ, and all will be right.”

faq.q: Who was Krupabai Satthianadhan?
faq.a: Krupabai Satthianadhan (1862–1894) was an Indian Christian writer from western India, remembered as one of the first Indian women to write novels in English. She wrote Saguna: A Story of Native Christian Life and Kamala: A Story of Hindu Life, studied medicine for a year at Madras Medical College, and started a school for Muslim girls at Ootacamund before dying of a long illness at thirty-two.

faq.q: What family was she born into?
faq.a: She was born at Ahmednagar in the Bombay Presidency on 14 February 1862, the thirteenth child of Haripunt and Radhabai Khisty, remembered as the first Brahmin converts to Christianity in that presidency. Her father gave up wealth, position and family to follow Christ and became a Christian missionary, and her mother, at first bitterly opposed, came in time to share his faith.

faq.q: Who was her brother Bhasker?
faq.a: Bhasker was her much older brother, who encouraged her studies and became the great spiritual influence of her childhood. On a mountain-top in the Deccan he asked her to promise that her life would be devoted to God's glory, and the two knelt and prayed together. His early death left her in deep grief for many months.

faq.q: How did she come to faith in Christ herself?
faq.a: At the Zenana Mission school in Bombay she felt lonely and misjudged, and in her autobiographical novel Saguna she describes weeping in the garden after being called ungodly. There she prayed to her brother's God, longing for Christ who understood human longings, and wrote, "Him I needed, and He came and I found joy." Her prayer was, "Stand by me, Christ, and all will be right."

faq.q: Is Saguna a true story?
faq.a: Saguna is a novel, and its scenes and names are shaped and idealised, so it should be read with care. But the friend who wrote her memoir, who knew her from her student days, called it essentially an autobiography, and its accounts of her parents' conversion, her brother and her schooling follow her own life closely.

faq.q: What happened when she studied medicine?
faq.a: Inspired by an American woman doctor, she went alone from Bombay to Madras Medical College, which had just opened to women, and lived with the family of the Rev. W. T. Satthianadhan. Her memoirist says the students rose and cheered her as the first Indian lady among them, and she won several prizes in her first year. Her health then broke down, and she was never able to resume her studies.

faq.q: Whom did she marry?
faq.a: In 1881 she married Samuel Satthianadhan, the son of the household that had welcomed her in Madras, who had just returned from Cambridge. She wrote that their feet were planted on the Rock of Ages and that Christ, God and heaven were theirs. They lived at Ootacamund, Rajahmundry, Kumbakonam and Madras as his educational work took them.

faq.q: What work did she do besides writing?
faq.a: At Ootacamund she visited women in their zenanas, helped improve the teaching at the Hobart School for Indian girls, and started a small school for Muslim girls, which later grew under the Church Missionary Society. She also began writing articles for local papers under the name of an Indian lady.

faq.q: What sorrows did she face?
faq.a: She suffered long illnesses, including a year as an invalid at Rajahmundry. Her only child died after a few months, and her husband wrote that she was never herself after that loss. She was then told her illness, tuberculosis, would prove fatal, and soon afterward she lost her husband's parents, whom she dearly loved.

faq.q: How did her life end?
faq.a: She kept writing, dictating the last chapters of Kamala to her husband with a high fever and saying she wanted to show that a simple Indian girl could do something useful. Her friend wrote that her strong faith burned more brightly as death approached. She died in Madras in August 1894, aged thirty-two, and was buried beside her child; memorials in her name were set up in Madras soon afterward.

fields.name: Dora Yu
fields.bio: Chinese evangelist and revival preacher (1873–1931). A trained doctor who gave up medicine to preach by faith, she founded a Bible school in Shanghai and led the 1920 Fuzhou meetings at which Watchman Nee and his mother came to Christ.
fields.bio_html:
Dora Yu was born in 1873 in the compound of the American Presbyterian Mission in Hangzhou, where her father was studying to become a preacher. He had come a long way to that compound. Her father, the son of a wealthy Confucian family, had studied medicine and practised as a physician until the Taiping Rebellion, when the rebels took him prisoner. He won their favour by doctoring their soldiers, but never felt safe among them, and one night he escaped. Afterwards, in Hangzhou, he heard the gospel and became a Christian, and at forty he married. Dora and her sister, three years older, were the only children.

She grew up in parsonages, first in the tea country outside Hangzhou and then in the towns where her father served as pastor. She was a slow pupil beside her bright sister, and remembered herself as a child who believed everything she was told and could never quite see a joke. But her faith came early and stayed. She could not remember a time, she wrote, when she forgot to pray, and “Christ was a very real Person to me, and I loved Him.” Her sister was afraid of the dark; Dora used to ask herself, “If Jesus is here, why should I fear?”

I often think that when I stand in my glorified body for the first moment in the presence of my Lord, my first exclamation will be—“Grace! Wonderful Grace!”

— Dora Yu

A medical student alone in the world

In 1888, at fifteen, she left home for Suzhou (then spelled Soochow) to study Western medicine at the women’s hospital and medical school there. Three months later her father died. Within two years her mother, who for six winters had been unable to lie down because of heart disease, died too. Her parents had prayed to be spared until their girls were old enough to be left; that prayer, she said, was answered — but the loneliness was very great, and for years afterwards she could hardly bear to see a family gathered together. In the holidays, when every other student went home, she stayed behind.

She had made her own choice of a husband and was engaged, but as the wedding drew near (in 1892, according to her Chinese biographers) she found she could not go through with it. She feared, she wrote, that her love for God would be divided. Engagements were not easily broken in China, and for two weeks she wept and pleaded with God to set her free, promising to be His servant for the rest of her life — though she had first to be willing to say yes if He willed her to marry. The engagement was broken. Friends criticized her; she felt God telling her to take it quietly and show her sincerity by her life rather than her words. She never married.

“Lord, is this Thy love?”

She had read her Bible and prayed three times a day since childhood. Yet in 1895, a year before she was due to graduate, she woke one morning under a crushing sense of condemnation, convinced that she had committed a sin that could not be forgiven. For two weeks she could scarcely eat. She cried aloud for mercy day and night. A missionary friend begged her to believe in Christ for forgiveness, and she tried, but did not know how. Then a harder question was put to her: if it was God’s will that she spend the rest of her life as an invalid, would she accept it? She paused before the dark future that opened up, and then, deciding that no bodily suffering could be worse than the terror she was in, she cried out, “Yes, Lord, I am willing.”

In those weeks God brought her sins to mind, small and large, and taught her — she had not known it was in the Bible — that true repentance meant confession and restitution. Even a handful of corks once taken from the hospital dispensary without asking had to be paid for. Then one night, before the lamp was put out, the darkness broke. “All of a sudden God opened heaven to me, and filled me with His divine love,” she wrote. She cried out, “Lord, is this Thy love? I have never known it before.” She got out of bed to pray and could only say, three times over, “Lord, I thank Thee.” The next day even the sun seemed to shine more brightly.

She graduated in 1896 — she and a classmate were the school’s first women graduates — and stayed on at the hospital. She lived, she said, a year and a half in that heavenly joy, and then by her own account she drifted, grieving the Holy Spirit by ambition, until the world began to look attractive and real again.

Wanderings in Korea

In October 1897 her missionary friend, Josephine Campbell, invited her to Korea, where Campbell was opening the women’s work of the Southern Methodist mission in Seoul. Dora accepted at once — and later judged that she had gone “without permission from the King.” She titled this chapter of her life “Wanderings in the Wilderness.” She learned Korean, practised medicine and preached, did the work of a Bible-woman, and taught Chinese embroidery and lacework to the girls of the mission school. But her health collapsed. In 1899 she was sent home to China, where doctors told her she would likely be an invalid for life. She recovered enough to go back to Seoul in January 1900, then declined again for years — sleepless, living on drugs, weeping at the smallest trouble. Once, in the darkest stretch, the thought came to take a strong dose of a drug and be done with it; she answered, “No, I am going to wait God’s time.”

Just before her return to Korea, her sister fell gravely ill shortly after giving birth to her sixth child. Dora lay awake at night with a heavy heart, having asked God to carry the burden for her.

As she lay sleepless, Dora Yu heard the Lord rebuke her worry: she had asked Him to bear the heavy load, “But how can I do it unless you lay it down?” Ashamed of her unbelief, she asked forgiveness and went to sleep. At five the next morning she found her sister’s fever gone; the sister who had been unconscious the night before knew her. “How grateful I was to God!”

For two years she felt God telling her to go home to China, but she lingered, clinging, she said, to something He had told her to put aside. In the summer of 1903 she finally gave way.

With only twenty-six cents in the bank, Dora Yu prayed, “Lord, if Thou dost want me to return to China, give me some money.” Within a month she received five times her usual amount, for no reason she ever discovered “except that God answered prayer.” She sailed for China in the autumn of 1903.

Living by faith

Back in China she resolved to take no salary, though she could have supported herself by medicine. In January 1904 she rented a house near her sister’s home in order to preach the gospel to anyone she met. Before she moved in, the promised subscriptions collapsed, and her family feared her mind was not quite right. She went ahead, leaning on Jeremiah’s promise of “an expected end,” and gave up medicine for good. It became, she said, one of the most precious years of her life. Needs were met as they came. Late in 1904 her sister, her brother-in-law and their two eldest children were converted in revival meetings; he later became an evangelist himself.

At the second series of those meetings, the missionary women who were to lead the women’s sessions sent word they could hardly come, and the work fell to Dora — a woman who had lisped as a child and told stories badly.

On the first morning Dora Yu rose at five, earnestly asking God for a message, and none seemed to come. As the church bell rang she went in “in fear and trembling,” hearing the Lord say, “I will put my own words into your lips when the time comes.” “Lord,” she answered, “the time has come, the bell has rung, and the people are gathering.” There was blessing in the meeting, and she spoke for ten days in succession.

From then on she was sent from mission to mission to preach. In the winter of 1907, sensing that she was working because she had become known as a worker rather than for love’s sake, she withdrew with a handful of pastors who felt the same need and confessed that she had left her “first love.” She found companions in the books of Andrew Murray, D. L. Moody and others. In 1908, with two friends, she prayed for a quiet place in Shanghai where Chinese Christians could “come apart and rest awhile,” and a gift from an American visitor rented the house she named the Bible Study and Prayer House. Bible readings began in Chinese, English and Korean, and the rooms were soon outgrown. A summer Bible school followed, drawing preachers’ wives, Bible-women and teachers from ten provinces through the August heat.

Revival in the south

Her first call to South China came in the spring of 1909. She could not speak a word of the southern dialects; she preached in English and missionaries translated. Before she left, she recalled one more old sin — glancing at notes during her final medical examination — and made it right. In the meetings that followed, she wrote, “God indeed visited us in mighty power”: pastors, preachers and church members pushed through the crowded church to take one another’s hands in tears, confessing their wrongs. Revival preaching took her across the country after that, and Chinese believers came to say that the north had Ding Limei and the south had Dora Yu.

In 1913–14 she travelled around the world for thirteen months. She came home grieved at what she had seen of “Higher Criticism” in the West and now in China, and she said plainly that it would be better for a missionary to stay home or go into business “than to be engaged in preaching a Christless Gospel.” She returned in December 1914 with a plan for a small house at Jiangwan (Chiangwan), outside Shanghai, where believers could be trained not only to search the Scriptures but to live them. Chinese Christians gave most of the money unasked, some selling their jewellery. The Bible school opened in 1916 with room for twelve. That year she published, in English, the little memoir God’s Dealings with Dora Yü: A Chinese Messenger of the Cross, later reissued in London.

It is only in proportion to my height in the heavenly places that I am able to come down low enough for God to use me.

— Dora Yu

The meetings at Fuzhou

In the spring of 1920 she held revival meetings at the Methodist Church of Heavenly Peace in Fuzhou. Among those who came was Lin Heping, a churchgoing mother who was converted there. Soon afterwards, in April 1920, Lin’s seventeen-year-old son, Ni Shuzu, also gave his life to Christ. He became known as Watchman Nee, and he later said simply that he had been saved through a woman believer, Dora Yu. For a time he studied at her Bible school in Shanghai, and she is also credited with introducing him to the English missionary Margaret Barber, who became his chief mentor. Through Nee and his mother, the fruit of those Fuzhou meetings ran on through Chinese Christianity for generations.

In 1927 Dora Yu went to England and spoke at the Keswick Convention — a rare honour for a Chinese Christian. Reports of her addresses say she pleaded with Western churches to stop sending missionaries who preached liberal theology to China. She returned to Shanghai by way of the United States in 1929.

Occupying till He came

Her health had been fragile all her life, and her last years were years of illness. She died in Shanghai in the spring of 1931, in her late fifties. She had prayed, near the end of her little book, that God would keep her “watching and waiting for His return,” and willing to fill any vacancy below until that coming.

She would not have wanted praise; God’s servants, she wrote, must “forward all the praises” to Him. Her own life was full of failures she refused to hide — the hasty journey to Korea, the bromide, the temper, the cooling of first love — and every one of them she told so that others passing through the same trials might take heart. Yet she had learned to live by faith with no salary, to preach without a script, and to wait for orders from what she called “the Almighty Captain.” Her book ends with a prayer and a plea that its readers would pray for her work, closing with the Bible’s own last prayer: “O Lord, come quickly. Amen.”

faq.q: Who was Dora Yu?
faq.a: Dora Yu (Yu Cidu, 1873–1931) was a Chinese evangelist, revival preacher and Bible teacher. Trained in Western medicine, she gave up practice to preach by faith without a salary, founded the Bible Study and Prayer House and a Bible school in Shanghai, and led the 1920 meetings in Fuzhou through which Watchman Nee and his mother came to faith.

faq.q: What was her early life like?
faq.a: She was born in 1873 in the American Presbyterian Mission compound in Hangzhou, where her father, a former physician who had escaped captivity among the Taiping rebels, was training to be a preacher. She and her older sister were the only children. She wrote that she could not remember a time when she forgot to pray, and that Christ was a very real Person to her as a child.

faq.q: Where did she study medicine?
faq.a: In 1888, at fifteen, she left home to study Western medicine at the women's hospital and medical school in Suzhou (Soochow). Her father died three months after she arrived and her mother within two years, leaving her very much alone. She graduated in 1896 as one of the school's first two women graduates.

faq.q: How did she come to a deep assurance of God's love?
faq.a: In 1895 she was seized for two weeks by a terrible sense of condemnation, believing her sin could not be forgiven. She confessed and made restitution for wrongs God brought to mind and finally told the Lord she was willing even to be an invalid for life. One night, she wrote, God opened heaven to her and filled her with His love, and she could only say, Lord, I thank Thee.

faq.q: What did she do in Korea?
faq.a: In October 1897 she went to Seoul with the Southern Methodist missionary Josephine Campbell, where she practised medicine, preached, did the work of a Bible-woman and taught in the mission school. She later called those years her wanderings in the wilderness, because she felt she had gone without God's leading. Serious illness dogged her there, and she returned to China in 1903 after praying for, and receiving, the money for the journey.

faq.q: How did her preaching ministry begin?
faq.a: Back in China in January 1904 she rented a house to preach the gospel, refusing a salary and giving up medicine, though her family feared for her. When she was unexpectedly left to lead the women's revival meetings in her sister's city, she prayed for a message and went in trembling, and found blessing for ten days in succession. From then on she was invited from mission to mission to preach.

faq.q: What was the Bible Study and Prayer House?
faq.a: In 1908 she and two friends prayed for a quiet place in Shanghai where Chinese Christians could come apart to pray and study Scripture, and a gift from an American visitor rented the house. Bible readings, prayer meetings and a summer Bible school followed, drawing women workers from ten provinces. In 1916 she opened a small residential Bible school at Jiangwan outside Shanghai, built largely with gifts from Chinese Christians.

faq.q: How was she connected with Watchman Nee?
faq.a: In spring 1920 she led revival meetings at the Church of Heavenly Peace in Fuzhou, where Lin Heping was converted. Soon afterwards, in April 1920, Lin's seventeen-year-old son, Watchman Nee, also gave his life to Christ. He later studied for a time at her Bible school in Shanghai, and she is credited with introducing him to the missionary Margaret Barber.

faq.q: Did she preach outside China?
faq.a: Yes. Besides her years in Korea, she travelled around the world for thirteen months in 1913–14, and in 1927 she spoke at the Keswick Convention in England. There she urged Western churches to stop sending missionaries who preached liberal theology to China. She returned to Shanghai by way of the United States in 1929.

faq.q: How did Dora Yu's life end?
faq.a: Her health had been fragile all her life, and she died in Shanghai in the spring of 1931 after years of illness. She left a short memoir, God's Dealings with Dora Yu, in which she told her failures as honestly as her blessings so that others in the same trials might take heart. She is remembered as a pioneer of Chinese revival preaching who lived by faith.

fields.name: Mary Stone (Shi Meiyu)
fields.bio: Chinese Christian physician (1873–1954), one of the first Chinese women to earn a US medical degree, who ran the Danforth Memorial Hospital in Jiujiang, trained China’s nurses, and co-founded the Bethel Mission in Shanghai.
fields.bio_html:
On the first day of the third moon of 1873, in the river city of Kiukiang — today’s Jiujiang, in Jiangxi province — a young Chinese pastor knelt beside his wife and gave their newborn daughter back to God. They named her Maiyü, “Beautiful Gem,” and before she was a day old they had agreed on something almost unheard of in Central China: her feet would never be bound. Her father was a pastor of the Methodist Episcopal mission, in charge of a chapel in Kiukiang; her mother was the first convert of the missionary Gertrude Howe’s work among Chinese women, and ran a day school for girls. The child would grow up as Shi Meiyu, and the English-speaking world would come to know her as Dr. Mary Stone.

Margaret Burton, who gathered her story from family and friends in 1912, records that on the day Maiyü was born her father knelt by his wife’s side and, together with her, “reverently consecrated to the service of the Divine Father” the little daughter God had given them.

The decision cost the girl something. Unbound feet marked her out for ridicule from adults and children alike. One day an older girl stopped her on the road to school and refused to let her pass unless she knelt and bowed to her own bandaged feet; little Maiyü would not, and only her mother’s help got her through. Relatives warned that no family would ever take her as a daughter-in-law.

Her mother taught her at home, and before she was eight she had memorized the Gospel of Matthew and the catechism in Chinese. Then her father did something even more startling than leaving her feet alone. Impressed by the work of the American medical missionary Dr. Kate Bushnell among the women and children of Kiukiang, he brought his eight-year-old daughter to her and said, “Here is my little girl. I want you to make a doctor of her.” There was no such thing as a Chinese woman physician. Maiyü was placed under Gertrude Howe at the mission’s girls’ boarding school, and spent most of the next ten years there, studying in Chinese and English for a medical course that did not yet exist for anyone like her.

Ann Arbor

In 1892 Miss Howe took Maiyü and her friend Ida Kahn (Kang Cheng), who had grown up in Howe’s own household, to the United States. Both girls passed the entrance examinations of the University of Michigan’s medical department — arithmetic, algebra, rhetoric, history, physics and Latin — and their progress was watched with real curiosity. Professors struggled with her name, so she took its English meaning: Shi is “stone,” and Mary Stone she became.

While she studied, the cause of her childhood followed her across the ocean. Her mother had kept her own feet bound, so that no one could say she had spared her daughters out of ignorance rather than conviction; now Mary wrote urging her to unbind them, and at the mission’s 1894 meeting Mrs. Shi stood before a large crowd and explained why she was doing so. The last shoes she wore bound and the first she wore free were mailed to her daughter in Michigan.

In 1896 Mary Stone and Ida Kahn received their medical degrees, among the very first Chinese women to earn one in the United States. After a summer in the clinics of Chicago — where Dr. I. N. Danforth, who became her lifelong friend, opened the city’s hospitals to her — the two young physicians sailed home and reached Kiukiang in the autumn.

The hospital at Kiukiang

They had expected months of suspicion. Instead patients arrived on their third day home and kept coming. By December they had rented dispensary rooms and rebuilt a Chinese house as a hospital, and by July 1897 they had seen more than two thousand dispensary patients. The building was soon packed beyond bearing. In 1898 Mary wrote home that twenty-one sleepers were crowded into a room the size of a small cottage, an oven by evening in the summer heat.

“We are looking forward all the time for signs or signals from the women of America to build our new hospital,” Mary Stone wrote in 1898, “but not a letter comes to bring us this kind of message. Still we are thankful for the hope of building some time.” Almost at once Dr. Danforth, who wished to honour his late wife, gave the gift that built the Elizabeth Skelton Danforth Memorial Hospital, from plans the two young doctors drew themselves.

The new building was ready in 1900 — on the very day the furniture went in, the American consul ordered foreign women and children out of Kiukiang as the Boxer violence spread, and the missionaries persuaded the two Chinese doctors to go with them to Japan. They came back after six months to find the hospital untouched. But that troubled season left a wound in the family: Mary’s father, travelling the country on a preaching tour at the time of the Boxer uprising, was beaten by a mob, and Burton records that those injuries were probably the cause of his death. The hospital was formally opened in December 1901.

Soon after, Ida Kahn went to open medical work in Nanchang, and Mary carried Kiukiang alone. Her day began with prayers in the hospital chapel, then rounds, then a class of nurses, then hours in the dispensary, then house calls on women who could not come to her. She stood on a stool to reach her operating table, and Danforth judged that no Chicago surgeon was doing better work. She charged the rich and spent it on the poor:

So often I find in the morning I earn a good fee, and in the evening I spend it on a very poor case.

— Mary Stone

When the Yangtze flooded in 1901 and refugees poured to her gates, she gave out rice and quilts with the medicine, and at Christmas fed them a square meal. It gave the staff, she wrote, an opportunity to tell them “of the greatest Gift to mankind,” and though they were too rushed even to sit down to their own meals, “we felt it was the happiest Christmas we have ever had.”

An army of nurses

The work that may have mattered most was the one she began out of necessity. With a hundred beds and sometimes a hundred and twenty outpatients a day, she said, she “had to multiply myself by training workers,” and she chose young women from the Christian schools and gave them a course modelled on American training schools. When an American nurse was offered to help her, she gently declined: she wanted the hospital to show Chinese women that they could do things they had never dreamed of, and to show the world that only lack of opportunity had held them back. She trusted her nurses, and she believed God did too.

Surely the Lord values the workers as well as His work, and we who want our work to prosper cannot afford to ignore the interests of those upon whom we depend so largely for success.

— Mary Stone

Her faith ran through every part of the work. Each morning she led a service in the chapel while the nurses held another upstairs; Bible women, among them her own mother, taught the waiting crowds in the dispensary; nurses spent their afternoons off visiting patients’ homes with the gospel, and went out with Bible women to villages beyond reach of any doctor. A missionary walking through the wards one evening heard a low murmur and realized that at every bed someone was praying.

An old woman, terrified of an operation set for the next morning, told one of the youngest nurses that the Christian God might help others but would not help her, for she had never worshipped Him. The nurse knelt beside her bed and taught her to pray. When Dr. Stone came in that night she met a radiant face: “Oh, doctor, I’m not afraid now of the operation. I’ve been talking to your God.” She recovered, and as she left for home she begged the doctor to come and tell her village about Jesus.

In 1907, after eleven years of almost unbroken labour, an attack of appendicitis forced her to America for surgery in Chicago under Danforth’s care. She went with Jennie Hughes, a young Methodist missionary teacher at Kiukiang who would become her companion and co-worker for the rest of her life. Convalescence turned into a speaking tour. Danforth called her appendix “that blamed thing.” She called it “that blessed thing, because it brought me to this country and people have been so kind to me.” She came home to build a new wing and a nurses’ home. During the 1911 Revolution she turned her hospital over to the care of the wounded, declined the revolutionaries’ white badge so that she could treat both sides, and with two nurses cared for the captured Manchu governor, whom no one else dared approach, until he died.

Leaving the mission

In 1918 Mary handed the Danforth Hospital to her younger sister, Dr. Phebe Stone, and spent a year of advanced study at Johns Hopkins on a Rockefeller scholarship. When she returned to China in 1920, she and Jennie Hughes broke with the Methodist mission they had served for nearly a quarter of a century.

The break should be told plainly and fairly. Stone and Hughes understood it as a matter of conscience: they were troubled by the liberal, modernist theology then gaining ground in the mission boards, which seemed to them to treat social service as a substitute for the gospel rather than its fruit, and they wanted to keep the old-fashioned faith in the authority of Scripture and the need for conversion. Historians who have studied the records, notably Connie Shemo, add other strands — a long dispute between Hughes and mission leaders over what the Bible school should teach, frustration at foreign control of the hospital Mary had built, and the unequal pay of Chinese and foreign workers. These are not contradictory accounts. The quarrel over modernism was real and fierce across China in those years, and it was tangled with a deeper longing that Chinese Christians should lead their own church.

Bethel

With Phebe Stone, the two women founded the Bethel Mission in Shanghai in 1920, independent of any denomination and supported by faith. Within less than a decade it held a hospital and nursing school — Mary’s domain — primary and secondary schools, an orphanage, and, after a revival in 1925, a Bible school under Hughes. Mary still taught a weekly Bible class to her student nurses, praying that they would go out as nurse-evangelists. She and Hughes raised a household of orphaned and needy children in their own home.

Out of Bethel’s students came the Bethel bands: small teams of young evangelists, musically gifted and earnest, who went from church to church holding revival meetings. In 1931 Andrew Gih and fellow Bethel graduates formed the Bethel Worldwide Evangelistic Band, and that same year the young preacher John Sung accepted Mary Stone’s invitation to join it. For nearly three years the band criss-crossed China, holding thousands of meetings during one of the great awakenings of Chinese Protestant history, before Sung parted from it to preach on his own. Much of the independent Chinese church that weathered the decades ahead was shaped by the men and women Bethel trained.

Then came war. In 1937 the Japanese assault on Shanghai brought the compound to ruin, and Bethel’s people scattered inland and to Hong Kong, where the work took root again and continues today. Mary and Jennie went to the United States to raise support, and by 1939 they had settled in Pasadena, California, with their adopted daughters. Jennie Hughes died in 1951, after some forty-five years at her friend’s side.

A gem that was not marred

Mary Stone died in Pasadena on 30 December 1954, at eighty-one. She had been born into a world where a woman doctor was undreamed of and an unbound foot was a disgrace, and she had answered both with patience rather than protest — by doing the work, training others to do it, and pointing her patients past herself to the Great Physician. Christians may weigh the 1920 split differently, but no one who met her in the wards doubted where her strength came from. Writing of the open doors in the homes of rich and poor alike, she put her hope in workers more than in buildings:

The cry now is not for open doors, for we have free entrance into the homes of the rich and poor. What we need now is an efficient force of trained evangelistic workers to … follow up the seed thus sown broadcast on such receptive soil.

— Mary Stone

Her parents had prayed, on the day she was born, that their Beautiful Gem would belong to God and never be marred. Thousands of women in Jiangxi, Shanghai and Hong Kong — patients, nurses, orphans and evangelists — came to know the Saviour because that prayer was answered.

faq.q: Who was Mary Stone (Shi Meiyu)?
faq.a: Mary Stone, born Shi Meiyu (1873–1954), was a Chinese Christian physician from Jiujiang who in 1896 became one of the first Chinese women to earn a medical degree in the United States. She ran the Danforth Memorial Hospital in Jiujiang for some twenty years, trained a generation of Chinese nurses, and in 1920 co-founded the independent Bethel Mission in Shanghai.

faq.q: What was her childhood like?
faq.a: She was born in Kiukiang (Jiujiang) in 1873 to a Methodist pastor and his wife, a teacher who was the first convert of missionary Gertrude Howe's work among women. Her parents dedicated her to God at birth and refused to bind her feet, so she grew up mocked for her natural feet. Before she was eight she had memorized the Gospel of Matthew.

faq.q: Why did she become a doctor?
faq.a: Her father admired the American medical missionary Dr. Kate Bushnell and brought his eight-year-old daughter to her, asking that she be made a doctor. She studied for about ten years under Gertrude Howe at the mission girls' school to prepare for a medical course.

faq.q: Where did she study medicine?
faq.a: In 1892 Gertrude Howe took her and her friend Ida Kahn to the University of Michigan, where both earned medical degrees in 1896. She adopted the English form of her name, Mary Stone, because Shi means stone. While she studied, her mother publicly unbound her own feet at a mission meeting in 1894.

faq.q: What was the Danforth Memorial Hospital?
faq.a: After returning in 1896, Stone and Kahn treated patients in a crowded rented house in Kiukiang. Dr. I. N. Danforth of Chicago gave a new hospital in memory of his wife, built from the young doctors' own plans; it was ready in 1900 and formally opened in December 1901. Stone later ran it alone, sometimes seeing over two thousand patients a month.

faq.q: How did she train nurses?
faq.a: With a hundred beds and heavy outpatient crowds, she said she had to multiply herself by training workers. She gave young Christian women a course modelled on American nursing schools and declined an American nurse, wanting the hospital to show what Chinese women could do. Her nurses also prayed with patients and carried the gospel to villages.

faq.q: How did her faith shape the hospital?
faq.a: Each day began with prayers in the hospital chapel, Bible women taught waiting patients, and nurses visited homes with the gospel. She charged wealthy patients and spent the fees on the poor. One frightened patient, taught to pray by a young nurse, faced her operation unafraid and went home asking the doctor to tell her village about Jesus.

faq.q: Why did she leave the Methodist mission in 1920?
faq.a: After a year of study at Johns Hopkins, she and her colleague Jennie Hughes left the Methodist mission in 1920. They saw it as a stand against the modernist theology spreading through the mission boards, which they felt put social service in place of the gospel. Historians add other factors, including disputes over the Bible school, foreign control of the hospital, and unequal pay for Chinese workers.

faq.q: What was the Bethel Mission?
faq.a: Founded in Shanghai in 1920 by Mary Stone, her sister Dr. Phebe Stone and Jennie Hughes, Bethel was an independent faith mission with a hospital and nursing school, schools, an orphanage and a Bible school. Its student evangelistic bands held revival meetings across China, and in 1931 the preacher John Sung joined the Bethel Worldwide Evangelistic Band at her invitation.

faq.q: How did her life end?
faq.a: When Japan attacked Shanghai in 1937, Bethel moved to Hong Kong, where its work continues, and Stone and Hughes went to the United States to raise support, settling in Pasadena, California. Hughes died in 1951, and Mary Stone died in Pasadena on 30 December 1954, aged eighty-one.

fields.name: Samuel Davies
fields.bio: Samuel Davies (1723–1761) was the leading Presbyterian preacher of the Great Awakening in colonial Virginia. From Hanover County he won legal toleration for dissenters, taught enslaved Africans to read, and wrote hymns. In 1759 he succeeded Jonathan Edwards as president of the College of New Jersey, and died there two years later, aged thirty-seven.
fields.tagline: Great Awakening preacher in Virginia, and president of the College of New Jersey.

fields.name: Thomas Chalmers
fields.bio: Thomas Chalmers (1780–1847) was the most celebrated Scottish preacher of his age. Converted while minister of Kilmany, he drew crowds to the Tron and St John's churches in Glasgow, where he also ran a famous experiment in parish care of the poor. A professor at St Andrews and Edinburgh, he led the Disruption of 1843 and was the first Moderator of the Free Church of Scotland.
fields.tagline: Glasgow preacher, parish reformer, and first Moderator of the Free Church of Scotland.

fields.name: Horatius Bonar
fields.bio: Horatius Bonar (1808–1889) was a Scottish minister and hymn writer. For nearly thirty years he served the Free Church congregation at Kelso, then the Chalmers Memorial Church in Edinburgh. He wrote some six hundred hymns, among them "I heard the voice of Jesus say", and gospel books such as God's Way of Peace, and in 1883 he was Moderator of the Free Church General Assembly.
fields.tagline: Scottish Free Church minister at Kelso and Edinburgh, and writer of hundreds of hymns.

fields.name: Frederick W. Robertson
fields.bio: Frederick William Robertson (1816–1853) was an Anglican preacher whose six years at Trinity Chapel, Brighton, made him one of the most widely read preachers of the Victorian age. He published almost nothing in his lifetime; his sermons were printed after his early death, from his own notes and his hearers' records, and went through edition after edition.
fields.tagline: Preacher of Trinity Chapel, Brighton, whose sermons were read across the Victorian world.

fields.name: Francis de Sales
fields.bio: Francis de Sales (1567–1622) was a Savoyard priest and Bishop of Geneva, a see whose city he could never enter, remembered for his patience and gentleness. His Introduction to the Devout Life taught that holiness belongs to people in every walk of life, not only to monks and nuns.
fields.bio_html:
Francis de Sales was Bishop of Geneva for twenty years and was never able to live in Geneva. The city was in Calvinist hands, its cathedral closed to him, and he governed his diocese from the little town of Annecy, some twenty miles to the south. It is a fitting picture of the man. He spent his life on the far side of a divide he did not make, among people who often distrusted him, and he answered that distrust not with force or with sharpness but with a patience so steady that it became proverbial. The book he is best loved for grew out of that same patience. It was written for people who could not leave the world — wives, courtiers, soldiers, tradesmen — and it told them, kindly and firmly, that holiness was meant for them too.

A son of Savoy

He was born two months early on 21 August 1567, at the Château de Sales in the Duchy of Savoy, the mountainous country between France and Italy. His family was among the noblest in the land. His father, known as M. de Boisy, had plans for him from the start: Francis was the first of six sons, and he was to be a magistrate, a man of law and public standing. In 1578, after schooling at La Roche-sur-Foron and Annecy, he was sent to Paris to study rhetoric and the humanities at the Jesuit Collège de Clermont. To please his father he also took lessons in riding, dancing and fencing, the accomplishments of a gentleman. He is described as tall and well built, with blue-grey eyes, intelligent, reserved and quiet.

The dark winter in Paris

Then, in 1586, something broke. Francis attended a theological discussion on predestination — the question of whether God has, from all eternity, chosen some souls for salvation and passed over others — and came away convinced that he himself was among the lost. For weeks he lived inside that conviction. The despair was so heavy that it made him physically ill, and for a time he could not leave his bed. The man later famous for calm and sweetness first knew, as a young student, what it is to believe oneself shut out from the love of God.

The turn came at the end of that year or the beginning of the next, in the old Paris church of Saint-Étienne-des-Grès.

Sick with the certainty that he was damned, the young student went to the church of Saint-Étienne-des-Grès and knelt before the statue known as Our Lady of Good Deliverance. There he prayed the Memorare, the old prayer that begins by reminding the Virgin that no one who fled to her protection was ever left unaided, and gave himself to God, vowing to live in chastity. The despair that had held him through the winter lifted. He came away resting on a single truth from the First Letter of John — that God is love — and so concluded that God had good in store for him.

His later teaching, sometimes called the Way of Divine Love, is in a sense the long working-out of what he learned on his knees that winter.

The heir who chose the altar

Francis finished at Clermont and went on to the University of Padua, in Italy, where he studied law and theology together, taking a Jesuit priest, Antonio Possevino, as his spiritual director. In 1592 he received his doctorate, and with it he settled what had been forming in him for years: he would be a priest. After a pilgrimage to Loreto he went home to Savoy.

Home was not easy. His father had arranged a seat for him as a senator and had chosen a wealthy noble heiress to be his bride. Francis refused the marriage, and his father at first refused to accept a priesthood in place of the career he had planned. What eased the deadlock was a cousin, Canon Louis de Sales, who persuaded the Bishop of Geneva to secure for Francis the post of provost of the cathedral chapter — the highest office in the diocese. M. de Boisy yielded. Francis signed over his title and his rights as heir to a younger brother, and in December 1593 he was ordained.

He preached in Annecy’s cathedral and its parish churches, and people came to hear him. His voice was deep and rich, his speech slow and measured, and his sermons were short and plain, without the displays of learning his age admired. He avoided controversy and took one thing at a time: a duty, a virtue, a vice to be corrected. Though only twenty-seven, he was soon made the diocese’s chief confessor, and found himself spending long hours hearing confessions.

A mission in the Chablais

In 1594 the Duke of Savoy asked for a missionary to go to the Chablais, the country along the southern shore of Lake Geneva that had long been held by the Swiss and had become almost wholly Calvinist. The work would be hard and could be dangerous. Francis volunteered, over his family’s objections, and set out with only his cousin Louis for company. At first they had to return each night to the fortress of Allinges; later Francis moved into the town of Thonon and lodged with a widow.

The welcome was cold and sometimes worse. Ministers from Geneva called him a sorcerer. His landlady once hid him from armed men, and more than once he escaped men who meant to kill him. When his mother managed to send him linen and money, he gave them to the poor. He began writing short pamphlets setting out the Catholic faith, which were later gathered into the book known as The Catholic Controversy — the reason the Church would one day name him patron of writers and journalists. Much of his teaching was done quietly, person to person. Slowly, and only slowly, the mission began to bear fruit.

This was a contest between Christians, in a bitter age, and Francis held his Church’s convictions without apology. What set him apart was the manner of it, summed up in his motto: “He who preaches with love, preaches effectively.”

In 1599 he was named coadjutor to the Bishop of Geneva, and in 1602 he was sent to Paris to negotiate with King Henry IV over the restoring of Catholic worship in the district of Gex. He preached the Lenten sermons at the royal chapel, before a notoriously worldly court, and the king grew fond of him and is said to have called him “a rare bird” — devout, learned and a gentleman all at once.

That same year Bishop Granier died, and on 8 December 1602 Francis was consecrated Bishop of Geneva. Shut out of his cathedral city, he made Annecy his home, and the diocese he built there became known across Europe for its good order, its zealous clergy and its well-taught people. He is remembered too for a small, telling kindness: wanting to teach a deaf man about God, he worked out signs to do it, and so is honoured as patron of the deaf. His goodness, patience and mildness, the record says simply, became proverbial.

Friendship, letters and a book for the world

Preaching the Lenten sermons at Dijon in 1604, he met a widow, Jane Frances de Chantal, who placed herself under his direction. Their friendship, carried on largely through letters, became one of the great spiritual friendships of the Church, and on 6 June 1610 the two of them founded at Annecy the Order of the Visitation of Holy Mary, a community of women. Archbishop Denis-Simon de Marquemont required its sisters to keep a strict cloister.

Out of the same habit of patient direction came his most famous book. A woman bound to him by various ties — usually identified as Madame de Charmoisy, the wife of a cousin — asked his private help to live more devoutly, and he let her keep written notes of his counsels. She showed them to a learned religious, who pressed Francis to publish them, and he gathered and enlarged the papers, “with scarce a moment’s leisure,” as he admits in his preface. The Introduction to the Devout Life appeared in 1609. Unusually for its time, it was written for lay people, and above all for women, and it put love before penance as the way to grow in holiness. He said plainly whom he meant it for:

It is an error, nay more, a very heresy, to seek to banish the devout life from the soldier’s guardroom, the mechanic’s workshop, the prince’s court, or the domestic hearth.

— Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, Part I

Nor did he write as one who had arrived. In the same preface, the bishop of an important diocese told his reader frankly that he was still learning what he taught:

It is too true that I who write about the devout life am not myself devout, but most certainly I am not without the wish to become so, and it is this wish which encourages me to teach you.

— Francis de Sales, Preface to the Introduction to the Devout Life

Francis did not ask busy people to leave their work in order to pray; he asked them to carry prayer into it. In the Introduction he urges his reader to slip away often through the day into “the solitude of your own heart,” even in a crowd, and to lift the heart to God in brief, ardent words — offering the soul to Him “a thousand times a day.” Such a pause, he says, is like a pilgrim stopping for a draught of wine: it does not delay the journey but lightens it.

The gardener’s hut at Lyon

He went on writing — a longer, more mystical Treatise on the Love of God, and a great many letters of spiritual direction — while carrying the ordinary load of a bishop. In December 1622 he was required to travel with the Duke of Savoy on the duke’s Christmas journey through his lands. At Lyon he chose to stay in the gardener’s hut at the Visitation convent there. While he was there he suffered a stroke, and he died on 28 December 1622, at the age of fifty-five.

Lyon kept his heart; his body was carried home and buried in January 1623 in the Visitation church at Annecy, where Jane de Chantal was later buried too. He was beatified in 1661 and canonised in 1665, and in 1877 Pope Pius IX declared him a Doctor of the Church. Vincent de Paul, who met him in Paris, was profoundly shaped by his writings, and in the nineteenth century a whole family of religious communities, the Salesians of Don Bosco among them, took his name and spirit as their own.

A gentle guide for ordinary lives

The Introduction to the Devout Life, published here in a public-domain English translation, is addressed to “Philothea,” a name he chose because it means one who loves God, and so belongs to any reader. It leads her in five parts: from a first desire for God to a settled resolution; into prayer and the sacraments; through the practice of particular virtues such as patience, humility and gentleness; past the temptations that would turn her back; and finally to a time of rest and renewal. It is full of homely pictures — bees and honey, birds and their nests — and never asks a reader to be anyone but who they are. What makes it worth reading four centuries on is its tenderness toward human weakness. Francis knew that people grow angry with themselves for being angry, and despair over their own falls, and he would have none of it. When you fail, he says, speak to your heart as a kind parent would:

Poor heart! so soon fallen again into the snare! Well now, rise up again bravely and fall no more.

— Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, Part III

That is the voice of a man who once lay sick with the fear that God had shut him out, and who found instead that God is love. He spent the rest of his life saying so, gently, to anyone who would listen — and he is saying it still.

faq.q: Who was Francis de Sales?
faq.a: Francis de Sales was a Catholic priest from the Duchy of Savoy who served as Bishop of Geneva from 1602 until his death in 1622. He is known for his gentle approach in a land divided by the Reformation and for his books on the spiritual life, above all the Introduction to the Devout Life.

faq.q: Where and when was Francis de Sales born?
faq.a: He was born two months premature on 21 August 1567 at the Château de Sales in the Duchy of Savoy, into one of its noblest families. He was the first of six sons, and his father intended him for a career as a magistrate.

faq.q: What was his crisis of despair as a student?
faq.a: While studying in Paris in 1586, he attended a discussion on predestination and became convinced that he was damned, a despair so heavy that it made him ill. Around the turn of 1587 he prayed the Memorare before the statue of Our Lady of Good Deliverance in the church of Saint-Étienne-des-Grès, gave himself to God, and came away trusting that God is love.

faq.q: How did he become a priest?
faq.a: After earning a doctorate in law and theology at Padua in 1592, he refused the marriage and the senator’s seat his father had arranged. His cousin helped secure him the post of provost of the Geneva cathedral chapter, his father gave way, and he was ordained in December 1593.

faq.q: What happened on his mission to the Chablais?
faq.a: In 1594 he volunteered to preach in the Chablais, a largely Calvinist region on Lake Geneva, with only his cousin Louis beside him. He was called a sorcerer, was hidden once from armed men, and escaped would-be assassins, and he wrote pamphlets later gathered as The Catholic Controversy. Slowly the mission began to show fruit.

faq.q: Why did the Bishop of Geneva live in Annecy?
faq.a: Geneva was controlled by the Calvinist Republic of Geneva and was closed to him, so after his consecration on 8 December 1602 he governed the diocese from Annecy. His diocese became known across Europe for its good organisation, zealous clergy and well-instructed laity.

faq.q: What was his friendship with Jane Frances de Chantal?
faq.a: He met Jane Frances de Chantal, a widow, when he preached the Lenten sermons at Dijon in 1604, and became her spiritual director, largely by letter. Together they founded the Order of the Visitation of Holy Mary at Annecy on 6 June 1610.

faq.q: What is the Introduction to the Devout Life about?
faq.a: Published in 1609, it grew out of counsels he gave to a woman seeking to live more devoutly, and it is addressed to Philothea, a name meaning one who loves God. Unusually for its time it was written for lay people, and it teaches in five parts how anyone, in any calling, can grow in prayer, virtue and gentleness toward others and oneself.

faq.q: How did Francis de Sales die?
faq.a: In December 1622 he travelled with the Duke of Savoy on the duke’s Christmas journey and, at Lyon, stayed in the gardener’s hut at the Visitation convent. There he suffered a stroke and died on 28 December 1622, aged fifty-five; his body was buried at Annecy and his heart kept in Lyon.

faq.q: Why is Francis de Sales a Doctor of the Church and patron of writers?
faq.a: He was canonised in 1665 and declared a Doctor of the Church by Pope Pius IX in 1877 for the lasting value of his teaching. In 1923 Pope Pius XI named him patron of writers and journalists because of his use of broadsheets and books, and he is also honoured as patron of the deaf for devising signs to teach a deaf man about God.

fields.name: Catherine of Siena
fields.bio: Catherine of Siena (1347–1380) was an Italian mystic and Dominican laywoman who nursed the sick, counselled popes, and urged Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome. She dictated The Dialogue, a conversation between God and the soul, and in 1970 was named a Doctor of the Church.
fields.bio_html:
Catherine of Siena lived only thirty-three years. She was a dyer’s daughter in a Tuscan hill town, never a nun, and for most of her life she could not write. Yet she wrote — or rather spoke, to secretaries who took down her words — to popes and queens, to mercenary captains and city councils, to prisoners and housewives, and she travelled to Avignon to urge the pope himself to come home to Rome. The best way into her is the one she herself recommended: not through the fame or the politics, but through the small inner room where she met God.

The dyer’s daughter

She was born Caterina di Jacopo di Benincasa on 25 March 1347, shortly before the Black Death swept through Europe. Her father, Jacopo, was a cloth dyer who ran his business with the help of his sons; her mother, Lapa, was the daughter of a local poet. Catherine was a twin, the twenty-third or twenty-fourth child of a very large family, and her twin sister died in infancy. As a little girl she was so merry that the family called her by a Greek pet name, Euphrosyne — “joy.”

Her confessor and first great biographer, Raymond of Capua, records that at five or six, walking home with a brother from a married sister’s house, she saw a vision of Christ in glory with the apostles Peter, Paul and John, and that at seven she vowed to give her whole life to God. Those stories come to us through Raymond, writing after her death to make her holiness known, and should be received as he gave them.

A cell inside the mind
