When Catherine was sixteen her older sister Bonaventura died in childbirth, and her parents soon proposed that Catherine marry the widower. She refused absolutely. She began a strict fast in protest, and when her mother urged her to make herself attractive to a husband, she cut off her long hair. Her family answered by taking away her privacy, so that she had no room of her own to pray in. Catherine’s response became one of the most lasting lessons she ever gave.

Denied any place or time of her own for prayer, the teenage Catherine built one inside herself. Years later she gave Raymond of Capua the same counsel for times of trouble: “Build a cell inside your mind, from which you can never flee.” Her family could interrupt her outward solitude, but not the inward recollection she kept with God — and she came to believe that no circumstance could take it away. Two centuries later Francis de Sales was still commending her “little interior oratory” to his readers.

She learned, too, to serve her family as a way of serving Christ, imagining her father in his place, her mother as the Virgin, her brothers as the apostles. In the end her parents gave up and let her live as she wished, unmarried. She did not enter a convent. Instead, after a serious illness, she was allowed to join the Mantellate, a local association of devout women, mostly widows, who lived at home in the spirit of the Dominican order. They taught her to read, and for some years she lived in almost complete silence and solitude in her room in the family house, fasting hard and praying long.

Out into the streets of Siena

According to Raymond, when she was about twenty-one Catherine experienced what she called a mystical marriage with Christ, and soon after was told to leave her withdrawn life and go out into the world. She did. From about 1367 to 1374 she gave herself to the sick and the imprisoned of Siena, nursing in the great hospital of Santa Maria della Scala and in the homes of her neighbourhood. People began to call her santa donna, a holy woman, and a circle of followers gathered around her — women and men, who called her “mother.”

Her fasting deepened in these years, and it is right to name it as the struggle it was. She ate less and less, until at last she seemed to live on little more than the Eucharist, which she received almost daily. The clergy and her own sisters thought it unhealthy; Raymond ordered her to eat properly. Catherine answered that she could not, and called her inability an illness. Whatever we make of it, it would in the end help to wear her out.

Letters to a pope

By 1374 Catherine’s reputation had spread beyond Siena. That year she went to Florence, probably to be questioned by the Dominican authorities, though the details are disputed; it seems to have been then that Raymond of Capua became her confessor and director. From 1375 she began dictating letters, first to friends and disciples, then to people of power, pleading for peace between the warring cities of Italy, for the reform of the clergy, and for the pope to return from Avignon, where the papacy had lived in exile for decades. Some 382 survive. To Pope Gregory XI she wrote with startling directness, often calling him Babbo — something like “dearest daddy” — and following a bold rebuke with a humble apology.

In June 1376 she went to Avignon herself as an envoy of Florence, which was then under papal interdict. The Florentines disowned her mission and negotiated on their own terms, but while she was there Catherine pressed Gregory to go back to Rome. In January 1377 he did. How much that was her doing is still debated by historians; she was one voice among several. But her confidence that she spoke with God’s authority was unmistakable, and so was her loyalty. She criticised corrupt clergy fiercely, yet insisted that Christians must remain obedient to the pope even when churchmen failed them — not for their virtue, but for the sake of God.

The years that followed were full of danger. She founded a house for women outside Siena, spent much of 1377 on a mission of peacemaking and preaching at Rocca d’Orcia, south of Siena, and was then sent again to Florence. There, in the riots of June 1378, she was nearly killed. She also remained, as Algar Thorold’s introduction puts it, a consoler of the suffering “in the condemned cell or in the hospital ward”; one of her best-known letters describes her accompanying a young man named Niccolò di Tuldo to his execution and receiving his head into her hands.

The Dialogue and the Bridge

In the autumn of 1377, while at Rocca d’Orcia, Catherine had the experience that led to her book, and around the same time she learned to write. Over the following year she dictated The Dialogue to her secretaries; her contemporaries agree that much of it was spoken while she was in ecstasy, though she may have revised it afterwards. It opens with a soul making four requests of God — for herself, for the reform of the Church, for the peace of the world, and for one particular need — and the rest of the book is God’s answer.

At its heart is a single picture. The road between heaven and earth, the Father tells her, was broken by sin; and so He made a bridge, His own Son, reaching from heaven to earth, joining our humanity to God:

I have made a Bridge of My Word, of My only-begotten Son, and this is the truth.

— the Father speaking, in Catherine of Siena’s Dialogue

Again and again the book returns to what Catherine calls “the cell of self-knowledge” — the place where the soul learns both its own smallness and the greatness of God’s goodness. It is the inner cell of her girlhood, grown into a whole teaching. And when, at the very end, the soul turns to give thanks, Catherine’s own voice breaks out in one of the great prayers of the Christian tradition:

You, oh eternal Trinity, are a deep Sea, into which the deeper I enter the more I find, and the more I find the more I seek; the soul cannot be satiated in Your abyss, for she continually hungers after You, the eternal Trinity, desiring to see You with light in Your light.

— Catherine of Siena, The Dialogue

Rome, and the long dying

Peace between Florence and the pope was agreed in July 1378, but by then Gregory XI was dead, and that autumn the Church split. Rival popes claimed the throne of Peter in what became known as the Great Western Schism. In late November 1378 Pope Urban VI summoned Catherine to Rome, and she spent her last months there, meeting nobles and cardinals and writing letter after letter to persuade princes that Urban was the true pope.

It cost her everything. Her disciple Barduccio Canigiani, who was with her, wrote an account of her last months that survives at the end of this book. From the beginning of 1380 she could hardly eat or drink at all. Yet her prayer, he wrote, was so fervent that it seemed a miracle.

In the Lent of 1380, already gravely ill, Catherine would rise each morning after communion so spent that she seemed dead, and then, an hour or two later, walk the good mile to St Peter’s, where she stayed in prayer until vespers. She came home, Barduccio writes, “so worn out that she seemed a corpse.” Barduccio ties her sufferings to her grief over the sins committed against God and the dangers facing the Church.

From the third Sunday of Lent she could no longer rise. She lay for eight weeks in terrible pain, and whenever a new torment came, Barduccio says, she raised her eyes to God and thanked Him. Near the end she passed through a dark hour of spiritual struggle.

On her last night, after receiving the last rites, Catherine seemed to suffer fierce assaults, and for a long time she cried out, “I have sinned! Oh Lord, have mercy on me!” and then, “Holy God, have mercy on me!” Barduccio, kneeling by her, saw her prayer answered: “her face suddenly changed from gloom to angelic light,” and her tearful eyes became serene and joyous, as of one saved from a deep sea. She sat up, fixed her eyes on the crucifix, and turned to prayer and confession.

She asked pardon of her spiritual children, blessed them, and prayed for the Church and for Pope Urban. Her last prayer, as Barduccio set it down, was this:

You, oh Lord, call me, and I come to You, not through my merits, but through Your mercy alone, which I ask of You, in virtue of Your Blood!

— Catherine of Siena, on her deathbed, as recorded by Barduccio Canigiani

Then, with the words “Father, into Your Hands I commend my soul and my spirit,” she died, on 29 April 1380.

What she leaves us

She was buried in Rome in the church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, where her body lies today, while Siena keeps her head. Pope Pius II canonised her in 1461. She was named a patron of Rome in 1866, of Italy in 1939, and of Europe in 1999, and on 4 October 1970 Pope Paul VI declared her a Doctor of the Church, days after Teresa of Ávila had become the first woman to receive that title.

The Dialogue appears here in the English translation of Algar Thorold, first published in 1896; this text follows the abridged edition he prepared in 1907. Thorold tried to translate as literally as he could while keeping the rhythm of Catherine’s Tuscan speech, and he warns the reader that she “has no style as such” — a sea, a vine and a plough may tumble into the same sentence. This is not a polished treatise but a woman talking with God about the things every Christian is taught: sin and mercy, tears and prayer, the bridge that is Christ, and the obedience that leads home. Read slowly, it is like being let into her cell.

It is easy to be dazzled by Catherine — the visions, the fasts, the letters to popes. Underneath all of it is something simpler and nearer. A girl with no room of her own made a room inside herself and met God there; and she spent the rest of her short life inviting everyone she could reach to find the same deep sea, where the more you find, the more you seek.

faq.q: Who was Catherine of Siena?
faq.a: Catherine of Siena was an Italian Catholic mystic who lived from 1347 to 1380. A dyer’s daughter who never became a nun, she nursed the sick, wrote hundreds of letters to popes and rulers, and dictated The Dialogue, and she is honoured as a saint and a Doctor of the Church.

faq.q: What was her family background?
faq.a: She was born Caterina di Jacopo di Benincasa on 25 March 1347 in Siena, the daughter of Jacopo, a cloth dyer, and Lapa, the daughter of a local poet. She was a twin and one of the youngest of some two dozen children, and her family nicknamed her Euphrosyne, meaning joy.

faq.q: Why did Catherine refuse to marry?
faq.a: From childhood she wanted to give her life to God, and when her sister Bonaventura died in childbirth her parents proposed that Catherine marry the widower. She refused, fasted in protest and cut off her hair, and eventually her parents allowed her to live unmarried.

faq.q: What does it mean to build a cell inside the mind?
faq.a: When her family took away her time and place for prayer, Catherine made an inner place of recollection where she could always be with God. She later advised Raymond of Capua, ‘Build a cell inside your mind, from which you can never flee,’ and the idea runs through The Dialogue as the cell of self-knowledge.

faq.q: Was Catherine of Siena a nun?
faq.a: No. She joined the Mantellate, a local association of devout women, mostly widows, who lived at home in the spirit of the Dominicans. From about 1367 to 1374 she cared for the sick and imprisoned of Siena, including at the hospital of Santa Maria della Scala.

faq.q: How did Catherine influence the pope’s return from Avignon?
faq.a: From 1375 she dictated letters urging peace in Italy, reform of the clergy and the pope’s return to Rome, and in June 1376 she went to Avignon as an envoy of Florence. Pope Gregory XI returned to Rome in January 1377, though historians still debate how much this was due to her.

faq.q: What is The Dialogue of Catherine of Siena?
faq.a: The Dialogue is a conversation between God the Father and a soul, dictated by Catherine to her secretaries in 1377 and 1378, much of it reportedly while she was in ecstasy. It begins with her four petitions and teaches about self-knowledge, tears, prayer, providence and obedience, with Christ pictured as the Bridge between heaven and earth. The edition published here is Algar Thorold’s English translation.

faq.q: What did Catherine do during the Great Western Schism?
faq.a: When the Church divided in 1378, Pope Urban VI summoned her to Rome in late November. She spent her last months there, meeting nobles and cardinals and writing letters to persuade others that Urban was the true pope.

faq.q: How did Catherine of Siena die?
faq.a: Worn out by fasting, illness and labour for the Church, she could barely eat or drink from early 1380 and was bedridden for her last eight weeks. Her disciple Barduccio Canigiani recorded that she died praying, with the words ‘Father, into Your Hands I commend my soul and my spirit,’ on 29 April 1380 in Rome, aged thirty-three.

faq.q: When was Catherine of Siena made a saint and a Doctor of the Church?
faq.a: Pope Pius II canonised her in 1461, and on 4 October 1970 Pope Paul VI declared her a Doctor of the Church, days after Teresa of Ávila. She is a patron saint of Rome, of Italy with Francis of Assisi, and since 1999 of Europe.

fields.name: Jeremy Taylor
fields.bio: Jeremy Taylor (1613–1667) was an English Anglican priest, Royalist chaplain and bishop, called the “Shakespeare of Divines” for his prose. Writing in Welsh exile during the Civil War, he gave a persecuted church The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living and its companion, Holy Dying.
fields.bio_html:
Jeremy Taylor wrote his best-loved book in exile, in years when the prayers he had been ordained to say were forbidden. His church had lost its bishops, his king had been beheaded, his parish had been taken from him, and he had been a prisoner of war. He was living in Wales on the kindness of a nobleman. Out of that wreckage came The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living, a calm, orderly, deeply practical guide to living every hour before God. Later readers called him the “Shakespeare of Divines” for the music of his prose. But the music was learned in hard places, and the man behind it knew grief, poverty and failure as well as eloquence.

The barber’s son

He was baptized on 15 August 1613 at Holy Trinity Church in Cambridge, the son of Nathaniel Taylor, a barber. Nathaniel was an educated man who taught his son grammar and mathematics himself. The family claimed descent from Rowland Taylor, a Protestant martyr under Queen Mary, though the claim has never been proved. In 1626 the boy went up to Gonville and Caius College as a sizar, a “poor scholar” who paid for his education by waiting on wealthier students.

In 1633, still below the usual age, he was ordained. A college friend asked him to stand in for a while as lecturer at St Paul’s Cathedral, and the young preacher’s fervour drew notice. William Laud, the Archbishop of Canterbury, sent for him. The story is told that Laud objected only to his youth, and that Taylor begged his grace to pardon the fault, promising that if he lived he would amend it. Laud took him under his wing, secured him a fellowship at All Souls College, Oxford, and made him his chaplain. Soon he was also chaplain to King Charles I.

In 1638 he became rector of Uppingham in Rutland and settled into the life of a country priest. In 1639 he married Phoebe Langsdale. Several children were born to them, and several were buried young. From these years a suspicion followed him for life: that he leaned secretly toward Rome. It came from his friendship with a Franciscan friar, his link with Laud, and his own ascetic habits. He preached to clear himself, but he never fully shook it off.

The great storm

Then England went to war with itself. In 1642 Taylor published a defence of bishops, Episcopacy Asserted, and was made Doctor of Divinity by the king’s command. He joined Charles at Oxford and served the royal army as chaplain. Parliament took his living. Laud was beheaded in January 1645, and a few weeks later, on 4 February, Taylor was captured with other Royalists at the siege of Cardigan Castle in Wales.

He was not held long, but he had nothing left. With two other ejected clergymen he opened a school in Carmarthenshire to support his family. He later described himself as shipwrecked on the coast of Wales, his anchor lost, saved only because God had provided him a plank. Writing without a library, he produced The Liberty of Prophesying in 1646, a plea for Christians to bear with one another’s honest differences. It was one of the first great English arguments for religious toleration.

When the king was a prisoner, his chaplains were allowed to visit him, and Charles gave Taylor his watch and some jewels from the case of his Bible. By 1649 the king was dead, and the Church of England had been driven from public life. Taylor described what he saw:

I have lived to see religion painted upon banners, and thrust out of churches…

— Jeremy Taylor, dedication to The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living

Golden Grove

Shelter came from Richard Vaughan, Earl of Carbery, who had led the Royalists in South Wales. His house at Golden Grove stood near Taylor’s school, and Taylor became his chaplain. The earl’s wife Frances was a constant friend. Under that roof, while the churches were closed to men like him, Taylor preached a yearly course of sermons to the household and its neighbours. Few writers have used an exile so fully. Within a few years he wrote a life of Christ, The Great Exemplar; a defence of set forms of prayer; the Golden Grove sermons; and the two books that would make him loved, Holy Living in 1650 and Holy Dying in 1651.

In the years when the old forms of worship were forbidden, Taylor kept praying them. He defended set prayers in print, and in 1655 he published Golden Grove, a manual of daily prayers and litanies for households that could no longer hear them in church. His prayers cost him his liberty more than once. The last time he was sent to prison, it was because his publisher had decorated a book of his services with a picture of Christ at prayer.

Death came close in those years. Lady Carbery died, and early in 1651 so did Taylor’s wife Phoebe. Holy Dying was written in that shadow. He married again, to Joanna Bridges, who owned an estate at Mandinam in Carmarthenshire. People said she was a natural daughter of Charles I, but there is no good evidence for it. He remained a marked man. His preface to Golden Grove offended the authorities, and he was imprisoned. In 1655 he was held for months in Chepstow Castle, where he wrote that his keepers were “civil to my person.” In 1657 he was sent to the Tower, and his friend the diarist John Evelyn pleaded until he was freed.

In the middle of all this he lost more children. Writing to Evelyn about the death of a small son, he put a whole theology of grief into one sentence:

But now he rejoices in his little orb while we think, and sigh, and long to be as safe as he is.

— Jeremy Taylor, in a letter to John Evelyn

A book for a scattered church

Holy Living was written for people who had lost the ordinary helps of religion. Their clergy were scattered and there was no pastor at hand to advise them. Taylor wanted to give them, in one book, the counsel a wise spiritual guide would have given in person. Some said that a church so beaten down must have been forsaken by God. Taylor answered that the marks of a Christian were never revenues, assemblies or armies. They were faith, prayer, purity, mercy, justice, humility, and patience under suffering, and no government could take them away:

And now the case is so with us that we are reduced to that religion which no man can forbid, which we can keep in the midst of a persecution; by which the martyrs, in the days of our fathers, went to heaven; that by which we can be servants of God, and receive the Spirit of Christ, and make use of his comforts, and live in his love, and in charity with all men: and they that do so cannot perish.

— Jeremy Taylor, dedication to The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living

Its first chapter sets out three instruments of a holy life: care of our time, purity of intention, and the practice of the presence of God. The other three chapters, on sobriety, justice and religion, follow St Paul’s call to live soberly, righteously and godly, in our conduct toward ourselves, our neighbour and God. Each section ends with prayers. Taylor is a strict teacher who will not let a reader waste an hour. He is also a humane one. He warns against anxious scruples, and he holds that honest work offered to God is itself service: the ploughman and the merchant are, in their callings, “the ministers of the Divine Providence.”

Taylor’s rule of prayer was meant for busy people. Think first of God on waking, and let him close your eyes at night. Set apart some part of every day for solemn devotion, and in the middle of work turn to him often in short prayers. When the clock strikes, pray briefly, so that “the parts and returns of devotion may be the measure of your time.” Before sleep, look back over the day for causes of sorrow or thanksgiving.

He was gentle with readers who felt they had no time to pray. A short prayer breathed in the middle of a trade, he promised, is no lesser offering:

God is present at thy breathings and hearty sighings of prayer, as soon as at the longer offices of less busied persons

— Jeremy Taylor, The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living, Chapter I

A bishop in a hard country

In 1658, again through Evelyn, Lord Conway offered Taylor a lectureship at Lisburn in the north of Ireland. He went reluctantly, for the pay was meagre. At Conway’s house of Portmore on Lough Neagh he finished his great work on cases of conscience, Ductor Dubitantium. Even there he was informed against, partly for making the sign of the cross at a private baptism, and he was summoned to Dublin in midwinter. The journey left him seriously ill.

At the Restoration he hoped to be recalled to England. Instead he was made Bishop of Down and Connor, and he was consecrated in Dublin in January 1661. The diocese of Dromore was soon added, with a seat on the Irish privy council and the vice-chancellorship of the University of Dublin, which he found in disorder and set on a sound footing. He commissioned a new cathedral at Dromore. He also warned the Irish parliament, as it dealt with confiscated land, not to let “the pretence of a different religion” excuse oppressing any man in his just rights.

In his own diocese, honesty requires saying that he fell short of that standard. The north was full of Presbyterian ministers who would not accept bishops. The author of The Liberty of Prophesying now had the power to practise the tolerance he had argued for, and he did not use it. He gave the ministers a single choice: accept a bishop’s ordination or be removed. At his first visitation he declared thirty-six churches vacant, and he wrote that he felt “thrown into a place of torment.” With the Irish-speaking Catholic majority he did no better, writing a Dissuasive from Popery but never urging his clergy to learn the people’s language. Some of the gentry were won by his evident sincerity. But his deepest gifts were for the study and the household, not for governing a divided land.

The last sorrows

His last years brought fresh grief. According to his nineteenth-century biographer, his two surviving sons both died young: one was killed in a duel, and the other died of consumption in England. On 3 August 1667 Taylor fell ill with a fever, and on 13 August he died at Lisburn, in his mid-fifties. No account of his last hours survives. He was buried at Dromore. His wife outlived him by many years.

What he leaves

Taylor was no flawless saint. He was a loyal party man in a savage age, and he argued for toleration that he failed to practise when he had power. But he was also a pastor who held a shattered church together with prayer books and sermons in a country house, a scholar who wrote masterpieces without a library, and a father who buried child after child and still wrote tenderly of heaven. Anglican churches remember him each year on 13 August.

The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living is the best place to meet him. It is a book of rules that reads like a wise friend’s counsel, firm about sin and generous about weakness, and always turning back to prayer. It has kept its place with devout readers for more than three and a half centuries. It was written for people who had lost almost everything outward, and it shows them what remains: the religion, as Taylor said, which no man can forbid.

faq.q: Who was Jeremy Taylor?
faq.a: Jeremy Taylor (1613–1667) was an English priest of the Church of England, chaplain to King Charles I, and later Bishop of Down and Connor in Ireland. He is remembered as one of the great prose writers in English, sometimes called the “Shakespeare of Divines,” and above all for his devotional books Holy Living and Holy Dying.

faq.q: Where did Jeremy Taylor come from?
faq.a: He was baptized in Cambridge on 15 August 1613, the son of a barber, Nathaniel Taylor, who taught him grammar and mathematics. He went to Gonville and Caius College in 1626 as a sizar, a poor scholar who paid his way by serving wealthier students.

faq.q: How did Jeremy Taylor come to the notice of Archbishop Laud?
faq.a: Ordained in 1633 while still under the usual age, he filled in for a friend as lecturer at St Paul’s Cathedral, and his preaching reached the ears of Archbishop William Laud. Laud took him under his protection, secured him a fellowship at All Souls College, Oxford, and made him his chaplain.

faq.q: What happened to Jeremy Taylor in the English Civil War?
faq.a: He sided firmly with the king, served as a Royalist chaplain, and lost his parish of Uppingham to Parliament. In February 1645 he was captured at the siege of Cardigan Castle, and afterwards he kept a school in Carmarthenshire to support his family.

faq.q: What was The Liberty of Prophesying?
faq.a: Published in 1646, it was Taylor’s plea for Christians to bear with one another’s honest differences of opinion, and it is counted among the earliest great English arguments for religious toleration. He wrote it in poverty, without a library.

faq.q: What was Golden Grove?
faq.a: Golden Grove was the Carmarthenshire home of Richard Vaughan, Earl of Carbery, who sheltered Taylor as his chaplain. There Taylor preached to the household and wrote his most famous works, and he gave the house’s name to his 1655 manual of daily prayers.

faq.q: Why was Jeremy Taylor imprisoned?
faq.a: Under Cromwell’s government he was imprisoned more than once: over a preface to his Golden Grove prayer manual, in Chepstow Castle in 1655, and in the Tower in 1657 after his publisher put a picture of Christ at prayer in a book of his services. His friend John Evelyn pleaded for his release.

faq.q: What is The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living about?
faq.a: Published in 1650, it is a practical guide to the whole Christian life, written for believers who had lost their churches and clergy. It begins with care of time, purity of intention and the practice of God’s presence, then treats sobriety, justice and religion, with prayers for every part of the day and every need.

faq.q: What kind of bishop was Jeremy Taylor in Ireland?
faq.a: Made Bishop of Down and Connor after the Restoration, and given Dromore as well, he worked hard to reform the University of Dublin and was respected for his sincerity. But he refused to tolerate the Presbyterian ministers of his diocese and declared thirty-six churches vacant, and he did little to reach the Irish-speaking Catholic population.

faq.q: When did Jeremy Taylor die and how is he remembered?
faq.a: After the deaths of his last two sons, he fell ill with a fever and died at Lisburn on 13 August 1667, and he was buried at Dromore. Anglican churches remember him each year on 13 August, and Holy Living is still read as a classic of devotion.

fields.name: Henry Scougal
fields.bio: Henry Scougal (1650–1678) was a Scottish minister and Professor of Divinity at King’s College, Aberdeen, who died of consumption at about twenty-eight. His letter to a friend, The Life of God in the Soul of Man, defined true religion as “a union of the soul with God” and later helped awaken George Whitefield.
fields.bio_html:
Henry Scougal lived only twenty-eight years, held no office grander than a professor’s chair in a small northern university, and left behind one short book that began life as a private letter. He never led a movement or, so far as anyone knows, preached to a crowd. Yet a century after his death, young men at Oxford were passing his letter from hand to hand, and one of them would say it taught him for the first time what true religion was. Scougal’s life is thinly documented, and an honest account of him has to admit how much is simply not known. But what is known is enough to show a quiet, scholarly, prayerful young man who understood the heart of Christianity with unusual clarity, and wrote it down for a friend.

A bishop’s son in Aberdeen

He was born in June 1650, probably at Leuchars in Fife, the second son of Patrick Scougal and his wife Margaret Wemys. His father was a minister of the Church of Scotland who later became Bishop of Aberdeen. In the years after 1661 the Church of Scotland was governed by bishops, and the country was bitterly divided between those who accepted that order and the Covenanters who resisted it. Henry grew up a bishop’s son in an age of fierce church quarrels. His younger brother James would later sit as a judge under the title Lord Whitehill.

The few accounts of his boyhood agree on one thing: he was a serious child, raised from his infancy in religion, who spent his free hours not in games but in reading, meditation and prayer. He loved the historical books of the Old Testament in particular. The sources are too thin to bear much embroidery, but it fits everything that comes after. The boy who sat with the stories of Israel became the man who could write about the inward life of God with the ease of someone describing his own home.

From his youth, the records say, Henry Scougal gave his spare hours to reading, meditation and prayer. It was not a phase he grew out of. The book he wrote as a young professor reads like the work of someone who had long been in the habit of withdrawing to speak with God, and who knew from the inside what he called “the great secret of devotion”.

A young professor at King’s College

In 1665, at about fifteen, he entered King’s College in Aberdeen, and he graduated Master of Arts in 1668. He was clearly gifted. Soon after graduating he was made a teacher of philosophy in the college, one of the regents who in Scottish universities of the time took a class of students through their whole course. He is said to have known Latin and Hebrew well, along with some other Eastern languages.

Then, in his early twenties, he stepped out of the university for a season. In 1672 or 1673 (the records differ) he was ordained and became minister of Auchterless, a country parish some twenty miles from Aberdeen. He stayed only about a year. He was called back to King’s College to become Professor of Divinity, the chair responsible for training the ministers of the north of Scotland, and he held it for the rest of his short life, from around 1674 until his death. His Latin treatise on the proper object of religious worship, De Objecto Cultus Religiosi, was printed at Aberdeen in 1674.

How he spent his days, what his students thought of him, how he stood in the controversies around him: none of this has come down to us in a form that can be trusted. What survives is his writing, sermons, essays and meditations published long after his death, and above all the letter that made his name.

A letter to a friend

The Life of God in the Soul of Man was written to a friend who had asked for spiritual counsel. The friend is never named, and no reliable source identifies him. He writes as to “my dear friend” throughout, apologising for his length and pausing at the end of each part to pray. It is a pastor’s answer to a single question: what is real religion, and how can anyone come to have it?

He begins by clearing away counterfeits. Some people, he says, place religion in correct opinions, and can tell you only which party they belong to among “those many sects whereinto Christendom is most unhappily divided.” Others place it in outward duties: going to church, keeping a sober diet, giving a little to the poor. Others place it in feelings, in rapturous hearts and melting devotion. All of these, he grants, may be means to religion or parts of it. None of them is the thing itself. Then he gives his own definition, the sentence for which he is remembered:

They know by experience that true religion is a union of the soul with God, a real participation of the divine nature, the very image of God drawn upon the soul, or, in the apostle’s phrase, “It is Christ formed within us.”

— Henry Scougal, The Life of God in the Soul of Man, Part I

Religion, for Scougal, is a life. It is not a sudden fit of feeling that flares and fades, but a steady inward principle, as natural to the renewed soul as breathing. He calls it divine because it comes from God, worked in the soul by the Holy Spirit, and because it makes the soul resemble God. Its root is faith, and its branches are four: love to God, charity to all people, purity, and humility. He then turns to Christ as the perfect pattern of all four: his nights of prayer, his meekness toward Judas, his humility in refusing to be made a king. The Christian life, as Scougal draws it, is the life of Jesus reproduced in ordinary men and women.

In the second part he sets out why such a life is worth wanting. His most searching passage is about love, which he believed shapes a person into the likeness of whatever is loved:

The worth and excellency of a soul is to be measured by the object of its love.

— Henry Scougal, The Life of God in the Soul of Man, Part II

Love placed on any creature, he argues, will always disappoint: the beloved is too small to fill the heart, may not love us back, may be taken from us. Love placed on God meets none of these griefs. The man who has given his heart to God can find, as Scougal puts it, that the darkest prison or the wildest desert becomes not only bearable but delightful, because the one he loves is never absent.

The means of grace

Scougal knew that a description of the divine life could leave a reader in despair, and the third part of his letter is written for exactly that reader, the one who sees the goal and says, “I am quite of another constitution”. He answers with encouragement rather than reproach. Holiness is the work of God, he insists, yet we must not “lie loitering in the ditch, and wait till Omnipotence pull us from thence.” He sets out plain, practical means: to stop doing what we know to be wrong; to review each day before sleep, an old practice he admits he learned from a pagan writer; to think long and seriously about the truths of the faith until they move the heart; to make use of the Lord’s Supper. And above all, to pray.

In prayer we make the nearest approaches to God, and lie open to the influences of heaven; then it is that the Sun of Righteousness doth visit us with his directest rays, and dissipateth our darkness, and imprinteth his image on our souls.

— Henry Scougal, The Life of God in the Soul of Man, Part III

He distinguishes three kinds of prayer: prayer spoken aloud, prayer formed silently in words within the mind, and a third, deeper kind, in which the soul, after long meditation, reaches toward God “in sighs and groans, and thoughts too big for expression.” This inward prayer he calls “the great secret of devotion,” though he does not despise the simpler kinds, and admits that the deepest prayer is tiring and cannot be kept up for long.

Scougal broke his letter into three parts and closed each with a prayer of his own, so that his friend would not only read about the divine life but ask for it. The first, written for one who has just begun to see what religion truly is, ends: “And let me never cease my endeavours, till that new and divine nature prevail in my soul, and Christ be formed within me.”

An early death

Scougal’s letter reached print in London in 1677, without his name on it. Gilbert Burnet, a Scottish clergyman then in London who would later become Bishop of Salisbury, saw it through the press and wrote its preface; one account says this was done with the author’s consent. Scougal did not have long to see what became of it. He fell ill with consumption, the old name for tuberculosis, and died at Aberdeen in June 1678, at about twenty-eight. Even the day is uncertain: different sources give the 13th, the 16th, or the 20th. He was buried in the chapel of King’s College, and his colleague George Garden preached his funeral sermon.

No deathbed story survives. His book had already said what he had to say about death: that the soul is “a divine spark, capable to know, and love, and enjoy our Maker”, and that though it is now weighed down by the body, it can live without it “as well as that can do without the clothes which we throw off at our pleasure.” A young man dying of a wasting disease had written those words a year or two before.

A book that kept travelling

The letter outlived its author by centuries. It went through edition after edition in Scotland and England, was translated into French in 1727, and became a quiet favourite among readers who cared more for the heart of faith than its quarrels. Its most famous reader came more than half a century after Scougal’s death. At Oxford in the 1730s, John and Charles Wesley gathered a small group of earnest students, mocked by others as the Holy Club, and Scougal’s book circulated among them. A copy came into the hands of a poor young servitor named George Whitefield; Charles Wesley is usually named as the friend who gave it to him. Whitefield later said that he had never known what true religion was until he read that treatise. He went on to become one of the great preachers of the evangelical revival in Britain and the Great Awakening in America.

It is a striking chain: a private letter from Aberdeen awakens a young man three generations later, and through him reaches crowds on two continents. Scougal belonged to the episcopal side of a divided Scottish church; Whitefield was a Calvinist field-preacher; the Wesleys were Arminian Anglicans. All of them found in this little book the same thing, because Scougal had written it beneath the level where those arguments happen.

Scougal’s final prayer in the letter gathers up everything he had taught into a single petition for grace: “Let us neither presume on our own strength, nor distrust thy divine assistance: but while we are doing our utmost endeavours, teach us still to depend on thee for success.” It is the prayer of a man who believed holiness was both God’s gift and our labour.

Why read him now

The Life of God in the Soul of Man is short enough to read in an evening and deep enough to return to for years. Its English is that of the seventeenth century, but its argument is plain and its warmth unmistakable. It is worth reading because it asks the question every believer eventually has to face, whether faith has become merely opinion, habit, or feeling, and answers it not with a scolding but with a picture of what God can do in a soul: the life of Christ himself, formed within.

Henry Scougal did not live to be thirty, and we know frustratingly little about him. But he left exactly what a good pastor would want to leave: a letter to a friend that still speaks to strangers, telling them that religion is not a performance but a union with God, and inviting them, as he invited his friend, to pray for it.

faq.q: Who was Henry Scougal?
faq.a: Henry Scougal (1650–1678) was a Scottish minister and theologian who taught at King’s College, Aberdeen, and served as its Professor of Divinity. He is remembered for one short book, The Life of God in the Soul of Man, written as a letter of spiritual counsel to a friend.

faq.q: Where was Henry Scougal born, and who were his parents?
faq.a: He was born in June 1650, probably at Leuchars in Fife, the second son of Patrick Scougal and Margaret Wemys. His father later became Bishop of Aberdeen, at a time when the Church of Scotland was governed by bishops, and his younger brother James became a judge as Lord Whitehill.

faq.q: What was Henry Scougal like as a boy?
faq.a: The accounts of his youth describe a serious child, raised in religion from infancy, who spent his free hours in reading, meditation and prayer. He especially loved the historical books of the Old Testament.

faq.q: Where did Henry Scougal study and teach?
faq.a: He entered King’s College, Aberdeen, in 1665 and graduated Master of Arts in 1668, after which he taught philosophy there. He was known as a fine linguist, with Latin, Hebrew and some other Eastern languages.

faq.q: Was Henry Scougal ever a parish minister?
faq.a: Yes, briefly. In 1672 or 1673 (the records differ) he was ordained and became minister of Auchterless, a parish about twenty miles from Aberdeen, and served there for roughly a year. He then returned to King’s College as Professor of Divinity, which he remained until his death.

faq.q: What is The Life of God in the Soul of Man about?
faq.a: It is a long letter to an unnamed friend explaining what true religion is and how to attain it. Scougal sets aside religion as mere opinion, outward duty or feeling, and describes it instead as a divine life in the soul, rooted in faith and growing in love to God, charity to all, purity and humility, with Christ as its pattern and prayer as one of its chief means.

faq.q: How did Henry Scougal define true religion?
faq.a: He wrote that true religion is “a union of the soul with God, a real participation of the divine nature, the very image of God drawn upon the soul,” or, in the apostle’s phrase, Christ formed within us. He called it a divine life because it comes from God and makes the soul resemble him.

faq.q: How was the book first published?
faq.a: It was printed in London in 1677 without Scougal’s name, with a preface by Gilbert Burnet, the Scottish clergyman who later became Bishop of Salisbury. It went through many later editions and was translated into French in 1727.

faq.q: How and when did Henry Scougal die?
faq.a: He died of consumption, or tuberculosis, at Aberdeen in June 1678, at about twenty-eight; sources give the day variously as the 13th, 16th or 20th. He was buried in the chapel of King’s College, and his colleague George Garden preached his funeral sermon.

faq.q: How did Scougal’s book influence the Wesleys and George Whitefield?
faq.a: The book circulated among John and Charles Wesley’s Holy Club at Oxford in the 1730s, and a copy reached the young George Whitefield, usually said to have been given him by Charles Wesley. Whitefield later said he had never known what true religion was until he read it, and went on to become a leading preacher of the evangelical revival in Britain and the Great Awakening in America.

fields.name: Philip Doddridge
fields.bio: Philip Doddridge (1702–1751) was an English Congregationalist minister, tutor and hymn-writer who led a Dissenting academy at Northampton. His Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul guides a reader from first awakening to a Christian death, and helped lead William Wilberforce to faith.
fields.bio_html:
Philip Doddridge spent his life in a Midlands market town, running a small college for ministers, preaching to one congregation, and writing whenever he could find the time. He was thin, often ill, and endlessly busy. Yet a book he wrote in that crowded life, The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul, crossed oceans and centuries. It was translated into several languages and helped turn William Wilberforce toward Christ, and churches still sing hymns that Doddridge wrote to close his Sunday sermons. He prayed that the book would reach readers who were not yet born, and it did.

The Bible on the chimney tiles

He was born in London on 26 June 1702, the last of the twenty children of Daniel Doddridge, a dealer in oils and pickles. Dissent ran in the family. His grandfather John Doddridge, rector of Shepperton, had been ejected from his parish in 1662 for refusing to conform to the Church of England. His mother Elizabeth was the orphaned daughter of a Lutheran pastor who had fled persecution in Prague. She was the deeper influence on him. Before Philip could read, she taught him the stories of the Old and New Testaments from the blue Dutch tiles around the fireplace of their sitting room.

She died in 1711, when he was eight, and his father died in 1715. The guardian left in charge of the boy squandered his inheritance, and at thirteen Philip was an orphan with nothing, at school in St Albans. There Samuel Clarke, the local Presbyterian minister, took him in and treated him as a son. Clarke guided his studies and encouraged his sense of a call to the ministry. Doddridge never forgot it. Preaching at Clarke’s funeral decades later, he said that to him, under God, he owed “even myself and all my opportunities of public usefulness in the church.”

Offers came that would have led the clever orphan into the Church of England, or into the law. He turned them down. In 1719, with Clarke’s support, he entered the Dissenting academy at Kibworth in Leicestershire under John Jennings. Dissenters, the Protestants who would not conform to the national church, were shut out of the universities, and academies like Kibworth trained their ministers. In 1723, still only about twenty-one, he briefly succeeded Jennings and settled as minister of a small village congregation.

Northampton

He was soon asked to lead a new academy for Dissenting ministers at Market Harborough. In 1729 he accepted a call from an Independent congregation at Northampton, and the academy moved with him. For the next twenty-two years he was both pastor of the Castle Hill church and head of the college. He lectured on philosophy and theology, and some two hundred young men passed through his hands. In 1736 both universities at Aberdeen made him a Doctor of Divinity.

On 22 December 1730 he married Mercy Maris of Worcester after a seven-month courtship. They had nine children, and only four lived to grow up. Their first, Elizabeth, whom they called Tetsey, died just before her fifth birthday in 1736 and was buried beneath the floor of the chapel where her father preached. Many of the letters between Philip and Mercy survive, and they give a rare window into their life together.

His preaching was plain and practical. Its aim was to bring hearers into a devout, prayerful frame of mind rather than to win arguments. He liked to end a sermon with a new hymn summing up its lesson, so the congregation could sing back what they had heard. He wrote some four hundred of these. None was published in his lifetime, but a collection of three hundred and seventy appeared after his death, and several are still sung today: “O God of Bethel, by whose hand,” “Hark the glad sound! the Saviour comes,” and “Awake, my soul, stretch every nerve.”

A friend to all who loved Christ

Doddridge lived in an age of quarrelling religious parties, and he refused to join any of them. He kept up a wide correspondence with ministers of many kinds and worked for a united Nonconformity that could hold together educated and uneducated believers. When he wrote his great book, he asked readers to take it as a whole, because he had watched Christians seize on single parts of the truth “as if each had been all.” In the preface he prayed:

I pray God to give to all his ministers and people more and more of the spirit of wisdom, and of love, and of a sound mind

— Philip Doddridge, preface to The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul

That generous spirit cost him something. When the evangelical revival began to stir England, Doddridge welcomed it. In 1743 he preached at George Whitefield’s Tabernacle in London and then opened his own Northampton pulpit to Whitefield. His friend Isaac Watts, the great hymn-writer, rebuked him for lowering the dignity of a Dissenting minister and tutor, and other Dissenting ministers sharply censured him. It was the price of his openness, and he paid it.

A book for every reader

The book itself began with Watts. In the preface Doddridge explains that Watts had sketched the plan of such a work, but illness kept him from writing it, and he “in a very affectionate and importunate manner” urged Doddridge to take it on. Doddridge did, and Watts lived to see it finished and to read much of it. It appeared in 1745, dedicated to him.

The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul follows a single reader through the whole Christian life in thirty short chapters. It begins with a careless person who has never thought seriously about God. It goes on through conviction of sin and the good news of salvation in Christ, then a solemn dedication of oneself to God and the Lord’s Supper. After that come the ordinary disciplines of daily devotion, and the hard seasons of spiritual dryness, relapse and affliction. It ends at the deathbed. Each chapter closes with a written prayer that the reader can make their own. Doddridge wrote it for the humblest reader he could imagine:

I have studied in this Treatise the greatest plainness of speech, that the lowest of my readers may, if possible, be able to understand every word

— Philip Doddridge, preface to The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul

He was also careful not to make his map a rule. He added a caution in the preface: not everyone comes to faith through the same stages of terror and conviction. Some, especially those raised in godly homes, are drawn to God “by such gentle and insensible degrees” that they cannot tell the story of their conversion at all. They should not doubt their faith because their story is quiet.

As a young minister, in 1727, Doddridge wrote a letter to a devout young friend describing how a day might be spent with God, and he later put it into the book. On waking, lift the heart to God. Then, on your knees, offer praise, renew your dedication to God, look ahead at the day’s duties and dangers, and pray over a few verses of Scripture with the Bible open in front of you. Through the day, send up short prayers. At night, examine the day and lie down in peace. The friend died a few months after receiving the letter. Doddridge hoped he had lived long enough to put it into practice.

Labours beyond his strength

He had a weak constitution from childhood, and he gave himself more work than a strong man could have carried. Alongside the church and the academy he wrote The Family Expositor, a paraphrase of and commentary on the whole New Testament, in six volumes from 1739. John Wesley acknowledged a debt to it in his own notes on the New Testament. Doddridge also wrote a Life of Colonel Gardiner (1747), sermons and treatises, and a vast number of letters. In 1750 he started a scheme to give poor but able boys a grammar-school education so that they could go on to train for the ministry. The scheme did not survive him.

The record admits that all this took a toll. His engagements and his correspondence grew so heavy that they interfered with his preaching and teaching. His body paid for it too. In December 1750 he travelled to St Albans to preach the funeral sermon of Samuel Clarke, the man who had rescued him as a boy, and on that journey he caught a cold that he never shook off. In July 1751 he preached to his Northampton congregation for the last time.

Lisbon

By then he had tuberculosis. His friends hoped a warmer climate might save him, and they raised three hundred pounds to send him to Lisbon. The Countess of Huntingdon gave a third of it. He sailed at the end of September 1751. The voyage did not help. He died at Lisbon on 26 October 1751, aged forty-nine, and was buried in the British Cemetery there, where his grave can still be seen.

He had already written, in the last chapter of his book, what he hoped his dying would show. He had asked that certain promises of Scripture be read to him on his deathbed, with pauses between them, so that he could rest on each. And he made it plain that the book had been written from experience, not theory:

And I can truly and cheerfully say, that I have marked out to you the path which I myself have trod, and in which it is my desire still to go on.

— Philip Doddridge, The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul, Chapter XXX

Readers yet unborn

His academy outlived him. In time it became New College, London, and went on training ministers for generations. But his widest influence came through the book. It was reprinted again and again and translated into several languages. Charles Spurgeon called it “that holy book.” Long after Doddridge’s death, William Wilberforce read it with his friend Isaac Milner, and it set him on the spiritual journey that ended in his conversion.

At the end of the first chapter, Doddridge wrote a prayer for the book itself. He asked God that it might “reach to those that are yet unborn, and teach them thy name and thy praise, when the author has long dwelt in the dust.” If that was too much to ask, he would be grateful for even one soul saved. He died six years after it was published. Wilberforce read it long afterwards, and it is still being read today.

Readers who open it today will find it serious, searching and tender. It does not hurry, and it does not flatter. Doddridge writes, as he promised, “as a friend to a friend,” stepping aside after each short address to let the reader pray. Its prayers alone make it worth reading. They give words to people at every stage, from the first stirring of conscience to the last hour of life. He wrote it in the gaps of an exhausting life for anyone who might pick it up, and it is still doing what he asked of it.

faq.q: Who was Philip Doddridge?
faq.a: Philip Doddridge (1702–1751) was an English Nonconformist minister of the Congregational, or Independent, tradition. He was pastor of a church in Northampton for twenty-two years, ran an academy that trained Dissenting ministers, and wrote hymns, a New Testament commentary and The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul.

faq.q: What was Philip Doddridge’s childhood like?
faq.a: He was born in London on 26 June 1702, the last of twenty children of an oil merchant. His mother taught him Bible stories from the Dutch tiles around their fireplace before he could read. She died when he was eight and his father when he was thirteen, and a guardian then squandered his inheritance.

faq.q: Who was Samuel Clarke to Philip Doddridge?
faq.a: Samuel Clarke was the Presbyterian minister at St Albans who took in the orphaned and penniless Doddridge, treated him as a son, guided his education and encouraged his call to the ministry. They stayed friends for life, and Doddridge said he owed Clarke, under God, even himself.

faq.q: Why did Philip Doddridge train at a Dissenting academy?
faq.a: He turned down openings that would have led him into the Church of England or the law, choosing instead to serve the Dissenters. In 1719 he entered the academy at Kibworth in Leicestershire under John Jennings, whom he briefly succeeded.

faq.q: What did Philip Doddridge do in Northampton?
faq.a: From 1729 until 1751 he was pastor of an Independent congregation at Northampton and head of an academy for ministers, where some two hundred students studied with him. In 1736 the universities of Aberdeen made him a Doctor of Divinity.

faq.q: What hymns did Philip Doddridge write?
faq.a: He wrote some four hundred hymns, often to close a sermon by summing up its lesson. They were published after his death, and several are still sung, including “O God of Bethel, by whose hand” and “Hark the glad sound! the Saviour comes.”

faq.q: What was Philip Doddridge’s connection with Isaac Watts and George Whitefield?
faq.a: Isaac Watts was a close friend who sketched the plan for The Rise and Progress and urged Doddridge to write it. In 1743 Watts rebuked him for preaching at George Whitefield’s Tabernacle, and Doddridge was censured by other Dissenting ministers when he opened his own pulpit to Whitefield.

faq.q: What is The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul about?
faq.a: Published in 1745 and dedicated to Isaac Watts, it follows a reader through the Christian life in thirty short chapters, from careless indifference through conviction, faith and dedication to God, daily devotion, spiritual trials, and finally death. Each chapter ends with a prayer, and Doddridge wrote it as plainly as he could so that anyone could follow it.

faq.q: How did Philip Doddridge die?
faq.a: His health had always been weak, and in 1751 he had tuberculosis. Friends raised money to send him to a warmer climate, and he sailed for Lisbon at the end of September, but he died there on 26 October 1751 and was buried in the British Cemetery.

faq.q: What is Philip Doddridge’s legacy?
faq.a: His academy later became New College, London, and his hymns are still sung. The Rise and Progress was often reprinted and translated, Charles Spurgeon called it a holy book, and William Wilberforce began the spiritual journey that led to his conversion by reading it.

fields.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
fields.bio: Cyril of Jerusalem (313–386) was bishop of Jerusalem and the teacher behind the Catechetical Lectures, the only complete course of instruction for new Christians to survive from the early church. Driven from his city three times amid the Arian controversy, he was cleared in old age and named a Doctor of the Church in 1883.
fields.bio_html:
Cyril of Jerusalem is the only bishop of the ancient church whose classroom we can still sit in. He left the very words he spoke, one Lent in the fourth century, to the men and women about to be baptized in the church built over the tomb of Christ. He was a teacher first, and remained one through a life the quarrels of his age made very hard. He was driven from his city three times, accused of theft, suspected of heresy by friends and enemies alike, and only cleared in his old age. Through all of it he went on doing the plain work of a pastor: telling ordinary people what the Church believes, and helping them to believe it.

A child of the holy city

Almost nothing is known of his early years, and it is honest to say so. He was born about 313 — the year is a reasonable guess, not a record — probably in or near Jerusalem. The names of his parents have not survived. The old calendars of the saints say only that he was “born of pious parents, professing the orthodox Faith,” and his lectures bear that out: he never speaks as a convert from paganism, and he writes of honouring father and mother with the warmth of a son who had been given a Christian upbringing and knew it.

He seems to have known Jerusalem before the great buildings went up. In his lectures he recalls that the place of the Nativity had lately been wooded, and that a rock-cut cave once stood before the door of the Sepulchre until it was cut away for the Emperor Constantine’s new church. If he spoke from memory, he saw the holy places as a boy, before the empire dressed them in marble. An early tradition adds that he lived as an ascetic, one of the “Solitaries” — Christians vowed to chastity who lived not in the desert but in their own houses in the city, giving themselves to strict discipline and works of charity.

He was ordained a deacon, probably by Bishop Macarius, around 335. That same year Jerusalem saw one of the most splendid and troubling scenes of the age. Bishops gathered from every province to dedicate Constantine’s Church of the Resurrection, and in that glittering assembly Arius, the priest who taught that the Son of God was a creature and not truly God, was received back into communion, while Athanasius, his great opponent, had just been deposed. The young deacon watched it all. It is to his credit that the triumph of the Arian party did not carry him with it.

Forty days of teaching

Later he was ordained priest by Bishop Maximus, and by about 348 he had been given one of the weightiest tasks in the Jerusalem church: preparing the candidates for baptism. Those who wished to be baptized at Easter gave in their names at the start of Lent and gave the forty days to it — fasting, prayer, confession, exorcism and daily instruction. Gifford’s careful dating points to the Lent of 348; it cannot have been much later.

Cyril opened the course with an address to the whole congregation, and it is full of the tenderness and bluntness that mark everything he says. He knew why some of them had come. A young man might be there to court a young woman, a slave to please his master, a friend to oblige a friend. Cyril did not turn them away. He welcomed them, and told them what had really happened to them:

Jesus is angling for thee, not in order to kill, but by killing to make alive: for thou must die and rise again.

— Cyril of Jerusalem, Procatechesis

Then, over the following weeks, he walked them through the Creed of the Jerusalem church, article by article: the one God, the Father; the Son, eternally begotten; the cross, the burial and the resurrection; the Holy Spirit; the Church, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body. The Creed itself he would not write down. The candidates were to learn it by heart and keep it there, not on paper, and to say nothing of the mysteries to outsiders. He was building a house, he told them, stone by stone. And he was clear about whose work it finally was:

For it lies in me to speak, but in thee to set thy mind upon it, and in God to make perfect.

— Cyril of Jerusalem, Procatechesis

He asked them to pray as well as listen, and he did not mean only in church.

Cyril told his candidates to pray more often, so that God might make them worthy of the mysteries they were about to receive — and not to stop by day or by night. When they lay awake, he said, they were to let the mind be free for prayer, and when a shameful thought rose up, to turn it toward the judgment of God and so remember their salvation.

What comes through most in the lectures is a teacher who loves his hearers and wants them safe. He warns them against the serpent by the roadside, and he describes the coming of the Holy Spirit not as something fearsome but as a gentle arrival, fragrant and light, coming “to save, and to heal, to teach, to admonish, to strengthen, to exhort, to enlighten the mind.”

He wanted the faith to reach into the smallest hours of the day. “Let us not then be ashamed to confess the Crucified,” he told them, and asked them to make the sign of the cross on the brow over their bread and their cups, coming in and going out, before sleep and on rising, on the road and at rest — a prayer traced with the fingers, so that the whole of life was marked as Christ’s.

Bishop of Jerusalem

Around 350, on the death of Maximus, Cyril became bishop himself. He was consecrated with the approval of Acacius, the bishop of Caesarea, who leaned to the Arian side, and enemies later said he had bought his see with compromise. Jerome, plainly hostile, repeated the rumours; the shadow lay over him for thirty years.

His episcopate opened with a wonder. On the morning of Pentecost, 7 May 351, a great cross of light appeared in the sky over Jerusalem, stretching from Golgotha to the Mount of Olives and visible for hours. The whole city crowded into the church, and Cyril wrote to the Emperor Constantius of it as a sign of God’s favour. Gifford, the translator of the lectures, thinks it was probably some rare natural phenomenon; the event itself is too well attested to doubt.

When famine struck Jerusalem and the poor came to their bishop in crowds, Cyril, who had no money of his own to give, sold the church’s treasures and sacred hangings to buy them bread. It was this act of mercy that his enemies turned into a crime. Acacius, as metropolitan of the province, claimed authority over Jerusalem; Cyril, as bishop of “the Mother of all the Churches,” refused it. The dispute festered, and the sale of church goods became the charge.

Three times driven out

For two years Cyril refused to stand trial before Acacius and his allies, judges who could hardly be impartial. Around 357 they deposed him in his absence, and he was driven out of Jerusalem. He took refuge in Tarsus, where Bishop Silvanus let him go on preaching because the people loved his teaching, and appealed to a higher court. In 359 the Eastern bishops met at Seleucia; Acacius refused to answer for his own charges and was himself deposed, and Cyril seems to have returned home. It did not last. Acacius carried his complaints to the imperial court, and in 360 a council at Constantinople deposed Cyril a second time, and the emperor sent him into exile.

The death of Constantius in 361 brought him back. The new emperor, Julian, recalled every exiled bishop — in the hope, the historians suspected, that the Christians would tear one another apart. One small story from that return survives. The son of a pagan priest at court had secretly become a Christian, and his father beat him and burned him with hot irons. The young man escaped, was hidden by a deaconess and brought to Bishop Meletius of Antioch, who handed him to Cyril; and they set out by night for Palestine. When Julian later tried to rebuild the Temple, Cyril was said to have foretold its failure. Gifford finds no proof of any prophecy — only a bishop who, on the strength of the Gospels, calmly said the work could not stand.

Then, around 367, the Emperor Valens, who favoured the Arians, ordered every bishop exiled under Constantius and restored under Julian to be driven out again. Cyril’s third exile was his longest, about eleven years, and almost nothing is known of it. He came home only after Valens died at the battle of Adrianople in 378. He found his church split by rival factions and, by the grieving report of Gregory of Nyssa, who visited soon after, sunk in every kind of vice. The old bishop, now in his mid-sixties, set about gathering it together again.

Cleared at last

In 381 the Emperor Theodosius summoned the bishops of the East to Constantinople to settle the long quarrel over the Nicene faith. Cyril came, and was counted among the leaders of the orthodox party. The question that had dogged him was whether he truly held the faith of Nicaea. For years he had been wary of the council’s key word, homoousios — “of one substance” with the Father — fearing it as an addition to the creeds. But his lectures had taught its meaning all along: that the Son is truly God, equal with the Father. Some historians said he changed his mind at Constantinople; Gifford rejects that as unfounded. Either way, he stood with the Nicene faith at the council that confirmed it.

The next year the same bishops, writing to the bishops of the West, did him the justice he had waited thirty years for:

Of the Church in Jerusalem, the Mother of all the Churches, we make known that Cyril the most reverend and most beloved of God is Bishop; and that he was canonically ordained long ago by the Bishops of the province, and that he has very often fought a good fight in various places against the Arians.

— The Synod of Constantinople, 382

It is the last thing the records tell us of him. Jerome says he held his see in peace for eight years under Theodosius, and he died, by the traditional reckoning, on 18 March 386, the day the Church still keeps as his feast. He was not a flawless man. He could be stubborn about the rights of his see, and he once named a bishop for Caesarea on authority that Gifford thinks doubtful. But Gifford’s judgment on him is generous and seems right: it was his prudence, moderation and love of peace that exposed him, in those days of bitter controversy, to suspicion he did not deserve. In 1883 Pope Leo XIII named him a Doctor of the Church; he is honoured as a saint in the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican traditions alike.

The lectures he left

The book we publish is The Catechetical Lectures, in the nineteenth-century translation of E. H. Gifford. It holds the opening address, or Procatechesis, and eighteen lectures to the candidates during Lent, followed by five Mystagogic Lectures — talks to the newly baptized in Easter week, explaining the baptism, anointing and communion they had just received. Scholars still debate whether the Mystagogic Lectures are Cyril’s own, perhaps from later in his life, or the work of his successor John; Gifford defends them as Cyril’s. Together they are the only complete course of instruction for new Christians to survive from the early centuries.

But they are worth reading less as history than because they still do what they were meant to do. Cyril wrote for beginners, and he never talks down to them. If you have recited a creed for years without quite knowing why each line is there, or if you are coming to the faith for the first time, he will walk you through it as patiently as he walked those candidates long ago — one stone at a time, until the house stands.

faq.q: Who was Cyril of Jerusalem?
faq.a: Cyril was a fourth-century bishop of Jerusalem, born about 313 and died in 386, best remembered for the lectures he gave to candidates for baptism. He was exiled three times during the Arian controversy and is honoured as a saint in the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican traditions.

faq.q: What is known about Cyril of Jerusalem’s early life?
faq.a: Very little. He was probably born in or near Jerusalem, the names of his parents are unknown, and the old calendars of the saints say he was born of pious, orthodox parents. His lectures suggest he saw the holy places as a boy, before Constantine’s great buildings went up.

faq.q: When was Cyril ordained?
faq.a: He was ordained a deacon, probably by Bishop Macarius, around 335, and later a priest by Bishop Maximus. By about 348 he had been given the task of preparing the candidates for baptism in the Jerusalem church.

faq.q: How were candidates for baptism prepared in Cyril’s Jerusalem?
faq.a: They gave in their names at the start of Lent and spent the forty days in fasting, prayer, confession, exorcism and daily instruction on the Creed. They were baptized at Easter, and in Easter week were taught the meaning of the sacraments they had received.

faq.q: When did Cyril become bishop of Jerusalem?
faq.a: He succeeded Bishop Maximus around 350. His first recorded act as bishop was a letter to the Emperor Constantius about a cross of light seen in the sky over Jerusalem on 7 May 351.

faq.q: Why was Cyril accused of selling church property?
faq.a: During a famine, having no money of his own, he sold church treasures and sacred hangings to feed the poor of Jerusalem. Acacius, the bishop of Caesarea, who claimed authority over Jerusalem, used this as the charge on which he deposed him.

faq.q: Why was Cyril exiled three times?
faq.a: He was deposed by Acacius around 357, deposed again by a council at Constantinople in 360 and exiled by Constantius, and driven out a third time around 367 under the Arian Emperor Valens. He returned for good after Valens died in 378.

faq.q: Did Cyril accept the Nicene faith?
faq.a: For years he avoided the Nicene word homoousios, of one substance, but his lectures teach that the Son is truly God, equal with the Father. At the Council of Constantinople in 381 he stood with the Nicene party, and in 382 the bishops wrote that he had often fought a good fight against the Arians.

faq.q: What are Cyril of Jerusalem’s Catechetical Lectures?
faq.a: They are an opening address, eighteen Lenten lectures on the Creed for candidates for baptism, and five Mystagogic Lectures on baptism, anointing and the Eucharist for the newly baptized. Scholars debate whether the Mystagogic Lectures are Cyril’s own or his successor John’s, and the translation published here is E. H. Gifford’s.

faq.q: How did Cyril of Jerusalem die, and how is he remembered?
faq.a: He held his see in peace in his last years and died in 386, traditionally on 18 March, which remains his feast day. In 1883 Pope Leo XIII named him a Doctor of the Church.

fields.name: Ignatius of Loyola
fields.bio: Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556) was a Basque soldier who, after a cannonball shattered his leg at Pamplona, turned to God and founded the Society of Jesus. His Spiritual Exercises, a retreat of prayer and discernment drawn from his own conversion, have guided seekers for nearly five centuries.
fields.bio_html:
Ignatius of Loyola is remembered as the founder of the Jesuits, one of the most disciplined and far-reaching religious orders the church has known. It is worth beginning somewhere humbler: with a vain young soldier lying in bed in his family’s house with a shattered leg, bored, asking for romances of knights and ladies to pass the time, and being handed instead a life of Christ. Nearly everything that followed — the order, the schools, the missions to the ends of the earth — grew out of what happened to him in that bed, and out of what he learned there about the movements of his own heart. He wrote it down as a handbook for helping others find God: The Spiritual Exercises.

A courtier with a sword

He was born Íñigo López de Oñaz y Loyola, probably in 1491 — the traditional date is 23 October, though some historians think he was born a little earlier — in the castle of Loyola near Azpeitia, in the Basque province of Gipuzkoa in northern Spain. He was the youngest of thirteen children of a family of the minor nobility, proud and quarrelsome. His mother died soon after his birth, and the boy was nursed by the wife of the local blacksmith. His native tongue was Basque, not Spanish, a fact his translators still notice in the plainness of his written style.

As a youth he became a page in the household of Juan Velázquez de Cuéllar, treasurer of the kingdom of Castile, and there he learned the life of a courtier: dancing, fencing, gambling, the pursuit of women, and duelling. He modelled himself on the heroes of the chivalric romances, above all Amadís de Gaula, and he wanted fame. One biographer calls him a fancy dresser and a rough swordsman, sensitive to insult. At about eighteen he entered the service of the Duke of Nájera.

The cannonball at Pamplona

On 20 May 1521, a French and Navarrese army attacked the fortress of Pamplona, which Íñigo was helping to defend. A cannonball, ricocheting off a wall, smashed his right leg. He was carried home to Loyola, and there, with no anaesthetic, he underwent a series of operations in which the bones were set, broken again and reset. He survived, but the leg was left shorter than the other. He would limp for the rest of his life, and his military career was over.

The convalescence was long. To fill the hours he asked for the romances of chivalry he loved, but there were none in the castle. His sister-in-law, Magdalena de Araoz, brought him what there was: the Life of Christ by Ludolph of Saxony, and a collection of lives of the saints. Ludolph taught his readers to place themselves in imagination inside the Gospel scenes — to stand by the manger, to watch and listen — and that way of praying would become the heart of the Exercises.

His mind still wandered off into daydreams of the great deeds he would do for his king and for a royal lady he loved. But he began to notice something. When he dreamed of worldly glory, the dream delighted him while it lasted and left him dry and dissatisfied afterwards. When he dreamed of following Christ as the saints had, the joy remained long after the dream had ended. It was the first lesson in what he would later call the discernment of spirits: learning to read the after-effects of one’s thoughts and desires, and to tell which come from God and which do not.

A sword left at Montserrat

When he could walk again, he resolved to go as a pilgrim to Jerusalem and to do penance for his past life. In March 1522 he came to the Benedictine monastery of Montserrat, high in the mountains of Catalonia. There he examined his whole life and made a full confession. He gave away his fine clothes to the poor and put on a garment of sackcloth.

At Montserrat Íñigo kept an all-night vigil at the shrine of the Virgin, and there he hung up his sword and dagger at her altar. The soldier left his weapons with Our Lady and walked down the mountain as a pilgrim.

From Montserrat he walked to the nearby town of Manresa, and stayed there about a year. He begged for his keep, later doing chores at a local hospital in exchange for food and lodging, and practised a hard, rigorous penance. He knew deep consolation there, and he also learned to be wary of spiritual experience itself: a beautiful shape that appeared to him again and again in the air and filled him with delight he came in the end to judge was not from God.

At Manresa Íñigo gave himself to prayer for about seven hours a day, much of it in a cave outside the town. Out of those months of prayer, struggle and consolation came the first outline of the Spiritual Exercises — a book that began not as a theory but as notes on what God had done with one soul.

The pilgrim goes to school

In 1523 he finally reached Jerusalem, hoping to spend his life there near the places where Christ had walked. The Franciscans who had charge of the holy places would not allow it, and within weeks he was sent home. He concluded that, if he was to help souls, he needed an education. So, at about thirty-three, the former courtier sat down among schoolboys in Barcelona to learn Latin grammar.

From there he went on to the University of Alcalá, studying theology and Latin in 1526 and 1527. Devout groups known as alumbrados, “the enlightened,” were then under the Inquisition’s suspicion, and a layman with no degree in theology preaching in the street looked dangerous. At Alcalá he was singled out and questioned by the Inquisition, and later released.

In Paris he studied at the strict Collège de Montaigu and then at the Collège Sainte-Barbe, and around this time he began to use the Latin name Ignatius, probably as a variant of Íñigo that foreigners understood better. In Paris he gathered companions — Peter Faber, Francis Xavier, Diego Laínez, Alfonso Salmerón, Nicolás Bobadilla and Simão Rodrigues. On 15 August 1534, in a chapel on the hill of Montmartre, Ignatius and six companions, only one of them a priest, took solemn vows together, binding themselves to the work of their lives.

The Society of Jesus

The companions planned to go to the Holy Land, but war between Venice and the Ottoman Empire made the voyage impossible. In 1537, at Venice, Ignatius and most of the others were ordained priests. Instead of Jerusalem they went to Rome and offered themselves to the pope. In 1540 Pope Paul III approved their new order, the Society of Jesus, and in 1541 Ignatius was elected its first Superior General. To the usual vows of poverty, chastity and obedience he added a fourth: a special vow of obedience to the pope to go wherever he might send them.

From Rome Ignatius governed the young order, drafting the Society’s Constitutions with his secretary Juan Alfonso de Polanco, and sending his companions out — Francis Xavier to India and the East, others across Europe to preach, teach and found schools. Its guiding principle became Ad maiorem Dei gloriam, “for the greater glory of God.”
