In 1548 Paul III formally approved the Spiritual Exercises. The examiners, his bull records, had found them “full of piety and holiness.” It is a set of instructions for the one who guides a retreat, laid out over four “Weeks” lasting about thirty days. It opens with a single sentence that sets out the purpose of human life:

Man is created to praise, reverence, and serve God our Lord, and by this means to save his soul.

— Ignatius of Loyola, The Spiritual Exercises, Principle and Foundation

Everything else follows from that. If we are made for God, then health or sickness, riches or poverty, honour or dishonour, a long life or a short one, are to be desired only so far as they help us toward him. The first Week leads the person through the reality of sin; in its first meditation he is asked to imagine Christ on the cross before him and to speak with him, asking “what I have done for Christ, what I am doing for Christ, what I ought to do for Christ.” The later Weeks move through the life, death and resurrection of Jesus, inviting the one praying to enter each scene with all the senses, as Ludolph had taught Ignatius in his sickbed. Again and again Ignatius insists that the point is not information but encounter:

For it is not knowing much, but realising and relishing things interiorly, that contents and satisfies the soul.

— Ignatius of Loyola, The Spiritual Exercises, Second Annotation

Woven through the book are the rules for the discernment of spirits, the fruit of his own experience at Loyola and Manresa. He describes consolation and desolation with a precision that still helps people today, and gives counsel born of hard experience: “In time of desolation never to make a change.” There are also rules for thinking with the church, written in the age of the Reformation, which ask the retreatant to put the judgment of the church above his own. One of them, which says that “the white which I see, is black, if the Hierarchical Church so decides it,” has troubled many readers. It belongs to Ignatius’s conviction that the same Spirit guides both the believer and the church.

A last offering

Ignatius was not an easy man. He was a soldier who had become a saint, and he kept a soldier’s will; the Constitutions he wrote asked his men for an absolute self-denial and obedience. Yet the Exercises open with a plea for charity in judging others — that every good Christian should be “more ready to save his neighbor’s proposition than to condemn it” — and the last Week closes with a contemplation on the love of God, which begins with the note that “love ought to be put more in deeds than in words.” At its centre is the prayer for which he is best known, the offering of a whole life back to the one who gave it:

Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my intellect, and all my will—all that I have and possess. Thou gavest it to me: to Thee, Lord, I return it! All is Thine, dispose of it according to all Thy will. Give me Thy love and grace, for this is enough for me.

— Ignatius of Loyola, The Spiritual Exercises, Contemplation to Gain Love

In his last years his health failed. Around 1553 he dictated the story of his early life to a younger Jesuit, the account through which we know most of what happened at Loyola and Manresa. He died in Rome on 31 July 1556, probably of the “Roman fever,” a severe form of malaria; an autopsy found that he had also long suffered from stones in his kidneys and bladder. He was buried in Rome, and his remains now lie in the Church of the Gesù. He was beatified in 1609 and canonized on 12 March 1622, and in 1922 Pope Pius XI named him patron of spiritual retreats.

Why read the Exercises

The edition offered here is Father Elder Mullan’s translation of 1914, made directly from the Spanish “Autograph” — the copy Ignatius himself corrected and used in giving the Exercises. Mullan kept close to Ignatius’s plain wording, so that readers could feel sure they were reading the saint’s own words, and he warned that the book is not meant to be read quickly but to be “pondered word for word and under the direction of a competent guide.” Read straight through, it can seem dry. Prayed slowly, it has formed saints, missionaries and ordinary believers for nearly five hundred years.

What Ignatius leaves is less a method than a way of looking: the conviction that God is at work in every created thing and in the stirrings of every heart, and that a person can learn, with patience and honesty, to notice where he is leading. It began with a wounded man who was handed the wrong book. He spent the rest of his life helping others find what he had found, and learn to say with him, “Give me Thy love and grace, for this is enough for me.”

faq.q: Who was Ignatius of Loyola?
faq.a: Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556) was a Basque nobleman and soldier who became a priest and founded the Society of Jesus, the Jesuits. He is best known for The Spiritual Exercises, his handbook of prayer and discernment.

faq.q: What was Ignatius like as a young man?
faq.a: Born Íñigo López de Oñaz y Loyola, the youngest of thirteen children, he grew up as a page in the household of the treasurer of Castile. He loved dancing, fencing, gambling, duelling and tales of chivalry, and he longed for fame as a soldier.

faq.q: What happened to Ignatius at Pamplona?
faq.a: On 20 May 1521, while the fortress of Pamplona was under attack by a French and Navarrese army, a cannonball shattered his right leg. Painful operations without anaesthetic left him with a limp for life and ended his military career.

faq.q: How was Ignatius converted?
faq.a: During his convalescence at Loyola there were no romances of chivalry to read, so he read a life of Christ by Ludolph of Saxony and lives of the saints. He noticed that dreams of worldly glory left him dry, while dreams of following Christ left lasting joy, and this was the beginning of his teaching on discernment.

faq.q: What did Ignatius do at Montserrat and Manresa?
faq.a: In March 1522 at the monastery of Montserrat he made a full confession, gave away his fine clothes, and after an all-night vigil hung his sword and dagger at the altar of the Virgin. He then spent about a year at Manresa in poverty and penance, praying some seven hours a day and drafting the first outline of the Spiritual Exercises.

faq.q: Why did Ignatius go back to school?
faq.a: After a pilgrimage to Jerusalem in 1523, where he was not allowed to stay, he decided he needed an education to help souls. He studied Latin grammar in Barcelona at about thirty-three, then at Alcalá, where the Inquisition questioned him and released him, and finally at the University of Paris.

faq.q: How did the Society of Jesus begin?
faq.a: In Paris Ignatius gathered companions including Peter Faber and Francis Xavier, and on 15 August 1534 they took solemn vows together at Montmartre. Ordained in Venice in 1537, they offered themselves to the pope, and Paul III approved the Society of Jesus in 1540, with Ignatius elected its first Superior General in 1541.

faq.q: What is The Spiritual Exercises?
faq.a: It is a set of instructions for guiding a retreat of about thirty days in four “Weeks,” moving from the purpose of human life and the reality of sin through the life, death and resurrection of Christ. It includes rules for the discernment of spirits and the prayer “Take, Lord, and receive,” and was approved by Pope Paul III in 1548; the edition published here is Elder Mullan’s 1914 translation from the Spanish Autograph.

faq.q: What is the Principle and Foundation?
faq.a: It is the opening meditation of the Exercises, which begins “Man is created to praise, reverence, and serve God our Lord, and by this means to save his soul.” From it Ignatius teaches that all created things are to be used only so far as they help a person toward that end.

faq.q: When did Ignatius die, and how is he remembered?
faq.a: He died in Rome on 31 July 1556, probably of malaria, and his remains lie in the Church of the Gesù. He was canonized on 12 March 1622, his feast is kept on 31 July, and in 1922 Pope Pius XI named him patron of spiritual retreats.

fields.name: Boethius
fields.bio: Boethius (c. 480–524) was a Roman senator, consul and Christian philosopher who carried Greek learning into the Latin West. Condemned for treason by King Theodoric, he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison before his execution, and is venerated at Pavia as St Severinus Boethius.
fields.bio_html:
Sometime around the year 524, in a cell near Pavia in northern Italy, a condemned man sat down to write. A few years earlier he had been one of the most honoured men in the Roman world: a consul, the father of two consuls, the chief minister of the king. Now his property was gone, his name was disgraced, and he was waiting to die for a treason he swore he had not committed. What he wrote in that cell was not a protest or a plea, but a long conversation with Wisdom about fortune, happiness, evil and the providence of God. For a thousand years afterward, almost every educated person in Europe read it. Its author was Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, and the book was The Consolation of Philosophy.

A child of old Rome

Boethius was born in Rome around 480, a few years after the last emperor of the West had been forced from his throne. Italy was now ruled by barbarian kings, but the great Roman families still kept their wealth, their titles and their pride. His own family, the Anicii, had produced emperors and many consuls, though by his birth its fortunes had faded. His father, also a consul, died while Boethius was still young, and the boy was taken in and raised by another noble, Quintus Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, who introduced him to philosophy and literature. The bond between them was deep. Boethius later married Symmachus’s daughter, Rusticiana, and they had two sons.

He grew up with a rare gift for that age in the West: a complete command of Greek. Older writers claimed that he studied for many years in Athens, and some modern historians have suggested Alexandria, but the evidence for either is weak, and he may have learned all he knew without leaving Italy. What is certain is the use he made of it. As a young man he set himself an enormous task: to translate all the works of Plato and Aristotle into Latin, with commentaries, and to show that the two great philosophers were, at bottom, in agreement.

Scholar and statesman

He never finished that work, but what he did finish shaped the mind of Europe. His Latin versions of Aristotle’s writings on logic were, for some six hundred years, almost the only Aristotle that Western Christians could read. He wrote handbooks on arithmetic and on music that were studied in schools throughout the Middle Ages; a modern historian called him “the schoolmaster of medieval Europe.” It was largely through him that the West kept any thread of connection with Greek philosophy at all.

Yet Boethius did not think a philosopher should stay in his library. Plato had taught that cities would be happy if wise men governed them, and Boethius took the lesson to heart. He entered the service of Theodoric, the Ostrogothic king of Italy, a capable ruler who governed his Roman subjects with considerable respect. Boethius rose quickly. He was a senator young and consul in 510. In 522 came the proudest day of his life, when both his sons were made consuls together and he stood between them in triumph before the people. In the same period he became master of offices, head of the king’s government and household.

He used the post to fight corruption, and he made enemies doing it. In the Consolation he recalls standing up to powerful officials who were plundering the poor, and using the king’s authority to stop a requisition of grain that would have deepened a famine in the south. These were honourable acts. They were not safe ones.

A Christian thinker

Boethius was a Christian, and a learned one. Alongside his philosophy he wrote short theological treatises, the Opuscula sacra, on the central doctrines of the faith. The most important, On the Trinity, defends the Catholic teaching that God is three persons in one undivided nature. Another, Against Eutyches and Nestorius, works out how Christ can be both fully God and fully man. In these little works he brought the precise tools of Greek logic to bear on Christian doctrine, and later medieval theologians learned much of their method from him.

This mattered politically. Theodoric and his Goths were Arian Christians, who held that the Son was not fully equal with the Father. Boethius, like most of the old Roman aristocracy, held the Catholic faith of the creed. In the last years of Theodoric’s reign, as Catholic Romans looked increasingly toward the emperor in Constantinople, the king grew suspicious of the senators around him, and a learned Catholic nobleman with ties to the East was an easy man to suspect.

Accused at Verona

The blow fell in 523. At a meeting of the royal council in Verona, an official named Cyprianus accused a former consul, Albinus, of treasonous letters to the emperor. Boethius sprang to his defence, declaring, according to the ancient accounts, that if Albinus had done it, then so had he and the whole Senate with him. It was a brave and loyal thing to say. Cyprianus promptly accused Boethius too, and produced witnesses whom Boethius later described as disgraced men, one dismissed for debt and two exiled for fraud. He was charged, in his own words, with having “desired the safety of the Senate”, and with forged letters hoping for the freedom of Rome. He was condemned without being allowed to answer for himself in person.

Nay, I did desire the safety of the Senate, nor shall ever cease to desire it.

— Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book I

He was imprisoned near Pavia, and there, awaiting death, he wrote the Consolation.

The visitor in the cell

The book opens with Boethius in tears, writing sad verses about his fall. Then a woman appears standing over him, of great majesty, her eyes burning, her robe torn and dimmed with neglect. She drives away the weeping Muses, sits on the end of his bed, and dries his eyes with a fold of her dress. He realises who she is: Philosophy, the nurse in whose rooms he had spent his life. What follows, in five books of alternating prose and verse, is her treatment of a sick soul.

She begins gently. He pours out his grievances, and the deepest of them is not the loss of wealth but the memory of happiness:

For of all suffering from Fortune, the unhappiest misfortune is to have known a happy fortune.

— Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II

Philosophy answers that Fortune never truly belonged to him. Fortune is a wheel, and its whole nature is to turn; to complain that it has turned is to complain that it is Fortune. Wealth, office, fame and pleasure all promise happiness and cannot give it, because each can be lost and none is complete. True happiness can only be found in the highest good, which cannot be lost because it is God himself.

In the first book, before Philosophy’s counsel has begun to take hold, Boethius cries out to God in a long lament: “Founder of the star-studded universe, resting on Thine eternal throne whence Thou turnest the swiftly rolling sky, and bindest the stars to keep Thy law”. Everything in heaven keeps its appointed order, he says; why then are the lives of men left to the cruelty of chance? It is a prisoner’s honest complaint, like those of the psalms, and the rest of the book is the slow answer to it.

At the turning point of the whole work, in the third book, Philosophy asks how they should seek that highest good. Boethius answers, “Call … upon the Father of all, for if we do not do so, no undertaking would be rightly or duly begun.” And Philosophy sings a hymn, known by its Latin opening O qui perpetua, to the One who rules the universe by everlasting law. It ends in plain petition:

“Grant then, O Father, that this mind of ours may rise to Thy throne of majesty; grant us to reach that fount of good. Grant that we may so find light that we may set on Thee unblinded eyes; cast Thou therefrom the heavy clouds of this material world.” It is the still centre of the whole book: a philosopher’s argument turning, at its heart, into prayer.

Thou art our beginning, our progress, our guide, our way, our end.

— Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book III

The last two books take up the hardest questions: why the wicked seem to prosper and the good to suffer, and how God can know the future without forcing it. Philosophy’s answer to the second has been admired ever since. God does not see events before they happen, as we do with our guesses; he lives in an eternal present, and sees all of time at once, as we see a man walking and the sun rising in the same glance, without making either happen by our seeing. Providence is better called a looking forth than a looking forward. Human freedom is real, and so prayer is not wasted.

Hopes are not vainly put in God, nor prayers in vain offered: if these are right, they cannot but be answered.

— Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book V

The question of his faith

Here an honest reader meets a puzzle. The Consolation never mentions Christ. It does not quote Scripture, speak of the cross, or name the Church. The comfort it offers is the comfort of reason, given by Philosophy rather than by a priest. Some scholars have concluded that in his last extremity Boethius’s Christianity simply fell away. Others reply that his theological works prove beyond doubt that he was a Christian, and orthodox. The editor of the old English translation published here observed that there is no Christian doctrine relied upon in the book, but also nothing that conflicts with Christianity.

Perhaps the fairest reading is that Boethius set out to show how far reason alone could carry a suffering man toward God, and found that it carried him a long way: to a good and loving Father who governs the world, to prayer, to the hope of seeing God face to face. He wrote as a philosopher, in the language his education had given him. Many Christian readers since have found that this makes the book more useful, not less, because it meets the grieving where they are and leads them, step by reasoned step, toward the One whom faith names more fully.

Death and remembrance

Boethius was put to death in 524 at an estate in the countryside near Pavia. The ancient sources disagree about how; the most likely account is that he was tortured with a cord tightened around his head and then beaten to death. Not long afterwards Theodoric had Symmachus, his father-in-law, executed as well. His wealth was confiscated and Rusticiana was left in poverty. His remains were laid in the church of San Pietro in Ciel d’Oro in Pavia, where the bones of Augustine of Hippo also rest.

The centuries that followed honoured him as a martyr who had died at the hands of an Arian king. That judgement is debated, since his condemnation was political rather than plainly religious. But the devotion was real and lasting. In the diocese of Pavia he has long been venerated as Saint Severinus Boethius, and in 1883 the Church confirmed that local custom, with a feast day on 23 October. Dante placed him in Paradise among the great teachers, in the heaven of the Sun.

His book had an even longer life. King Alfred the Great translated it into Old English; Chaucer and Queen Elizabeth I translated it after him; it fed the poetry of Dante, Chaucer and many others, and gave the Middle Ages its favourite image of Fortune’s wheel.

The translation on these pages is W. V. Cooper’s English version of 1902. It is a book for anyone who has lost what they loved and wondered whether God is still in charge. Boethius does not pretend that grief is small or injustice unreal; he begins in tears and is allowed to say everything. But he is led, patiently, out of self-pity toward a larger view: that Fortune is not God, that nothing we can lose was ever our true good, and that the eternal Father sees us, governs all things, and hears our prayers. He wrote it under sentence of death. Few books on suffering have been written with more right.

faq.q: Who was Boethius?
faq.a: Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524) was a Roman senator, consul and philosopher who served Theodoric, the Ostrogothic king of Italy. He translated Greek philosophy into Latin, wrote Christian theological treatises, and is best remembered for The Consolation of Philosophy, written in prison before his execution.

faq.q: Where did Boethius come from?
faq.a: He was born in Rome around 480 into the Anicii, an ancient noble family that had produced emperors and many consuls. His father died while he was young, and he was raised by the nobleman Symmachus, whose daughter Rusticiana he later married; they had two sons.

faq.q: What did Boethius do as a scholar?
faq.a: He set out to translate all of Plato and Aristotle into Latin, with commentaries, and to show that the two philosophers agreed. He never finished, but his versions of Aristotle’s logic were for about six centuries almost the only Aristotle available in the Latin West, and his handbooks on arithmetic and music were studied throughout the Middle Ages.

faq.q: What offices did Boethius hold?
faq.a: He became a senator young and consul in 510. In 522 both his sons were made consuls together, and he became master of offices, the head of Theodoric’s government and household, where he made enemies by opposing corrupt officials.

faq.q: Was Boethius a Christian?
faq.a: Yes. He wrote short theological treatises, including On the Trinity, defending the Catholic doctrine of God as three persons in one nature, and Against Eutyches and Nestorius on the two natures of Christ. Because The Consolation of Philosophy never mentions Christ, some scholars have doubted how much his faith shaped his final years, but many scholars hold that he was an orthodox Christian to the end.

faq.q: Why was Boethius arrested?
faq.a: In 523, at the royal council in Verona, he defended the former consul Albinus against a charge of treasonous correspondence with the emperor in Constantinople, and was then accused of the same crime himself. Theodoric, an Arian Christian increasingly suspicious of the Catholic Senate, had him imprisoned near Pavia.

faq.q: What is The Consolation of Philosophy about?
faq.a: Written in prison, it is a dialogue in prose and verse between the grieving Boethius and Philosophy, who appears to him as a majestic woman. She teaches him that Fortune is a turning wheel, that no earthly good can give true happiness, that the highest good is God, and that God’s providence sees all time in an eternal present without destroying human freedom.

faq.q: Does The Consolation of Philosophy contain prayers?
faq.a: Yes. In Book III Philosophy sings the hymn known as O qui perpetua to the Father who rules the universe by everlasting law, ending with the petition that our minds may rise to his throne and reach the fount of good. The book closes by urging the reader to send up prayers, since they are not offered in vain.

faq.q: How did Boethius die?
faq.a: He was executed in 524 at an estate near Pavia; the sources disagree on the method, but he was most likely tortured with a cord around his head and beaten to death. His property was confiscated, his father-in-law Symmachus was executed soon afterwards, and his remains were laid in San Pietro in Ciel d’Oro in Pavia.

faq.q: Is Boethius a saint, and what is his legacy?
faq.a: He is venerated in the diocese of Pavia as Saint Severinus Boethius, a local cult confirmed in 1883 with a feast on 23 October, though whether his death counts as martyrdom is debated. The Consolation was translated by King Alfred, Chaucer and Queen Elizabeth I, and Dante placed him in Paradise.

fields.name: Basil of Caesarea
fields.bio: Basil of Caesarea (330–379) was the archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia remembered as Basil the Great, a founder of Eastern monastic life and one of the Cappadocian Fathers. He fed the hungry in the famine of 368, built the Basileias for the poor and sick, and wrote On the Holy Spirit.
fields.bio_html:
Basil of Caesarea is one of the few people the church has simply called “the Great,” and the title fits him in more ways than one. His short book on the Holy Spirit helped settle what Christians confess about God. He shaped the monastic life of the Eastern church, fed a starving city with his own hands, and faced down an emperor. But he was also a hard, proud, worn-out man who could wound his dearest friend and never quite mend it. The record keeps both sides.

A household of saints

He was born about 330 — the year most scholars accept — probably at Caesarea in Cappadocia, in the uplands of what is now central Turkey, though Neocaesarea in Pontus has also been named. His family was wealthy and deeply Christian, with the scars of persecution still on it. His father’s parents had suffered severe hardships in the last great persecution; his mother Emmelia’s father had died for Christ. His father, also called Basil, was a respected advocate and teacher of rhetoric. Of the ten children, several are venerated as saints: his elder sister Macrina, his brother Gregory, later bishop of Nyssa, and his youngest brother Peter, later bishop of Sebasteia.

He was brought up on the family estate at Annesi, on the river Iris, by his grandmother Macrina, who taught him the faith she had learned from the tradition of Gregory the Wonderworker, the missionary bishop of Pontus. Then came the best education the empire could give, at Caesarea, Constantinople and, from 351, Athens. There he formed the friendship of his life with another young Cappadocian, Gregory of Nazianzus. Their fellow students knew the pair for their hard work, their clean and devout lives, and their love for one another; Gregory later wrote that they had everything in common and were as one soul. Among the other students was a young prince, Julian, who would one day abandon the faith and rule as emperor.

A clever young man, turned around

Basil came home around 356 and taught rhetoric at Caesarea with great success. His brother Gregory is frank that he was then rather pleased with himself. It was their sister Macrina, Gregory says, whose persuasion and example turned him to a life of self-denial. He was baptized, probably in 357, and soon made a reader in the church. He then travelled to see the monks of Palestine, Mesopotamia, Syria and Egypt, and came back resolved to live as they did.

He settled in a mountain glen across the Iris from the family home and gave himself to a discipline that would ruin his health: the poorest food, one inner and one outer garment, and haircloth at night, but not by day, lest he seem to be showing off. What was new in Basil’s monasticism, and what lasted, was its shape. Monks had mostly lived alone or in twos and threes. Following the example of the ascetic Eustathius of Sebaste, Basil gathered them into communities that worked, prayed and served together, and the rules he wrote for them became the foundation of monastic life in the Eastern churches. He also had a dry wit about half-measures. A later writer, John Cassian, tells of a senator who came to join him, announcing that he had renounced his property except for enough to spare him manual labour. “You have spoilt a senator,” said Basil, “without making a monk.”

Bread for a starving city

Basil was ordained priest around 364 by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea — not wholly willingly. His very usefulness soon caused friction, and some bishops were ready to set him up in Eusebius’s place. Basil would not divide the church for his own advancement: he withdrew to Pontus, and came back only when he could serve Eusebius loyally.

His great test as a priest came in 368, when drought and famine struck Caesarea. Speculators were hoarding grain to sell at famine prices. Basil moved them to open their stores. He gave lavishly from his own means, and he served the hungry in person. His friend Gregory left a picture of him standing in a crowd of men, women and children, some scarcely able to breathe, while servants brought in food fit for the starving and Basil handed it out with his own hands and cheered the sufferers with his own voice.

On the outskirts of Caesarea he built a great house for travellers, the poor and the sick, so large that people called it the “New Town,” and later the Basileias. It is often counted among the first Christian hospitals, and it became the mother of smaller houses across the countryside.

The bishop and the emperor

When Eusebius died in 370, in Basil’s arms, Basil was elected to succeed him as archbishop of Caesarea, with authority over a wide sweep of the provinces around. The election was bitterly fought; the elder Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus and father of Basil’s friend, old and ill, had himself carried to Caesarea in a litter to cast his vote.

His great trial came at the end of 371. The Emperor Valens favoured the Arian party, who denied that the Son is truly God, and he was travelling through Cappadocia intending to bring its churches into line. His prefect Modestus summoned Basil and threatened him with confiscation, exile, torture and death. As the story has come down to us, Basil answered that he owned nothing but a few rags and a few books; that no exile could send him out of God’s earth; that torture could not hurt a body already as good as dead; and that death would only be a friend, hurrying him home. Modestus said that no one had ever spoken to him like that. “Perhaps,” replied Basil, “you never met a bishop before.”

Valens himself came to the church at the Epiphany and was so shaken by the sight of Basil and his people at worship that he staggered as he brought his offering to the altar. He even gave lands for Basil’s hospital. But Basil would not admit the Arians to communion, and the order for his exile was drawn up.

On the very night his exile was to be enforced, the emperor’s little son Galates fell dangerously ill, and Valens sent for the bishop he had meant to banish and asked him to pray over the child. Basil came and prayed. There was a brief rally, then a relapse, and the boy died. The decree of exile was never carried out, and after that the emperor let him be.

Friendships lost and kept

It is in these same years that Basil’s hardness shows most painfully. When Valens split Cappadocia into two provinces, the bishop of the new capital, Tyana, claimed equal standing with Caesarea. To strengthen his hand, Basil set up new bishoprics and, against his friend’s will, made Gregory of Nazianzus bishop of Sasima, an insignificant little town at a fork in the road that Gregory loathed. Gregory soon gave up the post, and he never fully forgave him. Even in his funeral oration for Basil, Gregory owned that he still felt the smart. Basil had won a point of church politics and lost the friend of his youth.

Other friendships failed through no fault of his. Eustathius of Sebaste, the ascetic he had once revered, broke communion with him and circulated an old letter of Basil’s doctored with heretical phrases. Some of his own side doubted him, too. At a dinner party at Nazianzus a guest with a reputation for piety complained that Basil preached splendidly on the Father and the Son but would not clearly call the Spirit God. Gregory defended him: Basil, he said, had to weigh every word, with exile always hanging over him.

Yet he kept friends too: the old bishop Eusebius of Samosata, whom he loved like a son, and young Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, to whom he was a spiritual father. A conversation with Amphilochius in the autumn of 374 produced his most enduring book.

A book about a preposition, and about God

On the Holy Spirit began with a prayer. Leading his people in worship, Basil had given glory to the Father sometimes “with the Son together with the Holy Ghost,” and sometimes “through the Son in the Holy Ghost.” Some who heard him objected that he was bringing in new and contradictory terms. Amphilochius asked him to explain himself, and the treatise, written about 375, is the answer. It can look like an argument about prepositions, but Basil insists that no word of worship is small:

Truth is always a quarry hard to hunt, and therefore we must look everywhere for its tracks.

— Basil of Caesarea, On the Holy Spirit, chapter 1

From there he shows from Scripture and from the church’s worship that the Spirit is not a creature or a servant but shares the one glory of the Father and the Son. Some of his loveliest pages describe what the Spirit does in a human life — illuminating, healing and drawing the soul toward God:

Through His aid hearts are lifted up, the weak are held by the hand, and they who are advancing are brought to perfection.

— Basil of Caesarea, On the Holy Spirit, chapter 9

Along the way he defends the unwritten customs the church had handed down, many of them customs of prayer: praying facing east, and standing to pray on Sundays and through the fifty days from Easter to Pentecost.

Basil wanted Christians to understand even the posture of their prayers. “Thus we all look to the East at our prayers,” he wrote, “but few of us know that we are seeking our own old country, Paradise, which God planted in Eden in the East.” Standing to pray on the day of resurrection, he said, turns the mind from the present toward the age to come.

The last chapter is a cry of grief. Basil likens the church of his day to a naval battle fought in a storm, friend striking friend in the dark. He would rather have kept silent, he says, but love would not let him:

Wherefore we too are undismayed at the cloud of our enemies, and, resting our hope on the aid of the Spirit, have, with all boldness, proclaimed the truth.

— Basil of Caesarea, On the Holy Spirit, chapter 30

Worn out at fifty

His last years were dark. A chronic liver complaint, years of fasting and endless travel had broken his body; by 376, he told Amphilochius, he had lost all his teeth. Athanasius died in 373, and his appeals to the West for help went unanswered. Then, in 378, Valens was killed by the Goths at Adrianople, and the new emperor Gratian recalled the exiled bishops. Basil lived just long enough to see the tide turn.

He died, by the traditional reckoning, on 1 January 379, at about the age of fifty — though historians have disputed the date. Gregory was not with him, but left an account of the end. Crowds surrounded the house, praying for his recovery and ready to give their lives for his.

Having given his last words of counsel, Basil died with the prayer of Christ on the cross on his lips: “Into thy hands I commend my spirit.” At his funeral Jews and pagans mourned alongside Christians, and the press of people was so great that some were killed in the crowd.

He did not live to see the Council of Constantinople in 381, which confessed the Holy Spirit as “the Lord, the giver of life,” worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son — very nearly the position he had spent his last years defending. With his brother Gregory of Nyssa and his friend Gregory of Nazianzus he is remembered as one of the three Cappadocian Fathers. The Eastern churches still celebrate a Divine Liturgy bearing his name, its prayers preserving at least the memory of his work, and in Greek homes 1 January is still St Basil’s Day.

The book we publish is On the Holy Spirit, in Blomfield Jackson’s nineteenth-century translation, with the editor’s account of Basil’s life. It is short and sometimes demanding, but it shows how the early church thought: not by spinning theories, but by listening closely to Scripture and to its own prayers. Anyone who has ever said “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit” and wondered what they were saying will find in Basil a patient, passionate guide.

faq.q: Who was Basil of Caesarea?
faq.a: Basil, called Basil the Great, was a fourth-century archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, born about 330 and died in 379. He is remembered as a theologian of the Trinity, a founder of Eastern monastic life, and one of the three Cappadocian Fathers.

faq.q: What was Basil of Caesarea’s family like?
faq.a: He was one of ten children of a wealthy, devout family that had suffered in the persecutions. His grandmother Macrina raised him in the faith, and his sister Macrina and his brothers Gregory of Nyssa and Peter of Sebasteia are also venerated as saints.

faq.q: Where was Basil educated?
faq.a: He studied at Caesarea, Constantinople and, from 351, Athens. At Athens he formed a lifelong friendship with Gregory of Nazianzus, and the future emperor Julian was also a student there.

faq.q: What turned Basil to the monastic life?
faq.a: After returning home around 356 he taught rhetoric with success, and his brother Gregory credits their sister Macrina with turning him to a life of self-denial. He was baptized around 357, visited the monks of Palestine, Mesopotamia, Syria and Egypt, and settled in a retreat near the family estate at Annesi.

faq.q: How did Basil shape monastic life?
faq.a: Where most ascetics had lived alone or in very small groups, Basil gathered monks into communities that worked, prayed and served together. The rules he wrote for them became foundational for monastic life in the Eastern churches.

faq.q: What did Basil do during the famine of 368?
faq.a: When drought and famine struck Caesarea, he moved grain hoarders to open their stores, gave generously from his own means, and handed out food to the starving with his own hands. On the edge of the city he built a great house for travellers, the poor and the sick, later called the Basileias and often counted among the first Christian hospitals.

faq.q: How did Basil stand up to the Emperor Valens?
faq.a: When the Arian emperor’s prefect Modestus threatened him with confiscation, exile, torture and death, Basil answered that none of these frightened him, and told the astonished prefect that perhaps he had never met a bishop before. Valens drew up an order for his exile but it was never carried out.

faq.q: Why did Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus fall out?
faq.a: In a dispute with the bishop of Tyana, Basil made Gregory bishop of Sasima, an insignificant town Gregory loathed, against his wishes. Gregory soon gave up the post and never fully forgave his old friend.

faq.q: What is Basil’s book On the Holy Spirit about?
faq.a: Written about 375 for his friend Amphilochius of Iconium, it defends the way Basil gave glory to the Father with the Son together with the Holy Spirit, and argues from Scripture and the church’s worship that the Spirit shares the one glory of the Father and the Son. The translation published here is Blomfield Jackson’s.

faq.q: When did Basil die, and how is he remembered?
faq.a: He died worn out by illness and austerity, by the traditional reckoning on 1 January 379, praying the words Into thy hands I commend my spirit. He is honoured as a saint and Doctor of the Church, a Divine Liturgy bears his name, and 1 January is kept as St Basil’s Day in Greek tradition.

fields.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
fields.bio: Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390) was a Cappadocian bishop, poet and orator, called “the Theologian.” His Five Theological Orations, preached in a small Constantinople chapel in 380, defended the faith in the Trinity, and he briefly led the Council of 381 before resigning for the sake of peace.
fields.bio_html:
The church gave Gregory of Nazianzus a title it has given to almost no one else: the Theologian. He shares it among the early Fathers with the apostle John alone. It is a strange honour for a man who wanted, above all, quiet — books, prayer, a friend to share them with — and was given noise. He was ordained against his will, consecrated a bishop against his will, called to the capital of the empire against his will, and, when he had won the argument he was sent there to win, he resigned and went home. In between, in a borrowed house turned chapel, he preached five sermons on the Trinity that the whole church still reads.

A son promised to God

He was born around 329 at Arianzus, a country estate of his family near the small Cappadocian town of Nazianzus, in what is now central Turkey. The exact year is uncertain. His father, also named Gregory, had belonged to a little sect called the Hypsistarians, who worshipped one “Most High” God but rejected the Trinity. He was brought to Christian faith by his wife, Nonna, and was soon afterwards made bishop of Nazianzus. Nonna was a woman of deep holiness, and Gregory believed she had dedicated him to God even before he was born. He had a sister, Gorgonia, and a brother, Cæsarius, who became a physician at the imperial court.

The family was wealthy, and Gregory was given the finest education the fourth century had to offer: schools at Cæsarea in Cappadocia, then Cæsarea in Palestine, then Alexandria, and at last Athens. Like many Christians of his day he had put off baptism, and he was still unbaptized when, eager to reach Athens, he set sail out of season, in November.

The storm and the vow

In sight of Cyprus a storm struck the ship so violently that the crew said they had seldom seen its like. Gregory, telling the story years later at his father’s funeral, said plainly what frightened him most: “spiritual death was what I was most afraid of,” for he was about to die unbaptised. He cried out to God and begged for a respite, and his shipmates, in their own danger, joined their cries to his.

In Gregory’s own account, his parents at home learned of his danger in a vision by night, and “aided me from the land, soothing the waves by prayer, as I afterwards learned by calculating the time.” A boy on board dreamed that he saw Gregory’s mother walk upon the sea and drag the ship to land. Then the sea began to grow calm, and they reached Rhodes. Gregory kept his side of the bargain: “we promised ourselves if we were saved, to God, and, when we had been saved, gave ourselves to Him.”

At Athens he met again a young man he had first known at school in Cæsarea: Basil, later bishop of Cæsarea and remembered as Basil the Great. The two became inseparable. “Two ways were known to us,” Gregory later wrote, one leading to the church and its teachers, the other to their lectures. Looking back on that friendship after Basil’s death, Gregory put it in a sentence that has been quoted ever since:

We seemed to have one soul, inhabiting two bodies.

— Gregory of Nazianzus, Funeral Oration on Basil

He stayed in Athens until he was about thirty. When he came home he was baptized, most likely around this time, and at his baptism he vowed never to swear and to give his whole strength to the glory of God. He longed for the life of a monk. For some years he went back and forth between his aging parents and Basil’s retreat in the wilds of Pontus, where the two friends divided their days between prayer, study and manual work.

The noble tyranny

The quiet ended at Christmas, probably in 361. His father, old and failing, wanted his son beside him, and the people of Nazianzus wanted it too; together they had Gregory ordained a priest more or less by force. Gregory was stung, and fled to Basil in Pontus. Even in old age he called that ordination an act of tyranny. But he thought better of the flight, and was back in the church at Nazianzus for Easter 362, where he preached his first sermon as a priest. In it he offered his own pardon “for the noble tyranny which I have suffered (for I can now call it noble).” He also wrote a long defence of his flight, which became a treatise on the priesthood. In it he called the guiding of human souls “the art of arts and science of sciences,” and both John Chrysostom and Gregory the Great built their own books on pastoral care upon it.

The same pattern came round again. Around 372 Basil, now archbishop of Cæsarea and locked in a dispute over church boundaries, consecrated his friend bishop of Sasima, a wretched little village on a disputed border, to strengthen his own side. Gregory, as his editors put it, “bent his neck, but not his will.” A rival bishop held Sasima with soldiers, and Gregory probably never administered it at all. The wound to the friendship was real and long, and Gregory never pretended otherwise — nor stopped loving Basil.

He served instead as his father’s assistant at Nazianzus. When both his parents died in 374, he cared for the diocese for a time, gave away most of his inheritance, and then, after a serious illness, withdrew to Seleucia in Isauria, where he lived for some three or four years near the church of St Thecla. It was there that word reached him of Basil’s death.

Five sermons in a borrowed chapel

In 379 the small company of Christians in Constantinople who held to the faith of the Council of Nicaea asked him to come to them. For forty years the capital had been ruled by bishops of the Arian party, who taught that the Son of God was a creature, not truly God. Gregory resisted for a long time, then went. A relative gave him a house, and he turned part of it into a chapel and named it Anastasia — “Resurrection” — as the place where the faith of the church was to rise again.

There, in 380, he preached the five sermons now called the Theological Orations. His opponents, the followers of Eunomius, claimed that human logic could define the very essence of God. Gregory began by telling his hearers that this was not a subject for idle talk: “Not to every one, my friends, does it belong to philosophize about God.” It required a cleansed life, a quiet mind, and reverence. That did not mean God should be thought of seldom — just the reverse:

For we ought to think of God even more often than we draw our breath; and if the expression is permissible, we ought to do nothing else.

— Gregory of Nazianzus, The First Theological Oration

The second sermon dwells on how far beyond our grasp God is. The third and fourth defend the full divinity of the Son from the Scriptures, answering the texts his opponents used against it. The fifth does the same for the Holy Spirit. There, to describe how the Spirit comes from the Father in a way different from the Son’s being begotten, Gregory says he must “coin a word for the sake of clearness,” and the word he uses, procession, has shaped Christian teaching about the Spirit ever since. At the heart of it all is not a puzzle but a Person, the Christ who is both truly God and truly man:

He hungered—but He fed thousands; yea, He is the Bread that giveth life, and That is of heaven. He thirsted—but He cried, If any man thirst, let him come unto Me and drink.

— Gregory of Nazianzus, The Third Theological Oration

The preaching drew growing crowds, and it was dangerous work. One Easter vigil an Arian mob burst into the chapel during worship; Gregory was wounded and another bishop was killed. At his farewell he would ask his flock simply to “Remember my stonings.” He was also deceived by an adventurer named Maximus, who won his trust and then had himself secretly consecrated bishop of the city while Gregory lay ill. The people drove Maximus out, but the fashionable capital looked down on the plain provincial who would not play the showman in the pulpit.

Farewell, my throne

In late 380 the new emperor Theodosius came to Constantinople, expelled the Arian bishop and put Gregory in possession of the city’s churches. In 381 the emperor called the council of about one hundred and fifty Eastern bishops that is now counted as the Second Ecumenical Council. It confirmed Gregory as archbishop of the capital, and when its president, Meletius of Antioch, died, Gregory was chosen to lead it. The council divided over a dispute in Antioch, and late-arriving bishops from Egypt challenged his right to the see at all, arguing that a bishop could not lawfully move from one see (Sasima) to another. Rather than become the cause of a new division, Gregory resigned.

His farewell sermon to the council is among the most moving things he wrote. He was honest about his exhaustion: “I am weary of being charged with my gentleness.” He compared himself to a pilot struggling at the helm, “contending alike with the sea and the passengers,” and asked only to be dismissed with their prayers. Then he took leave of everything he loved there — the little Anastasia, the cathedral, the choirs and the night-long vigils, the widows and orphans and “ye eyes of the poor, turned towards God and towards me” — and ended with the God he had spent his strength defending:

Farewell, O Trinity, my meditation, and my glory.

— Gregory of Nazianzus, The Last Farewell

The garden at Arianzus

He went home to Cappadocia and looked after the church at Nazianzus once more, fighting the teaching of the Apollinarians, who denied that Christ had a full human mind. Around the end of 383, his health too frail for the work, he saw a bishop named Eulalius chosen for Nazianzus and withdrew for good to the family estate at Arianzus.

His last years were spent writing — hundreds of poems, among them a long autobiographical poem on his own life, along with letters and epitaphs for friends — and praying. Before leaving Constantinople he had made his will, leaving his property in the end to the poor of Nazianzus.

The account of his last days printed with his orations says that he spent them in continual devotion, that his knees were worn with kneeling, and that he slept on straw under sackcloth, with a single tunic for clothing — the former archbishop of the imperial city, praying alone by a fountain in the Cappadocian hills.

He died at Arianzus, by the date most commonly given on 25 January 390; the exact year is uncertain, and some older writers place it a year earlier or later. He is honoured as a saint and Doctor of the Church in the West, and in the East as one of the Three Holy Hierarchs, with Basil and John Chrysostom.

Why the Orations still matter

Gregory was not a flawless man. He was sensitive and easily hurt, sometimes sharp in his judgments, quicker to resolve than to persevere, and more at home in solitude than in the rough politics of the church. But he forgave readily and held no grudges. He was generous to the poor and never flattered the powerful. And when holding on to his throne would have split the church, he let it go.

The Five Theological Orations, given here in the translation of Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, are the reason the church calls him the Theologian. They are short, dense, sometimes fierce, and alive: a great orator saying with every gift he had that the God Christians worship as Father, Son and Holy Spirit is one God, to be adored rather than dissected. A reader who comes to them slowly, as Gregory asked, will find something rarer than a clever argument: a man for whom the Trinity was not a doctrine to win but, as he said on the day he gave up everything else, his meditation and his glory.

faq.q: Who was Gregory of Nazianzus?
faq.a: Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390) was a bishop, preacher and poet from Cappadocia, in what is now central Turkey, and one of the three Cappadocian Fathers with Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa. The church calls him “the Theologian,” a title it shares among the early Fathers only with the apostle John.

faq.q: Where did Gregory of Nazianzus grow up?
faq.a: He was born on his family’s estate at Arianzus, near Nazianzus. His father, also Gregory, was brought to Christian faith by his wife Nonna and became bishop of Nazianzus, and Gregory believed his mother had dedicated him to God before he was born.

faq.q: What happened during Gregory’s voyage to Athens?
faq.a: Sailing to Athens out of season, still unbaptized, he was caught in a violent storm and feared spiritual death more than drowning. In his own telling, his parents prayed for him at home after learning of his danger in a vision, the sea grew calm, and he gave himself to God as he had promised.

faq.q: What was Gregory’s friendship with Basil the Great like?
faq.a: The two became inseparable as students at Athens, and later lived together for a time as monks in Pontus. Gregory said they seemed to have “one soul, inhabiting two bodies,” though the friendship was badly strained when Basil made him bishop of Sasima for church-political reasons.

faq.q: Why did Gregory call his ordination a “tyranny”?
faq.a: Around Christmas 361 his aging father and the people of Nazianzus had him ordained a priest against his will, and he fled to Basil in Pontus. He soon returned, and in his first Easter sermon forgave what he called “the noble tyranny” he had suffered.

faq.q: Why did Gregory go to Constantinople?
faq.a: In 379 the Nicene Christians of the capital, long oppressed under Arian bishops, asked him to lead them. He turned part of a relative’s house into a chapel named Anastasia, “Resurrection,” and preached there despite mob violence.

faq.q: What are the Five Theological Orations?
faq.a: They are five sermons Gregory preached in Constantinople in 380 defending the doctrine of the Trinity: two on God and how far he surpasses human understanding, two on the full divinity of the Son, and one on the divinity of the Holy Spirit. They are the reason he is called the Theologian, and the translation published here is Browne and Swallow’s.

faq.q: Why did Gregory resign as archbishop of Constantinople?
faq.a: In 381 he presided over the Council of Constantinople, but some bishops challenged his right to the see because he had already been consecrated for Sasima. Rather than divide the church, he resigned and gave a farewell sermon ending “Farewell, O Trinity, my meditation, and my glory.”

faq.q: How did Gregory spend his last years?
faq.a: He returned to Cappadocia, cared for the church at Nazianzus until a bishop was chosen around 383, and then withdrew to his family estate at Arianzus. There he wrote many poems, including a long poem on his own life, and lived simply in prayer.

faq.q: When did Gregory of Nazianzus die, and how is he remembered?
faq.a: He died at Arianzus, most often dated to 25 January 390, though the exact year is uncertain. He is honoured as a saint and Doctor of the Church in the West and, in the East, as one of the Three Holy Hierarchs with Basil and John Chrysostom.

fields.name: Justin Martyr
fields.bio: Justin Martyr (c. 100–165) was a Greek-speaking philosopher from Samaria who found in Christ the “true philosophy” after years in the schools. He taught the faith in Rome, defended Christians before the emperor in his First Apology, and was beheaded for refusing to sacrifice to the gods.
fields.bio_html:
Justin is one of the few saints who carries his whole story in his name. He was a philosopher who became a Christian and never stopped thinking of himself as a philosopher, and he died a martyr, a witness, rather than give up what he had found. He left us some of the earliest surviving defences of the faith addressed to a Roman emperor, one of the earliest descriptions of Christian Sunday worship, and a moving account of his own long search for God. He was not a polished writer, nor always fair to those he argued with, but he was brave and honest.

A seeker from Samaria

He was born in Flavia Neapolis, a Roman city in Samaria built near the ancient town of Shechem, where Nablus stands today. The date is uncertain; modern scholars usually put it about the year 100, though the older translators of his works suggested a decade or so later. His family was not Jewish. He opens his First Apology by naming himself “Justin, the son of Priscus and grandson of Bacchius,” a Latin name and a Greek one, and he speaks of himself as a Gentile, uncircumcised, with little knowledge of Hebrew.

He was well educated and had means enough to travel and study. What he wanted was not a career but to know God, and in his world that search was called philosophy.

The schools of the philosophers

Years later, in his Dialogue with Trypho, Justin told the story with humour at his own expense. He first gave himself to a Stoic teacher, but after a long time learned nothing more about God, “for he did not know himself, and said such instruction was unnecessary.” He moved on to a Peripatetic, a follower of Aristotle, who after a few days asked him to settle the fee; Justin decided he was no philosopher at all. A famous Pythagorean told him he must first master music, astronomy and geometry, and sent him away when he admitted he had not. Impatient, he turned at last to the Platonists.

Here, for a time, he thought he had arrived. A respected Platonist had lately settled in his city, and Justin spent every hour he could with him. “And the perception of immaterial things quite overpowered me, and the contemplation of ideas furnished my mind with wings,” he wrote, “so that in a little while I supposed that I had become wise; and such was my stupidity, I expected forthwith to look upon God, for this is the end of Plato’s philosophy.”

Something else was working on him too. In his Second Apology he tells how, while he was still delighting in Plato, he heard Christians slandered as monsters and then saw them face death without fear. No one living in secret wickedness, he reasoned, would welcome death like that.

An old man by the sea

He liked to walk alone in a field not far from the sea, where he could think without interruption. One day he became aware that an old man, “exhibiting meek and venerable manners,” was following him at a little distance. They fell into conversation, and the old man began gently to question him. What is philosophy? What is God? Can the mind see God by its own power? One by one Justin’s confident answers gave way.

Then Justin asked the question that every seeker reaches in the end: if not even the philosophers have the truth, where can anyone turn? The old man pointed him to the prophets, men older than all the philosophers, who “spoke by the Divine Spirit,” foretold what would come and what was now taking place, and proclaimed the Son of God, the Christ.

The old man ended not with an argument but with a charge to pray. “But pray that, above all things, the gates of light may be opened to you,” he told Justin, “for these things cannot be perceived or understood by all, but only by the man to whom God and His Christ have imparted wisdom.” Justin had spent years trying to climb to God by reasoning; the truth he wanted was a gift, to be asked for.

Then the old man went away, and Justin never saw him again. He never even tells us his name. But he tells us what happened inside him:

But straightway a flame was kindled in my soul; and a love of the prophets, and of those men who are friends of Christ, possessed me; and whilst revolving his words in my mind, I found this philosophy alone to be safe and profitable.

— Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho, chapter 8

Where this happened is not certain. It is commonly placed at Ephesus, but it may have been anywhere on the road between Palestine and Rome. What is certain is the direction of his life from then on.

The philosopher’s cloak

Justin did not stop being a philosopher; he simply believed he had found the true philosophy. He went on wearing the plain cloak that marked a philosopher in the street, and it opened doors. The Dialogue begins with a stranger greeting him in a public colonnade, “Hail, O philosopher!”, simply because of what he wore.

In the reign of the Emperor Antoninus Pius (138–161) he came to Rome and opened his own school, teaching the faith to whoever came. One of his pupils was a young Syrian named Tatian, who would later become a writer himself and who remembered his teacher as “the most admirable Justin.” It was a dangerous calling: a Christian could be denounced and put to death simply for bearing the name.

A petition to the emperor

It was against that injustice that Justin wrote his most famous work. The First Apology, usually dated about 155, is addressed to Antoninus Pius, to his adopted sons, one of them the future Marcus Aurelius, to the Senate and to the whole Roman people. An “apology” here means a defence, a speech for the accused. Justin presents it “in behalf of those of all nations who are unjustly hated and wantonly abused, myself being one of them.”

His request is simple: try Christians for what they have done, not for their name. If they are criminals, punish them; if they are not, stop putting them to death. And he speaks with a freedom that must have startled its readers:

For as for us, we reckon that no evil can be done us, unless we be convicted as evil-doers or be proved to be wicked men; and you, you can kill, but not hurt us.

— Justin Martyr, First Apology, chapter 2

To the rumours that Christians were atheists and worse, Justin replies by describing how they actually live. Those who once loved money now share what they have with anyone in need; those who once hated people of other nations now live alongside them, “and pray for our enemies.” He argues at length from the prophets that Jesus is the one they foretold.

He also offers a bold and generous idea. Christ, he says, is the Word, the divine Reason (in Greek, the Logos), and every race of human beings has shared in him. Wherever philosophers or poets said something true, they said it by a seed of that Word sown in them; Socrates, he argues, lived by reason, and was put to death on the charge of bringing in new gods. In the Second Apology he puts it in a single sentence:

Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians.

— Justin Martyr, Second Apology, chapter 13

Justin did not mean that Plato and Christ were the same; he says plainly that their teachings are “not in all respects similar.” He meant that the whole truth, glimpsed in part by the wise, is found in Christ.

Near the end of the book Justin opened the door of the church and let the emperor see what Christians do when they gather: how a new believer is baptised, how the bread and wine are blessed and shared, and what happens every week.

“And on the day called Sunday,” Justin wrote, “all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place.” The memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read “as long as time permits”; the president teaches; and then “we all rise together and pray.” Bread and wine and water are brought, prayers and thanksgivings are offered, the people answer “Amen,” and the deacons carry a portion to those who are absent. A collection is made for widows, orphans, prisoners and strangers. It is one of the earliest pictures we have of Christian worship, and it is still recognisable in churches across the world.

A long conversation with Trypho

The Dialogue with Trypho, written a few years later, is the longest of Justin’s surviving works. It records, or recreates, a debate over two days with Trypho, a Jew who had fled the recent war in Judaea, probably the revolt of Bar Kokhba, and was living in Greece. After telling the story of his conversion, Justin argues through page after page of Scripture that Jesus is the Messiah of whom the law and the prophets speak.

It must be said honestly that the Dialogue is hard reading today. Justin is often harsh toward the Jewish people, and later writers took up such arguments in ways that did real harm; historians count works like this among the roots of Christian hostility to Jews. Yet the two men argue as friends. Trypho admits at the end that he has been “particularly pleased with the conference,” and asks Justin to remember them as friends when he sails away.

The Dialogue ends in prayer. As Trypho and his companions leave, wishing him a safe voyage, Justin prays for them: “I can wish no better thing for you, sirs, than this, that, recognising in this way that intelligence is given to every man, you may be of the same opinion as ourselves, and believe that Jesus is the Christ of God.” Earlier he had told Trypho that Christians pray for him and for all who hate them, because Christ taught them to pray even for their enemies.

A witness in Rome

Justin seems to have known how his story would end. In the Second Apology he wrote that he expected to be plotted against, perhaps by a Cynic philosopher named Crescens, whom he had questioned in public and found to know nothing of what he attacked. According to Tatian and the historian Eusebius, that is very nearly what happened: in the reign of Marcus Aurelius, after disputing with Crescens, Justin was denounced to the authorities.

He was tried with six companions, among them two slaves he had taught, before Junius Rusticus, the prefect of Rome. An ancient account of the trial, the Martyrdom of Justin, survives. In one English rendering, when the prefect ordered them all to sacrifice to the gods, Justin answered, “No one in his right mind gives up piety for impiety.” Threatened with torture, he said that to suffer for the Lord Jesus Christ and so to be saved was their desire. They were scourged and beheaded. The exact year is unknown, but Rusticus held office from 162 to 168, and the date usually given is about 165.

The young man who had once expected to look upon God by the power of his own mind died for the God who had shown himself in Christ. He had written years before that Christians welcome death as a debt that every person owes; now he paid it.

What he leaves us

The church remembered him at once. Irenaeus spoke of his martyrdom, and Tertullian, a generation later, called him both philosopher and martyr. He is honoured as a saint by Catholic, Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox Christians, by Lutherans and Anglicans, and his feast is kept on 1 June. A church at Sacrofano, a few miles north of Rome, claims his relics.

We publish his First Apology, in the nineteenth-century translation of Marcus Dods and George Reith, and we plan to publish the Dialogue with Trypho as well. The Apology is not elegant, but it is a rare window into the church barely a century after the apostles: how Christians prayed, worshipped, shared their goods and faced the courts. And it is the voice of a man who had searched every school for the truth, found it, and was willing to say so to the most powerful ruler on earth.

faq.q: Who was Justin Martyr?
faq.a: Justin Martyr, also called Justin the Philosopher, was a second-century Christian teacher and apologist, born about 100 and martyred in Rome about 165. He is remembered for his First and Second Apologies, written in defence of Christians, and for his Dialogue with Trypho.

faq.q: Where was Justin Martyr born?
faq.a: He was born in Flavia Neapolis in Samaria, near ancient Shechem, where Nablus stands today. He was a Gentile, not a Jew, and names himself the son of Priscus and grandson of Bacchius.

faq.q: Which philosophers did Justin study with before he became a Christian?
faq.a: By his own account he tried a Stoic, who taught him nothing about God, then a Peripatetic, who asked for his fee, then a Pythagorean, who sent him away for not knowing music, astronomy and geometry. He then became a Platonist and for a time expected to look upon God through Plato’s philosophy.

faq.q: How was Justin Martyr converted?
faq.a: Walking alone in a field near the sea, he met an old man who questioned his philosophy and pointed him to the Hebrew prophets, who foretold Christ, and told him to pray that the gates of light would be opened to him. Justin writes that a flame was kindled in his soul, and he found the Christian faith to be the only safe and profitable philosophy.

faq.q: Why did Justin keep wearing a philosopher’s cloak?
faq.a: He believed that in Christ he had found the true philosophy, so he went on dressing and teaching as a philosopher. In the Dialogue with Trypho a stranger greets him in the street as a philosopher simply because of his dress.

faq.q: What did Justin do in Rome?
faq.a: In the reign of Antoninus Pius he settled in Rome and opened a school where he taught the Christian faith. One of his pupils was Tatian, who later called him “the most admirable Justin.”

faq.q: What is Justin Martyr’s First Apology about?
faq.a: Written about 155 and addressed to the Emperor Antoninus Pius, his sons, the Senate and the Roman people, it asks that Christians be judged by their deeds and not condemned for their name alone. It describes how Christians live, argues from the prophets that Jesus is the Christ, and gives one of the earliest descriptions of baptism, the Eucharist and Sunday worship. The translation published here is that of Marcus Dods and George Reith.

faq.q: What did Justin teach about the Word, or Logos?
faq.a: He taught that Christ is the Word of God, in whom every race of people has had some share, so that whatever was rightly said by philosophers and poets belongs to Christians. He saw the fullness of that truth in Christ, while the wise before him had only seeds of it.

faq.q: What is the Dialogue with Trypho?
faq.a: It is Justin’s longest surviving work, an account of a debate with Trypho, a Jew who had fled the war in Judaea, in which Justin tells his conversion story and argues from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Messiah. It is often harsh toward the Jewish people, yet it ends with the two men parting as friends and Justin praying for them.

faq.q: How did Justin Martyr die?
faq.a: In the reign of Marcus Aurelius, after he had disputed with the Cynic philosopher Crescens, he was denounced and tried with six companions before Junius Rusticus, the prefect of Rome. They refused to sacrifice to the gods and were scourged and beheaded, about 165; his feast is kept on 1 June.

fields.name: Clement of Alexandria
fields.bio: Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–c. 215) was a convert from paganism who studied under Pantaenus and taught the faith in Alexandria until the persecution of 202 drove him away. In his Exhortation to the Heathen he calls the Greeks to Christ, the “New Song,” bringing their learning to his feet.
fields.bio_html:
Clement of Alexandria is one of those early Christians we know far better by his voice than by his life. The facts of his biography would fit on a single page, and his nineteenth-century translator said as much, plainly: after setting down a handful of dates and names, he wrote, “The above is positively the sum of what we know of Clement’s history.” Yet the books he left behind are among the largest and liveliest that survive from the church’s second century. Through them we meet a man of enormous reading and restless curiosity, a former pagan who came to believe that every scattered gleam of truth he had found in them was a ray from one Light. This is the story of what can honestly be said about him, and of the book in which his voice rings out most clearly.

A seeker from the old world

His full name was Titus Flavius Clemens. When and where he was born, no one knows. He is usually placed around 150, and the old writers disagree about the city: one tradition says Athens, another Alexandria. Almost everything about his early years has to be read back from his writing. He was, it seems, born to pagan parents, and the ease with which he describes the Greek mystery cults, their rites and their secret words, suggests a man who had once stood close to them. His pages are thick with quotations from Greek authors whose works have otherwise perished.

At some point, how and when we are not told, he became a Christian. What we do know is what he did next. Like a student going from teacher to teacher, he travelled widely through Greece, Italy, Palestine, the East and Egypt, looking for the best Christian teachers he could find. He remembered them with reverence: an Ionian he met in Greece, an Assyrian in the East, a Hebrew, and others. Later readers have tried to put names to some of them, but they are guesses. Only one can be identified for certain, and Clement thought him the greatest of them all.

The bee of Alexandria

That teacher was Pantaenus, who taught the faith in Alexandria, the great harbour city at the mouth of the Nile. Clement seems to have reached him around 180, and there his long search came to rest. Clement speaks of him with deep reverence, and the old editors of his works call Pantaenus “the Sicilian bee,” gathering and storing up wisdom for his pupils.

The city held the most famous library of the ancient world, a meeting-place of Greek, Jewish and Egyptian learning; it was here, centuries before, that the Hebrew Scriptures had been put into Greek. Around Pantaenus a school had grown up for teaching the faith, the “catechetical school,” so called because it prepared catechumens, those learning the faith before baptism, and went on to train the more learned. Historians still debate how formal that school was in Clement’s day. But it is clear that Clement studied with Pantaenus, that he was ordained a presbyter, an elder of the church, and that he came to teach in his master’s place, probably around 189, when Pantaenus is said to have gone away on a mission to the East.

For a dozen years or so Clement taught in Alexandria with great distinction. The old accounts count among his pupils the young Origen, who would become the most famous Christian scholar of the next generation. Another was Alexander, later bishop of Jerusalem, who never forgot what he owed him. Writing years afterwards of the teachers who had gone before him into glory, Alexander named them with love:

the truly blest Pantænus, I mean, and the holy Clemens, my teacher, who was to me so greatly useful and helpful.

— Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, on his teacher

A new song for the Greeks

It was in these Alexandrian years, about 195, that Clement wrote the Exhortation to the Heathen, known by its Greek name as the Protrepticus, an appeal to his pagan neighbours to turn to Christ. It was the first of three books he seems to have planned as a ladder. The Exhortation calls the outsider in; The Instructor (the Paedagogus) then trains the new believer in daily Christian living, down to food, dress and table manners; and the sprawling Miscellanies (the Stromata) lead the mature believer on toward deeper knowledge of God. Over all three stands one figure: Christ, the Word of God, the true Teacher.

The Exhortation opens not with an argument but with music. Clement retells the old Greek tales of minstrels whose songs charmed fish and beasts and raised the walls of Thebes, and then turns on his readers. You believe that singers tamed animals, he says, and yet you look with incredulous eyes on the truth. He offers them another song, “the New Song,” which is Christ himself. That song, he writes, has made men out of stones and men out of beasts; it tuned the whole universe into harmony, and above all it tunes the human being, whom he calls a beautiful breathing instrument made by God. And what does the Singer want? “To open the eyes of the blind, and unstop the ears of the deaf,” and to reconcile disobedient children to their father.

The heart of it is the incarnation. The Word who made the world has come among us as a man, as our Teacher, so that we might share his life. Clement put it in a sentence that Eastern Christians have pondered ever since:

And now the Word Himself clearly speaks to thee, shaming thy unbelief; yea, I say, the Word of God became man, that thou mayest learn from man how man may become God.

— Clement of Alexandria, Exhortation to the Heathen, chapter 1

He did not mean that people become gods in their own right. He meant what the Eastern churches call theosis, or deification: that by grace men and women can be drawn into the very life and likeness of God. To readers who scorned the faith as a novelty, he answered in a single line:

Error seems old, but truth seems a new thing.

— Clement of Alexandria, Exhortation to the Heathen, chapter 1

Learning brought to the feet of Christ

Much of the middle of the Exhortation makes hard reading. Clement goes through the gods, mysteries and sacrifices of Greece one by one, exposing them with fierce, mocking energy. Even his nineteenth-century editor wished he had spared some of the details. But he had a reason: he wanted his readers to see what they were actually worshipping, and to see that many of their own best minds had seen it first.

For Clement was no enemy of learning. That is perhaps the most important thing to know about him. Many Christians of his day thought Greek philosophy useless or dangerous. Clement believed that philosophy had been, for the Greeks, something like what the law was for the Hebrews: a schoolmaster to bring them toward Christ. In the Exhortation he quotes Plato and the poets again and again, not to set them beside Scripture, but to show that they had glimpsed fragments of a truth now whole in Christ. He is honest that they only glimpsed it: “that which the chiefs of philosophy only guessed at,” he wrote, “the disciples of Christ have both apprehended and proclaimed.”

And he never let learning become a reason to keep God at a distance from ordinary life. One of the most attractive passages in the book is an invitation to people in every trade:

Practise husbandry, we say, if you are a husbandman; but while you till your fields, know God. Sail the sea, you who are devoted to navigation, yet call the whilst on the heavenly Pilot.

— Clement of Alexandria, Exhortation to the Heathen, chapter 10

Clement’s arguments keep breaking into prayer. Near the end of a long chapter against idols he stops to pray for the very readers he has been rebuking: “May God grant that you may at length awake from this slumber, and know God”. Here the teacher is also an intercessor, and his whole book was written so that this prayer would be answered.

Exile and silence

In 202 the storm broke. Under the emperor Septimius Severus, persecution fell on the church at Alexandria. Clement left the city, and as far as we know he never returned to teach there.

His going has sometimes been questioned. It is fair to remember what he himself taught: that every Christian must be ready to die for Christ, but that to rush forward and seek out death was not courage but a failure to honour God’s gift of life. He seems to have lived by that. The next glimpses of him come from his old pupil Alexander, by then a bishop. About 211 Alexander gave Clement a letter commending him to the church at Antioch, and spoke of him as a blessed presbyter, a man illustrious and approved. The letter suggests that Clement had spent some of the intervening years near Alexander, perhaps in Cappadocia or in Jerusalem.

After that, silence. He is thought to have died about 215, but where and how, no one recorded. Alexander later counted him among the blessed fathers who had gone before.

The Exhortation rises at one point into a hymn of praise to the Light that had found him: “Hail, O light! For in us, buried in darkness, shut up in the shadow of death, light has shone forth from heaven, purer than the sun, sweeter than life here below.” His Instructor ends in the same spirit, with a prayer and a hymn.

A disputed saint and a lasting teacher

Later generations honoured Clement highly. Jerome called him the most learned of the ancients; Theodoret said he surpassed all others and was a holy man; Eusebius called him an incomparable master of Christian philosophy. His name stood in the Western calendar of saints for centuries, with a feast on 4 December.

But he was also a pioneer, and pioneers leave rough edges. He wrote before the great creeds had settled the language of Christian doctrine, and some of his phrases, especially in works now lost, troubled later readers; the ninth-century patriarch Photius criticised several of his ideas sharply, though it is not clear that Photius always read him fairly.
