At the end of the sixteenth century his name was removed from the Roman Martyrology, on the grounds that his life was little known and some of his teaching doubtful. The Coptic Church still keeps him as a saint, and Anglicans commemorate him. One Victorian writer said he did not know where to look for a purer or a truer man.

His great achievement was to show that a Christian could be both deeply learned and wholly devoted to Christ. His nineteenth-century editors called him, after Justin and Irenaeus, the founder of Christian literature. With Clement, and then with Origen after him, a Christian intellectual tradition began in Alexandria that would shape theology for centuries. And under all the learning was a simple conviction, which he put in one short sentence of the Exhortation: “The instrument of God loves mankind.”

Reading the Exhortation today

The book we publish is the Exhortation to the Heathen, in William Wilson’s translation from the Ante-Nicene Fathers, with the editors’ introductory note on Clement’s life and works. The catalogue of pagan gods can be wearying, but a reader who keeps going will be rewarded. The opening chapter on the New Song is among the most beautiful pages in early Christian literature, and the closing chapters are a sustained, tender appeal: to the sailor, to the old blind seer Tiresias, to anyone who has heard the sirens’ song, “bound to the wood of the cross, thou shalt be freed from destruction”.

Above all, the book shows how an educated Christian of the second century spoke to a world that thought his faith new, foreign and foolish. He did not retreat from that world or flatter it. He took what was true in it, named what was false, and pointed past both to the Word who had become man. He sums it up himself: “Good is the whole life of those who have known Christ.” Little as we know of Clement’s own life, the book suggests he found that to be true.

faq.q: Who was Clement of Alexandria?
faq.a: Titus Flavius Clemens, known as Clement of Alexandria, was a Christian teacher and writer who lived from about 150 to about 215. He taught the faith in Alexandria, and his surviving books are among the largest that remain from the church’s second century.

faq.q: Where was Clement of Alexandria born?
faq.a: No one knows for certain. One ancient tradition says Athens and another says Alexandria, and his birth year is also uncertain, usually given as about 150.

faq.q: How did Clement become a Christian?
faq.a: He seems to have been born to pagan parents, and his writing shows close knowledge of the Greek mystery religions. The details of his conversion are not recorded, but afterwards he travelled widely through Greece, Italy, Palestine and the East looking for the best Christian teachers.

faq.q: Who was Pantaenus, and what did he mean to Clement?
faq.a: Pantaenus was a Christian teacher in Alexandria, the only one of Clement’s teachers who can be identified with certainty, and the one Clement regarded as the greatest. Clement reached him around 180, studied under him, and later taught in his place.

faq.q: What was the catechetical school of Alexandria?
faq.a: It was the circle in Alexandria where the faith was taught to catechumens, people preparing for baptism, and to more advanced students. Clement taught there from about 189, and the old accounts count Origen and Alexander, later bishop of Jerusalem, among his pupils, though historians debate how formal the school was in his day.

faq.q: What is Clement’s Exhortation to the Heathen about?
faq.a: Written about 195, it is an appeal to pagan Greeks to leave their idols and mysteries and turn to Christ, whom Clement calls the New Song. It exposes the old religions sharply, draws on Plato and the poets as witnesses to partial truth, and ends with a warm invitation to come to the Word of God. The translation published here is William Wilson’s, from the Ante-Nicene Fathers.

faq.q: What did Clement think about Greek philosophy?
faq.a: Unlike many Christians of his day, he valued it. He taught that philosophy prepared the Greeks for Christ as the law prepared the Hebrews, and that whatever truth it held came in fragments from the one truth found whole in Christ.

faq.q: What other books did Clement write?
faq.a: Besides the Exhortation, his surviving works are The Instructor, a guide to daily Christian living, the Miscellanies or Stromata, a long and wide-ranging work on Christian knowledge, and the short treatise Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? Many other writings are lost or survive only in fragments.

faq.q: Why did Clement leave Alexandria?
faq.a: In 202 persecution under the emperor Septimius Severus fell on the church in Alexandria, and Clement left the city. About 211 his former pupil Alexander, by then a bishop, gave him a letter commending him to the church at Antioch.

faq.q: When did Clement die, and is he a saint?
faq.a: He died about 215, at a place no one recorded. He was long honoured in the Western calendar with a feast on 4 December, but his name was dropped from the Roman Martyrology at the end of the sixteenth century; the Coptic Church still venerates him as a saint and Anglicans commemorate him.

fields.name: Gregory of Nyssa
fields.bio: Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–c. 394) was bishop of Nyssa in Cappadocia and one of the three Cappadocian Fathers, with his brother Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus. Turned to God by his sister Macrina, he defended the Nicene faith and wrote The Great Catechism, a guide for teachers of new believers.
fields.bio_html:
Gregory of Nyssa was the shy one in a family of saints. His elder brother Basil was a born leader, a famine-fighter and a defier of emperors; his friend Gregory of Nazianzus was the great orator of the age. Gregory was quieter, more bookish, slower to commit, and for years he was not sure he wanted the church at all. He made real mistakes, some of them embarrassing. Yet the Second Council of Nicaea, four centuries later, could speak of him as the one all called “the father of fathers,” and many readers today count him the deepest thinker of the three Cappadocian Fathers. Much of the credit, the old accounts agree, belongs to a woman: his elder sister Macrina.

A house of saints

He was born about 335, most probably at Caesarea in Cappadocia, in the uplands of what is now central Turkey, though some place his birth at Neocaesarea in Pontus. His family was wealthy and deeply Christian. In the last great persecution his grandparents had fled to the mountains of Pontus and suffered great hardship there; his mother’s father is said to have lost both life and property. His father, Basil, was a teacher of rhetoric who died young, leaving ten children in the care of their grandmother Macrina and their mother Emmelia.

Of those ten, several are remembered as saints: Basil, later archbishop of Caesarea; Peter, later bishop of Sebaste; and, above all, the eldest daughter, Macrina, named for her grandmother. The editor of Gregory’s works calls her “the angel in the house.” She helped to raise and teach the younger children, and there was not one of them, he writes, who did not owe to her their settlement in the faith. Her own betrothed had died young; she never married, and with her mother she founded a community of women on the family estate at Annesi, on the river Iris in Pontus.

Gregory, the third son, was delicate in health and retiring by temperament. He did not go to Athens as Basil had; he seems to have been taught at home. His mother and Macrina gave him his faith, and Basil, several years older, gave him his learning: Gregory called him his “Master” all his life, and once said that whatever was good in his writing was Basil’s and whatever was poor was the pupil’s.

A dream at a martyrs’ vigil

For years he remained unbaptized, which was not unusual then, and drifted. The turn, when it began, came through his mother. She begged him to come to Annesi for a festival in honour of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste, much loved in Cappadocia. He went unwillingly. The service ran far into the night, and, tired from the journey, he went out and fell asleep in the garden.

As the story is told, Gregory dreamed that the martyrs appeared to him, rebuked him for his indifference and beat him with rods. He woke filled with remorse and at once began to pray earnestly for mercy and forgiveness. Under the impression of that night he agreed to serve the church as a reader.

It did not last. Some unfitness, and a love of eloquence that never quite left him, drew him away again, and he took up his father’s profession as a rhetorician, a teacher of public speaking. Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus both rebuked him sharply for it. Tradition places his marriage to Theosebeia around this time, but the evidence is thin and disputed.

What finally turned him was Macrina. The prolegomena to his works calls her “the master spirit of the family”, and says that by her powerful persuasion, “after much struggle,” he changed his whole way of life. She had already turned Basil from worldly success to a life of self-denial; now she did the same for Gregory. He gave up his secular work and withdrew to Basil’s monastery in the wild, beautiful country beside the Iris, near the women’s community where his mother and sister lived.

Years of study by the river

There he stayed for several years, reading Scripture and the works of Origen, the great third-century teacher whose bold mind shaped so much of Eastern theology. There, too, his love of nature deepened. Few ancient Greek writers describe nature with such delight; later he would write of a river gliding “like a golden ribbon” between its banks, and of vines covering the hillsides “like a green mantle.” His treatise On Virginity came out of these years of quiet.

A reluctant bishop

The quiet ended in 372. Basil, now archbishop of Caesarea, was struggling against the Arian party, who denied that the Son is truly God and enjoyed the favour of the emperor Valens. To strengthen his hand he made Gregory, over his emphatic protest, bishop of Nyssa, a small town in western Cappadocia. When a friend wondered that he had chosen so obscure a place for such a man, Basil replied that he did not want his brother to gain distinction from his see, but to bring distinction to it.

Gregory was not a natural administrator, and the record is honest about it. In one well-meant but foolish scheme he tried to reconcile Basil with their uncle, also a bishop, by forging a letter from the uncle asking for peace; the forgery was discovered and only widened the breach, though peace came later.

Then came real persecution. His opponents accused him of irregularity in his ordination and of mismanaging church funds. Soldiers were sent to bring him before a synod; the rough journey left him ill with fever. In 376 a synod at Nyssa itself deposed him in his absence, and the emperor banished him. For about two years he wandered, often moving from place to place. His own letters from this time are lost, but the replies of Gregory of Nazianzus show how crushed and despondent his gentle spirit had become.

In 378 Valens was killed fighting the Goths at Adrianople, and the new emperor allowed the exiled bishops to return. Gregory came home to Nyssa, and the people greeted him with joy.

Macrina’s last lesson

The joy was short-lived. Soon afterwards Basil was dead, worn out before he was fifty, and Gregory preached his panegyric. Later that same year he travelled to Annesi to see Macrina, whom he had not seen for many years, and found her dying. He wrote of their last conversations in two books: a Life of Macrina and a dialogue, On the Soul and the Resurrection, in which she is the teacher and he the grieving pupil. To the end she was, as his editor says, “the great teacher of her family.” She strengthened his faith in the resurrection of the dead and gently reproved his grief, reminding him not to sorrow as those who have no hope.

In his Life of Macrina Gregory records that as she lay dying, lying on two planks on the ground, she stopped speaking with those around her and turned to pray. Her prayer thanked God for taking away the fear of death and asked him to receive her soul. She made the sign of the cross, and her breath ended with her prayer.

When her body was prepared for burial, a ring holding a fragment of the cross and a small iron cross were found on her. Gregory kept one and gave the other to a sister of the community, and he buried Macrina in the chapel at Annesi beside their parents.

Defender of the faith

With Basil and Macrina both gone, Gregory stepped into a much larger life. He took his brother’s place among the defenders of the faith of Nicaea and wrote a long defence of Basil’s teaching against Eunomius, a theologian who taught that the Son did not share the Father’s essence. In 381 he was one of the bishops at the Council of Constantinople, which confirmed the Nicene faith; he preached there, including the funeral sermon for Meletius of Antioch, the council’s first president. Afterwards he was sent to try to set in order the troubled churches of Arabia, which he found beyond his power to reform, and he visited Jerusalem, where he was so disturbed by what he saw of pilgrims’ conduct that he wrote warning against pilgrimage as an aid to faith.

His mind was bold and original. He was among the first Christian writers to insist that God is infinite, so that the soul’s journey into God never ends. He was one of the earliest voices in the ancient world to condemn slavery itself as a sin against the image of God in every person. He also hoped, following Origen, that in the end God’s purifying love would restore all creation, so that every being would join in thanksgiving. Christians have weighed that hope differently ever since; it is part of who Gregory was, and he held it as an expression of the goodness of God.

The Great Catechism

About 385 Gregory wrote the book we publish, The Great Catechism, sometimes called the Catechetical Oration. It is not a catechism for children. It is a handbook for the teachers who instructed converts, showing them how to explain the faith to Greeks, to Jews and to those who had wandered into heresy. Its first rule is pastoral: “The method of recovery must be adapted to the form of the disease.”

From there he walks through the whole faith: the Trinity; the creation of humanity out of God’s “superabundance of love”; the free will that made sin possible; evil as nothing more than the absence of good, as darkness is the absence of light. He likens death to a potter who breaks a spoiled vessel in order to remould it in its original beauty. Above all he asks why God became man, and answers simply:

Our diseased nature needed a healer. Man in his fall needed one to set him upright.

— Gregory of Nyssa, The Great Catechism, chapter 15

The power of God, he says, is shown more clearly in this coming down than in the stars themselves, as a flame that streamed downwards would be a greater marvel than one that rose. Some of his images, such as Christ’s humanity as bait hiding the hook of divinity from the devil, trouble many readers, and Gregory himself stopped to answer the charge that it made God a deceiver. But the centre of the book is clear and warm:

This is what we are taught and learn from the Revelation of the truth, that God in the beginning made man and saved him when he had fallen.

— Gregory of Nyssa, The Great Catechism, chapter 8

Gregory taught that the new birth of baptism rests on prayer. It is, he wrote, “prayer and the invocation of heavenly grace, and water, and faith, by which the mystery of regeneration is accomplished”. God has promised to come when he is called upon, and so the church begins with prayer.

He ends not with doctrine but with life. If a baptized person goes on living as before, he says boldly, “the water is but water.” The proof of a new birth is a new character:

If, then, you have received God, if you have become a child of God, make manifest in your disposition the God that is in you, manifest in yourself Him that begot you.

— Gregory of Nyssa, The Great Catechism, chapter 40

The star of Nyssa

Little is known of Gregory’s last years. The last record of him is at a synod in Constantinople in 394, where his name stood among those of the great metropolitans, and Basil’s prophecy came true: the obscure town of Nyssa was honoured by its bishop. He probably died soon after, in 394 or 395. The Eastern churches keep his memory on 10 January; the Church of England remembers him together with Macrina on 19 July.

The translation we publish is by William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, from the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, with the editors’ account of his life and teaching. The Great Catechism is closely argued and sometimes demanding, but it is one of the first attempts to set out the whole Christian faith as a single reasonable whole, written by a man who knew that the truth must finally be lived. The shy brother who nearly walked away became a teacher of the church, and he never forgot the sister who had taught him first.

faq.q: Who was Gregory of Nyssa?
faq.a: Gregory was a fourth-century bishop of Nyssa in Cappadocia, born about 335 and died about 394. With his elder brother Basil of Caesarea and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus he is remembered as one of the three Cappadocian Fathers.

faq.q: What was Gregory of Nyssa’s family like?
faq.a: He was one of ten children of a wealthy Christian family whose grandparents had suffered in the persecutions. His grandmother Macrina, his mother Emmelia, his sister Macrina and his brothers Basil and Peter of Sebaste are all honoured as saints.

faq.q: Who taught Gregory of Nyssa?
faq.a: He was taught at home rather than at Athens. His mother and his sister Macrina gave him his faith, and his elder brother Basil gave him his learning; Gregory called Basil his Master all his life.

faq.q: What happened at the vigil of the Forty Martyrs?
faq.a: As the story is told, Gregory went unwillingly to a night festival for the Forty Martyrs at his mother’s request, fell asleep in the garden, and dreamed that the martyrs rebuked him and beat him with rods. He woke in remorse, prayed for mercy, and agreed to serve as a reader in the church, though he soon left to teach rhetoric.

faq.q: How did his sister Macrina influence Gregory of Nyssa?
faq.a: Macrina, the eldest daughter, helped raise and teach the younger children, and it was by her persuasion, after much struggle, that Gregory gave up his secular career and withdrew to Basil’s monastery in Pontus. She had earlier turned Basil to a life of self-denial in the same way.

faq.q: How did Gregory become bishop of Nyssa?
faq.a: In 372 his brother Basil, archbishop of Caesarea, made him bishop of the small town of Nyssa over his strong protest, to strengthen the Nicene side against the Arians. Basil said he wanted his brother not to gain distinction from his see but to bring distinction to it.

faq.q: Why was Gregory of Nyssa deposed and exiled?
faq.a: Arian opponents accused him of irregular ordination and of mismanaging church funds, and in 376 a synod deposed him and the emperor Valens banished him. After Valens died at Adrianople in 378 he was allowed to return to Nyssa, where the people welcomed him with joy.

faq.q: What happened at Macrina’s deathbed?
faq.a: In 379, the year Basil died, Gregory visited Macrina at Annesi and found her dying. She strengthened his faith in the resurrection and reproved his grief, and he later wrote her life and the dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection from their last conversations.

faq.q: What is The Great Catechism by Gregory of Nyssa?
faq.a: Written about 385, it is a handbook for those who taught converts, showing how to explain the Christian faith to Greeks, Jews and heretics. It covers the Trinity, creation, the problem of evil, the Incarnation, baptism and the Eucharist, and ends by insisting that a true new birth must show in a changed life. The translation published here is William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson’s.

faq.q: When did Gregory of Nyssa die, and how is he remembered?
faq.a: He was last recorded at a synod in Constantinople in 394 and probably died soon afterwards. He is honoured as a saint, remembered in the Eastern churches on 10 January and in the Church of England with Macrina on 19 July, and is known for his teaching on the infinity of God and his condemnation of slavery.

fields.name: Tertullian
fields.bio: Tertullian (c. 155–c. 220) was a Christian writer of Carthage, the first to produce a large body of Christian work in Latin. His Apology defended persecuted Christians before Rome’s magistrates and declared that “the blood of Christians is seed.” In later life he was drawn to the strict New Prophecy movement.
fields.bio_html:
Tertullian is the first great Christian writer in Latin, the man who gave the Western church much of the vocabulary it still uses to speak about God. He was brilliant, funny, fierce, and at times unbearable. He could defend his fellow believers before the magistrates of Rome with a courage and wit that still leap off the page, and he could turn the same sharp pen on fellow Christians he thought too lax. Late in life he was drawn to a strict movement that the wider church came to reject. The record keeps all of this, and so should we. But the book we publish comes from his strongest years, when he stood up for persecuted Christians and told the empire, in effect: look at how we actually live before you kill us.

A son of Carthage

He was born Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus in Carthage, the great port city of Roman Africa, on the coast of what is now Tunisia. The year is uncertain; modern scholars usually say about 155, while older editors suggested ten years earlier. Jerome, writing two centuries later, says his father was a centurion serving the Roman governor of Africa. Tertullian once called himself “Punic among Romans,” a man of the old Carthaginian stock living in a Roman world, and he claimed Africa as his homeland.

He was born a pagan and received an excellent education. Roman Africa was famous for its orators, and Tertullian wrote like one: vivid, compressed, full of paradox and sudden jokes. He could also write Greek, and composed at least three books in it, all now lost. Ancient writers thought he had been a lawyer, and his works are full of legal argument, though modern historians point out that a good Roman education would explain that too. Whether he was ever ordained a presbyter, an elder of the church, is also disputed. Jerome says so, but in his own writings he seems to count himself among the laity.

Made, not born

We do not know when or how he became a Christian. Some place it about 185, others about 197. He tells us almost nothing about it directly. But he plainly remembered what it was to stand outside and scoff, and his conversion seems to have been sudden and decisive. In the Apology, explaining the Christian hope of resurrection and judgment, he stops to admit:

Once these things were with us, too, the theme of ridicule. We are of your stock and nature: men are made, not born, Christians.

— Tertullian, The Apology, chapter 18

That last phrase has become one of his most famous. He could not imagine a Christian life that had not been chosen with open eyes. He was married to a Christian wife, and two little books he wrote to her survive.

The African church of his day was large, and it paid for its faith; its persecutions were cruel. Christians were being condemned in the courts simply for the name they bore. It was for them that he wrote his most famous book.

A voice for the accused

The Apology was written about 197; scholars have argued for dates from 197 to as late as 217, but most place it near the end of the second century. It is addressed to the “Rulers of the Roman Empire,” the magistrates who sat in judgment over Christians. Because they would not hear the Christians openly, Tertullian sends the truth to them, he says, “by the secret pathway of a noiseless book.” The truth knows she is a stranger on earth and expects enemies here. She asks only one thing:

One thing, meanwhile, she anxiously desires of earthly rulers—not to be condemned unknown.

— Tertullian, The Apology, chapter 1

He writes like the lawyer he may have been. In every other case, he says, the accused is questioned, may defend himself, and is tortured, if at all, to make him confess. Only Christians are tortured to make them deny, and are condemned for the name alone. He answers the rumours one by one: that Christians murder and eat a child at their secret rites, that they commit incest, that they are traitors to the emperor. He turns the charges back on the accusers, showing from their own customs and stories where such cruelty is really found. And he mocks the habit of blaming Christians for every disaster: “If the Tiber rises as high as the city walls, if the Nile does not send its waters up over the fields, if the heavens give no rain, if there is an earthquake, if there is famine or pestilence, straightway the cry is, ‘Away with the Christians to the lion!’”

He also wants the magistrates to see how much the Christians already are among them. “We are but of yesterday,” he writes, “and we have filled every place among you,” the cities and islands, the army camp, the palace and the senate. If Christians were really enemies of the empire, they had numbers enough to do it harm. Instead, they pray for it.

How Christians pray

Some of the warmest pages of the Apology describe the prayer and common life of the church. Christians would not burn incense before the emperor’s image, and so they were called public enemies. Tertullian answers that they do something better for the emperor: they pray for him to the only God who can help him.

“Thither we lift our eyes, with hands outstretched, because free from sin; with head uncovered, for we have nothing whereof to be ashamed; finally, without a monitor, because it is from the heart we supplicate.” So Tertullian describes Christians at prayer: hands raised, heads bare, praying from the heart with no one to prompt them, for long life for the emperor, a secure empire, brave armies, a faithful senate, a virtuous people and a world at rest. And he adds that the very attitude of a Christian at prayer, arms stretched out to God, is a readiness for whatever punishment may come.

He describes the gatherings themselves with the same plainness. Christians meet to read the Scriptures, to encourage and correct one another, and to pray together. Each brings a small gift once a month, if he wishes and can, and the money is spent not on feasts but on burying the poor, feeding orphans, caring for the old and the shipwrecked, and helping those condemned to the mines or prisons for their faith. Their neighbours, he says, look on and remark, “See,” they say, “how they love one another.”

“We meet together as an assembly and congregation,” Tertullian wrote, “that, offering up prayer to God as with united force, we may wrestle with Him in our supplications. This violence God delights in.” Their simple common meal, the agape or love-feast, began and ended in prayer, and after it each was invited to stand and sing a hymn to God, from the Scriptures or of his own making. In time of drought, he says, while the pagans held processions to Jupiter, Christians fasted and prayed in sackcloth and ashes until they had touched God’s heart.

He was bold enough to claim answered prayer as evidence, too. He appeals to letters of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius which, he says, bore witness that a drought afflicting the army in Germany was ended by rain obtained through the prayers of Christian soldiers. A sudden storm on that campaign was remembered by pagan writers as well, who credited it to their own gods or to the emperor; the letter later circulated in Marcus’s name is judged a forgery, and we cannot now be sure what happened. But it shows what Tertullian believed: that the prayers of despised Christians were holding up the world.

The blood of Christians

The Apology ends with its most famous lines. Why, the magistrates might ask, do Christians complain of persecution if they are so eager to suffer? Tertullian answers that they want suffering only as a soldier wants battle: not for itself, but for the victory. Every time Christians die without denying Christ, more people stop to ask what kind of faith could do this, and many of them believe:

The oftener we are mown down by you, the more in number we grow; the blood of Christians is seed.

— Tertullian, The Apology, chapter 50

It is sometimes quoted as “the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church.” His own words are shorter and harder. He was writing to men who had the power to kill his friends, and he was telling them that they could not win.

A hard and restless mind

The Apology was only the beginning. More than thirty of his works survive. He wrote on prayer, on patience, on baptism and on repentance; he wrote to encourage Christians in prison awaiting martyrdom. He wrote at length against the heretic Marcion, who rejected the God of the Old Testament, and against Praxeas, who taught that the Father and the Son were simply one person under two names. In that work Tertullian became the first writer in Latin known to use the word trinitas, “Trinity,” and he gave Latin theology terms such as “person” and “substance” that later theology would build on. Not all of his own teaching was later judged sound; his way of describing the Son as subordinate to the Father was set aside. But it is no exaggeration that he has been called the father of Latin Christianity. He was suspicious of mixing the gospel with Greek philosophy, and asked a question that has been repeated ever since: “What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?”

He was also a rigorist, a man for whom there could be no halfway Christianity. He told believers to stay away from the theatre and the arena, urged women to give up jewellery, insisted that virgins be veiled, and grew ever harsher against second marriage. Jerome remembered him as a man “of a sharp and vehement temper.” That temper, which made him so formidable against persecutors, could make him hard on weaker Christians too.

In the middle of his life, perhaps about 207, he was drawn to the “New Prophecy,” the movement begun by Montanus in Asia Minor and later called Montanism. Its followers believed that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete Jesus had promised, was still speaking through their prophets, calling the church to stricter fasting and a firmer discipline. Jerome thought that Tertullian had been driven to it by the envy and insults of the Roman clergy, but that is doubtful, and his own temperament was already close to the movement’s strictness. How far he went is now debated. Older writers spoke of him leaving the church; most scholars today doubt that he ever formally left it or was excommunicated, and the North African followers of the New Prophecy seem to have kept most of the church’s doctrine. What is clear is that his later writings are sharper against the leaders of the mainstream church, and that the church as a whole did not follow him. Two centuries later Augustine knew of a small group in Carthage called “Tertullianists,” whose church building passed in his own day to the main body of Christians.

The master Cyprian read

Jerome says that Tertullian lived to a great age. The year of his death is unknown; it is usually put about 220, and possibly later. He is not counted among the saints, and the church has always read him with some caution. Yet it has never stopped reading him. Cyprian, the martyr bishop of Carthage a generation later, is said to have read some of Tertullian every day, and to have asked for his books with the words, “Give me my master.” Through Cyprian, and later through Augustine and Jerome, much of the language and the temper of Western Christianity passed through Tertullian’s hands.

We publish his Apology in the nineteenth-century translation of S. Thelwall. It is not a gentle book; Tertullian is sarcastic and sometimes unfair to the pagans he mocks. But it is a brave one, written for people who were being killed for their faith, and it gives us a vivid picture of how the church lived and prayed under persecution: their worship, their common purse, their care for the poor, their prayers for the very rulers who condemned them. Its last sentence says what all of it was for:

As the divine and human are ever opposed to each other, when we are condemned by you, we are acquitted by the Highest.

— Tertullian, The Apology, chapter 50

faq.q: Who was Tertullian?
faq.a: Tertullian, in full Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus, was a Christian writer of Carthage in Roman Africa, born about 155 and dying about 220 or later. He was the first Christian author to write a large body of work in Latin, and has been called the father of Latin Christianity.

faq.q: Where did Tertullian come from?
faq.a: He was born a pagan in Carthage, on the coast of what is now Tunisia. Jerome says his father was a centurion serving the Roman governor of Africa, and Tertullian called himself Punic among Romans and claimed Africa as his homeland.

faq.q: Was Tertullian a lawyer or a priest?
faq.a: Ancient writers said he was a lawyer, and his works are full of legal argument, but modern historians note that a good Roman education would explain this. Jerome calls him a presbyter, yet in his own writings he seems to count himself among the laity, so both claims are uncertain.

faq.q: How did Tertullian become a Christian?
faq.a: Little is known; the date is put anywhere from about 185 to about 197, and he says almost nothing about it directly. In the Apology he admits that Christian teaching was once a joke to him too, and insists that Christians are made, not born. He was married to a Christian wife, and two books he wrote to her survive.

faq.q: What is Tertullian’s Apology about?
faq.a: Written about 197 to the magistrates of the Roman Empire, it asks that Christians not be condemned unknown, answers rumours of child murder, incest and treason, and describes how Christians actually live, worship and pray for the emperor. The translation published here is that of S. Thelwall.

faq.q: What did Tertullian say about how early Christians prayed?
faq.a: He describes Christians praying with hands outstretched and heads uncovered, from the heart, for the emperor, the empire and the world at rest. He says they met to pray together as if wrestling with God in their supplications, a violence God delights in, and that their common meal began and ended with prayer.

faq.q: Did Tertullian say the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church?
faq.a: That popular saying comes from the last chapter of his Apology, where he tells the persecutors that the more often Christians are mown down, the more they grow, because the blood of Christians is seed. His own words are shorter than the familiar version.

faq.q: What did Tertullian contribute to the doctrine of the Trinity?
faq.a: In his work against Praxeas he became the first writer in Latin known to use the word trinitas, Trinity, and he used terms such as person and substance that later theology built on. Some of his teaching, such as his way of describing the Son as subordinate to the Father, was later set aside.

faq.q: Did Tertullian become a Montanist?
faq.a: In middle life, perhaps about 207, he was drawn to the New Prophecy, or Montanism, a strict movement that believed the Holy Spirit was still speaking through its prophets. Jerome blamed the envy of the Roman clergy, but that is doubtful, and most scholars today doubt that he formally left the church or was excommunicated, though his later writings are sharper against its leaders.

faq.q: When did Tertullian die, and how is he remembered?
faq.a: Jerome says he lived to a great age; the year of his death is unknown and is usually put about 220. He is not counted among the saints, but Cyprian of Carthage is said to have read him daily and called him his master, and through Cyprian, Augustine and Jerome he shaped the language of Western theology.

fields.name: John Henry Newman
fields.bio: John Henry Newman (1801–1890) was an English priest, theologian and writer who led the Oxford Movement in the Church of England and in 1845 was received into the Catholic Church. His Apologia Pro Vita Sua tells that journey in his own words. He became a cardinal and was canonised in 2019.
fields.bio_html:
In the spring of 1864 a sixty-three-year-old priest in Birmingham sat down to answer a charge that he was a liar. The novelist Charles Kingsley had written that “Truth, for its own sake, had never been a virtue with the Roman clergy,” and had named John Henry Newman as his example. Newman’s reply was the story of his own soul, told week by week as he wrote it: how a London boy became an Evangelical, an Oxford clergyman, the leading voice of a movement that shook the Church of England, and at last, at forty-four, a Catholic. He called it Apologia Pro Vita Sua, a defence of his life, and its candour won over many readers who never shared his conclusions.

A boy who read the Bible

He was born in the City of London on 21 February 1801, the eldest of six children of a banker, John Newman, and Jemima Fourdrinier, who came of a family of French Huguenot refugees. At seven he went to school at Ealing, a bookish boy who skipped the games and read Walter Scott’s novels as they came out. He had been brought up “from a child to take great delight in reading the Bible,” he wrote, but had “no formed religious convictions till I was fifteen.”

Then, in the autumn of 1816, his last year at school, everything changed. A master named Walter Mayers, himself recently converted, talked with him and put books into his hands, all of the Calvinist school. Newman trusted what happened next for the rest of his life.

When I was fifteen (in the autumn of 1816) a great change of thought took place in me. I fell under the influences of a definite creed, and received into my intellect impressions of dogma, which, through God’s mercy, have never been effaced or obscured.

— John Henry Newman, Apologia Pro Vita Sua

Of that inward conversion he was still, he said, “more certain than that I have hands and feet.” The writer who marked him most was the Evangelical commentator Thomas Scott, to whom “(humanly speaking) I almost owe my soul,” and for years he used two of Scott’s sayings almost as proverbs: “Holiness before peace,” and “Growth is the only evidence of life.” That same autumn he became convinced that God was calling him to a single life, and he kept to it always.

Oxford, and two great blows

He went up to Trinity College, Oxford, in 1816. Anxiety ruined his final examinations, yet in April 1822 he was elected a fellow of Oriel, then the centre of Oxford’s intellectual life. Richard Whately, a senior don, took him in hand and taught him, Newman said, “to see with my own eyes and to walk with my own feet.” He was ordained in 1824 and 1825, served as curate of St Clement’s in Oxford, and in 1828 became vicar of St Mary’s, the university church.

He was honest about where his cleverness was taking him: “I was beginning to prefer intellectual excellence to moral; I was drifting in the direction of liberalism.” He was woken at the end of 1827 “by two great blows—illness and bereavement,” the bereavement being the death of his sister Mary in January 1828. Afterwards he began reading the early Church Fathers through in order, and found in them a Church visible, ancient and holy. Two friends shaped him now: John Keble, the quiet poet of The Christian Year, and Hurrell Froude, brilliant and fearless, who taught him to look with admiration on the Catholic past.

A work to do in England

In December 1832 he sailed with Froude and Froude’s father for the Mediterranean. He went back alone to Sicily and fell dangerously ill with fever at Leonforte. His servant thought he was dying, but Newman said, “I shall not die, for I have not sinned against light,” words he admitted he never understood. Recovering, he was overcome by the sense that God had kept him for a purpose.

Before starting from my inn in the morning of May 26th or 27th, I sat down on my bed, and began to sob bitterly. My servant, who had acted as my nurse, asked what ailed me. I could only answer, “I have a work to do in England.”

— John Henry Newman, Apologia Pro Vita Sua

Sailing home in an orange boat, he was becalmed for a week in the Straits of Bonifacio, and there wrote the lines “Lead, kindly light,” later a much-loved hymn. He reached England in July 1833. On 14 July Keble preached a sermon at Oxford called “National Apostasy,” and Newman wrote: “I have ever considered and kept the day, as the start of the religious movement of 1833.”

That movement, the Oxford or Tractarian Movement, set out to remind the Church of England that it was no department of the state but part of the one ancient Church, with bishops in succession from the apostles, real sacraments, and the faith of the Fathers. Newman began the Tracts for the Times that gave the movement its name, and for eight years his Sunday afternoon sermons at St Mary’s held a generation of undergraduates.

The death-bed of a conviction

Doubt came, as Newman tells it, through study. In 1839, reading the history of a fifth-century controversy, he met a sentence of St Augustine, “Securus judicat orbis terrarum,” roughly “the judgment of the whole world is sure.” “By those great words of the ancient Father,” he wrote, “the theory of the Via Media was absolutely pulverised.” The via media was the middle way between Rome and popular Protestantism that he had defended for years.

He tried to hold his ground. In February 1841 he published Tract 90, arguing that the Thirty-Nine Articles, the Church of England’s statement of doctrine, could be read in harmony with the ancient Catholic faith. The outcry was enormous. Senior tutors denounced it, the Bishop of Oxford asked that the Tracts stop, and for three years bishop after bishop condemned it.

From the end of 1841, I was on my death-bed, as regards my membership with the Anglican Church, though at the time I became aware of it only by degrees.

— John Henry Newman, Apologia Pro Vita Sua

In 1842 he withdrew to Littlemore, a village in his parish where he had built a church, and lived there with a few younger men in a quiet, semi-monastic way. It was hard, he said, to have to tell newspaper editors “that I went up there to say my prayers.” In February 1843 he publicly withdrew the hard things he had said against Rome, confessing they owed much “to an impetuous temper, a hope of approving myself to persons I respect, and a wish to repel the charge of Romanism.” In September he resigned St Mary’s and preached his last Anglican sermon, “The Parting of Friends.”

At Littlemore Newman gave his days to prayer and study. When a dear and old friend died in 1844, he had hoped the death-bed would bring him light; it did not, and he wrote that he sobbed over the coffin, still dark “as to what the way of truth was, and what I ought to do in order to please God and fulfil His will.” He asked his friends to “kindly remember me and my trial in their prayers.”

He never pretended the Church he was leaving was empty of God. Even then, he wrote, his “firm belief that grace was to be found in the Anglican Church remained too.” He set himself to write an Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine, resolving that if his convictions had not weakened by its end he would act. On 8 October 1845 he told his friends he was expecting Father Dominic Barberi, an Italian Passionist, and meant to ask him for “admission into the one Fold of Christ.” He was received the next day at Littlemore.

Leaving Oxford

Friendships broke and families divided. Keble and Pusey stayed in the Church of England, as did most of the movement, which went on shaping Anglican life long after he had gone. Newman left Oxford on 23 February 1846, remembering the snapdragon on the wall opposite his first rooms at Trinity, which he had taken “as the emblem of my own perpetual residence even unto death in my University.” Writing in 1864, he added, “I have never seen Oxford since, excepting its spires, as they are seen from the railway.”

He was ordained a Catholic priest in Rome in 1847 and came home as a member of the Oratory, the community of priests founded by St Philip Neri. He settled at Edgbaston in Birmingham and lived there most of the next forty years among factory workers, Irish immigrants and tradespeople, who remembered him as a caring pastor. The Catholic years had their own trials. In 1852 a jury found him guilty of libel against an ex-friar, Giacinto Achilli, and he was fined £100. From 1854 he spent four years as first rector of the struggling Catholic University of Ireland, whose lectures became The Idea of a University. Pius IX mistrusted him, and he clashed with Henry Manning, another Oxford convert.

Peace, and a friend

In the Apologia he summed up his life since 1845 in a few lines. He had no more changes of opinion to report, and none of the anguish of the years before.

I was not conscious of firmer faith in the fundamental truths of revelation, or of more self-command; I had not more fervour; but it was like coming into port after a rough sea; and my happiness on that score remains to this day without interruption.

— John Henry Newman, Apologia Pro Vita Sua

He felt the difficulties of faith as keenly as anyone; but “Ten thousand difficulties do not make one doubt.” He dedicated the book to the priests of the Birmingham Oratory, and above all to Ambrose St John, who had joined him at Littlemore in 1843: “whom God gave me, when He took every one else away; who are the link between my old life and my new.”

The Apologia ends not with an argument but with a prayer for all the friends he had loved at Oxford, those who had followed him and those who had not: “that all of us, who once were so united, and so happy in our union, may even now be brought at length, by the Power of the Divine Will, into One Fold and under One Shepherd.”

The book changed how England saw him. The Dream of Gerontius, a poem of the soul’s passage through death, followed in 1865, and A Grammar of Assent in 1870. In 1879 Pope Leo XIII made him a cardinal; he asked to stay in Birmingham, and took as his motto Cor ad cor loquitur, “Heart speaks to heart.” Ambrose St John had died in 1875, a grief Newman compared to the loss of a husband or wife.

What he left

Newman died of pneumonia at the Birmingham Oratory on 11 August 1890, aged eighty-nine, and at his own wish was buried in Ambrose St John’s grave at Rednal. Their memorial stone reads Ex umbris et imaginibus in veritatem, “Out of shadows and phantasms into the truth.” He was beatified by Benedict XVI in Birmingham in 2010, canonised by Pope Francis on 13 October 2019, and in 2025 named a Doctor of the Church by Leo XIV. The Church of England, which he left, still remembers him on the day of his death.

Apologia Pro Vita Sua is the book we publish here. Its opening parts answer Kingsley directly; its heart is the long “History of My Religious Opinions” that follows, from the Bible-reading boy to the man received at Littlemore. It is not a book of easy devotion, and it does not ask the reader to agree with where Newman arrived. What it offers is rarer: a careful, humble, sometimes painful account of a Christian trying for thirty years to follow the truth as he saw it, whatever it cost him in friends and place.

The schoolboy who wished the Arabian Tales were true became a man convinced that the unseen world was more real than the seen. He followed the light he was given one step at a time, and told the truth about every step. That honesty, more than any argument, is what the Apologia still gives its readers.

faq.q: Who was John Henry Newman?
faq.a: John Henry Newman (1801–1890) was an English clergyman, theologian, poet and writer. As an Anglican at Oxford he led the Oxford Movement; in 1845 he was received into the Catholic Church, and in 1879 he was made a cardinal.

faq.q: Where did John Henry Newman grow up?
faq.a: He was born in the City of London on 21 February 1801, the eldest of six children of a banker, John Newman, and Jemima Fourdrinier, who came of a Huguenot family. He went to school at Ealing and was raised to love reading the Bible.

faq.q: How did John Henry Newman become a committed Christian?
faq.a: In the autumn of 1816, at fifteen, he went through an inward conversion under the influence of his schoolmaster Walter Mayers and the books he lent him. Newman said he was more certain of that conversion than that he had hands and feet, and he looked back on it all his life.

faq.q: What did Newman do at Oxford?
faq.a: He studied at Trinity College, was elected a fellow of Oriel in 1822, was ordained in the Church of England in 1824 and 1825, and in 1828 became vicar of St Mary’s, the university church, where his sermons drew a generation of students.

faq.q: When did Newman write “Lead, Kindly Light”?
faq.a: He wrote it in June 1833 while sailing home from Sicily, when his orange boat was becalmed for a week in the Straits of Bonifacio. He had just recovered from a dangerous fever, convinced that he had a work to do in England.

faq.q: What was the Oxford Movement?
faq.a: It was a movement within the Church of England, dated by Newman from John Keble’s sermon of 14 July 1833, which sought to recover the Church’s ancient and Catholic inheritance: the apostolic succession, the sacraments and the teaching of the Fathers. Newman began its Tracts for the Times.

faq.q: What was Tract 90?
faq.a: Tract 90, published in February 1841, argued that the Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England could be read in harmony with the ancient Catholic faith. It caused an uproar, the Tracts were brought to an end, and bishops condemned it over the following years.

faq.q: When and why did Newman become a Catholic?
faq.a: After years of study and doubt at Littlemore, he came to believe that the Catholic Church was the Church of the apostles, though he still held that grace was found in the Church of England. He resigned St Mary’s in 1843 and was received into the Catholic Church by Father Dominic Barberi on 9 October 1845.

faq.q: What is Apologia Pro Vita Sua about?
faq.a: It is Newman’s account of his religious opinions from childhood to 1845, written in weekly parts in 1864 to answer Charles Kingsley’s charge that he did not value truth. Its candour changed how many in England saw him, and it is read by people of many traditions.

faq.q: How did Newman’s life end, and how is he remembered?
faq.a: He lived his later years at the Birmingham Oratory, was made a cardinal in 1879, and died on 11 August 1890; at his wish he was buried in the grave of his friend Ambrose St John. He was canonised by Pope Francis on 13 October 2019 and named a Doctor of the Church in 2025, and the Church of England also remembers him on 11 August.

fields.name: Irenaeus of Lyons
fields.bio: Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–c. 202) was a Greek bishop of Lyons in Roman Gaul who as a boy had heard Polycarp of Smyrna. His Against Heresies, written around 180, answered the Gnostic teachers with one good God, one Christ, and the faith handed down from the apostles.
fields.bio_html:
Irenaeus lived a long way from the places where the church’s story usually gets told. He grew up in the Greek East, among people who remembered the apostles, and spent his working life on the far western edge of the Christian world, in a river town in Gaul where he says he mostly used “a barbarous dialect.” His Greek name comes from the word for peace. Yet he is remembered chiefly for a fight: the long, patient, five-book argument against the Gnostic teachers that we call Against Heresies. He wrote it not as a man who enjoyed controversy but as a pastor who saw his people being drawn away, and who wanted to keep both the faith and the flock.

A boy who listened to Polycarp

We know very little about his early life. He is generally thought to have come from Smyrna, the busy port on the Aegean coast of Asia Minor (today İzmir in Turkey), though one nineteenth-century editor thought he may have been born in Syria and brought to Smyrna as a boy. His birth year is uncertain. The editors of the Ante-Nicene Fathers place it “somewhere between a.d. 120 and a.d. 140,” and their heading gives 120; many accounts settle around 130. Unlike many Christians of his age, he seems to have been raised in the faith rather than converted as an adult.

The one fixed point of his youth is a person. Smyrna’s bishop was Polycarp, an old man said to have heard John, the disciple of the Lord. Irenaeus tells us himself that Polycarp was one “whom I also saw in my early youth, for he tarried [on earth] a very long time,” and who died “having always taught the things which he had learned from the apostles.” Polycarp was martyred around 155. It was a living chain: the apostles taught Polycarp, Polycarp taught his church, and a boy in the congregation carried that teaching for the rest of his life. When teachers later claimed a secret tradition from Jesus, Irenaeus could answer that he had sat under a man who knew the apostles and heard no such thing.

To the banks of the Rhone

How he came to Gaul is not recorded, but there was a brisk trade between Smyrna and Marseilles, and the gospel had travelled with it. At Lyons — then the Roman city of Lugdunum — the church was led by a venerable bishop named Pothinus. Old tradition, followed by the ANF editor, says that Polycarp had sent Pothinus into Gaul as an evangelist, and that Irenaeus joined him there as a presbyter, an elder of the church. In 177, under the emperor Marcus Aurelius, that small congregation was struck by one of the most terrible persecutions of the century, and “the martyrs of Lyons and Vienne,” its neighbouring town, became famous throughout the church. Pothinus was among those who died.

While the persecution was under way, members of the church awaiting martyrdom sent Irenaeus to Rome, with a letter to Eleutherus, the bishop there. The historian Eusebius records the errand; the letter is said to have concerned the Montanists, a movement of new prophecy. He may also have written the surviving account of the martyrs’ sufferings, though that is uncertain. When he came home he found Pothinus dead, and he was chosen to succeed him, probably about 177 — the second bishop of Lyons — in a church that had just buried its leaders.

Even in the middle of his argument, Irenaeus stopped to pray. In the third book of Against Heresies he turns from his readers to address God directly: “Wherefore I do also call upon thee, Lord God of Abraham, and God of Isaac, and God of Jacob and Israel, who art the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He asks, through Christ, for “the governing power of the Holy Spirit,” and then makes a request that reaches across eighteen centuries: “give to every reader of this book to know Thee, that Thou art God alone, to be strengthened in Thee, and to avoid every heretical, and godless, and impious doctrine.”

The teachers of a secret knowledge

The danger he saw was not persecution but persuasion. Through the second century a number of teachers offered what they called gnosis, “knowledge” — a hidden wisdom for the spiritually advanced. Irenaeus studied most closely the system of Valentinus and his followers. In their account the true God dwelt far off in a fullness (the pleroma) of divine beings called Æons. One of the youngest, Sophia, or Wisdom, longed to grasp the unknowable Father and fell into passion and grief, and from that fall the material world eventually came to be, shaped by a lesser maker, the Demiurge. Human beings fell into classes — material, psychic and spiritual — and only the spiritual would be fully redeemed, freed from body and soul alike.

It is right to be fair to them. The ANF translators, no friends of Gnosticism, grant that it was trying “to solve the two grand problems of all religious philosophy”: how to account for evil, and how to reconcile the finite with the infinite. Some modern historians, notably Elaine Pagels, have charged that Irenaeus painted Gnostics as libertines when some were stricter ascetics than the orthodox. Since the Nag Hammadi library was found in 1945, the broad scholarly judgement has been that Irenaeus reported their beliefs fairly accurately, though the groups were more varied than any one summary allows.

What troubled Irenaeus was close at hand. Followers of a teacher named Marcus were at work, he says, “in our own district of the Rhone,” and he had read the Valentinians’ writings and talked with some of them himself. So he set himself, as the ANF editor puts it, to study these systems “like a wise physician,” so that others could recognise them. He began with an apology for his plain style:

Thou wilt not expect from me, who am resident among the Keltæ, and am accustomed for the most part to use a barbarous dialect, any display of rhetoric, which I have never learned, or any excellence of composition, which I have never practised, or any beauty and persuasiveness of style, to which I make no pretensions.

— Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book I, Preface

One God, one Christ, one story

Against the picture of a distant God, a botched creation and an elite saved out of the body, Irenaeus set a single, sweeping story. There is one good God, who made the world himself and has never stopped caring for it. He made humanity young and unfinished, meaning it to grow slowly into his likeness. When Adam fell, God did not abandon the plan; he sent his Son to take it up from within. Irenaeus called this recapitulation, a “summing up”: Christ, the new Adam, passes through every stage of human life and undoes the old disobedience by his obedience — the tree of the cross answering the tree in the garden. He was the first writer we know of to set Mary’s faithfulness against Eve’s faithlessness. And because the Word truly became flesh, the flesh itself will be saved; the fifth book is given to the resurrection of the body. Salvation is not escape from creation but its healing.

For the glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God.

— Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book IV

But how could anyone tell whose reading of Scripture was true, when both sides quoted it? Irenaeus pointed to what the churches held in common: the Scriptures; the rule of faith, a short summary of belief much like the later Apostles’ Creed; and the teaching handed down by the bishops of the apostles’ churches, whose names could be listed back to the beginning. He gave Rome as his chief example, saying every church should agree with it “on account of its pre-eminent authority” — a passage Catholics and Protestants have argued over for centuries. And he is the earliest surviving writer to insist on four Gospels, no more and no fewer, “four pillars, breathing out immortality on every side.”

He had his oddities, which his translators name plainly: he held that Christ lived to be an older man, with a ministry of many years, and he looked for a literal earthly reign of Christ before the end.

For all the sharpness of his argument, Irenaeus closed his third book by praying for the very teachers he had been refuting — that they would leave “the pit which they themselves have dug,” be “converted to the Church of God,” and “that Christ may be formed in them.” Then he added the line that explains the whole work: “We pray for these things on their behalf, loving them better than they seem to love themselves.” It would not weary him, he promised, “to endeavour with all our might to stretch out the hand unto them.”

The peacemaker

Little is known of his years as bishop; the reports of his missionary labours in southern Gaul are late and uncertain. The last thing told of him, by Eusebius, best suits his name. The churches of Asia Minor, his homeland, kept Easter on the fourteenth day of the Jewish month of Nisan, the day of the Passover, whatever day of the week it fell on; they were called Quartodecimans, the fourteenth-day keepers. Rome kept it on a Sunday. Polycarp and the Roman bishop Anicetus had once agreed to differ in peace. But around 190 Victor, bishop of Rome, moved to cut the Asian churches off from communion.

Irenaeus wrote to him — only a fragment of the letter survives — warning, as the ANF editors summarise it, that if he persisted the effect would be “to rend the Catholic Church in pieces.” The letter “had the desired result,” and the question was debated more temperately until the Council of Nicaea settled it. When Pope Francis named Irenaeus a Doctor of the Church in 2022, he gave him the added title Doctor unitatis, “Doctor of Unity.” The man who wrote five books against division also kept his own church from causing one.

An uncertain end

We do not know when or how Irenaeus died. It was at the end of the second century or the beginning of the third; the traditional date is about 202. The story that he was martyred goes back to Jerome, writing long afterwards, and the ANF translators note that neither Tertullian nor Eusebius, nor other early authorities, mentions it. The Catholic Church and some in the Orthodox Church honour him as a martyr; the honest answer is that the early record is silent. He was buried in Lyons under the Church of St John, later renamed for him.

His influence was immediate: Hippolytus and Tertullian drew freely on him. He is honoured as a saint across the Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran traditions, on 28 June in the West and 23 August in the Orthodox East. One other short work, the Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching, was found in an Armenian copy in 1904; the rest of his books are lost.

Reading him now

Against Heresies — in full, A Refutation and Subversion of Knowledge falsely so called — was written around 180. Its Greek is lost except for much of the first book, quoted by later writers; it survives whole in an ancient Latin version. Our text is Alexander Roberts and W. H. Rambaut’s translation from the Ante-Nicene Fathers of 1885, and the translators warn honestly that Irenaeus is often obscure, and that the reader’s patience is “sorely tried” by the first two books, which describe and refute the Gnostic systems in detail. A reader may fairly begin with Books III to V, where Irenaeus sets out the faith itself.

It repays the effort. Few books bring us closer to a church still within living memory of the apostles, already sure that the truth was not a secret for the few but a gift for all. Irenaeus ends the preface to his fifth book with the line that is the heart of his legacy, and the reason the boy who listened to Polycarp spent his life on the banks of the Rhone:

the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who did, through His transcendent love, become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself.

— Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book V, Preface

faq.q: Who was Irenaeus of Lyons?
faq.a: Irenaeus was a second-century Greek Christian from Asia Minor who became the second bishop of Lyons in Roman Gaul. He is best known for Against Heresies, his five-book refutation of the Gnostic teachers, and is honoured as a saint across the Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran traditions.

faq.q: When and where was Irenaeus born?
faq.a: His birth year is uncertain: the Ante-Nicene Fathers editors place it somewhere between 120 and 140, and many accounts settle around 130. He is generally thought to have come from Smyrna in Asia Minor, though one nineteenth-century editor suggested he was born in Syria and moved to Smyrna as a boy.

faq.q: What was his connection to Polycarp?
faq.a: As a young man in Smyrna, Irenaeus saw and heard Polycarp, the city's aged bishop, who was said to have been taught by John the disciple of the Lord. Irenaeus treated that memory as a living link to the apostles' own teaching, and appealed to it against those who claimed a secret tradition.

faq.q: How did Irenaeus come to Lyons?
faq.a: The details are not recorded, but there was a brisk trade between Smyrna and Marseilles, and the gospel came to southern Gaul from Asia Minor. Tradition says Polycarp sent the evangelist Pothinus to Gaul, and Irenaeus served under Pothinus at Lyons as a presbyter, or elder.

faq.q: What happened during the persecution at Lyons in 177?
faq.a: Under the emperor Marcus Aurelius the churches of Lyons and Vienne suffered a terrible persecution, and the martyrs of Lyons and Vienne became famous throughout the church; the aged bishop Pothinus was among those who died. During the persecution Irenaeus was sent to Rome with a letter to Bishop Eleutherus, and on his return he succeeded Pothinus as bishop, probably about 177.

faq.q: Who were the Gnostics Irenaeus opposed?
faq.a: They were second-century teachers, notably the followers of Valentinus, who offered a hidden knowledge, or gnosis, for the spiritually advanced. Many taught that the material world came from a fall among divine beings and was shaped by a lesser maker, and that the spiritual few would be freed from the body; modern scholars broadly judge that Irenaeus reported their beliefs fairly accurately, though the groups varied widely.

faq.q: What did Irenaeus teach against them?
faq.a: He taught one good God who made the world and guides all of history, and a humanity created young and meant to grow into God's likeness. Christ, the new Adam, sums up and heals human life, undoing Adam's disobedience by his obedience, and the body itself will be raised. He appealed to the Scriptures, including four Gospels, to the rule of faith, and to the teaching handed down by the bishops of the apostolic churches.

faq.q: How did Irenaeus help settle the Easter controversy?
faq.a: Around 190, Victor, bishop of Rome, moved to cut off the churches of Asia Minor, which kept Easter on the fourteenth day of the Jewish month of Nisan rather than on a Sunday. Irenaeus wrote warning him that this would rend the church in pieces, and the letter had the desired result; Pope Francis later named him the Doctor of Unity.

faq.q: How did Irenaeus die?
faq.a: Nothing certain is known about his death, which came at the end of the second century or the beginning of the third; the traditional date is about 202. The tradition that he was martyred goes back to Jerome, writing long afterwards, and is not mentioned by Tertullian, Eusebius or other early authorities.

faq.q: What is Against Heresies, and is it worth reading today?
faq.a: Against Heresies, written around 180, is a five-book description and refutation of the Gnostic systems and a defence of the apostolic faith; it survives whole in an ancient Latin version, here in the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers translation by Alexander Roberts and W. H. Rambaut. The first two books are heavy going, but Books III to V set out the faith itself and contain lines such as 'the glory of God is a living man.'

fields.name: Origen of Alexandria
fields.bio: Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) was an Alexandrian teacher, preacher and biblical scholar, one of the most influential and most debated theologians of the early Church. He wrote On First Principles, the first ordered account of Christian doctrine, and died after torture in the Decian persecution.
fields.bio_html:
Few Christians have been so loved and so argued over as Origen of Alexandria. In his lifetime bishops sat at his feet like pupils, and the bishop of his own city drove him out. After his death the great theologians of the East learned from him, and three centuries later an emperor ordered his books burned. He was one of the most prolific writers of the ancient world. Yet the record of his life leaves something plainer than all that: a man who gave his days to the Scriptures, owned almost nothing, taught whoever would come, and in old age suffered torture rather than deny Christ.

A father’s son in Alexandria

Origen was born around 185 in Alexandria, the great Greek-speaking city of Roman Egypt. Almost everything we know of his life comes from the church historian Eusebius, who wrote about fifty years after Origen’s death, admired him deeply, and sometimes relied on hearsay. His father, Leonides, was a Christian teacher of literature who gave his son a full Greek education and, Eusebius says, had him learn and recite passages of Scripture every day. The boy soon asked questions about the deeper meaning of the texts that his father could not answer. Leonides told him to be content with the plain sense, but inwardly rejoiced.

Eusebius preserves a tender picture of Leonides’ devotion. He used to uncover the breast of his sleeping son and kiss it, as the temple of the Holy Spirit, and he gave thanks to God for having made him the father of such a child. Origen’s life of prayer began in a house where a father gave thanks to God over his sleeping son.

In 202, when Origen was about seventeen, persecution broke out under the emperor Septimius Severus, and Leonides was imprisoned. Origen longed to share his father’s fate and give himself up. Eusebius tells the story that his mother hid all his clothes, so that he could not leave the house. Instead he wrote to his father in prison, urging him to stand firm and not to change his mind for the sake of his family. Leonides was beheaded, the family’s property was confiscated, and Origen, the eldest son, was left to provide for his mother and younger brothers.

Teacher at eighteen

He began to earn his living as a teacher of grammar, the ancient study of language and literature, and his pupils soon included young men drawn to the faith. When persecution struck again, many of them were martyred, and Origen stood by them so openly that more than once he had to flee from house to house to escape the mob. At about eighteen, Bishop Demetrius gave him a post teaching catechumens, those preparing for baptism. The editor’s Life in our edition says he became head of the school; some modern scholars think a teaching post more likely. Either way, he gave himself to it entirely. He sold his books for a small daily income of four obols and lived on it for years. He taught all day and studied Scripture far into the night, slept on the bare ground, fasted often, went barefoot and owned a single cloak.

Eusebius adds a darker story: that the young Origen, reading literally Christ’s words about those who make themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 19:12), castrated himself. Some modern scholars accept the account; others doubt it, or think it gossip spread by his enemies. Origen himself never mentions it, and when he later commented on that verse he condemned the literal reading in the strongest terms.

He kept learning. He handed the beginners to his former pupil Heraclas, studied philosophy under Ammonius Saccas so that he could meet educated pagans on their own ground, and visited Rome. He also won a friend who changed his life. Ambrose, a wealthy man whom Origen had brought out of a Gnostic sect, gave him a house, relays of stenographers to take down his dictation and copyists to make fair copies, and paid for all of it to be published.

The bishop and the exile

When the emperor Caracalla turned his soldiers on Alexandria and its scholars around 215, Origen fled to Palestine, where Bishop Alexander of Jerusalem and Bishop Theoctistus of Caesarea asked him to explain the Scriptures in church. He was still a layman. Demetrius, protesting that such a thing had never been heard of, ordered him home, and Origen obeyed.

Around 230, travelling to Greece on church business, he passed again through Caesarea, and his friends there ordained him a presbyter, or priest. To Demetrius this was insubordination. Synods he summoned declared Origen unfit to teach, excommunicated him from the church of Alexandria and stripped him of the priesthood, though the churches of Palestine, Phoenicia, Arabia and Achaia refused the sentence. Rumours followed him: Eusebius says Demetrius published the castration story, and Demetrius also accused him of teaching that even the devil would be saved, which Origen denied in a Letter to Friends in Alexandria. Demetrius died about a year later, but the charges never quite went away. Origen did not go back. Caesarea, on the coast of Palestine, was his home for the rest of his life.

A school, a library and a pulpit

The Caesarea years were the fullest of his life. He founded a school there, aimed especially at young pagans drawn to the faith, and led his students from reasoning to the study of the natural world, and only then to theology, the crown of all they had learned. One of them, Gregory, later called the Wonderworker, stayed five years and wrote a warm tribute to his teacher. When Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, taught a mistaken view of Christ, Origen reasoned with him until he came round. A record of a similar meeting, the Dialogue with Heracleides, found in Egypt in 1941, shows him questioning a bishop with unusual courtesy.

He preached in Caesarea, at first on Wednesdays and Fridays and later daily, and hundreds of his sermons survive. He built up the great Christian library of Caesarea, at whose heart stood the Hexapla, setting the Hebrew Old Testament beside a Greek transliteration and several Greek translations in parallel columns. He wrote commentaries on John, Matthew, Romans and the Song of Songs, which he read as the love of the Word for the believing soul, and late in life Against Celsus, a reply to a pagan philosopher’s attack on Christianity.

At the request of Ambrose and a woman named Tatiana, Origen wrote a treatise On Prayer. It explains the kinds of prayer found in Scripture, works carefully through the Lord’s Prayer, and closes with counsel on the posture, place and attitude of the one who prays. For him prayer was the door into theology itself: in On First Principles he confesses that the hardest questions about God’s justice cannot be explained by any human power or language “unless as prostrate suppliants we pray to the Word, and Wisdom, and Righteousness Himself, who is the only-begotten Son of God.”

When the emperor Maximinus turned on Christian leaders in 235, Origen went into hiding in the house of a Christian woman named Juliana. Ambrose and Protoctetus, a priest of Caesarea, were arrested, and for them he wrote his Exhortation to Martyrdom, urging them to stand firm as he had once urged his father.

Thinking aloud before God

On First Principles belongs to his Alexandrian years, between about 220 and 230. It sets out the faith as an ordered whole: God, Christ and the Holy Spirit; angels and the world; free will, sin and redemption; and how to read Scripture. Origen begins with what the apostles taught plainly and the Church holds without question. Then he turns to the questions they left open, and insists more than once that here he is exploring, not deciding.

These subjects, indeed, are treated by us with great solicitude and caution, in the manner rather of an investigation and discussion, than in that of fixed and certain decision.

— Origen, On First Principles, Book I

Two of these explorations were later rejected by the Church. The first concerned the origin of souls. Troubled that people are born into such unequal lives, and unwilling to think God unjust, Origen suggested that God first created rational spirits, equal and free, devoted to contemplating him; that as their love cooled they fell, some further than others, becoming angels, human beings or demons; and that the variety of the world reflects their own free choices. The second was a hope about the end. Because “the end is always like the beginning,” he wondered whether all things might at last be restored to unity with God, and he believed God’s punishments are meant to heal. He presented this as a possibility rather than a doctrine, and in his letter to Alexandria he denied that the devil would be saved. Beneath both ideas lies a conviction he states plainly: that the mind’s longing for God is God’s own gift.

This desire, this longing, we believe to be unquestionably implanted within us by God; and as the eye naturally seeks the light and vision, and our body naturally desires food and drink, so our mind is possessed with a becoming and natural desire to become acquainted with the truth of God and the causes of things.

— Origen, On First Principles, Book II

The iron collar

In 250 the emperor Decius ordered a general persecution of Christians, and this time Origen did not escape. Eusebius describes his “bodily tortures and torments under the iron collar and in the dungeon,” his feet stretched for many days in the stocks. The governor ordered that he was not to be killed until he had publicly renounced Christ. He would not. When Decius died in 251 Origen was released, but his body, worn by a lifetime of fasting and night study, was broken. He died around 253, at about sixty-nine. An old tradition, followed by the editor of our edition, places his imprisonment and death at Tyre, though some modern historians give it little weight.

A contested inheritance

For generations the East revered him. Athanasius learned from him, and so did Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa; monks especially loved him. But his followers pressed his ideas in different directions, and controversy came. In the late fourth century Epiphanius and Jerome attacked him while Rufinus and Bishop John of Jerusalem defended him, John holding that a man could not be condemned as a heretic after his death. In 397 Rufinus translated On First Principles into Latin and, believing that heretics had tampered with it, altered passages to fit the orthodoxy of his own day. In 543 the emperor Justinian condemned Origen and ordered his writings burned.

Anathemas against Origen are associated with the Second Council of Constantinople in 553, but how far they touched Origen himself is still debated. Some scholars think his name was added to the council’s text later, or that the anathemas belong to an earlier local synod; many conclude that the teachings condemned were those of later Origenist monks rather than his own. So much of his work was destroyed that the question cannot be fully settled. He is not generally counted a saint, yet he has never lacked admirers: Erasmus prized him above almost every Christian writer, and Pope Benedict XVI called him “not only a brilliant theologian but also an exemplary witness of the doctrine he passed on.”

The book we are publishing is On First Principles, in Frederick Crombie’s 1885 translation for the Ante-Nicene Fathers. Most of it survives only in Rufinus’s smoothed Latin; where Origen’s own Greek survives, this edition follows the Greek. It is not an easy book. But it is the first attempt to map the whole of Christian doctrine, and its fourth book, on reading the Bible in its literal, moral and spiritual senses, shaped Christian interpretation for centuries. Above all, it lets a reader watch a great mind at prayer and at work, asking every question it can and confessing how much remains beyond it.

For however far a man may advance in his investigations, and how great soever the progress that he may make by unremitting study, assisted even by the grace of God, and with his mind enlightened, he will not be able to attain to the end of those things which are the object of his inquiries.

— Origen, On First Principles, Book IV

faq.q: Who was Origen of Alexandria?
