faq.a: Origen was a Christian teacher, preacher and biblical scholar born around 185 in Alexandria in Roman Egypt. He was one of the most prolific writers of the ancient world, and he died around 253 after being tortured for his faith in the persecution under the emperor Decius.

faq.q: What happened to Origen’s father?
faq.a: His father, Leonides, a Christian teacher of literature, was imprisoned and beheaded in the persecution under Septimius Severus in 202, when Origen was about seventeen. Eusebius says Origen wanted to give himself up too, but his mother hid his clothes so he could not leave the house; he wrote to his father urging him to stand firm instead.

faq.q: How did Origen become a teacher?
faq.a: After his father’s death left the family poor, he supported them by teaching grammar, and at about eighteen Bishop Demetrius gave him a post teaching those preparing for baptism in Alexandria. He lived very simply, selling his books for a small daily income, studying Scripture late into the night, fasting often and owning a single cloak.

faq.q: Did Origen really castrate himself?
faq.a: The story comes from Eusebius, who says the young Origen took Matthew 19:12 literally. Some modern scholars accept it, while others doubt it or think it gossip from his enemies; Origen never mentions it, and later he condemned the literal reading of that verse.

faq.q: Why did Origen leave Alexandria?
faq.a: He was ordained a priest around 230 by friendly bishops in Caesarea without the consent of his own bishop, Demetrius, who saw this as insubordination. Synods in Alexandria excommunicated him and stripped him of the priesthood, and he made Caesarea in Palestine his home for the rest of his life.

faq.q: What did Origen do in Caesarea?
faq.a: He founded a Christian school, preached regularly in the church, and built up a great library whose centrepiece was the Hexapla, an edition of the Old Testament setting the Hebrew beside several Greek versions in parallel columns. He also wrote biblical commentaries, the treatise On Prayer, the Exhortation to Martyrdom and Against Celsus.

faq.q: What is On First Principles about?
faq.a: Written in Alexandria between about 220 and 230, On First Principles is the first attempt to set out Christian teaching as an ordered whole, covering God and the Trinity, angels and the world, free will, sin and redemption, and how to read Scripture. It survives mostly in Rufinus’s Latin translation of 397, which altered some passages to fit later orthodoxy.

faq.q: Which of Origen’s ideas were later rejected?
faq.a: Origen explored the idea that souls existed before their bodies and fell from an original contemplation of God, and he hoped that all things might at last be restored to God. He offered these as possibilities rather than settled doctrine, but the Church later rejected his teaching on the pre-existence of souls.

faq.q: How did Origen die?
faq.a: In the persecution under Decius, which began in 250, he was imprisoned and tortured with an iron collar and the stocks, and the governor ordered that he not be killed until he renounced Christ, which he refused to do. He was released after Decius died in 251 but never recovered, and died around 253; tradition places his death at Tyre.

faq.q: Was Origen condemned as a heretic?
faq.a: Controversy over his teaching broke out in the late fourth century, and in 543 the emperor Justinian condemned him and ordered his writings burned. Anathemas against him are associated with the Second Council of Constantinople in 553, but scholars still debate whether they belonged to the council and how far they touched his own teaching rather than that of later Origenists.

fields.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
fields.bio: Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339) was a bishop and scholar of Palestine, the pupil of the martyr Pamphilus and the father of church history. He lived through the Great Persecution, signed the Nicene Creed, befriended Constantine, and wrote The Church History.
fields.bio_html:
Much of what we know about the first three centuries of the church, we know because one man in a city on the coast of Palestine sat down to write it out. Eusebius of Caesarea was not a martyr, though he mourned his dearest friend as one. He was not a great theologian, and in the heat of controversy he said things the church later refused. He was a reader and a copier of other men’s words, and because he copied them, bishops and martyrs who would otherwise have vanished still speak. He is remembered as the father of church history. He is also one of the most argued-over figures of his age, and an honest account of him has to hold both.

A son of Pamphilus

He was born around 260, most likely in or near Caesarea Maritima, on the Mediterranean coast. Nothing is known of his parents. What Eusebius tells us himself is that he learned the creed of the Caesarean church as a child, was baptized into it, and later served that church as a presbyter, or priest. As a young man he also saw the young Constantine pass through Caesarea in the train of the emperor Diocletian.

The decisive figure of his youth was Pamphilus, a learned presbyter who settled in Caesarea in the later third century. Pamphilus revered Origen, the great Alexandrian scholar who had made Caesarea his home and left his books to its church. He built that bequest into a great library, and gathered a household of students who lived together, studied the Scriptures, and copied and corrected manuscripts of the Bible and of Origen’s works. Eusebius became his closest disciple, so close that he took the name Eusebius Pamphili, Eusebius the son of Pamphilus — a name that may also mean he was Pamphilus’s heir.

Those years among the books seem to have been the happiest of his life. Out of them came the Chronicle, a table of world history set out in parallel columns, and the beginnings of a history of the church itself; how early its first edition appeared is still debated.

The years of the furnace

In 303 the quiet ended. The persecution of Diocletian, remembered as the Great Persecution, broke upon the church, in McGiffert’s phrase, almost like a thunderbolt out of a clear sky. Eusebius watched churches torn down and Scriptures burned in the market-places, and for seven years Caesarea was a city of trials and executions. He was present at martyrdoms in Tyre, and in the Thebais, the upper Nile country of Egypt, he recorded a single day of slaughter: “We, also being on the spot ourselves, have observed large crowds in one day; some suffering decapitation, others torture by fire.”

What stayed with him from Egypt was not only the cruelty but the worship. He wrote that the condemned received their sentence of death with joy, even with laughter, and that they sang hymns and gave thanks to God until their last breath. Among the historian’s memories of the persecution was this one: people praying as they died.

The persecution reached his own household. Apphianus, a young student who lived under the same roof, kept his plan even from his housemates, then seized the governor’s hand as he was about to sacrifice; he was tortured and killed. In the fifth year Pamphilus himself was arrested. He spent two years in prison, and Eusebius spent much of that time with him; together they wrote a Defence of Origen. Whether Eusebius was ever imprisoned himself is not known. In the seventh year of the persecution, about 309 or 310, Pamphilus was put to death with eleven companions, and Eusebius wrote of him with a grief that has not faded:

Among these was my dearest friend Pamphilus, who was by reason of every virtue the most illustrious of the martyrs in our time.

— Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine

He wrote a life of Pamphilus, now all but lost, and the Martyrs of Palestine, an account of those who died in his own province. How he himself came through those years unharmed, he never explained. That silence would one day be used against him.

Bishop of a rebuilt church

Not long after peace came, Eusebius became bishop of Caesarea. The year is uncertain — about 313 to 315 is commonly given, though McGiffert allowed anything from 311 to 318 — and he held the see for the rest of his life. One of his first duties was to preach at the dedication of a great new church at Tyre, built by his friend Paulinus., and he copied the sermon into his History without naming himself.

Eusebius saw the rebuilding of the churches as an answer to the church’s prayers. Describing the dedication feasts after the persecution, he called them “the sight which had been desired and prayed for by us all”: bishops assembling, strangers arriving from abroad, psalms sung in the new buildings, and people of every age giving honour to God in prayers and thanksgiving.

In these years he completed the Church History, carrying it down to Constantine’s victory over his last rival, Licinius, in 324, and dedicating its last book to Paulinus.

Arius, Nicaea, and a letter home

About 318 a dispute broke out in Alexandria that would shadow the rest of his life. A presbyter named Arius taught that the Son of God was a creature, the highest of all, but not eternal: there was a time, his party said, when the Son was not. Excommunicated by his bishop, Alexander, Arius found a friend in Eusebius. The historian Sozomen reports that Eusebius and other Palestinian bishops let Arius gather his people for worship, while urging him to make peace with his bishop. Fragments survive of letters in which Eusebius rebuked Alexander for misrepresenting Arius, in language plainly sympathetic to the Arian side. McGiffert’s judgement was that for a few years Eusebius was an Arian as he understood Arianism, out of conviction and not mere friendship, but that he had not grasped how far Arius went.

In 325 Constantine summoned the bishops to Nicaea. Sozomen says it was Eusebius who gave the opening address in Constantine’s honour, though other ancient writers name other speakers. He put forward the creed of his own church. Constantine declared it orthodox, but asked that one word be added: homoousios, of one substance with the Father. The council then drew up a fuller creed, with condemnations of the Arian slogans attached. Eusebius hesitated, asked what the new phrases meant, was satisfied by the explanations, and signed. Then he wrote home to explain himself. His letter to the church of Caesarea, preserved by the historian Socrates, gives his reasons:

On this account we assented to the sense ourselves, without declining even the term ‘One in substance,’ peace being the object which we set before us, and steadfastness in the orthodox view.

— Eusebius, letter to the church of Caesarea

Readers still argue whether that letter shows an honest mind changing under argument or a man bending to the emperor’s wish. McGiffert found that after Nicaea Eusebius never again defended Arian teaching in his writings, though he never grew fond of the word homoousios. He held what McGiffert called a mild orthodoxy, and feared above all the opposite error, Sabellianism, which blurred the Father and the Son into one.

Tyre, and an old accusation

That fear shaped his later years. He quarrelled with Eustathius of Antioch, a firm defender of Nicaea, each accusing the other of heresy, and a council at Antioch deposed Eustathius. The church there then asked Eusebius to be its bishop, one of the great sees of the East. He refused, and Constantine wrote to praise him for it.

He also stood with the enemies of Athanasius, Alexander’s successor and the champion of the Nicene faith. In 335 Athanasius was tried at a council in Tyre on charges his defenders have always called slander. Eusebius was there, and may have presided; the sources disagree. There Potamo, an Egyptian bishop who had lost an eye for the faith in the persecution, turned on him. According to Epiphanius, he asked: “How wast thou released from prison unless thou didst promise those that put upon us the pressure of persecution to do that which is unlawful, or didst actually do it?” Eusebius rose in anger and dismissed the council.

The charge that he had sacrificed to the gods to save himself has followed him ever since, and it should be said plainly: it was never proven. Potamo claimed no knowledge of any act; he reasoned that a man who left prison unhurt must have given way. Athanasius said only that Eusebius had been “accused of sacrificing,” and never called him a sacrificer, as he did others. Eusebius was made bishop in the very city where his conduct in the persecution must have been known, and he wrote sternly of those who lapsed. Perhaps friends in authority protected him; perhaps he was released when the persecution ended, like many others. The accusation remains an accusation.

The emperor’s friend

Through all of this ran his friendship with Constantine. He corresponded with him, preached before him, and in 336 delivered the oration for the thirtieth year of his reign. When Constantine died in May 337, Eusebius, now an old man, began his Life of Constantine, which tells of the vision of a cross of light that, he said, the emperor himself had described to him. It is a eulogy, not a neutral history, and it was criticised as such in antiquity: Socrates complained that its author cared more for the emperor’s praises than for an accurate account of the facts.

Eusebius died soon after his friend, probably in 339, though some put it early in 340. An ancient Syriac martyrology keeps his memory on 30 May, and his pupil Acacius succeeded him at Caesarea.

The man who kept the record

His reputation has never settled. Some of the Fathers counted him a heretic; others honoured him. He was long commemorated as a saint in parts of the West, until his name was struck from the Roman Martyrology in its revision under Pope Gregory XIII, and the Syrian Orthodox Church venerates him still. Modern critics have been harsh: Edward Gibbon distrusted his account of the martyrs, and Jacob Burckhardt called him “the first thoroughly dishonest historian of antiquity.” Others, Bishop Lightfoot and McGiffert among them, answer that where his quotations can be tested they prove faithful, that he tells the reader openly what he is leaving out, and that his real faults lie elsewhere — careless chronology, too ready a trust in a few doubtful documents, and a fondness for the men he admired that could blind him to their faults. Read him with care, they say, and with gratitude.

The gratitude is owed. The Church History, the book we publish, is the first full history of the church, ten books running from Christ to the peace under Constantine. Much of what survives of early writers such as Papias and Hegesippus survives in its pages, and it preserves two of the noblest records of martyrdom from the ancient church, the death of Polycarp and the sufferings of the churches of Lyons and Vienne. Eusebius knew he was attempting something new:

But at the outset I must crave for my work the indulgence of the wise, for I confess that it is beyond my power to produce a perfect and complete history, and since I am the first to enter upon the subject, I am attempting to traverse as it were a lonely and untrodden path.

— Eusebius, The Church History, Book I

He set out on that path with a prayer. In the opening chapter of the History, before a single bishop or martyr is named, he wrote, “I pray that I may have God as my guide and the power of the Lord as my aid,” for he could find only scattered fragments left by those who had gone before.

McGiffert’s translation of 1890 includes the Martyrs of Palestine, and it rewards slow reading. It is uneven and digressive. But it was written by a man who had seen his friends die for Christ and then seen the churches rebuilt, and who could not bear that their witness, or the witness of the generations before them, should be lost. That he did not let it be lost is his monument.

faq.q: Who was Eusebius of Caesarea?
faq.a: Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339) was bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, a biblical scholar, and the author of the first full history of the church. He is remembered as the father of church history.

faq.q: Where and when was Eusebius born?
faq.a: He was born around 260, most likely in or near Caesarea Maritima in Palestine; nothing is known of his parents. He learned the creed of the Caesarean church as a child, was baptized there, and later served it as a presbyter.

faq.q: Who was Pamphilus, and why was Eusebius called Eusebius Pamphili?
faq.a: Pamphilus was a learned presbyter of Caesarea who built Origen’s bequest of books into a great library and gathered students to study and copy the Scriptures. Eusebius was his closest disciple and took the name Eusebius Pamphili, Eusebius the son of Pamphilus.

faq.q: What did Eusebius experience during the Great Persecution?
faq.a: From 303 he saw churches destroyed and Scriptures burned, and he was an eyewitness of martyrdoms in Caesarea, Tyre and Egypt. Pamphilus spent two years in prison, where the two wrote a Defence of Origen together, and was martyred with eleven companions about 309 or 310.

faq.q: Did Eusebius sacrifice to the gods to escape martyrdom?
faq.a: There is no proof that he did. At the Council of Tyre in 335 the Egyptian bishop Potamo asked how he could have left prison unharmed without giving way, but this was an inference, not an eyewitness charge, and even Athanasius said only that Eusebius was accused of sacrificing.

faq.q: When did Eusebius become bishop of Caesarea?
faq.a: He became bishop not long after the persecution ended; the year is uncertain, though about 313 to 315 is commonly given. He held the see for the rest of his life and refused a later invitation to become bishop of Antioch.

faq.q: What was Eusebius’s attitude to Arius?
faq.a: When Arius was excommunicated in Alexandria about 318, Eusebius supported him and wrote to Bishop Alexander complaining that Arius’s views had been misrepresented. Historians disagree about how far he shared Arius’s teaching; his translator McGiffert judged that he was an Arian for a few years as he understood it, but left that position at Nicaea.

faq.q: What part did Eusebius play at the Council of Nicaea?
faq.a: At Nicaea in 325 he presented the creed of his church at Caesarea, which Constantine accepted with the addition of the word homoousios, of one substance. After questioning the meaning of the council’s new phrases he signed its creed, and he explained his reasons in a letter to his church, saying that peace was the object he set before him.

faq.q: What was his relationship with Constantine?
faq.a: Eusebius first saw Constantine as a young man in Caesarea and became one of the emperor’s most trusted bishops. He preached before him, gave the oration for his thirtieth year as emperor in 336, and after Constantine’s death in 337 wrote the Life of Constantine, a eulogy that even ancient historians criticised for its praise.

faq.q: What is The Church History by Eusebius?
faq.a: The Church History is the first full history of the Christian church, in ten books, from Christ to the peace under Constantine around 324. It preserves passages from many early writers otherwise lost; critics fault its chronology and some of its judgements, but it remains the main source for the early church. This is the translation by Arthur Cushman McGiffert (1890), with the Martyrs of Palestine.

fields.name: Lactantius
fields.bio: Lactantius (c. 250–c. 325) was a North African teacher of rhetoric, called by Diocletian to Nicomedia, who lost his career in the Great Persecution and turned his eloquence to defending the faith. Later tutor to Constantine’s son Crispus, he wrote The Divine Institutes and is remembered as “the Christian Cicero.”
fields.bio_html:
Lactantius spent the first half of his life teaching young men how to win an argument. He was good at it — good enough that an emperor sent for him across the sea to teach Latin eloquence in a Greek city. Then he came to believe that the art he had mastered had been used to train his pupils, as he later put it, “not to virtue, but altogether to cunning wickedness.” He did not throw the art away. He turned it around, and spent the rest of his life using the finest Latin of his age to plead for a faith the Roman state was trying to destroy. The Renaissance would call him the Christian Cicero. He might rather have been remembered as a man who changed what his words were for.

A rhetorician from Africa

Little about his early life is certain, and the oldest notices of him admit it. He was probably born around 250 in Roman North Africa, into a family that was not Christian; he is usually described as of Berber origin, though his translator, William Fletcher, records that some once argued for a birth in Italy. Even his full name, usually given as Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius, is unsettled; Fletcher mentions the old guess that “Lactantius” was a nickname for the milky softness of his style. An inscription at Cirta in Numidia names a certain L. Caecilius Firmianus, and that city may have been his home.

One thing the record does hold is his teacher. According to Jerome he studied under Arnobius, who taught rhetoric at Sicca Veneria, in what is now Tunisia. Rhetoric — the art of persuasive speaking and writing — was the crown of an ancient education and the road to a public career, and the pupil’s fame soon outstripped his master’s. He taught in Africa until the emperor Diocletian invited him to become an official professor of Latin rhetoric at Nicomedia, the imperial capital in Bithynia, in what is now north-western Turkey.

A professor at Diocletian’s court

Nicomedia put him close to power. He moved in the imperial circle, and there he first met Constantine, and Galerius, whom he would later cast as the villain of the persecutions. Yet the post was not the triumph it seemed. A Latin teacher in a Greek-speaking city found few pupils, and Fletcher records that he was reduced to extreme poverty.

Somewhere in these years he became a Christian. When and how, no source tells us. Fletcher wondered whether his poverty and his change of religion were connected; the American editor of the same volume answered in a footnote that he saw no force in the idea, since a man converting then could expect nothing but worse suffering. What that editor did insist on was that Lactantius was not a “fair-weather Christian,” but confessed the faith amid the last and most terrible of the great persecutions.

Diocletian published his first edict against the Christians on 24 February 303. Modern accounts say Lactantius had already resigned his post; either way, his public career was over. In the fifth book of The Divine Institutes he remembers what he saw. While he was teaching rhetoric in Bithynia, he writes, the temple of God was overthrown, and two men in the same city seized the moment to publish attacks on the Christians: a philosopher who praised frugality and lived in luxury, and a judge who had urged the persecution and then wrote books pretending to advise its victims kindly. He recalls, too, a governor in Bithynia exulting as if he had conquered a nation of barbarians, because one Christian who had held out for two years seemed at last to give way. It was out of that grief, he says, that he took up the task of answering them — moved by their arrogance, by the consciousness of truth itself, “and (as I think) by God.”

Turning the art around

Stripped of his chair, Lactantius lived in poverty, Jerome says, and eked out a living by writing. Around 303 or 304 he wrote On the Workmanship of God, on the human body as evidence of its Maker’s wisdom, dedicated to a former pupil. And he began the great work of his life, The Divine Institutes, written between about 303 and 311.

The title borrows from the law courts. Roman jurists wrote Institutes of civil law to settle the quarrels of citizens; Lactantius would write the divine Institutes, which would speak not of rain-droppings and water rights and the pressing of claims, but of hope, of life, of salvation, of immortality, and of God. In the preface he says plainly why a professor of rhetoric should turn to such a subject:

For they, the philosophers, were considered teachers of right living, which is far more excellent, since to speak well belongs only to a few, but to live well belongs to all.

— Lactantius, The Divine Institutes, Preface

He did not despise his training: truth, he says, flows more powerfully into the mind when it is set out clearly and well. And he knew whom he was writing for. Educated pagans, he thought, scorned Christianity partly because it lacked defenders who could write in a way they respected. Even Cyprian, the great bishop of Carthage, had in his view answered a pagan critic with Scriptures the man did not believe, when such a reader needed to be led by reason, step by step, “that he might not be dazzled.” So Lactantius met the learned on their own ground — Cicero and Virgil, Seneca and the philosophers, and the Sibylline oracles that Romans revered — and tried to show them where it all was pointing.

Seven books on true wisdom

The Divine Institutes runs to seven books. The first three clear the ground: the false worship of the gods, the origin of that error, and the false wisdom of the philosophers. The fourth makes his central claim, that true wisdom and true religion cannot be separated: the philosophers sought wisdom without God, the cults worshipped without wisdom, and the two meet only in the one God made known in Christ. It was the first attempt to set out Christian teaching as a whole system in Latin.

The fifth book, on justice, was written while Christians were still being tortured, and it argues that worship cannot be forced, because “nothing is so much a matter of free-will as religion.” Christians call one another brethren, he says, because they believe themselves equal, rich and poor, master and servant alike. And he turns the persecutors’ claim to be defending religion against them:

For religion is to be defended, not by putting to death, but by dying; not by cruelty, but by patient endurance; not by guilt, but by good faith.

— Lactantius, The Divine Institutes, Book V

The sixth book turns from argument to life. It is about true worship, and much of it is practical: works of mercy, repentance and forgiveness, the governing of the passions. Worship, for Lactantius, is not costly gifts or the blood of animals, for God needs nothing:

His offering is innocency of soul; His sacrifice praise and a hymn.

— Lactantius, The Divine Institutes, Book VI

Lactantius left no account of his own hours of prayer, but he left a plain rule for them. The worshipper, he wrote, should always ask God’s mercy and pray for pardon, give thanks when good comes and in evil too, and not keep this for the temple only, “but at home, and even in his very bed” — always having God with him, consecrated in his heart, since he himself is a temple of God.

The seventh book, on the happy life, looks to the end. Lactantius sets out a vivid millenarian hope: that when six thousand years of history are complete, Christ will come, the righteous will reign on earth for a thousand years, and then the world will be renewed. He drew much of it from the Sibyls and other apocalyptic sources. He even reckoned the end no more than two hundred years away, though nothing of the kind need be feared while the city of Rome still stood.

Having traced what he believed the last days would bring, Lactantius asks his readers to pray. While Rome stands, he writes, the end is held back, and so “the God of heaven is to be entreated by us and implored” — if indeed his decrees can be delayed — that the final tyrant may not come sooner than we think.

Later Christian thought did not follow him everywhere. The church came to see attempts to fix the date of the end as at odds with Christ’s word that no one knows the day or the hour, and his earthly millennium was not the view that prevailed. In the third book he also ridiculed philosophers who thought the earth round, with people on the far side whose footsteps would be higher than their heads; Copernicus later called this mockery childish. His statements of doctrine could be loose, and his grasp of Scripture thin. Jerome put both sides in a sentence that has stuck: “Lactantius has a flow of eloquence worthy of Tully: would that he had been as ready to teach our doctrines as to pull down those of others!” None of this cancels what he got right. He is best read as what he was: an earnest convert making the case for Christ to the world he had come out of.

Tutor to an emperor’s son

The persecution ended, and Lactantius lived to see what had seemed impossible: a Roman emperor who honoured the God of the Christians. Constantine, whose Christian policy he is said to have helped guide in its first stages, became his patron and appointed him, already old, as Latin tutor to his son Crispus. The sources date this differently — some say 309–310, Fletcher about 315 — but the work took him to Gaul, and he is said to have followed Crispus to Trier in 317, when the young man was made Caesar.

Some manuscripts of the Institutes open several of its books with addresses to Constantine, praising him as the first Roman prince to repudiate error and honour the one true God. Other manuscripts lack them, but the editors judged them true to the style and spirit of Lactantius, and they show the work reaching for a new reader: no longer a hostile magistrate but a ruler who might be won to a deeper faith. He also wrote On the Anger of God, against philosophers who held that God is moved by nothing men do, and On the Deaths of the Persecutors, on the fates of the emperors who had attacked the church — written by a man who had known both Diocletian’s court and Constantine’s, and still a valuable witness to its events, including Constantine’s vision of the Chi Rho.

How his life ended, we do not know. Fletcher says he is believed to have died at Trier around 325, but in truth the time and circumstances of his death are unknown.

The Christian Cicero

His reputation had a strange afterlife. For reasons that are not clear, he came to be thought somewhat suspect, and the sixth-century Gelasian Decree counted his works among those not to be read. A thousand years later the humanists of the Renaissance fell in love with his Latin and named him Cicero Christianus, the Christian Cicero. An edition of his works printed at the Abbey of Subiaco in 1465 was the first book printed in Italy to carry a date.

The book on this page is The Divine Institutes in William Fletcher’s translation, published in 1886 in the Ante-Nicene Fathers. It is worth reading for more than its style. It is a picture of the church at the hinge of its history, written by a man who saw the church at Nicomedia overthrown and lived to tutor an emperor’s son, and who never stopped trying to persuade the educated, sceptical reader that wisdom and worship belong together. Its pages on justice, mercy and freedom of conscience still speak, and near its close he gave his readers a sentence any of them could carry:

We can take nothing with us, except a well and innocently spent life.

— Lactantius, The Divine Institutes, Book VII

He began his life teaching young men to speak well. He ended it trying to teach them to live well, which, he said, belongs to everyone.

faq.q: Who was Lactantius?
faq.a: Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius was an early Christian writer and teacher of Latin rhetoric who lived from about 250 to about 325. He is best known for The Divine Institutes, a reasoned defence of Christianity written for educated pagans, and Renaissance humanists called him the Christian Cicero for the elegance of his Latin.

faq.q: Where was Lactantius born?
faq.a: He was probably born in Roman North Africa into a family that was not Christian, and Wikipedia describes him as of Berber origin. The exact place is unknown; an inscription at Cirta in Numidia naming a L. Caecilius Firmianus suggests it may have been his home, though some older scholars argued for Italy.

faq.q: Who taught Lactantius?
faq.a: According to Jerome, he was a pupil of Arnobius, who taught rhetoric at Sicca Veneria in North Africa. Lactantius taught rhetoric in Africa himself, and his fame came to outstrip his master’s.

faq.q: Why did Lactantius go to Nicomedia?
faq.a: The emperor Diocletian invited him to become an official professor of Latin rhetoric at Nicomedia, the imperial capital in Bithynia. There he moved in the imperial circle and first met the future emperor Constantine, though as a Latin teacher in a Greek-speaking city he found few pupils and fell into poverty.

faq.q: When did Lactantius become a Christian?
faq.a: No source records when or how he converted. It was evidently before or during the Great Persecution that began in 303, and his editor stressed that he was no fair-weather Christian but confessed the faith while Christians were being persecuted.

faq.q: What happened to Lactantius in the Great Persecution?
faq.a: His public career at Nicomedia ended when Diocletian turned against the Christians in 303; Wikipedia says he resigned his post before the first edict was published. He saw the church in the city overthrown, lived afterwards in poverty, and supported himself by writing.

faq.q: What is The Divine Institutes about?
faq.a: Written between about 303 and 311, The Divine Institutes is a defence of Christianity in seven books, addressed to educated readers who did not yet believe. It exposes the false worship of the gods and the limits of the philosophers, argues that true wisdom and true religion are one, and teaches on justice, true worship and the happy life, ending with the last things. This page presents William Fletcher’s 1886 translation from the Ante-Nicene Fathers.

faq.q: What did Lactantius teach about freedom of religion?
faq.a: In the fifth book of The Divine Institutes he argued that worship cannot be forced, since nothing is so much a matter of free will as religion. Religion, he wrote, is to be defended not by putting to death but by dying, not by cruelty but by patient endurance.

faq.q: Which views of Lactantius did later Christians not follow?
faq.a: He held a millenarian view of the end, expecting a thousand-year reign of the righteous on earth and reckoning the end no more than two hundred years away, and he ridiculed the idea of a round earth with people on the far side. Later Christian thought did not follow him on these points, and Jerome, while praising his eloquence, wished he had been as ready to teach Christian doctrine as to pull down pagan ideas.

faq.q: How did Lactantius end his life?
faq.a: Constantine became his patron and appointed him, in old age, as Latin tutor to his son Crispus, and he followed Crispus to Trier in Gaul. The time and circumstances of his death are unknown; he is traditionally believed to have died at Trier around 325.

fields.name: Minucius Felix
fields.bio: Minucius Felix (fl. c. 200) was a Roman advocate and convert who wrote the Octavius, one of the first Christian books in Latin. Set on the beach at Ostia, it shows his friend Octavius answering a pagan’s charges against the Christians, and winning him to the faith.
fields.bio_html:
Some writers leave a life behind them; Minucius Felix left a single day. Nearly all we know of him comes from one short book about someone else: his friend Octavius, who had died by the time it was written. Minucius sat down to remember him, and what he remembered was a walk by the sea, a quarrel among friends, and a long argument that ended with all three of them going home glad. Out of that memory came the Octavius, one of the earliest and most graceful Christian books in Latin.

A lawyer of Rome

Jerome, writing in the late fourth century, calls him a notable advocate at Rome; Lactantius, earlier, had said more modestly that he was not unknown among the advocates of the city. The word both use is causidicus, literally a case-speaker: a courtroom pleader, not a learned jurist. The Octavius fits this. Minucius mentions in passing that the holidays of the courts at vintage-time had freed him from his cares, and the whole dialogue is shaped like a trial, with charges, a defence, and Minucius in the judge’s seat.

He was a convert, one who in his own words “emerged from the abyss of darkness into the light of wisdom and truth,” and Caecilius reminds him that he had known both kinds of life and chosen one. Jerome knew of a second treatise under his name, now lost, which Wallis, his translator, thought probably wrongly ascribed. He is often thought to have had African roots, because the Latin Christian writing of his age was largely North African and because his pagan friend speaks of “our Cirtensian,” a man of Cirta in Numidia, as one of his own. It is a guess and no more. We do not know when he was born or when he died.

A walk by the sea at Ostia

The book opens in grief and turns at once to delight. Octavius had come to Rome on business and to visit, leaving at home his wife and his small children, whose half-uttered words Minucius calls “a language all the sweeter for the very imperfection of the faltering tongue.” After a day or two of catching up, in the mild weather of early autumn, they went down to Ostia, Rome’s port at the mouth of the Tiber, so that Minucius could take the sea-bathing. With them came Caecilius Natalis, Minucius’s constant companion, still a pagan.

Minucius remembers Octavius as the other half of himself:

You would think that one mind had been shared between us two.

— Minucius Felix, The Octavius, ch. 1

As they walked toward the sea, Caecilius passed an image of Serapis, an Egyptian god, raised his hand to his mouth and kissed it, as common people did. Octavius rebuked not Caecilius but Minucius, for letting so close a friend give himself up to carved stones in broad daylight. They walked on along the shore, wetting their feet in the waves, and on the way back watched some boys skimming shells across the water, each wanting his to go furthest and leap most often. Everyone laughed except Caecilius, who stood apart, stung by the remark about Serapis, and asked for a proper debate. They sat down on the stone breakwater that ran out into the sea, with Minucius between them as arbiter, and Caecilius began.

The case against the Christians

Caecilius argues well. Nothing in human affairs is certain, he says, so it is wiser to keep the religion of one’s ancestors, which made Rome great, than to presume to know the mind of heaven. Then he turns on the Christians: an unlettered crowd of the lowest sort, meeting at night, “silent in public, but garrulous in corners,” without temples, altars or images, worshipping a God they cannot show. He repeats the common rumours: that they adore an ass’s head; that a novice is made to stab an infant hidden under meal, and the company drinks its blood; that at their feasts a dog tied to the lamp is made to knock it over so that in the darkness they may commit incest. He mocks their hope of resurrection and asks where their God is when they are poor and tortured.

What Octavius answered

Octavius answers point by point, with a friend’s patience. The poor and unschooled can reason as well as anyone, for wisdom is not given to wealth. The order of the heavens declares one Maker. The best philosophers had reached toward the same truth, so that one might think “either that Christians are now philosophers, or that philosophers were then already Christians.”

The most striking pages are a confession. We were once the same as you, Octavius says; we believed these stories too, and when Christians were accused we would not even hear them, but pressed them under torture to deny the name, never to confess the crimes they were charged with. Against the charge of infant murder he answers that Christians may not even watch a killing, and will not eat the blood of animals. Against incest he sets their marriages to one wife, their sober meals, and their love for one another:

Thus we love one another, to your regret, with a mutual love, because we do not know how to hate.

— Octavius, in Minucius Felix, The Octavius, ch. 31

Why no temples? Because man himself is the image of God, and the whole world cannot contain him. Why so poor? Poverty is their glory, and suffering is not punishment but warfare. And the dead will rise as the trees bud again after winter:

We must wait also for the spring-time of the body.

— Octavius, in Minucius Felix, The Octavius, ch. 34

The Octavius gives a glimpse of how these Christians prayed. Octavius sees the sign of the cross “when a man adores God with a pure mind, with hands outstretched.” He speaks, too, of evil spirits driven from the afflicted “by the torments of our words and by the fires of our prayers,” calling on the only true God.

Their worship, Octavius insists, was a life before it was a rite. Among them, he says, “he who cultivates innocence supplicates God,” and he who snatches a man from danger offers the most acceptable sacrifice. And if they asked God for anything, it was not riches: “we desire rather innocency, we rather entreat for patience.”

When Octavius finished, they sat in silence. Then Caecilius broke out that he did not need a verdict: Octavius had conquered him, and he had conquered his own error. He yielded to God, keeping a few questions for tomorrow, since the sun was setting. “After these things we departed, glad and cheerful,” he writes: Caecilius because he had believed, Octavius because he had won, and Minucius because of both.

Which came first

The book’s date is still an open question. Many passages closely resemble Tertullian’s Apology, written about 198, and one writer must have borrowed from the other. If Minucius borrowed, he wrote in the early third century; if Tertullian did, the Octavius may date from about 166, under Marcus Aurelius. Scholars have argued both ways for generations, and the question is not settled. What is certain is that Cyprian of Carthage later borrowed from it. The book was almost lost: a single manuscript survives, in Paris, copied as the eighth book of Arnobius; only in 1560 did Franciscus Balduinus recognise its true author.

Why read the Octavius

The Octavius is not a book of theology. It never names Jesus Christ, is silent on the sacraments, and draws more on Cicero than on Scripture, because it was written for educated pagans who had heard only slanders. It sets out to show them, courteously and in Latin a later historian likened to the golden age of Roman prose, that Christians were neither monsters nor fools. It also shows ordinary Christians around the year 200 as they saw themselves: without temples, praying with open hands, refusing the games and the sacrificial meat, burying rather than burning their dead, and facing the courts without shame. Octavius sums it up in one plain line: “we do not speak great things, but we live them.”

And it is a book about friendship. Minucius did not write a treatise; he wrote down how his dearest friend once won another friend to the faith, gently, on a beach, and how they all went home rejoicing. Of his own life, that is what he chose to leave us.

faq.q: Who was Minucius Felix?
faq.a: Marcus Minucius Felix was a Christian advocate at Rome, probably writing around the year 200, and one of the earliest Christian authors in Latin. He is known for a single surviving book, the Octavius, a dialogue in which he acts as judge between a pagan and a Christian friend.

faq.q: What do we know about his life?
faq.a: Very little. Jerome calls him a notable advocate at Rome, and Lactantius says he was not unknown among the city’s pleaders; nearly everything else comes from hints in the Octavius itself, which shows him to be a convert who had once shared his pagan friends’ beliefs. His dates of birth and death are unknown.

faq.q: Was Minucius Felix from Africa?
faq.a: Possibly, but it is not known. Scholars have often guessed at African roots because early Latin Christian writing was largely North African and because the pagan Caecilius speaks of “our Cirtensian,” a man of Cirta in Numidia, as one of his own.

faq.q: Who was Octavius?
faq.a: Octavius Januarius was Minucius’s closest friend, a Christian with a wife and small children who lived away from Rome, and who had died by the time the book was written. Minucius says one mind seemed to have been shared between the two of them.

faq.q: Where and how does the Octavius take place?
faq.a: On an autumn holiday from the law courts, Minucius, Octavius and the pagan Caecilius Natalis walk along the shore at Ostia, Rome’s port. After Octavius rebukes Minucius for letting Caecilius kiss an image of Serapis, and while boys skim shells across the waves, Caecilius asks for a debate, and they sit on a breakwater with Minucius as arbiter.

faq.q: What charges against Christians does Caecilius repeat?
faq.a: He calls them an unlettered, secretive crowd without temples or altars, and repeats the rumours of the day: that they worshipped an ass’s head, killed and ate an infant at their initiations, and committed incest at their night-time feasts. He also mocks their hope of resurrection and asks where their God is when they are poor and tortured.

faq.q: How does Octavius answer those charges?
faq.a: He argues that the order of the world declares one God, that the best philosophers agreed, and that the pagan gods were once men. He admits that he too once believed the slanders, and answers that Christians will not even watch a killing, keep to one marriage, eat sober meals, and love one another because they do not know how to hate.

faq.q: What does the Octavius show about Christian worship around 200?
faq.a: It describes Christians without temples or images, who held that man himself is God’s image, prayed with hands outstretched, drove out evil spirits by prayer, and counted a just and innocent life as their true sacrifice. They kept away from the games and sacrificial food, buried rather than burned their dead, and faced trial without shame.

faq.q: Did Minucius Felix write before or after Tertullian’s Apology?
faq.a: No one knows for certain. Many passages closely match Tertullian’s Apology of about 198, so one borrowed from the other: if Minucius borrowed, he wrote in the early third century, and if Tertullian did, the Octavius may date from around 166. The question is still debated.

faq.q: Why read the Octavius today?
faq.a: It is a short, courteous and beautifully written defence of the faith, aimed at educated pagans, that ends with the doubter won over and all three friends going home glad. It also gives a rare picture of how ordinary Christians around the year 200 lived, prayed and were seen by their neighbours.

fields.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
fields.bio: Polycarp of Smyrna (c. 69–c. 155) was bishop of Smyrna, remembered by tradition as a hearer of the apostle John. His Epistle to the Philippians survives, and his church’s letter tells how, burned at the stake, he said, “Eighty and six years have I served Him.”
fields.bio_html:
The early church left us mostly argument — letters against error, careful explanations of the faith. Polycarp of Smyrna left a little of that too. But what the church has treasured about him for almost nineteen centuries is not an argument. It is an old man, arrested at supper-time, who had food set out for the men who came to take him, asked for an hour to pray, and prayed for two. It is the same old man, hours later, in a roaring stadium, refusing to curse the Lord he had served for eighty-six years.

A hearer of the apostles

Almost nothing is known of Polycarp’s early life, and it is better to say so than to fill the gap. The traditional dates, about 69 to about 155, are worked backward from his own words at his trial. What we have instead is a memory. Irenaeus, later bishop of Lyons in Gaul, heard Polycarp as a boy and never forgot him:

I could describe the very place in which the blessed Polycarp sat and taught; his going out and coming in; the whole tenor of his life; his personal appearance; how he would speak of the conversations he had held with John and with others who had seen the Lord.

— Irenaeus, remembering his teacher

That John, Irenaeus understood, was the apostle. Tertullian says the same, and Jerome adds that John himself ordained Polycarp bishop of Smyrna, a busy port on the Aegean coast of what is now western Turkey. It is an early tradition, and a cherished one, but it rests largely on Irenaeus’s boyhood memory set down many years later, and it is fair to hold it in that light. The old scholar James Ussher even wondered whether Polycarp was the “angel” — the messenger or leader — of the church in Smyrna, to whom the risen Christ says in Revelation, “Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.” That is only a guess. Anyone who reads the end of his story will see why someone wanted to make it.

A friend in chains

Polycarp first steps clearly into history receiving a prisoner. Early in the second century Ignatius, bishop of Antioch in Syria, was being taken under guard toward Rome to die, and his guards stopped at Smyrna. Polycarp welcomed him; a later account says the two had once been fellow disciples of John. Ignatius, moving on, wrote a letter to Polycarp himself, counselling him as a father might.

Polycarp kept faith with his friend. When the church at Philippi asked for Ignatius’s letters, he gathered all he had and sent them, asking in return for any certain news of what had become of him. It is partly because of that small act of care that those letters reach us at all.

A letter to Philippi

That reply, the Epistle to the Philippians, is the only writing of Polycarp’s that survives. It is short, plain and pastoral, woven almost entirely out of Scripture. He writes, he says, only because they asked, and neither he nor anyone like him can come up to the wisdom of “the blessed and glorified Paul.” He even admits they know the Scriptures better than he does. What he offers is the faith as it was handed down: Christ, who suffered for our sins and whom God raised from the dead; salvation “by grace … not of works”; and a life of love, honesty and mercy that answers to it.

At its heart is a sorrow. Valens, once a presbyter, or elder, at Philippi, had fallen into covetousness and disgraced his office. Polycarp does not soften the sin, but he prays that the Lord would grant Valens and his wife true repentance, and tells the church to call them back “as suffering and straying members.” Firm, and with the door left open.

With false teaching he was sterner. Some said Christ had only seemed to have a body. Whoever does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, Polycarp writes, echoing John, is antichrist, and whoever twists the Lord’s words to deny the resurrection and judgment is “the first-born of Satan” — a phrase Irenaeus says he once used to the face of the teacher Marcion. His remedy was simple: “let us return to the word which has been handed down to us from the beginning.” And with it, endurance:

Let us then be imitators of His patience; and if we suffer for His name’s sake, let us glorify Him.

— Polycarp, Epistle to the Philippians

The letter asks the Philippians to widen their prayers as far as they will go: “Pray for all the saints. Pray also for kings, and potentates, and princes, and for those that persecute and hate you, and for the enemies of the cross.” He wrote that under an empire that could kill Christians, and he would one day pray that way himself.

A visit to Rome

Late in life, when Anicetus was bishop of Rome, Polycarp travelled west to meet him. Their churches kept Easter differently: Polycarp, following the custom of Asia — and, Eusebius records, what he had kept with John — on the fourteenth of the Jewish month of Nisan, the day of Passover, whatever the weekday; Rome always on a Sunday. Irenaeus says they quickly agreed on other matters, but neither could persuade the other on this. So they disagreed and stayed in full communion, and Anicetus invited Polycarp to celebrate the Lord’s Supper in his own church, a mark of great honour.

Eighty and six years

His death is told by the church of Smyrna itself, in a letter to the church at Philomelium and through it to the whole church — one of the earliest accounts of a Christian martyrdom outside the New Testament. Persecution had broken out; after a young man named Germanicus faced the beasts bravely, the crowd shouted, “Away with the Atheists; let Polycarp be sought out!” — atheists, because Christians refused the gods. The letter honestly records a man named Quintus who volunteered for martyrdom and then lost his nerve and sacrificed, and draws the lesson: the gospel does not teach us to hand ourselves over.

Polycarp did not. At his people’s urging he withdrew to a farmhouse. Three days before his arrest, while praying, he saw his pillow as if on fire, and said to those with him, “I must be burnt alive.” He moved again, but a young servant of his household was tortured until he told where he was.

At the farmhouse, the letter says, he did “nothing else night and day than praying for all men, and for the Churches throughout the world, according to his usual custom.” The prayers of his last days were not a new crisis-devotion. They were what he had always done.

They came on a Friday evening, armed as if against a robber. He could have slipped away, but said, “The will of God be done,” and went down to meet them. Struck by his age, some wondered why so much effort had been spent to catch such a venerable man. He had food and drink set before them and asked only for an hour to pray.

He stood and prayed, the letter says, so full of the grace of God that he could not stop for two full hours, remembering everyone who had ever crossed his path, “both small and great, illustrious and obscure,” and the whole church throughout the world. Many of the men who had come to arrest him began to be sorry they had come.

On the road into the city, officials urged him to say “Lord Cæsar” and offer incense; when he would not, they pushed him from their carriage and he hurt his leg, and walked on as if nothing had happened. As he entered the stadium, the letter says, a voice came from heaven: “Be strong, and show thyself a man, O Polycarp!” No one saw the speaker, but the Christians there heard it.

The proconsul, the Roman governor, tried to spare him: think of your age; swear by the fortune of Cæsar; revile Christ, and I will let you go. Polycarp answered:

Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?

— Polycarp, before the proconsul

Whether those years were his whole life or the years since he came to faith, we cannot say; the traditional birth year of 69 assumes the first. Either way, the sentence is less about arithmetic than about a Master who had never dealt unjustly with him. Threatened with beasts, he told the governor to call them. Threatened with fire, he said:

Thou threatenest me with fire which burneth for an hour, and after a little is extinguished, but art ignorant of the fire of the coming judgment and of eternal punishment, reserved for the ungodly.

— Polycarp, in the stadium at Smyrna

The crowd roared that this was “the teacher of Asia, the father of the Christians,” and demanded he be burned. When they moved to nail him to the stake he asked to be left as he was: the One who gave him strength to bear the fire would hold him still. So they only bound him, and he looked up to heaven and prayed.

“I give Thee thanks,” he said to the Father, “that Thou hast counted me worthy of this day and this hour, that I should have a part in the number of Thy martyrs, in the cup of thy Christ.” It ends not in pleading but in praise: “I praise Thee for all things, I bless Thee, I glorify Thee.”

What followed, the Smyrnaean Christians say they saw. The fire arched around him like a ship’s sail filled with wind, and he glowed within it like bread baking or gold in a furnace, with a fragrance like incense. When it did not consume him, an executioner stabbed him, and from the wound, they write, came a dove and so much blood that it put out the fire. These are the church’s own words, offered as testimony. The version Eusebius quoted lacks some of these wonders, and our translation’s editors suspect “the dove” is a copyist’s slip. What no one has doubted is the courage at the centre of the story.

The birthday of his martyrdom

Fearing the Christians would worship him, the authorities had his body burned. The church’s reply is one of the clearest early statements of where devotion belongs: Christ, as the Son of God, they adore; the martyrs, as disciples of the Lord, they love. They gathered his bones, “more precious than the most exquisite jewels,” and resolved to meet each year on the anniversary of his death — one of the earliest witnesses to that custom. His day is still kept on 23 February.

The year is less certain. The letter names the proconsul Statius Quadratus, and from that many date the martyrdom to about 155 or 156; Eusebius placed it later, in the 160s. A date in the later 150s fits best with the memories of Ignatius and John, but it remains a reckoning, not a certainty.

Reading Polycarp today

Our book brings his two witnesses together in the 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers translation of Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson: Polycarp’s own Epistle to the Philippians and the Smyrnaean church’s Martyrdom of Polycarp. Both can be read in a sitting. The first lets us hear a pastor a generation or two after the apostles — humble, steeped in Scripture, gentle with the fallen and firm against error. The second shows that same pastor when everything was at stake, and finds him unchanged.

He did not seek martyrdom, and he did not flee it. He fed the men who arrested him and prayed for them. He kept faith with a friend in chains and a church in trouble, and kept communion with a brother he could not agree with. And at the end, offered his life for a single word against Christ, he looked back over eighty-six years and found no wrong his King had ever done him. It is a long faithfulness, quietly kept, and still worth following.

faq.q: Who was Polycarp of Smyrna?
faq.a: Polycarp was a second-century bishop of Smyrna, a port city on the Aegean coast of what is now western Turkey. He is counted among the Apostolic Fathers and is honoured as a saint and martyr by Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches alike.

faq.q: Did Polycarp really know the apostle John?
faq.a: That is the early tradition. Irenaeus, who heard Polycarp as a boy, remembered him speaking of his conversations with John and others who had seen the Lord, and Tertullian and Jerome say the same; Jerome adds that John ordained him. The tradition rests largely on Irenaeus’s boyhood memory, written down many years later.

faq.q: When was Polycarp born?
faq.a: No record of his birth survives. The traditional year of about 69 is worked backward from his words at his trial, “Eighty and six years have I served Him,” which may mean his age or the years since he came to faith.

faq.q: What was Polycarp’s connection with Ignatius of Antioch?
faq.a: When Ignatius was being taken under guard toward Rome to die, his guards stopped at Smyrna, where Polycarp welcomed him, and Ignatius later wrote a letter to Polycarp. Afterward Polycarp gathered Ignatius’s letters and sent them to the church at Philippi, which helped preserve them.

faq.q: What does Polycarp’s Epistle to the Philippians teach?
faq.a: It is a short pastoral letter, woven out of Scripture, that urges faith in Christ who suffered and rose, salvation by grace, and a life of love, honesty and mercy. It grieves over a fallen presbyter named Valens and asks the church to call him back, while warning firmly against those who denied that Christ came in the flesh.

faq.q: Why did Polycarp visit Anicetus in Rome?
faq.a: Late in life he travelled to Rome to talk with its bishop, Anicetus, about differences between the churches of Asia and Rome. They could not agree on the date of Easter, which Polycarp kept on the fourteenth of Nisan and Rome on a Sunday, but they stayed in full communion, and Anicetus let Polycarp celebrate the Lord’s Supper in his church.

faq.q: How was Polycarp arrested?
faq.a: During a persecution in Smyrna he withdrew to the countryside at his people’s urging, but a servant of his household was tortured into revealing where he was. When the searchers came he refused to escape, saying “The will of God be done,” had food set before them, and prayed for two hours.

faq.q: What did Polycarp say at his trial?
faq.a: When the proconsul urged him to revile Christ and go free, he answered, “Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He never did me any injury: how then can I blaspheme my King and my Saviour?” Threatened with fire, he replied that the governor’s fire burned only for an hour, while the fire of the coming judgment was eternal.

faq.q: How did Polycarp die, and when?
faq.a: He was bound to a stake and burned, and the Smyrnaean letter says the fire arched around him without consuming him, so that he was stabbed and his blood put out the flames. The letter dates it to the proconsulship of Statius Quadratus, usually reckoned about 155 or 156, though Eusebius placed it later and the year remains uncertain; his feast is kept on 23 February.

faq.q: What is The Epistle and Martyrdom of Polycarp?
faq.a: It brings together Polycarp’s only surviving writing, his Epistle to the Philippians, and the Martyrdom of Polycarp, the Smyrnaean church’s letter describing his arrest and death, in Roberts and Donaldson’s 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers translation. Both are short, and together they show a humble pastor’s teaching and the faith he kept to the end.

fields.name: Hermas
fields.bio: Hermas (fl. c. 140) was a Christian of Rome and a former slave who wrote The Shepherd, a book of visions, commandments and parables calling believers to repentance and an undivided heart. Little else is known of him, but his book was read as Scripture in many early churches.
fields.bio_html:
Most writers on these shelves left a life that can be told. Hermas left one book, The Shepherd, and the few things it lets slip about the man who wrote it down. He was a Christian of Rome and a former slave, married, with children who had grieved him, once rich and rich no longer. Yet for two or three centuries his book was among the most loved in the church, read aloud in congregations and copied into Bibles.

A former slave in Rome

The book opens abruptly, in the first person: “He who had brought me up, sold me to one Rhode in Rome.” That is all we know of his childhood. Years later he met Rhode again and came to love her as a sister. Once, helping her out of the Tiber, he thought how happy he would be with a wife so beautiful and good. That passing thought, he says, was all.

The rest comes in pieces, mostly through rebukes. His wife, he is told, “does not restrain her tongue”; his sons have blasphemed the Lord and betrayed their parents, and Hermas, who loved them, failed to correct them. He had been in business, and not honestly. When the Shepherd tells him to love the truth, he weeps that “I never spake a true word in my life”. He had lost his money too. “When you were rich, you were useless,” he is told; “but now you are useful and fit for life.” His visions come to him out in the country, and many readers have pictured him working land outside the city, though the book never quite says so.

Which Hermas?

Who this man was has been argued over since antiquity, and the claims do not fit together. The most widespread ancient view tied him to the apostles. In Romans 16:14 Paul greets a Christian in Rome named Hermas. Origen thought this was our author, and Eusebius and Jerome repeated the idea. If the Clement named in the book is Clement of Rome, its story is set around the year 90.

The Muratorian fragment, an early list of the church’s books usually dated around 170, says otherwise: “Hermas wrote The Shepherd very recently, in our times, in the city of Rome, while bishop Pius, his brother, was occupying the chair of the church of the city of Rome.” Pius led the Roman church around 140 to 155. On this account Hermas was not Paul’s friend but a bishop’s brother, two generations later.

Both cannot be true. Some modern critics have thought Hermas a character invented for the story. The editor of our edition conjectured that Hermas and his brother were grandchildren of the Hermas Paul greeted. The book was written in Rome, in Greek, most likely in the first half of the second century, by a man who calls himself Hermas.

The old woman who grew young

In the first vision Rhode appears from the opened heavens to accuse him. Then an old woman in a splendid robe sits before him on a great white chair. God is angry, she says, less for that thought than for his neglected household; he must keep warning his sons. A year later she gives him a little book to copy. He copies it letter by letter without understanding it, and its meaning comes only after fifteen days of fasting and prayer. A young man in a dream tells him who she is. She is not the Sibyl, the prophetess of Roman legend, as Hermas had guessed: “It is the Church.” She is old because she was created first of all.

Before his third vision Hermas went alone to a quiet place in the country and knelt to confess his sins, as he had done before. The old woman came and stood behind him, listening as he prayed. Then she touched him and told him to stop praying always for his sins, and to pray for righteousness, that he might have a portion of it at once in his house.

She then shows him a great tower rising on the waters, built of shining square stones that fit so closely the joins cannot be seen. The tower is the Church. Other stones are cracked, too short, or round, and each stands for a kind of believer: the quarrelsome, the half-hearted, the rich whose wealth must be cut away before they can be squared. Some are set aside but not far off, because they may yet be used if they repent while the tower is still building.

Across the visions the woman changes. First she is very old and must sit. Then her face is youthful though her hair is white. Then she is young and joyful, and at last she meets him dressed as a bride. The change, Hermas learns, was in him and his fellow believers. Their spirits had grown old through doubt and worldly cares, and as they repented they were made young. “Those, therefore, who repent completely and with the whole heart,” he is told, “will become young and firmly established.”

The shepherd at the door

The fifth vision gives the book its name. Hermas has been praying at home when a man of glorious appearance comes in, dressed as a shepherd in a white goatskin, with a staff in his hand. He has been sent to live with Hermas for the rest of his days. He is the angel of repentance, and he gives Hermas twelve commandments and ten similitudes, or parables, to write down.

The commandments are plain moral teaching, and their theme is the undivided heart. Believe in one God. Be simple and guileless, like a child. Speak evil of no one. Give to the needy without fretting over who deserves it. Tell the truth. The Shepherd keeps warning against the man he calls “double-souled,” who half trusts and half doubts and has the Lord on his lips but not in his heart. When Hermas protests that the commandments are too hard, the Shepherd answers that they are hard only to a divided heart:

Put, therefore, ye who are empty and fickle in your faith, the Lord in your heart, and ye will know that there is nothing easier or sweeter, or more manageable, than these commandments.

— Hermas, The Shepherd, Commandment Twelfth

The ninth commandment brings this to prayer. Hermas is not to talk himself out of asking because he has sinned so much, but to ask with all his heart and without doubting, and to keep asking when the answer is slow.

For He is not like men, who remember evils done against them; but He Himself remembers not evils, and has compassion on His own creature.

— Hermas, The Shepherd, Commandment Ninth

Walking alone on the Campanian road, Hermas prayed that God would complete what he had begun to show him and give repentance to all who were going astray. A huge beast rose out of the dust ahead of him, and he wept and called on the Lord to rescue him. Then, he writes, he remembered the word he had heard, “Doubt not, O Hermas,” and went on past it in faith.

A book the early church read

The book travelled far, into Latin, Coptic, Ethiopic and other tongues. Our translator calls it perhaps the most popular book in the church of the second, third and fourth centuries. He records that Irenaeus quoted it as Scripture, Clement of Alexandria said it spoke divinely, and Origen thought it divinely inspired. Its Greek text was copied at the end of the great manuscript Bible known as Codex Sinaiticus. Others held back. The Muratorian fragment allowed private reading but not public reading in church, since the book came after the apostles, and Tertullian scorned it as apocryphal. In the end the church did not receive it into the New Testament.

Two teachings were debated then and still are. The first is repentance after baptism. The Shepherd agrees with teachers who said baptism is the only repentance, then announces that by God’s mercy a believer who falls has “opportunity to repent but once.” Some heard a stern limit, and the rigorist Novatian is said to have drawn on it; others heard a door opened where it had seemed shut. The second is its way of speaking about Christ. One parable describes the pre-existent Holy Spirit dwelling in a chosen flesh that served it faithfully, which some read as Jesus being adopted as Son. J. N. D. Kelly called the book’s Christology “an amalgam of binitarianism and adoptionism,” while Bogdan Bucur reads the passage differently. Yet the same book calls the Son of God “older than all His creatures”. A reader need not settle these questions to profit from it.

Reading the Shepherd today

We publish The Shepherd of Hermas in F. Crombie’s translation from the Ante-Nicene Fathers of 1885, with all five Visions, twelve Commandments and ten Similitudes. Its translator compared its old popularity to that of Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress. It is a long, homely allegory, sometimes repetitive and sometimes very moving, in which ordinary Roman Christians are called to wholehearted repentance.

Its author stays in shadow. What we can see is the man the book shows: a sinner who did not hide his sins, a father who learned late to speak to his children, a doubter told again and again not to doubt. The aged woman grew young before his eyes because he and those like him turned back to God with their whole hearts. A tired and divided heart can be made young again, and the tower is still being built.

faq.q: Who was Hermas?
faq.a: Hermas was a Christian of Rome, probably of the early second century, who wrote The Shepherd, one of the most widely read Christian books of the second, third and fourth centuries. Almost everything known about him comes from what the book says of itself.

faq.q: What does The Shepherd tell us about Hermas’s life?
faq.a: It says he was raised in another’s household and sold as a slave to a woman named Rhode in Rome. He was married, his wife is rebuked for her tongue, and his sons had blasphemed the Lord and betrayed their parents; he confesses that he had been dishonest in business and is told that he had once been rich but was now useful because his riches were gone.

faq.q: Was Hermas the Hermas greeted by Paul in Romans 16:14?
faq.a: Origen thought so, and Eusebius and Jerome repeated the idea, which would place the book in the first century. Only a minority have followed it since, and it conflicts with the other ancient claim that Hermas was the brother of a second-century bishop of Rome.

faq.q: Was Hermas the brother of Pope Pius I?
faq.a: The Muratorian fragment, an early list of the church’s books usually dated around 170, says Hermas wrote The Shepherd “very recently, in our times” while his brother Pius was bishop of Rome, around 140 to 155. This cannot be reconciled with the view that he was Paul’s friend, and some modern critics think Hermas is a character invented for the story.

faq.q: When was The Shepherd of Hermas written?
faq.a: The date is uncertain. The mention of a Clement, if he is Clement of Rome, would set the story around the year 90, while the Muratorian fragment points to the time of Pius, about 140 to 155; most place the book in Rome in the first half of the second century.

faq.q: Who is the old woman in Hermas’s visions?
faq.a: She is the Church, old because she was created first of all. Over the visions she grows younger, from a weak old woman in a chair to a joyful young woman and at last a bride, and Hermas is told the change reflects believers whose weary spirits are renewed as they repent with the whole heart.

faq.q: What is the tower in The Shepherd of Hermas?
faq.a: The tower, built on the waters out of square stones, is the Church, and the stones are believers. Well-fitted stones are those who lived faithfully and at peace, while cracked, short or round stones stand for the quarrelsome, the half-hearted and the rich, some of whom may still be used if they repent while the tower is building.

faq.q: What is in The Shepherd of Hermas, and who is the Shepherd?
faq.a: The book has five Visions, twelve Commandments and ten Similitudes, or parables, published here in F. Crombie’s 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers translation. The Shepherd is the angel of repentance, sent to live with Hermas, and his commandments call for a simple, undivided heart, warning against the double-souled believer who half trusts and half doubts.

faq.q: What does Hermas teach about prayer?
faq.a: The ninth commandment tells Hermas not to hold back from asking God because he has sinned much, but to ask with all his heart and without doubting, since God does not remember evils as men do. If the answer is slow he is to keep asking rather than waver.

faq.q: Why is The Shepherd of Hermas not in the Bible?
faq.a: Some early writers treated it as Scripture and it was copied into Codex Sinaiticus, but the Muratorian fragment allowed only private reading because it came after the apostles, and Tertullian rejected it as apocryphal. The church did not receive it into the New Testament, and its teaching that a believer may repent only once after baptism and its way of speaking about Christ have long been debated.

fields.name: Theophilus of Antioch
fields.bio: Theophilus of Antioch (died c. 183) was a second-century bishop of Antioch in Syria, a pagan who came to faith by reading the Hebrew prophets. His To Autolycus, three books to a pagan friend, is the earliest surviving Christian work to use the word trias, Trinity, of God, his Word and his Wisdom.
fields.bio_html:
Almost everything we know about Theophilus of Antioch comes from one long answer to one man: Autolycus, a learned pagan friend who had mocked him for being a Christian and challenged him to produce his God. Theophilus answered in three short books, and they are all that survive of him. They never mention even the office he held. But they give us the voice of a second-century pastor explaining, patiently and sometimes sharply, why he had stopped believing in the old gods and what he had found instead.

A pagan who read the prophets

He was born a pagan. His birth year is unknown; one nineteenth-century editor guessed around 115, and said it was a guess. Describing the rivers of Eden, Theophilus remarks that the Tigris and Euphrates “border on our own regions,” a hint, many think, that he was born not far from them. Beyond that, the record of his early life is empty.

What he did leave, in one paragraph of his first book, is the story of how he came to faith. Autolycus did not believe that the dead are raised. Neither, Theophilus admits, had he: “I myself also used to disbelieve that this would take place, but now, having taken these things into consideration, I believe.” What changed him was reading: “I met with the sacred Scriptures of the holy prophets,” he says, and found in them things foretold that had come to pass as spoken. It is a quiet conversion: a thoughtful man reading the Bible and finding that it would not let him go. He offers Autolycus the same road.

A bishop in the city of the name

He became bishop of Antioch in Syria, the great city where, as the book of Acts records, the disciples were first called Christians. Eusebius, the fourth-century church historian, counts him the sixth bishop there after the apostles, in a line running back through Ignatius; others make him the seventh. He took office around 168 or 169, in the eighth year of the emperor Marcus Aurelius.

Eusebius remembered him as one of the faithful shepherds of that generation who laboured to drive the heretics away from the flock of Christ, and he singled out Theophilus’s book against Marcion, who rejected the Old Testament and its God, as “of no mean character.” He and Jerome knew of other works too — against the teacher Hermogenes, for the instruction of new believers, and commentaries that Jerome doubted were his. All are lost.

“Show me yourself”

Autolycus had boasted of his gods of wood and stone and used the word Christian as a sneer. Theophilus takes the name gladly — “I, for my part, avow that I am a Christian” — and then turns the challenge back on the man who made it.

But if you say, “Show me thy God,” I would reply, “Show me yourself, and I will show you my God.”

— Theophilus of Antioch, To Autolycus, Book I

His point is that God is seen not with the eyes of the body but with the eyes of the soul, and those eyes can be clouded. Sin, he says, is like rust on a mirror: as long as it is there, no face can be seen in it. The question is not only whether God exists, but whether the one asking is willing to be made clean, and Theophilus lists the vices of the pagan city one by one and asks his friend to show that he is free of them.

Yet the book is not only rebuke. When Theophilus tries to describe God, his language rises into worship — “For in glory He is incomprehensible, in greatness unfathomable, in height inconceivable” — and he finds God known through the seasons, the stars, and the rain that falls in its time. And for the man whose eyes are clouded there is a remedy.

Entrust yourself to the Physician, and He will couch the eyes of your soul and of your heart. Who is the Physician? God, who heals and makes alive through His word and wisdom.

— Theophilus of Antioch, To Autolycus, Book I

To couch an eye was the old surgical word for removing a cataract. The healing ends in resurrection: “God will raise thy flesh immortal with thy soul,” and then the one who believes shall see the Immortal. When Autolycus scoffs, Theophilus points to seasons that die and return, and the seed of wheat that rots and rises as a stalk. Even the mocked name is a kind of promise: “we are called Christians on this account, because we are anointed with the oil of God.”

God, his Word, and his Wisdom

The second book followed another conversation, after which the friends parted “with much mutual friendliness.” Theophilus, “not educated to the art of speaking,” sets the poets’ accounts of the beginning beside the prophets’, and most of the book becomes a commentary on the opening chapters of Genesis.

The prophets, he says, taught that God made all things out of nothing.
