God had his Word within him, and when he willed to create, he brought the Word forth with his Wisdom and made all things through him. It was this Word, “who is also His Son,” who walked in the garden and spoke with Adam, and here Theophilus quotes the opening of John’s Gospel by name. He seems to call the Holy Spirit God’s Wisdom, as his contemporary Irenaeus did, though his terms move freely.

In his commentary on the six days of creation he writes the sentence for which he is best remembered. The sun, always full, is a picture of God; the waning and returning moon, of man and the resurrection. And the days before the sun and moon were made carry a meaning of their own: “In like manner also the three days which were before the luminaries, are types of the Trinity, of God, and His Word, and His wisdom.” This is the earliest surviving Christian use for God of the Greek word trias, a group of three, which Dods translates Trinity. He does not seem to be coining it, so it was probably already in use among Christians.

The commentary is full of such pictures, some lovely, some strained. As the sea has islands with good harbours, he says, so God has given the storm-tossed world “holy churches,” where those who wish to be saved may find refuge, while heresies are barren rocks where ships are wrecked. On Adam he is tender. The tree of knowledge was good, he says; the death was in the disobedience. Adam was still “an infant in age,” and God put him out of Paradise so that he would not remain in sin for ever. Man was made “neither mortal nor immortal,” but capable of both, and free.

It is fair to say that later Christians did not follow him in every step. The church came to state more carefully that the Son is eternally begotten rather than brought forth at the moment of creation, and to name the three as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. And in this book Theophilus never uses the name Jesus, nor does he go on to speak of the incarnation or of Christ’s atoning death. He treats the Sibylline oracles, verses of uncertain origin, as true prophecy, and some of his derivations of words are fanciful. He wrote before many questions had been settled, to a man who did not yet believe in one God at all.

Older than Homer

The third book answers the slanders Autolycus had half believed: that Christians held their wives in common, committed incest and ate human flesh, and that their faith was a recent novelty. He answers by setting out what Christians are taught: the Ten Commandments, care for the stranger, repentance, justice for the widow and the fatherless, chastity of heart and love of enemies. Christians, he adds, may not even watch the gladiators, lest they become partakers in murder.

But far be it from Christians to conceive any such deeds; for with them temperance dwells, self-restraint is practiced, monogamy is observed, chastity is guarded, iniquity exterminated, sin extirpated, righteousness exercised, law administered, worship performed, God acknowledged: truth governs, grace guards, peace screens them; the holy word guides, wisdom teaches, life directs, God reigns.

— Theophilus of Antioch, To Autolycus, Book III

To the charge of novelty he answers with history. Drawing on Moses, Josephus, the Egyptian and Chaldean historians and the Roman lists, he reckons the years from Adam to the death of the emperor Marcus Aurelius, 5,698 in all, to show that Moses and the prophets are older than all the Greek poets and lawgivers. He is honest about his sums: if he has erred by fifty, a hundred or even two hundred years, at least it is not by thousands, as the Greek authors had.

Before he begins his long reckoning of the ages, Theophilus stops to pray, and writes the prayer into the book: “And I pray for favour from the only God, that I may accurately speak the whole truth according to His will, that you and every one who reads this work may be guided by His truth and favour.” The bishop who prays over his tables of dates is praying, in the end, for his friend.

He can be scornful of Greek learning, sometimes misquoting the authors he dismisses, and his sums belong to his century. But he believed the God of the prophets had acted in real history, and took the trouble to show it.

Theophilus would not worship the emperor, but he would not stop praying for him. “Wherefore I will rather honour the king [than your gods], not, indeed, worshipping him, but praying for him,” he told Autolycus, and he counselled the same: “honour the king, be subject to him, and pray for him with loyal mind; for if you do this, you do the will of God.” He wrote it while, as he says, those who worshipped God were still being persecuted.

A letter that outlived the writer

Theophilus died around 183; the old sources give 181 or 188, and modern accounts place his death probably between 183 and 185. No account of his death has come down, and Maximus followed him as bishop. Only the books to Autolycus survived, quoted in the West by Lactantius and honoured centuries later by Archbishop James Ussher, who paid him tribute as a founder of Christian biblical chronology.

To Autolycus repays a reader who comes to it as it was written: not as a treatise, but as one man’s long answer to a friend, severe with idols and gentle with the idolater. He quotes the Old Testament on almost every page, because the prophets had brought him to believe, and he hoped they would do the same for Autolycus. We do not know whether they did. The book ends with an invitation rather than a victory: study these things carefully, he tells his friend, “that you may have a compendium and pledge of the truth.” It is an invitation still open to anyone who will read.

faq.q: Who was Theophilus of Antioch?
faq.a: Theophilus was a second-century bishop of Antioch in Syria, the city where the disciples were first called Christians. He is known today for one surviving work, To Autolycus, a defence of the Christian faith written to a learned pagan friend around 180.

faq.q: How did Theophilus become a Christian?
faq.a: He was raised a pagan and, by his own account, once disbelieved in the resurrection. He came to faith by reading “the sacred Scriptures of the holy prophets,” in which he found things foretold that had come to pass as they were spoken.

faq.q: Where did Theophilus come from?
faq.a: Nothing certain is known of his birthplace or birth year. Describing the rivers of Eden, he says the Tigris and Euphrates “border on our own regions,” which many take as a hint that he was born not far from them.

faq.q: When was he bishop of Antioch?
faq.a: Eusebius counts him the sixth bishop of Antioch after the apostles, in the line of Ignatius, and says he took office in the eighth year of Marcus Aurelius, around 168 or 169; other reckonings make him the seventh. The length of his episcopate is uncertain.

faq.q: What else did Theophilus write?
faq.a: Eusebius and Jerome knew of works against the heretics Marcion and Hermogenes, writings for the instruction of new believers, and commentaries on the Gospels and Proverbs, though Jerome doubted the commentaries were his. Eusebius called the book against Marcion “of no mean character.” All of these are lost.

faq.q: What is To Autolycus?
faq.a: To Autolycus is three short books written to a pagan friend who had mocked Theophilus for being a Christian. The first speaks of the unseen God and the resurrection, the second compares the poets with the prophets and comments on the six days of creation, and the third answers slanders against Christians and argues that Moses is older than the Greek writers. It is read here in Marcus Dods’s 1885 translation for the Ante-Nicene Fathers.

faq.q: What did Theophilus mean by “Show me yourself, and I will show you my God”?
faq.a: Autolycus had demanded, “Show me thy God.” Theophilus answered that God is seen with the eyes of the soul, and that sin clouds them as rust clouds a mirror; God, the Physician, heals those eyes through his Word and wisdom.

faq.q: Was Theophilus the first to call God a Trinity?
faq.a: His is the earliest surviving Christian use for God of the Greek word trias, a group of three, which Dods translates Trinity: he calls the three days before the sun and moon “types of the Trinity, of God, and His Word, and His wisdom.” He names the three as God, his Word and his Wisdom rather than Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and later Christians stated the doctrine with more care.

faq.q: How did Theophilus answer the charges against Christians?
faq.a: To rumours that Christians shared wives and ate human flesh, he set out what they are taught, from the Ten Commandments to love of enemies, and said that among them chastity is guarded and God reigns. To the charge that the faith was new, he built a chronology from Adam to the death of Marcus Aurelius, 5,698 years, to show that Moses and the prophets are older than the Greek poets.

faq.q: When did Theophilus die?
faq.a: He died around 183, though the year is uncertain: older sources give 181 or 188, and modern accounts place his death probably between 183 and 185. No account of how he died survives, and he was followed as bishop by Maximus.

fields.name: Hippolytus of Rome
fields.bio: Hippolytus of Rome (c. 170–c. 235) was a Greek-speaking presbyter and theologian of the Roman church whose clash with Bishops Zephyrinus and Callistus led later historians to call him the first antipope. Exiled to Sardinia with Pope Pontian, he died there, reconciled, and is honoured as a martyr.
fields.bio_html:
Hippolytus of Rome is one of the most learned voices of the early church and one of the hardest to pin down. He preached, expounded Scripture and wrote a huge attack on every heresy he knew. He was a presbyter of the Roman church who fell out so badly with two of its bishops that later historians called him the first antipope. Yet he died an exile in Sardinia, probably in its mines, beside the very bishop of Rome his party had opposed, and the church that buried them both now honours them on the same feast day. It is a story of truth held fiercely, a long quarrel, and a peace that came at the end.

A Greek voice in the Roman church

Almost nothing about his early life is certain. He was probably born around 170, though some put it a few years earlier, and nobody knows where. Even Eusebius and Jerome, who had read his books, could not say where he served. An old tradition makes him a disciple of Irenaeus of Lyons, and through Irenaeus a spiritual grandchild of Polycarp and of the apostle John. The ninth-century scholar Photios passes it on, and the editors of our translation treat it as settled; modern scholars are less sure. It is best received as cherished, unproven tradition.

What is clearer is the man in his prime. He seems to have been a presbyter, or elder, of the church at Rome in the years when Zephyrinus was its bishop (199–217), and he was known for his learning and eloquence. According to one old account, the young Origen heard him preach during a visit to Rome. He wrote on a remarkable range of subjects: commentaries on Daniel and on the Song of Songs, a treatise On Christ and the Antichrist from around 200, a chronicle of the world from creation down to the year 234, and works on church order. His Commentary on Daniel holds the earliest known reference to Christ’s birth being kept on 25 December. In the same book he warned against those who predicted that Christ’s return was close at hand.

The quarrel with the bishops

His conflict with the Roman bishops began over the doctrine of God. A teaching was spreading in Rome, brought by followers of one Noetus of Smyrna, that Father and Son are simply two names for one and the same divine person. Historians call this modalism. Its defenders meant to protect the oneness of God; Hippolytus believed it meant that the Father himself was born and suffered. He held instead to the Logos theology of earlier Greek writers such as Justin Martyr, which distinguished the Father from his Word, or Logos. In the ninth book of the Refutation he says that Bishop Zephyrinus tolerated the new teaching and was steered by his adviser Callistus. He says that he and his friends refused to give way, and that Callistus answered by calling them “Ditheists,” worshippers of two gods.

The second quarrel was over sin and forgiveness. When Callistus became bishop in 217, he received back into communion Christians who had committed grave sins such as adultery, and he was more lenient about the marriages of clergy. To Hippolytus, a strict moralist, this looked like the church surrendering its holiness. To Callistus’s supporters it was mercy to sinners in a church filling with new converts from paganism. Hippolytus himself records that Callistus appealed to the parable of the wheat and the tares and to Noah’s ark, which held clean and unclean animals alike.

What Hippolytus did next is disputed. The older view, still widely held, is that he let himself be chosen as a rival bishop of Rome and led a separate congregation through the time of Callistus and his successors Urban and Pontian. That is why he is often called the first antipope. Others think Rome then had no single bishop in the later sense, but a network of house-churches, and that Hippolytus led one of them, perhaps a Greek-speaking community gathered round a teacher like a school of philosophy. The sources do not settle it; we do not fully know how far he went.

Reading Book IX with open eyes

The quarrel survives only in Hippolytus’s own telling, and that telling is hostile. He describes Callistus as a slave who lost his master’s money and the deposits of widows, fled and threw himself into the sea, and was sent to the Sardinian mines after a disturbance in a synagogue. He then charges him with buying influence over a bishop he calls ignorant and greedy, and with opening a school that welcomed sinners for the sake of numbers. Some of it may be true, but it is the account of a bitter opponent, written after Callistus’s death, with no reply from the other side. The church remembers Callistus as a pope, and his side of the story is simply lost. Book IX is a precious window into the Roman church of the early third century. It is not a fair trial.

Hippolytus could be harsh, and he was sure he was right. Yet he believed that what God is and how God forgives were at stake, and he would not trade them for peace.

But none will refute these, save the Holy Spirit bequeathed unto the Church, which the Apostles, having in the first instance received, have transmitted to those who have rightly believed.

— Hippolytus, The Refutation of All Heresies, Book I

A labyrinth of heresies

The Refutation of All Heresies was written after 222, near the end of his life. It was planned in ten books. The first surveys the Greek philosophers; the second and third, now lost, dealt with Egyptian mysteries and Chaldean astrology; the fourth treats astrologers and magicians. Books V to IX then work through the Christian heresies one school at a time, and Book X sums up and sets out what the author himself believes.

His argument is simple and polemical: every heresy, he claims, is stolen not from Scripture but from pagan philosophy, mystery religion and astrology, dressed up in Christian words. Most were Gnostics, who taught that salvation comes through secret knowledge, often with long chains of heavenly powers between the true God and this world. They included the Naassenes and Ophites, Simon Magus, Valentinus, Basilides and Marcion. The reader need not master their systems. His family tree of errors is a polemicist’s case and should be read as one. But in building it he copied out a great deal of what his opponents actually wrote, and so preserved sayings of the philosopher Heraclitus, passages of Basilides, and much of the Greek of Irenaeus’s own work against the heresies.

At the start of the Refutation the author explains why he took up so heavy a task, and part of the reason is gratitude. Labouring “with every energy of body and soul,” he writes, he still cannot repay his “Divine Benefactor” as he ought, and so he means to hand on without grudging whatever the Holy Spirit supplies. His long, hard book of controversy began as an offering of thanks.

Then the tone changes. Book X turns to what the author calls the doctrine of the truth: one God who made the world from nothing and made nothing evil, and the Word, born of a virgin, who lived through every stage of human life to be a pattern for all, and endured hunger, thirst and weariness:

He did not protest against His Passion, but became obedient unto death, and manifested His resurrection.

— Hippolytus, The Refutation of All Heresies, Book X

Exile in Sardinia

In 235, during the persecution under the emperor Maximinus Thrax, Hippolytus and Pontian, bishop of Rome, were exiled together to Sardinia, where they very likely died in the mines. The man whose book mocks Callistus for his years in the Sardinian mines ended his own life there. There, it seems, the long division ended. The two old opponents, sharing the same exile, appear to have made their peace; later accounts say Hippolytus urged his followers to return to unity with the church.

The evidence is quiet but telling. Under Pope Fabian the bodies of Pontian and Hippolytus were brought back to Rome, and a Roman record known as the Chronography of 354 says that they were buried on 13 August, probably in 236. Hippolytus was buried on the Via Tiburtina, his funeral led by one Justin the Confessor. The same document shows that by about 255 he was counted a martyr, and it gives him the rank of presbyter, not bishop. This strongly suggests he died at peace with the church he had once opposed. The later tale that he was dragged to death by wild horses grew from confusion with other men of the same name.

The Refutation does not end in triumph over its enemies. It ends in a plea to the nations: Greeks and Barbarians, Egyptians, Indians, Celts and Latins. The author calls himself their adviser because he is “a disciple of the benevolent Logos,” and he urges them to turn back while there is time, to be washed from sin and made new. In its last lines the old controversialist sounds less like a prosecutor than a pastor praying over his people.

Be not therefore inflamed, O ye men, with enmity one towards another, nor hesitate to retrace with all speed your steps. For Christ is the God above all, and He has arranged to wash away sin from human beings, rendering regenerate the old man.

— Hippolytus, The Refutation of All Heresies, Book X

A statue and a lost manuscript

Writing in Greek, his name tangled with legends of other saints called Hippolytus, he was nearly forgotten in the West. Two discoveries brought him back. In 1551, during digging near the church of St Lawrence on the Via Tiburtina, a marble seated statue came to light. It had been heavily restored, but on its chair were carved a table for finding Easter and a list of writings matched to Hippolytus. An inscription of Pope Pius IV named it as Saint Hippolytus. Modern study has shown that the original figure was a woman, perhaps a personification of one of the sciences, so the monument’s purpose is debated again.

Then, in 1842, the Greek scholar Minoïdes Mynas brought from a monastery on Mount Athos a manuscript holding Books IV to X of a lost work against the heresies. Emmanuel Miller published it at Oxford in 1851 under the name of Origen. Book I had long been printed among Origen’s writings under the title Philosophumena. Most nineteenth-century scholars soon assigned the whole to Hippolytus, and controversialists on both sides of Protestant and Catholic debates about the papacy seized on it. Recent scholarship is more cautious, and many now treat the Refutation as the work of an unknown author, probably Roman. The same caution surrounds the Apostolic Tradition, a church order identified as his in the early twentieth century. Its attribution is now hotly contested.

If the Apostolic Tradition is his, Hippolytus is the source of some of the oldest prayers the church still uses. The work contains the earliest known ritual of ordination, and the words now used in the Catholic Church for ordaining bishops come from it. Its twenty-first chapter holds what may be an early form of the Apostles’ Creed.

Why read his book now

The book we publish is J. H. MacMahon’s translation from the Ante-Nicene Fathers (1886), with the editors’ introductory notice. It is long, and in places a slog: Books II and III are lost, Book IV is a catalogue of astrology and conjuring tricks, and its judgments are not gentle. But it is also a first-hand witness to the church of the early third century, written by someone who says he took part in the events he describes. It shows what Roman Christians argued about and why the doctrine of God mattered so much to them. And it ends with a warm invitation to faith.

Hippolytus is a strange companion: brilliant, stubborn, often unfair, and devoted to the truth as he saw it. His life warns how zeal for doctrine can harden into division; his death shows that divided Christians can still be brought home. His closing counsel still stands:

Do not devote your attention to the fallacies of artificial discourses, nor the vain promises of plagiarizing heretics, but to the venerable simplicity of unassuming truth.

— Hippolytus, The Refutation of All Heresies, Book X

faq.q: Who was Hippolytus of Rome?
faq.a: Hippolytus was a learned Greek-speaking presbyter of the church at Rome in the early third century, a preacher, biblical commentator and writer against heresy. He quarrelled bitterly with the Roman bishops of his day, was exiled to Sardinia with Bishop Pontian in 235, and died there; the church honours him as a saint and martyr.

faq.q: When and where was Hippolytus born?
faq.a: Nobody knows where he was born, and the date is uncertain; around 170 is commonly given, though some place it a few years earlier. Even Eusebius and Jerome, who had read his works, could not say where he served.

faq.q: Was Hippolytus a disciple of Irenaeus?
faq.a: An old tradition, passed on by the ninth-century scholar Photios and accepted by the nineteenth-century editors of the Ante-Nicene Fathers, makes him a disciple of Irenaeus of Lyons. Modern scholars regard the claim as doubtful, so it is best treated as tradition rather than established fact.

faq.q: What did Hippolytus write?
faq.a: He wrote on a wide range of subjects, including commentaries on Daniel and the Song of Songs, a treatise On Christ and the Antichrist, a chronicle of the world down to 234, and works on church order. His Commentary on Daniel contains the earliest known reference to Christ’s birth being kept on 25 December.

faq.q: Why did Hippolytus clash with Zephyrinus and Callistus?
faq.a: He accused them of tolerating or teaching modalism, the view that Father and Son are only two names for one divine person, and he held instead to the Logos theology that distinguished the Father from the Word. He also opposed Callistus for readmitting Christians who had committed grave sins and for relaxing rules about the marriages of clergy.

faq.q: Why is Hippolytus called the first antipope?
faq.a: The older and still common view is that he was chosen as a rival bishop of Rome and led a separate congregation through the time of Callistus, Urban and Pontian. Some modern scholars think Rome was then a network of house-churches without a single bishop in the later sense, so how far he set up a rival church remains disputed.

faq.q: Is his account of Callistus reliable?
faq.a: It should be read with caution. Book IX of the Refutation portrays Callistus as a dishonest former slave and a lax, scheming churchman, but it was written by a bitter opponent after Callistus’s death, and no reply from Callistus’s side survives.

faq.q: How did Hippolytus die?
faq.a: In 235, during the persecution under the emperor Maximinus Thrax, he and Bishop Pontian were exiled together to Sardinia, where they probably died in the mines. It appears the two were reconciled there; under Pope Fabian their bodies were brought back to Rome, and an early Roman record names Hippolytus a martyr with the rank of presbyter.

faq.q: What is The Refutation of All Heresies?
faq.a: It is a ten-book work arguing that each heresy of the early church, especially the Gnostic systems, was borrowed from pagan philosophy, mystery religion and astrology rather than Scripture; Books II and III are lost. We publish J. H. MacMahon’s 1886 Ante-Nicene Fathers translation, a polemical but first-hand witness to the Roman church of the early third century that ends with a warm appeal to all nations to know the true God.

faq.q: Did Hippolytus really write the Refutation and the Apostolic Tradition?
faq.a: Books IV to X of the Refutation were found on Mount Athos in 1842 and first published in 1851 under the name of Origen; nineteenth-century scholars mostly assigned the work to Hippolytus, but many today treat it as the work of an unknown, probably Roman, author. Whether the Apostolic Tradition, a church order containing the earliest known ordination ritual, is his is also hotly contested.

fields.name: Jerome
fields.bio: Jerome (c. 342–420) was a Latin scholar, ascetic and Church Father who translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew and gave the West its Vulgate Bible. From his monastery at Bethlehem he wrote letters of counsel, controversy and grief that bring his age vividly to life.
fields.bio_html:
Jerome is the saint painters loved to put in a study: an old man bent over a book, a skull on the desk, a lion dozing at his feet. The lion is a legend, added long after his death. The books are not. For half a century this restless, brilliant, quarrelsome man gave himself to the words of Scripture, and the Latin Bible he made was the Bible of Western Christendom for a thousand years. He was also, by the witness of his own letters, proud, thin-skinned and quick to wound. Both things are true, and his life is worth telling only if both are told.

A student in Rome

He was born Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus at Stridon, a small town near Aquileia on the borders of Dalmatia and Pannonia. The year is uncertain; it is usually given as about 342, though his translator Fremantle preferred 345 and others place it as late as 347. His parents were Catholic Christians of moderate wealth, but he was not baptised as a child. As a young man he went to Rome with his friend Bonosus to study rhetoric under the grammarian Aelius Donatus, and there he fell in love with Cicero, Virgil and Plautus and began to collect a library.

He also, he later confessed, fell into sin, and suffered bouts of guilt afterwards. Yet on Sundays he and some young Christian friends would go down into the catacombs among the tombs of the martyrs and apostles, where the darkness and the lines of the dead brought home to him the terror of judgment. Somewhere in those years the drift turned into faith, and he was baptised in Rome, probably around 366.

After some years in Gaul and at Aquileia, where a band of young friends, among them Rufinus, gathered round him to live for God, Jerome set out for the East about 373 and came at last to Antioch, worn out and ill. There, in the middle of Lent, he fell into a fever so severe that his friends began to prepare his funeral, and there he had the dream which became the most famous page of his letters. He had been fasting, he admits, only so that he might go back afterwards to Cicero; when he turned to the prophets their style seemed rude and repellent. Now he found himself dragged before the judgment seat of Christ:

Asked who and what I was I replied: “I am a Christian.” But He who presided said: “Thou liest, thou art a follower of Cicero and not of Christ. For ‘where thy treasure is, there will thy heart be also.’”

— Jerome, Letter XXII, to Eustochium

Scourged in the dream, he cried out for mercy and swore that if he ever again possessed or read worldly books he would have denied his Lord. He woke with his eyes drenched with tears, and insisted it had been no idle dream. In later life he did quote the pagan authors, and his enemies never let him forget the oath. But the night at Antioch settled the direction of his life: from then on his great love was the Bible, and the classics he had mastered became tools in its service.

The desert and the call to Rome

Around 374 Jerome went out into the desert of Chalcis, east of Antioch, a wilderness so full of hermits that it was called the Syrian Thebaid. For four or five years he lived in a cell, wore sackcloth and fasted hard. It was not the peace he had hoped for. Years later he told Eustochium, without sparing himself, how the memories of Rome pursued him there, and how, with a body wasted by fasting, his mind still burned with desire. In the desert he also began to learn Hebrew from a converted Jew, a study of much toil that he kept up all his life, he said, lest the language leave him.

In the desert, Jerome wrote, when temptation came he would cast himself helpless at the feet of Jesus, water them with his tears and wipe them with his hair. He remembered crying aloud all night until daybreak, until tranquillity returned at the chiding of the Lord. Among the valleys and cliffs he made his place of prayer, and sometimes, when he had wept and strained his eyes towards heaven, he felt himself among the angelic hosts and sang for joy.

Church quarrels at Antioch drove him out of the desert in 379. Bishop Paulinus ordained him a presbyter, though he declined, then and always, the active ministry. He sat under Gregory of Nazianzus at Constantinople, and in 382 came to Rome for a council. Pope Damasus quickly saw what kind of scholar he had. He kept sending Jerome questions about the Bible, and asked him to revise the Latin Gospels and the Psalter, which circulated in many differing copies. That request was the beginning of the work we now call the Vulgate.

The women of the Aventine

In Rome Jerome found a circle hungry for what he had to give. In the house of the widow Marcella on the Aventine hill, noble Roman women met to pray, to sing the psalms in Hebrew, which some learned for the purpose, and to read the Scriptures under his guidance. Among them were the widow Paula, heiress of one of the great families of Rome, and her daughters Blesilla and Eustochium. To Eustochium he addressed his long treatise on virginity, Letter XXII, telling her to make the Bible her pillow: “Let sleep overcome you, the roll still in your hands; when your head falls, let it be on the sacred page.”

Here a modern reader, and especially a Protestant one, meets the Jerome who is hardest to love. He held, as many in his age did, that consecrated virginity was a higher calling than marriage, and said so with relish: “I praise wedlock, I praise marriage, but it is because they give me virgins.” His satire of the Roman clergy was savage. And his counsel had a cost. Blesilla, a young widow, took up the hard life he urged and died within a few months; at her funeral the crowd cried “The monks to the Tiber!”, and his letter urging Paula to restrain her grief struck many as heartless. When Damasus died in December 384, Jerome lost his protector. Rumours about his friendship with Paula led to an inquiry by the Roman clergy, and in August 385 he left Rome for good.

On board ship at Ostia, overwhelmed with grief and tears, Jerome wrote to Asella, one of the Roman circle, denying the charges against him. Yet he thanked God that he was counted worthy of the world’s hatred, and he asked for her prayers: that after Babylon he might see Jerusalem once more, and that by her intercessions she would calm the waves of the sea.

Bethlehem and the Hebrew truth

Paula and Eustochium followed him East, and in 386 they settled at Bethlehem for the rest of their lives. With Paula’s fortune they built a monastery for men under Jerome, a convent for women under Paula, and a guest-house for pilgrims from every corner of the world. Paula gave so freely that she died in debt, and Jerome and his brother sold what remained of their family property to keep the houses going.

In his cell, surrounded by his books, Jerome did the work of his life. He had first revised the Latin Old Testament from the Greek Septuagint, but he saw that the Greek versions disagreed and that the only way to settle them was to go back to the Hebrew, the Hebraica veritas, the Hebrew truth, as he called it. Between about 391 and 405 he translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew, helped by a Jewish teacher who came to him by night like Nicodemus. Most Christians, Augustine among them, held the Septuagint to be inspired, and Jerome was attacked as an innovator. He kept going. To the Roman senator Paulinus he wrote about the study of the Bible in words that still speak to anyone who loves it:

I beg of you, my dear brother, to live among these books, to meditate upon them, to know nothing else, to seek nothing else. Does not such a life seem to you a foretaste of heaven here on earth?

— Jerome, Letter LIII, to Paulinus

Commentaries on the prophets, a catalogue of Christian writers called On Illustrious Men, and letters to Spain, Gaul and Africa flowed from his pen. Sulpicius Severus, who visited him, said he was always reading or writing and never rested day or night.

A sharp pen

These years were also full of controversy, and here honesty is needed. When the Roman monk Jovinian taught that virginity, marriage and widowhood were equal in God’s sight for those who lived in faith, Jerome answered with such contempt that his own friends in Rome tried to keep the book from circulating, thinking he had exalted virginity at the expense of marriage. When Vigilantius, a priest of Gaul, preached against the veneration of relics and night vigils, Jerome wrote against him what his translator judged the most violent and the least reasonable of all his controversial writings. Worst was the break with his old friend Rufinus over the writings of Origen, a public quarrel Jerome kept up even after Rufinus died.

Yet the picture is not only dark. He was remembered as kind to the weak and the poor and entirely free of greed. His correspondence with the younger Augustine began badly: a critical letter of Augustine’s went astray for years and circulated before it reached Bethlehem, and Jerome, suspecting an ambush, warned him that an old man could still be a dangerous opponent. But Augustine answered with patience and deep respect, and the friendship that followed was real. In his last years Jerome hailed him as “the restorer of the ancient faith.”

When the city fell

Jerome’s last years were heavy with loss. Paula died in January 404, whispering the psalms, “Lord, I have loved the habitation of thy house”, until her breath failed. Then, in August 410, Alaric and the Goths took Rome. Refugees crowded into Bethlehem, and Jerome, who had left the city in disgrace a quarter of a century before, wept for it. Writing to Principia about the death of Marcella, he could hardly go on:

My voice sticks in my throat; and, as I dictate, sobs choke my utterance. The City which had taken the whole world was itself taken; nay more famine was beforehand with the sword and but few citizens were left to be made captives.

— Jerome, Letter CXXVII, to Principia

Jerome passes on what eyewitnesses told him of Marcella’s last days. When Gothic soldiers broke into her house and beat her for gold she did not have, she threw herself at their feet and pleaded with tears for young Principia, who was with her. The soldiers brought them both to the basilica of St Paul, and Marcella, it is said, burst into great joy and thanked God for having kept Principia unharmed in answer to her prayer. A few days later she fell asleep in the Lord.

Around 416 a mob sympathetic to Pelagius, whom Jerome had written against, attacked the monasteries at Bethlehem, killing some inside and burning the buildings; Jerome escaped in a tower. Eustochium died in 418. He worked on his commentary on Jeremiah until his last illness cut it short, tended, it is believed, by the younger Paula and Melania. He died at Bethlehem in 420, traditionally on 30 September, and was buried near the cave of the Nativity beside Paula and Eustochium.

The letters he left

The Letters of St. Jerome, in the 1893 translation by W. H. Fremantle and his collaborators, gathers 150 letters, most of them his own. Few books from the ancient church bring us so close to a living person. Here are the dream at Antioch, the tears in the desert, his letter on the best way to translate, his counsel to monks, widows and young mothers, his grief for Paula and his lament for Rome. Readers will find things to argue with, above all in his views of marriage and the ascetic life. But they will also find a man who loved the Scriptures with his whole heart, and who, with all his faults, spent his life making God’s word speak to people in their own tongue.

faq.q: Who was Jerome?
faq.a: Jerome (Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus, c. 342–420) was a priest, scholar and ascetic, one of the four great Latin Fathers of the church. He is best known for the Latin translation of the Bible that became the Vulgate, and for his letters.

faq.q: Where was Jerome born and educated?
faq.a: He was born at Stridon, near Aquileia on the borders of Dalmatia and Pannonia, to Christian parents of moderate wealth. As a young man he studied rhetoric in Rome under the grammarian Aelius Donatus and came to love the Latin classics.

faq.q: When was Jerome baptised?
faq.a: He was not baptised as a child. After a student youth he later confessed was sinful, and Sunday visits to the tombs of the martyrs in the catacombs, he was baptised in Rome, probably around 366.

faq.q: What was Jerome’s Ciceronian dream?
faq.a: During a severe fever at Antioch around 374 he dreamed he stood before the judgment seat of Christ, said he was a Christian, and was told, “Thou liest, thou art a follower of Cicero and not of Christ.” He tells the story in Letter XXII, and it turned him from pagan literature to the study of Scripture.

faq.q: What did Jerome do in the Syrian desert?
faq.a: For four or five years, from about 374, he lived as a hermit in the desert of Chalcis east of Antioch, fasting, praying and fighting temptation. There he also began to learn Hebrew from a converted Jew.

faq.q: What did Jerome do in Rome under Pope Damasus?
faq.a: From 382 to 385 he was a trusted adviser to Pope Damasus, who asked him to revise the Latin Gospels and Psalter, the beginning of the Vulgate. He also taught the Scriptures to a circle of Roman women, including Marcella, Paula and Eustochium.

faq.q: Why did Jerome leave Rome?
faq.a: His sharp satire and ascetic teaching made enemies, and the death of the young widow Blesilla after taking up the hard life he urged turned many against him. After Damasus died in 384, rumours about his friendship with Paula led to an inquiry by the Roman clergy, and he left Rome in August 385.

faq.q: What did Jerome do at Bethlehem?
faq.a: From 386 until his death he lived at Bethlehem, heading a monastery built with Paula’s fortune beside her convent and a guest-house for pilgrims. There, between about 391 and 405, he translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew and wrote commentaries on the prophets.

faq.q: Who were Jerome’s main opponents?
faq.a: He wrote fiercely against Jovinian, who held virginity and marriage equal in God’s sight, and against Vigilantius, who opposed the veneration of relics, and he broke publicly with his old friend Rufinus over Origen. His early exchanges with Augustine were tense, but they ended in a warm friendship.

faq.q: What is The Letters of St. Jerome?
faq.a: It is the 1893 English translation by W. H. Fremantle and his collaborators of 150 letters, most of them Jerome’s own. They include his account of the Ciceronian dream, his counsel to monks and widows, his memorial of Paula, and his lament for the sack of Rome in 410, ten years before his death at Bethlehem in 420.
